bappa-rawal.story:
## Bappa Rawal — the cowherd who became the regent of Shiva

*Much of Bappa Rawal's life comes to us through the traditions of Mewar: the bardic chronicles, the Ekalinga Mahatmya and the memory kept at the temple of Eklingji. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

In the early years of the eighth century, the Guhila clan held small territories in the hills of what is now southern Rajasthan and northern Gujarat. They traced their line to **Guhadatta**, and further back to the solar race of Rama. Their power was modest: a few hill towns, a few forts, and the loyalty of the forest tribes.

Tradition says that Bappa was born into this house as the son of a Guhila chief, and that his father was killed while the boy was still an infant. The bards tell of a night of fire and swords, of a palace that fell, and of a mother who fled into the hills with her child held against her chest. Whether the enemy was a rival chief or a rebellious hill clan, the story agrees on one thing: the heir of the Guhilas survived because someone carried him out of the flames and hid him.

He was taken to **Nagda**, a quiet settlement in a green valley north of where Udaipur stands today. There he was raised not as a prince, but as an ordinary boy in a Brahmin household. Nobody spoke his lineage aloud. His name, *Bappa*, was not even a name at first. It was an affectionate word, something like "little father", the kind of name a village gives a child it loves.

As a boy, Bappa's work was to take the village cows out to graze in the forests around Nagda. He knew every path in those hills, every stream and every cave. The forest tribes, the Bhils, knew him too, and in later years they would stand beside him in war.

Among the cows in his care was one that came home every evening with no milk. The Brahmin who owned her suspected the boy of drinking it on the way. Bappa, hurt by the accusation, followed the cow one day. Deep in a thicket he saw her stop above a stone and let her milk flow onto it of her own accord.

When Bappa cleared away the leaves, he found a **Shiva linga**, and beside it an old ascetic deep in meditation. This was **Harit Rishi**, a sage of the Pashupata tradition. When the sage opened his eyes, tradition says, he looked at the cowherd boy for a long time and told him who he really was.

For years after that day, Bappa served the sage and the hidden shrine. He brought water, gathered flowers, and guarded the place from wild animals. In return, Harit Rishi taught him. The lessons were not only prayers. They were lessons about duty, about the purpose of power, and about the difference between a king and a robber with an army.

The most important lesson became the foundation of a dynasty. The land, the sage said, belongs to **Ekalinga**, the lord Shiva of that shrine. The king is only his servant, his *dewan*, who governs in his name. For more than twelve centuries afterwards, the rulers of Mewar called themselves the **Dewan of Eklingji**, and every Maharana bowed before the shrine as a servant, not a master.

When the time came for the sage to leave the world, the legends say he wished to bless Bappa with immortality, and that Bappa, reaching up too slowly, received the blessing on his body but not his life. Whatever the meaning of the story, he left the forest of Nagda with a sense of purpose that never left him.

As the years passed, the boy grew into a young man. The young man who came down from the hills had little: a sword, a small band of companions, the friendship of the Bhils, and a name the forest people already trusted. He took service, tradition says, with the ruler of **Chittor**, **Man Mori**, of the Maurya (Mori) line that then held that great rock fortress. Some chronicles make Man Mori his maternal uncle.

In Chittor, Bappa rose quickly. He was bold in war and generous in victory, and soldiers followed him gladly. The older nobles of the court resented the newcomer. When an enemy army threatened Chittor, the story goes, those nobles refused to march, and Bappa led the defence with his own men and won.

The victory made him the most powerful man in Chittor. Around **734 CE**, according to Mewar's traditional date, Bappa took the fortress for himself. The bards say the nobles who had abandoned Man Mori opened the way to him. Chittor would remain the heart of Mewar for more than eight hundred years, until Akbar's siege of 1568.

These were dangerous years for all of western India. In the decades after the Arab conquest of Sindh in 712, the governors of the Umayyad Caliphate sent raiding armies east, into Rajasthan, Gujarat and Malwa. Under **Junaid**, the governor of Sindh, these raids reached deep into the region in the 720s and 730s. Old kingdoms fell, and cities were plundered.

The tide was turned by the Indian kings of the region. **Nagabhata I** of the Pratiharas drove the invaders back from Malwa, and in **739 CE** the Chalukya general **Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin** defeated them decisively at **Navsari** in Gujarat. After these defeats, the Arab raids into the interior of India ended for centuries.

Mewar's tradition places Bappa Rawal among the defenders of this age, fighting the invaders and driving them back towards Sindh. The bards go further, telling of a march to the west as far as **Ghazni** and Khorasan. Historians cannot confirm Bappa's exact part in these wars, and the far western campaign is legend. But the memory is important: Mewar has always remembered its founder as a ruler who stood against invasion when the whole region was under threat.

Bappa was not only a warrior. Holding Chittor and Nagda, he had to make the hill country into a state. He bound the Bhil chiefs to the Guhila house with gifts and honour, a bond that lasted for centuries: at the coronation of a Maharana, a Bhil chief traditionally marked the new ruler's forehead with blood from his own thumb.

He also kept faith with the shrine where his life had changed. Tradition credits Bappa with founding the temple of **Eklingji**, near Nagda, around 734 CE, as the seat of the kingdom's true lord. The present temple was rebuilt many times, most of all by **Rana Raimal** in the fifteenth century, but the lineage of worship goes back to him.

A gold coin found at Ajmer, bearing the name **"Shri Voppa"** together with Shaiva symbols, has been linked by many scholars to Bappa. If the attribution is right, it is one of the very few objects that may come from his own reign.

Historians have long asked which Guhila ruler of the inscriptions "Bappa" really was. *Bappa* and *Rawal* are titles of affection and rank rather than a personal name, and the later inscriptions of the dynasty, such as the **Atpur inscription of 977 CE**, list the Guhila kings without using it. Many scholars identify him with **Kalabhoja**, a Guhila ruler of the eighth century. Others suggest different names. What is certain is that the later rulers of Mewar, from the Guhilas to the Sisodias, all looked back to Bappa Rawal as the founder of their kingdom.

Every tradition of Bappa ends in the same way: not on a battlefield, but in renunciation. Having established his kingdom, Bappa is said to have handed power to his son and turned back towards the life of the forest that had formed him. He took up the life of an ascetic in the service of Ekalinga, as his teacher had once lived.

He died around **753 CE**. His *samadhi*, the memorial over his last resting place, is shown near **Nagda**, close to the valley where a cow once gave her milk to a hidden stone, and where a cowherd boy learned that a king is only a servant of something greater.

## Highlights of his life

- **Survival and upbringing at Nagda.** Saved as an infant after his father's death, he was raised in secret as a cowherd in the hills.
- **Disciple of Harit Rishi.** From the sage he received the idea that the ruler is the *dewan* (servant) of Ekalinga. This principle defined Mewar's kingship for over twelve hundred years.
- **Founder of the Eklingji tradition.** Tradition credits him with founding the temple of Eklingji around 734 CE.
- **Conquest of Chittor (c. 734 CE).** He took the fort from the Mori ruler Man Mori, making it the capital of Mewar for over eight centuries.
- **Defender in the age of the Arab raids.** He is remembered as one of the rulers who resisted the Umayyad raids of the 720s and 730s. The decisive victories of 739 CE were won by Nagabhata I and Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin.
- **Alliance with the Bhils.** He bound the forest tribes to the Guhila house, a bond later honoured at every coronation.
- **Renunciation.** He gave up the throne for the life of an ascetic and died around 753 CE near Nagda.

mahayik.story:
## Mahayik — a name in the stone roll of the Guhila kings

*Almost nothing is known of Mahayik (Mahayaka) beyond his name and his place in the Guhila genealogy. This short account gives only what can be said with confidence.*

Mahayik, written **Mahayaka** in the inscriptions, was a king of the **Guhila** dynasty of Mewar, the house founded by Bappa Rawal. His name survives in the **Atpur inscription of 977 CE**, set up in the reign of **Shaktikumara**, which lists the Guhila rulers in order from the founder Guhadatta. There he stands after the second **Khumman** (Khuman II) and before the third. That places his reign in the **ninth century**. Popular lists sometimes put him directly after Bappa Rawal, in the eighth century, but the tenth-century inscription, written far closer to his time, does not support this.

No record tells us whose son he was, how long he reigned, what he built, or whom he fought. What can be described is the world he ruled in. The Guhila kingdom was a hill state centred on **Nagda** and the valleys around the shrine of **Eklingji**, where its kings ruled as servants of the god Ekalinga. North India in his century was dominated by the **Gurjara-Pratihara** empire of Kannauj, which reached its height under **Mihira Bhoja**, and the Rajput houses of Rajasthan lived in its shadow, most of them as its allies or vassals. The Guhila kings relied on their kinsmen, on the Bhil chiefs of the forests, and on the Pashupata ascetics who kept the worship of Eklingji.

After Mahayaka, the inscription names a third Khumman, whose reign carried the line into the tenth century, followed by Bhartripatta II, Allata and Naravahana. Mahayaka's own deeds are lost, but the line he held passed on unbroken.

## Highlights of his life

- **Guhila king of the ninth century.** The Atpur inscription of 977 CE names him among the kings of Mewar, between Khuman II and Khuman III.
- **Ruler in the Pratihara age.** He reigned while the Gurjara-Pratihara empire dominated north India.
- **Servant of Ekalinga.** Like every king of his house, he ruled as the *dewan* of the lord of Eklingji.
- **A link in an unbroken line.** He passed the kingdom on to the third Khumman, carrying Bappa Rawal's house towards the tenth century.

khuman-ii.story:
## Khuman II — the name the bards gave to Mewar

*Khuman II survives in the historical record mainly as a name in the Guhila genealogies carved in stone in the tenth century. Most of what is told about him comes from the much later Khuman Raso and from the bardic traditions that Colonel James Tod collected in the nineteenth century. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

More than a century after Bappa Rawal had laid down his sword and gone back to the forest of Nagda, the house he founded still held the hill country of Mewar. Its kings ruled the green valleys around **Nagda**, the shrine of **Eklingji** where the lord of the land was worshipped, and the farming country along the rivers that drain the Aravalli hills towards the Banas. The kingdom had survived its first hundred years. It had not yet become great. It was one hill state among many, in a north India dominated by powers far larger than itself.

The order of its kings is known to us from the stone records the dynasty left behind, above all the **Atpur inscription of 977 CE**, set up in the reign of **Shaktikumara**. It lists the Guhila rulers one after another, from the founder **Guhadatta** down to its own day. After **Kalabhoja**, whom many scholars identify with Bappa Rawal, it names **Khumman**, then **Mattata**, **Bhartripatta** and **Simha**, and then a second **Khumman**. After him come **Mahayaka** and a third Khumman. This second Khumman is the ruler remembered as Khuman II. Some modern lists, including the order followed in this archive, place Mahayaka before him, but the tenth-century inscription, written far closer to his time, puts Mahayaka after him.

The inscription does not say whose son he was, nor when he came to the throne, nor how long he ruled. Most historians place his reign in the first half of the **ninth century**. Beyond that, the stone is silent. No record tells of his childhood. Like every prince of his house, he would have grown up between the palace and the temple, learning to ride and to use the sword and the bow, learning the old story of Bappa and the sage Harit, and learning above all the rule that Mewar's kings held sacred: the land belongs to Ekalinga, and the king is only his servant, his *dewan*.

The world into which he was born was a dangerous one. For more than a generation the great powers of India had been fighting over **Kannauj**, the old imperial city on the Ganga. From the west came the **Gurjara-Pratiharas**, whose kings had their roots in Rajasthan itself. From the east came the **Palas** of Bengal. From the Deccan, again and again, came the armies of the **Rashtrakutas**. Around the year 800 the Rashtrakuta king **Govinda III** marched north and defeated the Pratihara king **Nagabhata II**, and for a time it seemed that no northern power could hold its own. But the Pratiharas recovered. Nagabhata took Kannauj and made it the capital of an empire that would dominate north India for most of the ninth century.

Every one of these wars sent armies along the roads of Rajasthan. The small hill kingdoms that lay across those roads had to choose their friends carefully. Most of the Rajput houses of the region, it seems, accepted the overlordship of the Pratiharas and sent their soldiers to fight in Pratihara wars. Another branch of the Guhila family, settled at **Chatsu** near present-day Jaipur, served the Pratihara emperors faithfully, and its own later inscription proudly records the deeds its chiefs performed in their service. The Guhilas of Mewar left no such record of their relations with the empire, but they lived in its shadow, and their safety depended on how they managed it.

To the west there was another power. The Arabs had held **Sindh** since 712. The great raids of the eighth century, which Bappa's generation had faced, had been turned back in the 730s, but the governors of Sindh, now ruling for the **Abbasid caliphs** of Baghdad, still fought the neighbouring Indian kingdoms on their borders. An Arab merchant named **Sulaiman**, writing around 851, described the king of the Gurjaras as the strongest of Indian rulers and the most determined enemy of the Arabs. The frontier between Sindh and Rajasthan was never fully quiet in Khuman's lifetime.

It is against this background that the bards of Mewar set the greatest legend attached to his name. The legend is preserved in the **Khuman Raso**, a long poem in the language of Rajasthan. It is credited to a Jain poet named **Dalpat Vijay**, and in the form we have it today it was composed many centuries after Khuman's death; it even carries its story forward to much later Maharanas. It is a work of devotion and pride, not a chronicle, but it tells the story the bards had long been singing.

In that story, an army came out of the west to attack **Chittor**. Colonel Tod, reading the bardic accounts in the nineteenth century, identified it with the forces of the Abbasid caliph **al-Ma'mun**, who ruled from 813 to 833. When the news reached the fortress, the bards say, Khuman sent riders across the whole of Rajasthan, and the chiefs came. They came from the deserts and the hills and the river valleys, each with his own banner and his own band of horsemen, until the plateau below Chittor was full of their camps.

The poets imagine a night council before the battle. The chiefs sat around the fires, and some of them doubted. "The enemy is many," one of them said. "Their horses have crossed rivers we have never seen. Why should we die for a rock that is not ours?" Khuman, the story says, stood and answered them. "This rock is not mine either. It belongs to Ekalinga. I am only his servant. If you fight tonight, you do not fight for Khuman. You fight for the land your fathers are buried in." The chiefs, the bards say, rose and swore to stand with him.

The battles that followed, in the telling of the Raso, were many and hard. Khuman is said to have driven the invaders back from Chittor, pursued them, and captured their commander, whom he later released. The bards count his battles in the dozens and make every one of them a victory. In their verses, Khuman stands at the gate of India, and the army of the caliph breaks against him like water against the rock of Chittor.

Historians cannot confirm any of this. No Arab history and no contemporary Indian inscription records an invasion of Mewar in this period, and as far as the evidence goes, the Arab governors of the ninth century did not carry their wars so deep into Rajasthan. Since the Guhila line had three kings named Khumman, it is not even certain which of them the bards meant; the hero of the Raso may well be a memory that gathered together the deeds of several generations. Historians also debate whether the Guhilas of this early period held Chittor at all, or whether their power was centred on Nagda and the valleys around it. The Raso is not evidence for these events. It is evidence of how deeply Mewar wished to remember its kings as defenders.

And in one way the legend proved more lasting than any inscription. The name of Khuman became a title. For centuries afterwards the bards addressed the rulers of Mewar as **Khuman**, as though every king of the line carried something of that ancient defender in him. Poets spoke of the Maharanas as the Khumans of Chittor, and the name passed into songs that were still sung at the courts of Udaipur long after Chittor itself had fallen. Few rulers whose deeds are so poorly recorded have left their name so deeply in the speech of their people.

What the real Khuman II did with his years on the throne, the stones do not say. Like every ruler of his house, he had to hold together a state built on loyalty rather than on great wealth. The Guhila kings depended on their kinsmen, who held villages and forts in their name, and on the **Bhil** chiefs of the forests, whose alliance with the dynasty went back to Bappa's days. The valleys gave grain, the hills gave timber and shelter, and the roads that ran from Gujarat towards the Ganga plain brought traders, pilgrims and news. A king who kept those roads safe, kept his kinsmen loyal, and kept peace with the great empire beyond his borders had done the work that his age required.

He ruled, too, as the servant of a god. The worship of Shiva at Eklingji was in the hands of ascetics of the **Pashupata** tradition, the tradition of Harit Rishi, and the kings of Mewar honoured them as the guardians of the dynasty's faith. In the century after Khuman, under a later king, **Naravahana**, a temple of **Lakulisha**, the great teacher of the Pashupatas, was built at Eklingji, and its inscription of 971 CE is one of the oldest dated records of the dynasty. The Shaiva faith that Khuman's line protected there would shape Mewar for a thousand years.

When and how Khuman II died, no record tells. The Atpur inscription simply moves on to the next name. After him came **Mahayaka**, and after Mahayaka a third Khumman, whose reign carried the dynasty into the tenth century. The line then passed through **Bhartripatta II**, **Allata**, under whom the town of **Aghata** (Ahar, near Udaipur) became a flourishing centre of the kingdom, and Naravahana. The hill kingdom that Khuman had held through a dangerous century survived, and the stones that record its kings record his name among them.

That is almost all that history can say of Khuman II. A name on a stone, a place in a line of kings, a century of empires at war around a small hill state that endured. And over that silence the bards built a hero, the defender of Chittor, whose name became a title for every ruler who came after him. Between the stone and the song lies the real man, whom we cannot see clearly. But Mewar never forgot to call its kings by his name.

## Highlights of his life

- **A king of the Guhila line.** The Atpur inscription of 977 CE names him as the second Khumman of the dynasty, after Simha and before Mahayaka, in the ninth century.
- **Ruler in the age of empires.** He held the hill kingdom of Mewar while the Pratiharas, Palas and Rashtrakutas fought for control of north India.
- **Hero of the Khuman Raso.** The bardic poem, composed centuries later, remembers a Khuman who defended Chittor against an invasion from the west; historians cannot confirm it, and which Khumman the bards meant is uncertain.
- **A name that became a title.** For centuries the bards addressed the rulers of Mewar as Khuman, keeping his name alive in the kingdom's poetry.
- **Servant of Ekalinga.** Like every king of his house, he ruled as the *dewan* of the lord of Eklingji, under the Shaiva tradition of the Pashupatas.
- **Continuity of the dynasty.** He passed the kingdom on to Mahayaka, and through his successors the Guhila line continued into the tenth century and beyond.

bharttripatta-i.story:
## Bharttripatta I — a Guhila king between two ages

*Almost nothing is known of Bharttripatta I (Bhartripatta) beyond his name and his place in the Guhila genealogy. This short account gives only what can be said with confidence.*

Bharttripatta I, written **Bhartripatta** in the inscriptions, was a king of the **Guhila** dynasty of Mewar. His name appears in the **Atpur inscription of 977 CE**, which lists the Guhila rulers in order from the founder Guhadatta. There he comes after **Mattata** and before **Simha**, in the generations after Khumman I, who succeeded Kalabhoja, the king many scholars identify with Bappa Rawal. That places his reign around the **turn of the ninth century**. Some modern lists, including the order followed in this archive, place Khuman II before him, but in the inscription the second Khumman comes later, after Simha. He is called "the First" because a later king of the same name, **Bhartripatta II**, ruled in the tenth century.

No record tells us whose son he was, how long he ruled, or what he built or fought. His years fell in a turbulent time. The **Gurjara-Pratiharas**, the **Palas** of Bengal and the **Rashtrakutas** of the Deccan were fighting for **Kannauj** and the mastery of north India, and around 800 the Rashtrakuta king **Govinda III** marched far into the north and defeated the Pratihara **Nagabhata II**. Armies on these campaigns crossed Rajasthan, and small hill kingdoms like Mewar had to keep their footing among the great powers.

The Guhila state of his day was centred on **Nagda** and the valleys around the shrine of **Eklingji**, where the kings ruled as servants of Ekalinga, supported by their kinsmen, the Bhil chiefs and the Pashupata ascetics of the shrine. After Bhartripatta, the inscription names Simha as the next king, and the line continued unbroken.

## Highlights of his life

- **Guhila king of Mewar.** The Atpur inscription of 977 CE names him between Mattata and Simha.
- **Ruler at the turn of the ninth century.** He reigned as the Pratiharas, Palas and Rashtrakutas fought for north India.
- **Servant of Ekalinga.** Like every king of his house, he ruled as the *dewan* of the lord of Eklingji.
- **First of his name.** A second Bhartripatta ruled the Guhila kingdom in the tenth century.

## Sinha Raj — a Guhila king in the shadow of Kannauj

There he follows **Bhartripatta I** and comes before the second **Khumman**, the king remembered as Khuman II. That places his reign in the **ninth century**, probably in its earlier decades. Some modern lists, including the order followed in this archive, name a different successor for him, but in the inscription the king who comes after Simha is Khumman II.

No record tells us whose son he was, how long he ruled, what he built or whom he fought. The age he lived in, however, is well known. The **Gurjara-Pratihara** king **Nagabhata II** had made **Kannauj** the capital of a great empire, and under his successors, above all **Mihira Bhoja**, that empire dominated north India for most of the century. The Rajput houses of Rajasthan lived in its shadow; a branch of the Guhila family itself, settled at **Chatsu** near present-day Jaipur, served the Pratiharas in their wars. To the west, the Arab governors of **Sindh** still fought the Indian kingdoms on their borders.

The Guhila state of Simha's day was a hill kingdom centred on **Nagda** and the valleys around the shrine of **Eklingji**, where the kings ruled as servants of the god Ekalinga. They depended on their kinsmen, on the Bhil chiefs of the forests, and on the Pashupata ascetics who kept the shrine. Simha's own deeds are lost, but he passed the kingdom to Khumman II, whose name the bards of Mewar would make famous.

## Highlights of his life

- **Guhila king of Mewar.** The Atpur inscription of 977 CE names him between Bhartripatta I and Khuman II.
- **Ruler in the Pratihara age.** He reigned in the ninth century, when the Gurjara-Pratihara empire of Kannauj dominated north India.
- **Servant of Ekalinga.** Like every king of his house, he ruled as the *dewan* of the lord of Eklingji.
- **Predecessor of Khuman II.** He handed the kingdom to the second Khumman, whose name later became a title of Mewar's rulers.

kshitij-raj.story:
## Kshitij Raj — a name the stones do not hold

*No ruler named Kshitij Raj can be found in the surviving Guhila inscriptions. This short account explains where the name stands and what is known of the period in which it is placed.*

Kshitij Raj appears in modern lists of the rulers of Mewar as a king of the **Guhila** dynasty in the **tenth century**, placed after Sinha Raj and before Narvahan Raj. The dynasty's own records, however, do not name him. The **Atpur inscription of 977 CE**, set up in the reign of **Shaktikumara**, lists the Guhila kings in order from the founder Guhadatta, and in the generations before **Naravahana** it names the third **Khumman**, **Bhartripatta II** and **Allata**, with no king called Kshitij. The name may be a later variant or title of one of these rulers, or a mistake in the lists, but it cannot be identified with confidence, and nothing can be said of his life.

The century in which he is placed is better known. The Guhila kingdom was then growing beyond its old heartland around **Nagda** and **Eklingji**. Under **Allata**, the town of **Aghata** (Ahar, near Udaipur) became a flourishing centre of the kingdom, and under Naravahana a temple of **Lakulisha** was built at Eklingji, its inscription dated **971 CE**. The power of the **Gurjara-Pratiharas** of Kannauj, which had overshadowed Rajasthan for a century, was declining after the Rashtrakuta king **Indra III** sacked Kannauj around 916, and new neighbours were rising, among them the **Paramaras** of Malwa, whose king **Munja** attacked Aghata later in the century.

Whoever the name of Kshitij Raj was meant to recall, the Guhila line in this century passed on unbroken from Bhartripatta II to Allata, Naravahana, Shalivahana and Shaktikumara.

## Highlights of his life

- **A name without a record.** No king called Kshitij Raj appears in the Atpur inscription of 977 CE or other surviving Guhila records.
- **Placed in the tenth century.** Modern lists set him before Narvahan Raj, where the inscription names Khumman III, Bhartripatta II and Allata.
- **An age of growth.** In this century Aghata (Ahar) rose as a centre of the Guhila kingdom and the Lakulisha temple was built at Eklingji.
- **A changing north India.** The Pratihara empire declined, and the Paramaras of Malwa became Mewar's powerful new neighbours.

narvahan-raj.story:
## Narvahan Raj — the king in whose reign Eklingji found its voice

*What we know of Narvahan Raj, called Naravahana in the inscriptions, comes from a few carved stones: above all the Lakulisha temple inscription of 971 CE at Eklingji and the Atpur inscription of 977 CE set up in his grandson's reign. Where the record is silent, this story says so rather than filling the silence with invention.*

By the second half of the tenth century, more than two hundred years had passed since the age that Mewar remembers as the time of Bappa Rawal. The Guhila house still held the hill country of southern Rajasthan, the green valleys around **Nagda**, which the inscriptions call Nagahrada, and the shrine of **Ekalinga** in the hills above it. But the kingdom had grown. Its newest and busiest city lay a few miles to the south, at **Aghata**, the place we now call Ahar, on the edge of modern Udaipur. Into this kingdom, in a year no record has kept, Naravahana was born.

Modern lists of the rulers of Mewar often place him early in the tenth century, before Bharttripatta II and Allata. The dynasty's own inscriptions tell a different and clearer story. The **Atpur inscription of 977 CE**, which lists the Guhila kings in order from the founder **Guhadatta**, names Naravahana as the successor of **Allata**, and Allata as the successor of **Bhartripatta II**. Naravahana was therefore not the grandfather of those kings but their descendant: the son of Allata and the grandson of Bhartripatta II. His story belongs to the middle and later decades of the century.

His family was more widely connected than the image of a remote hill dynasty might suggest. His grandmother, Bhartripatta II's queen **Mahalakshmi**, came from a family of the **Rashtrakutas**, the great name of the Deccan in that age. His mother, Allata's queen **Hariyadevi**, was a princess of the **Hunas**, descendants of the Central Asian peoples who had settled in western India centuries before and had long since become part of its society of ruling clans. Hariyadevi is remembered in the inscriptions for founding a town called **Harshapura**. A boy born into such a house would have grown up hearing many accents at his father's court and understanding that alliances by marriage were as much a part of kingship as the sword.

The court in which he grew up was a lively one. Under Allata, Aghata had become a prosperous centre. An inscription of **953 CE** from Aghata records the endowment of a temple there in Allata's reign, and speaks of the officers of state who governed the kingdom and of the traders who came to its markets from distant regions. The prince who would become Naravahana must have known those markets, the temple courtyards, the river that ran past the town and the roads that led west towards Gujarat and east towards Malwa. We do not know the names of his teachers or the details of his education. A Guhila prince of his time would have been trained in riding, arms and the duties of rule, and, in a court that patronised temples and learned men, in the Sanskrit learning that gave a king his dignity. The later inscription of his reign, written in polished Sanskrit verse, shows that such learning was honoured in his kingdom.

His father's reign also taught him that power had to be defended. The Atpur inscription records that Allata killed an enemy named **Devapala** in battle. Historians have debated who this Devapala was; some identify him with a king of the **Gurjara-Pratihara** dynasty of that name who ruled in the middle of the century. Whoever he was, the victory showed that the Guhilas of Mewar were no longer content to be quiet vassals in the hills.

That change was happening across all of northern India. For more than a century the **Pratiharas** of Kannauj had been the greatest power of the north, and the kings of Rajasthan had lived in their shadow. Then, around **916 CE**, the Rashtrakuta king **Indra III** marched north and sacked Kannauj itself. The Pratiharas recovered their capital, but not their old strength. Over the next decades their feudatories one by one became independent kings. In Malwa the **Paramaras** were rising; in the north of Rajasthan the **Chahamanas** of Shakambhari were growing stronger; in Gujarat, **Mularaja** founded the **Chaulukya** kingdom of Anahilapataka. Naravahana came of age in a world where the old order had broken and every ruling house had to find its own footing.

We do not know the year in which Allata died or in which Naravahana took his place. What is certain is that by **971 CE** Naravahana was ruling the Guhila kingdom. He sealed one of the most important alliances of his house by marriage. According to the Atpur inscription, his queen was a daughter of **Jejaya**, a prince of the Chahamana family. The Chahamanas were the Guhilas' powerful neighbours, and a marriage tie with them gave Mewar a measure of security on its northern side in an unsettled age.

The event for which Naravahana is truly remembered, however, did not happen on a battlefield. It happened in the hills above Nagda, at the shrine of Ekalinga. In his reign, ascetics of the **Pashupata** order, the Shaiva tradition that honoured the teacher **Lakulisha** as its founder, built a temple to Lakulisha at Eklingji. Lakulisha is shown in sculpture as a seated teacher holding a staff, the *lakuta* from which his name comes. The Pashupatas were among the most influential Shaiva communities of western India, and their ascetics served at many great shrines. The temple they raised at Eklingji still stands, one of the oldest surviving buildings at the site.

On that temple, the builders set a long Sanskrit inscription dated **971 CE**. It is the oldest dated inscription at Eklingji and one of the most important records of the dynasty. It praises the Guhila kings of Nagahrada and speaks of the learning of the ascetics who served the shrine. Above all, it is one of the earliest inscriptions to name **Bappa** as a ruler of the Guhila line at Nagahrada. Long before the bards of later centuries told the full story of the cowherd boy, the sage Harit Rishi and the hidden linga, the stone raised in Naravahana's reign was already joining the name of Bappa to the place.

One can imagine the day of the consecration: the cold morning air in the valley, the smoke of the sacrificial fires, the chanting of the priests, and the king standing among his nobles while the ascetics in their ash and matted hair performed the rites. Such scenes are imagined; the inscription does not describe them. But the meaning of the event is clear from the record itself. In Naravahana's reign, the shrine of Ekalinga was no longer simply a sacred spot in the forest. It was a centre of organised religious life, with learned ascetics, endowments and a written memory of the kings who protected it. The idea that the kings of Mewar ruled as the servants of Ekalinga, which later generations would make the foundation of their kingship, grew out of exactly this close bond between the dynasty and the shrine.

The religious life of the kingdom was not narrow. The same land that honoured Shiva at Eklingji held temples to Vishnu at Aghata, and the inscriptions of the region speak of Jain communities and traders as well. A ruler of this period was expected to protect all the faiths of his subjects, to grant land and revenues to temples and learned Brahmins, and to keep the roads safe for merchants. Naravahana's kingdom, with its towns, its trade and its shrines, depended on that kind of steady rule.

The inscriptions do not record any war fought by Naravahana. Modern accounts that credit him with defending the frontier and putting down revolts are guesses, not history. What can be said is that he held the kingdom together in dangerous decades, kept the alliances his family had made, and handed it on intact. In the years around his death, the danger was growing. In **972 CE** the Paramara king **Siyaka II** sacked **Manyakheta**, the capital of the Rashtrakutas, and his successor **Munja** soon became the most feared king in the region. Within a few years of Naravahana's reign, Munja's armies would fall upon Aghata itself. Naravahana did not live to see that blow, but the storm was gathering on his eastern horizon.

We do not know when or how Naravahana died. The Atpur inscription names his son **Shalivahana** as the next king, and after him Shalivahana's son **Shaktikumara**, who was ruling by **977 CE**. The fact that his grandson was on the throne only six years after the Eklingji inscription suggests that Naravahana's reign ended in the early or middle 970s, and that Shalivahana's reign was short. The line of Guhila kings ran on unbroken through him.

Narvahan Raj left no great victories for the bards to sing and no fortress that bears his name. His legacy is quieter and more lasting. In his reign, the shrine of Ekalinga received the oldest dated record that survives there, and the name of Bappa was first set firmly into stone beside it. Every later Maharana who bowed at Eklingji as the dewan of its lord was walking a path that had been made clearer in the time of Naravahana.

## Highlights of his life

- **Son of Allata.** The Atpur inscription of 977 CE names him as the son and successor of Allata and the grandson of Bhartripatta II, not their predecessor as modern lists suggest.
- **A Chahamana alliance.** He married a daughter of the Chahamana prince Jejaya, binding Mewar to its powerful northern neighbours.
- **The Lakulisha temple at Eklingji.** In his reign Pashupata ascetics built a temple to Lakulisha at Eklingji, one of the oldest surviving buildings at the site.
- **The inscription of 971 CE.** The temple's inscription is the oldest dated record at Eklingji and one of the earliest to name Bappa as a Guhila ruler of Nagahrada.
- **Steady rule in a broken age.** He held the kingdom together as the Pratihara empire declined and new powers rose around Mewar.
- **An unbroken succession.** He was followed by his son Shalivahana and his grandson Shaktikumara, who was ruling by 977 CE.

bharttripatta-ii.story:
## Bharttripatta II — the Guhila who married into the house of the Rashtrakutas

*Bharttripatta II, called Bhartripatta in the inscriptions, is known to us from the Atpur inscription of 977 CE, which lists the Guhila kings in order, and from inscriptions of the early 940s CE that bear his name. Few details of his life survive; this story tells what the record holds and sets it in the real history of his age.*

In the first half of the tenth century, the kingdom of the Guhilas lay in a country of low, wooded hills, narrow valleys and seasonal rivers in what is now southern Rajasthan. Its heart was the old town of **Nagda**, called Nagahrada in the inscriptions, and the shrine of **Ekalinga** in the hills nearby, the god whom the dynasty already regarded as its protector. A few miles to the south, the town of **Aghata**, today's Ahar on the edge of Udaipur, was beginning its rise into the chief city of the kingdom. This was the land that Bhartripatta II would inherit.

The modern lists of the rulers of Mewar often place him in the wrong position, after a king called Narvahan Raj and before Allata. The dynasty's own record sets the order straight. The **Atpur inscription of 977 CE**, which counts the Guhila kings from the founder **Guhadatta** down to the reigning king **Shaktikumara**, places Bhartripatta II after **Khumman III**, and before **Allata** and **Naravahana**. Bhartripatta II was not Naravahana's successor but his grandfather. His name honoured an earlier king of the line, **Bhartripatta I**, who had ruled in the ninth century; the Guhilas, like many Indian dynasties, often gave their princes the names of their ancestors.

We do not know the year of his birth, the name of his mother, or the course of his childhood. What we can know is the world into which he was born, because it was one of the most turbulent periods in the history of northern India. For more than a century, the **Gurjara-Pratiharas** of Kannauj had been the greatest power of the north, and the chiefs of Rajasthan, among them the Guhilas, lived within the circle of their power. In the ninth century, branches of the Guhila clan in Rajasthan are known to have served the Pratiharas in war, and the Guhilas of Mewar were very likely their subordinate allies as well.

Then the balance broke. Around **916 CE**, the Rashtrakuta king **Indra III**, ruler of the Deccan from his capital at Manyakheta, led his army north and sacked Kannauj itself. The Pratihara king **Mahipala I** was driven from his capital for a time. He returned, and the Pratiharas would survive for another century, but their prestige never recovered. Across Rajasthan, Malwa and Gujarat, the families who had been their vassals began to look to their own strength. Whether Bhartripatta was a boy or a young man in those years, he grew up in their aftermath, in a world where the great overlord of the north could no longer be relied upon and every hill kingdom had to secure itself.

For a small kingdom in such a world, there were two kinds of strength: the strength of its own fighting men and forts, and the strength of its friendships. The Guhilas had long relied on the first. Their hills were hard to invade, their forest allies, the Bhils, knew every path, and their warriors were used to defending the valleys. Bhartripatta II is remembered in the inscriptions for the second kind of strength.

The Atpur inscription records that his queen was **Mahalakshmi**, a princess of the **Rashtrakuta** family, and that she was the mother of Allata. The name Rashtrakuta in that age carried enormous weight. The imperial Rashtrakutas of Manyakheta were the masters of the Deccan and the very dynasty whose king had humbled Kannauj. There were also lesser branches of the Rashtrakuta clan in Rajasthan itself, such as the family that ruled at **Hastikundi**, not far to the west of Mewar. The inscription does not tell us which branch Mahalakshmi came from, and historians have not settled the question. Either way, the marriage linked the Guhilas to one of the most respected names of the time and drew Mewar out of its old isolation.

One can picture the arrival of such a bride in the hill country: the long procession on the roads, the camels and bullock carts carrying her household and gifts, the drums at the gates of the Guhila town, and the women of the palace coming out to receive her. The details are imagined, but the meaning of the marriage is not. Marriages between ruling houses in medieval India were treaties as much as unions. They created ties of kinship that could bring help in war, protection on the roads and a place among the families who counted. The fact that the composers of the Atpur inscription, writing a generation later, chose to record Mahalakshmi's family shows how much the connection mattered to the dynasty.

The inscriptions of the early 940s that carry Bhartripatta's name show that he was then the ruling king of the Guhilas. Like most records of the period, they are concerned with the ordinary business of kingship: grants, endowments and the dating of a reign. They tell us that the kingdom was organised, that it kept records, and that its rulers were part of the world of Sanskrit learning and temple patronage that extended across northern India. They do not describe wars, and no battle fought by Bhartripatta II is known. Modern accounts that credit him with campaigns against regional enemies or with reforms of the army are not based on any surviving record.

What kind of kingdom did he govern? The evidence of his son's reign gives us a glimpse. Within a few years of Bhartripatta's death, Aghata was a busy town with temples, officers of state and markets visited by traders from distant parts of India. Such a town does not appear overnight. The growth of Aghata, which reached its height under Allata, must already have been under way in his father's time. The road through Aghata linked the plains of Malwa to the east with Gujarat and the western sea ports, and a king who kept that road safe could draw wealth from the trade that passed along it.

The religious life of the kingdom was centred on Shiva. The shrine of Ekalinga in the hills above Nagda was served by ascetics of the **Pashupata** tradition, who would, a generation later, raise a temple there to their founder Lakulisha. At Aghata, temples were rising too, and in the reign of his son one of them, dedicated to Vishnu in his boar form, would receive a recorded endowment. A Guhila king of this period was expected to protect these shrines, to grant land to learned Brahmins and to honour holy men of every school. We do not know Bhartripatta's personal devotions, but he ruled within this tradition and handed it on.

The great dynasties around him continued to shift as his reign went on. In Malwa, the **Paramaras** were growing from vassals into a power in their own right. To the north, the **Chahamanas** of Shakambhari were strengthening their hold on the lands around Sambhar. In Gujarat, a new house, the **Chaulukyas** of Anahilapataka, was about to be founded by **Mularaja**. Mewar stood between all of these. A ruler in Bhartripatta's position needed patience as well as courage, and the evidence suggests that he kept his kingdom secure and passed it on intact.

We do not know when or how Bhartripatta II died. The Atpur inscription simply names his son **Allata**, born of the Rashtrakuta queen Mahalakshmi, as the next king. Allata's reign shows what kind of inheritance he received. Allata was strong enough to defeat and kill in battle an enemy king named **Devapala**, to marry a princess of the **Hunas**, and to make Aghata a flourishing centre of trade and worship. Allata's son **Naravahana** in turn presided over the building of the Lakulisha temple at Eklingji in 971 CE. A dynasty that could do all this in the decades after Bhartripatta's death had clearly been left in good order.

Bhartripatta II is one of the many Guhila kings whose personal story is almost lost. We have no portrait of him, no saying, no tale of a single day of his life. Yet he stands at an important turning point. Before him, the Guhilas of Mewar were a hill dynasty in the shadow of the Pratiharas. After him, under his son and grandson, they were a confident regional power with a flourishing city, wide alliances and a famous shrine. The marriage he made with the house of the Rashtrakutas is the first clear sign of that change, and the son born of it carried the kingdom into its next stage.

## Highlights of his life

- **His true place in the line.** The Atpur inscription of 977 CE places him after Khumman III and before his son Allata and grandson Naravahana.
- **A name of the ancestors.** He bore the name of Bhartripatta I, an earlier Guhila king of the ninth century.
- **King in the early 940s.** Inscriptions of the early 940s CE bear his name as the ruling Guhila king.
- **The Rashtrakuta marriage.** His queen Mahalakshmi came from a Rashtrakuta family, linking Mewar to one of the most powerful names of the age.
- **An age of change.** He ruled as the Pratihara empire weakened after Indra III's sack of Kannauj around 916 CE and new powers rose around Mewar.
- **Father of Allata.** His son Allata made Aghata a flourishing centre and raised the Guhilas to new strength.

allata.story:
## Allata — the king who made Aghata a city

*Allata is one of the best-attested Guhila kings of the tenth century. He is known from the Atpur inscription of 977 CE, set up in the reign of his great-grandson, and from an inscription of 953 CE found at Aghata itself. Where the record is silent, this story says so and does not invent.*

On the eastern edge of modern Udaipur, beside a small river, lies the old town of **Ahar**. Today it is known for its museum, for the ancient mound where archaeologists have found traces of a farming culture thousands of years old, and for the white cenotaphs of the later Maharanas of Mewar. A thousand years ago it had another name, **Aghata**, and for a time it was the most important city of the Guhila kingdom. The king whose reign marked its rise was Allata.

Modern lists of the rulers of Mewar often put Allata in the wrong place, after Bharttripatta II but before a ruler called Nagarbhatta, and set him too early or too vaguely in time. The dynasty's own records are clearer. The **Atpur inscription of 977 CE**, which lists the Guhila kings from the founder **Guhadatta** down to **Shaktikumara**, names Allata as the son and successor of **Bhartripatta II** and the father of **Naravahana**. His own inscription of **953 CE** shows him on the throne in the middle of the tenth century.

His mother was **Mahalakshmi**, a princess of a **Rashtrakuta** family, whose marriage to Bhartripatta II had linked the Guhilas to one of the great names of the age. We know nothing of Allata's childhood itself, not the year of his birth nor the names of his tutors. But we can imagine the world he grew up in: a hill kingdom with its old centre at **Nagda** and the shrine of **Ekalinga** in the hills, its growing town at Aghata in the valley to the south, its warriors and Bhil allies, and its court where a Rashtrakuta queen brought the customs and connections of a wider world. A Guhila prince of his time was trained in riding, archery and swordsmanship, in the conduct of war and the duties of rule, and in the Sanskrit learning that the kings of India prized.

The age into which he was born was unsettled. Around **916 CE** the Rashtrakuta king **Indra III** had sacked **Kannauj**, the capital of the **Gurjara-Pratiharas**, who had long been the overlords of the north. The Pratiharas survived, but they were never again the power they had been. Across Rajasthan and Malwa, their old vassals were becoming independent kings, and every ruler had to decide whether to defend what he had or to reach for more. Allata, when his turn came, reached for more.

We do not know the year in which Bhartripatta II died and Allata became king. What the Atpur inscription records, in the language of royal praise, is the deed that made his name: Allata killed in battle an enemy king named **Devapala**. The inscription tells us nothing about the place or the course of the fight, and historians have long debated who Devapala was. Some identify him with **Devapala**, a king of the Pratihara dynasty who ruled at Kannauj around the middle of the tenth century; if they are right, a Guhila king of Mewar had defeated and killed a ruler of the old imperial house, a sign of how far the Pratiharas had fallen. Others think Devapala was a less famous neighbouring chief. Either way, the victory was large enough for Allata's descendants to set it in stone more than twenty years later as the defining achievement of his life.

Warfare in that age was a matter of horsemen and foot soldiers, archers and war elephants, fought with swords, spears and bows. A king rode at the head of his own men, and the nobles of his clan rode beside him with their followers. In the hill country of Mewar, the Bhils, with their bows and their knowledge of the forest paths, often fought alongside the Guhilas. We do not know which of these forces Allata led against Devapala, or how the battle unfolded. We know only its outcome: the enemy king was dead, and the Guhila king returned victorious.

Allata's marriage was as remarkable as his war. His queen was **Hariyadevi**, a princess of the **Hunas**. The Hunas had entered India from Central Asia centuries before; by the tenth century their ruling families were settled in western and central India and married into other royal houses like any other clan. The inscriptions remember Hariyadevi for founding a town called **Harshapura**. That a queen could found a town in her own name says much about her wealth and standing at the Guhila court. With a Rashtrakuta mother and a Huna wife, Allata's family reached far beyond the hills of Mewar.

The greatest work of his reign, though, was the growth of Aghata. Tradition holds that Allata made it the chief city of his kingdom, and the evidence supports that its importance reached a high point in his time. The inscription of **953 CE**, found at Aghata, records the building and endowment of a temple of **Vishnu** in his boar form, **Varaha**, during Allata's reign. It names the officers who served in his government, showing that the Guhila state now had a regular administration of ministers and officials. It also records levies on goods traded in the town, set aside for the temple's upkeep, and speaks of merchants who came to Aghata from distant regions, including **Karnata** in the south, **Lata** in southern Gujarat and **Madhyadesha**, the heartland of the Ganges plain.

From these few lines a picture of the city emerges. Caravans came down the roads from Malwa and from Gujarat and paused at Aghata. Merchants from the far south and from the Ganges valley traded side by side in its markets. Temples rose along the river, their builders and priests supported partly by the trade that passed through. Officials kept accounts, collected dues and recorded grants. Above it all stood a king who kept the roads safe enough for this commerce to flourish. The details of the scene are imagined, but every element of it is drawn from the record of 953.

Allata's kingdom was Shaiva at its core. The shrine of Ekalinga above Nagda remained the dynasty's spiritual centre, served by ascetics of the **Pashupata** tradition. But the Varaha temple at Aghata shows that Vishnu was honoured too, and that the Guhila king acted as protector of all the faiths of his subjects. The temples of the region, including the ruins that still stand at Ahar, belong to the great tradition of temple building that spread through Rajasthan in these centuries, carved with gods and goddesses, guardians and scenes from the epics.

We do not know of any other wars fought by Allata, and no record tells us of revolts, treaties or defeats. Modern accounts that speak in general terms of his frontier defence and military campaigns are guesses. What can be said is that he was victorious in the one battle the inscriptions record, that he strengthened his house with a powerful marriage, and that he left his kingdom richer and better organised than he found it.

The world around Mewar continued to change in his lifetime. In Malwa, the **Paramaras** were growing stronger, and within a generation their king **Munja** would become the most feared ruler in the region. To the north, the **Chahamanas** of Shakambhari were consolidating their power; Allata's son would take a Chahamana bride. In Gujarat, **Mularaja** was founding the **Chaulukya** kingdom. A city as rich as Aghata would draw the eyes of these neighbours, and in the 970s or 980s, after Allata's time, the armies of Munja would indeed fall upon it. But in Allata's reign the city was at peace and prospering.

We do not know when or how Allata died. The Atpur inscription simply names his son **Naravahana** as the next king. Naravahana was ruling by **971 CE**, when ascetics of the Pashupata order raised a temple to their founder **Lakulisha** at Eklingji and inscribed on it the oldest dated record at that site. After Naravahana came **Shalivahana** and then **Shaktikumara**, whose Atpur inscription of 977 preserved the memory of Allata's victory over Devapala.

Allata's name is little known today compared with those of Bappa Rawal or the later Maharanas. Yet his reign marks the moment when the Guhilas of Mewar stepped out of the hills and became a confident regional power with a real city at its heart. The museum, the ancient mound and the royal cenotaphs at Ahar draw visitors now; few of them know that the town once flourished as the capital of a king who defeated a Devapala, married a Huna princess and welcomed merchants from the far ends of India.

## Highlights of his life

- **Son of Bhartripatta II.** The Atpur inscription of 977 CE names him as the son of Bhartripatta II and his Rashtrakuta queen Mahalakshmi, and the father of Naravahana.
- **Victory over Devapala.** He killed an enemy king named Devapala in battle, possibly a ruler of the declining Pratihara dynasty.
- **Marriage to a Huna princess.** His queen Hariyadevi, a princess of the Hunas, founded the town of Harshapura.
- **The rise of Aghata.** Under him Aghata (Ahar) became the leading city of the Guhila kingdom and a meeting place of merchants from across India.
- **The inscription of 953 CE.** It records a Varaha temple endowed at Aghata in his reign and the officials of his government.
- **A strong inheritance.** He passed a richer and better organised kingdom to his son Naravahana.

nagarbhatta.story:
## Nagarbhatta — a name between two centuries

*No Guhila ruler called Nagarbhatta can be found in the surviving inscriptions of the dynasty. This short account explains where the name stands, which real names it may echo, and what is known of the period around it.*

Nagarbhatta appears in modern lists of the rulers of Mewar as a king of the **Guhila** line, set after **Allata** and before **Shakti Kumar**, and dated vaguely to the eighth or ninth century. Both the place and the date are doubtful. The dynasty's own genealogy, the **Atpur inscription of 977 CE**, names the kings who followed Allata as his son **Naravahana** and grandson **Shalivahana**, after whom came **Shaktikumara**. No ruler called Nagarbhatta stands among them, nor anywhere else in the list from the founder **Guhadatta** onwards. Allata himself ruled in the middle of the tenth century, so a successor of his cannot belong to the eighth or ninth.

The name may be an echo of others. The Atpur inscription does name an early Guhila king called **Naga**, who ruled in the seventh century, long before Allata. The bardic chronicles of Mewar remember a **Nagaditya**, whom tradition makes the father of **Bappa Rawal**, killed while his son was still an infant. And the eighth and ninth centuries were the age of two famous kings named **Nagabhata**, both of the **Gurjara-Pratihara** dynasty: **Nagabhata I**, who drove back the Arab raids from Malwa, and **Nagabhata II**, who made Kannauj the Pratihara capital. A compiler mixing these names could easily have produced a "Nagarbhatta", but which of them lies behind it cannot be known, and nothing can be said of his own life.

What is certain is that the Guhila succession in the tenth century ran on unbroken: from Bhartripatta II to Allata, then to Naravahana, in whose reign the Lakulisha temple at Eklingji was built in 971, then to Shalivahana and Shaktikumara.

## Highlights of his life

- **A name without a record.** No king called Nagarbhatta appears in the Atpur inscription of 977 CE or other surviving Guhila records.
- **A misplaced date.** Modern lists date him to the eighth or ninth century but place him after Allata, who ruled in the mid-tenth century.
- **Possible echoes.** The name may recall the early Guhila king Naga, the bardic Nagaditya, or the Pratihara kings Nagabhata I and II.
- **The real succession.** After Allata, the inscriptions name Naravahana, Shalivahana and Shaktikumara.

shakti-kumar.story:
## Shakti Kumar — the king who set his ancestors in stone

*Shakti Kumar, called Shaktikumara in the inscriptions, is known above all from the Atpur inscription of 977 CE, set up in his own reign, and from an inscription of 997 CE at Hastikundi that tells of the Paramara attack on his city of Aghata. Where the record is silent, this story says so rather than inventing what it does not tell.*

In the year **977 CE**, at Aghata in the valley of Mewar, the place we now call Ahar on the edge of Udaipur, stonecutters finished carving a long Sanskrit inscription. It named the reigning king, **Shaktikumara**, and then did something that gives it a special place in the history of Rajasthan. It counted back his ancestors, king by king, through some twenty generations to the founder of the line, **Guhadatta**. That stone, known today as the **Atpur inscription**, is the backbone of all serious study of the early Guhilas of Mewar. Without it, the order of the kings before him would be lost in the confusion of later lists.

Modern lists often blur Shakti Kumar into a vague "early medieval period" and set him after a king called Nagarbhatta, a name the inscriptions do not contain. The record of his own reign is clearer. Shaktikumara was the son of **Shalivahana**, the grandson of **Naravahana** and the great-grandson of **Allata**. He ruled in the last quarter of the tenth century, and he is one of the few early Guhila kings whose reign can be fixed to an exact year.

He was born into a confident house. His great-grandfather Allata had killed an enemy king named **Devapala** in battle and made Aghata a flourishing city, where merchants from Karnata, Lata and the Ganges plain traded side by side. His grandfather Naravahana had married a daughter of the **Chahamana** prince **Jejaya**, and in his reign, in **971 CE**, Pashupata ascetics had raised a temple to **Lakulisha** at the shrine of **Ekalinga** above Nagda. We do not know the year of Shaktikumara's birth, but as a young prince he may well have known that new temple and the ceremonies around it. He grew up in Aghata among temples, markets and the officers of a settled state, and he would have been trained, as Guhila princes were, in arms, riding, the conduct of war and the Sanskrit learning of the court.

His father Shalivahana's reign was brief. Naravahana was still ruling in 971, and by 977 his grandson was on the throne, so Shalivahana can have held power for only a few years. We do not know how he died. Shaktikumara came to the throne young enough to rule for a good many years, and old enough to understand what his house had achieved and what it needed to protect.

The Atpur inscription shows what mattered to him. A king who orders his ancestors to be listed in stone is making a claim: that his family is ancient, that its right to rule is long established, and that he stands in an unbroken line from a founder. The inscription remembers not only the kings but some of the queens and the families they came from: the **Rashtrakuta** queen **Mahalakshmi** of Bhartripatta II, the **Huna** princess **Hariyadevi** of Allata, and the Chahamana bride of Naravahana. It records Allata's victory over Devapala. In a world of rising and falling dynasties, it was a declaration that the Guhilas of Mewar were a royal house of the first rank. The old Guhila inscriptions of the seventh century, such as that of **Shiladitya** at Samoli in 646 CE and that of **Aparajita** near Nagda in 661 CE, had recorded individual reigns; Shaktikumara's record gathered the whole story into one.

He needed that confidence, because the world around Mewar had grown dangerous. In **972 CE** the **Paramara** king **Siyaka II** of Malwa sacked **Manyakheta**, the capital of the Rashtrakutas, and soon afterwards his successor **Vakpati Munja** came to the throne. Munja was one of the most remarkable kings of his age: a poet and patron of poets, whose court at Ujjain and Dhara welcomed scholars, and at the same time a relentless conqueror. His armies struck in every direction, against the **Kalachuris** of Tripuri, the Chahamanas of Naddula, the **Hunas** and the rulers of Gujarat and Rajasthan. Mewar, rich and close to Malwa, lay directly in his path.

Malwa was not the only danger. To the north, the Chahamana king **Vigraharaja II** of Shakambhari, whose Harsha inscription is dated **973 CE**, was at the height of his power and led his armies as far as Gujarat against **Mularaja**, the founder of the **Chaulukya** kingdom of Anahilapataka. Mularaja in turn was building a strong state on Mewar's south-western flank. Shaktikumara's kingdom lay in the middle of these rising powers, each of them larger and richer than his own. A small hill kingdom could survive among them only by the strength of its hills, the loyalty of its warriors and the friendships it had made.

The blow fell on Aghata. An inscription of **997 CE** set up at **Hastikundi**, near Bali in the Godwar region, by the **Rashtrakuta** chief **Dhavala**, records that when **Munja** destroyed Aghata, the chief city of **Medapata** (Mewar), Dhavala gave shelter to the army of its ruler. The inscription does not name the Guhila king, but the attack is generally placed in the reign of Shaktikumara, since Munja's reign of conquest fell in the last decades of the tenth century, when Shaktikumara ruled.

We cannot describe that day with certainty. The record tells us only that the city was destroyed and that the Guhila army had to seek refuge in the hills to the west. One can imagine what such a defeat meant: the smoke rising over the temples and markets that Allata had made famous, the merchants fleeing, the king's soldiers falling back along the roads into the Aravallis, and the long march to a friendly chief's stronghold. It was the worst disaster the house had suffered for generations. The proud city of the Atpur inscription was in ruins, perhaps within only a few years of the inscription itself.

Yet the Guhila kingdom did not end. Dhavala of Hastikundi, a chief of the Rashtrakuta clan, the clan from which Shaktikumara's great-great-grandmother Mahalakshmi had come, stood by Mewar in its hour of need. The army survived. The hill country around Nagda and Eklingji, which had sheltered the Guhilas since the days of their founders, remained in their hands. Munja's empire was itself built on conquest rather than lasting rule, and it would not survive him; in the 990s he was defeated and killed by the Chalukya king **Tailapa II** of the Deccan, against whom he had marched once too often.

The damage to Mewar, however, was real. In the decades that followed, the great fortress of **Chittor**, the rock that Mewar's tradition linked to Bappa Rawal, appears in the hands of the Paramaras; Munja's nephew **Bhoja** would later be remembered as a builder there. The Guhilas would not hold Chittor firmly again for a long time. Aghata itself recovered as a town, and in later centuries Ahar would become the resting place of the Maharanas, whose white cenotaphs still stand there. But the age of Aghata as the confident capital of an expanding kingdom ended in Shaktikumara's reign.

Of his religious life we know only what was common to his house. He ruled under the protection of **Ekalinga**, the lord of the shrine above Nagda, where the Lakulisha temple of his grandfather's time now stood, and his kingdom also honoured Vishnu, whose Varaha temple at Aghata had been endowed in Allata's day. Modern accounts that credit him with particular campaigns or reforms are not based on any surviving record, and no other war of his reign is known.

We do not know when or how Shaktikumara died. The Guhila genealogies of later centuries name his successor as **Ambaprasada**, who would face a new enemy in the **Chahamanas** of Shakambhari and die in battle against their king **Vakpatiraja II**. After Ambaprasada came **Shuchivarman**, **Naravarman** and **Kirtivarman**, and the line of the Guhilas ran on into the eleventh century, diminished but unbroken.

Shakti Kumar's reign holds both the high point and the fall of tenth-century Mewar. At its beginning he set up the stone that preserved the memory of his ancestors for a thousand years. Within his reign, the city where that stone stood was struck down by one of the greatest conquerors of the age. That the dynasty survived the blow, and that the stone survived to tell its story, is his true legacy.

## Highlights of his life

- **Son of Shalivahana.** He was the son of Shalivahana, grandson of Naravahana and great-grandson of Allata, and was ruling by 977 CE.
- **The Atpur inscription (977 CE).** His inscription lists the Guhila kings from the founder Guhadatta, and is the foundation of the early history of Mewar.
- **Memory of a royal house.** The inscription records the dynasty's marriages with Rashtrakuta, Huna and Chahamana families and Allata's victory over Devapala.
- **The fall of Aghata.** The Paramara king Munja destroyed Aghata, an attack generally placed in his reign and recorded in the Hastikundi inscription of 997 CE.
- **Survival through alliance.** The Rashtrakuta chief Dhavala of Hastikundi gave shelter to the Guhila army after Aghata fell.
- **An unbroken line.** He was succeeded by Ambaprasada, and the Guhila line continued into the eleventh century.

ambaprasad.story:
## Ambaprasad — the king who fell before the Chahamanas

*Ambaprasad, called Ambaprasada in the sources, is known from the Guhila genealogies and from a single event recorded by his enemies: the Chahamana court poem* Prithviraja Vijaya *tells that he was killed in battle by the Chahamana king Vakpatiraja II. Little else of his life survives, and this story says so where the record falls silent.*

At the close of the tenth century, the Guhila kingdom of Mewar was a wounded state. Only a few years earlier, in **977 CE**, its king **Shaktikumara** had set up the **Atpur inscription** at **Aghata**, the city on the edge of modern Udaipur that we now call Ahar, proudly listing his ancestors back to the founder **Guhadatta**. Soon afterwards, the armies of the **Paramara** king **Munja** of Malwa had fallen upon Aghata and destroyed it, and the Guhila army had found refuge only with the **Rashtrakuta** chief **Dhavala** of Hastikundi. The kingdom survived, but its confidence was shaken. Into this inheritance came Ambaprasada.

Modern lists of the rulers of Mewar place him vaguely in an "early medieval period" and name his successor as Narvarman. The Guhila genealogies of later centuries are more precise. They name Ambaprasada as the successor of Shaktikumara, and he is generally taken to have been his son. After him, they name **Shuchivarman**, and only then **Naravarman** and **Kirtivarman**. His reign belongs to the last years of the tenth century or the early years of the eleventh, though no inscription fixes its exact dates.

We know nothing of his childhood, not the year of his birth, his mother's name nor the names of his teachers. We can say what kind of world shaped him. If he was Shaktikumara's son, he grew up at Aghata in its last years of splendour, among the temples his ancestors had endowed and the markets where merchants from distant regions had traded. He may have been old enough to remember the day Munja's army came, the flight into the hills and the long return to a ruined city. Whether or not he saw it with his own eyes, the fall of Aghata was the great fact of his youth. A Guhila prince of that generation learned early that his house was no longer the rising power it had been in his great-great-grandfather Allata's time, but a small kingdom that had to fight to survive among larger ones.

The powers around Mewar were formidable. In Malwa, the Paramaras remained the dominant force. Munja himself was defeated and killed in the 990s by the Chalukya king **Tailapa II** of the Deccan, but the dynasty soon recovered, and in the early eleventh century his nephew **Bhoja** would make the Paramara court at Dhara one of the most brilliant in India. The great fortress of **Chittor**, which Mewar's tradition linked with its founder Bappa Rawal, was now in Paramara hands, and Bhoja would later be remembered as a builder there. To the south-west, in Gujarat, the **Chaulukyas** of Anahilapataka, founded by **Mularaja**, were growing into a major kingdom. And to the north lay the **Chahamanas** of Shakambhari, the kingdom around the salt lake of Sambhar, whose kings had already shown their strength by carrying war as far as Gujarat.

The Chahamanas were an old clan of Rajasthan. For generations they had served the Pratiharas, but as the Pratihara empire weakened they became masters of their own land. Their king **Vigraharaja II**, whose inscription on the hill of **Harsha** near Sikar is dated **973 CE**, had led his armies against Mularaja of Gujarat, and his successors kept up the same ambition. Their kingdom lay across the open country to the north of Mewar, and its later kings would found **Ajmer**. For a weakened Guhila state, such a neighbour was both a possible ally and a constant threat.

The Guhilas had long had ties with the Chahamanas. Ambaprasada's great-grandfather **Naravahana** had married a daughter of the Chahamana prince **Jejaya**. But marriages between ruling houses did not prevent war, and the frontier between the Chahamana lands and the hills of Mewar was a natural place for quarrels over territory, tribute and the control of roads. We do not know what caused the conflict between Ambaprasada and the Chahamanas, or which side began it.

What we know comes from the other side. More than a century and a half later, in the court of the Chahamana king **Prithviraj III** at Ajmer, the poet **Jayanaka** composed the Sanskrit poem *Prithviraja Vijaya*, celebrating the victories of Prithviraj's ancestors. Among the deeds of the Chahamana king **Vakpatiraja II**, the poem records that he killed **Ambaprasada**, the ruler of Aghata, in battle. This is the one event of Ambaprasada's life that the surviving sources describe.

The poem tells us the outcome but not the place, the date or the course of the battle. We can imagine it only in general terms. Armies of that age were made of horsemen and foot soldiers, archers and, in the larger kingdoms, war elephants. A Rajput king rode at the head of his clansmen, and the nobles of his house fought around him. To fall in battle was, in the warrior ideals of the time, the most honourable of deaths for a king. The Chahamana poet, writing to glorify his own patrons, naturally presents Ambaprasada's death as a triumph for Vakpatiraja. From Mewar's side, no account survives. We do not know whether Ambaprasada was defending his own land or had marched against the Chahamanas, whether he was outnumbered, or how many of his men died with him. We know only that he did not come home.

It is worth pausing on what this single fact tells us. The poets of the Chahamana court thought it worth remembering, generations later, that their king had killed the ruler of Aghata. That means Ambaprasada was a king of standing, an enemy whose defeat was a matter of pride. Even in decline, the Guhilas of Mewar were a dynasty that their neighbours took seriously.

The years of Ambaprasada's reign were also the years when a new danger appeared on the western horizon of India. From the year **1000 CE**, **Mahmud of Ghazni** began his raids into the subcontinent from his kingdom in Afghanistan. Over the next quarter of a century he struck again and again, at the Punjab, at Mathura and Kannauj, and finally, in **1025 CE**, across the deserts of western Rajasthan to the temple of **Somnath** in Gujarat. We do not know whether Ambaprasada was still alive when these raids began, and there is no record that his kingdom was touched by them. But the world in which his successors ruled was shaped by that storm from the north-west, which shattered the old powers of northern India and left the Rajput kingdoms of Rajasthan to face the future on their own.

Of Ambaprasada's government, his religious life and his building works, nothing specific is known. Modern accounts that credit him with administrative continuity and cultural patronage describe what was expected of any king of his line, not anything recorded of him. He ruled, like his ancestors, as the servant of **Ekalinga**, the lord of the shrine above **Nagda**, where the temple of Lakulisha raised in Naravahana's reign still stood. His kingdom honoured Shiva and Vishnu, protected its temples and Brahmins, and relied on the hill country and its Bhil allies for its defence. That much was the inheritance of every Guhila king, and he would have kept it as they did.

After his death, the genealogies name **Shuchivarman** as the next king, followed by **Naravarman** and **Kirtivarman**. The Guhilas of the eleventh century were a lesser power than they had been in Allata's time. Chittor remained in other hands, and the kingdom was hemmed in by the Paramaras, the Chaulukyas and the Chahamanas. Yet the line did not break. Over the following generations it endured, and in later centuries the Guhilas recovered their strength, regained Chittor and grew into the kingdom whose rulers, the Rawals and later the Maharanas, would become the most famous royal house of Rajasthan.

Ambaprasad's story is almost entirely lost. He is remembered by his own dynasty only as a name in a list, and by his enemies only as a king they killed. But that one line of an enemy poet is enough to show that he died as a Rajput king was expected to die, on the field, defending the inheritance of his house in one of its hardest centuries. The dynasty that he could not save from defeat survived him, and that survival was itself a kind of victory.

## Highlights of his life

- **Successor of Shaktikumara.** The Guhila genealogies name him as Shaktikumara's successor, and he is generally taken to have been his son.
- **Heir to a wounded kingdom.** He inherited Mewar after the Paramara king Munja had destroyed Aghata and Chittor had passed into Paramara hands.
- **Among powerful neighbours.** He ruled between the Paramaras of Malwa, the Chaulukyas of Gujarat and the Chahamanas of Shakambhari.
- **Death in battle.** According to the *Prithviraja Vijaya*, he was killed in battle by the Chahamana king Vakpatiraja II.
- **A king of standing.** That the Chahamana poets remembered his death shows he was an enemy of rank.
- **An unbroken line.** He was followed by Shuchivarman, Naravarman and Kirtivarman, and the Guhila dynasty survived to rise again.
