narvarman.story:
## Narvarman — a Guhila king in the shadow of Malwa

*Almost nothing is known of Narvarman (Naravarman) beyond his name and his place in the Guhila genealogy. This short account gives only what can be said with confidence.*

Narvarman, written **Naravarman** in the inscriptions, was a king of the **Guhila** dynasty of Mewar, the house of Bappa Rawal. His name survives in the genealogies carved by his descendants in the thirteenth century, such as the inscription of **Rawal Samarasimha** at Mount Abu of **1285 CE**. There he follows **Shuchivarman** and comes before **Kirtivarman**. Modern lists often place him directly after **Ambaprasad**, but the inscriptions name Shuchivarman between the two. His reign falls in the **eleventh century**.

No record tells us how long he reigned, what he built or whom he fought. What can be described is the danger of his age. His predecessor Ambaprasad, as a later Chahamana inscription claims, had been killed in battle by **Vakpatiraja II** of Shakambhari. In the late tenth century, the Paramara king **Munja** of Malwa had sacked **Aghata**, the Guhila capital. In the early eleventh century the Paramara **Bhoja** held **Chittor**, where he built the temple of Tribhuvana Narayana that still stands as the Samiddheshvara temple. In **1025** Mahmud of Ghazni marched across western Rajasthan on his way to Somnath. Squeezed between Malwa, the Chahamanas and Gujarat, the Guhila kings held on to their hill country around Aghata, Nagda and the shrine of **Eklingji**, ruling as servants of the god Ekalinga.

After Naravarman the inscriptions name Kirtivarman, Yogaraja and Vairata, carrying the line towards the twelfth century. Some modern lists name **Shalivahan** as his successor, but the tenth-century inscriptions show that Shalivahana ruled earlier, as the father of Shaktikumara. Naravarman's own deeds are lost, but the line he held survived one of its hardest centuries.

## Highlights of his life

- **Guhila king of the eleventh century.** The dynasty's own inscriptions name him between Shuchivarman and Kirtivarman.
- **Ruler in a dangerous age.** He reigned when Paramara Malwa held Chittor and Chahamana and Ghaznavid armies threatened the region.
- **Servant of Ekalinga.** Like every king of his house, he ruled as the *dewan* of the lord of Eklingji.
- **A link in an unbroken line.** He carried Bappa Rawal's house through the eleventh century.

shalivahan.name: Shalivahan
shalivahan.title: Guardian of the Dynastic Tradition
shalivahan.significance: Guhila ruler of Mewar between Naravahana and Shaktikumara, named in the Atpur inscription of 977 CE
shalivahan.legacy: Shalivahan is known only as a name in the Guhila genealogy; his son Shaktikumara's Atpur inscription preserves his place in the line.
shalivahan.story:
## Shalivahan — the brief king between Naravahana and Shaktikumara

*Almost nothing is known of Shalivahan (Shalivahana) beyond his name and his place in the Guhila genealogy. This short account gives only what can be said with confidence.*

Shalivahan, written **Shalivahana** in the inscriptions, was a king of the **Guhila** dynasty of Mewar, the house of Bappa Rawal. He was the son of **Naravahana**, whose reign is recorded in an inscription of **971 CE** at the Lakulisha temple beside the shrine of **Eklingji**, and the father of **Shaktikumara**, whose **Atpur inscription of 977 CE** lists the Guhila kings from the founder Guhadatta down to his own day. Between those two dates there is room for only a short reign, so Shalivahan ruled for a few years in the **970s**.

This places him earlier than some modern lists suggest. Those lists put him after **Narvarman**, but the inscriptions of the dynasty itself make Shalivahana a king of the tenth century, with Naravarman coming several generations later.

No record tells us what Shalivahana did as king. Later lists describe him as a patron of religion and culture, but no record of his time confirms it. What can be described is his world. The Guhila capital was **Aghata**, the trading town of Ahar near present-day Udaipur, where merchants and Jain communities flourished and where his son set up the Atpur inscription. Close by stood Nagda and the shrine of Eklingji, where the Pashupata ascetics of the Lakulisha tradition kept the worship of the god the Guhila kings served. Beyond the hills, the power of the Gurjara-Pratiharas of Kannauj was fading, and new kingdoms were rising in their place: the **Paramaras** of Malwa, the **Chahamanas** of Shakambhari and the **Chaulukyas** of Gujarat. Within a few years of Shalivahana's death, in his son's reign, the Paramara king **Munja** would sack Aghata.

Shalivahana passed the kingdom to Shaktikumara. His own deeds are lost, but his son's inscription keeps his name, and with it the unbroken line of Bappa Rawal's house.

## Highlights of his life

- **Guhila king of the tenth century.** The son of Naravahana and father of Shaktikumara, he ruled for a few years in the 970s.
- **Named in the Atpur inscription.** His son's inscription of 977 CE records him in the line of Guhila kings.
- **Ruler at Aghata.** He reigned from the Guhila capital at Ahar, near the shrine of Eklingji.
- **Ruler in a changing age.** His reign came as the Pratihara empire faded and the Paramaras, Chahamanas and Chaulukyas rose around Mewar.

samant-singh.story:
## Samant Singh — the king who lost Mewar and founded Vagad

*Samant Singh, written Samantasimha in the inscriptions, is known from the genealogies of the Guhila house, from records of his own time and from the praise-poems of his neighbours. The bards say little about him. Where the record is silent, this story says so.*

In the middle of the twelfth century, the Guhila kingdom of **Medapata**, the land we call Mewar, was not the proud power it would later become. Its kings were the heirs of Bappa Rawal and ruled, as their ancestors had, as servants of the god Ekalinga at the shrine of **Eklingji**. Their seat was **Aghata**, the town of Ahar beside the little river that still flows past the edge of Udaipur, with Nagda and the temple valley a short ride to the north. But the great fort of **Chittor** was not securely theirs, and the kingdom sat among neighbours far stronger than itself.

To the south-west lay the **Chaulukya** kingdom of Gujarat, the richest power of western India. Its kings **Jayasimha Siddharaja** and **Kumarapala** had pushed their influence deep into Rajasthan, and an inscription of Kumarapala, set up at Chittor itself around **1150 CE**, shows how far Gujarat's reach extended into the Guhila homeland. To the north stood the **Chahamanas** of Shakambhari and Ajmer, and to the west their kinsmen of **Naddula**, the Chauhans of Nadol. To the south-west, on the mountain of Abu, ruled a branch of the **Paramaras**, the loyal vassals of Gujarat. A Guhila king of this age had to be watchful, patient and quick to act when the balance shifted.

Samant Singh was born into this world as the son of **Kshemasimha**, the Guhila king, and the grandson of **Ranasimha**, also called Karnasimha. We do not know the year of his birth or the name of his mother. Tradition remembers that his grandfather's house had already divided into two lines. Kshemasimha's descendants held the throne, with the title of *Rawal*, while Kshemasimha's brother **Rahapa** took an estate at **Sisoda** in the hills and founded the line of the Ranas, the ancestors of the later Sisodias. Samant Singh also had a brother, **Kumarasimha**, whose fortunes would one day be tied to his own in a way neither could have expected.

Nothing is recorded of his childhood, but we know the world that shaped it. A Guhila prince grew up among horsemen and archers, in a court where the priests of Eklingji, the Jain merchants of Aghata and the chiefs of the Bhil forests all had their place. He would have learned to ride the stony tracks between Ahar and Nagda, to read the movements of armies from the passes, and to understand that his family's survival depended on choosing its moments well. He would also have heard, again and again, the story of Bappa Rawal and the hidden linga, and the lesson that a king of Mewar holds his land only in Ekalinga's name.

He came to the throne after his father, probably around the beginning of the **1170s**. Inscriptions place his reign in that decade. The moment was a turning point for all of western India. Kumarapala of Gujarat, who had ruled for some thirty years, died around **1171**, and his successor **Ajayapala** began a short and troubled reign. After decades in which Gujarat had seemed unbreakable, its grip on its neighbours suddenly loosened.

Samant Singh struck. The details of the war are lost, and no record names the field where it was fought. But its outcome was remembered even by Gujarat's own allies. Almost sixty years later, in **1230 CE**, a long praise-poem was carved at the Jain temple of Lunavasahi on Mount Abu. In praising the Paramara princes of Abu, it records that **Prahladana**, the brother of the Paramara king Dharavarsha, protected the king of Gujarat at a time when that king's strength had been broken in battle by Samantasimha. The poem's purpose was to glorify Prahladana, but in doing so it preserved the fact that a Guhila king had defeated the ruler of the most powerful kingdom in the west.

It is easy to picture the scene that followed the fighting, even if the record gives us only its result: the Guhila horsemen pressing forward, the Gujarat army giving way, and the Abu prince bringing his men in to shield the defeated king. Prahladana was himself a remarkable figure, a warrior who was also a poet and the author of a Sanskrit play, the *Partha-Parakrama*. That such a man is remembered for rescuing a king from Samant Singh shows how serious the defeat had been.

A victory of this kind brought glory, but it also brought danger. Gujarat recovered quickly from its troubles. Ajayapala was killed around **1175**, and power passed to a child king, **Mularaja II**, under the regency of his mother **Naikidevi**. In **1178** the Gujarat army and its allies defeated the invading army of **Muhammad of Ghor** at **Kasahrada**, near Mount Abu, one of the few defeats the Ghurid ruler ever suffered in India. Among the allies of Gujarat in those years was **Kirtipala**, a prince of the Chahamana house of Nadol who was carving out a new kingdom of his own at **Jalor**.

It was Kirtipala who brought Samant Singh's rule in Mewar to an end. The later inscriptions of the Guhilas remember an enemy they call **Kitu**, who seized the Guhila lands and drove the king from them, and historians identify Kitu with Kirtipala of Jalor. The Chahamana prince occupied **Aghata**, the Guhila capital, sometime in the 1170s. We do not know whether Samant Singh lost a pitched battle or was simply outmatched, and the record does not tell us how long he held out. We know only that the king who had once broken the strength of Gujarat now found himself without his ancestral seat.

He did not give up his crown. Samant Singh went south and east, into the hill country of **Vagad**, the land of the Mahi river and its broken ridges, where the modern districts of Dungarpur and Banswara lie today. It was a wild country of forest and Bhil villages, far from the great trade roads, and it offered what a dispossessed king needed most: distance, defensible hills and people who could be won as allies. There he established himself as a ruler again. Inscriptions found in Vagad record his rule there, showing that the exile became the founder of a new Guhila kingdom.

Meanwhile Mewar itself did not remain lost. Samant Singh's brother **Kumarasimha** took up the struggle for the old homeland. The later Guhila inscriptions say that Kumarasimha recovered the kingdom from Kitu, and that he did so by winning the favour of the king of Gujarat. The Chaulukyas, who had once been beaten by Samant Singh, now helped restore his brother. In politics as in war, the balance had turned again. From Kumarasimha the line of the Rawals of Mewar ran on through Mathanasimha and Padmasimha to **Jaitrasimha**, who would fight the armies of the Delhi Sultanate, and later to **Samarasimha** and **Ratnasimha**, the last Rawal of Chittor.

So the house of Ranasimha came to have three branches: the Rawals of Mewar descended from Kumarasimha, the Ranas of Sisoda descended from Rahapa, and the Guhilas of Vagad descended from Samant Singh. Each would have its own long history.

Samant Singh's branch proved the most lasting in its own land. His descendants ruled Vagad as Rawals for centuries. Its old capital was at Vatapadraka, the village of Baroda in Dungarpur district, and in the fourteenth century the town of **Dungarpur** was founded and became the seat of the line. In the sixteenth century, after **Rawal Udai Singh** of Vagad died fighting beside Rana Sanga at **Khanwa** in 1527, the kingdom was divided between his sons, and the separate state of **Banswara** was born. Both Dungarpur and Banswara continued to trace their royal line to Samant Singh until the end of the princely states in the twentieth century.

Of Samant Singh's religion and character we can say a little. Like every king of his house, he would have held the land as the *dewan* of Ekalinga, and the Shaiva faith of Eklingji was the faith of his family. His kingdom, like Mewar, was home to Jain merchants and temples as well, and the old shrines of the region, such as the temple of the goddess Ambika at **Jagat**, stood within the lands of his house. His career suggests a man who was bold rather than cautious: a king who saw the moment of Gujarat's weakness and seized it, and who, when the wheel turned against him, refused to be erased and built a new kingdom out of the hills.

Some later writers have wondered whether the bardic hero **Samarsi** of Chittor, whom the *Prithviraj Raso* makes a brother-in-law of Prithviraj Chauhan, preserves a distorted memory of Samant Singh, who really was a contemporary of Prithviraj. The record does not support any such link, and the Raso's Samarsi is usually understood as a confused memory of the much later Rawal Samarasimha. It is one more sign of how quickly the real Samant Singh faded from the songs of the bards, even as his descendants ruled on.

We do not know when or how Samant Singh died. His last years were spent in Vagad, probably in the 1180s or soon after, among the hills that had given him refuge. No *samadhi* of his is known, and no bard sang his death. Yet the kingdom he founded outlived the Rawals of Chittor, outlived the Delhi Sultanate and outlived the Mughals. The king who lost Mewar left behind a line of rulers who held their own corner of Rajasthan for more than seven hundred years.

## Highlights of his life

- **Heir of the Guhila house.** The son of Kshemasimha and grandson of Ranasimha, he became king of Mewar around the early 1170s.
- **Victory over Gujarat.** He defeated the Chaulukya king Ajayapala; the Mount Abu inscription of 1230 CE remembers that the Paramara prince Prahladana had to protect the Gujarat king after Samantasimha broke his strength in battle.
- **Loss of Mewar.** He was driven from the Guhila capital Aghata by Kirtipala of Jalor, remembered in Mewar's inscriptions as "Kitu".
- **Founder of the Guhila kingdom of Vagad.** In exile he established a new kingdom in the hills of Vagad, recorded in inscriptions found there.
- **Ancestor of Dungarpur and Banswara.** His descendants ruled Vagad for centuries; Dungarpur and Banswara both traced their royal line to him.
- **Brother of the restorer.** His brother Kumarasimha recovered Mewar, continuing the line of the Rawals of Chittor.

kshetra-singh.story:
## Kshetra Singh — the Guhila king whose sons divided Mewar's fate

*Very little is known of this Kshetra Singh beyond his name and his place in the Guhila genealogy. This short account gives only what can be said with confidence.*

The Kshetra Singh who stands at this point in the line of Mewar is the Guhila king written **Kshemasimha** in the inscriptions, often called **Kshem Singh**. He should not be confused with the much better-known **Maharana Kshetra Singh**, the son of Rana Hammir, who ruled Mewar from 1364 to 1382. The earlier Kshemasimha was the son of the Guhila king **Ranasimha**, also called Karnasimha, and he ruled in the **middle of the twelfth century**, his reign ending before the early 1170s.

His father's house had divided. Kshemasimha kept the throne and the title of *Rawal*, while his brother **Rahapa** received the estate of **Sisoda** and, tradition says, founded the line of the Ranas, the ancestors of the later Sisodias. No record tells us what Kshemasimha himself built or fought. His kingdom, ruled from **Aghata** near the shrine of **Eklingji**, lived in the shadow of the **Chaulukyas** of Gujarat: around **1150 CE** the Chaulukya king **Kumarapala** set up an inscription at Chittor itself. The **Chahamanas** of Ajmer and Nadol pressed on Mewar from the north and west.

Kshemasimha's importance lies in his sons. **Samantasimha** succeeded him, defeated the Chaulukya king Ajayapala, then lost Mewar to Kirtipala of Jalor and founded the Guhila kingdom of **Vagad**, the ancestor of Dungarpur and Banswara. His other son, **Kumarasimha**, recovered Mewar and carried on the line of the Rawals of Chittor down to Ratnasimha. Kshemasimha's own deeds are lost, but through his sons and his brother, all three branches of the later Guhila house trace back to his generation.

## Highlights of his life

- **Guhila king of the twelfth century.** The son of Ranasimha, he ruled Mewar in the mid-twelfth century as a king of the Rawal line.
- **Brother of Rahapa.** His brother founded the Rana branch at Sisoda, from which the Sisodias descend.
- **Ruler in Gujarat's shadow.** He reigned when the Chaulukyas under Kumarapala held sway as far as Chittor.
- **Father of two lines.** His sons Samantasimha and Kumarasimha founded the Vagad line and continued the Rawals of Mewar.

rahap.story:
## Rahap — the prince of Sisoda who took the title of Rana

*Rahap, written Rahapa in Sanskrit records, comes to us mainly through the genealogies of the Rana line set down in fifteenth-century Mewar, and through the bardic chronicles that Colonel James Tod retold in the nineteenth century. His name and his place in the family are secure; most of his deeds are tradition. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

In the twelfth century, the Guhila house of Mewar was an old dynasty in a difficult age. Four hundred years had passed since Bappa Rawal, and his descendants still ruled the hill country around **Aghata**, **Nagda** and the shrine of **Eklingji** as servants of the god Ekalinga. But the kingdom lived in the shadow of greater powers: the **Chaulukyas** of Gujarat, whose king Kumarapala set up an inscription in Chittor itself around 1150 CE, and the **Chahamanas** of Ajmer and Nadol, who pressed on its northern and western borders.

Rahap was born into this house as a son of **Ranasimha**, the Guhila king who is also called Karnasimha. We do not know the year of his birth or the name of his mother. What we do know is that he was not the son who would inherit the throne. That place belonged to his brother **Kshemasimha**, whose line kept the kingship of Mewar and the old title of *Rawal*. Kshemasimha's sons, **Samantasimha** and **Kumarasimha**, would later rule in turn, and Samantasimha would found the Guhila kingdom of Vagad. Rahap's path lay elsewhere.

In Rajput kingdoms, a younger son of the royal house was usually given an estate of his own, a share of the land from which he could support his household and his followers while remaining bound in loyalty to the king. Rahap's share was **Sisoda**, a village in the hills of Mewar. It was not a great prize: a cluster of houses, some fields, the hills around and the duty to ride when the king called. But from this small place would come one of the most famous names in Indian history. The family that held Sisoda came to be called the **Sisodias**, and it was their line that would one day rule all of Mewar.

The bards have their own version of these events, and it differs in its details from the inscriptions. In Tod's retelling, Karan, the father, had two sons named **Mahup** and **Rahup**. Mahup was the elder, but he went away to his mother's people and settled in the south, where his descendants are said to have founded the line of Dungarpur. Rahup stayed in Mewar and received Sisoda. Historians prefer the record of the inscriptions, which make **Samantasimha**, Rahap's nephew, the founder of the Vagad line of Dungarpur, but the bardic story shows how Mewar's memory linked all these branches back to one father.

The most famous story told of Rahap concerns his title. Tod records the tradition that around **1201 CE** Rahap fought **Mokal**, a Parihar prince of **Mandor**, the old Pratihara seat in Marwar, and took him captive. The prince carried a title of honour, *Rana*. Rahap, the bards say, stripped him of it and took it for himself, and from that day his descendants were called Ranas.

The bards' Rahap is easy to imagine in this moment. Picture him standing in his courtyard at Sisoda, the captured Parihar brought before him, dust still on the horses outside.

"You came to my hills as a Rana," Rahap says, in the way the bards might tell it. "You will go home as a man who has given his title to the Guhilas."

Mokal, the story goes, could only bow his head. Then he was sent back to Mandor, while Rahap kept the title that his descendants would carry for six hundred years.

Historians treat this tale with caution. The word *Rana* was already an old title of rank in western India, and it was used by many chiefs. No contemporary record describes Rahap's war with Mandor, and the date belongs to the bardic tradition rather than to an inscription. What is certain is that the line descended from Rahap used the title of Rana from early on, and that it distinguished them clearly from their cousins, the Rawals, who ruled from Aghata and Chittor.

Some modern lists place Rahap in the eleventh century, but his father Ranasimha belongs to the middle of the twelfth, and his nephews ruled in the 1170s and 1180s. Rahap's own life therefore ran through the second half of the twelfth century and probably into the early thirteenth. This was one of the most violent periods in the history of north India.

When Rahap was a grown man, his nephew Samantasimha defeated the king of Gujarat and then lost Mewar to **Kirtipala** of Jalor. Another nephew, Kumarasimha, won the kingdom back with Gujarat's help. Then, in **1192**, **Prithviraj Chauhan** of Ajmer was defeated and killed by **Muhammad of Ghor** at the second battle of **Tarain**. Within a few years the Ghurid armies held Ajmer and Delhi. In **1197** the Ghurid general **Qutb al-Din Aibak** marched through Rajasthan into Gujarat and sacked the Chaulukya capital at Anahilapataka. The old order of the Rajput kingdoms, in which Guhilas, Chahamanas, Paramaras and Chaulukyas fought one another for local advantage, had suddenly been joined by a much more dangerous power from the north.

For a chief at Sisoda, these were years when loyalty to the house of Eklingji mattered more than ever. The Ranas were the king's kinsmen and vassals, and their place in war was beside the Rawal. Tradition does not record any particular campaign that Rahap fought for his cousins, and this story will not invent one. But the duty of the Rana line was clear, and it was passed down from father to son: when Chittor or Aghata was threatened, the men of Sisoda would ride.

After Rahap, the later genealogies of the Rana branch give a list of names: Narapati, Dinakara, Jasakarna, Nagapala and others, generation after generation, each holding Sisoda and the title of Rana. Most of them are names and little more. The Rawals, meanwhile, fought on against the Delhi Sultanate. In the reign of **Jaitrasimha**, in the 1220s or 1230s, an army of the Sultan **Iltutmish** ravaged Nagda, and the Guhila capital moved to the safety of **Chittor**.

The moment for which Rahap's line would be remembered came a century after his death. In **1303 CE** Sultan **Alauddin Khalji** of Delhi besieged Chittor. The defender was **Rawal Ratnasimha**, the last king of the old Rawal line. Beside him fought his kinsman **Lakshmasimha**, the Rana of Sisoda and a descendant of Rahap, with his sons. The fort fell, and tradition says that Lakshmasimha and most of his sons died in its defence.

One grandson of Lakshmasimha survived to carry the line: **Hammir**, son of Arisimha. Around **1326**, Hammir recovered Chittor from the governors whom the Delhi Sultanate had left there, and from that time the Ranas of Sisoda became the rulers of Mewar. The title Rahap had carried home to his small estate became the title of the kingdom. Under the Sisodia Ranas and Maharanas, Mewar produced **Rana Kumbha**, **Rana Sanga** and **Maharana Pratap**, and stood for centuries as the most famous of the Rajput states.

So Rahap is remembered not for a great reign, but for a beginning. He never ruled Mewar. He held a village in the hills, a title that the bards say he won with his sword, and a line of sons who kept faith with their cousins on the throne. When the Rawal line ended in the fire of 1303, it was Rahap's line that rose from the ashes.

Of his religion we can say what is true of all his house: he would have worshipped **Ekalinga** at Eklingji as the true lord of the land, and his descendants, when they became kings, called themselves the *dewan* of that god as Bappa Rawal had done. Of his character the bards speak in the language of pride. They describe a man who would not accept a lesser place for his family, and who turned a younger son's small estate into the root of a royal house.

We do not know when or how Rahap died, and no memorial of his is known. His descendants at Sisoda took up his estate and his title, and the name of the village became the name of a dynasty. Every Maharana of Mewar who sat on the gaddi of Udaipur, down to the twentieth century, was a Sisodia, and every one of them traced his line through the Ranas of Sisoda back to Rahap.

## Highlights of his life

- **Son of Ranasimha.** A son of the Guhila king Ranasimha (Karnasimha) and brother of Kshemasimha, he founded a younger branch of the royal house.
- **Lord of Sisoda.** He received the estate of Sisoda in the hills of Mewar, the village that gave the Sisodia clan its name.
- **The title of Rana.** Tradition says he won the title of Rana around 1201 CE by capturing Mokal, a Parihar prince of Mandor; historians treat the story as bardic tradition.
- **Founder of the Rana line.** His descendants held Sisoda as Ranas, loyal kinsmen of the Rawals of Mewar, for more than a century.
- **Ancestor of the Sisodia rulers.** Through his descendants Lakshmasimha and Hammir, his line took the throne of Mewar after 1303 and ruled it until the twentieth century.
- **A life in a turbulent age.** His lifetime saw the fall of Prithviraj Chauhan at Tarain in 1192 and the arrival of the Ghurid and Delhi Sultanate armies in Rajasthan.

nagar-singh.story:
## Nagar Singh — a Rana of Sisoda in the age of the Sultanate

*Nagar Singh cannot be clearly identified in the surviving records of Mewar. This short account gives only what can be said with confidence about his place and time.*

Nagar Singh is placed in modern king-lists of Mewar after **Rahap**, the founder of the Rana branch of the Guhila house at **Sisoda**. The name itself does not appear in that form in the genealogies of the Rana line set down in fifteenth-century Mewar. Those genealogies give Rahapa's successors as **Narapati**, **Dinakara**, **Jasakarna**, **Nagapala** and others. The name Nagar Singh may be a later form of one of these, perhaps Nagapala, but this cannot be confirmed. If he belongs at this point, he lived in the **thirteenth century**, as a Rana of Sisoda rather than a king of all Mewar.

In that century the Ranas held their estate in the hills as kinsmen and vassals of the **Rawals**, who ruled Mewar from Nagda and then **Chittor**. It was a hard age. After Prithviraj Chauhan's defeat at Tarain in **1192**, the Delhi Sultanate became the great power of north India. In the reign of **Rawal Jaitrasimha**, in the 1220s or 1230s, an army of Sultan **Iltutmish** ravaged **Nagda**, and the Guhila capital moved to the safety of Chittor. The Ranas of Sisoda were bound to stand with their cousins in such wars, though no record names any battle fought by a Rana called Nagar Singh.

Modern lists name **Bharttripatta III** as his successor, but no ruler of that name is known in the Rana line; the Bhartripattas of the inscriptions were Guhila kings of earlier centuries. The line of Rahap continued, generation after generation, to **Lakshmasimha**, who died defending Chittor against Alauddin Khalji in 1303, and to **Hammir**, who won Mewar back around 1326 and made the Sisodias its rulers.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Rana of the Sisoda line.** Modern lists place him after Rahap, the founder of the Rana branch of the Guhilas.
- **An uncertain name.** He cannot be clearly matched with any name in the fifteenth-century genealogies of the Ranas.
- **A life in the Sultanate age.** His century saw Iltutmish's army ravage Nagda and the Guhila capital move to Chittor.
- **A link towards Hammir.** The line he belonged to led to Lakshmasimha and Hammir, who made the Sisodias rulers of Mewar.

bharttripatta-iii.name: Bharttripatta III
bharttripatta-iii.title: Guhil Ruler
bharttripatta-iii.period: Not attested; the known kings of the name ruled c. 800 CE and in the 10th century CE
bharttripatta-iii.significance: A name not found in the Guhila inscriptions; probably a repeated entry for Bhartripatta I or II
bharttripatta-iii.legacy: No reign can be confirmed for a third Bhartripatta; the name belongs to two real Guhila kings of the ninth and tenth centuries.
bharttripatta-iii.story:
## Bharttripatta III — a name at the edge of the record

*No third king named Bharttripatta (Bhartripatta) is found in the inscriptions of the Guhila dynasty. This short account explains what is known of the name and the age in which this archive places him.*

The name **Bhartripatta** belongs to the **Guhila** kings of Mewar, the house of Bappa Rawal that ruled from **Nagda**, **Ahar** and **Chittor** as servants of the lord **Ekalinga**. The great **Atpur inscription of 977 CE**, which lists the Guhila rulers in order from the founder Guhadatta, names two kings of this name. **Bhartripatta I** ruled around the turn of the ninth century, between Mattata and Simha. **Bhartripatta II**, a son of Khumman III, ruled in the middle of the tenth century; his queen, **Mahalakshmi**, came from the Rashtrakuta family, and their son **Allata** made **Ahar** a great centre of the kingdom.

A Bhartripatta III does not appear in these lists, nor in the later genealogies of Mewar. The name in this archive, placed between **Nagar Singh** and **Kshetra Singh II**, probably comes from a confused or repeated entry in a modern king-list, and no reign, date, deed or family can honestly be given to him. If he was a real person, he is most likely one of the two known Bhartripattas counted a second time.

What can be said is that the kings who bore this name ruled in a hard age. Between the eighth and tenth centuries Mewar lay between the great powers of the **Gurjara-Pratiharas**, the **Rashtrakutas** of the Deccan and, later, the **Paramaras** of Malwa. The Guhila kings kept their hill kingdom by alliance, marriage and the strength of their forts, and passed the line of Bappa Rawal on, generation after generation, to the Rawals and Ranas of later centuries.

## Highlights of his life

- **An unattested name.** No third Bhartripatta is found in the Atpur inscription or the later genealogies of Mewar.
- **Two real kings of the name.** Bhartripatta I ruled around 800 CE, and Bhartripatta II in the tenth century.
- **A Rashtrakuta alliance.** Bhartripatta II married the Rashtrakuta princess Mahalakshmi, mother of King Allata.
- **The Guhila tradition.** Every king of the name ruled as the *dewan* of Ekalinga, the true lord of Mewar.

kshetra-singh-ii.story:
## Kshetra Singh II — the son of Hammir who widened Mewar

*This archive lists two kings named Kshetra Singh. The first is the twelfth-century Guhila king Kshemasimha; this second is Maharana Kshetra Singh, also called Khetal or Khetsi, the son of Rana Hammir. His reign is known mainly from the genealogies and praise-inscriptions of later Sisodia kings and from the traditions of the bards, and few of its details can be checked. Where the story rests on tradition, it says so.*

Kshetra Singh was born into a house that had just risen from ruin. In **1303** the Delhi Sultan **Alauddin Khalji** had besieged and taken **Chittor**, and the last Rawal of the old Guhila line, **Ratnasimha**, had lost his kingdom. In that siege the Ranas of **Sisoda**, the junior branch of the Guhila house descended from Rahapa, had fought beside their kinsmen. Tradition says that **Rana Lakshmanasimha** of Sisoda and seven of his sons died defending the fort, among them **Arisimha**, whose young son **Hammir** survived. Chittor passed to a son of the Sultan, and later into the keeping of the **Songara Chauhan** chief **Maldeva** of Jalor, who held it for Delhi.

Hammir grew up in the hills, and as a young man he began to win back the country of his fathers piece by piece. The bards tell a famous story of how Maldeva, hoping to bind the young Rana to him, offered him his daughter in marriage, and how Hammir accepted even though the bride had been widowed young. The princess, the tale goes, helped her new husband win the loyalty of the garrison, and around **1326** Hammir took Chittor and made it once again the seat of Mewar. From this Rana of Sisoda the later Maharanas, the **Sisodias**, take their name and their line. Tradition says that Kshetra Singh was the son of this marriage, born to the Songara princess at a time when his father was still fighting to secure his throne.

He grew up, then, in a Chittor that had been won back but not made safe. The walls still bore the marks of the great siege. The temples of the fort were being restored, and the old nobles were returning to their estates. The Sultanate of Delhi under **Muhammad bin Tughluq** remained the strongest power of north India, and Mewar's tradition tells of a great battle at **Singoli** in which Hammir defeated a Tughluq army; historians have not been able to confirm it from the Delhi side, and it is best remembered as a claim of the bards. What is sure is that by the end of Hammir's long reign, Mewar was again a real kingdom, with Chittor at its heart and the shrine of **Eklingji** at its spiritual centre, where every Rana ruled as the *dewan* of the lord Ekalinga.

Kshetra Singh came to the throne around **1364**, on the death of his father. He took power in a changing world. **Firuz Shah Tughluq**, who ruled Delhi from 1351 to 1388, was a builder of canals and towns rather than a conqueror, and he did not press hard on the Rajput kingdoms. The great provinces of the Sultanate, among them Gujarat and Malwa, were drifting away from Delhi's control under their governors, though they would not become independent sultanates until after Kshetra Singh's death. Between these weakening powers lay open country, and the kings of Rajasthan moved to fill it.

The other Rajput houses of the region were also on the move in these years. The **Rathores**, still a clan of modest chiefs in the sandy country of Marwar, were building the strength that would carry them to **Mandore** before the century ended. The **Bhatis** held the desert around **Jaisalmer**, and the **Kachhwahas** of Amber were not yet a great power. Among them all, Mewar had the strongest claim to ancient dignity, for its kings traced their line through the Guhilas to Bappa Rawal and beyond, and the memory of Chittor's fall and recovery gave its rulers a fame that the bards carried far beyond their borders.

A Rana of this age ruled through his kinsmen. The great nobles of Mewar, most of them descended from earlier Ranas or from the old Guhila house, held their estates in return for service in war, and they gathered at Chittor with their horsemen whenever the Rana called. The Bhil chiefs of the southern and western hills, bound to the house since Bappa's time, guarded the forest passes. A ruler who wished to widen his kingdom needed the trust of these men above all, and a Rana who led them to victory and rewarded them with land could count on them for generations.

Kshetra Singh took that chance. Later Mewar tradition and inscriptions credit him with extending the kingdom far beyond the hills his father had won. He is said to have brought **Ajmer**, **Jahazpur** and **Mandalgarh** under Mewar's control, and the forested hill tract of **Chhappan** in the south. The details of these campaigns are not recorded, and some of these places changed hands many times in the following century. But the direction of his reign is clear: under him Mewar grew from a recovered fortress into a regional power reaching towards the plains of central Rajasthan. The praise-poems of his descendants also speak of victories over Muslim commanders on his borders; their names and the places of the battles cannot now be checked, and this story does not invent them.

His wars brought him into conflict with the **Hada Chauhans**, who had founded the kingdom of **Bundi** in the 1340s in the hills east of Mewar. Mandalgarh and the country around it lay between the two powers, and their quarrels were long and bitter. Tradition says that Kshetra Singh's death came out of this rivalry. The bards tell that he went to the Hada country around **1382**, some say to seek the hand of a Hada princess, and that at **Bambavda**, near Bundi, a dispute broke out between his men and those of the Hada chief, and the Rana was killed in the fighting. The story is told in more than one form, and its details are uncertain, but it is agreed that his reign ended in violence on the Bundi frontier.

One can imagine the news reaching Chittor: riders coming up the long ramp of the fort with dust on their clothes, the drums falling silent, the queens and nobles gathering in the palace to hear that the Rana would not return. Mewar had lost its king on a frontier he had pushed outward himself, and the kingdom now passed to a son who would have to hold everything his father had won.

Of his life at court even less is known. The Sisodia kings of his age continued the restoration of Chittor that Hammir had begun, and they kept faith with Eklingji, where the line of worship went back to Bappa Rawal. The bards remember Kshetra Singh as a bold and restless ruler, a warrior more than a builder. They also remember, without approval, a darker side of his household. Tradition says that he had two sons, **Chacha** and **Mera**, by a woman of humble birth outside his marriages. They were never counted as heirs, but they lived on at court, and in **1433** their resentment would end in the murder of his grandson, **Rana Mokal**, an event that opened the troubled first years of Rana Kumbha's reign.

His heir was his son **Lakshasimha**, remembered as **Rana Lakha**, who succeeded him around 1382. Lakha's reign brought the wealth that Kshetra Singh's conquests had prepared: silver and zinc were found at **Jawar**, south of the later site of Udaipur, and the treasury of Mewar grew rich. In Lakha's time, tradition says, a Banjara trader dug the lake of **Pichola**, which would one day reflect the palaces of Udaipur. Lakha's own marriage to the Rathore princess **Hansa Bai** of Mandore, and the famous renunciation of his eldest son **Chunda**, who gave up his right to the throne so that Hansa Bai's son Mokal might rule, belong to the story of the next reign.

From Kshetra Singh's line came Mokal, then **Rana Kumbha**, the builder of Kumbhalgarh, then **Rana Sanga**, and in time **Maharana Pratap**. In the long story of the Sisodias, Kshetra Singh stands in the second generation after the recovery of Chittor: the king who took the kingdom his father had won back and pushed its frontiers outwards, preparing the ground on which his great descendants would build.

## Highlights of his life

- **Son of Rana Hammir.** By tradition the son of Hammir and his Songara Chauhan queen, born as his father was rebuilding Mewar after the fall of Chittor in 1303.
- **Accession around 1364.** He succeeded Hammir as Rana of Mewar, ruling from the recovered fortress of Chittor.
- **Expansion of Mewar.** Tradition credits him with bringing Ajmer, Jahazpur, Mandalgarh and the Chhappan hills under Mewar's control.
- **Rivalry with the Hadas of Bundi.** His wars on the eastern frontier set Mewar against the Hada Chauhans.
- **Death at Bambavda (c. 1382).** Tradition says he was killed in a conflict with the Hada chief near Bundi.
- **Father of Rana Lakha.** His son Lakha inherited a larger, richer kingdom, and his line led on to Kumbha, Sanga and Pratap.

maharana-pratap.story:
## Maharana Pratap — the king who would not bow

*Maharana Pratap's life is unusually well recorded, in the Persian chronicles of Akbar's court, in the memoirs of men who fought against him, and in the bardic traditions of Mewar. Where the chronicles end and the legends begin, this story says so.*

Pratap was born, by the traditional reckoning of Mewar, on **9 May 1540**, in the fortress of **Kumbhalgarh**, high on the ridges of the Aravallis. The fort had been built a century earlier by his great ancestor Rana Kumbha, and in 1540 it was a refuge as much as a palace. His father, **Udai Singh II**, was then fighting to win back the throne of Mewar from the usurper Banbir, who had murdered Udai Singh's brother. The boy's mother was **Jaiwanta Bai**, a Songara Chauhan princess of Pali. Pratap was the eldest son, and the bards say that his birth came in the very year his father's fortunes turned, when Udai Singh retook Chittor and was seated firmly on the throne of his forefathers.

He grew up in a Mewar that remembered its glory and feared for its future. His grandfather, **Rana Sanga**, had been the strongest Hindu king of north India until his defeat by Babur at Khanwa in 1527. Chittor had been sacked by Bahadur Shah of Gujarat in 1535. The boy learned to ride and fight in the hills, and tradition says that he spent much of his youth among the **Bhils** of the forest, learning their paths and earning a trust that would one day save his kingdom. The Bhils called him *Kika*, a word for a little one, and the name stayed with him in the songs of the hills.

In 1567 the new Mughal emperor, **Akbar**, marched on Chittor. Udai Singh, on the advice of his council, withdrew into the hills, leaving the fortress in the care of **Jaimal Rathore** and **Patta Chundawat**. The siege lasted from October 1567 to **February 1568**. When the walls were breached, the women of the fort performed jauhar, the garrison went out to die, and Akbar ordered a massacre of the defenders and the people who had sheltered in the fort. Pratap, then a young man of twenty-seven, was not in Chittor; but the fall of the ancestral capital shaped everything he did afterwards. Udai Singh built a new seat in the valley he had already chosen, beside the lake that bears his name, and there the city of **Udaipur** began to grow.

Udai Singh died at **Gogunda** in **February 1572**. In his last years he had favoured **Jagmal**, his son by a younger queen, and named him heir. But the great nobles of Mewar would not accept him. Led by **Krishnadas Chundawat** and other chiefs, tradition says they took Jagmal by the arm as he sat on the throne and led him to a lower seat, and then placed Pratap on the gaddi at Gogunda on **28 February 1572**. Jagmal left in anger for Akbar's court, and later received the town of Jahazpur from the emperor. The quarrel showed the danger Pratap faced: a divided family, a lost capital, and an empire that was growing stronger every year.

By 1572 almost every great Rajput house had made terms with Akbar. The Kachhwahas of Amber had become his kinsmen by marriage, and Bikaner, Jaisalmer and Bundi had accepted his overlordship. Akbar wanted Mewar too, and he tried first with diplomacy. Over the next two years he sent four embassies to the new Rana: **Jalal Khan Qorchi**, then **Raja Man Singh** of Amber, then Man Singh's father **Bhagwant Das**, and finally **Raja Todar Mal**. Each was received with courtesy. Pratap even sent his son **Amar Singh** to Bhagwant Das as a mark of goodwill. But he would not go to court himself and bow before the emperor, and that was the one thing Akbar required. Later legend made the meeting with Man Singh a scene of insult at a feast; the chronicles only say that the talks failed.

War came in 1576. Akbar sent Man Singh, with **Asaf Khan** and a strong army, from Ajmer towards Gogunda. Pratap chose to meet them in the narrow country of the Aravallis, at the pass of **Haldighati**, named for the yellow, turmeric-coloured earth of its hills. On **18 June 1576** the armies met near **Khamnor**. Pratap's force was smaller, perhaps three thousand horse against Man Singh's five thousand or more, but it held men of every kind: the Sisodia chiefs, the old Tomar king **Ram Shah Tanwar** of Gwalior and his sons, the Afghan commander **Hakim Khan Sur** leading the vanguard, and the Bhils under **Rana Punja**, who guarded the hills on the flanks.

The first charge of the Mewar army drove the Mughal front back in confusion, and for a time it seemed that the day would be Pratap's. The historian **Badayuni**, who rode with the Mughal army, left a vivid account of the fighting and admitted the force of that charge. But the Mughal reserves held, and the imperial war elephants and the steadier Mughal line slowly turned the battle. Pratap himself fought in the thick of it. Tradition says he rode his horse **Chetak** straight at Man Singh's elephant and struck at the Raja with his lance, and that Chetak's leg was cut by the sword on the elephant's trunk.

As the Mughals closed around the wounded Rana, **Jhala Man**, the chief of Bari Sadri, took the royal umbrella and insignia upon himself, drew the enemy towards him, and died in Pratap's place. Ram Shah Tanwar and three of his sons fell in the same fight. Pratap escaped from the field. The legend that Chetak carried him across a stream on three legs and then died is told all over Rajasthan, and a memorial to the horse stands near Haldighati today. The chronicles agree that Pratap withdrew with much of his army intact, and that the Mughals, exhausted and wary of an ambush in the hills, did not pursue.

Haldighati was a defeat, but it was not the end. Man Singh occupied Gogunda, yet his army could find little food in a country whose people had fled to the hills, and Akbar was displeased with the result. In the autumn of 1576 the emperor himself came to Mewar and took Gogunda, Udaipur and the surrounding country. Over the next years he sent his commander **Shahbaz Khan** on three campaigns. In **1578** Shahbaz Khan captured Kumbhalgarh, Pratap's birthplace, after a hard siege. Pratap was driven from one stronghold to the next, and his family lived through years of hardship in the forests.

The bards remember this time with stories of hunger: of the Rana's children eating bread made from wild grass, of a wild cat snatching that bread from a child's hand, and of Pratap's resolve almost breaking. They also tell of letters exchanged with **Prithviraj Rathore** of Bikaner, a poet at Akbar's court, who reminded him in verse of his duty. These are beloved legends, not documented history, but they hold a real truth: the war was long, and the cost was paid by the whole family and the whole land.

What saved Mewar was the method Pratap now chose. He would not risk his men in open battle again. Instead, with the Bhils as his scouts and the hills as his fortress, he struck Mughal convoys and outposts and vanished. He forbade his people to cultivate the plains, so that the Mughal garrisons would find nothing to feed on. His minister **Bhamashah**, tradition says, brought him a great treasure at the darkest hour, enough to raise and pay an army again. In **1580** the Khan-i-Khanan **Abdul Rahim** was sent against him; a story told in Mewar says that Amar Singh captured the women of Rahim's household, and that Pratap ordered them returned with honour.

The turning point came at **Dewair** in **1582**. In a pass in the north of Mewar, Pratap and Amar Singh attacked the Mughal post commanded by **Sultan Khan**. Tradition says that Amar Singh drove his lance through Sultan Khan and his horse together. After Dewair, the Mughal outposts across Mewar fell one after another, and some thirty-six of them, the chronicles of Mewar say, were abandoned or taken. Kumbhalgarh was won back. In **1584** Akbar sent **Jagannath Kachhwaha** on one last major campaign, but after 1585 the emperor moved to Lahore to face the dangers of the north-west, and Mewar was largely left alone.

In those last twelve years Pratap rebuilt. He made **Chavand**, in the southern hills, his capital, and built there a palace and a temple to the goddess **Chamunda**. He recovered nearly all of Mewar, except **Chittor**, **Mandalgarh** and the country around them. Scholars and poets came to his court, among them **Chakrapani Mishra**, who wrote works on statecraft and ritual under his patronage, and the beginnings of the Chavand school of painting date from these years. The land that had been laid waste was resettled and farmed again.

Pratap never saw Chittor again. The bards say that he took a vow not to sleep on a bed, eat from gold or silver plates, or live in a palace of comfort until the old capital was free, and that for centuries afterwards the rulers of Mewar placed a leaf beneath their dishes and straw beneath their beds in memory of it. He died at Chavand on **19 January 1597**, aged fifty-six. Tradition says that his death followed an injury suffered while drawing a hard bow during a hunt. His *chhatri*, his memorial, stands at **Bandoli**, near Chavand, beside a small stream.

He was succeeded by his son **Amar Singh I**, who carried on the war for eighteen more years before making an honourable peace with Akbar's son Jahangir in 1615, on the condition that no Maharana would ever have to attend the Mughal court in person. Pratap's refusal had become the law of his house. In the centuries since, his name has stood across India for the right of a people to remain free, and the hills of Haldighati still remember the man the Bhils called Kika.

## Highlights of his life

- **Birth at Kumbhalgarh (1540).** Born to Udai Singh II and Jaiwanta Bai in the fortress built by Rana Kumbha.
- **Accession at Gogunda (1572).** The nobles of Mewar set aside Jagmal and crowned Pratap as Maharana.
- **Refusal of Akbar's embassies (1572–1573).** He received four Mughal envoys but would not attend the imperial court.
- **Haldighati (18 June 1576).** He led a smaller army against Man Singh; Jhala Man died in his place, and Pratap escaped to fight on.
- **The long hill war.** With the Bhils under Rana Punja and the support of Bhamashah, he wore down the Mughal garrisons from the forests.
- **Victory at Dewair (1582).** Pratap and Amar Singh broke the Mughal outposts, and he went on to recover most of Mewar.
- **Capital at Chavand.** He rebuilt the kingdom from Chavand, patronising scholars and building the temple of Chamunda.
- **Death at Chavand (1597).** He died undefeated in spirit, and his son Amar Singh I continued the struggle.

rana-kumbha.story:
## Rana Kumbha — the scholar-king who built in stone and song

*Rana Kumbha is known from his own inscriptions, above all the great praise-poem carved at Chittor in 1460, from the Sanskrit works written under his name, and from the Persian histories of his enemies in Malwa and Gujarat. Each side claimed victories the other denied; where the record is uncertain, this story says so.*

Kumbhakarna, whom history remembers as **Rana Kumbha**, was born in the early fifteenth century into the Sisodia house that had ruled Mewar from Chittor since Rana Hammir won the fortress back in the previous century. His father was **Rana Mokal**, and his grandfather was **Rana Lakha**, in whose reign silver had been found at Jawar and the treasury of Mewar had grown rich. His grandmother, **Hansa Bai**, was a Rathore princess of Mandore, and through her the Rathores had come to hold great influence at the court of Chittor.

The boy grew up in a court of learning. Mewar's princes were taught to ride and fight, but Kumbha was also taught Sanskrit, grammar, music and the sacred texts, and he loved them all his life. He was still young when disaster struck. In **1433**, while on campaign, Rana Mokal was murdered by **Chacha** and **Mera**, his own kinsmen, sons of an earlier Rana by a lesser wife. The killers fled into the hills, and the young Kumbha was placed on the throne of a kingdom suddenly in danger.

The man who restored order was **Rao Ranmal Rathore**, Hansa Bai's brother and Mokal's uncle. He hunted down the murderers and destroyed them. But Ranmal then made himself master of the court, filling the great offices with Rathores and pushing aside the Sisodia nobles. He brought about the death of **Raghavdev**, the respected brother of **Chunda**, the prince who had long ago given up his right to the throne and gone into exile in Malwa. The Sisodia chiefs began to fear that Mewar would become a Rathore possession.

In **1438** the matter was settled with violence. Ranmal was killed at Chittor by a plot of the Sisodia nobles, and his son **Jodha** fled for his life towards Marwar. Chunda, who had returned to Mewar, pursued him and occupied **Mandore** itself. For years Mandore was held by Mewar, until Jodha recovered it in 1453. In the end Kumbha made peace with him and fixed a boundary between their lands, and Jodha went on to found the city of **Jodhpur** in 1459. With the Rathore danger at court ended, Kumbha could rule in his own right.

His great enemy was the sultanate of **Malwa**, ruled from Mandu by the ambitious **Mahmud Khalji**. Malwa had given shelter to enemies of Mewar, and in **1437** Kumbha marched against it. Near **Sarangpur** he defeated the Sultan's army. The Chittor inscriptions say that Mahmud was taken prisoner and held at Chittor for some months before Kumbha released him without ransom, a gesture of royal generosity that the Rajput tradition loved to remember. The Malwa histories tell the story differently, and historians still argue about the details, but there is no doubt that Sarangpur was a great victory for Mewar.

Mahmud Khalji did not forget. In the 1440s he invaded Mewar again and again. He attacked Kumbhalgarh, marched on Chittor, and tried more than once to take the strong fort of **Mandalgarh**. Some of these campaigns did real damage, and both sides claimed success: Mahmud even built a tower of victory of his own at Mandu. But Mewar held its ground, and none of the Sultan's invasions broke the kingdom.

To the west lay the sultanate of **Gujarat**. When the ruler of **Nagaur**, **Firuz Khan**, died in the early 1450s, a struggle over the succession gave Kumbha a chance to intervene. He backed one claimant, then turned on him when the promised terms were broken, and around **1456** he took Nagaur by force. Gujarat answered with war. Sultan **Qutbuddin Ahmad Shah II** marched against Sirohi and Kumbhalgarh, and in **1456** he and Mahmud Khalji agreed, by the treaty of Champaner, to attack Mewar together and divide it between them. It was the gravest danger of Kumbha's reign. Yet the allied attacks of the following years failed to take the great forts, and Mewar survived the combined assault of its two neighbours.

Kumbha was also a ruler of the hills and frontiers. He brought the Hada chiefs of the Bundi country, the rulers of **Abu** and the princes of the south under his power, and he strengthened Mewar's border with a chain of fortresses. Tradition says that of the eighty-four forts that defended Mewar, thirty-two were built or rebuilt by him. He rebuilt the fort of **Achalgarh** on Mount Abu, strengthened Chittor, and raised new strongholds wherever an enemy might enter.

The greatest of them was **Kumbhalgarh**. Begun around **1443** and completed in **1458** under the architect **Mandan**, it rises more than a thousand metres above sea level on a ridge of the Aravallis. Its wall runs for about thirty-six kilometres over hill and valley, wide enough, it is said, for several horsemen to ride side by side. Inside it stood palaces, gardens, water tanks and dozens of temples. It was almost never taken by force. A popular legend says that the walls kept collapsing until a man offered himself as a sacrifice, and that a shrine marks the place where his head fell; this is a tale told by local people, not recorded history.

At Chittor he raised his most famous monument, the **Vijay Stambha**, the Tower of Victory. Built in the 1440s to celebrate his triumph over Mahmud Khalji, it rises nine storeys, about thirty-seven metres, and its walls are covered inside and out with sculptures of the gods of the Hindu world, each labelled with its name. Its architect was **Jaita**, working with his sons. The tower is often confused with the older **Kirti Stambha** nearby, a Jain tower of the twelfth century that Kumbha did not build.

Kumbha's reign also saw the building of the great Jain temple of **Ranakpur**, begun in **1437** by the merchant **Dharna Shah** under the king's patronage, with its forest of more than a thousand carved pillars. It is a sign of the confidence and wealth of Mewar in his time that such a temple could be built while its armies were at war.

Kumbha himself was a devotee of Vishnu as well as of Ekalinga, the lord whom every king of his house served as *dewan*. At Chittor he built up the temple now called **Kumbhashyam**, dedicated to Vishnu, and within Kumbhalgarh rose shrines to many gods. Yet he gave his patronage freely to the Jain merchants and monks of his kingdom, whose wealth and learning were part of Mewar's strength. Picture the Rana in the cool of an evening at Chittor: the drums of the temples sounding across the rock, the masons' scaffolding still standing around his tower, a court poet reading verses to him while the messengers of the frontier wait outside with news of the Sultan's armies. That was the double life of his reign, war on the borders and building at the centre, and he seems to have carried both with the same restless energy.

Above all, Kumbha was a scholar. Works on music under his name include the vast *Sangitaraja*, a treatise covering song, instrument and dance. He wrote the *Rasikapriya*, a commentary on Jayadeva's *Gita Govinda*, and works on the theory of music and drama are attributed to him. He patronised the architect Mandan, whose books on building are still studied, and his court was full of poets, scholars and craftsmen. The **Chittor prashasti of 1460**, the great Sanskrit inscription set up in his tower of victory and composed by the poets **Atri** and his son **Mahesha**, records his deeds and the genealogy of his house. A popular belief makes the saint-poet Mirabai his queen; she was in fact the wife of a grandson of Rana Sanga and lived in the following century.

The end of this great reign was dark. In his last years, tradition says, Kumbha suffered from a disturbance of the mind and withdrew from the business of the state. In **1468**, at Kumbhalgarh, he was murdered by his own son **Udaysimha**, known as **Uda**, who wanted the throne. Tradition says he was killed while at prayer at a shrine within the fort. Uda was shunned by the nobles of Mewar as a parricide, and within about five years his brother **Raimal** drove him out and took the throne. Raimal's son would be **Rana Sanga**.

Kumbha ruled for thirty-five years. He found Mewar shaken by murder and the ambitions of its neighbours, and left it the strongest kingdom of Rajasthan, ringed by forts and adorned with towers, temples and books. His grandsons would fight the Lodis and the Mughals from the fortresses he raised, and the walls of Kumbhalgarh, the birthplace of Maharana Pratap, still climb over the hills he chose.

## Highlights of his life

- **Accession in crisis (1433).** He came to the throne after the murder of his father, Rana Mokal, and freed the court from Rathore domination in 1438.
- **Victory at Sarangpur (1437).** He defeated Mahmud Khalji of Malwa; Mewar's inscriptions say the Sultan was captured and later released.
- **Survival against Malwa and Gujarat.** He held off repeated invasions, including the combined attack planned by the two sultans in 1456.
- **Capture of Nagaur (c. 1456).** He took Nagaur during its succession struggle, extending Mewar's power to the north-west.
- **Builder of Kumbhalgarh (c. 1443–1458).** He raised the great hill fortress with its thirty-six-kilometre wall, and many other forts of Mewar.
- **The Vijay Stambha.** He built the Tower of Victory at Chittor to celebrate his triumph over Malwa.
- **Scholar-king.** He wrote or sponsored the *Sangitaraja* and a commentary on the *Gita Govinda*, and patronised Mandan and the builders of Ranakpur.
- **Death at Kumbhalgarh (1468).** He was murdered by his son Uda, whose brother Raimal soon took the throne.

rana-sanga.story:
## Rana Sanga — the scarred king who challenged Babur

*Rana Sanga's life is known from the chronicles of Mewar and the bards of Rajasthan, from the Persian histories of the sultanates he fought, and from the memoirs of his last great enemy, Babur. Where the bardic tales go beyond the record, this story says so.*

**Sangram Singh**, remembered by everyone as **Rana Sanga**, was born in **1482**, a son of **Rana Raimal** of Mewar and a grandson of the great builder-king **Rana Kumbha**. His father had taken the throne after driving out Kumbha's murderer, his own brother Uda, and Mewar under Raimal was a strong kingdom, guarded by the forts that Kumbha had built. But the court was full of ambitious princes, and Sanga was not the eldest. His brothers **Prithviraj** and **Jaimal** were bold, quarrelsome young men, and each of the three believed he deserved the throne.

The bards tell how the rivalry broke into open violence. The three brothers, they say, went to a Charan priestess of the goddess to ask which of them would rule, and when she declared for Sanga, Prithviraj drew his sword in fury. In the fight that followed Sanga lost the sight of one eye. Wounded and in danger of his life, he fled from Mewar. For a time, tradition says, he lived in disguise, and took service with **Karmachand Panwar**, a chief of the Ajmer country, as an ordinary soldier, until his bearing and courage gave away his birth.

Fate removed his rivals one by one. Jaimal was killed in a quarrel far from home, and Prithviraj, a famous and reckless warrior, died of poison given to him, tradition says, by his own brother-in-law of Sirohi. Sanga was recalled as heir, and when Raimal died in **1508**, he became Rana of Mewar. He was about twenty-six years old, already marked by war, and determined to make Mewar the first power of north India.

The moment was favourable. The sultanate of Delhi under the Lodis was weakening, Malwa was torn by quarrels among its nobles, and Gujarat was busy with its own wars. Sanga brought the Rajput chiefs of the region together under his leadership, through marriage, friendship and the force of his reputation. The houses of Marwar, Amber, Gwalior, Ajmer, Chanderi and many others came to follow him in war. His Persian enemies recognised him as the greatest of the Rajput rulers of his time.

His first great contest was with Malwa. When the nobles of Malwa rose against **Sultan Mahmud Khalji II**, the Rajput minister **Medini Rai** gained great power at Mandu, and when the Sultan turned against him, Medini Rai turned to Sanga. Medini Rai held **Chanderi** and the country around it under Mewar's protection. In **1519** Mahmud marched against him, and at **Gagron** Sanga met the Sultan's army and defeated it. Mahmud himself was wounded and taken prisoner. Sanga treated him with honour, had his wounds cared for, and later released him, keeping a pledge of loyalty and territory in return, an echo of what Mewar remembered of Kumbha's victory at Sarangpur.

To the west, Sanga fought **Gujarat** over the small kingdom of **Idar**. Two Rathore princes claimed its throne, Gujarat backed one and Sanga the other, a prince who had found refuge at Chittor and was betrothed to Sanga's daughter. The quarrel grew into a war. Around **1517** Sanga marched into Gujarat, placed his candidate on the throne of Idar, and raided as far as Ahmednagar in Gujarat, carrying off rich plunder. Gujarat answered with a great expedition against Mewar in the following years, but Sanga's forts and his alliance held.

To the north stood the Lodi sultans of Delhi. **Ibrahim Lodi**, who came to the throne in 1517, tried to check Sanga's rise. At **Khatoli**, near the border of the Delhi sultanate, around **1517**, the armies met, and the Rajputs won. In that battle, tradition says, Sanga lost an arm to a sword stroke and was lamed in one leg by an arrow. Another clash came near **Dholpur** soon after, and again Sanga prevailed and extended his power towards the Chambal and Bayana. The bards say that he won eighteen pitched battles against the sultans of Delhi and Malwa, and that his body carried the scars of eighty wounds. The numbers are poetic, but the picture is true. With one eye, one arm and a crippled leg, the Rana still led his armies from the front.

Then, in **1526**, everything changed. **Babur**, the Timurid prince of Kabul, invaded India and destroyed the army of Ibrahim Lodi at **Panipat** on 21 April, killing the Sultan. Delhi and Agra fell to him. Babur later wrote in his memoirs that Sanga had sent him word promising to attack Ibrahim from the other side, and accused him of failing to keep his word; Rajput tradition remembers the matter differently, and the truth of those early messages cannot now be known. What is clear is that after Panipat, Sanga saw a foreign conqueror in the place where the weakened Lodis had been, and he decided to drive him out before he could take root.

Sanga gathered the greatest Rajput army of the age. With him came the Rajput chiefs of Marwar, Amber, Vagad, Chanderi and Merta, and with him too came Afghans who had lost everything at Panipat: **Hasan Khan Mewati** of Alwar and **Mahmud Lodi**, a brother of Ibrahim, who hoped to recover his family's throne. Early in **1527** Sanga's advance guard defeated a Mughal force near **Bayana**, and fear spread through Babur's camp. Babur wrote that his men were disheartened. He answered by breaking his wine cups, renouncing drink, and calling his army to holy war.

On **16 March 1527** the two armies met at **Khanwa**, near Fatehpur Sikri. Babur fought as he had at Panipat: a line of carts chained together protected his matchlockmen and his cannon, with cavalry on the flanks ready to wheel around the enemy. Sanga's horsemen charged again and again into the guns. For hours the battle hung in the balance, and the Rajput attacks pressed hard on Babur's right. But the cannon and the turning cavalry wore them down. In the midst of the fighting Sanga was struck by an arrow and fell unconscious. His companions carried him from the field, and **Ajja Jhala** took the royal insignia so that the army would not know its leader had fallen. Without him, the Rajput army broke. Among the dead were **Rawal Udai Singh** of Vagad, **Hasan Khan Mewati** and many chiefs of Mewar and Marwar.

Babur's victory was complete. He took the title of **Ghazi**, and, as he himself recorded, raised a tower of the heads of the slain on a hill near the field, as the Timurid conquerors before him had done. Rajput tradition remembers the defeat with bitterness, and tells that **Silhadi**, the chief of Raisen, deserted to Babur in the course of the battle and weakened Sanga's line; the story is widely told, but historians are divided on whether it is true. What is certain is that Babur's guns and his disciplined tactics, still new to the warfare of north India, had broken an army of horsemen that would have swept any other foe from the field. The victory secured the Mughal hold on Delhi and Agra far more firmly than Panipat had done.

Sanga woke far from the battlefield and was told that the day was lost. Tradition says he swore that he would not return to Chittor until he had defeated Babur. Within months he was raising a new army. In January 1528 Babur marched against Chanderi, still held by Medini Rai, and Sanga moved to help his old ally. He never reached him. At **Kalpi**, on **30 January 1528**, Rana Sanga died. Tradition says that he was poisoned by his own nobles, who feared another war that they believed could not be won. He was about forty-six years old.

He left a powerful widow, **Rani Karnavati**, a Hada princess of Bundi, and several sons. His son **Ratan Singh II** succeeded him, followed by **Vikramaditya**, and then by **Udai Singh II**, the father of Maharana Pratap. Through his son **Bhoj Raj**, who died before him, Sanga was also the father-in-law of the saint-poet **Mirabai**, whose devotion to Krishna made the court of Chittor famous in another way.

Khanwa ended the hope that a Rajput king would rule from Delhi, and opened the way for the Mughal empire. Yet even Babur, in his memoirs, wrote of Sanga with respect, saying that he had risen to his greatness by his own valour and sword. In Rajasthan he is remembered as **Hindupat**, the champion of the Hindu kings of his age, a warrior who gave an eye, an arm and finally his life to a cause he would not abandon.

## Highlights of his life

- **Exile and return.** Wounded and driven out by his brothers' rivalry, he lived in disguise before returning as heir and becoming Rana in 1508.
- **Leader of the Rajput chiefs.** He gathered the Rajput houses of north and central India under his leadership, making Mewar the strongest power in the region.
- **Victory at Gagron (1519).** He defeated and captured Sultan Mahmud Khalji II of Malwa, and released him with honour.
- **War with Gujarat over Idar (c. 1517).** He placed his candidate on the throne of Idar and raided deep into Gujarat.
- **Victories over Ibrahim Lodi.** At Khatoli and Dholpur he defeated the Sultan of Delhi, losing an arm and the use of a leg in the fighting.
- **Khanwa (16 March 1527).** He led a great Rajput and Afghan alliance against Babur, and was carried wounded from the field when the battle was lost.
- **Death at Kalpi (1528).** He died while marching to fight Babur again, poisoned, tradition says, by his own nobles.

khuman-i.story:
## Khuman I — the son who kept Bappa's kingdom

*Khuman I (Khummana) is known only from his place in the Guhila genealogies and from the traditions of Mewar. This short account gives what can be said with confidence.*

Khuman I, written **Khummana** in the inscriptions, was a king of the **Guhila** dynasty of Mewar in the **eighth century**. The **Atpur inscription of 977 CE**, which lists the Guhila kings in order, names him directly after **Kalabhoja**, the ruler whom many scholars identify with **Bappa Rawal**. Mewar's tradition agrees, remembering him as Bappa's son and successor, and gives his reign as about **753 to 773 CE**. These dates are traditional rather than recorded, but they place him in the generation after the founder.

He inherited a young kingdom. Bappa had won **Chittor** and bound the hill country around **Nagda** and the shrine of **Eklingji** to the Guhila house, with the loyalty of the Bhil chiefs as one of its foundations. Tradition says that Bappa gave up the throne for the life of an ascetic, and Khuman's task was to show that the kingdom could outlive the man who had made it. He ruled, as every king of his line would, as the *dewan*, the servant, of Ekalinga.

No record names his battles, his queens, or his buildings, and the wars and campaigns credited to him in some modern lists cannot be confirmed. His years were a time of rebuilding in western India. The Umayyad raids from Sindh had been broken in 739, and the **Gurjara-Pratiharas** were rising into the great power of Rajasthan and Malwa. Small kingdoms like Mewar had to keep their footing beside them. That the Guhila line passed safely from Khuman to his successor **Mattata**, and on through the generations, is the clearest sign that he did so.

His name lived on. A later king, **Khuman II**, carried it again, and the bards made *Khuman* a title of honour for the rulers of Mewar, celebrated in the *Khuman Raso*.

## Highlights of his life

- **Successor of Bappa Rawal.** The Atpur inscription names him after Kalabhoja, and Mewar's tradition calls him Bappa's son.
- **Keeper of a young kingdom.** He held Chittor and the Nagda country in the generation after the founder.
- **Servant of Ekalinga.** Like every king of his house, he ruled as the *dewan* of the lord of Eklingji.
- **A name that became a title.** The name Khuman was borne by later kings and became an honoured title for the rulers of Mewar.
