hammir-singh.story:
## Hammir Singh — the lion of the hard passes who brought Chittor home

*Hammir's life comes to us through the inscriptions of his descendants, above all those of Rana Kumbha, through Kumbha's commentary Rasikapriya, and through the bardic chronicles of Mewar gathered centuries later. The inscriptions remember him as a victorious king; the bards fill in the story of his youth and his return. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

In the first years of the fourteenth century, the house of Bappa Rawal came close to vanishing from the earth. In **1303 CE** the Delhi Sultan **Alauddin Khalji** laid siege to **Chittor**, the great rock fortress that had been the heart of Mewar for centuries. The siege lasted for months. When it ended, the ruler **Rawal Ratan Singh** was dead or lost, the women of the fort had chosen the fire of *jauhar*, and the fortress belonged to Delhi. Alauddin renamed it **Khizrabad** after his son **Khizr Khan** and left it in his hands.

Among those who fell in those years were the men of a junior branch of the Guhila house, the lords of **Sisoda**, a village in the hills to the north-west of Chittor. Mewar's tradition says that **Lakshman Singh** of Sisoda died defending the fort together with many of his sons. One of those sons was **Ari Singh**. And Ari Singh, the bards say, had left behind a small boy named **Hammir**.

The bards tell a gentle story about the boy's mother. Ari Singh, they say, was out hunting one day near a village in the hills when a wild boar broke through a field of millet. A young woman of the Chandana Rajputs, working on a raised platform in the field, struck the beast down with a single stone from her sling before the prince could reach it. Ari Singh asked her father for her hand, and from that marriage Hammir was born. The tale cannot be checked, but it says something the bards wanted remembered: that the restorer of Mewar grew up not in a palace but among the farming people of the hills.

So the boy grew up in the years when Chittor was a Sultanate garrison. He learned to ride and to use the bow in the rough country of the Aravallis, the region of narrow passes, thorn forest and hidden valleys that would always be Mewar's refuge in bad times. The surviving Sisodia and Guhila retainers gathered around him. Tradition remembers that his uncle **Ajay Singh**, who now led the Sisoda family, recognised the boy's courage and chose him as the heir of the branch over his own sons.

Meanwhile Delhi's grip on Chittor loosened. Holding a distant hill fortress surrounded by hostile country was expensive and dangerous. Within a few years Alauddin gave Chittor to a Rajput ally, **Maldeo**, a **Songara Chauhan** chief related to the house of **Jalore**, who held it as a vassal of the Sultan. Alauddin himself died in **1316**, and Delhi entered a time of murder and confusion until the **Tughluq** dynasty took power in **1320**. In all these years the Sisodias kept up a quiet war from the hills, raiding the lands around the fort and waiting.

The bards tell how Chittor was finally won back, and their story is one of the most famous in Mewar. Maldeo, they say, wished to make peace with the troublesome young chief of the hills, and offered Hammir his daughter in marriage. Hammir's companions warned him that it was a trap, but he went. At the wedding, the bride told her new husband the truth: she had already been married as a child and widowed, and her father had given her away to shame the Sisodia prince. Instead of anger, the story says, the two found trust. She told Hammir she would help him win back the fort of his ancestors. When their son was born, she took the child to Chittor to visit her family, and through her the gates were opened to Hammir's men.

Historians treat the details of this tale with caution. What is certain is that around **1326 CE**, after the death of Maldeo, Hammir took Chittor from his successors and made it the seat of his family once again. More than two decades after the great siege, the fort was back in the hands of Bappa Rawal's descendants.

This return changed the dynasty itself. The old main line of the Guhilas, who had ruled as **Rawals**, had been broken in 1303. Hammir belonged to the Sisoda branch, whose chiefs bore the title **Rana**. From his time onward, the rulers of Mewar were the **Sisodias**, and they kept the title Rana, later Maharana, until the end of princely rule in the twentieth century. Every later Maharana, from Kumbha and Sanga to Pratap, descended from Hammir.

Winning Chittor was one thing; keeping it was another. The new Tughluq Sultan, **Muhammad bin Tughluq**, who came to the throne in **1325**, ruled the largest empire Delhi had ever held, and he could not be expected to accept the loss of the fortress quietly. Mewar's tradition tells of a great battle at **Singoli**, in which Hammir defeated an army sent from Delhi, captured the Sultan himself, and held him prisoner for three months until he paid a heavy ransom, including lands such as **Ajmer**, **Ranthambhor** and **Nagaur**.

This is the most famous claim about Hammir, and the place where history and legend clearly part ways. No Persian chronicle of the Sultanate mentions such a defeat or the capture of a Sultan, and Muhammad bin Tughluq was never anyone's prisoner. Most historians believe the bards have built a great story on a smaller truth. What the inscriptions do show is that Hammir fought hard and successfully against Muslim commanders in the region and kept Chittor against them. The inscriptions of his great-great-grandson Kumbha praise him as having defeated Muslim armies, and give him a proud title: **Vishamaghati Panchanana**, "the lion of the hard passes", a name that remembers exactly the kind of war he fought, in the narrow valleys of the Aravallis where a small army could stop a great one.

The times were in his favour. Muhammad bin Tughluq's reign was full of rebellions, failed projects and costly campaigns, and by the 1330s and 1340s province after province was breaking away from Delhi. A Sultan fighting rebels in the Deccan, Bengal and Gujarat had little strength to spare for a hill kingdom in Rajasthan. Hammir used these years well. He brought back under his rule the chiefs who had scattered after 1303, won the loyalty of the Bhils of the hills as Bappa had done, and steadily widened the territory of Mewar around Chittor.

Mewar's chronicles describe Hammir as a strong and fair ruler who restored order to a land that had suffered years of war. Fields that had been abandoned were farmed again, and travellers and traders returned to the roads below the fort. He rebuilt what he could of the damaged fortress and its shrines.

He was also a devout man. Tradition links him with the goddess, and the temple of **Annapurna** inside Chittor fort is traditionally credited to him; the bards say he honoured a local goddess of the Charans, **Barbadi**, who had blessed his enterprise. Like every ruler of his line, he governed in the name of **Ekalinga**, the lord of Mewar, and counted himself as Shiva's *dewan*, the servant who rules on the god's behalf.

Hammir's reign was long. He ruled for close to four decades, and when he died around **1364 CE** he left behind a kingdom very different from the scattered hill holdings of his youth. Chittor was secure, the Sisodia line was firmly established, and Mewar was once again one of the leading powers of Rajasthan. He was succeeded by his son **Kshetra Singh**, often called **Rana Kheta**, who continued to expand the state, fighting the rulers of Malwa and the neighbouring chiefs.

Later generations never forgot what Hammir had done. When Mewar's greatest builder, Rana Kumbha, recorded the history of his family on the walls of Kumbhalgarh and in the verses of his books, he placed Hammir at the beginning of the line's revival, the man who had taken a fallen house and set it upright again. The story of the boy from the hills who brought Chittor home became one of the foundation stories of Mewar, told and retold for six hundred years.

## Highlights of his life

- **A childhood in the hills.** Born into the Sisoda branch of the Guhilas, he grew up after the fall of Chittor in 1303, when his grandfather Lakshman Singh and father Ari Singh had died in its defence.
- **Recovery of Chittor (c. 1326 CE).** He took the fortress back from the successors of the Songara chief Maldeo, returning it to Bappa Rawal's descendants after more than two decades.
- **Founder of the Sisodia line of rulers.** From his reign the rulers of Mewar were Sisodias who bore the title Rana; every later Maharana descended from him.
- **"Lion of the hard passes."** Kumbha's inscriptions praise him as Vishamaghati Panchanana, a victor over Muslim armies in the passes of the Aravallis.
- **The legend of Singoli.** Mewar's bards say he defeated and captured Muhammad bin Tughluq; no Sultanate source records this, and historians regard the capture as legend.
- **Restorer of the kingdom.** He gathered the scattered chiefs, won over the Bhils, rebuilt the fort's shrines and widened Mewar's lands.
- **A long reign.** He ruled for nearly four decades and died around 1364 CE, succeeded by his son Kshetra Singh.

udai-singh-ii.story:
## Udai Singh II — the prince saved by a nurse's sacrifice, who built a city by the lake

*Udai Singh's life is recorded in the Mughal histories of Akbar's reign, above all Abul Fazl's Akbarnama, and in the chronicles and bardic traditions of Mewar. The Mughal sources tell of his wars; the traditions of Mewar keep the stories of his childhood and of the founding of Udaipur. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

**Udai Singh** was born in **1522**, the son of the greatest warrior-king of his age, **Rana Sanga** of Mewar, and of **Rani Karnavati**, a princess of the Hada Chauhans of **Bundi**. He was a younger son, far from the throne, and the world he was born into was about to break apart. In **1527**, when he was a small child, his father led the Rajput confederacy against **Babur** at **Khanwa** and was defeated. Sanga died in **1528**, and Mewar's long age of greatness began to crumble.

Udai's elder half-brother **Ratan Singh II** ruled for a few years and was killed in a quarrel in 1531. The throne passed to Udai's full brother **Vikramaditya**, a young, harsh and quarrelsome ruler who drove many nobles away from the court. Mewar's enemies saw their chance. In **1535** **Bahadur Shah**, the Sultan of Gujarat, besieged Chittor with a powerful army and artillery. Karnavati led the defence of the fort while her young sons were sent to safety at Bundi, her own family's home. When the walls could no longer hold, the Rajput defenders rode out to die, and the women of Chittor, with Karnavati among them, entered the fire of the second great *jauhar*. Udai Singh was about thirteen. He had lost his father, and now he lost his mother.

Bahadur Shah did not hold Chittor for long. The Mughal emperor **Humayun** attacked Gujarat, and Vikramaditya returned to the fort. But the danger now came from inside. **Banbir**, a son of Sanga's brother Prithviraj by a woman of lower birth, had gained great power at court. In **1536** he murdered Vikramaditya, and then, Mewar's tradition says, went through the dark palace with his sword to kill the last true heir: the boy Udai Singh.

What happened that night is the most famous story in Mewar. The boy's nurse, **Panna Dai**, a woman of the Gujar community who had raised him, heard the cries from the royal quarters and understood what was coming. She hid Udai in a fruit basket and had a trusted servant carry him out of the fort. In the prince's bed she laid her own son, **Chandan**, of the same age. When Banbir burst in and demanded to know where the heir was, Panna pointed silently to the bed, and watched her own child die. The story has been told for nearly five hundred years, and it remains the purest image of loyalty that Rajasthan knows.

Panna then slipped away herself and carried the prince from one place of refuge to another. Several chiefs, fearing Banbir, would not take them in. At last they reached **Kumbhalgarh**, the great mountain fortress built by Rana Kumbha, whose keeper was **Asha Shah Depura**, a Jain official. Tradition says Asha Shah's mother rebuked her son when he hesitated, telling him that a servant of Mewar does not count the cost of loyalty. Asha Shah sheltered the boy, and passed him off at first as his own nephew while the nobles of Mewar were quietly told the truth.

One by one, the chiefs who hated Banbir came to Kumbhalgarh. Around **1537** Udai Singh was crowned there. Over the next three years his supporters gathered strength. In **1540** his army defeated Banbir's forces near **Mavli**, and Udai Singh entered Chittor as Rana. Banbir fled and disappeared from history.

That same year brought joy to the young ruler's household. His wife **Jaiwanta Bai**, a Songara Chauhan princess, gave birth on **9 May 1540**, at Kumbhalgarh, to a son named **Pratap**. Udai Singh would have many wives and more than twenty sons, but it was this first-born who would become the most famous of all the Maharanas.

The 1540s were the years of the Afghan **Sher Shah Suri**, who drove Humayun out of India. In **1544**, after defeating the Rathores of Marwar, Sher Shah turned towards Mewar. Udai Singh, whose kingdom was still weak after years of war, judged that he could not fight him. He sent the keys of Chittor to Sher Shah as a sign of submission. Sher Shah accepted, posted an officer in the fort, and left Mewar largely to itself. It was a cautious decision, and later writers have criticised Udai Singh for it, but it preserved his kingdom. Sher Shah died the next year.

The following years were spent in the ordinary struggles of Rajput kings: contests with neighbours, quarrels among the nobles, and shifting alliances. In **1557** Udai Singh fought the Afghan commander **Haji Khan**, who was supported by **Rao Maldeo** of Marwar, at **Harmada**, and was defeated. Meanwhile a much greater power was rising in the north. Humayun had returned to Delhi in 1555, and after his death in 1556 his young son **Akbar** set out to build an empire that would cover all of northern India.

It was in these years that Udai Singh carried out the work for which he is best remembered. The plains around Chittor were open to invasion, and Udai Singh saw that his family needed a refuge deep in the hills. Tradition says that while hunting in the valley around the **Pichola** lake, among the Aravalli hills, he met a holy man meditating on a hilltop, who blessed him and told him that a city built in this place would never be easily taken. Around **1559** Udai Singh began building there. The new city was named **Udaipur** after him, and the first parts of the great **City Palace** rose on the ridge above the lake.

He also built water works for the dry land of Mewar. To the east of the new city he raised a great dam across the Berach river, creating **Udai Sagar**, one of the largest lakes of the region, completed in the 1560s. Lakes, wells and stepwells were the lifeblood of Mewar's farming, and Udai Singh's lake served his people for centuries.

The clash with Akbar came soon. Udai Singh gave refuge to **Baz Bahadur**, the Sultan of Malwa, after Akbar's armies drove him out in 1562, and he refused to come to the Mughal court as other Rajput rulers had begun to do. Mewar's tradition adds that his son **Shakti Singh**, who had quarrelled with his father and gone to Akbar's camp, overheard the Emperor's plans and rode home to warn him. In **October 1567** Akbar himself marched on Chittor with a large army, siege engineers and artillery.

Udai Singh now made the most debated decision of his life. On the advice of his council, he did not stay to defend the fort himself. He withdrew with his family and his treasury into the hills to the west, around **Gogunda** and Udaipur, so that the royal line could not be destroyed in one siege. The defence of Chittor was entrusted to **Jaimal Rathore** of Merta and **Patta Sisodia** of Kelwa, with about eight thousand Rajputs.

The siege lasted four months. Akbar's men dug trenches, laid mines under the walls and built a covered approach towards the fort. The Rajputs defended every breach with great courage. One night in **February 1568** Akbar, firing his musket at a figure directing repairs on the wall, killed Jaimal. The fort's last hope went with him. The women of Chittor performed the third *jauhar*, and on **23 February 1568** the defenders rode out to their deaths. Akbar, angered by the long resistance, ordered a massacre, and Abul Fazl records that around thirty thousand people were killed. Chittor, the capital of Bappa Rawal's descendants for more than eight hundred years, never again became the seat of Mewar.

Some writers, starting with the colonial historian James Tod, have judged Udai Singh harshly for leaving the fort, comparing him unfavourably with his father and his son. Modern historians are kinder. By leaving, he saved the dynasty, the treasury and the army, and made sure that Mewar could go on fighting from the hills. The policy of retreating into the mountains and continuing the struggle from there, which his son Pratap would follow so famously, began with him.

Udai Singh spent his last years in the hills, ruling from Gogunda and his new city of Udaipur. Mewar had lost Chittor and the eastern plains, but the heart of the kingdom remained free, and the Rana never went to the Mughal court. He died at **Gogunda** on **28 February 1572**. Before his death he had named as his heir **Jagmal**, his son by his favourite queen **Dhir Bai Bhatiyani**. But the leading nobles of Mewar would not accept him. Gathering at Gogunda after the funeral, they set Jagmal aside and placed Pratap, the eldest son, on the throne.

Udai Singh is often overshadowed by the father before him and the son after him. Yet the boy who survived because of a nurse's terrible sacrifice lived to save his kingdom twice, from Banbir and from Akbar, and to give Mewar the city that would be its capital for the next four centuries.

## Highlights of his life

- **Saved by Panna Dai (1536).** When Banbir murdered Vikramaditya, his nurse Panna Dai put her own son in his place and carried him to safety at Kumbhalgarh.
- **Crowned at Kumbhalgarh and recovery of Chittor.** Crowned around 1537 with the help of Asha Shah Depura, he defeated Banbir and entered Chittor in 1540.
- **Father of Maharana Pratap.** His eldest son Pratap was born to Jaiwanta Bai at Kumbhalgarh on 9 May 1540.
- **Founder of Udaipur (c. 1559).** He began the city and the City Palace beside Lake Pichola, which became the capital of Mewar.
- **Builder of Udai Sagar.** He dammed the Berach river to create one of the largest lakes of the region.
- **Siege of Chittor (1567–1568).** He withdrew to the hills and left the fort to Jaimal and Patta; Chittor fell to Akbar on 23 February 1568.
- **The policy of the hills.** His retreat preserved the dynasty and began Mewar's long resistance from the Aravallis. He died at Gogunda on 28 February 1572.

amar-singh-i.story:
## Amar Singh I — the son of Pratap who fought for eighteen years and made an honourable peace

*Amar Singh's reign is described both in the Mughal sources, above all the memoirs of the Emperor Jahangir, and in the chronicles of Mewar such as the Amar Kavya and the later bardic histories. The two sides tell the same war from opposite banks; where they differ, or where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

**Amar Singh** was born on **16 March 1559** at **Chittor**, the first son of **Pratap Singh** and his chief queen **Ajabde Punwar**. His grandfather **Udai Singh II** still ruled Mewar from the ancient fortress, and the new city of **Udaipur** was only beginning to rise beside Lake Pichola. Amar was a child of eight when everything changed. In 1567 the Mughal Emperor **Akbar** marched on Chittor, and the royal family withdrew into the hills. In February 1568 the fort fell. Amar would grow up in a Mewar that had lost its old capital and would spend the rest of the century fighting to keep the rest.

His boyhood was spent in the camps and hill towns of the Aravallis, at Gogunda, Kumbhalgarh and Udaipur. In 1572 his grandfather died, and his father became **Maharana Pratap**. Amar was thirteen. From then on he lived in the shadow of the long war between his father and the Mughal Empire. He was a young man of seventeen in **1576**, the year of **Haldighati**, when Pratap's army met the Mughal force under **Raja Man Singh** of Amber. Mewar's traditions place Amar in the campaigns of the years that followed, when Pratap's men retreated into the hills, cut Mughal supply lines and slowly won back much of the country.

There is a story, told in many versions, about the hardest of those years, when the royal family lived in the forests and sometimes went hungry. Tradition says that a wild cat once snatched a piece of bread made from grass seed out of the hands of one of Pratap's children, and that the father's heart nearly broke. Whatever its truth, the story reminds us what Amar's youth was like: not a prince's life of palaces, but years of hardship, movement and constant danger.

The bards also tell a quieter story of Amar's character. During one campaign, they say, Amar captured the women of the household of the Mughal general **Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan**, the poet-statesman of Akbar's court. Pratap rebuked his son and ordered that the women be returned with honour, and Rahim never forgot the courtesy. The story may be legend, but it is how Mewar wished its princes to behave.

By the late 1580s Pratap had won back most of Mewar apart from Chittor and the area around Mandalgarh, and he built a new capital at **Chavand** in the southern hills. It was there, on **19 January 1597**, that Pratap died, and Amar Singh, now thirty-seven, became Maharana of Mewar. He inherited his father's war, his father's nobles, and the duty never to bow before the Mughal throne.

Akbar did not leave the new Maharana in peace for long. In **1599** he sent an army under his eldest son, Prince **Salim**, with Raja Man Singh, to subdue Mewar. Amar Singh fell back into the hills and harassed the Mughal posts. Salim showed little interest in the campaign and soon left it to rebel against his own father. In these years Amar Singh's forces attacked and took several Mughal outposts. The best known of these fights is the attack on the fort of **Unthala**, and around it the bards built one of Mewar's most famous stories. Two great clans of Mewar's nobility, the **Chundawats** and the **Shaktawats**, quarrelled over who had the right to lead the vanguard. Amar Singh, the story says, declared that the honour would go to whichever clan first entered Unthala. The Shaktawat chief **Ballu** tried to break the gate with an elephant, which would not charge into the spikes; Ballu pressed his own body against the spikes and ordered the elephant forward. The Chundawat leader **Jait Singh**, already wounded on the wall, ordered his men to cut off his head and throw it over the wall, so that the Chundawats would be inside first. Whether every detail is true or not, the tale has been told for four centuries as a picture of Mewar's fierce pride.

In **1605** Akbar died, and Prince Salim became Emperor as **Jahangir**. The new Emperor was determined to finish what his father had left undone. In **1605–06** he sent an army under his son Prince **Parviz**. Mewar's chronicles describe a great victory for Amar Singh at **Dewair** in these years, in the same pass where Pratap had once won; the Mughal sources describe the campaign as indecisive. Either way, Parviz achieved little. In 1608 Jahangir sent **Mahabat Khan**, and then, from 1609, **Abdullah Khan**, who pressed hard into the hills and fought several engagements against the Rajputs. Commander followed commander: Raja **Basu** of Mau, and later **Mirza Aziz Koka**. Each campaign burned villages and destroyed crops, and each time Amar Singh's men melted into the hills and returned when the Mughals left.

Yet the war was slowly exhausting Mewar. Pratap had fought one long war; Amar Singh fought another for almost two decades, against an empire far richer and stronger than in his father's day. The fields of Mewar lay waste, the people fled from the plains, and the nobles had lost brothers and sons in every year of fighting.

In **1613** Jahangir moved his court to **Ajmer** to direct the war himself, and sent his ablest son, Prince **Khurram**, the future **Shah Jahan**, into Mewar with a very large army. Khurram did not chase Amar Singh through the hills. Instead he placed garrisons across the country, cut the Rajputs off from food and supplies, and drove the people out of the valleys. By the end of 1614 Mewar was close to ruin.

Amar Singh now faced the hardest choice any Maharana had faced. Some of his nobles wished to fight on whatever the cost. Others, and his son and heir **Karan Singh** among them, argued that the land and its people could not survive more war, and that an honourable peace was possible. After long debate the Maharana sent envoys, **Shubh Karan** and **Haridas Jhala**, to Khurram. Jahangir, eager to end the war and to win honour by bringing Mewar to terms, offered generous conditions.

The treaty was settled early in **1615**. Amar Singh accepted the Emperor as overlord, but on terms no other Rajput ruler had received. The Maharana himself would never have to appear at the Mughal court; his heir would go in his place. Mewar would not have to give a daughter in marriage to the imperial family. **Chittor** and the lands of Mewar taken by the Mughals would be returned, though the fort was not to be repaired or rebuilt. Amar Singh met Khurram briefly, and soon afterwards Karan Singh went to Ajmer, where Jahangir received him with great honour. Jahangir was so pleased that he had marble statues of Amar Singh and Karan Singh made and set up in the palace garden at Agra, below the window where he appeared to his people.

For Amar Singh himself, the peace was bitter. Tradition says that the man who had fought for eighteen years felt the treaty as a deep personal grief, even though it saved his kingdom. He handed most of the work of government to Karan Singh, withdrew from public life, and spent his last years largely in retirement at Udaipur, which once more became the capital of Mewar.

Amar Singh's reign was not only war. At **Chavand**, the wartime capital, painters working at his court produced the **Chavand Ragamala** of **1605**, one of the earliest dated works of the Mewar school of painting, made by the painter **Nisardi**. Out of the hardships of his reign came the beginnings of the rich artistic tradition that later Maharanas would develop in Udaipur. Amar Singh also honoured the temples and religious institutions of his kingdom, and like all his line ruled as the *dewan* of **Ekalinga**.

He died at Udaipur on **26 January 1620**. His cenotaph at **Ahar**, outside the city, was among the first of the great royal memorials there, where the rulers of Mewar were cremated for generations afterwards. He was succeeded by **Karan Singh II**, who used the peace to rebuild the country his father had defended.

History has often judged Amar Singh in his father's shadow. But for eighteen years he held out against the full power of the Mughal Empire at its height, and when he finally made peace he did so on terms that kept Mewar's pride and spared its people. The treaty of 1615 gave Mewar a special place among the Rajput states that it kept for the rest of the Mughal age.

## Highlights of his life

- **A childhood of war.** Born at Chittor on 16 March 1559, he was eight when the fort fell to Akbar, and grew up in his father Pratap's hill campaigns.
- **Maharana at Chavand (1597).** He succeeded Pratap on 19 January 1597 and continued the war against the Mughals.
- **Resistance to two emperors.** He held out against campaigns sent by Akbar and Jahangir under Salim, Parviz, Mahabat Khan, Abdullah Khan and others for nearly two decades.
- **Unthala and Dewair.** Mewar's tradition remembers the storming of Unthala and a victory at Dewair as high points of his war.
- **The treaty of 1615.** Under Khurram's pressure he made peace with Jahangir on unique terms: no personal attendance at court, no marriage alliance, and the return of Chittor.
- **Patron of the Mewar school.** The Chavand Ragamala of 1605, painted at his court, is one of the earliest dated Mewar paintings.
- **Death and memorial.** He died at Udaipur on 26 January 1620; his cenotaph at Ahar stands among the royal memorials of Mewar.

lakha-singh.story:
## Rana Lakha — the builder of a rich Mewar and the father who lost his heir to a jest

*Rana Lakha's reign is known mainly from the later inscriptions of his descendants, especially those of Rana Kumbha, and from the chronicles and bardic traditions of Mewar, which James Tod gathered in the nineteenth century. Few documents survive from his own time, so many details of his life are tradition. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

**Lakha**, also written **Laksha Singh** or **Lakshasimha**, was born in the middle of the fourteenth century into the house that **Hammir Singh** had raised up from ruin. His grandfather Hammir had won back **Chittor** around 1326 and made the **Sisodias** the rulers of Mewar. His father, **Kshetra Singh**, known in the chronicles as **Rana Kheta**, came to the throne around 1364 and spent his reign widening the borders his father had secured, fighting the neighbouring chiefs and the governors who ruled Malwa for the Delhi Sultanate.

Lakha grew up as the heir of a kingdom on the rise. The great fortress of Chittor was again a royal seat, its walls repaired and its temples once more in use. The young prince was trained, as all Rajput heirs were, in riding, archery and the sword, and in the duties of a ruler who governed in the name of **Ekalinga**, the lord Shiva of Mewar. Tradition says that his father was killed around **1382** in a feud with the Hada Chauhans, the clan that held the hill country of Bundi to the east, and that Lakha then became Rana of Mewar.

He came to power at a fortunate time. The Delhi Sultanate, which had once taken Chittor, was growing weaker. **Firuz Shah Tughluq**, the last strong Sultan of his line, died in **1388**, and after him came a decade of quarrels over the throne. In **1398** the Central Asian conqueror **Timur** sacked Delhi, and after that blow the Sultanate never recovered its old power. Its distant provinces became independent kingdoms: **Gujarat** under **Zafar Khan**, who took the title of Sultan in **1407**, and **Malwa** under **Dilawar Khan** around **1401**. Even **Nagaur**, on Mewar's northern border, passed into the hands of an independent Muslim ruling family. For Mewar this meant that the great enemy in the north was gone, but that new and ambitious neighbours were rising on every side.

Lakha used these years to make his kingdom strong. Mewar's chronicles describe him as a ruler who fought to secure his borders, and they remember especially his campaigns in the rugged country to the north-east of Chittor, where the **Mer** tribes held the hills. Tradition says that he subdued the Mers and took the area around **Badnore**, bringing new land under Mewar's control. Other traditions credit him with victories over neighbouring chiefs and the Sultanate's commanders, but the details are uncertain, and the chronicles of his own time do not survive to confirm them.

What his descendants remembered most clearly was not war but wealth. In Lakha's reign, Mewar's tradition says, rich deposits of silver and lead were opened at **Zawar**, in the hills south of the later city of Udaipur. Mining at Zawar is very ancient, and the region was also one of the world's earliest centres of zinc smelting; but it was in Lakha's time that the mines became a great source of royal income. The silver of Zawar filled the treasury of Chittor.

Lakha spent that wealth on rebuilding. Mewar had never fully recovered from the siege of 1303, when Alauddin Khalji's army had broken temples and palaces in the fort. Tradition credits Lakha with repairing many of these buildings and with raising new temples, palaces and water works. The chronicles name him as a patron of Brahmins and pilgrims, and as a ruler who gave generously to the shrines of his kingdom.

One of the most lasting works of his age was not built by the Rana himself. Tradition says that during Lakha's reign a **Banjara**, one of the travelling grain traders who moved with their bullock trains across Rajasthan, built a dam across a stream in the valley of the village of **Picholi**, to water his cattle and hold the rains. The lake that formed behind it was named **Pichola**. Nearly two centuries later, **Udai Singh II** would build his new capital, Udaipur, on its shore.

Tradition also tells of a journey of faith. The bards say that Lakha led an expedition to **Gaya**, the holy city in the east where Hindus perform rites for their ancestors, because pilgrims there were being forced to pay a heavy tax. They say that he won freedom from the tax for the pilgrims of his time. This story cannot be confirmed from other sources, but it shows how Mewar remembered him: as a protector of the faith whose reach went far beyond his own hills.

The best-known story of Lakha's life, though, is a story of his household, and it shaped the history of Mewar for generations. Lakha's eldest son was **Chunda**, a brave and capable young man whom everyone expected to be the next Rana. One day, the bards tell, a coconut arrived at the court of Chittor from **Rao Chunda Rathore** of **Mandore**, the ruler of Marwar, carried by his son **Ranmal**. In Rajput custom the coconut was a formal offer of marriage, and it was meant for the heir: the Rathore princess **Hansa Bai** was offered to Prince Chunda.

Prince Chunda was away when the envoys arrived. The old Rana, the story says, looked at the coconut and laughed. "I suppose," he said, stroking his grey beard, "that this is not meant for an old man like me." It was a joke, the kind of thing a father says lightly in his own hall. But when Chunda returned and heard of it, he refused the marriage. A coconut his father had joked about in that way, he said, could only be for his father now.

The Rathores were offended, and refusing the alliance would have been an insult to Marwar. Ranmal then agreed that his sister could marry Lakha himself, but he set a hard condition. A son born to Hansa Bai, he said, would be only a younger son with no hope of the throne, unless Chunda gave up his right of succession. Chunda, the story says, gave that promise at once and without hesitation. He swore before the court that the son of Hansa Bai would be Rana of Mewar, and that he himself would serve that brother as a loyal noble.

So Lakha married Hansa Bai, and in time she bore him a son, **Mokal**. Chunda kept his vow. For his sacrifice, the chronicles say, he and his descendants were given the first place among the nobles of Mewar and the right to set his mark beside the Rana's on royal grants, and the right to lead the vanguard in war. His descendants, the **Chundawats**, became the most powerful noble clan of Mewar. Later writers often called Chunda the **Bhishma of Mewar**, after the prince of the Mahabharata who gave up his throne for the sake of his father's marriage.

The story is told in the chronicles, and historians accept its core: that Chunda, the eldest son, stood aside so that Mokal, the son of the Rathore queen, could become Rana. Its consequences were real and serious. The Rathore alliance brought Ranmal and his followers into the life of Chittor, and in the next reign their influence would bring both help and great danger to Mewar.

Lakha's last years were spent at the head of a prosperous and respected kingdom. Mewar was stronger and richer than it had been at any time since 1303, and its rulers were once again counted among the leading powers of Rajasthan. Lakha died around **1421**. His son Mokal was still a boy, and it was Chunda, faithful to his promise, who placed his young half-brother on the throne and stood beside him as guardian of the kingdom.

Lakha's reign is often overshadowed by the more famous rulers who came after him, above all his grandson **Rana Kumbha**. But the foundations of Kumbha's great age were laid in Lakha's time: the treasury filled by the mines of Zawar, the buildings restored after a century of damage, the borders pushed outward, and a Mewar once again able to face its neighbours with confidence.

## Highlights of his life

- **Heir to Hammir's revival.** Son of Rana Kshetra Singh and grandson of Hammir, he became Rana around 1382 and continued the rise of the Sisodias.
- **Secure borders.** Tradition credits him with subduing the Mer tribes and adding the region around Badnore to Mewar.
- **The mines of Zawar.** In his reign, tradition says, the silver and lead mines of Zawar became a great source of royal wealth.
- **Rebuilding Mewar.** He used that wealth to restore temples and palaces damaged since the siege of 1303 and to build new ones.
- **The lake of Pichola.** Tradition says the lake was made in his reign by a Banjara grain trader; Udaipur was later built on its shore.
- **The coconut and Chunda's vow.** A jest over a marriage offer from Mandore led his eldest son Chunda to give up the throne, so that Hansa Bai's son Mokal became heir.
- **A strong kingdom left behind.** He died around 1421, leaving a rich and stable Mewar that prepared the way for the age of Kumbha.

mokal-singh.story:
## Rana Mokal — the boy king of a brother's sacrifice, struck down on the road to war

*Rana Mokal's reign is known from inscriptions set up in his own time, above all the Chittor inscription of 1428 at the temple of Samadhishvara, from the later inscriptions of his son Kumbha, and from the chronicles and bardic traditions of Mewar. The inscriptions give us his buildings and his wars; the bards give us the story of his court. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

**Mokal** was born in the early years of the fifteenth century, the son of **Rana Lakha** of Mewar and of his Rathore queen **Hansa Bai**, a princess of **Mandore** in Marwar. He was born a younger son, and by every rule of Rajput custom he should never have ruled. His eldest half-brother, **Chunda**, was the heir to the throne. But Mokal's life had been shaped before he was born, by a coconut and a jest.

The bards tell that when Hansa Bai's family first sent a marriage offer to Chittor, it was meant for Chunda. The old Rana joked that such a gift could not be for a greybeard like himself, and Chunda, hearing of it, refused to accept a bride his father had spoken of in that way. To save the alliance with Marwar, Lakha married Hansa Bai himself, and Chunda swore that her son would inherit Mewar in his place. Mokal was that son. He grew up in the palaces of **Chittor** as the chosen heir of a kingdom, knowing that his elder brother had given up a crown for him.

Rana Lakha died around **1421**, when Mokal was still a boy, perhaps about twelve years old. Chunda kept his vow faithfully. He placed his young half-brother on the throne, bowed before him as the first of his nobles, and governed the kingdom as regent in the boy's name. For a time Mewar was ruled by one of the most honourable arrangements in its history: a man who could have been king serving a child who had become king because of him.

The arrangement did not last. Hansa Bai, the queen mother, did not trust Chunda. The chronicles say that she suspected him of wanting the throne after all, and that she accused him of plotting against her son. Chunda, deeply hurt, would not stay where his loyalty was doubted. He left Mewar with his followers and went to **Mandu**, the capital of the Sultanate of **Malwa**, where Sultan **Hoshang Shah** received him with honour. He left behind his younger brother **Raghudev** to watch over the boy king.

Into the space that Chunda left came the queen's brother, **Ranmal Rathore**. A great warrior and an ambitious man, Ranmal came to Chittor with his Rathore followers and soon held the real power at court. Rathores took important posts in the fort and the kingdom, and Mewar's own nobles grew uneasy. For the time being, however, Ranmal served his nephew well. He was a skilled commander, and with Rathore help Mewar's armies were strong.

As Mokal grew into a young man, he began to rule in his own right. He came to power in a dangerous neighbourhood. To the south-west, the Sultans of **Gujarat** were building a strong kingdom under **Ahmad Shah**, the founder of Ahmedabad. To the south-east, the Sultans of **Malwa** were powerful and ambitious. To the north lay **Nagaur**, held by a Muslim ruling family related to the Gujarat Sultans, whose lands touched Mewar's borders. Each of them was a threat, and each of them watched the young Rana carefully.

The inscriptions of Mokal's own reign speak of his wars with pride. They credit him with a victory over **Firuz Khan**, the ruler of **Nagaur**, and with campaigns to the north towards **Sambhar**, the old Chauhan country of the salt lake. Later inscriptions of his son praise him as a ruler who humbled the Muslim rulers around him. As with all royal inscriptions, the language is the language of praise, and the battles are not described in detail. But they show that the young Rana was an active and successful soldier, and that under him Mewar held its own against its strong neighbours.

Mokal is remembered even more for what he built and for the learning he supported. The most lasting record of his reign stands in Chittor itself. In **1428** he restored the old temple of Shiva known as **Samadhishvara**, on the southern part of the fort, and set up a long inscription in Sanskrit verse there, recording the history of his family and his own good deeds. The temple is still sometimes called the temple of **Mokalji** after him. The inscription of 1428 is one of the most important sources for the history of the Guhila and Sisodia rulers, and it shows a court where poets and scholars were honoured.

Tradition credits Mokal with other works too. He is said to have built and repaired temples, gates and water works in Chittor and in the country around **Eklingji**, the shrine of the lord of Mewar. Like every ruler of his line, he governed in the name of **Ekalinga** and counted himself the god's servant. Under him, the craftsmen and sculptors whose skills would make his son's reign so brilliant were already at work. The great age of **Rana Kumbha**, with its temples, forts and books, did not begin from nothing. It began in the court of Mokal.

Mokal's family grew in these years. His queen **Saubhagya Devi**, a princess of the Paramara line, bore him a son, **Kumbha**, who would become the greatest builder and one of the greatest warriors in Mewar's history. Mokal had other sons as well, but it was Kumbha who was raised as heir.

Danger, though, was gathering around the Rana from inside his own family. His grandfather **Rana Kshetra Singh** had left sons by a woman of humble birth, **Chacha** and **Mera**, who had been raised at court but could never hope to inherit. Mokal's uncles by blood, they held positions of trust in his household. The chronicles say that they nursed a bitter resentment over their low standing, and that they found an ally in **Mahpa Panwar**, a noble of the court.

In **1433** news came that **Ahmad Shah** of Gujarat was moving with an army towards the southern frontier of Mewar. Mokal gathered his forces and marched out to meet him. On the way, the army camped at **Jilwara**, in the hill country south of Chittor. Tradition tells a bitter story of what happened there. Mokal, it says, pointed to a tree and asked Chacha and Mera what it was called. To the brothers the question seemed a cruel taunt about their mother's humble caste, as if only men of low birth would know the names of the common trees of the village, and in front of the assembled nobles the insult burned. Whether that was really the spark or not, Chacha and Mera, with Mahpa Panwar, attacked the Rana in his camp and killed him.

Mokal was still a young man, perhaps in his middle twenties. His reign had lasted about twelve years. The murder shocked Mewar. The army that had marched out against Gujarat did not fight the Sultan; it broke up in confusion, and the murderers fled into the hills. Ahmad Shah, for his part, did not press into Mewar's heartland.

The nobles placed Mokal's young son Kumbha on the throne. Ranmal Rathore, the uncle of the murdered Rana, took up the duty of revenge. With Kumbha's support he hunted down Chacha and Mera in the hills where they had taken refuge, and killed them. Mahpa Panwar escaped to Mandu. Later, when Ranmal's own power grew too great, Chunda would return from Malwa to protect Kumbha against him, and Mewar's story would turn again.

Mokal's life was short and its end was violent, but its place in Mewar's history is secure. He was the boy for whom an elder brother gave up a throne, the young ruler who held Mewar firm against strong neighbours, the patron who restored the temple of Samadhishvara and left one of the most precious inscriptions of the dynasty, and the father of Rana Kumbha.

## Highlights of his life

- **The son of a promise.** Born to Rana Lakha and Hansa Bai of Mandore, he became heir because his elder brother Chunda gave up the throne.
- **A boy king (c. 1421).** He came to the throne as a child, with Chunda as his regent until the queen mother's suspicion drove Chunda away to Malwa.
- **Ranmal at court.** His uncle Ranmal Rathore became the power behind the throne and a strong commander for Mewar.
- **Wars with his neighbours.** Inscriptions credit him with a victory over Firuz Khan of Nagaur and with campaigns towards Sambhar.
- **Restorer of Samadhishvara (1428).** He rebuilt the Shiva temple at Chittor and set up the Sanskrit inscription that is a key source for Mewar's history.
- **Father of Rana Kumbha.** His court and patronage prepared the way for his son's great age of building and learning.
- **Murdered at Jilwara (1433).** On the march against Ahmad Shah of Gujarat, he was killed in his camp by his uncles Chacha and Mera with Mahpa Panwar.

rana-raimal.name: Rana Raimal
rana-raimal.title: Avenger of Kumbha - Rana Raimal
rana-raimal.significance: Overthrew his brother Uda, Kumbha's murderer; defended Mewar against Malwa and rebuilt the Eklingji temple
rana-raimal.ancestry: Sisodia branch of the Guhilas; son of Rana Kumbha
rana-raimal.legacy: Rana Raimal kept Mewar united and prepared the way for the great age of Rana Sanga.
rana-raimal.story:
## Rana Raimal — the son who avenged Kumbha and rebuilt the house of Ekalinga

*Rana Raimal's reign is recorded in the inscriptions of his own time, above all the great Eklingji inscription of 1488, and in the chronicles and bardic traditions of Mewar, which preserve the story of his family's quarrels. The inscriptions speak in the language of royal praise; the bards add drama and prophecy. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

**Raimal** was a son of **Rana Kumbha**, the greatest builder and one of the greatest warriors in the history of Mewar. He grew up in the most brilliant court Mewar had ever known. In the years of his boyhood his father raised the walls of **Kumbhalgarh** on a mountaintop, set up the **Vijay Stambh**, the Tower of Victory, at **Chittor**, saw the great Jain temple at **Ranakpur** rise under his patronage, and wrote books on music and poetry. Kumbha fought the Sultans of **Malwa** and **Gujarat** for decades and held his kingdom against them both. To be his son was to grow up among architects, poets, musicians and soldiers, and to learn from childhood what a great Rana looked like.

That world ended in murder. In **1468** Kumbha was killed at Kumbhalgarh, and the killer was his own son, Raimal's brother **Udai Singh**, remembered in Mewar as **Uda**. Mewar's tradition says that in his last years Kumbha was troubled by illness of the mind, and that Uda struck him down while he sat at prayer. Whatever the full story, the crime filled Mewar with horror. The bards would never call Uda by his name without adding the word *hatyara*, the murderer.

Uda took the throne, but he could not hold the loyalty of the nobles. To buy support from his neighbours, the chronicles say, he gave away lands that Kumbha had won: territory around **Sambhar** and **Ajmer** to **Rao Jodha** of Marwar, and **Abu** to the Deora Chauhans of Sirohi. The nobles of Mewar grew more angry each year. Raimal, meanwhile, was living away from the court. Tradition says that he had taken refuge at **Idar**, in the hills on the borders of Gujarat, where he had family ties by marriage.

The leading nobles of Mewar sent for him. Around **1473** Raimal returned with his followers, and the chiefs of Mewar gathered under his banner. The chronicles describe several battles between the two brothers, at places such as **Jawar**, **Darimpur** and **Pangarh**, in which Raimal's forces defeated Uda's. Uda fled from Mewar. Raimal entered Chittor and was crowned Rana. The murder of Kumbha had been avenged, and the throne was in the hands of a son the nobles could trust.

Uda went to **Mandu**, the capital of Malwa, to seek help from Sultan **Ghiyath Shah Khalji**, the old enemy of his father. Tradition says that he offered his own daughter to the Sultan in return for an army to win back Mewar, and that as he left the Sultan's presence he was struck by lightning and killed. The bards saw it as the judgement of heaven on a parricide. Whether or not the lightning story is literally true, Uda disappears from history at this point.

Raimal's first years were spent in restoring order. The kingdom had been shaken by the murder and the civil war that followed, and some of the lands Uda had given away were lost for good. The new Rana had to win back the confidence of the nobles, punish those who had supported the murderer, and keep Mewar's powerful neighbours from taking advantage of its weakness.

The most dangerous of those neighbours was Malwa. Ghiyath Shah, despite his reputation as a ruler who preferred his palace and his large household of women to the battlefield, sent his armies against Mewar. Uda's sons, **Sahasmal** and **Surajmal**, came with the Malwa forces, hoping to win their father's throne. Mewar's inscriptions and chronicles record that Raimal defeated these attacks and drove the Malwa army back, and the Eklingji inscription of 1488 praises him as a victor over the Sultan of Malwa. As with all such inscriptions, the language is proud and the details are few, but it is clear that under Raimal Mewar held its frontier against Malwa and kept its independence.

Raimal is remembered above all as a builder of shrines. The temple of **Eklingji**, near Nagda, the seat of Mewar's true lord, had been damaged in the wars of the fifteenth century. Raimal rebuilt it on a grand scale, and much of the temple that stands today, with its great tower and its four-faced image of Shiva, is his work. In **1488** he set up a long inscription there in Sanskrit verse, recording the history of the Guhila and Sisodia rulers from Bappa Rawal to his own time. The Eklingji inscription of Raimal is one of the most important sources for Mewar's history. By rebuilding the shrine, Raimal renewed the bond on which the whole dynasty rested: the Rana as the *dewan*, the servant, of Ekalinga.

His family shared in this work. His queen **Shringar Devi**, a princess of the Rathores of Marwar, built a great stepwell at **Ghosundi**, near Chittor, and her inscription there, dated **1504**, records her gifts and her husband's line. Wells and stepwells were the lifeblood of the dry country, and royal women of Rajasthan often built them as acts of piety.

Raimal's own household, however, was troubled. He had many sons, and three of them were men of great ability and great ambition: **Prithviraj**, the eldest, **Jaimal**, and **Sangram Singh**, who would become famous as **Rana Sanga**. The quarrels among these brothers fill the bardic histories of Raimal's reign.

The bards tell a famous story about how the quarrel began. The three princes, wishing to know which of them would one day rule, went together to the shrine of a Charan priestess at **Nahar Magra**, a holy woman believed to have the gift of prophecy. When she spoke, she said that it was Sangram who would rule Mewar. Prithviraj, hot-tempered and proud, drew his sword and attacked his younger brother on the spot. In the struggle Sangram was wounded and lost the sight of one eye. The tale may have grown in the telling, but it is certain that Sanga lost an eye in his youth and that he fled from the court in fear of his brothers.

Sangram, tradition says, found shelter with a Rathore warrior named **Bida** at **Sevantri**, who defended him against his pursuers and was killed protecting him. Afterwards the prince lived for years in hiding, serving under other chiefs, without revealing who he was.

The other two brothers met tragic ends. Jaimal, the bards say, went to the court of the Solanki chief **Rao Surtan**, who had lost his town of **Toda** to Afghan invaders, and sought the hand of his daughter **Tara Bai**, famed for her beauty and courage. He behaved so insolently that Rao Surtan killed him. When Raimal heard what had happened, he did not seek revenge, saying that his son had earned his death by his own conduct.

Prithviraj, a bold and restless warrior known as **Udna Prithviraj**, "Prithviraj the swift", then won Tara Bai's hand by promising to recover Toda for her father, and the bards say he kept his promise in a daring night attack. He was the hero of many adventures in the songs of Mewar. But his end was sad. His sister had been married to **Jagmal**, the ruler of **Sirohi**, who treated her badly. Prithviraj rode to Sirohi and forced his brother-in-law to promise better behaviour. Jagmal pretended friendship, but tradition says he gave Prithviraj poisoned sweets as he left, and the prince died near **Kumbhalgarh**, within sight of the fortress his grandfather had built. Tara Bai, the bards say, followed him onto the funeral pyre.

So the old Rana lost two of his sons, and the third was living as a fugitive. In his last years Raimal sent for Sangram, the son the prophecy had named. Sanga came home and was recognised as heir. When Raimal died in **1509**, after a reign of about thirty-six years, Sangram Singh succeeded him as **Rana Sanga**.

Raimal's reign is often seen only as the bridge between two giants, his father Kumbha and his son Sanga. But it was a bridge that had to be built. He took a kingdom shamed by a father's murder and torn by civil war, avenged the crime, defended the borders against Malwa, restored the temple of Ekalinga, and handed on to his son a Mewar strong enough for Sanga to make it, for a time, the leading power of northern India.

## Highlights of his life

- **Son of Rana Kumbha.** He grew up in the court of Mewar's greatest builder and warrior king.
- **Avenger of his father (c. 1473).** After Kumbha's murder by Uda in 1468, the nobles called Raimal back from Idar; he defeated Uda in several battles and took the throne.
- **Defender against Malwa.** He repulsed attacks from Ghiyath Shah's Malwa, which came with Uda's sons in its train.
- **Rebuilder of Eklingji.** Much of the present temple of Eklingji is his work, and his inscription of 1488 is a key source for Mewar's history.
- **A family of builders.** His queen Shringar Devi built the stepwell at Ghosundi, recorded in an inscription of 1504.
- **Father of Rana Sanga.** The quarrels of his sons Prithviraj, Jaimal and Sangram fill Mewar's legends; Sangram survived to become his heir.
- **A long reign.** He ruled for about thirty-six years and died in 1509, succeeded by Rana Sanga.

udai-singh-i.name: Udai Singh I
udai-singh-i.title: The Interval after Kumbha - Udai Singh I
udai-singh-i.significance: Seized Mewar's throne by killing his father Rana Kumbha; overthrown by his brother Raimal
udai-singh-i.legacy: Remembered in Mewar as Uda Hatyara, Uda the murderer. His brief, unloved reign weakened Mewar until Raimal restored the kingdom.
udai-singh-i.story:
## Udai Singh I — the prince who killed a great king and lost a kingdom

*What we know of Udai Singh I, remembered in Mewar as Uda, comes mostly from the later chronicles of Mewar and Marwar, the bardic tradition, and the history James Tod gathered from them in the nineteenth century. The outline of his reign is accepted; many of its details are tradition, and where they are, this story says so.*

In the middle of the fifteenth century, Mewar stood at the height of its medieval power. Its ruler was **Rana Kumbha**, who had come to the throne in **1433** after the murder of his own father, Rana Mokal. Kumbha had spent thirty-five years making Mewar the strongest kingdom of Rajasthan. He fought the sultans of Malwa and Gujarat again and again and held his ground against both. He raised the **Vijay Stambh**, the tower of victory at Chittor, and built the great fortress of **Kumbhalgarh** high in the Aravallis, with walls that wind for miles across the ridges. He was a scholar as well as a soldier, a writer on music and a patron of temples, poets and architects. Under him, Chittor was the proudest court in western India.

Udai Singh, whom the chronicles mostly call **Uda** or Udaykaran, was one of Kumbha's sons. Nothing certain is known of his birth or of his mother. He grew up in a court of victories, among nobles who had ridden with his father against the sultans, in the shadow of towers and temples that carried his father's name. Like every prince of his house, he would have been trained in arms and horsemanship and in the duties owed to **Eklingji**, the lord whom the rulers of Mewar served as *dewan*.

Kumbha had several sons, and the question of who would follow him was not settled. Another son, **Raimal**, is said by tradition to have fallen out with his father and to have been living away from Mewar, at **Idar** in the hills to the south-west. Uda remained close to the centre of power. The chronicles suggest that he was impatient for the throne. Some later traditions add that Kumbha, in his last years, had become troubled in mind and difficult to serve, and that this unsettled the court. How much of this is true cannot be known. What is remembered is what happened next.

In **1468**, at Kumbhalgarh, Uda killed his father. Tradition says that the old Rana was struck down while at prayer, near a temple within the fortress he had built. The man who had survived three decades of war with the sultans died by the hand of his own son. In a land where loyalty to one's father and one's lord stood at the very centre of Rajput honour, no crime could have been worse. Mewar never forgave it. In its memory, the new ruler would be known for ever as **Uda Hatyara**, Uda the murderer.

Uda took the throne, but he could not take the loyalty of the kingdom. The great nobles of Mewar, the chiefs of the clans who had fought beside Kumbha, turned away from him. Many withdrew to their own estates. Some refused to attend his court. A Rana of Mewar depended on these men for his armies, and without them his power was hollow. Uda sat on the throne of Chittor, but around him there was silence.

To buy the support he could not command, Uda began to give away the lands his father had won. The chronicles say he offered territory to neighbouring rulers in return for their friendship. Tradition holds that **Abu** went to the Deora Chauhans of Sirohi, and that **Ajmer** and **Sambhar** passed to **Rao Jodha** of Marwar, the founder of Jodhpur. Historians treat these grants with caution, as the details come from later accounts, but they agree on the meaning: the kingdom Kumbha had enlarged was being broken up to keep his murderer in power. Each grant made the nobles of Mewar more bitter.

The bards describe these five years as a time of shame and unease. Chittor was still a great fortress, its temples still full of worship, but the court was hollow. Old warriors refused to sit in the hall where the Rana held audience. Messages passed quietly between the estates of the nobles and the hills of Idar, where Raimal waited. In their verses, the poets imagine the ghosts of Kumbha's battles watching from the walls, but the truth was simpler: a kingdom cannot be held by a man whom its own warriors will not follow.

At last the nobles acted. They sent for Raimal and declared for him as the rightful heir. Raimal came out of Idar and gathered an army from the clans who had refused Uda. The chronicles speak of battles between the two brothers' forces, at **Jawar** and at **Darimpur** among other places, and in each Raimal's side prevailed. Uda, losing men and ground, fell back on Chittor. Raimal's army followed, and the fortress that had been Uda's only real strength now became his trap.

Around **1473**, Uda's hold collapsed. Raimal entered Chittor and was recognised as Rana of Mewar. Uda fled. Here history and legend become hard to separate. The chronicles agree that he went out of Mewar to seek the help of a Muslim sultan, hoping to come back with a foreign army behind him. Tod's account says he went to the court of Delhi; other traditions point to the sultan of Malwa. The bards tell that he offered the sultan a daughter in marriage in return for help, and that, as he left the court after the bargain, he was struck dead by lightning. To the people of Mewar, this ending seemed like the judgement of heaven on a man who had killed his father and was now ready to sell his family's honour. Historians cannot confirm the story. It is remembered as a moral tale, not as recorded fact.

What is better attested is that Uda's line did not give up at once. His sons, according to the chronicles, took refuge with **Ghiyas Shah**, the Khalji sultan of Malwa, who had come to the throne in 1469. Malwa had suffered heavily at Kumbha's hands, and its sultans had every reason to support a rival claimant. The chronicles say a Malwa force entered Mewar on their behalf and that Raimal turned it back. After that, the claim of Uda's sons faded, and Raimal's rule was secure.

Raimal ruled Mewar until **1509**, a reign of thirty-six years. He restored much of what had been lost, worked to repair the state and rebuilt the great temple of **Eklingji** near Nagda, the shrine that tradition traced back to Bappa Rawal. His sons would carry the story of Mewar forward: one of them, **Rana Sanga**, became the most powerful Rajput king of the early sixteenth century and faced Babur at Khanwa in 1527. Uda's five years became a gap in the honoured line of the house, a reign mentioned but never celebrated. Some later lists of the rulers of Mewar pass over him almost in silence.

It is worth asking why Mewar remembered Uda so harshly when other princes also took power by violence. Kumbha himself had come to the throne after his father Mokal was murdered by relatives, and the history of many Indian kingdoms is full of brothers and cousins killing one another for a throne. But the murder of a father by his son, and of a ruler as revered as Kumbha, struck at something deeper. Mewar's kings saw themselves as servants of Eklingji, holding the land in trust. A man who killed his father to seize that trust had broken the very idea of kingship. His later gifts of territory to outsiders only confirmed, in the eyes of the nobles, that he cared for the throne more than for the kingdom.

Uda's reign also shows how power worked in the Rajput states of that age. A Rana was not an absolute monarch. He depended on the great nobles, the heads of the clans, who held their own lands and brought their own warriors to his banner. When they withdrew their loyalty, the throne could not stand for long, however strong its fortresses. In 1473 the nobles of Mewar decided who would be king, and their choice was not the man who held Chittor, but the brother who came back from exile.

Kumbha's death at his son's hand also marked the end of an age. Under Kumbha, Mewar had been the leading power of Rajasthan. The years of Uda's rule, with lands given away and the nobles divided, weakened that position. Marwar under Rao Jodha grew stronger in the same years, and the sultans of Malwa and Gujarat watched for chances. Raimal had to spend much of his reign rebuilding. The full recovery came only under Sanga, a generation later.

The forts and towers Kumbha raised still stand: the Vijay Stambh rising over Chittor, and the walls of Kumbhalgarh running along the ridges. No monument stands to Uda. He left no buildings, no inscriptions of victory and no songs in his praise. His memory survives in the chronicles as a warning, told by the bards to every generation of Mewar's princes: that the throne of Eklingji could be seized by a crime, but could not be kept by one.

## Highlights of his life

- **Son of Rana Kumbha.** Uda was born into the house of Mewar at the height of its power, under the great builder and warrior Rana Kumbha.
- **Parricide (1468).** He killed his father at Kumbhalgarh to seize the throne, a crime for which Mewar remembered him as "Uda Hatyara", Uda the murderer.
- **A reign without loyalty (c. 1468–1473).** The nobles of Mewar refused to serve him, leaving his rule weak despite his hold on Chittor.
- **Loss of territory.** The chronicles say he gave away lands such as Abu, Ajmer and Sambhar to neighbouring rulers to buy their support.
- **Overthrown by his brother.** The nobles called back Raimal from Idar, whose forces defeated Uda's and took Chittor around 1473.
- **A death remembered as judgement.** He fled to seek a sultan's help; legend says he was killed by lightning, though this cannot be confirmed.

ratan-singh-ii.name: Ratan Singh II
ratan-singh-ii.title: Leadership after Sanga - Ratan Singh II
ratan-singh-ii.significance: Son of Rana Sanga who held Mewar after the defeat at Khanwa, amid family rivalry and the rise of Gujarat
ratan-singh-ii.legacy: Ratan Singh II held Chittor through the difficult years after Khanwa and died in a fight with Rao Surajmal Hada of Bundi in 1531.
ratan-singh-ii.story:
## Ratan Singh II — the heir of Sanga and the hunt in the hills of Bundi

*The short reign of Ratan Singh II is known from the chronicles of Mewar and Bundi, from a passing mention in the memoirs of Babur, and from the history James Tod built on the bardic tradition. The main events are clear; the story of his death is told in more than one way, and this telling says where tradition takes over.*

Ratan Singh was born into the house of Mewar in the years when it was rising again to greatness. His father was **Rana Sanga**, Sangram Singh, who had come to the throne in **1509** and made Mewar the leading power of northern India's Rajput world. Sanga defeated the sultans of Delhi, Malwa and Gujarat, and he carried the scars of his wars on his body: tradition says he had lost an eye, an arm and the use of a leg, and bore some eighty wounds. To be a son of Sanga was to grow up in a camp as much as in a palace, among nobles who measured a man by his courage.

Sanga had many sons by several queens. The eldest, **Bhojraj**, was the heir, and he is remembered above all as the husband of the poet-saint **Mirabai**. But Bhojraj died young, before his father, and the succession passed to Ratan Singh. Two younger half-brothers, **Vikramaditya** and **Udai Singh**, were the sons of Sanga's queen **Karnavati**, a Hada princess from Bundi. Sanga, in his later years, granted the great fortress of **Ranthambore** to Karnavati's sons. That grant would trouble Mewar long after his death.

Ratan Singh was a grown man when his father's fortunes turned. In **1526**, **Babur** defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat and took Delhi and Agra. Sanga gathered the largest Rajput coalition of the age and marched against him, and on **17 March 1527**, at **Khanwa** near Bayana, the two armies met. Babur's artillery and matchlocks, and his disciplined cavalry, broke the Rajput charge. Sanga was wounded and carried from the field. He survived and swore to fight again, but in **January 1528**, while preparing a new campaign, he died. Tradition says some of his own nobles, unwilling to face Babur once more, poisoned him.

So Ratan Singh came to the throne of Chittor in 1528, in the shadow of defeat. Mewar had lost many of its best warriors at Khanwa, and the alliance of Rajput houses that Sanga had built fell apart after his death. The new Rana's first task was simply to hold the kingdom together.

His greatest difficulty lay inside his own family. Karnavati was a determined and capable queen, and she wished to secure the future of her sons. Ranthambore, one of the strongest forts in India, was in their hands, and with it a power base that could rival Chittor. The memoirs of Babur record that envoys came to him in 1528 from the mother of Vikramaditya, offering Ranthambore in return for Babur's support for her son. Nothing lasting came of these talks, but they show how deeply divided the house of Mewar had become. Ratan Singh could not ignore a rival claim backed by a fortress and, perhaps, by the new power at Agra.

Ratan Singh's position was further complicated by the Hadas of Bundi. Karnavati's kinsman, **Rao Surajmal Hada** of Bundi, many accounts call him her brother, stood close to her sons and to Ranthambore. Bundi was a vassal state of Mewar, its Hada chiefs bound to the Rana by service and by marriage, but Surajmal was a proud and warlike ruler. Between the Rana of Chittor and the Rao of Bundi, suspicion grew.

Meanwhile, the world beyond Mewar was changing quickly. Babur, the victor of Khanwa, died in **December 1530**, and his son **Humayun** inherited a new and unsteady empire. To the south-west, a more immediate danger was rising. **Bahadur Shah**, the ambitious sultan of Gujarat, was building one of the strongest armies in India, with a large artillery train. In **1531** he overran Malwa and took the fortress of **Mandu**, ending the Khalji sultanate there. His borders now pressed directly against Mewar. Ratan Singh's reign thus fell between two powers: the young Mughal state to the north and an expanding Gujarat to the south. The Mughals, busy securing their own new conquests, did not press on Mewar in those years. The real threat came from Gujarat, and within a few years it would fall on Chittor.

Of Ratan Singh's government little is recorded. He is remembered as brave and quick-tempered, a true son of Sanga in his love of arms, but he did not have time to build monuments or to recover what Khanwa had cost. The chronicles describe a court still grieving, nobles whose loyalties had been strained, and a young Rana who had to show that he was worthy of his father's name.

His end came in **1531**, and it came not on a battlefield but in the hunting grounds of the hills near Bundi. The traditions agree on the outcome: Ratan Singh and Rao Surajmal Hada met, quarrelled and fought, and both men died of their wounds. They disagree on why.

One version, the one Tod recorded from the bards, tells it as a tale of honour and a bride. Tod's story says that Ratan Singh had been promised, or secretly married, to a princess of the Kachhwaha house of Amber, and that she was afterwards given in marriage to Surajmal instead. Ratan Singh nursed the insult. When the spring hunting festival came, the bards say, the Rana went out with Surajmal into the forests, two chiefs riding among their companions in apparent friendship. At a moment when they were apart from the others, the quarrel broke into the open. Swords and daggers were drawn. Each man struck the other, and both fell, the Rana of Mewar and the Rao of Bundi dying together among the trees.

In the bards' telling, the scene has all the shape of a Rajput tragedy: the hunting horns falling silent, the attendants running through the undergrowth, the two bodies lying in the leaves where the deer had passed a moment before. The details of the scene are the bards' own colouring, but the bitterness behind it was real.

The other way of seeing it is political. Surajmal was the protector of Karnavati's sons and of Ranthambore, and Ratan Singh had every reason to fear him. The quarrel may have been about power as much as honour, about who would control Ranthambore and the future of the Mewar throne. Historians generally accept that Ratan Singh and Surajmal killed each other in a personal fight in 1531; the true cause is not certain, and it is likely that pride, rivalry and the dispute over Karnavati's sons were all mixed together.

Ratan Singh left no son to succeed him. The throne of Chittor passed to his half-brother **Vikramaditya**, the elder of Karnavati's sons, the very prince whose claims had darkened his reign. In Bundi, Surajmal's death brought his own son to the throne. The two houses that had been joined by marriage and service were left counting their dead.

Looking back, the three short years of Ratan Singh's reign stand at a turning point. Sanga's death had ended Mewar's age of expansion, and his sons now fought one another while new empires rose around them. Within four years of Ratan Singh's death, **Bahadur Shah** of Gujarat would besiege Chittor, in **1535**, and the fortress would fall, with a great *jauhar* led by Karnavati herself. The divisions inside the house of Sanga, which Ratan Singh had not been able to heal, left Mewar weaker against that storm.

Yet Ratan Singh is not remembered with shame. He held Chittor through the dangerous years after Khanwa, he kept Mewar's independence in a time when the Rajput alliance had collapsed, and he died sword in hand, as his father would have understood. The chronicles of Mewar give him a short place among its rulers, a brave prince who came to the throne too soon after a defeat and left it too soon after a quarrel.

## Highlights of his life

- **Son of Rana Sanga.** He grew up in the camp of the greatest Rajput king of his age, and became heir after the early death of his elder brother Bhojraj.
- **Accession after Khanwa (1528).** He took the throne after Sanga's death in January 1528, with Mewar weakened by the defeat of 1527.
- **A divided house.** He faced the rival claims of his half-brothers Vikramaditya and Udai Singh, whose mother Karnavati held Ranthambore and opened talks with Babur.
- **Between Gujarat and the Mughals.** His reign saw Babur's death in 1530 and Bahadur Shah of Gujarat's conquest of Malwa in 1531, which brought a powerful enemy to Mewar's border.
- **Death at Bundi (1531).** He and Rao Surajmal Hada of Bundi killed each other in a fight during a hunt; the cause is told differently in different traditions.
- **Succession.** Leaving no son, he was succeeded by his half-brother Vikramaditya.
