vikramaditya-singh.story:
## Vikramaditya Singh — the young Rana in the storm over Chittor

*The reign of Vikramaditya is known from the chronicles of Mewar, the Persian histories of Gujarat and the Mughals, and the bardic tradition that James Tod later wrote down. The two sieges of Chittor are well recorded; some of the stories around them, such as the rakhi sent to Humayun, are tradition, and this telling says so.*

Vikramaditya was the elder son of **Rana Sanga** and his Hada queen **Karnavati** of Bundi. He and his younger brother **Udai Singh** were born in the last years of their father's reign, when Mewar was still the strongest Rajput state in India. They were far down the line of succession. Their elder half-brothers came first, and Sanga gave Karnavati's sons the great fortress of **Ranthambore** as their share, rather than any hope of the throne of Chittor.

Then everything changed. Sanga was defeated by **Babur** at **Khanwa** in **1527** and died in **January 1528**. The throne passed to Vikramaditya's half-brother **Ratan Singh II**. Karnavati, determined to protect her sons, held Ranthambore for them and even sent envoys to Babur, as his memoirs record, offering the fortress in return for his support. Then, in **1531**, Ratan Singh was killed in a fight with **Rao Surajmal Hada** of Bundi during a hunt. He left no son. The boy Vikramaditya, still in his teens, became Rana of Mewar.

He came to the throne at the worst possible moment. To the south-west, **Bahadur Shah** of Gujarat had conquered Malwa in 1531 and now stood on Mewar's border with one of the most powerful armies in India, including a large train of artillery handled by Ottoman and Portuguese-trained gunners. Mewar, still weak after Khanwa, needed a strong and wise ruler who could unite its nobles. Vikramaditya was neither.

The chronicles agree that the young Rana was proud, hot-tempered and careless of the old customs. He kept company with wrestlers and foot soldiers and favoured them over the great nobles. He mocked the veterans of his father's wars and, tradition says, publicly insulted senior chiefs in his own court. In a kingdom where the Rana's power rested on the loyalty of the clan chiefs, this was dangerous folly. Many of the nobles withdrew to their estates. Karnavati, who had fought so hard for her son's rights, now had to hold together a court that he was driving apart.

Tradition also links Vikramaditya to one of the most famous stories of Mewar. **Mirabai**, the poet-saint, was the widow of his half-brother Bhojraj. Her songs speak of a "Rana" who persecuted her for her devotion to Krishna, sending her poison and a snake in a basket, which turned into harmless things in her hands. Many traditions identify this Rana with Vikramaditya. Historians cannot be certain who it was, and the miracles are legend, but Mirabai did leave Chittor in these years, going first to her family at Merta and later to Vrindavan and Dwarka.

The storm from Gujarat broke first in **1532–33**. Bahadur Shah marched on Chittor and laid siege to it. Mewar's defenders held, but Bahadur's guns battered the walls, and the Rana's divided court could not raise a relieving army. Peace was made in **1533**. As its price, Mewar gave back the territories of Malwa it had held, and handed over the jewelled crown and golden belt of **Sultan Mahmud Khalji II** of Malwa, which Sanga had taken when he captured the sultan at Gagron in 1519. Bahadur withdrew, but he had seen how weak Chittor had become.

He returned in **1534**. This time he meant to take the fortress. His army was vast, and his artillery, commanded by the gunner known as **Rumi Khan**, was the best in India. The nobles of Mewar, whatever they thought of their Rana, came to defend Chittor. They knew it could not hold for long. Karnavati and the chiefs decided that the royal line must survive. The two princes, Vikramaditya and the young Udai Singh, were sent away to safety at **Bundi**, Karnavati's own home.

Command of the defence was given to **Rawat Bagh Singh** of Deolia, a kinsman of the royal house, who was to hold the fortress in the Rana's name. Here the story enters the most famous legend of the siege. Tradition says that Karnavati sent a *rakhi*, the thread of sisterly protection, to the Mughal emperor **Humayun**, asking him, as a brother, to come to her help. Humayun is said to have accepted it and set out. The story is told in later sources and is not found in the contemporary histories. What is certain is that Humayun was at war with Bahadur Shah himself, that he moved slowly, and that he did not arrive in time to save Chittor.

Through the winter of 1534–35 the guns pounded the walls. A great breach was opened by a mine. In **March 1535**, when the fall could no longer be prevented, the women of Chittor chose death over capture. Led by Karnavati herself, thousands of women entered the fire in the second great *jauhar* of Chittor, after that of 1303. The men put on saffron robes, opened the gates and rode out to die. Bagh Singh fell fighting at the gate, and Bahadur Shah's army entered the fortress.

Bahadur did not keep Chittor long. Humayun now turned on him in earnest, defeated him near **Mandsaur** in 1535, and drove him from Malwa and then from much of Gujarat itself. The Gujarat garrison left Chittor, and the Rajputs of Mewar returned to the ruined fortress. Vikramaditya came back from Bundi and was restored to the throne of his ancestors, now a fortress of burned palaces and fresh graves.

He had learned nothing. The chronicles say he returned as arrogant as before, still insulting the nobles who had bled for Chittor while he was safe in Bundi. The chiefs of Mewar had lost their sons and their wives in the siege, and their patience was gone. They decided that the boy-king could not be allowed to rule. But Udai Singh, the only other living son of Sanga, was still a child. They needed a regent.

They turned to **Banbir**, the son of Sanga's elder brother **Prithviraj** by a concubine. As the son of an unequal union, he could not claim the throne by right, and that may be why the nobles trusted him to govern for Udai Singh. It was a terrible mistake. Banbir wanted the throne for himself.

In **1536** (some accounts say 1537), Banbir entered the palace at night and killed Vikramaditya with his sword. Then he went in search of Udai Singh. The story that follows is the most loved in Mewar's history. The child's nurse, **Panna Dai**, heard the noise and knew what was coming. She put the young prince in a fruit basket and had him carried out of the palace by a trusted servant, and laid her own son, **Chandan**, in the prince's bed. When Banbir came and asked where Udai Singh was, she pointed to the sleeping boy. Banbir killed him before her eyes. Panna then left Chittor, followed the basket and carried the prince across the hills to **Kumbhalgarh**, where its governor gave him shelter.

Vikramaditya was dead, and he left no son. Banbir ruled at Chittor for a few years, but the nobles came to recognise Udai Singh, raised at Kumbhalgarh, as their true Rana. Around **1540** Udai Singh's supporters defeated Banbir and took back Chittor. **Udai Singh II** would later found the city of **Udaipur**, and his son would be **Maharana Pratap**.

The life of Vikramaditya is a hard one to admire. He came to power as a boy, surrounded by danger, and he made it worse by quarrelling with the very men he needed most. In his years, Chittor was twice besieged, once surrendered its treasures and once fell in fire. Yet his story is also a reminder of how heavily the age pressed on the house of Sanga. Within eight years, Mewar lost a great king, two of his sons by violence and its fortress to a foreign army. Out of that chaos, through the sacrifice of Karnavati, Bagh Singh and Panna Dai, the line of Mewar survived.

## Highlights of his life

- **Son of Rana Sanga and Karnavati.** He was raised with his brother Udai Singh as heir to Ranthambore, far from the throne of Chittor.
- **An unexpected Rana (1531).** He came to the throne as a youth after the death of his half-brother Ratan Singh II.
- **A ruler who divided his court.** His arrogance and his insults to senior nobles cost him the loyalty of the chiefs of Mewar.
- **First siege of Chittor (1532–33).** Bahadur Shah of Gujarat besieged the fortress; peace was bought with Malwa lands and the crown of Mahmud Khalji II.
- **Second siege and jauhar (1534–35).** Sent to safety at Bundi, he lost Chittor in March 1535, when Karnavati led the jauhar and Bagh Singh died defending the gate.
- **Restoration and murder.** He regained Chittor after Humayun defeated Bahadur Shah, but was killed by Banbir in 1536, an event that led to Panna Dai's famous sacrifice.

karan-singh-ii.story:
## Karan Singh II — the prince who made peace and rebuilt Mewar

*Karan Singh's life is recorded in the chronicles of Mewar and, unusually for a Rajput prince of his time, in the memoirs of the Mughal emperor Jahangir, who wrote about meeting him. Some stories told of him, such as the exchange of turbans with Prince Khurram, are tradition, and this telling says so.*

Karan Singh was born in **1584**, the son of **Amar Singh**, the eldest son of **Maharana Pratap**. He came into the world in the hardest years of Mewar's history. Chittor had fallen to Akbar in 1568, the battle of **Haldighati** had been fought in 1576, and Pratap was carrying on his long war from the hills, moving between hidden camps and fortresses while Mughal armies held the plains. The prince's earliest years were spent in that world of forest forts, Bhil allies and constant movement, among warriors who had sworn not to bow to the emperor.

When Karan was still a boy, the tide in the hills began to turn. In the last decade of his life Pratap recovered much of Mewar, and he made **Chavand** his capital. He died there in **January 1597**, and Karan's father became **Maharana Amar Singh I**. The new ruler inherited his father's war and his father's oath. For nearly twenty years Amar Singh fought the armies of Akbar and then of **Jahangir**, who came to the throne in 1605.

Karan grew to manhood in these campaigns. Jahangir sent one commander after another against Mewar: his son Parvez, then Mahabat Khan, then Abdullah Khan and others. The Mewar forces fought from the hills, raided Mughal posts and won some notable successes, but each campaign destroyed more villages and burned more fields. As heir, Karan shared in the councils of war and in their burdens, and tradition remembers him riding with his father's forces in these years.

The decisive campaign came in **1613**. Jahangir moved his court to **Ajmer** to direct the war and gave command to his favourite son, **Prince Khurram**, the future Shah Jahan. Khurram did not try to win a single battle. Instead, he spread his troops in posts across Mewar, burned the crops, cut off supplies and drove the people from the valleys. Mewar, after nearly half a century of war, was exhausted. Its people were starving and its nobles had lost sons in every generation. They urged Amar Singh to make peace.

In **1615** the treaty was made. Its terms were generous by the standards of the age, and they shaped Mewar for the next two centuries. Mewar accepted Mughal overlordship, but the Maharana himself would never be required to attend the imperial court in person. His heir would go in his place. There was no demand for a marriage between the two royal houses. Chittor and the lands taken by the Mughals would be returned, but the fortress of Chittor was not to be repaired or refortified.

It was Karan Singh who carried the treaty into the Mughal world. Amar Singh, unable to bear the thought of bowing before an emperor, sent his son. In **1615** Karan rode to Ajmer and was presented to Jahangir. The emperor wrote of the meeting in his memoirs with clear satisfaction. He received the prince with honour, gave him rich gifts, horses, elephants and jewels, and seated him near the throne. He granted Karan a mansab, an imperial rank, of **5,000**, a high honour. Jahangir also recorded that he had life-size marble statues of Amar Singh and Karan made and set up in the garden below the palace window at Agra.

For Karan, these must have been strange days: the son of a family that had fought the Mughals for three generations, now a guest of the emperor, watched by the whole court. He carried himself, the sources suggest, with dignity, and he returned to Mewar having gained peace on terms that left his house its pride. It is from this meeting that the friendship between Karan and **Prince Khurram** began.

Amar Singh never recovered from the grief of the treaty. He gave up most of the business of government, withdrew from public life and, tradition says, shut himself away from the world. He died in **January 1620**, and Karan Singh became Maharana of Mewar at about thirty-six years of age.

Karan's reign was the first true age of peace in Mewar for almost a century. He turned at once to the work of recovery. The villages that Khurram's campaign had emptied were resettled. Fields were brought back under the plough, and the roads and markets reopened. The capital was **Udaipur**, founded by Udai Singh II on the shores of **Lake Pichola**, and for the first time in decades its rulers could think of beauty as well as defence.

Peace had its own price, and Karan felt it. Under the treaty, Mewar's contingent of horsemen now served in the imperial armies, often far away in the Deccan, under the command of a prince of the house or a senior noble. Chittor, the old capital, stood within Mewar again, but its broken walls could not be mended, and its palaces stayed empty. For a family whose pride was rooted in that rock, it was a daily reminder that independence had been traded for survival. Karan's task was to show that the bargain had been worth it, by giving his people prosperity in place of glory.

He also had to rebuild the bonds within Mewar. The great noble clans, the Chundawats, the Shaktawats and others who had fought in the hills for two generations, had grown used to war and to the power that war gave them. In peace, their estates had to be settled, their ranks fixed, and their old rivalries kept from turning into feuds. The chronicles credit Karan with handling the nobles carefully, rewarding the families who had suffered most in the long war and keeping the court united around the throne.

His most lasting work was on the lake itself. On an island in Pichola, Karan began building a palace that would become the **Jag Mandir**. The earliest part, the domed pavilion known as the **Gul Mahal**, is credited to him. His son would complete the island palace and give it its present name.

The Gul Mahal soon received a famous guest. In **1622–23** Prince Khurram rebelled against his father Jahangir, and after his defeat he was a fugitive, moving between the Deccan, Bengal and western India. Karan Singh, remembering the prince who had made the peace of 1615, gave him shelter at Udaipur. Khurram stayed in the palace on the island in Pichola. Tradition says that the Maharana and the prince exchanged turbans as a sign of brotherhood, and a turban said to be Khurram's is still shown at Udaipur. Historians cannot confirm the story in detail, but Karan's protection of the rebel prince is well remembered.

Karan's younger brother, **Bhim Singh**, went further. He joined Khurram's service and became one of the boldest commanders of the rebellion. He died fighting for the prince in **1624**, in a battle against the imperial army in the east. For the house of Mewar, it was a sign of how far it had come: a Sisodia prince now fought and died in the civil wars of the Mughal empire as a sworn ally.

Karan's loyalty was repaid. In **1627** Jahangir died, and in early **1628** Khurram took the throne as **Shah Jahan**. The friendship between the new emperor and the house of Mewar would, for a time, keep the peace that Karan had built. But Karan himself did not live to enjoy it. He died in **1628**, in the same year as Shah Jahan's accession, after a reign of about eight years.

He was succeeded by his son **Jagat Singh I**, who completed the Jag Mandir, built the great Jagannath temple at Udaipur, and continued the age of building that Karan had begun.

Karan Singh's place in Mewar's story is a quiet one beside the heroes of Haldighati and Chittor. He did not win a famous battle or die in a famous siege. But in a land worn down by fifty years of war, he did something just as hard. He carried a painful peace with dignity, won the respect of an emperor, sheltered a fugitive prince, and gave his people the first years of rest they had known in living memory. The palace he began on the island in Lake Pichola still floats on the water, a monument to the peace that followed the long war.

## Highlights of his life

- **Grandson of Maharana Pratap.** Born in 1584, he grew up during the long resistance of Pratap and Amar Singh I against the Mughals.
- **Envoy of the 1615 treaty.** He went to Jahangir's court at Ajmer in his father's place, received a mansab of 5,000, and was honoured with a marble statue at Agra.
- **Maharana of the peace (1620–1628).** He resettled villages, restored farming and trade, and gave Mewar its first long years of peace in a century.
- **Builder of the Gul Mahal.** He began the island palace on Lake Pichola that his son completed as the Jag Mandir.
- **Shelter to Prince Khurram.** He gave refuge at Udaipur to the rebel prince who later became Shah Jahan; tradition says they exchanged turbans.
- **Succession.** He died in 1628 and was succeeded by his son Jagat Singh I.

jagat-singh-i.story:
## Jagat Singh I — the Maharana who built in marble and paint

*Jagat Singh's reign is recorded in the chronicles of Mewar, in the Sanskrit inscriptions of his own temples, and in the paintings his workshop produced. The broad story is well known; where tradition adds to it, this telling says so.*

Jagat Singh was born into a Mewar that was just coming out of war. His grandfather, **Maharana Amar Singh I**, had fought the armies of Akbar and Jahangir for nearly twenty years before making peace in **1615**. His father, **Karan Singh II**, had carried that peace to the Mughal court at Ajmer and won the friendship of **Prince Khurram**. Jagat Singh grew up in the first generation of Sisodia princes who did not expect to spend their lives fighting in the hills. His world was Udaipur, the city on the shores of **Lake Pichola**, where his father was beginning to build palaces rather than forts.

As a young prince, Jagat Singh would have watched the most remarkable visitor his father ever received. In **1623**, Prince Khurram, in rebellion against his father Jahangir, came to Udaipur as a fugitive and was sheltered by Karan Singh in the new pavilion on an island in the lake. Five years later, in **1628**, Khurram became the emperor **Shah Jahan**. In the same year Karan Singh died, and Jagat Singh became Maharana of Mewar.

He inherited a kingdom bound by the treaty of 1615. Mewar accepted Mughal overlordship and sent a contingent to serve in the imperial armies, but its Maharana did not attend the Mughal court in person, and no marriage tied the two houses. In return, Mewar was left to govern itself. For Jagat Singh, the friendship between his father and the new emperor was a valuable inheritance, and for most of his reign the peace held.

That peace allowed him to spend the wealth of Mewar on building, worship and art on a scale not seen since the days of Rana Kumbha. His first great work was to finish the palace his father had begun on the island in Pichola. Around Karan Singh's domed pavilion, the **Gul Mahal**, Jagat Singh added courtyards, gardens and halls, and the whole island palace came to be known after him as the **Jag Mandir**. Its terraces, its rows of carved stone elephants rising from the water, and its views of the city across the lake made it one of the most beautiful pleasure palaces in Rajasthan.

The island palace carried a memory as well as a name. It was here that Khurram had lived as a hunted rebel, and the emperor he became did not forget the house that had sheltered him. Local tradition in Udaipur goes further and says that the domes and inlaid stone of the island palace gave Shah Jahan ideas he later used in his own buildings, even in the Taj Mahal. No record confirms this, and it is told as a story of the city's pride rather than as history. What is certain is that, under Jagat Singh, the palace became the setting for the court's festivals, where the Maharana and his nobles gathered on the water on summer evenings.

Jagat Singh's greatest monument was a temple. In the heart of Udaipur, close to the royal palace, he built a great shrine to Vishnu as **Jagannath**, the lord of the world. It was completed in **1651**. The temple stands on a high plinth, reached by a steep stairway guarded by stone elephants, and its walls are covered with carvings of dancers, musicians, riders and gods. A long Sanskrit inscription set up in the temple praises the Maharana and records the history of his house. Today it is known as the **Jagdish Temple**, and it remains the most important temple in the city.

The temple shows something about Jagat Singh's faith. The rulers of Mewar had always served **Eklingji**, the Shiva of their kingdom, as his *dewan*, and Jagat Singh kept that service faithfully. But the seventeenth century was also an age of growing Vaishnava devotion in Rajasthan, and Jagat Singh's temple to Jagannath placed the worship of Vishnu at the very centre of his capital. The chronicles describe him as devout and generous, giving great gifts to Brahmins and temples. They record that he performed the ceremony of *tula dan*, in which a ruler was weighed against gold or silver that was then given away in charity.

He was also one of the great patrons of painting in Indian history. In the royal workshop at Udaipur, artists created works that defined the Mewar style for generations. The most celebrated of them was **Sahibdin**, who led the painting of a vast illustrated **Ramayana** between about **1649** and **1653**, with hundreds of paintings in bright colours of red, yellow and blue. Another master, **Manohar**, worked on other volumes of the same great project. Sahibdin and his workshop also illustrated poetry such as the *Rasikapriya* and the *Gita Govinda*. These paintings, filled with palaces, forests, armies and lovers, are now treasured in museums around the world. They began in the court of Jagat Singh.

The style of these paintings was bold and direct. Instead of the soft shading of the Mughal workshops, the Mewar painters used flat fields of strong colour and clear outlines. A single page often showed several moments of a story at once, so that Rama might appear three times in the same forest, travelling, resting and fighting. The effect was like a story told aloud by a bard, moving from scene to scene. In these pages the epics of India were retold in the dress, the architecture and the landscape of Mewar, so that Ayodhya and Lanka look much like the palaces and hills around Udaipur.

Not everything in his reign was peaceful. Mewar had long claimed overlordship over the smaller Rajput states of the south, such as **Dungarpur** and **Banswara**, whose rulers were kinsmen of the Sisodias. The chronicles record that Jagat Singh sent forces to assert Mewar's authority over these neighbours. Such campaigns were small affairs compared with the wars of his grandfather's time, but they mattered, because the Mughal court regarded these chiefs as its own vassals too, and every quarrel risked imperial displeasure.

The greatest risk Jagat Singh took was at **Chittor**. The treaty of 1615 had returned the old capital to Mewar on one condition: its walls and gates were not to be repaired. For the Sisodias, Chittor was more than a fortress. It was the place of the three great *jauhars*, the seat of Bappa Rawal, Kumbha and Sanga, the heart of their memory. Jagat Singh began to repair its gates and walls. Whether he meant it as a quiet act of pride or a careful test of the emperor's patience, it was a breach of the treaty. Shah Jahan took note. The full answer did not come in Jagat Singh's lifetime: in **1654**, two years after his death, the emperor sent his minister **Saadullah Khan** with an army to pull down the new works. The Chittor repairs became the first crack in the peace between Mewar and the Mughals.

In his own court, Jagat Singh lived as a ruler of a rich and confident state. Udaipur grew around its palace and its lake, its markets busy with traders, its temples crowded with pilgrims. The chroniclers of Mewar remember his reign as a time of plenty, of festivals on the water and processions through the city, after the long hunger of the war years. In a sense, he gave Udaipur the shape and the beauty that visitors still see today.

Jagat Singh died in **1652**, after a reign of twenty-four years. He was succeeded by his son **Raj Singh I**, a very different kind of ruler, who would carry on the repairs at Chittor and, in time, stand against the emperor **Aurangzeb** himself.

Jagat Singh does not appear in the songs of battle that fill Mewar's chronicles. His achievements were of another kind. He turned a peace that had been won at great cost into an age of building and art. The island palace of the Jag Mandir, the great Jagdish Temple, and the pages of Sahibdin's Ramayana are his legacy, and they made Udaipur not only the seat of a kingdom but one of the jewels of Rajput culture.

## Highlights of his life

- **Heir to the peace of 1615.** Son of Karan Singh II, he became Maharana in 1628, the year his father's friend Khurram became the emperor Shah Jahan.
- **Builder of the Jag Mandir.** He completed and enlarged the island palace on Lake Pichola that bears his name.
- **The Jagdish Temple (1651).** He built Udaipur's great temple to Vishnu as Jagannath, with a long Sanskrit inscription on the history of his house.
- **Patron of Mewar painting.** His workshop, led by Sahibdin and Manohar, produced the great illustrated Ramayana of about 1649–1653.
- **Devotion and charity.** He gave generously to temples and Brahmins and performed the tula dan.
- **Repairs at Chittor.** He began repairing the old capital's defences in breach of the treaty, which led Shah Jahan to order their demolition in 1654.

raj-singh-i.story:
## Raj Singh I — the Maharana who stood against Aurangzeb

*Raj Singh's life is unusually well recorded: in the Persian histories of the Mughal court, in the chronicles of Mewar, and above all in the Raj Prashasti, the great Sanskrit poem carved in stone on the banks of the lake he built. Some famous stories about him, such as the rescue of the princess of Kishangarh, are tradition, and this telling says so.*

Raj Singh was born on **24 September 1629**, the son of **Maharana Jagat Singh I**. He grew up in the most peaceful and prosperous Mewar for a century. His grandfather **Karan Singh II** had made friends with Prince Khurram, now the emperor **Shah Jahan**, and his father filled Udaipur with temples, palaces and paintings. The young prince watched the Jagdish Temple rise in the heart of the city and the painters of the royal workshop at work on their great Ramayana. But he also inherited a quieter tradition: the memory of Pratap and of Chittor, and a deep pride in Mewar's freedom.

He became Maharana in **1652**, at the age of twenty-two. Almost at once he was tested. His father had begun to repair the walls and gates of **Chittor**, the ancient capital, against the terms of the treaty of 1615, and Raj Singh continued the work. Shah Jahan would not accept it. In **1654** he sent his minister **Saadullah Khan** with a large army into Mewar. Raj Singh, unable to fight the whole empire, did not resist. The Mughal troops pulled down the new walls and gates, and some of Mewar's districts were taken away. It was a bitter lesson for the young Maharana, and he did not forget it.

His chance came only a few years later. In **1657** Shah Jahan fell ill, and his four sons began a war for the throne. Raj Singh used the confusion. As a new ruler, he revived the old custom of the **Tika Daur**, the ceremonial raid with which a Rana of Mewar marked his accession, and turned it into a real campaign. In **1658** his forces swept through Mughal-held districts on Mewar's borders, recovering lost lands and plundering rich towns such as **Malpura**. At the same time he took care to stand on the winning side. He sent his support to **Aurangzeb**, who defeated his brothers and became emperor in 1658, and the new emperor confirmed Raj Singh's gains.

For some years, Raj Singh and Aurangzeb were at peace. But the Mewar chronicles remember an early clash of honour. Around **1660**, they tell, Aurangzeb demanded the hand of **Charumati**, a princess of the Rathore house of **Kishangarh**. The princess refused to marry the emperor and sent a message to Raj Singh, begging him to save her. The bards describe the Maharana riding to Kishangarh with his warriors, and marrying the princess himself. Historians accept the marriage, but the details of the story come mainly from tradition, and Mughal sources are silent on it. In Mewar, it became a symbol of the Maharana as protector of Rajput honour.

In these same years, a great disaster struck Mewar. Around **1661–62**, a terrible famine fell on the land after the rains failed. Raj Singh answered it with the work for which he is best remembered. Near **Kankroli**, where the Gomati river flowed through the hills, he ordered a vast dam to be built to create a lake. The work gave food and wages to thousands of starving people. It went on for more than a decade, from **1662** to about **1676**. The result was **Rajsamand**, one of the largest artificial lakes in Rajasthan, with its great embankment of white marble, its graceful pavilions and its steps descending into the water, known as the **Nauchowki**.

On the embankment Raj Singh set up something even more remarkable. The court poet **Ranchhod Bhatt** composed a long Sanskrit poem, the **Raj Prashasti**, telling the history of Mewar from its legendary origins to Raj Singh's own deeds. It was carved on **twenty-five** great slabs of black stone and set into the walls of the lake's pavilions. It is the longest Sanskrit inscription known in India, and one of the most important sources for the history of Mewar.

The lake was not only a monument. It held the water of the monsoon through the long dry months, watered the fields of the villages around it and gave the region a reserve against the next failure of the rains. Raj Singh is said to have marked its completion with great ceremonies and gifts, and the chroniclers praised him for turning a time of hunger into a work that would feed his people for generations. More than three centuries later, Rajsamand still holds water, and its marble steps are still crowded at festival times.

Those who wrote about Raj Singh describe a ruler of strong will and deep faith, generous to priests and poets, careful with his nobles and quick to take an opportunity. He was not reckless. He gave way when he had to, as in 1654, and struck when the empire was divided, as in 1658. That patience made his final stand all the more striking.

Meanwhile, the empire was changing. Aurangzeb was a strict and devout Sunni ruler, and from the late 1660s his policies grew harder towards his Hindu subjects. In **1669** he ordered the destruction of a number of important temples. In the holy land of **Braj** around Mathura, the priests of the image of **Shrinathji**, the form of Krishna worshipped by the Vallabha sect, fled with their god. For a time they wandered from court to court, but many rulers feared to give them shelter. Raj Singh welcomed them. In **1672** the image was installed at the village of **Sihad**, in Mewar, which grew into the temple town of **Nathdwara**, the "gateway of the lord". Another sacred image, of **Dwarkadhish**, was given a home at Kankroli, on the shore of the new lake. Both remain among the most important places of pilgrimage in India.

In **1679** Aurangzeb reimposed the **jizya**, the poll tax on non-Muslims that Akbar had abolished more than a century before. Across Rajasthan there was anger. A famous letter of protest against the tax, defending the rights of the emperor's Hindu subjects, has been attributed to Raj Singh; other traditions attribute it to Shivaji, and its true author is uncertain. But Raj Singh's opposition to the jizya and to the policies behind it was clear, and it soon turned into war.

The spark came from Marwar. In **December 1678**, **Maharaja Jaswant Singh** of Jodhpur died at Jamrud, on the far north-western frontier. His heir, **Ajit Singh**, was born after his death. Aurangzeb took Marwar under direct control and tried to bring the infant to be raised at his court. In **1679** the Rathore noble **Durgadas** and his companions fought their way out of Delhi with the child and carried him to safety. Raj Singh gave shelter to Ajit Singh and support to the Rathore cause, joining Mewar and Marwar against the empire.

Aurangzeb answered with force. In late **1679** he marched into Mewar himself with a great army. Raj Singh did what his ancestors had done: he left the cities to the enemy and withdrew into the hills of the Aravallis. The Mughals occupied Udaipur and Chittor, and many temples were damaged, including his father's Jagdish Temple. But in the hills, the forces of Mewar, led by Raj Singh and his sons, cut Mughal supply lines and attacked isolated camps. The emperor's son, **Prince Akbar**, left to hold Chittor, suffered heavily.

Raj Singh did not live to see the end of the war. He died on **22 October 1680**, in the hills, in the middle of the struggle. Some accounts suggest he was poisoned, but this is not proven. His son **Jai Singh** succeeded him. Within months, in **January 1681**, Prince Akbar rebelled against his father with Rajput support. The rebellion failed, and in **1681** Jai Singh made peace with Aurangzeb on terms that kept Mewar's independence in its own affairs.

Raj Singh's life was the last great age of Mewar under the Mughals. He was a builder like his father and grandfather, but also a fighter like Pratap. He gave the famine-stricken a lake, gave the fleeing gods a home, gave the infant Ajit Singh a refuge, and stood against the most powerful emperor of his age when the Mughals were at the height of their strength. In the lines of the Raj Prashasti on the marble shores of Rajsamand, his memory is still written in stone.

## Highlights of his life

- **Raids of 1658.** During the Mughal war of succession, he turned the ceremonial Tika Daur into a campaign that recovered lost districts.
- **Rajsamand Lake (1662–1676).** Built as famine relief, it is one of Rajasthan's largest lakes, with its marble embankment and the Nauchowki.
- **The Raj Prashasti.** He set up the longest Sanskrit inscription in India, carved on twenty-five stone slabs, telling the history of Mewar.
- **Refuge for Shrinathji.** He gave the image of Shrinathji a home in 1672 at Sihad, which became Nathdwara.
- **Opposition to the jizya (1679).** He stood against Aurangzeb's reimposition of the poll tax on non-Muslims.
- **Protector of Ajit Singh.** He sheltered the infant heir of Marwar and joined the Rathores in war against Aurangzeb from 1679.
- **Death in the war (1680).** He died in the hills on 22 October 1680, still resisting; his son Jai Singh made peace in 1681.

jai-singh.story:
## Jai Singh — the Maharana who made peace and built a sea

*Jai Singh's reign is known from Mughal histories, the chronicles of Mewar and the great lake that still carries his name; where the bards add colour to the record, this story says so.*

In the year **1653**, a son was born in the palace at Udaipur to **Maharana Raj Singh**, who had come to the throne the year before and would prove one of the most determined rulers Mewar ever had. The child was named Jai Singh. He grew up in a court that was proud, devout and watchful. His ancestor **Maharana Pratap** had refused to bow to Akbar, and Pratap's son **Amar Singh I** had at last made an honourable peace with Jahangir in 1615. Since that peace, Mewar had lived in an uneasy balance with the Mughal empire: its rulers did not attend the imperial court in person, but they sent their heirs and their contingents, and they never forgot that Chittor, the old heart of the kingdom, had been taken from them.

Jai Singh's childhood was spent beside the waters of **Lake Pichola**, in the city that his ancestor Udai Singh II had founded. He learned to ride and to use the sword and the lance, as every Sisodia prince did. He also learned the worship of **Eklingji**, the form of Shiva whom the rulers of Mewar served as *dewan*. As the boy grew, he watched his father build. Raj Singh raised the great embankment of **Rajsamand**, a lake made to give work to the people in a time of famine, and he carved into its stones the long Sanskrit poem *Raj Prashasti*, the history of his house.

But the boy also grew up in the shadow of a gathering storm. In 1658 **Aurangzeb** seized the Mughal throne, and as his reign went on, his policies grew harder towards his Hindu subjects. Raj Singh defied him openly more than once. He married the princess of **Rupnagar (Kishangarh)**, whom the emperor had wished to take into the imperial harem, and he protested when the emperor reimposed the **jizya**, the tax on non-Muslims, in 1679.

The storm broke over the house of Marwar. When **Maharaja Jaswant Singh** of Jodhpur died in 1678, Aurangzeb tried to take control of his kingdom and his infant heir, **Ajit Singh**. The Rathore nobles, led by the famous **Durgadas Rathore**, smuggled the child out of Delhi. Raj Singh gave shelter to the cause of Marwar, and Mewar and Marwar went to war together against the empire.

Jai Singh was then in his twenties, and he lived through that war as a soldier and a prince. In the early months of 1680, a great Mughal army entered Mewar. The emperor's forces occupied **Udaipur** and **Chittor**, and temples in the capital were damaged. Raj Singh did what the rulers of Mewar had always done against a stronger enemy: he withdrew into the hills of the Aravallis and fought from the passes. Mewari bands cut off supplies, struck at Mughal outposts and vanished into the forests. The Mughal histories record that the imperial commanders found the hill war slow and costly.

In the middle of this struggle, in **1680**, Raj Singh died in the hills. Tradition in Mewar says that he was poisoned; the cause has never been proved. Jai Singh succeeded him in the camp, not in a palace, with an empire's armies inside his kingdom.

The new Maharana faced a choice that his ancestors had faced before. He could fight on in the hills, as Pratap had done, or he could seek a peace that kept his throne and his people. For a few months the war continued. Then, in January **1681**, came an event that shook the whole Mughal world. Aurangzeb's own son, **Prince Akbar**, who had been commanding against the Rajputs, rebelled against his father with the support of the Rathores and the Sisodias, and proclaimed himself emperor.

For a moment it seemed that the Rajputs might help to put a new emperor on the throne of Delhi. But Aurangzeb was a master of intrigue. A letter, written so that it would fall into Rajput hands, made it appear that Akbar was secretly working for his father and leading the Rajputs into a trap. The Rajput chiefs, suspicious, drew away from the prince in the night. Akbar's army melted away. Durgadas, who refused to abandon a man who had trusted him, took the young prince south to the court of the Maratha king **Sambhaji**, and Akbar later went into exile in Persia.

With the rebellion broken, the war in Mewar could only end in one way. In the summer of 1681, Jai Singh made peace with Aurangzeb through the emperor's son **Prince Muhammad Azam**. The terms were heavy, but they were not a surrender. In place of the jizya, Mewar gave up three of its districts, **Pur, Mandal and Badnor**. The Mughal armies withdrew from the kingdom, and Jai Singh was recognised as **Rana** with the rank and honours of an imperial *mansab*. The bards tell of the meeting between the Maharana and the Mughal prince, of the formal courtesies exchanged and of the silence of the Rajput nobles who watched their master sign away good land. Whatever they felt, the kingdom was free of foreign armies again.

Marwar did not accept the peace. The Rathores went on fighting for Ajit Singh for more than twenty years. Mewar's withdrawal from the war was remembered by some as prudence and by others as weakness. Colonel James Tod, who wrote the history of Rajasthan in the nineteenth century from the chronicles he collected, judged Jai Singh harshly, as a ruler who preferred comfort to glory. But Tod was writing long after the events, and the choice Jai Singh made was not an easy one. He had inherited a kingdom in ruins, with its capital occupied and its people driven into the hills. Peace gave Mewar seventeen years to recover.

He used those years to build. Southeast of Udaipur, the river **Gomati** flowed through a wide valley among the hills. Jai Singh ordered a great dam of stone to be thrown across it. Work went on for several years, and when it was finished, around **1691**, the water rose behind the dam and filled the valley, covering villages, fields and low hills and leaving their tops as islands. The new lake was called **Jaisamand**, the "sea of Jai". It was also known as **Dhebar**, after the pass where the dam stood. For a long time it was counted the largest artificial lake in Asia.

Tradition says that at the dedication of the dam the Maharana performed the *tula dan*, the ceremony in which a king is weighed against gold and silver that are then given away in charity, and that he walked along the embankment with his court as the water lapped at the steps. Marble chhatris and stairs lead down to the lake from the dam, with carved elephants facing the water. Small palaces rose on the ridges above it, where the royal women could take the cool air in summer. Like his father's lake at Rajsamand, Jaisamand was more than a monument. It gave water to fields and villages in a dry country, and it remained one of the great works of Mewar's later history.

The court of Jai Singh was not a happy one in his last years. A bitter quarrel broke out between the Maharana and his eldest son, **Amar Singh**. The chronicles say the cause lay within the palace: the favour shown to a rival queen and her son, and the fear of the heir that he might be set aside. Nobles took sides, and for a time the prince was in open revolt against his father. There were armed confrontations, and Mewar seemed on the edge of civil war. In the end the senior chiefs brought about a settlement. Amar Singh remained the heir, and Jai Singh spent much of his remaining time away from the tensions of Udaipur, often at his new lake.

The quarrel left marks on Mewar. It weakened the authority of the throne over the great nobles, who had learned that they could choose between father and son. It also made Amar Singh, when his turn came, determined to set the nobility in order.

Through all of this, the wider world was changing. Aurangzeb had gone south in 1681 to fight the Marathas, and he never returned to northern India. His long war in the Deccan drained the empire of men and money. In Rajputana, the Rathores fought on, and the imperial grip loosened year by year. Jai Singh kept his peace with the empire and did not join the war again. Under him, Mewar survived not by victory but by endurance.

Jai Singh was a devout ruler, as the house of Mewar expected. He worshipped at Eklingji and gave grants to temples and Brahmins. He was also a lover of comfort, of gardens and water, and of the quiet life of the lake palaces. The bards remember him less for his wars than for the water he left behind.

He died in **1698**, at about forty-five years of age. His son Amar Singh, the same prince who had once taken up arms against him, succeeded him as **Maharana Amar Singh II**. The kingdom Jai Singh left was smaller than the one his father had held, for Pur, Mandal and Badnor were still in Mughal hands. But it was at peace, its capital was restored, and in the hills to the southeast a new sea shone where a valley had been.

## Highlights of his life

- **Heir in a time of war.** Born in 1653 to Raj Singh I, he grew up as Mewar and Marwar went to war together against Aurangzeb in defence of the infant Ajit Singh.
- **Accession in the field (1680).** He became Maharana in the hills during the Mughal occupation of Udaipur and Chittor, after his father's death.
- **The rebellion of Prince Akbar (1681).** He lived through the brief Rajput support for Aurangzeb's rebel son, which collapsed through the emperor's intrigue.
- **Peace of 1681.** He made peace with Aurangzeb through Prince Azam, ceding Pur, Mandal and Badnor in place of the jizya, and freeing Mewar of imperial armies.
- **Builder of Jaisamand.** He dammed the Gomati river and created Jaisamand (Dhebar) Lake around 1691, long counted the largest artificial lake in Asia.
- **A troubled succession.** His quarrel with his heir Amar Singh nearly brought civil war, before the nobles arranged a settlement.
- **Death (1698).** He died after an eighteen-year reign and was succeeded by his son, Amar Singh II.

amar-singh-ii.story:
## Amar Singh II — the Maharana who gave shelter to kings

*Amar Singh II is known from the chronicles of Mewar, the Mughal and Rajput records of his age, and the paintings made at his court; where tradition adds to the record, this story says so.*

In **1672**, a son was born in the palace at Udaipur to **Jai Singh**, then the heir of Mewar and the son of Maharana Raj Singh. The boy was given the name **Amar Singh**, the name of the ancestor who had made peace with Jahangir more than half a century before. It was a name with weight. The child grew up as the grandson of a reigning Maharana, in a kingdom that was still at peace with the Mughal empire but deeply uneasy about it.

He was a small boy when that peace broke. In 1679 the emperor **Aurangzeb** reimposed the jizya, and Mewar under Raj Singh joined Marwar in the defence of the infant **Ajit Singh**, heir of Jodhpur. In 1680 the Mughal armies occupied Udaipur and Chittor, and the court retreated into the hills of the Aravallis. Amar Singh's earliest memories must have been of camps in the forest, of messengers riding in with news of the war, and of the death of his grandfather in those hills in 1680. His father became Maharana in the field, and in 1681 made peace with the emperor, giving up the districts of **Pur, Mandal and Badnor** in place of the jizya. The boy came back to a capital that had been occupied and damaged.

He grew up during the long peace that followed. He was trained as a Sisodia prince in arms and horsemanship, in the worship of **Eklingji**, and in the ways of the court. But the court of his father was divided, and as Amar Singh became a young man, the divisions turned against him. The chronicles say that Maharana Jai Singh showed great favour to another queen and to her son, and that the heir came to fear that he would be pushed aside. Nobles who had their own quarrels gathered around the prince.

In the early 1690s, the quarrel broke into open revolt. Amar Singh took up arms against his father, and for a time Mewar had two centres of power. There were armed confrontations, and the kingdom stood close to civil war. The bards say that the senior chiefs, fearing for the house of Bappa Rawal, went between father and son until a settlement was made. Amar Singh remained the heir. The experience shaped him for the rest of his life. He had seen how the great nobles of Mewar could make and unmake the peace of the kingdom, and how dangerous a throne could be when its authority was not fixed.

When Jai Singh died in **1698**, Amar Singh succeeded him as **Maharana Amar Singh II**. He was about twenty-six years old.

One of his first concerns was the nobility. Mewar's great chiefs held their lands in return for military service, and their rank at court, the place where each stood or sat in the durbar, was a matter of fierce pride. Disputes over precedence could lead to bloodshed. Tradition in Mewar credits Amar Singh II with ordering the chiefs into fixed ranks, the first-class nobles known as the **Solah**, the "sixteen", and the second-class known as the **Battis**, the "thirty-two", with the duties and honours of each defined. Historians debate how much of this system was his own creation and how much he formalised what already existed. But the memory in Mewar is clear: he was the Maharana who set the nobility in order, so that the quarrels of his youth would not be repeated.

He also had to manage the empire. Aurangzeb was still alive, fighting his endless war against the Marathas in the Deccan. Amar Singh II kept the peace his father had made, and he did not take Mewar back into war. He sent his contingents and his courtesies as the treaty required. But the loss of Pur, Mandal and Badnor rankled, and the Maharana waited.

His chance came with the old emperor's death in **1707**. Aurangzeb's sons fought each other for the throne, and the victor, **Bahadur Shah I**, came north into Rajputana in 1708. The new emperor intended to tighten his hold on the Rajput states. He took over the kingdom of **Amber** from its young ruler, **Sawai Jai Singh II**, and placed it under imperial control. He sent forces into **Jodhpur**, where Ajit Singh had at last won back his father's capital, and brought Marwar to heel. Both Rajput kings were made to follow the imperial camp.

Then, during the emperor's march south towards the Deccan, Jai Singh II and Ajit Singh slipped away from the imperial camp and rode for Mewar. They came to Udaipur, two kings without kingdoms, and asked Amar Singh II for help.

The meeting of the three rulers is one of the great scenes of the age. The bards tell of the guests received with full honour by the lake, of the solemn talks in the palace above Pichola, and of the old pride of Mewar, which had never sent its own daughters into the Mughal harem, being set before the two kings as a condition. From the meeting came a **Rajput alliance of 1708** between Mewar, Amber and Marwar. The three agreed to support one another in recovering their kingdoms. Amar Singh II gave his daughter, **Chandra Kunwari**, in marriage to Jai Singh II, on the condition, recorded in the histories, that her son would succeed to the throne of Amber ahead of any elder sons by other queens. The Rajput tradition also says that the kings of Amber and Marwar promised to give no more daughters in marriage to the Mughal house.

With the help of Mewar, the two kings returned to their lands. Ajit Singh retook Jodhpur and Jai Singh II recovered Amber, while Bahadur Shah was busy with the war against his brother **Kam Bakhsh** in the south and then with the rising of the Sikhs under **Banda Singh Bahadur** in the Punjab. Faced with so many troubles, the emperor came to terms with the Rajput kings and confirmed them in their states.

The alliance of 1708 was a sign of how much had changed since the days of Akbar. The Rajput kingdoms were no longer only servants of the empire. They could now act together, and the empire had to bargain with them. Yet the alliance also carried a seed of later trouble. The promise about the succession in Amber would, a generation later, lead to a bitter war between the sons of Jai Singh II, a war that drew Mewar in and opened Rajputana to the Marathas. That future could not be seen in 1708.

In the same years, the weakening of the empire let Mewar press against the districts it had lost in 1681. Mewari chiefs began to reoccupy the lands around Pur and Mandal. The question would come to open battle only after Amar Singh's death, but the claim was renewed in his reign.

Amar Singh II was also a patron of art and building. In the **City Palace** of Udaipur, he raised the garden courtyard known as **Amar Vilas**, also called the **Badi Mahal**, at the very top of the palace, where trees and a pool are set on a natural rise of rock, so that the garden seems to float above the city. It was a place of fountains, cool air and music, and it remained one of the favourite retreats of the rulers of Mewar.

His court was a great centre of painting. The painters of Udaipur in his reign began to make large pictures of the Maharana himself: Amar Singh II in durbar with his nobles, hunting in the hills, watching festivals, or seated in his gardens with his companions. Some of these works are painted in a delicate dotted technique, and the unknown master who made them is called by art historians the **"Stipple Master"**. These paintings opened a new chapter in the art of Mewar. Where earlier artists had painted mainly scenes from religious stories and poems, the painters of Amar Singh II's court made the ruler and his world their subject, a tradition that would grow richer under his successors.

He was, by the accounts that survive, a careful and dignified ruler, quicker to negotiate than to fight, but firm on the honour of his house. He kept his kingdom out of war with the empire, yet used the empire's weakness to strengthen Mewar's place among the Rajput states. He restored order among his own nobles after the troubles of his youth.

Amar Singh II died in **1710**, at the age of about thirty-eight. His son **Sangram Singh II** succeeded him. The young Maharana inherited a kingdom at peace within, allied with its neighbours, and ready to defend the lands it had begun to take back.

## Highlights of his life

- **A childhood in wartime.** Born in 1672, he was a boy during the war of 1679–1681 against Aurangzeb, when the court of Mewar took refuge in the hills.
- **Rebellion against his father.** As heir, he quarrelled with Maharana Jai Singh and took up arms, until the senior nobles brought about a settlement.
- **Ordering the nobility.** Tradition credits him with fixing the ranks of Mewar's chiefs into the Solah and the Battis.
- **The Rajput alliance of 1708.** He sheltered Sawai Jai Singh II of Amber and Ajit Singh of Marwar at Udaipur and joined them in an alliance to recover their kingdoms.
- **Marriage of Chandra Kunwari.** He gave his daughter to Jai Singh II on the condition that her son would succeed to Amber.
- **Builder of Amar Vilas.** He raised the hanging garden courtyard, the Badi Mahal, at the top of the City Palace of Udaipur.
- **Patron of painting.** His court began the great tradition of Mewar paintings showing the ruler and his court life.

sangram-singh-ii.story:
## Sangram Singh II — the careful guardian of a fading age

*Sangram Singh II is known from the chronicles of Mewar, the histories of the late Mughal age, and the gardens and temples he left behind; where tradition adds to the record, this story says so.*

In **1690**, a son was born in the palace at Udaipur to **Amar Singh**, the heir of Mewar. The kingdom was then ruled by the boy's grandfather, **Maharana Jai Singh**, and the court was not a peaceful place. Within a few years the child's father would be in open revolt against his grandfather, and the nobles of Mewar would be divided between the two. The boy, named **Sangram Singh** after the great Rana Sanga who had fought Babur, spent his earliest years in a house of quarrels.

The quarrel ended in a settlement, and in 1698 his father became **Maharana Amar Singh II**. Sangram Singh was eight years old. He grew up in a court that his father worked hard to put in order. The ranks of the great nobles were fixed, the honours of the durbar were defined, and the authority of the throne was made firmer. The prince learned the arts of a Sisodia ruler: riding and arms, the hunt in the Aravalli hills, the worship of **Eklingji**, and the long, patient business of governing a kingdom of proud chiefs.

He also learned the politics of a changing empire. When he was seventeen, the emperor **Aurangzeb** died in the Deccan, and the Mughal empire began to come apart. In 1708 the young prince saw two kings, **Sawai Jai Singh II** of Amber and **Ajit Singh** of Marwar, come to Udaipur as fugitives from the new emperor Bahadur Shah, and saw his father make an alliance with them. His sister **Chandra Kunwari** was married to Jai Singh II as part of that alliance. Sangram Singh learned early that Mewar's strength now lay as much in negotiation as in war.

Amar Singh II died in **1710**, and Sangram Singh succeeded him as **Maharana Sangram Singh II**, at about twenty years of age.

The first test came quickly. In the war of 1679–1681, Mewar had lost the districts of **Pur, Mandal and Badnor** to the empire. As Mughal power weakened, the chiefs of Mewar had begun to take those lands back. The imperial court did not accept this. In **1711** the Mughal government granted the area to **Ranbaz Khan Mewati**, a commander in imperial service, and he marched into Mewar with his troops to take possession of it.

The young Maharana did not give way. He sent his chiefs and their followers to meet the invader, and the two forces met at **Bandanwara**, in the borderlands of Mewar. The bards tell of the Rajput horsemen charging across the rough ground, of the clash of swords in the dust, and of the Mewari chiefs fighting under the eyes of their new lord's banner. The battle ended in victory for Mewar, and Ranbaz Khan's attempt to seize the districts failed. It was a small battle by the standards of the age, but it showed that Mewar would defend its lands, and that the empire could no longer simply take them.

In the years that followed, the Mughal throne passed from hand to hand. Bahadur Shah died in 1712. **Jahandar Shah** ruled for a few months and was overthrown by **Farrukhsiyar**, who was himself a puppet of the powerful **Sayyid brothers** and was deposed and killed in 1719. After a rapid succession of short reigns, **Muhammad Shah** came to the throne in 1719 and reigned for nearly thirty years, while real power slipped steadily from Delhi to the provinces. Through all of this, Sangram Singh II kept Mewar steady. He maintained correct relations with whoever held the throne, and he guarded what Mewar held.

The real danger now came from the south. The **Marathas**, who had fought Aurangzeb for a generation, were growing into a great power. Under the Peshwa **Baji Rao I**, who took office in 1720, Maratha armies pushed north across the Narmada into Malwa and Gujarat. They demanded *chauth* and *sardeshmukhi*, shares of the revenue, from every territory they reached. In 1728 they won a major victory over the Mughal governor of Malwa at **Amjhera**. Malwa lay directly on the southern and eastern borders of Mewar, and the Maharana could see that the Maratha tide would soon reach his own lands.

Sangram Singh II was cautious. He did not have the strength to fight the Marathas alone, and the empire could no longer protect anyone. Tradition says that in his last years he spoke of the need for the Rajput rulers to stand together against this new threat. The idea would take shape after his death, at the conference of Hurda in 1734, but in Mewar it was remembered as his.

Within Rajputana, his family ties drew him into the affairs of his neighbours. His sister Chandra Kunwari had borne Jai Singh II a son, **Madho Singh**, who by the agreement of 1708 was to have a claim to the throne of Amber. The boy was raised in close connection with the court of Udaipur, and Mewar gave him the district of **Rampura** for his support. These ties of blood and land would later lead Mewar into the war over Amber's succession. In Sangram Singh's lifetime, they were a sign of the closeness between the two houses.

At home, Sangram Singh II was remembered as a ruler of order and economy. The chronicles describe him as careful with the treasury, attentive to justice, and firm with nobles who overstepped their rights. Colonel James Tod, who collected the traditions of Mewar a century later, wrote of him with respect, as one of the last rulers who maintained the dignity of the kingdom before the troubles of the later eighteenth century. The bards tell that he was strict about the forms of the court and that he would not allow the old ranks his father had set to be disturbed.

He was also a builder, and the works of his reign are among the most loved in Udaipur. North of the city, near the lake now called Fateh Sagar, he laid out a garden that came to be called **Saheliyon ki Bari**, the "garden of the maidens". Tradition says it was made for the ladies of the royal household, who came there to walk and rest away from the palace. Its lawns and shaded walks are set around pools and fountains. Marble elephants stand at the corners of the water, and the fountains, fed by the lake, still play today. In a dry land, it was a place built to celebrate water.

He also raised the **Vaidyanath temple** at **Sisarma**, near Udaipur, dedicated to Shiva. The tradition of the temple says that it was built in honour of the Maharana's mother. It is a fine example of the temple architecture of Mewar in the early eighteenth century, with a tall spire and carved halls, and it shows the devotion to Shiva that ran through every generation of Bappa Rawal's line.

His court continued the painting tradition that had flourished under his father. The painters of Udaipur made pictures of the Maharana in durbar, at worship, at festivals and on the hunt, building the great record of court life that makes eighteenth-century Mewar one of the best-pictured courts in India.

By the early 1730s, Sangram Singh II had ruled for more than twenty years. Mewar was at peace within, its borders were held, and its treasury was in good order. But the world beyond its hills was becoming more dangerous every year. The empire was hollow, the Marathas were on the frontier, and the Rajput states were too often rivals rather than allies.

Sangram Singh II died in **1734**, at about forty-four years of age. His son **Jagat Singh II** succeeded him. Within months, the new Maharana would preside over the Rajput conference at Hurda, the gathering that tried to make real the unity Sangram Singh had hoped for. The age of careful stability that Sangram Singh had guarded was ending, and an age of Maratha armies and Rajput rivalries was about to begin.

## Highlights of his life

- **Born into a divided court.** Born in 1690, he grew up through his father's quarrel with Maharana Jai Singh and the reordering of Mewar's nobility that followed.
- **Witness to the alliance of 1708.** As a young prince, he saw Mewar shelter the kings of Amber and Marwar and join them in alliance.
- **Victory at Bandanwara (1711).** Early in his reign, Mewar's forces defeated Ranbaz Khan Mewati, who had been sent to take the districts of Pur and Mandal.
- **A steady hand in a crumbling empire.** He kept Mewar stable through the rapid changes of rulers in Delhi after 1712.
- **Watchful of the Marathas.** He saw the Maratha advance into Malwa and, tradition says, urged unity among the Rajput rulers.
- **Builder of Saheliyon ki Bari and the Vaidyanath temple.** He laid out the famous garden of fountains at Udaipur and raised the Shiva temple at Sisarma.
- **A ruler of order.** He was remembered as a just and economical ruler, one of the last to keep the old dignity of Mewar, and died in 1734.

jagat-singh-ii.story:
## Jagat Singh II — the Maharana of the lake palace and the Maratha storm

*Jagat Singh II is known from the chronicles of Mewar and its neighbours, the Maratha and Mughal records of his age, and an unusually rich body of court paintings; where tradition adds to the record, this story says so.*

In **1709**, a son was born in the palace at Udaipur to **Sangram Singh**, the heir of Mewar. His grandfather **Maharana Amar Singh II** was then on the throne, and only the year before, two kings without kingdoms, Jai Singh II of Amber and Ajit Singh of Marwar, had come to Udaipur as fugitives and made an alliance with Mewar. The child was named **Jagat Singh**, after the seventeenth-century Maharana who had built the palace of Jag Mandir on Lake Pichola.

The next year his grandfather died, and his father became **Maharana Sangram Singh II**. Jagat Singh grew up through that long, steady reign. He saw his father defend Mewar's lost districts at Bandanwara in 1711, keep the kingdom calm while the Mughal throne passed through a chain of weak emperors, and build the cool garden of Saheliyon ki Bari. He was trained as every Sisodia prince was, in riding, arms and the hunt, and in the worship of **Eklingji**. He also grew up with a taste for pleasure, music and festivity that the chronicles would note again and again.

By the time he was a young man, the shape of the world was changing fast. The **Marathas**, under the Peshwa **Baji Rao I**, were pressing north into Malwa and Gujarat, demanding shares of the revenue from every land they reached. The Mughal empire could no longer defend its provinces, and the Rajput states lay open to the south.

Sangram Singh II died early in **1734**, and Jagat Singh became **Maharana Jagat Singh II** at about twenty-five years of age. Within months, he stood at the centre of the most famous attempt at Rajput unity in the eighteenth century.

In July 1734, the rulers of Rajputana gathered at **Hurda**, a village in the borderlands of Mewar. Among them were **Sawai Jai Singh II** of Amber, **Abhay Singh** of Marwar and his brother **Bakht Singh**, and the rulers or representatives of **Kota**, **Bundi** and other states. As the head of the senior Rajput house, the Maharana of Mewar presided. The bards tell of the tents of many colours spread across the plain, of the banners of the clans, and of the old rivals sitting together in council. The rulers swore to stand together against the Marathas and agreed to assemble their armies after the rains.

But the unity of Hurda did not last. Each ruler had his own interests, and some were already in negotiation with the Marathas. When the time came to march, the armies did not gather as one. The conference became a symbol, remembered with pride and with regret, of what the Rajputs might have done together and did not.

The Marathas soon came to Mewar itself. Early in **1736**, Baji Rao I marched into Rajputana and came to Udaipur. The meeting of the Peshwa and the Maharana was full of ceremony. Tradition tells of the debate over seats and precedence, for the head of the house of Bappa Rawal would not lightly accept a Brahmin minister of the Maratha king as his equal, and of how a careful arrangement was found that satisfied the pride of both. Behind the courtesies lay a hard reality. Mewar agreed to pay the Marathas an annual tribute. It was the first time in centuries that the Maharanas had agreed to pay a regular tribute to a power from the south, and it opened a door that would never fully close.

Three years later, in **1739**, the Persian ruler **Nadir Shah** invaded India, defeated the Mughal army at Karnal and sacked Delhi. The empire never recovered. In Rajputana, the lesson was clear: there was no longer any imperial power to hold the balance, and every state would have to look after itself.

Jagat Singh II looked after his pleasures as well. Between about **1743** and **1746** he built the palace of **Jag Niwas** on an island in Lake Pichola. It is the building known today as the **Lake Palace**. Rising straight from the water in white marble and stone, with courtyards, fountains, gardens and pavilions, it seemed to float on the lake. The Maharana and his court went there by boat for festivals, music and moonlit evenings. The chronicles and the paintings of his reign are full of these pleasures. More pictures were made of Jagat Singh II than of almost any other ruler of Mewar: the Maharana at the festival of Holi, at the Gangaur procession by the lake, watching elephant fights and wrestlers, hunting boar in the hills, and seated among his nobles in durbar. His painters recorded his world with a care that makes his court one of the most vivid in Indian art.

But the costs of festivity and tribute were heavy, and the politics of the age soon drew Mewar into war. In **1743** Sawai Jai Singh II of Amber died. His eldest son, **Ishwari Singh**, succeeded him. But by the agreement of 1708, Jai Singh's son by the Mewar princess **Chandra Kunwari**, **Madho Singh**, was to have the throne. Madho Singh was Jagat Singh II's cousin, raised in close connection with the court of Udaipur. The Maharana took up his cause.

At first the dispute was pursued by negotiation, then by arms. Both sides sought help, and both found that the Marathas were willing to give it for a price. In **1747**, at **Rajmahal**, the army of Ishwari Singh met the forces of the coalition that supported Madho Singh, in which Mewar's troops fought alongside those of Kota and Bundi. Ishwari Singh's army won the field, and the coalition was defeated.

Madho Singh and his allies turned to the Maratha general **Malhar Rao Holkar**. In **1748**, at **Bagru**, near Jaipur, the coalition with Maratha support pressed Ishwari Singh hard, and he was forced to make concessions to his brother. The war dragged on. At last, in **1750**, with Maratha armies at the gates of his capital and his position hopeless, Ishwari Singh took his own life. Madho Singh became the ruler of Jaipur.

Mewar had won its point: the son of a Mewar princess sat on the throne of Amber, as the agreement of 1708 had promised. But the victory was bought at a terrible price. The Marathas had been paid, and they had learned that the quarrels of the Rajput houses were a source of profit. From now on, Maratha armies would return again and again to Rajputana, taking sides in every dispute and demanding tribute from every court. The treasury of Mewar, drained by war, payments and the Maharana's own spending, was far weaker than the one his father had left.

Colonel James Tod, writing in the nineteenth century from the traditions of Mewar, judged Jagat Singh II harshly as a ruler more interested in festivals than in statecraft. The judgement is too simple. He came to the throne at the moment when the old order of northern India was collapsing, and no ruler of Mewar could have stopped the Maratha advance alone. He tried the path of Rajput unity at Hurda, and it failed. He tried the path of agreement with the Peshwa, and it cost him tribute. He fought for his cousin's cause, and won it, but at a price that weakened all of Rajputana. Yet it is also true that his court spent freely while the kingdom's position grew weaker.

He kept the devotion of his house. He worshipped at Eklingji, gave grants to temples and Brahmins, and celebrated the festivals of the year with great splendour. The paintings of his reign show a ruler who loved his city, its lakes and its seasons.

Jagat Singh II died in **1751**, at about forty-two years of age. His son **Pratap Singh II** succeeded him. The new Maharana inherited the Lake Palace and the most beautiful court in Rajputana, and with them a drained treasury, restless nobles and the Maratha armies on the horizon.

## Highlights of his life

- **Heir of a stable reign.** Born in 1709, he grew up during the careful rule of his father Sangram Singh II and succeeded him in 1734.
- **President of the Hurda conference (1734).** He presided over the gathering of Rajput rulers that swore to unite against the Marathas, an alliance that did not hold.
- **Agreement with Baji Rao I (1736).** He received the Peshwa at Udaipur and agreed to pay the Marathas an annual tribute.
- **Builder of Jag Niwas.** He built the island palace of Jag Niwas, now the Lake Palace, on Lake Pichola between about 1743 and 1746.
- **Patron of court painting.** His reign produced one of the richest records of court life in Indian art.
- **The war for Amber's succession.** He backed his cousin Madho Singh against Ishwari Singh; Mewar's forces were defeated at Rajmahal in 1747, but Madho Singh gained Jaipur in 1750 with Maratha help.
- **Death (1751).** He died after a seventeen-year reign and was succeeded by his son Pratap Singh II.
