## Pratap Singh II — three years on a burdened throne

*Pratap Singh II reigned for only about three years, and the record of his life is thin, coming mainly from the chronicles of Mewar and from what is known of his father's and his son's reigns; where tradition fills the gaps, this story says so.*

Pratap Singh was born in the palace at Udaipur during the reign of his grandfather, **Maharana Sangram Singh II**, the careful ruler who had defended Mewar's lands at Bandanwara and kept the kingdom steady while the Mughal empire weakened. His father was the heir, **Jagat Singh**, a prince who loved music, festivals and the lakes of Udaipur. The boy was given the name of the most honoured of all the rulers of Mewar, **Maharana Pratap**, who had refused to submit to Akbar. It was a name that carried great expectations, and it would fall on a prince whose life was spent in a far harder and smaller time.

He grew up as the eldest son and heir of his house. In 1734, when his grandfather died, his father became **Maharana Jagat Singh II**, and the young prince became the heir apparent of Mewar. He was trained, as every Sisodia prince was, in riding, in the sword and the lance, in the hunt in the Aravalli hills, and in the worship of **Eklingji**, the form of Shiva whom the Maharanas served as *dewan*. He would have been taught the long history of his house, from Bappa Rawal to Rana Kumbha, from Rana Sanga to the great Pratap whose name he bore.

But the history he lived through was one of decline. In the same year his father came to the throne, the rulers of Rajputana met at **Hurda** and swore to stand together against the **Marathas**. The oath did not hold. In 1736 the Peshwa **Baji Rao I** came to Udaipur, and Mewar agreed to pay the Marathas an annual tribute. In 1739 **Nadir Shah** of Persia sacked Delhi, and the Mughal empire was shown to be helpless. From then on, every Rajput state had to fend for itself.

At court, the prince watched his father spend lavishly. Jagat Singh II built the island palace of **Jag Niwas** on Lake Pichola, now known as the Lake Palace, and filled his years with festivals, processions and hunts. The painters of Udaipur recorded these pleasures in hundreds of pictures. The heir must have been present at many of these occasions, though the paintings and chronicles say little about him.

The relationship between father and son was not easy. Tradition in Mewar, preserved in the chronicles that Colonel James Tod later collected, says that Jagat Singh II grew suspicious of his heir and of the nobles who gathered around him, and that the prince was kept under close restraint for a period during his father's reign. The details are uncertain, and the cause is not clearly recorded. But the story fits a pattern that Mewar knew well. Jai Singh had quarrelled bitterly with his heir Amar Singh II, and the great nobles of Mewar had learned long before that a discontented heir could become the centre of a party at court.

Meanwhile, the affairs of Rajputana grew more dangerous. When **Sawai Jai Singh II** of Amber died in 1743, his sons **Ishwari Singh** and **Madho Singh** fought for the throne. Madho Singh's mother was a princess of Mewar, and Jagat Singh II supported his claim. Mewar's forces were part of the coalition defeated by Ishwari Singh at **Rajmahal** in 1747. The war ended only in 1750, when Ishwari Singh, besieged by Maratha armies, took his own life and Madho Singh took the throne of Jaipur. The cost to Mewar was heavy. The Marathas had been paid to intervene, and they had learned that the quarrels of the Rajput houses brought them wealth and power. The treasury of Mewar was drained.

In **1751** Jagat Singh II died, and his son became **Maharana Pratap Singh II**. He came to the throne of a kingdom very different from the one his grandfather had ruled. The court was splendid, but the treasury was weak. The great nobles were restless, having grown used to taking sides in the quarrels of the royal house. And beyond the hills, the Maratha generals, above all **Malhar Rao Holkar** and the house of **Scindia**, were now the strongest powers in northern India after the collapse of Mughal authority.

His accession followed the ancient forms of the house. By the custom of Mewar, the new ruler went to worship at the shrine of Eklingji, where the Maharanas declared themselves the servants of the god, and the great nobles came to offer their allegiance in the durbar. The old tradition that a Bhil chief marked the new Maharana's forehead with the *tika* recalled the founding alliance of Bappa Rawal with the forest people. The chroniclers record these rites for the rulers of the age in general rather than describing Pratap Singh's coronation in detail, but no Maharana took the throne without them. Standing before the image of Shiva, the new ruler would have felt the full weight of a thousand years of his line.

The kingdom he received had shrunk in strength if not in pride. Mewar's revenues came from its villages in the valleys of the Banas and its tributaries, from the trade routes that passed through its hills, and from the lands held by its chiefs. Years of war and payments had left many of those sources stretched thin.

The new Maharana's reign was short, and the chronicles record no great war or treaty of his own. What can be said is what any ruler of Mewar faced in those years. The Marathas expected the tribute agreed in 1736 to be paid, and they were quick to send troops to collect arrears. The ruler had to find money for them from a drained treasury, while keeping his own chiefs loyal and his court in order. Every decision carried the risk that one noble faction or another would turn against him, or that a Maratha army would appear on the frontier.

The bards remember Pratap Singh II as a quieter ruler than his father. Whether that was his nature, or the result of years of restraint and the weight of debts he inherited, they do not say. He kept the worship of Eklingji and the round of court ceremonies that his position required. The festivals by the lake continued, and the painters of Udaipur went on recording the life of the court, though his reign was too brief to leave the deep mark his father's had.

He had a son, **Raj Singh**, born in **1743**, while Pratap Singh was still the heir. The boy was still a child when his father became Maharana, and no doubt Pratap Singh hoped to have many years to prepare him to rule.

He did not have them. Pratap Singh II died in **1754**, after a reign of about three years. The cause of his death is not clearly recorded, and the story makes no guess. His son, then only about eleven years old, succeeded him as **Maharana Raj Singh II**.

The early death of Pratap Singh II was a misfortune for Mewar. It placed a child on the throne at the very moment when the kingdom most needed a strong and experienced ruler. Power passed into the hands of the regents and great nobles, and the Maratha generals pressed their demands on a court that could not refuse them. The decline that had begun in his father's reign continued in his son's.

Pratap Singh II is one of the least remembered rulers of Mewar. He left no great lake, no palace and no battle bearing his name. Yet his short reign marks an important point in the history of the kingdom. It was the moment when the burden of the Maratha tribute and the weakness of the treasury passed from one generation to the next, and when it became clear that Mewar's troubles could not be solved by a single ruler. His life, spent in the shadow of a splendid father and cut short before he could leave his own mark, reflects the uncertain years of mid-eighteenth-century Mewar.

## Highlights of his life

- **Named after a great ancestor.** Born in the reign of his grandfather Sangram Singh II, he carried the honoured name of Maharana Pratap.
- **Heir in a time of decline.** He grew up as heir during his father Jagat Singh II's reign, which saw the failure of the Hurda conference, the agreement to pay tribute to the Marathas and Nadir Shah's sack of Delhi.
- **A difficult relationship with his father.** Tradition says that Jagat Singh II kept him under restraint for a time out of suspicion.
- **Accession (1751).** He became Maharana after his father's death, inheriting a drained treasury, restless nobles and heavy Maratha demands.
- **A short reign.** He kept the court and the worship of Eklingji through about three difficult years.
- **Death (1754).** He died young, leaving the throne to his son Raj Singh II, who was then a child.

## Raj Singh II — the boy king in the years of the Maratha tide

*Raj Singh II came to the throne as a child and died young, so the record of his own deeds is slight; his story comes mainly from the chronicles of Mewar and the history of the Maratha advance into Rajputana. Where tradition fills the gaps, this story says so.*

In **1743**, a son was born in the palace at Udaipur to **Pratap Singh**, the heir of Mewar. The kingdom was then ruled by the child's grandfather, **Maharana Jagat Singh II**, the lover of festivals who was building the island palace of **Jag Niwas** on Lake Pichola in those very years. The boy was named **Raj Singh**, after the great seventeenth-century Maharana who had defied Aurangzeb and built the lake of Rajsamand. Like his father, he was given a name that recalled Mewar's days of strength.

The world into which he was born was far less secure than his name suggested. In the year of his birth, **Sawai Jai Singh II** of Amber died, and a war began between his sons for the throne of Jaipur. Raj Singh's grandfather supported **Madho Singh**, whose mother was a princess of Mewar, against his elder brother **Ishwari Singh**. Mewar's forces were defeated at **Rajmahal** in 1747, and the war was decided only in 1750, when Ishwari Singh took his own life as Maratha armies closed in on his capital. Madho Singh won Jaipur, but the Marathas had been paid for their help, and they had learned that the quarrels of Rajputana were a rich source of tribute.

As a small boy, Raj Singh would have known the splendour of his grandfather's court: the music on the lake, the processions of Gangaur and the festival of Holi, the elephants and horses of the durbar. He would also have heard, as the children of royal houses always did, the anxious talk of the elders about money, debts and the demands of the Maratha generals.

In 1751 his grandfather died, and his father became **Maharana Pratap Singh II**. The boy was now the heir apparent of Mewar, at about eight years of age. His father's reign was short and difficult. The treasury was drained, the nobles were restless, and the Maratha generals, above all **Malhar Rao Holkar** and the house of **Scindia**, pressed for the tribute Mewar had agreed to pay in 1736.

In **1754** Pratap Singh II died, and Raj Singh became **Maharana Raj Singh II**. He was about eleven years old.

The coronation of a child-king was a solemn and uneasy event. By the custom of Mewar, the new ruler went to the shrine of **Eklingji** to declare himself the servant of the god, and the great nobles came to offer their allegiance. Tradition kept the old rite in which a Bhil chief marked the new Maharana's forehead, recalling the founding alliance of Bappa Rawal with the forest people. The bards tell of the small figure on the great cushion of the throne, and of the faces of the chiefs, each wondering what the new reign would bring to his own house.

A boy of eleven could not govern. Real power passed into the hands of the queen mother, the ministers and the senior nobles of the court. The chronicles do not describe the regency in detail, but its shape is clear from what followed. The great chiefs of Mewar, who had long since learned to take sides in the quarrels of the royal house, now had no grown ruler above them. Each looked to his own interest. The authority of the throne, which Amar Singh II and Sangram Singh II had worked so hard to build, weakened year by year.

Meanwhile the Maratha tide rose higher. These were the years when the Maratha empire under the Peshwa **Balaji Baji Rao**, the son of Baji Rao I, reached the height of its power in the north. Maratha armies crossed Rajputana again and again on their way to Delhi and the Punjab, and every crossing brought demands for tribute and arrears. The generals of the Holkar and Scindia houses held lands and claims in Malwa and along Mewar's borders. The district of **Rampura**, which Mewar had once given to Madho Singh, had passed into Maratha hands and became part of the Holkar domains. For a court with a child ruler and an empty treasury, there was little choice but to pay what could be paid and to delay what could not.

The Mughal empire, meanwhile, had become a shadow. The emperor in Delhi was a pawn of his own ministers and of the Marathas. In the northwest, a new power had appeared: **Ahmad Shah Abdali** (Durrani), ruler of Afghanistan, who raided into the Punjab and in 1757 sacked Delhi and Mathura. The Marathas pushed into the Punjab in 1758, and a great collision between the two powers became certain.

It came on **14 January 1761**, on the field of **Panipat**, north of Delhi. The Maratha army under **Sadashivrao Bhau** met the forces of Ahmad Shah Abdali and his Indian allies. The Third Battle of Panipat ended in a terrible Maratha defeat. Tens of thousands died, among them the Peshwa's son Vishwasrao and Sadashivrao Bhau himself. The news shook all of India. For the Rajput states, it brought a brief breathing space. The Maratha power in the north was broken for a time, and the demands on the courts of Rajputana eased for a few years.

The Rajput rulers had largely stayed out of the Panipat campaign, unwilling to fight for the Marathas who had drained their treasuries, and wary of the Afghan invader as well. Mewar, with a young ruler and a divided court, was in no position to play any part. The chronicles record no action of Raj Singh II in these great events.

The young Maharana was now about seventeen, close to the age when he might take the reins of government himself. The bards say little about his character. What can be said is that he grew up in a court that was splendid in its forms but weak in its power, and that he never had the chance to show what kind of ruler he might have become.

He died in **1761**, only a few months after Panipat, at about eighteen years of age. The chronicles do not record the cause of his death clearly, and this story makes no guess. He left no acknowledged son. The throne passed to his uncle, **Ari Singh II**, a younger son of Jagat Singh II.

The death of Raj Singh II without a clear heir opened one of the darkest chapters in Mewar's history. Ari Singh II was a harsh and quarrelsome ruler, and many of the great nobles turned against him. Some of them later put forward a young man named **Ratan Singh** as a son of Raj Singh II born after his death, and therefore the rightful Maharana. The claim was fiercely disputed then and has been doubted by historians since. But it became the banner for a long civil war, which brought Maratha armies, above all those of **Mahadji Scindia**, deep into Mewar, and cost the kingdom still more land and wealth.

None of that was Raj Singh's doing. His short life fell between the decline that began in his grandfather's time and the civil wars that came after him. He inherited a kingdom already in debt to the Marathas, ruled it in name while others governed in his place, and died before he could make his own mark. His reign is remembered as a time of transition, when the old strength of Mewar slipped away and the forces that would trouble it for half a century grew in power.

Yet the institutions of the kingdom survived him. The worship of Eklingji went on, the court kept its forms, and the painters of Udaipur continued to record the life of the palace. In the long history of the house of Bappa Rawal, there had been weak reigns and child rulers before, and the kingdom had endured them. Mewar would endure this one too, and in the nineteenth century it would find its footing again.

## Highlights of his life

- **Born in his grandfather's reign (1743).** He was born at Udaipur in the reign of Jagat Singh II, in the year the war for Amber's succession began.
- **Heir of a burdened house.** He grew up as Mewar's treasury was drained by war and Maratha tribute.
- **Accession as a child (1754).** He became Maharana at about eleven after his father Pratap Singh II's death, with real power held by regents and nobles.
- **Years of the Maratha tide.** His reign saw Maratha armies crossing Rajputana and pressing Mewar for tribute.
- **The age of Panipat.** The Maratha defeat at Panipat in January 1761 brought Rajputana a brief respite near the end of his life.
- **Early death (1761).** He died at about eighteen without an acknowledged heir and was succeeded by his uncle Ari Singh II.
- **A disputed legacy.** A claimant named Ratan Singh was later put forward as his posthumous son, a claim that fuelled civil war in Mewar.

ari-singh-ii.story:
## Ari Singh II — the stern Maharana of a divided Mewar

*Ari Singh II's reign is known from the court chronicles of Mewar, the Maratha records of the period and the accounts later gathered by James Tod; where the chroniclers disagree or drift into legend, this story says so.*

In the middle of the eighteenth century, the house of Mewar was the oldest and proudest royal line in Rajputana, and one of the weakest. The great Mughal empire that its rulers had resisted for generations was breaking apart after the death of Aurangzeb in 1707, but its fall did not bring peace. Into the gap came the armies of the Marathas, sweeping north from the Deccan into Malwa and then into Rajasthan, demanding tribute, taking sides in every quarrel and leaving every quarrel more bitter than before. For Mewar, which had once defied the Mughal emperors from its hills, this new age brought a slower and more humiliating kind of danger: debt, division and the constant arrival of creditors with armies.

**Ari Singh** was born into this world as a son of **Maharana Jagat Singh II**, who ruled from 1734 to 1751. Jagat Singh was a lover of pleasure, of festivals and of fine building, and he left behind him beautiful palaces, a famous school of painting and a treasury emptied by Maratha demands. Ari Singh was a younger son. The throne went first to his elder brother, **Pratap Singh II**, whose reign lasted only three years, and then to Pratap Singh's young son, **Raj Singh II**, who came to the throne as a boy in 1754.

For most of his youth, then, Ari Singh lived as a prince who was not expected to rule. He grew up in the palaces of Udaipur, between the lake and the hills, learning to ride, to hunt and to use the sword and the lance as every Sisodia prince did. He would have heard from childhood the stories of his ancestors: of Bappa Rawal and the shrine of Eklingji, of Rana Sanga and Maharana Pratap, of the long refusal to bow before Delhi. Those stories shaped the pride of every prince of Mewar. In Ari Singh, it seems, they shaped a temper that was proud, quick and unforgiving.

Raj Singh II did not live long. He died in **1761**, still a young man, without a son to succeed him. The crown of Mewar passed to his uncle, and Ari Singh, no longer a younger son on the edges of the court, became Maharana. The chronicles agree on one thing about the new ruler: he was a man of strong will and a harsh tongue. Where his father had charmed the nobles with festivals, Ari Singh tried to command them. He demanded obedience from the great chiefs, the lords of Salumbar, Deogarh, Begun and the other fiefs, who held the real military power of the state. He spoke to them sharply, punished slights and made it clear that he regarded himself as their master.

In a kingdom where the nobles were proud men with their own forts and their own armies, this was a dangerous way to rule. The great houses of Mewar, many of them descended from the royal line itself, had always seen themselves as partners of the Maharana rather than as his servants. Within a short time, many of them came to hate the new ruler.

They soon found a weapon against him. After Raj Singh's death, one of his queens was said to have given birth to a son, who was named **Ratan Singh**. The discontented nobles declared that this boy was the rightful heir, and that Ari Singh had no right to the throne at all. Ari Singh and his supporters said that the child was an impostor, brought in from outside to serve the nobles' ambitions. The truth of Ratan Singh's birth was never settled, and historians still treat it as uncertain. But true or false, the claim divided Mewar in two. Some of the great chiefs stood by Ari Singh. Others gathered around the boy and his guardians, and soon held parts of the country in his name.

A civil war inside Mewar was exactly the kind of quarrel the Marathas knew how to use. The rebel nobles turned for help to **Mahadji Scindia**, one of the most powerful Maratha commanders of the age, whose base was at Ujjain in Malwa. They promised him money if he would place Ratan Singh on the throne of Udaipur. Mahadji, always ready to profit from the disputes of the Rajput states, accepted.

Ari Singh's loyal chiefs gathered an army and marched out to meet the threat. In **1769**, near **Ujjain**, on the banks of the Kshipra, the forces of Mewar met Mahadji Scindia's army. The battle went badly for Mewar. The Maratha troops were trained and well supplied, and the Rajput horsemen, brave as they were, could not break them. Several great lords of Mewar fell on that field, among them **Raja Umaid Singh of Shahpura**, an old warrior who had come to fight for his Maharana. The survivors fell back towards Udaipur, and the way into the heart of Mewar lay open.

Mahadji Scindia advanced and laid siege to **Udaipur** itself, bringing the pretender Ratan Singh with him. For months the city was surrounded. It was in this moment of danger that a remarkable figure took charge of its defence: the minister **Amar Chand Barwa**. He was not a warrior noble but an administrator, a man known for honesty and an iron sense of duty. The chronicles remember him as perhaps the only person in Udaipur whom the stern Maharana truly trusted and who dared to speak plainly to him.

Amar Chand organised the city's walls and garrison. He gathered grain and armed the townspeople. When money was needed to pay the soldiers, the tradition says, he did not spare even the palace's treasures. The bards like to tell of the moment when the soldiers' pay was late and he sent the household silver and gold to the mint, saying that a kingdom was worth more than its ornaments. Whether that scene happened exactly so or not, it is clear that his firmness held Udaipur together through the siege.

Udaipur did not fall, but Mewar could not win either. In the end the two sides came to terms. Ari Singh kept his throne, but at a heavy price. He agreed to pay Mahadji Scindia a vast sum of money, many lakhs of rupees, and because the treasury could not pay it at once, rich districts in the east of the kingdom, among them **Jawad** and **Nimach**, were placed in Maratha hands as security. Those lands were never recovered by Mewar. The pretender Ratan Singh was abandoned by his Maratha ally, and though his supporters went on holding parts of the country for years, his cause slowly faded.

Mewar lost land in the west as well during these troubled years. The district of **Godwar**, on the border with Marwar, passed into the hands of the Rathore rulers of Jodhpur in this period and never returned to Mewar. The kingdom that Ari Singh had inherited was smaller and poorer than ever.

Yet Ari Singh did not change his nature. If anything, defeat and betrayal made him more suspicious. He trusted few, rewarded few and punished many. He took into his service bands of mercenary soldiers, Sindhis and others from outside Mewar, because he did not trust his own nobles to defend him. These hired men had to be paid regularly, and when their wages fell behind, they too became a danger. A kingdom divided between angry nobles, unpaid mercenaries and Maratha creditors was not a kingdom at peace.

Still, the court of Udaipur did not stop living. The palaces on the lake were kept up, the festivals of Holi and Gangaur were celebrated, and the painters of the court went on producing the bright miniatures for which Mewar was famous, now often showing the Maharana himself at the hunt, in procession or in council. Ari Singh, like his ancestors, worshipped at **Eklingji** as the servant of the god who was the true lord of Mewar. Whatever his faults as a ruler, he held to the ancient forms of his house.

Hunting was the great passion of the Sisodia princes, and it was during a hunt that Ari Singh's reign came to its sudden end. In **1773**, the Maharana went on a hunting expedition in the hills near the border of **Bundi**, the kingdom of the Hada Chauhans, joined by the Bundi prince **Ajit Singh**. Somewhere in the forest, as the hunting party spread out among the trees, Ajit Singh rode up to the Maharana and struck him down with his weapon. Ari Singh died there in the forest.

Why the prince of Bundi killed the Maharana of Mewar has been told in different ways. Some accounts speak of an old grievance between the two houses over land and honour; others suggest that Ari Singh's many enemies inside Mewar were behind the deed. The bards of Mewar added a darker ending of their own: they told that Ajit Singh did not live long after the murder, and that a curse fell upon the spring hunt between the two royal houses, so that for generations the meeting of Mewar and Bundi at the chase was feared as unlucky. That curse belongs to legend, but the killing itself is history, and it left a deep wound between Udaipur and Bundi.

Ari Singh II had reigned for about twelve years. He left behind a young son, **Hamir Singh II**, still a boy, who now inherited a throne surrounded by debt, rival factions and foreign armies. The faithful minister Amar Chand Barwa would serve the boy too, as he had served the father.

History has not been kind to Ari Singh's memory. The chroniclers describe him as harsh, proud and quick to anger, a ruler whose temper turned allies into enemies. But his reign must also be seen in its time. He came to the throne of a kingdom already broken by debt and Maratha pressure, in a century when every Rajput state was being torn by civil wars and foreign intervention. He held on to Udaipur through a civil war, a lost battle and a long siege, and he did not surrender the crown of Bappa Rawal to a pretender backed by a foreign army. That, too, was a kind of courage.

## Highlights of his life

- **An unexpected Maharana.** A younger son of Maharana Jagat Singh II, he came to the throne in 1761 after the early death of his nephew Raj Singh II.
- **A stern ruler.** His harsh treatment of the great nobles turned many of them against him and split Mewar into rival camps.
- **The pretender Ratan Singh.** Rebel chiefs raised a boy said to be Raj Singh II's posthumous son as a rival claimant, plunging Mewar into civil war.
- **Defeat at Ujjain (1769).** His army was beaten by Mahadji Scindia near Ujjain, where Raja Umaid Singh of Shahpura and other lords fell.
- **The siege of Udaipur.** With the minister Amar Chand Barwa leading the defence, Udaipur held out against Scindia's siege.
- **A costly peace.** He kept his throne but paid a huge indemnity, and eastern districts such as Jawad and Nimach passed into Maratha hands for good.
- **Death at the hunt (1773).** He was killed near the Bundi border by the Bundi prince Ajit Singh, and was succeeded by his young son Hamir Singh II.

## Hamir Singh II — the boy-king of a kingdom in debt

*Hamir Singh II reigned for only five years, and he left few records of his own; his story comes to us through the chronicles of Mewar and the later accounts of James Tod, and where these are uncertain, this story says so.*

In the spring of **1773**, the people of Udaipur woke to terrible news. Their Maharana, **Ari Singh II**, had gone hunting in the hills near the border of Bundi and had not come back alive. He had been struck down in the forest by the Bundi prince Ajit Singh. The stern ruler who had held on to his throne through civil war, a lost battle and a Maratha siege was dead, and the crown of Mewar now passed to his son, **Hamir Singh II**.

Hamir Singh was still a boy. He had been born in the early years of his father's troubled reign, and he had grown up inside a palace that was never at peace. As a child he would have seen the great nobles of Mewar coming and going in anger, some loyal to his father and many against him. He would have heard the talk of the pretender **Ratan Singh**, the boy whom the rebel chiefs called the true heir. He would have lived through the months when Mahadji Scindia's army surrounded Udaipur, when the drums sounded on the walls at night and the city's grain was counted day by day. Few princes of Mewar had a childhood so full of danger.

Now he was Maharana, the *dewan* of Eklingji, heir of Bappa Rawal and of Maharana Pratap, and he had no power at all. A boy cannot command proud nobles or bargain with Maratha generals. The real government of Mewar fell into the hands of those around him: his mother, the Rajmata, who guarded her son's interests with fierce determination; the chiefs who had stood by his father; and above all the minister who had saved Udaipur in the siege, **Amar Chand Barwa**.

The coronation of the young Maharana was held with the old ceremonies. He was seated on the throne of his ancestors, the sacred mark was placed on his forehead, and the nobles came forward one by one to offer their swords and their homage. But everyone in the hall knew how weak the kingdom was. The treasury was empty. Rich districts in the east, among them Jawad and Nimach, had been handed to the Marathas in pledge for a debt that Mewar could not pay. Godwar in the west had passed to Marwar. Parts of the country were still held by the supporters of the pretender. And the Maratha chiefs, Scindia and Holkar, regarded Mewar as a source of tribute to be collected whenever their armies passed that way.

The most immediate danger came from inside the city. Ari Singh, distrusting his nobles, had brought into his service bands of mercenary soldiers, Sindhis and others from outside Mewar. These men fought for pay, and their pay was long overdue. Soon after Hamir Singh came to the throne, the mercenaries grew mutinous. They gathered in arms in the capital and demanded their arrears, threatening violence if they were not paid. For a moment it seemed that the hired defenders of the palace might become its plunderers.

It was Amar Chand who faced them. The chronicles describe how the old minister, with no money in the treasury, refused to be frightened and refused to let the soldiers dishonour the young Maharana. He gathered what funds he could, including, the bards say, his own wealth, and paid the men enough to calm them. Tradition remembers that he gave everything he owned in the service of the state, and that he died poor. Whatever the exact details, his loyalty and honesty made him one of the most respected ministers in the history of Mewar, a man whose name was praised long after the kings he served were forgotten.

Amar Chand's firmness did not please everyone at court. He was a stern man who had no patience for waste, and he quarrelled at times with the Rajmata and with the courtiers around her, who wanted the state's scarce money spent in other ways. The palace of the boy-king was full of these struggles, as factions rose and fell around the throne. Not long after the crisis with the mercenaries, Amar Chand died. With him went one of the few people strong enough to hold the court together, and the government of Mewar fell more completely into the hands of competing nobles and palace favourites.

Outside the palace, the land suffered. The countryside of Mewar in these years was poor and insecure. Maratha bands and the troops of rival chiefs moved across it, demanding money from villages and towns. Traders feared the roads. Farmers who had once paid their dues to the Maharana now paid them to whoever was strongest in their district, or fled the land altogether. The great nobles, who were supposed to serve the crown, often behaved like independent princes, quarrelling with each other and seizing the crown lands near their estates. Among them, the rivalry between the two great clans of the Mewar nobility, the **Chundawats** and the **Shaktawats**, was growing sharper, and it would tear the kingdom apart in the following reign.

Mewar was not alone in its troubles. All across Rajputana in the 1770s, the old kingdoms were weak and divided. Jaipur and Jodhpur were fighting their own battles with the Marathas and with rebellious nobles. The Mughal emperor in Delhi was now little more than a name, protected first by one power and then by another. Far to the east, a new force was rising: the English **East India Company** had won control of Bengal and was becoming the strongest power in India. In Hamir Singh's lifetime, however, the Company was still distant from Rajputana, and the forces that pressed on Mewar were the Maratha armies and its own divided nobility.

What do we know of Hamir Singh himself? Very little that is certain. He was too young to rule in his own name, and the chronicles say little about his character. The bards, who loved to praise the Maharanas, describe him as a promising prince, brave in the hunt and courteous in the court, a boy in whom the people saw the hope of better days. Like every Maharana, he would have taken part in the great rites of the kingdom: worship at **Eklingji**, the festivals of Holi and Gangaur on the lake, the formal durbars at which the nobles appeared in their robes. In the paintings of the Udaipur court from these years, the young ruler appears in the same poses as his ancestors, seated in state or riding in procession, a small figure carrying the weight of an ancient crown.

Perhaps the most important thing about his short reign is what it preserved. Despite the empty treasury, the mutinous soldiers, the Maratha demands and the quarrelling nobles, Mewar did not fall apart in these years. The throne passed peacefully from father to son and, in time, from brother to brother. The old structure of the kingdom, with the Maharana at its centre as the servant of Eklingji, survived. That survival owed much to loyal servants like Amar Chand, and to the deep respect that the people of Mewar felt for the house of Bappa Rawal, even when its rulers were weak.

But Hamir Singh did not live to grow into his power. In **1778**, after only five years on the throne, he died, still in his teens, before he had ever governed in his own right. He left no son. The crown passed to his younger brother, **Bhim Singh**, who was only about ten years old. Once again, Mewar had a child on the throne.

Bhim Singh would reign for fifty years, the longest reign in the later history of Mewar. His time would see the worst of the Maratha raids, the bloody feud between the Chundawats and the Shaktawats, the tragedy of his daughter Krishna Kumari, and finally, in 1818, the treaty with the British that brought the long age of disorder to an end. Hamir Singh II saw none of this. His reign was brief, and his name is often passed over in histories of Mewar. Yet he held the throne of his ancestors through five dangerous years, and he handed it on, unbroken, to the brother who would carry Mewar into a new age.

In the long line of Mewar's rulers, some are remembered for great battles, some for great buildings and some for great sacrifices. Hamir Singh II is remembered for something smaller and sadder: a boy who became king in a time of grief and danger, who was surrounded by debt and division, and who died before he could show what kind of ruler he might have been. His story is a reminder that the history of a kingdom is also made by those who simply kept it alive through its darkest hours.

## Highlights of his life

- **A child on the throne.** He became Maharana in 1773 as a boy, after his father Ari Singh II was killed during a hunt near the Bundi border.
- **A kingdom in debt.** He inherited a Mewar weakened by civil war, Maratha demands and the loss of districts such as Jawad, Nimach and Godwar.
- **The mutiny of the mercenaries.** Early in his reign, unpaid mercenary troops threatened the capital until they were pacified by the minister Amar Chand Barwa.
- **The loyalty of Amar Chand Barwa.** The honest minister, remembered for giving his own wealth in the service of the state, guided the young Maharana's government until his death.
- **A court of factions.** His reign saw the government divided between the Rajmata, rival nobles and palace favourites, while the Chundawat–Shaktawat rivalry grew.
- **An unbroken succession.** He died young in 1778 without a son and was succeeded by his younger brother Bhim Singh, who would rule for fifty years.

bhim-singh.story:
## Bhim Singh — the gentle Maharana of Mewar's darkest years

*Maharana Bhim Singh's long reign is known from the Mewar chronicles, the Maratha and British records, and above all from James Tod, who knew him personally; where Tod's admiration or the bards' stories go beyond the record, this story says so.*

In **1778**, a boy of about ten was seated on the throne of Mewar. His name was **Bhim Singh**, and he was the younger son of **Maharana Ari Singh II**, who had been killed during a hunt near the Bundi border five years before. His elder brother, **Hamir Singh II**, had reigned for those five years as a boy-king and had died in his teens without a son. Now the crown of Bappa Rawal passed to another child. Nobody in Udaipur could have guessed that this boy would reign for fifty years, longer than any Maharana in the later history of Mewar, and that he would live to see the kingdom fall almost to ruin and then rise again under a new order.

Bhim Singh had been born in **1768**, in the middle of his father's troubled reign, and his earliest memories were of a palace at war with itself. He had been an infant when Mahadji Scindia's army besieged Udaipur. He had been a small child when his father was killed, and a boy when the old minister Amar Chand Barwa, who had held the state together, died. When he became Maharana, the treasury was empty, the eastern districts were in Maratha hands, and the great nobles of Mewar were more powerful than the crown.

Worst of all was the feud between the two great clans of the Mewar nobility. The **Chundawats**, descended from Chunda, the prince who had given up his right to the throne in the fifteenth century, held the first place among the nobles, led by the house of **Salumbar**. The **Shaktawats**, descended from Shakti Singh, the brother of Maharana Pratap, were their great rivals, led by the house of **Bhinder**. In Bhim Singh's youth, the rivalry between these clans grew into open war. Each side tried to control the young Maharana and the government in his name, and each used the other's power as a reason to seize land, forts and revenues.

For the first years of his reign, Bhim Singh was in the hands of the Chundawats. When he grew older and tried to escape their control, he turned for support to the Shaktawats and to a capable minister, **Somchand Gandhi**, who tried to restore the authority of the crown. The struggle that followed was bloody. Somchand was murdered by his enemies inside the palace itself, and the Chundawats, in rebellion, seized the great fortress of **Chittor**, the ancient heart of Mewar.

The young Maharana could not recover Chittor by his own strength. In **1791**, the great Maratha leader **Mahadji Scindia** came into Mewar, and with his help the rebels were forced to give up the fortress. But Maratha help always came at a price. Scindia left behind his officer **Ambaji Inglia** to manage the affairs of Mewar, and for years the Maratha agents collected the kingdom's revenues, paid themselves first, and treated the Maharana as their pensioner.

The years around 1800 were the darkest that Mewar had known since the wars with the Mughals. The Maratha chiefs, Scindia and **Holkar**, fought each other across Rajputana, and both demanded money from Mewar. Behind them came the **Pindaris**, bands of freebooting horsemen who lived by plunder, and the adventurer **Amir Khan**, whose army of mercenaries hired itself out to whichever prince would pay and robbed all the others. Villages were burned and abandoned. Trade died on the roads. Whole districts of Mewar returned to jungle, and the revenues of the crown fell to a small fraction of what they had once been. The Maharana of Mewar, heir of the proudest house in India, was at times so poor that he could barely keep up his household.

In the middle of this ruin came the tragedy for which Bhim Singh's reign is best remembered. His daughter, **Krishna Kumari**, was famous throughout Rajputana for her beauty and grace. As a child she had been betrothed to the ruler of Jodhpur, but he died before the marriage. A new proposal came from **Maharaja Jagat Singh of Jaipur**, and Bhim Singh accepted it. But the new ruler of Jodhpur, **Maharaja Man Singh**, declared that the princess's hand belonged to the throne of Jodhpur, and that he would not allow her to marry his rival.

The quarrel over Krishna Kumari became a war between Jaipur and Jodhpur, the two greatest states of Rajputana. Armies marched, Amir Khan and other mercenaries joined in, and the land between them was ravaged. Mewar, too weak to defend itself, was caught in the middle. In **1810**, Amir Khan, now with his army in Mewar, pressed the Maharana with a cruel choice: either the princess must marry Man Singh of Jodhpur, or she must die, so that the war over her would end.

What happened next is told with deep sorrow in the chronicles and in Tod's pages. It was decided that Krishna Kumari must die to save Mewar from further destruction. She was about sixteen years old. She was given poison. Tradition says that she received the cup calmly, comforted her weeping mother, and drank it, saying that she was a daughter of the Rajputs and was not afraid of death. Her mother, the story goes, died of grief soon afterwards. Some of the nobles of Mewar never forgave those who had advised the deed. Whatever the exact words spoken in the palace that day, the death of Krishna Kumari became a symbol of how far the ancient house of Mewar had fallen: unable to protect even the life of its own princess.

The end of this age of disorder came from an unexpected direction. By the second decade of the nineteenth century, the English **East India Company** had become the strongest power in India. In 1817 it went to war against the Pindaris and the Maratha chiefs, and it invited the Rajput states to accept its protection. One after another, they agreed. On **13 January 1818**, Mewar signed a treaty with the Company. Mewar would accept British protection and pay a yearly tribute, and in return the Company would protect the kingdom from outside attack and leave the Maharana as ruler of his own state. The Maratha claims on Mewar were ended.

A few weeks later, the first British Political Agent arrived in Udaipur. He was **Captain James Tod**, a soldier and scholar who loved Rajputana and its history. Tod found a kingdom in ruins. He set to work to restore the Maharana's authority: he persuaded the great nobles to give back the crown lands they had seized, settled the quarrels between them, brought back farmers and traders, and helped to revive towns such as **Bhilwara**, which had been almost deserted. Within a few years, the revenues of Mewar had begun to recover.

Tod came to know Bhim Singh well, and he described him with real affection. He wrote of a ruler who was gentle, courteous, deeply devoted to his faith and to the traditions of his house, generous to a fault and sincerely loved by his people. He also wrote, honestly, that the Maharana lacked firmness: he could not refuse a request, could not control his spending and could not stand up to the strong men around him. His court was famous for its festivals and ceremonies, which went on even in the poorest years. In Tod's great work, the *Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan*, much of what we know of Mewar's history was first gathered from the bards, chronicles and conversations of Bhim Singh's court.

The Maharana's love of beauty and ceremony is visible in the **City Palace** of Udaipur. The chamber known as **Bhim Vilas**, named after him, is decorated with glass inlay and paintings, and the painters of his court produced a great body of work showing festivals, processions, hunts and the Maharana at worship. Like all his ancestors, Bhim Singh ruled as the *dewan* of **Eklingji**, and his devotion to the god of Mewar was sincere throughout his life.

The last years of his reign were more peaceful than any he had known. The danger of Maratha armies and Pindari raids was gone. But the new order brought its own difficulties. The tribute to the Company was heavy, the nobles resented the loss of the lands they had seized, and the debts of the court kept growing. After Tod left India in the 1820s, the troubles of Mewar's finances returned, and the British agents began to press the Maharana to cut his spending.

Bhim Singh died in **1828**, after a reign of half a century. He had many children, but several of his sons died before him, and he was succeeded by his son **Jawan Singh**. His reign had begun in the depths of disorder and ended in the first years of British supremacy. He had not been a great warrior or a strong ruler, and he had lived through humiliations his ancestors would have found hard to bear. But he had kept the throne of Bappa Rawal, kept the faith and dignity of his house, and seen Mewar survive the worst century in its history.

## Highlights of his life

- **A child-king (1778).** He became Maharana at about ten years old, after the death of his brother Hamir Singh II.
- **The Chundawat–Shaktawat feud.** His early reign was torn by the war between the two great noble clans, in which the minister Somchand Gandhi was killed and Chittor seized by rebels.
- **Recovery of Chittor (1791).** With Mahadji Scindia's help the fortress was recovered, though Mewar then fell under the control of Maratha agents such as Ambaji Inglia.
- **The tragedy of Krishna Kumari (1810).** His daughter, sought by both Jaipur and Jodhpur, was given poison to end the war over her hand.
- **Treaty with the East India Company (1818).** On 13 January 1818 Mewar accepted British protection, ending the age of Maratha and Pindari raids.
- **Revival under James Tod.** With the Political Agent James Tod, the crown lands were restored and the ruined countryside began to recover.
- **Patron of court arts.** The Bhim Vilas of the City Palace and a rich body of court painting date from his long reign, which ended with his death in 1828.

jawan-singh.story:
## Jawan Singh — a Maharana in the shadow of the Company

*Maharana Jawan Singh's reign is thinly recorded beyond the Mewar chronicles and the reports of the British Political Agents at Udaipur; this story follows what those sources tell, and where the record is silent or uncertain, it says so.*

When **Jawan Singh** was born in **1800**, the kingdom of Mewar was close to ruin. His father, **Maharana Bhim Singh**, had been on the throne for more than twenty years, and in all that time the country had known little but war, debt and plunder. Maratha armies under Scindia and Holkar crossed the land demanding tribute. Pindari horsemen burned villages. The great nobles of Mewar, divided between the rival clans of the Chundawats and the Shaktawats, fought each other and seized the crown's lands. The palace at Udaipur, rising white above Lake Pichola, was still beautiful, but the treasury behind its walls was nearly empty.

Jawan Singh grew up in that palace in the last and worst years of the disorder. He was a boy of ten in **1810**, when his half-sister **Krishna Kumari**, the princess sought in marriage by both Jaipur and Jodhpur, was given poison so that the war over her hand might end. The grief of that event hung over the court for years. Every child of the royal household learned from it how weak Mewar had become, unable even to protect its own daughters.

Then, when Jawan Singh was about eighteen, the world changed. In **January 1818**, his father signed a treaty with the English **East India Company**. Mewar accepted British protection and agreed to pay a yearly tribute; in return, the Company promised to defend the kingdom and leave the Maharana as master of his own state. Within weeks the first British Political Agent, **James Tod**, arrived in Udaipur. The Maratha claims were ended, the Pindaris were destroyed, and for the first time in Jawan Singh's life, the roads of Mewar were safe.

The young prince thus came of age in a new kind of kingdom. His father's court was still the court of an ancient Rajput monarchy, with its bards, its festivals, its painters and its rituals at the shrine of **Eklingji**. But beside it now stood the Residency of the British agent, whose advice could not be ignored. Tod persuaded the nobles to return the crown lands they had seized, brought farmers back to the deserted villages and helped revive trade. For a few years, Mewar's fortunes rose. Tod left India in the early 1820s, but he did not forget Udaipur. In England he wrote his great *Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan*, built from the chronicles, bardic songs and conversations he had gathered at Bhim Singh's court, and its volumes appeared in 1829 and 1832, during Jawan Singh's own reign. Through that book, the story of Mewar, of Bappa Rawal, Padmini, Rana Sanga and Maharana Pratap, became known far beyond India, at the very moment when the kingdom itself had lost its old independence.

Several of Bhim Singh's sons died before their father, and Jawan Singh became heir to the throne. When Bhim Singh died in **1828**, after a reign of fifty years, Jawan Singh succeeded him as Maharana at the age of about twenty-eight. He was seated on the throne of Bappa Rawal with the ancient ceremonies, received the homage of the nobles, and took up the title of *dewan* of Eklingji, servant of the god who was the true lord of Mewar.

He inherited a kingdom at peace, but not a kingdom free of trouble. The greatest problem was money. The treaty of 1818 required Mewar to pay the Company a share of its revenue as tribute, and this burden was heavy for a country still recovering from decades of ruin. At the same time, the court had old debts to bankers, the household of the royal family was large and expensive, and the habits of spending formed in Bhim Singh's long reign did not change. Soon after Jawan Singh's accession, the tribute fell into arrears.

The chronicles and the British reports agree that Jawan Singh was not a strict administrator. He was remembered as a generous, pleasure-loving ruler, fond of music, festivals and the life of the court, and devoted in his worship. Like his father, he found it hard to refuse a request or to cut the expenses of his household. His critics among the British officers wrote of extravagance and of a court in which favourites and officials enriched themselves while the treasury fell further behind. These reports must be read with care, since the British agents had their own reasons to press the Maharana; but the problem of debt was real, and it shaped his whole reign.

The British response was to interfere more and more in the affairs of the state. The Political Agents at Udaipur pressed the Maharana to reduce his spending and to give the management of the finances to ministers they trusted. At times, they took an active hand in arranging the revenue and the payment of the tribute. For a Maharana of Mewar, heir of a line that had refused for centuries to bow before Delhi, this was a painful position. He remained the ruler in name and in ceremony, but in the matters that mattered most, the money and the relations with outside powers, he was no longer free.

Jawan Singh also had to manage the great nobles, who had never forgiven the loss of the lands Tod had made them return. Disputes over their duties to the crown, over the service they owed and the lands they held, ran on through his reign, and the British agents were often asked to settle them. The old feud between the Chundawats and the Shaktawats had cooled, but the nobility as a whole remained proud, restless and jealous of its rights.

In **1832**, the Governor-General of India, **Lord William Bentinck**, came to **Ajmer**, in the heart of Rajputana, and held a great durbar there. The Rajput princes were invited to meet him, and Jawan Singh was among them. For the Maharana of Mewar, the meeting with the head of the British government in India was a sign of the new order of things: the rulers of Rajputana now dealt not with Mughal emperors or Maratha generals, but with the representatives of a distant company of merchants that had become the master of India.

Of Jawan Singh's private life and character, the records say less than we would like. The court painters of Udaipur continued to work in his reign, and paintings from these years show the Maharana at festivals, on the lake, in procession and at worship, in the bright style for which Mewar was famous. The traditions of the palace remember him as a devout ruler who spent freely on religious gifts and ceremonies. He kept up the festivals of **Gangaur** and **Holi**, when the city came down to the shores of Pichola and the boats of the royal household moved across the water lit by lamps. In this he followed his ancestors, for whom such festivals were not only pleasures but duties of kingship.

What he did not leave behind was an heir. Jawan Singh had no son, and as his health failed, the old question that had troubled Mewar so often returned: who would sit on the throne of Bappa Rawal next? He died in **1838**, after a reign of about ten years, when he was still a man in his late thirties.

After his death, a successor was chosen from a branch of the royal family. **Sardar Singh**, from the house of **Bagor**, a line descended from an earlier Maharana, was adopted and placed on the throne. His reign was short, lasting only until 1842, and he too left no son. He was followed by his younger brother, **Swarup Singh**, who would reign for nearly twenty years and lead Mewar through the great revolt of 1857.

History has usually passed over Jawan Singh quickly. He fought no famous battles, built no great fortress and left no great reform. His reign was a time of transition, when the old independence of Mewar gave way to life under British supremacy, and when the debts of the past weighed heavily on the present. Yet his years were also years of peace, after decades of war, in which the villages of Mewar were rebuilt and the people of the kingdom could once again plant their fields without fear of raiders. For a land that had suffered as Mewar had, that peace was no small thing.

## Highlights of his life

- **Born in an age of ruin (1800).** He grew up during the worst years of Maratha and Pindari raids and the tragedy of his half-sister Krishna Kumari.
- **Witness to the treaty of 1818.** As a young prince he saw his father accept British protection, ending decades of disorder.
- **Accession (1828).** He succeeded his father Bhim Singh after a fifty-year reign, inheriting a kingdom at peace but burdened by debt.
- **The burden of tribute.** The yearly tribute to the East India Company fell into arrears, and British agents pressed for control of the state's finances.
- **Meeting with Lord William Bentinck (1832).** He was among the Rajput princes who met the Governor-General at Ajmer.
- **A devout and generous court.** He kept up the festivals, religious gifts and court painting of the Udaipur tradition.
- **Death without an heir (1838).** He died childless and was succeeded by Sardar Singh of Bagor, and then by Sardar Singh's brother Swarup Singh.

swarup-singh.story:
## Swarup Singh — the careful Maharana who saw the storm of 1857

*Maharana Swarup Singh's reign is documented in the Mewar chronicles, the later court history Vir Vinod, and the reports of the British Political Agents; where tradition adds to these, this story says so.*

In **1815**, when **Swarup Singh** was born, nobody expected him to become Maharana of Mewar. He was not a son of the ruling Maharana, **Bhim Singh**, but a child of the house of **Bagor**, a branch of the royal family descended from an earlier Maharana, Sangram Singh II. The Bagor princes lived close to the throne, with their own estates and their own place in the court of Udaipur, but they were cousins of the ruling line, not its heirs. Swarup Singh grew up as a younger son of that house, educated in the arts of a Rajput nobleman: horsemanship, arms, the traditions of his clan and the worship of **Eklingji**.

The world he grew up in was changing fast. Three years after his birth, in 1818, Mewar signed a treaty with the English **East India Company**, accepting British protection and agreeing to pay a yearly tribute. The decades of Maratha and Pindari raids came to an end, and a British Political Agent took up residence in Udaipur. Peace returned to the countryside, but the court remained deep in debt, and the British agents watched its finances closely.

Then, in the space of a few years, the line of the Maharanas failed twice. **Maharana Jawan Singh**, Bhim Singh's son and successor, died in **1838** without a son. To fill the throne, the court turned to the house of Bagor and chose Swarup Singh's elder brother, **Sardar Singh**, who was adopted into the main line. Sardar Singh's reign lasted only four years. He too had no son, and before his death in **1842**, he adopted his younger brother as his heir. So it was that Swarup Singh, a cousin from a side branch, came to sit on the throne of Bappa Rawal at the age of about twenty-seven.

The kingdom he inherited was at peace, but it was poor and weighed down by debt. The tribute to the British was often in arrears; the household of the court was large and expensive; officials and favourites had grown rich at the treasury's cost. Swarup Singh's first great task was to bring order to the finances of Mewar, and it is for this above all that he is remembered. Unlike his two predecessors from the main line, he was a careful, economical and strong-willed ruler. He cut down the expenses of the court, examined the accounts himself, dismissed corrupt officials and pressed for the collection of revenue that had been neglected. Slowly, the debts of the state were reduced, and the arrears of tribute were paid.

He also took a close interest in the coinage of his kingdom. During his reign, Udaipur minted new coins in his name, known as **Swarupshahi** coins, which became the standard money of Mewar for many years. Some of these coins, struck in the later part of his reign, carried an inscription proclaiming friendship with London, a small sign of the new alliance under which the kingdom now lived.

His firmness brought him into conflict with the great nobles of Mewar. Since Tod's time, the nobles had been made to return the crown lands they had seized, but they still held large estates and a strong sense of their rights. Swarup Singh demanded that they perform the military service and pay the dues they owed for their lands, and he tried to reduce the privileges that had grown up during the years of disorder. The nobles resisted, and for years there were bitter disputes between the Maharana and his chiefs. The British Political Agents were drawn in again and again to mediate, and agreements were drawn up to define what the nobles owed to the crown. These struggles did not end in his lifetime, but he showed that a Maharana could still stand up to the most powerful men in the kingdom.

Swarup Singh was also a builder. In Udaipur, he created the lake known as **Swarup Sagar**, which joins the waters of Lake Pichola with the lakes to the north, helping to manage the precious water of the city. In a land of hot summers and uncertain rains, such works were among the most valuable gifts a ruler could leave behind, and the lake still bears his name.

The old life of the court went on around these works. Swarup Singh kept the festivals of Gangaur and Holi on the lake, received the nobles in formal durbar, and worshipped at Eklingji as the *dewan* of the god, as every Maharana had done before him. Mewar was also home to **Nathdwara**, where the image of **Shrinathji**, brought from Braj in the seventeenth century, drew pilgrims from all over western India, and the Maharanas were its protectors. The painters of Udaipur continued to record the ruler's life in bright, detailed pictures, now and then showing, beside the familiar scenes of hunts and processions, the figures of British officers who had become part of the court's world.

In his reign, too, the British government in India began to press the princely states to end certain old customs. Under this pressure, orders were issued in Mewar against **female infanticide**, against the sale of children and against the persecution of women accused of witchcraft, who were sometimes tortured or killed by frightened villagers. On the old practice of **sati**, the burning of widows on their husbands' funeral pyres, Swarup Singh was more reluctant. The British had banned it in their own territories in 1829 and urged the Rajput rulers to do the same, but the Maharana, holding to the traditions of his house, long resisted a formal ban.

Then came the great storm of **1857**. In May of that year, Indian soldiers of the Company's army rose in revolt at Meerut, and within weeks the rising had spread across northern and central India. In early June, the troops at the British cantonment of **Neemuch**, on the eastern edge of Mewar, mutinied. The British officers and their families fled for their lives towards Udaipur, with the Political Agent of Mewar, **Captain Showers**, helping to bring the refugees to safety.

The Maharana now faced a difficult choice. Many in India saw the revolt as a chance to throw off British rule, and some among the nobles of Mewar sympathised with the rebels. But Swarup Singh had bound his kingdom to the treaty of 1818, and he chose to keep his word. He received the British refugees and housed them on the island palace of **Jag Mandir**, in the middle of Lake Pichola, where they were safe from attack. He supplied them with food and protection, and contingents of Mewar troops were sent to help the British restore order in the region around Neemuch.

Not all of Mewar followed its ruler. The tradition remembers that some nobles gave shelter to rebel leaders, among them the Thakur of **Auwa** from Marwar, who is said to have found refuge with a Mewar chief after his own rising failed. In **1858**, the rebel general **Tantia Tope** passed through parts of Mewar with his army, pursued by British columns, and the countryside was disturbed for months. Through all of this, Swarup Singh stayed loyal to the treaty, and when the revolt was crushed, the British remembered his help.

The years after 1857 brought a new order. The East India Company was abolished, and India passed under the direct rule of the British Crown. Queen Victoria's proclamation of 1858 promised to respect the rights and dignity of the Indian princes, and the threat that their states might be taken away for lack of a natural heir was lifted. For Mewar, which had so often struggled to find an heir, this promise mattered greatly: the princes were now allowed to adopt successors freely.

Swarup Singh had no son of his own. Like his brother before him, he adopted an heir from the Bagor branch of the family, a boy named **Shambhu Singh**. In **1861**, after a reign of nearly twenty years, the Maharana fell ill and died. Tradition remembers that at his funeral a woman of his household gave her life on his pyre, and his death is often named as the last time a sati took place at the funeral of a Maharana of Mewar. Soon afterwards, under the regency that governed for the young Shambhu Singh, the practice was formally forbidden in Mewar.

Swarup Singh was not a conqueror and did not fight great battles. His achievements were quieter: a treasury brought back from ruin, a kingdom kept loyal to its word in a time of revolt, a lake that still serves Udaipur, and a line of succession preserved. He was the first ruler of the Bagor branch to leave a lasting mark, and the strong, careful style of government he began would be carried further by his successors.

## Highlights of his life

- **A prince from the Bagor branch.** Born in 1815 into a cadet line of the royal family, he came to the throne in 1842 as the adopted heir of his brother Sardar Singh.
- **Restoring the treasury.** He cut the court's expenses, punished corrupt officials and reduced the debts and tribute arrears of the state.
- **The Swarupshahi coinage.** New coins struck in his name became the standard money of Mewar.
- **Swarup Sagar.** He built the lake in Udaipur that bears his name and links Lake Pichola with the lakes to the north.
- **Firm with the nobles.** He pressed the great chiefs to perform their service and pay their dues, leading to long disputes mediated by the British.
- **Social measures.** Orders were issued in his reign against female infanticide, the sale of children and the persecution of women accused of witchcraft.
- **Loyalty in 1857.** He sheltered British refugees from Neemuch on the island palace of Jag Mandir and kept Mewar bound to its treaty.

shambhu-singh.story:
## Shambhu Singh — the young Maharana who opened Mewar to a new age

*Maharana Shambhu Singh's reign is recorded in the Mewar court histories, above all the Vir Vinod compiled under his successor, and in the reports of the British Political Agents; where tradition adds to these, this story says so.*

In **1847**, a son was born in the house of **Bagor**, the branch of the royal family of Mewar that stood closest to the throne. He was named **Shambhu Singh**, after Shambhu, one of the names of Shiva, the god whom the rulers of Mewar served as Ekalinga. Like the other Bagor princes, he was born a cousin of the ruling line, not its heir. But in the nineteenth century, the main line of the Maharanas had twice failed to produce a son, and the Bagor house had already given Mewar two rulers: **Sardar Singh**, who reigned from 1838 to 1842, and his brother **Swarup Singh**, who followed him.

Swarup Singh, too, had no son. As he grew older, he looked among the young princes of his own family for an heir, and his choice fell on Shambhu Singh. The boy was adopted as the successor to the throne of Bappa Rawal. He grew up in the palaces of Udaipur, in the last years of a ruler known for his firmness, his careful management of the treasury and his loyalty to the British during the great revolt of 1857. As a child of ten, Shambhu Singh would have seen the British refugees from Neemuch rowed out to the island palace of **Jag Mandir**, where his adoptive father had given them shelter.

In **1861**, Swarup Singh died, and Shambhu Singh became Maharana at the age of about fourteen. He was too young to govern. Under the new order that followed the revolt, India was now ruled directly by the British Crown, and the government of a minor prince's state was placed in the hands of a **regency council** of Mewar nobles and officials, working under the close supervision of the British Political Agent. For four years, this council governed Mewar in the young Maharana's name.

The regency began with a change that marked the end of an old world. At Swarup Singh's funeral, tradition remembers, a woman of his household had died on his pyre, and his death is often named as the last time a sati took place at the funeral of a Maharana of Mewar. Soon after, the regency council, pressed by the British, formally forbade the practice of **sati** throughout Mewar. Other old customs were also forbidden, and the work of building a modern administration began.

While the council governed, the young Maharana studied. His education was planned with care, combining the traditional learning of a Rajput prince with the new knowledge that the British considered necessary for a ruler of the age. He learned to ride and to use arms, studied the history and religion of his house, and received lessons in English, in administration and in the affairs of the wider world. In **1865**, when he was about eighteen, he was given full powers as ruler of Mewar.

Shambhu Singh's reign as a ruling prince lasted less than ten years, but they were busy years. Building on the order that Swarup Singh had brought to the treasury, he and his ministers began to reshape the government of Mewar along new lines. Departments were created to handle revenue, justice, the police and public works. A central office of government, the **Mahakma Khas**, was set up to bring the business of the state under one roof. Courts of justice were organised, and the rules for collecting land revenue were made more regular, so that farmers would know what they owed and officials could not demand more at will.

The young Maharana took a special interest in education. In his reign, schools were opened in Udaipur where boys could learn not only Hindi and Sanskrit but also English and the modern subjects. The best known of these was the school named after him, which later grew into one of the important institutions of the city. Dispensaries were opened to bring Western medicine to the people, and roads were built to link Udaipur with the British cantonments and the towns of the plains. For a kingdom that had been almost cut off from the world by its hills, these were the first steps into a new age.

Not everything in his reign was progress. In **1868 and 1869**, the rains failed across Rajputana, and one of the worst famines of the century swept the land. Crops withered in the fields, wells dried up, and cattle died in great numbers. Thousands of people left their villages in search of food, and many died on the roads. The government of Mewar opened relief works, distributed grain and tried to protect the poorest, but the means of a small state were limited, and the famine left deep scars on the countryside. It was a hard lesson in the limits of the new administration, and it showed how much still remained to be done.

The court histories describe the young ruler as earnest and open to new ideas, willing to listen to his ministers and to the British officers, yet anxious that the changes should not wound the pride of his house. It was not an easy balance. Every reform touched someone's old rights: the officials who had grown used to collecting fees as they pleased, the nobles who disliked the new courts, the priests and elders who distrusted the new schools. Shambhu Singh moved carefully, often slowly, but he kept moving, and the direction of his reign was clear.

Like his predecessor, Shambhu Singh had to deal with the great nobles of Mewar, who still guarded their old privileges jealously. The disputes over the service and dues they owed to the crown, which had troubled Swarup Singh's reign, continued in his. The young Maharana tried to settle them through negotiation rather than force, with the British Political Agents again acting as mediators. He did not resolve the quarrel entirely, but he kept the peace between the crown and its chiefs.

He remained, at the same time, a faithful heir to the traditions of his house. He worshipped at **Eklingji** as the *dewan* of Shiva, the true lord of Mewar, and his very name was a sign of that devotion. He was a generous patron of temples and of religious festivals, and the court of Udaipur continued to celebrate **Gangaur**, **Holi** and the other great feasts of the year with the old splendour. The painters of the court went on recording the life of the Maharana, now sometimes alongside the new art of photography, which arrived in Udaipur in these years.

Shambhu Singh also left his mark on the great **City Palace** of Udaipur. The part of the palace known as **Shambhu Niwas**, built in his reign, became one of the principal residences of the royal family. Its rooms, looking out over Lake Pichola, mixed the old style of Rajput palaces with new fashions of decoration, much as his reign mixed the traditions of Mewar with the ideas of a new century. Shambhu Niwas remains part of the palace today.

The British government valued the young Maharana's cooperation, and he received high honours from the Crown, among them the insignia of the **Order of the Star of India**. For the ruler of a house that had once refused to send its princes to the Mughal court, these honours were a sign of how much the world had changed. Yet within his own kingdom, Shambhu Singh was still the Maharana, heir of Bappa Rawal and Maharana Pratap, and the old forms of the throne were carefully preserved.

His life was cut short. In **1874**, at the age of only about twenty-seven, Shambhu Singh fell ill and died. Like his two predecessors from the Bagor line, he left no son. Once again, the court of Udaipur turned to the Bagor house, and his young cousin, **Sajjan Singh**, a boy of about fifteen, was chosen to succeed him. Sajjan Singh would carry forward the work of reform, and under him the great history of Mewar, the *Vir Vinod*, would be written.

Shambhu Singh's reign was short, and it is easy to overlook. But in those thirteen years, Mewar changed more than it had in the century before. Sati was forbidden, schools and dispensaries were opened, courts and departments of government were set up, and the kingdom took its first steps into the modern world. The young Maharana who began his reign as a boy under a regency council left behind a state that was beginning to be governed in a new way, while still keeping faith with the god and the traditions that had defined Mewar for more than a thousand years.

## Highlights of his life

- **An heir from Bagor.** Born in 1847 in the Bagor branch of the royal family, he was adopted by Maharana Swarup Singh and succeeded him in 1861.
- **The regency and the end of sati.** During his minority a regency council governed Mewar, and the practice of sati was formally forbidden.
- **Full powers (1865).** He took up the government himself at about eighteen and began a programme of administrative reform.
- **A modern administration.** Departments of revenue, justice, police and public works were organised, along with a central office of government, the Mahakma Khas.
- **Schools and dispensaries.** He opened schools teaching English and modern subjects, and dispensaries offering Western medicine, in Udaipur.
- **The famine of 1868–69.** His government opened relief works and distributed grain during one of the worst famines of the century in Rajputana.
- **Shambhu Niwas.** He built the Shambhu Niwas in the City Palace of Udaipur, which became a principal residence of the royal family.
