sajjan-singh.story:
## Sajjan Singh — the young Maharana who opened Mewar to a new age

*Sajjan Singh's short reign is well recorded, in the state's own papers, in the British political reports on Rajputana, and above all in the great history his court poet Shyamaldas wrote at his command. Where tradition adds colour to the record, this story says so.*

In the autumn of **1874**, the court of Udaipur faced a question it had faced many times before. **Maharana Shambhu Singh** had died on 7 October, still a young man, and he left no son. The throne of Bappa Rawal and Rana Pratap could not stand empty, and in the old way of Mewar the choice of an heir fell to the leading nobles of the state, watched closely now by the British Political Agent who sat at Udaipur.

The choice fell on a boy of fifteen. **Sajjan Singh** had been born on **8 July 1859**, the son of **Maharaj Shakti Singh** of **Bagore**, a cadet branch of the ruling house descended from the Maharanas themselves. He was a cousin of the dead ruler, close enough in blood to be a natural heir and young enough to be shaped for the throne. On **8 October 1874**, a single day after Shambhu Singh's death, he was seated on the *gaddi* of Mewar.

It was not a calm beginning. Succession in a house without a direct heir always stirred old rivalries, and there were kinsmen and nobles who felt that their own claims, or their own counsel, had been passed over. The young Maharana also inherited a kingdom that had changed greatly in the half-century since Mewar signed its treaty with the East India Company in **1818**. The days when a Maharana could ride out at the head of his clans were over. Peace was guaranteed by the British, but that peace came with a Political Agent at the court, a careful eye on every appointment, and a steady pressure to govern in new ways.

Because Sajjan Singh was a minor, a council of regency managed the state for the first part of his reign, under the supervision of the Political Agent. The boy was not idle in these years. Those who knew him describe a quick, eager, curious mind. He read widely, listened to scholars, and asked questions about everything: about revenue and law, about the machines and newspapers of the outside world, about the history of his own house. He was soon given the full powers of a ruler, and he used them with energy.

The outside world came to meet him early. In **1875** the Prince of Wales, the future King Edward VII, made his long tour of India, and the young Maharana travelled to **Bombay** to meet him. Two years later, on **1 January 1877**, the Viceroy **Lord Lytton** held the great Imperial Assemblage at **Delhi**, where Queen Victoria was proclaimed Empress of India before the assembled princes. Sajjan Singh attended. For a Maharana of Mewar, whose ancestors had refused to stand in the Mughal court at Delhi, this was a strange and uneasy honour. The bards of Mewar never forgot that the house of Udaipur had kept its pride when others bowed, and the young ruler carried that memory with him even as he took his place in the new imperial order.

He chose to meet the new age rather than retreat from it. Over the following years Sajjan Singh reshaped the government of his state. He set up a council of state, the **Mahendraj Sabha**, around **1880**, to hear the most important judicial cases and advise him on matters of law, bringing the great nobles and the officials of the state together in one body. He reorganised the courts, departments and offices of the capital, so that justice and revenue would rest on written rules rather than on the will of whoever happened to hold power in a district. Work began on a survey and settlement of land revenue, a slow and difficult task in a state where village rights, noble estates and temple lands had grown together over centuries.

The capital itself began to change. Udaipur gained a municipal administration, better roads, and new public buildings. Schools were opened, and a hospital served the city. Like other Rajputana states in these years, Mewar entered into an agreement with the British over the manufacture of salt in **1879**, giving up local salt making in return for compensation. These were not dramatic reforms, but they mattered. They marked the moment when the old feudal state of Mewar began, slowly, to become a modern administration.

Not every change was welcome. In **1881** the Bhils of the southern hills, around **Kherwara** and the shrine of **Rishabhdeo**, rose in unrest. They feared that the new census, the counting of their homes and people, was the first step towards new taxes and new controls on the forests that sustained them. The rising was serious enough to alarm both Udaipur and the British. It was brought to an end by a mixture of force and negotiation, and by assurances that their customs would be respected. The old bond between the Bhils and the house of Bappa Rawal was strained, but not broken.

The same year brought the young Maharana his highest honour from the empire. In **1881** the Viceroy, **Lord Ripon**, came to **Chittorgarh** itself, the ancient fortress and the first capital of Mewar, to invest Sajjan Singh with the insignia of a **Knight Grand Commander of the Star of India**. For the ceremony to be held on the great rock where Padmini, Kumbha and Jaimal had once stood was a choice heavy with meaning, and the people of Mewar did not miss it.

What makes Sajjan Singh most remembered, however, is not his administration but his love of learning. He believed that his people should read, and that the knowledge of the world should reach Udaipur in its own language. To this end he founded a printing press in the capital, the **Sajjan Yantralaya**, and from it, in **1879**, came Mewar's first newspaper, the weekly *Sajjan Kirti Sudhakar*. It carried state notices, news and articles in Hindi, and for many years it was the public voice of the government of Udaipur.

He also gave his patronage to the man who would write the greatest history of the kingdom. **Kaviraja Shyamaldas**, a poet and scholar of the Charan community, was commissioned by Sajjan Singh to write a full history of Mewar. The work grew into *Vir Vinod*, a vast history in several volumes that drew on inscriptions, coins, Persian chronicles, bardic records and the state's own archives. It is still one of the most important sources for the history of Rajasthan. The young Maharana did not live to see it finished; its volumes were printed later, and for decades they lay largely unread, but the project began with his curiosity and his support.

In **1882**, a visitor arrived in Udaipur who would leave a deep mark on Sajjan Singh's mind. **Swami Dayananda Saraswati**, the founder of the **Arya Samaj**, came at the Maharana's invitation and stayed for several months, from the late summer of 1882 into early 1883, in the **Navlakha Mahal** in the gardens of Udaipur. Each day, it is recorded, the Maharana sat with him to study the *Manusmriti*, the principles of government, and the Vedic texts. The Swami saw in the young ruler a prince who might govern by the old ideals of the *rajarshi*, the king who is also a sage. During his stay he worked on his writings, and when he made his will, he named Sajjan Singh as president of the **Paropkarini Sabha**, the body he created to carry on his work. After the Swami's death at Ajmer in October 1883, the Maharana took up that charge.

Sajjan Singh's love of beauty showed in his buildings. He laid out and enlarged the great garden of Udaipur that became known as **Sajjan Niwas Bagh**, today's **Gulab Bagh**, with its trees, walks and pavilions. He also began to collect fine things from abroad. Records of the palace show that he ordered a large collection of crystal furniture and objects from the firm of **F. & C. Osler** in Birmingham, chairs, tables, beds and lamps of cut glass. He would never see them used. The crates arrived after his death, and much of the collection lay packed away for over a century before it was displayed in the City Palace.

His last great plan was the boldest. On the high peak of **Bansdara**, in the Aravalli hills west of Udaipur, he began to build a palace in **1884**. Tradition says he wished to watch from it the monsoon clouds rolling over the hills of his kingdom, and that he hoped to use it to observe the sky. From that summit a man could see Pichola, the city and the hills around it laid out like a painted map. The palace came to be called **Sajjangarh**, and today it is known as the **Monsoon Palace**. Its walls had only begun to rise when its builder's life came to an end.

Late in **1884**, Sajjan Singh fell ill. His illness grew worse through the autumn, and on **23 December 1884** he died in Udaipur. He was only **twenty-five** years old, and he had ruled for ten years. He left no son. Once again, the nobles of Mewar had to choose an heir, and their choice fell on **Fateh Singh** of the **Shivrati** branch of the house, a man of thirty-five who would rule for nearly half a century and complete many of the works his young predecessor had begun, among them Sajjangarh itself.

Mewar remembered Sajjan Singh with a particular tenderness. He was the young ruler who loved books, who invited sages to his court, who gave his people a newspaper and a history, and who began to turn a proud old kingdom towards the modern world without ever forgetting what it had been. His reign was short, but the press, the paper, the garden, the palace on the hill and the great history of *Vir Vinod* all carry his name, or his mark, to this day.

## Highlights of his life

- **Accession at fifteen (1874).** Chosen from the Bagore branch of the house after Maharana Shambhu Singh died without a son, he took the throne on 8 October 1874.
- **Administrative reform.** He set up the Mahendraj Sabha as a council and court of state, reorganised the departments of Udaipur and began the survey and settlement of land revenue.
- **Printing press and newspaper.** He founded the Sajjan Yantralaya press, which from 1879 published Mewar's first newspaper, the *Sajjan Kirti Sudhakar*.
- **Patron of Vir Vinod.** He commissioned Kaviraja Shyamaldas to write *Vir Vinod*, still one of the great histories of Mewar and Rajasthan.
- **Student of Dayananda Saraswati.** He hosted the founder of the Arya Samaj at Udaipur in 1882–83 and became president of the Paropkarini Sabha.
- **Imperial honour at Chittorgarh.** In 1881 Lord Ripon invested him with the Grand Commandership of the Star of India at the ancient fortress.
- **Sajjangarh and Sajjan Niwas Bagh.** He laid out the great garden of Udaipur and in 1884 began the palace on Bansdara hill now called the Monsoon Palace.
- **Early death.** He died on 23 December 1884, aged twenty-five, and was succeeded by Fateh Singh of Shivrati.

fateh-singh.story:
## Fateh Singh — the proud Maharana who would not bow at Delhi

*Fateh Singh's long reign is documented in the records of the Mewar state and of the British government of India, and it lives on in the songs and stories of Rajasthan. Where those stories go beyond the record, this story says so.*

On **23 December 1884**, the young **Maharana Sajjan Singh** died in Udaipur at the age of twenty-five, leaving no son. For the second time in ten years the throne of Mewar stood without a direct heir, and the nobles of the state gathered to choose a successor from among the branches of the royal house. Their choice was a man who had never expected to rule.

**Fateh Singh** had been born on **16 December 1849**, the son of **Maharaj Dal Singh** of **Shivrati**, one of the cadet branches descended from the Maharanas of the eighteenth century. He had grown up not in the palace on the shore of Pichola but in the quieter world of a noble estate, among horses, hunting grounds, temples and the old customs of the Rajput country. By the time the call came he was a man of thirty-five, tall, upright and serious, already formed in his habits and his beliefs. He was seated on the *gaddi* of Mewar on the day of Sajjan Singh's death, and he would hold it for more than forty-five years.

From the beginning, those who met him saw a ruler cut from older cloth than his predecessor. Sajjan Singh had been eager for newspapers, presses and new ideas. Fateh Singh was devout, reserved, deeply attached to ritual, and fiercely conscious of the dignity of his house. He rose early for worship, kept the great festivals of Mewar with full ceremony, and went regularly to the shrine of **Eklingji**, where, like every Maharana since Bappa Rawal, he bowed as the *dewan*, the servant, of Shiva. He spoke little, and when he did, people remembered it.

He did not, however, abandon the work Sajjan Singh had begun. The palace on **Bansdara** hill, which his predecessor had started in his last year, was completed under Fateh Singh and kept the name **Sajjangarh**. The great history of Mewar, *Vir Vinod*, was finished by **Kaviraja Shyamaldas** in these years. The administration that Sajjan Singh had reshaped continued to grow, with its courts, departments and revenue settlement. Fateh Singh was a conservative, but he was not a fool, and he understood that some things could not be turned back.

His greatest gift to Udaipur was water. In the hills north of the city lay an old lake, first dammed by **Maharana Jai Singh** in the late seventeenth century, whose embankment had been washed away by floods. Fateh Singh decided to rebuild it on a far grander scale. In **1889** the foundation stone of the new dam was laid by the **Duke of Connaught**, a son of Queen Victoria, and the embankment came to be called the **Connaught Bund**. Behind it rose a broad, shining lake that took the Maharana's name: **Fateh Sagar**. Linked to Pichola by a channel, it gave the city water, cooled its air, and added another great mirror to the landscape of the City of Lakes. Today it is one of the best-loved places in Udaipur.

He built within the city as well. In **1890** the **Victoria Hall** was opened in the gardens of Udaipur as a museum and library, built to mark Queen Victoria's jubilee. In the City Palace complex he completed the palace of **Shiv Niwas**, begun under Maharana Shambhu Singh, with its crescent-shaped courtyard looking over Pichola, and he built the **Fateh Prakash** palace. In **1909** the Viceroy **Lord Minto** laid the foundation stone of the great **Durbar Hall** within Fateh Prakash, a hall of chandeliers and portraits meant for the formal gatherings of the state.

Fateh Singh also brought the railway to Udaipur. The line from **Chittorgarh** to **Udaipur** was built by the state and opened in **1899**, linking the capital in the hills to the railway network of India. For the first time, a traveller could reach the city of the Maharanas without days on the road.

Yet the closing years of the century brought disaster. In **1899–1900**, the monsoon failed across western India, and the great famine remembered in Rajasthan as the *Chhappania Akal*, the famine of the year 1956 in the Vikram era, swept through Mewar. Wells dried, cattle died, and families left their villages in search of food. The state opened relief works and distributed grain, but the scale of the suffering was beyond what any government of the time could manage. Many thousands died in Mewar and across Rajputana. The memory of that year was kept in folk songs for generations.

The most famous moments of Fateh Singh's reign were not battles but refusals. In **1903** the Viceroy **Lord Curzon** held a great **Delhi Durbar** to celebrate the coronation of King Edward VII, where the princes of India were to appear in procession and pay homage. Fateh Singh set out for Delhi. A widely told story in Rajasthan says that the poet **Kesari Singh Barhath** sent him thirteen verses in Dingal, the *Chetavani ra Chungatya*, "the pricks of warning", reminding him that no Maharana of Mewar had ever bowed in the court at Delhi, not before Akbar, not before Jahangir, and that Rana Pratap had eaten bread of grass rather than submit. The story goes that the Maharana read the verses on his journey, and that, whatever moved him, he did not take part in the Durbar and returned to Udaipur. The verses became one of the best-known poems of Rajasthani literature.

In **1911** the scene was repeated. King **George V** came in person to India for the **Delhi Durbar** of that year, the only reigning British monarch ever to do so. Fateh Singh went to Delhi and received the King, but he did not take his place at the Durbar itself, and returned home. To the British it was an irritation. To the people of Mewar it was something else: proof that the pride of their house had survived the loss of its armies.

That pride was real, but it was not the whole picture of his reign. Mewar under Fateh Singh was still a deeply feudal state. Its great nobles held their estates, their courts and their rights over the villages with little change from earlier centuries, and the peasants who worked the land paid not only revenue but a long list of customary cesses and forced labour. In the estate of **Bijolia**, in the north-east of Mewar, the peasants began to protest these burdens as early as **1897**. Over the following two decades the protest grew into one of the earliest organised peasant movements in India. Led from **1916** by **Vijay Singh Pathik**, the farmers refused to pay, formed their own councils, and drew the attention of nationalist newspapers across the country. In the hills of the south, the Bhil leader **Motilal Tejawat** led a movement of the tribal peoples against heavy taxes and forced labour in the early 1920s.

The British, worried by the unrest and by what they saw as the old Maharana's refusal to reform the relations between the nobles and the peasantry, pressed for change. Fateh Singh resisted. He regarded the internal life of Mewar as his own concern and that of his nobles. In **1921**, under strong British pressure, a compromise was reached: Fateh Singh kept the title, honours and ceremonial place of the Maharana, but the day-to-day powers of government were handed to his son, **Maharaj Kumar Bhupal Singh**. It was a painful moment for a proud ruler, and he never entirely accepted it.

In his later years Fateh Singh lived much as he always had, among rituals, prayers and the hunting lodges in the hills around Udaipur. He was by then an old man with a long white beard, upright on his horse, a living link to a world before railways and telegraphs. Visitors from abroad described him as one of the most dignified of all the princes of India, a ruler who seemed to have stepped out of the pages of the old chronicles.

He died on **24 May 1930**, at the age of eighty. His reign had spanned nearly half a century, from the age of Queen Victoria to the years of Gandhi's movements, and he had seen the world around Mewar change beyond recognition. He was succeeded by his son **Bhupal Singh**, who had already governed the state for nine years and who would lead it into the new India.

Fateh Singh's legacy is double. He was a conservative who resisted reform at home and left real grievances unanswered among his peasants. He was also a builder who gave Udaipur its lake, its railway, its palaces and its museum, and a ruler whose refusal to bow at Delhi made him, for many in Rajasthan, the last living symbol of the old Mewar of Rana Pratap.

## Highlights of his life

- **Unexpected heir (1884).** Born at Shivrati in 1849, he was chosen by the nobles of Mewar after Sajjan Singh died without a son.
- **Fateh Sagar.** He rebuilt the old dam north of Udaipur on a grand scale; the Duke of Connaught laid its foundation stone in 1889, and the lake took his name.
- **Builder of Udaipur.** He completed Sajjangarh and Shiv Niwas, built the Fateh Prakash palace and its Durbar Hall, and opened the Victoria Hall museum and library in 1890.
- **Railway to Udaipur.** The Chittorgarh–Udaipur line, built by the state, opened in 1899.
- **The famine of 1899–1900.** His reign saw the great Chhappania famine, which brought terrible suffering to Mewar despite relief works.
- **Refusals at Delhi.** He did not take part in the Delhi Durbars of 1903 and 1911, an act long celebrated in Rajasthan as the pride of Mewar.
- **Peasant and tribal unrest.** The Bijolia peasant movement and Motilal Tejawat's Bhil movement grew in his reign, and in 1921 he was compelled to hand executive powers to his son Bhupal Singh.
- **Death (1930).** He died on 24 May 1930, aged eighty, after a reign of over forty-five years.

bhupal-singh.story:
## Bhupal Singh — the last ruling Maharana, who led Mewar into India

*Bhupal Singh's life belongs to the twentieth century, and it is recorded in the papers of the Mewar state, the reports of the British government, and the documents of India's integration of the princely states. Where popular memory adds to that record, this story says so.*

On **22 February 1884**, a son was born in the household of **Maharaj Fateh Singh** of **Shivrati**, a noble of one of the cadet branches of the royal house of Mewar. Nobody at his birth could have imagined that within a year his father would be Maharana, or that this child would one day be the last ruler of Mewar to govern as a sovereign prince. He was named **Bhupal Singh**.

In December of that same year, the young **Maharana Sajjan Singh** died without a son, and the nobles of Mewar chose Fateh Singh as his successor. The infant Bhupal Singh was carried from the estate of Shivrati to the palaces of Udaipur, and grew up as the **Maharaj Kumar**, the heir to the oldest surviving ruling house of Rajputana. He was educated privately in the palace, in the languages, scriptures and history of his house as well as in English and the subjects of a modern education, and he learned to ride and shoot like every Rajput prince of his time.

Then, in his youth, illness struck. Around the age of sixteen he was afflicted by **tuberculosis of the spine**, a disease that in those years had no cure. He survived, but it left him paralysed in the legs for the rest of his life. A prince of Mewar was expected to ride at the head of processions, to hunt in the hills, to embody the martial tradition of Rana Pratap. Bhupal Singh would do none of these things on his own feet. He moved by wheelchair or was carried, and he had to find other ways to carry the weight of his inheritance.

He found them in patience and in work. Those who served him spoke of a quiet, courteous, steady man who listened carefully and read his papers closely. His father, **Maharana Fateh Singh**, was proud, orthodox and stubborn, and by the time Bhupal Singh reached middle age the old ruler's relations with the British were badly strained. The peasants of **Bijolia** had been protesting their burdens for years, the Bhils of the south were stirring under **Motilal Tejawat**, and the British pressed for reforms that Fateh Singh refused to make.

In **1921** a compromise was forced upon the old Maharana. He kept his title and ceremonial dignity, but the executive powers of government were transferred to his son. At the age of thirty-seven, Bhupal Singh became the real head of the administration of Mewar, while his father still sat on the *gaddi*. It was a delicate position: he had to govern without humiliating his father, satisfy the British without surrendering the dignity of his house, and begin to answer the grievances of a peasantry that was no longer silent. Over the next years settlements were made with the peasants of Bijolia and other estates, some of the heaviest cesses and forms of forced labour were reduced, and the administration of the state was gradually reorganised.

Fateh Singh died on **24 May 1930**, and Bhupal Singh succeeded him as **Maharana**. He was forty-six years old, and he had already been governing the state for nine years. His reign coincided with the most turbulent quarter-century in modern Indian history: the national movement, the Second World War, Partition, independence and the integration of the princely states.

He was a builder of institutions rather than palaces. Education spread in his time. The **Bhupal Nobles' School**, founded in **1923** by a society for the education of the sons of Mewar's nobles and named in his honour, grew over the decades into a college and later a university. In **1931** the educationist **Dr Mohan Sinha Mehta** founded the **Vidya Bhawan** school at Udaipur, which became known across India for its progressive teaching. The main hospital of the capital came to bear the Maharana's name. Roads were improved, and the city of Udaipur, with its lakes and palaces, began to attract visitors from beyond Rajputana.

But the age of the old princely order was ending, and the people of Mewar wanted a voice in their own government. In **1938** the **Mewar Praja Mandal** was founded by **Manikya Lal Verma** to demand responsible government under the Maharana. The state banned it, and Verma was arrested. The ban was later lifted, and in **1942**, during the **Quit India Movement**, students, workers and Praja Mandal members in Udaipur joined the national protest. Many were imprisoned. Among the young men of the movement was **Mohan Lal Sukhadia**, who would later serve for many years as Chief Minister of Rajasthan. The Maharana's government moved slowly, often reluctantly, towards reform, and in **1947**, on the eve of independence, a new constitution for the state was announced, providing for ministers responsible in part to an elected assembly.

When the British announced that they would leave India in August **1947**, every princely state faced the same question. The paramountcy of the British Crown would lapse, and the rulers were asked to accede to either India or Pakistan. A few rulers dreamed of independence, and some were courted by those who wished to build a block of states outside the Indian Union. A widely told story in Rajasthan says that such an approach was made to Udaipur, and that Bhupal Singh replied that Mewar's choice had been made centuries earlier, by his ancestors who had stood for their land and their faith. Whatever the exact words, the decision was clear. **Mewar acceded to India in 1947**, among the first of the great Rajput states to do so, and its example carried weight with the others.

Accession was only the first step. The small and middling states of Rajputana could not survive as separate units in the new republic, and the Government of India, through **Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel** and **V. P. Menon**, began to bring them together into larger unions. On **18 April 1948**, Mewar joined the **United State of Rajasthan**, and **Jawaharlal Nehru** came to Udaipur to inaugurate it. Bhupal Singh was made its **Rajpramukh**, the constitutional head of the new state, and **Manikya Lal Verma**, the Praja Mandal leader his government had once imprisoned, became its prime minister. The thousand-year sovereignty of the house of Bappa Rawal ended not on a battlefield but in a ceremony of union.

A year later the remaining great states, Jaipur, Jodhpur, Bikaner and Jaisalmer, joined in, and on **30 March 1949** the larger state of Rajasthan was inaugurated at Jaipur by Sardar Patel. In honour of the antiquity and standing of his house, Bhupal Singh was given the unique title of **Maharajpramukh**, which he held for life, while **Maharaja Man Singh II** of Jaipur became Rajpramukh. Under the covenant of integration the Maharana received a privy purse, kept his personal properties and was recognised by the Government of India as the ruler of Mewar.

His last years were spent in Udaipur, among the palaces his ancestors had built on the lakes, and among the people who still called him Maharana and still bowed to him at festivals as their forefathers had. He had no son of his own. To continue the line he adopted a young kinsman of the Shivrati branch, **Bhagwat Singh**, born in 1921, who was formally recognised as his heir.

Bhupal Singh died on **4 July 1955**, aged seventy-one. He had lived through more change than any Maharana before him: born in a kingdom under the shadow of the British Raj, he died a citizen of the Republic of India. Paralysed from his youth, he had never led an army. Yet he had led his state through famine and unrest, through the national movement and the end of empire, and finally into the new nation. Mewar remembers him as the last Maharana who ruled, and as the one who chose India.

## Highlights of his life

- **Heir from Shivrati.** Born on 22 February 1884, he became Maharaj Kumar when his father Fateh Singh was chosen Maharana later that year.
- **Courage in illness.** Spinal tuberculosis left him paralysed in the legs from his youth, yet he governed Mewar for over a quarter of a century.
- **Executive powers from 1921.** He took over the administration from his father and began settling peasant grievances in Bijolia and elsewhere.
- **Maharana from 1930.** He succeeded Fateh Singh on 24 May 1930 and ruled through the national movement and the Second World War.
- **Education and institutions.** The Bhupal Nobles' School, the Vidya Bhawan and other institutions grew in Udaipur in his time.
- **Accession to India (1947).** Mewar acceded to the Indian Union in 1947, an example that influenced other Rajput states.
- **Rajpramukh and Maharajpramukh.** He became Rajpramukh of the United State of Rajasthan in 1948 and Maharajpramukh of Rajasthan for life in 1949.
- **Death (1955).** He died on 4 July 1955 and was succeeded by his adopted son Bhagwat Singh.

bhopal-singh.story:
## Bhopal Singh — a name, not a separate reign

*The list of Mewar's rulers is well documented for the twentieth century, in state records, the papers of India's integration of the princely states and the records of the house of Mewar itself. This short entry explains what those records show.*

Some lists of the rulers of Mewar place a **Maharana Bhopal Singh** between **Bhupal Singh** and **Bhagwat Singh**. The records of the twentieth century do not support a separate ruler of that name. *Bhopal* is simply another way of spelling and pronouncing **Bhupal**, both forms of the Sanskrit *bhupala*, "protector of the earth", and older English writings use both spellings for the same Maharana.

That Maharana, **Bhupal Singh**, was born on **22 February 1884**, the son of **Fateh Singh**. He took over the executive powers of the state in **1921**, succeeded his father on **24 May 1930**, led Mewar into the Indian Union in **1947**, became Rajpramukh of the United State of Rajasthan in **1948** and Maharajpramukh of Rajasthan in **1949**, and died on **4 July 1955**.

He had no son of his own. His heir was **Bhagwat Singh**, a kinsman of the Shivrati branch born in 1921, whom he adopted. On Bhupal Singh's death in 1955, Bhagwat Singh succeeded directly as head of the house of Mewar. No other ruler stood between them.

The entry for "Bhopal Singh" is therefore best read as a duplicate of Bhupal Singh, created when one name was written in two ways. His real life, with its illness, its reforms and its part in the making of modern Rajasthan, is told in full in the story of Maharana Bhupal Singh.

## Highlights of his life

- **A variant name.** "Bhopal Singh" is another spelling of Bhupal Singh, not a separate Maharana.
- **The real ruler.** Bhupal Singh reigned from 1930 to 1955 and led Mewar into India.
- **Direct succession.** Bhupal Singh was followed directly by his adopted son Bhagwat Singh in 1955.
- **Where to read more.** His full life is told in the story of Maharana Bhupal Singh.

bhagwat-singh-mewar.story:
## Bhagwat Singh Mewar — the Maharana without a kingdom

*Bhagwat Singh Mewar lived in modern times, and his life is recorded in public documents, court records, newspapers and the institutions he founded. Where family memory and public account differ, this story says so.*

When **Bhagwat Singh** was born on **20 June 1921**, Mewar was still a kingdom. Its ruler, the aged **Maharana Fateh Singh**, still sat on the *gaddi* at Udaipur, and that very year his son **Bhupal Singh** had taken over the powers of government. Bhagwat Singh was not born in the palace. He was a son of the **Shivrati** branch of the royal house, the same branch from which Fateh Singh had come, and so he was a close kinsman of the Maharanas, but no one at his birth could be sure that he would ever stand at the head of the house.

He grew up in the last years of the old princely India. Like many sons of the Rajput nobility of his generation, he was sent to **Mayo College** at **Ajmer**, the school founded in the 1870s to educate the princes of Rajputana. There he learned English, history, mathematics and the manners of a modern gentleman alongside the boys of other ruling houses, and he played sport with enthusiasm. He grew into a tall, confident, outgoing young man, at ease among people and fond of the outdoors.

His future was decided by the childlessness of his cousin. **Maharana Bhupal Singh**, paralysed since his youth by tuberculosis of the spine, had no son. Following the long custom of Mewar, in which the throne passed by adoption when the direct line failed, he chose Bhagwat Singh as his heir and adopted him. From then on the young man of Shivrati was the **Maharaj Kumar**, the heir apparent of Mewar.

He married **Sushila Kumari**, a princess of the house of **Bikaner**, and they had two sons, **Mahendra Singh**, born in 1941, and **Arvind Singh**, born in 1944, and a daughter, **Yogeshwari Kumari**. The children grew up in the palaces of Udaipur during the years in which the world of their elders was dissolving.

Bhagwat Singh was in his twenties when India became independent. He watched as his adoptive father took Mewar into the Indian Union in **1947**, became **Rajpramukh** of the United State of Rajasthan in **1948**, and then **Maharajpramukh** of the greater state of Rajasthan in **1949**. Kingdoms became districts, and the old administration of the Maharanas was absorbed into the new state government at Jaipur. When Bhupal Singh died on **4 July 1955**, Bhagwat Singh succeeded him. He was recognised by the Government of India as the ruler of Mewar, received the **privy purse** guaranteed to the princes when they merged their states, and kept the palaces and properties that belonged to the family. But he inherited a title, not a kingdom.

This was the great problem of his life. He was the head of the oldest ruling house of Rajputana, a line that traced itself back through Pratap, Sanga and Kumbha to Bappa Rawal, and the people of Mewar still came to him for blessings, still bowed when he passed, still looked to him at the festivals of **Gangaur** and **Dussehra**. Yet he had no army, no revenue, no courts and no power. The palaces of Udaipur, built for a royal household with hundreds of servants, guards, horses and elephants, now had to be maintained from a fixed allowance and whatever the family could earn. Many princely families of this period sold their treasures piece by piece, or let their palaces fall into ruin. Bhagwat Singh chose another path.

He saw that the beauty of Udaipur, its lakes, palaces and hills, could sustain the heritage of Mewar if it was opened to the world. The first and most famous step was taken on the waters of **Pichola**. The island palace of **Jag Niwas**, built by **Maharana Jagat Singh II** in the eighteenth century as a summer pleasure palace, was converted into a hotel and opened in **1963** as the **Lake Palace**. Its white walls seemed to float on the lake, and it soon became one of the most celebrated hotels in the world, visited by travellers, statesmen and film-makers. It was later managed by the **Taj** group. Parts of the **City Palace**, among them the palaces of **Shiv Niwas** and **Fateh Prakash**, were in time opened to guests as well, and the great palace complex on the shore of Pichola was opened to visitors as a museum.

The change was not easy, and not everyone approved. To some of the older nobles, turning the palaces of the Maharanas into hotels seemed a kind of humiliation, a selling of the family's dignity to strangers. Bhagwat Singh saw it differently. A palace that stood empty would decay; a palace that welcomed guests would earn the money to repair its roofs, clean its paintings and pay the families who had served the house for generations. Over the following decades Udaipur grew into one of the great destinations of India, and in **1983** its lakes and palaces reached cinema screens across the world when the James Bond film *Octopussy* was filmed there, with the Lake Palace among its settings.

He also understood that heritage was more than buildings. In **1969** he established the **Maharana of Mewar Charitable Foundation**, a trust to maintain the City Palace and its collections, support education and culture, and continue the charitable duties that the Maharanas had once carried out as rulers. Through it, the paintings, weapons, manuscripts and objects gathered by generations of Maharanas were preserved and displayed, and the foundation began to honour scholars, artists and citizens whose work served society, in the spirit of the old royal patronage.

His sense of duty extended to religion. As the head of the house that called itself the *dewan* of **Eklingji**, he continued the ancient rites at the shrine and at the temples of Mewar. He also took a public role in Hindu religious life beyond Mewar, serving as president of the **Vishva Hindu Parishad**, a position that reflected the standing his house held among Hindus across India as the line of Rana Pratap.

The 1970s brought a new blow. In **1971**, the **twenty-sixth amendment** to the Constitution of India abolished the privy purses and withdrew official recognition of the titles of the former rulers. From then on, in the eyes of the law, there was no Maharana of Mewar. Bhagwat Singh was simply a citizen with a famous name. For the people of Mewar, however, he remained the Maharana, and the ceremonies of the house continued. Without the privy purse, the hotels, the museum and the trusts he had built became even more important. They were what kept the palaces standing.

The last years of his life were troubled by a bitter conflict within his own family. His elder son, **Mahendra Singh**, disagreed with his father over the management and division of the family's properties, and in **1983** he went to court against him, seeking a partition of the ancestral estate. To a man who saw the palaces as the inheritance of the whole line, and the trusts as the way to keep them together, this was a deep wound. In his will and in the arrangements he made for his trusts, Bhagwat Singh named his younger son, **Arvind Singh**, as the executor and gave him responsibility for the foundation and its properties. The elder son was excluded from that role.

Bhagwat Singh Mewar died in Udaipur on **3 November 1984**, at the age of sixty-three. His death did not settle the dispute. A section of the nobles and supporters of the house recognised Mahendra Singh as the head of the house with a traditional ceremony, while Arvind Singh took charge of the City Palace, the trusts and the foundation as his father had directed. The two branches of the family, and their legal battles, would continue for decades.

His legacy is the Udaipur that the world knows today. He came to the head of his house at the moment when it lost its kingdom, and he found a way to keep its palaces alive, its collections intact and its name honoured, not by force or by law, but by opening them to the world. The Lake Palace on Pichola, the museum in the City Palace and the foundation that bears the name of Mewar are his monuments.

## Highlights of his life

- **From Shivrati to the heirship.** Born on 20 June 1921, he was adopted by the childless Maharana Bhupal Singh as heir to Mewar.
- **Educated at Mayo College.** He was schooled at Ajmer among the sons of the ruling houses of Rajputana.
- **Head of the house from 1955.** He succeeded Bhupal Singh on 4 July 1955, recognised by the Government of India as ruler of Mewar.
- **The Lake Palace (1963).** He converted the island palace of Jag Niwas on Pichola into the Lake Palace hotel, now famous across the world.
- **The Maharana of Mewar Charitable Foundation (1969).** He founded the trust that preserves the City Palace, its museum and its collections.
- **Through the end of the privy purses (1971).** He kept the heritage of Mewar alive after the abolition of princely titles and allowances.
- **Religious leadership.** He maintained the rites of Eklingji and served as president of the Vishva Hindu Parishad.
- **Death and divided succession (1984).** He died on 3 November 1984, having named his younger son Arvind Singh executor of his will and trusts.

arvind-singh-mewar.story:
## Arvind Singh Mewar — the custodian who carried Mewar into the world

*Arvind Singh Mewar's life belongs to our own times, and it is recorded in newspapers, court records and the work of the institutions he led. The headship of the house of Mewar was disputed within his family for much of his life; this story says so plainly and does not take sides where the courts and the family have not agreed.*

On **13 December 1944**, a second son was born in the palace at **Udaipur** to **Bhagwat Singh**, the heir of Mewar, and his wife **Sushila Kumari**, a princess of Bikaner. They named him **Arvind Singh**. His elder brother, **Mahendra Singh**, was three years old. Above them all, in the old palace on the shore of Pichola, their grandfather by adoption, **Maharana Bhupal Singh**, still ruled Mewar as a princely state within the British Indian empire.

That world would not last long enough for the boy to remember it clearly. Before he was three, India was independent. Before he was five, Mewar had merged into the new state of **Rajasthan**, and his grandfather had become its Maharajpramukh. When Bhupal Singh died in **1955**, Arvind's father became head of the house, and the boy grew up as the younger son of a Maharana who no longer had a kingdom.

He was educated at **Mayo College** in **Ajmer**, the old school of the princes of Rajputana, and at **Maharana Bhupal College** in Udaipur, which carried his grandfather's name. He was a natural sportsman. He played cricket at a high level, appearing in first-class matches for **Rajasthan**, and he loved polo, the horseman's game that had long been a passion of the Rajput nobility. Those who knew him in these years remembered an energetic, practical young man, more interested in how things worked than in ceremony.

His father had begun to open the palaces of Udaipur to the world, turning the island palace of **Jag Niwas** into the **Lake Palace** hotel in 1963. Arvind Singh decided to learn the trade properly. He went abroad, studying hotel management in **Britain** and working in the hotel industry in the **United States**. It was an unusual path for the son of a Maharana, and it shaped the rest of his life. He came home convinced that the heritage of Mewar could survive only if it paid its own way, and that this required the discipline of a modern business as well as the pride of an ancient house.

He married **Vijayaraj Kumari**, a princess of the house of **Kutch**. They had two daughters, **Bhargavi Kumari** and **Padmaja Kumari**, and a son, **Lakshyaraj Singh**, born in **1985**.

In **1971** the privy purses and the official recognition of the princes' titles were abolished. The house of Mewar now had to support its palaces, temples, staff and ceremonies entirely from its own resources. Arvind Singh worked closely with his father on the hotels and on the **Maharana of Mewar Charitable Foundation**, which Bhagwat Singh had founded in **1969** to care for the City Palace and its collections.

The family, however, was dividing. In **1983** his elder brother Mahendra Singh went to court against their father over the family's properties. Bhagwat Singh, deeply hurt, made his younger son the executor of his will and gave him charge of the trusts that held the palaces. When Bhagwat Singh died on **3 November 1984**, Arvind Singh took up that charge. A section of the nobles and supporters of the house, on the other hand, recognised Mahendra Singh as head of the house with a traditional ceremony. From then on the family had two branches, each with its own claim, and a long series of legal cases over the properties that would continue for decades.

Arvind Singh described his own role with a particular word: not as a king, but as the **custodian** of the house of Mewar. He drew on the oldest idea of his dynasty, the teaching remembered from the time of Bappa Rawal that the true ruler of Mewar is **Eklingji**, the lord Shiva of the shrine near Nagda, and that the Maharana is only his *dewan*, his servant. In that spirit, he presented himself as the trustee of an inheritance that belonged to the whole line and to the people of Mewar, not as its owner. He continued the rites at the temple of Eklingji and the great ceremonies of the house, such as the lighting of the **Holika** fire at the City Palace and the worship of horses on Dussehra, so that they would not die with the old order.

His greatest work was the transformation of the **City Palace** of Udaipur. Under the trusts he led, the vast palace complex was conserved, and much of it was opened to the public as a museum. Rooms that had been closed for generations were restored, paintings and weapons were cleaned and catalogued, and the old women's quarters, the **Zenana Mahal**, were brought back to life as galleries. In the **Fateh Prakash** palace he opened the **Crystal Gallery**, displaying the extraordinary collection of crystal furniture that **Maharana Sajjan Singh** had ordered from Birmingham in the nineteenth century and never lived to use. Pieces that had lain in their packing crates for more than a hundred years were at last brought into the light. In the old garage of the palace he created a gallery of the house's **vintage and classic cars**, the Rolls-Royces and other motor cars that had carried the Maharanas in the twentieth century.

He built the business side with the same energy. The **HRH Group of Hotels**, which he led as chairman, grew from the palaces of Udaipur into a chain of heritage properties. In the City Palace, the **Shiv Niwas** and **Fateh Prakash** palaces became hotels, and the island of **Jagmandir** on Pichola, where tradition says the young prince Khurram, the future Shah Jahan, once took refuge, became a venue for celebrations. The group also took in heritage properties beyond Mewar, among them the lakeside palace of **Gajner** near Bikaner. The money earned by the hotels supported the upkeep of the palaces, the staff and the work of the foundation.

The foundation itself grew under his leadership. Its annual awards honoured scholars, artists, public servants and ordinary citizens, and many of them were named after figures from Mewar's own history, such as **Panna Dhai**, the nurse who saved the infant Udai Singh, and **Hakim Khan Sur**, the Afghan commander who fought for Rana Pratap at Haldighati. An award named after **Colonel James Tod**, the British author of the *Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan*, honoured foreign scholars of India. The foundation also ran schools and a research institute, and supported the study and publication of the history of Mewar. Under the banner of **"Eternal Mewar"**, Arvind Singh presented the culture of his house, its festivals, crafts, music and history, to audiences in India and abroad.

Not everyone admired his approach. Critics, including members of his own wider family, accused him of turning a sacred inheritance into a commercial enterprise, and the legal battles over the properties of the house were long and bitter. His supporters answered that without his work the palaces would have fallen into ruin, as so many other royal palaces in India had. Both views were held sincerely, and both remain part of his story.

In his last years Arvind Singh suffered from a long illness, and his son **Lakshyaraj Singh** took on more and more of the work of the trusts and the hotels. In **November 2024**, his elder brother **Mahendra Singh** died. Mahendra Singh's son, **Vishvaraj Singh**, was then formally installed as head of the house by his supporters in a traditional ceremony at **Chittorgarh**, and when he tried to visit the family shrine inside the City Palace, the gates were closed against him, and tension spilled into the streets of Udaipur. The quarrel that had begun in the lifetime of Bhagwat Singh was still unresolved.

Arvind Singh Mewar died in Udaipur on **16 March 2025**, at the age of eighty. He was succeeded as custodian of the trusts and the City Palace by his son Lakshyaraj Singh. He had spent forty years at the head of the institutions of the house, longer than many Maharanas had reigned. He left behind a City Palace that welcomes visitors from every country, collections that are preserved and displayed, and a name that the world associates not with the wars of the past but with the beauty and memory of Mewar.

## Highlights of his life

- **Born into a vanishing kingdom (1944).** He was born in Udaipur on 13 December 1944, the younger son of Bhagwat Singh, while Mewar was still a princely state.
- **Sportsman and hotelier.** He played first-class cricket for Rajasthan and studied and worked in the hotel industry in Britain and the United States.
- **Custodian from 1984.** Named executor of his father's will and trusts, he led the institutions of the house from 1984, though his elder brother's branch disputed his position.
- **The City Palace Museum.** He conserved the City Palace and opened it as a museum, restoring the Zenana Mahal and creating galleries such as the Crystal Gallery.
- **HRH Group of Hotels.** He built a chain of heritage hotels whose earnings supported the upkeep of the palaces.
- **Foundation and awards.** Through the Maharana of Mewar Charitable Foundation he honoured scholars, artists and citizens with awards named after figures of Mewar's history.
- **Keeper of tradition.** He continued the rites of Eklingji and the ceremonies of the house under the idea of the ruler as custodian.
- **Death (2025).** He died on 16 March 2025, aged eighty, and was succeeded as custodian by his son Lakshyaraj Singh.

rao-jodha.story:
## Rao Jodha — the exile who built a fort on the Bird Hill

*Rao Jodha's life comes to us through the Marwar khyats, above all the chronicle of Muhnot Nainsi, through the court histories of Jodhpur, and through a few inscriptions such as the one his daughter left at Ghosundi. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

In the early fifteenth century the Rathores were still newcomers to power in the desert country of Marwar. For nearly two hundred years their clan had lived as chiefs of small holdings in the west, around Kher and the Luni valley, descendants of **Rao Siha**, who had come into the region in the thirteenth century. Only in the generation of **Rao Chunda** did they win a real capital. Around the end of the fourteenth century Chunda took **Mandore**, the ancient seat of the Pratiharas, and with it the beginnings of a kingdom.

Jodha was born in **1416**, the son of Chunda's son **Rao Ranmal**. He came into a family that was already restless and divided. Ranmal had been passed over for the throne of Mandore in favour of a younger brother, and like many Rajput princes without a seat of his own, he went to seek his fortune at a greater court. That court was **Chittor**. Ranmal's sister **Hansa Bai** had married **Rana Lakha** of Mewar, and her son **Mokal** became Rana. Through her, Ranmal rose to great power in Mewar, and after Mokal was murdered in 1433, he became the strongest man at the court of the young **Rana Kumbha**.

So Jodha grew up between two worlds: the sand and thorn of Marwar, and the great rock fortress of Chittor with its temples, its intrigues and its proud Sisodia nobility. He learned to ride and fight among his father's Rathore followers, and he learned, too, how quickly favour at a foreign court could turn to suspicion.

Ranmal's power in Mewar made enemies. The Sisodia nobles, and especially the followers of **Chunda Sisodia**, the elder half-brother of Mokal who had given up his own claim to the throne, believed that the Rathore was making Mewar into a Rathore possession. In **1438** the blow fell. Ranmal was killed inside Chittor. The bards tell that he was taken while he slept, that a maidservant had tied him to his cot, and that the old warrior rose with the bed still bound to his back and fought until he fell. Whether every detail is true or not, the murder itself is well remembered in both Mewar and Marwar.

Jodha was in Chittor or close by when his father died. He fled at once with a small band of Rathore horsemen. The Mewar forces pursued them, and many of Jodha's companions were cut down on the long ride west. The Sisodias followed through to **Mandore** itself and occupied it. At about twenty-two years old, the heir of the Rathores had lost his father, his followers and his capital in a single season.

For roughly fifteen years Jodha lived as an exile. He took shelter in the dry country to the north and west, around **Kahuni** and the edges of the Thar, gathering what men he could and raiding when he was strong enough. These were hard years. He had little money, few horses and many enemies, and his kinsmen were scattered.

A famous story belongs to this time, told across Rajasthan as a legend rather than as history. Tired and hungry, Jodha stopped one day at a peasant's hut. The woman of the house set before him a plate of hot *khichri*. Starving, he plunged his hand into the middle of it and burned his fingers. The woman laughed and said: "You are as foolish as Jodha. He attacks the centre of the enemy's land and gets burned, instead of eating from the edges where the food is cool." The prince, the story goes, took the lesson to heart. From then on he began to win back his country piece by piece, from the outside in.

Whether a peasant woman taught him or not, that is how the struggle went. Jodha built up support among the Rathore kinsmen and among neighbouring clans. Tradition remembers the help of **Harbu Sankhla**, a holy man and warrior of the Sankhla Parmar clan, who is still honoured in Marwar as a folk hero. Mewar, meanwhile, had many other concerns. Rana Kumbha was fighting the sultans of **Malwa** and **Gujarat**, and the garrison at Mandore was a distant burden.

Around **1453** Jodha struck. He retook Mandore and drove out the Mewar garrison. Over the next years he recovered the surrounding districts and pressed his raids towards Mewar's own borders. Tradition says it was Hansa Bai, the Rajmata of Mewar and Jodha's own aunt, who pressed for an end to the bloodshed between her two families. A settlement followed. The bards remember a boundary drawn through the countryside, and a saying about which trees grew on which side of it. What matters historically is that Mewar accepted the return of the Rathores to Mandore, and that Marwar and Mewar, for a time, made peace.

Jodha was now master of his inheritance, but he wanted more than to sit again in his grandfather's city. Mandore lay in a low valley, open and hard to defend. A few miles to the south rose a great ridge of rock, steep on every side, called **Bhakurcheeria**, the "hill of birds". On **12 May 1459**, according to the Jodhpur tradition, Jodha laid the foundation of a new fort on its summit. Around its foot he founded a new city and gave it his own name: **Jodhpur**.

Many legends cluster around that foundation. The hill, it is said, was the home of a hermit called **Cheeria Nathji**, the lord of the birds. When Jodha's men moved him from his cave to make way for the fort, the hermit cursed the place with drought. Local people say that Jodhpur's long struggle with water began that day, and that Jodha built a small shrine and a house near the cave to soften the curse. Tradition also says that **Karni Mata**, the warrior-saint of Deshnok who was revered by the Rathores, came to bless the foundation. And there is a darker story, still told with honour in Jodhpur: that a man named **Rajiya Bambhi**, of the Meghwal community, was buried alive in the foundations as an offering, so that the fort would never fall, and that Jodha granted land to his family in return. These are traditions, kept by the people of the city, not facts confirmed by any record of the time.

The fort that rose on the hill became **Mehrangarh**, the "fort of the sun". What Jodha built was smaller and plainer than the vast palace-fortress visitors see today. His successors added to it for four centuries. But the site was his choice, and it was a brilliant one. From the top of its walls a sentry could see far across the plain, and the rock itself was a barrier no army ever easily broke. Jodha brought the image of the goddess **Chamunda**, the patron of his family, from Mandore and installed her in the new fort. His queen **Jasmade**, a Hadi princess, built the tank called **Ranisar** within the walls to store precious rainwater.

From his new capital Jodha set about turning a clan holding into a state. He was a practical ruler. Rather than keep every conquest under his own hand, he sent his sons and brothers out to win and hold lands of their own, bound to Jodhpur by blood. His sons **Duda** and **Varsingh** took **Merta**, which became the seat of the Mertia Rathores. His brother **Kandhal** and his son **Bika** rode north into the dry lands of Jangladesh. Bika's mother was the Sankhla queen **Naurangde**, and the story goes that a jest at court about whether Bika meant to win a kingdom of his own sent him off to do exactly that. Over the following decades he founded the state and city of **Bikaner**, completed in **1488**. Other sons and kinsmen settled at Sojat, Phalodi and elsewhere. The Rathore lands spread across much of western Rajasthan.

This system had its strengths and its dangers. It made the Rathores the masters of a huge region within a single lifetime. It also created powerful branches that would later act as independent states. But in Jodha's own day, it gave the clan room to grow, and it gave his sons something better to do than fight one another for a single throne.

The old enmity with Mewar faded too. Jodha's daughter **Shringar Devi** was married to **Rana Raimal**, Kumbha's son, who ruled Mewar from 1473. Long after her father's death she built a stepwell at **Ghosundi**, near Chittor, and its inscription of **1504** proudly names her as Jodha's daughter. The houses whose quarrel had killed Ranmal were now joined by marriage.

Jodha's character, as the chronicles paint him, was that of a hard, patient and practical man. He had seen what pride and intrigue did at a great court, and he trusted his own kin and his own hills more than any alliance. He was a devotee of the goddess and a patron of the holy men of Marwar. He spent the first half of his adult life losing almost everything and the second half building something that would last for five hundred years.

Rao Jodha died in **1489**, at about seventy-three. He was succeeded by his son **Rao Satal**, who ruled only a few years, and then by another son, **Rao Suja**. The line that later produced **Rao Maldeo**, the great Rathore ruler of the sixteenth century, descended from Suja. The fort Jodha founded on the hill of birds was never taken by storm in all the centuries that followed, and the city at its foot, the blue city of Jodhpur, still carries his name.

## Highlights of his life

- **Survivor of his father's murder (1438).** After Rao Ranmal was killed at Chittor, he escaped with a handful of horsemen and lived for years as an exile.
- **Recovery of Mandore (c. 1453).** He rebuilt Rathore strength in the desert and took back the family capital from the Mewar garrison.
- **Peace with Mewar.** He ended the feud with the Sisodias, and his daughter Shringar Devi later married Rana Raimal.
- **Founder of Jodhpur and Mehrangarh (1459).** He chose the rocky Bhakurcheeria hill for a new fort and founded the city that bears his name.
- **Builder of a wider Rathore realm.** His sons and kinsmen founded or held Merta, Bikaner and other centres across western Rajasthan.
- **Patron of the goddess.** He installed Chamunda in Mehrangarh, and his queen Jasmade built the Ranisar tank within the fort.
- **Death and succession (1489).** He died at about seventy-three and was succeeded by his son Rao Satal.

rao-maldeo.story:
## Rao Maldeo — the lord of Marwar who nearly cost Sher Shah an empire

*Rao Maldeo's life comes to us through the Marwar khyats and the chronicle of Muhnot Nainsi, through Persian histories such as those of Abbas Khan Sarwani and Ferishta, and through the ballads of Rajasthan. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

When Maldeo was born in **1511**, the Rathore kingdom of Marwar was a smaller and weaker thing than its founder had left it. Rao Jodha had built Mehrangarh and sent his sons out to win lands of their own, but the branches they founded at Bikaner and Merta had grown into independent powers, and the throne at Jodhpur controlled little more than the country around the capital and Sojat. Maldeo's father, **Rao Ganga**, came to power in **1515** after a struggle with his own uncle, and his reign was spent holding together what remained.

Maldeo grew up in this tight, quarrelsome world of kinsmen and rivals. He was trained, as every Rathore prince was, in horse and sword, and he learned early that in Marwar a ruler's power depended on the loyalty of his nobles and the strength of his forts. In **1527**, when **Rana Sanga** of Mewar led the great Rajput confederacy against **Babur**, Marwar sent a contingent to the field of **Khanwa**. Tradition says the young Maldeo commanded it. The battle was lost, and Babur's guns and tactics broke the Rajput alliance. For a boy of sixteen, it was a hard first lesson in what the new power in Delhi could do.

In **1532** Rao Ganga died after falling from a window of the palace at Jodhpur. The khyats record a suspicion, repeated ever since, that Maldeo pushed him. It has never been proven, and it may be no more than the dark gossip that clings to ambitious princes. What is certain is that Maldeo, then about twenty, became Rao of Marwar, and that he meant to rule far more than his father had.

What followed was one of the most remarkable expansions in the history of Rajasthan. Within ten years Maldeo turned a small desert state into the strongest power in the region. He took **Bhadrajun** and **Nagaur**, where a Muslim dynasty of Khanzadas had ruled. He seized **Ajmer**, the old city and strategic prize of central Rajasthan. He drove his own cousin **Rao Biramdev** out of **Merta**, beginning a long and bitter feud with the Mertia Rathores. He took **Jalore**, **Siwana**, **Sambhar** and **Didwana**, and his armies reached far to the north and east. The Persian historian **Ferishta** later called him the most powerful prince of Hindustan, a judgement that was exaggerated but not absurd.

His most painful conquest was of his own kin. In **1542** he turned on **Bikaner**, the state founded by Rao Jodha's son Bika. Its ruler, **Rao Jaitsi**, was killed fighting in the battle that followed, and Maldeo took the city. Jaitsi's son **Kalyanmal** fled, and he and the dispossessed Biramdev of Merta carried their grievances to the one man in north India who might be strong enough to avenge them.

Maldeo had built his empire with relentless energy, and also with relentless suspicion. He garrisoned forts, strengthened walls and kept his nobles close. He built the walls of Jodhpur city, raised the strong fortress called the **Malkot** at Merta, and strengthened the defences of Sojat, Siwana and other strongholds across his realm. He was hard on enemies and quick to take offence.

That last quality shaped his marriages too. He married **Uma De**, a Bhati princess of **Jaisalmer**, and the bards tell that on the wedding night a misunderstanding over a maidservant wounded her pride so deeply that she never lived with him as his wife. She is remembered in the songs of Rajasthan as the **Ruthi Rani**, "the queen who was offended". Tradition says that after his death she still chose to honour him by becoming *sati*. The story is told as legend, but it captures something of how the people remembered Maldeo: a man of great power whose pride sometimes cost him dearly.

Meanwhile the politics of north India were changing fast. In **1540** the Afghan **Sher Shah Suri** defeated the Mughal emperor **Humayun** and drove him out of Hindustan. Humayun wandered west through the desert seeking help, and in **1542** he came towards Marwar, expecting support from Maldeo, who was said to have offered it. But by the time the fugitive emperor arrived, Maldeo had changed his mind, or had never truly meant it. Humayun, warned that he might be seized and handed over to Sher Shah, fled across the desert to **Amarkot** in Sindh. It was there, in October 1542, that his son **Akbar** was born.

Sher Shah had no wish to leave the most powerful Rajput ruler in the west at his flank. Kalyanmal and Biramdev urged him on. In late **1543** he marched into Marwar with a very large army, and Maldeo came out to meet him with a great Rathore host. The two armies faced each other near **Giri** and **Sumel**, between Ajmer and Jodhpur. For about a month neither side attacked. Sher Shah, the chroniclers say, grew anxious: the Rathore army was strong, the ground was difficult, and a defeat here could undo everything he had won.

So he turned to cunning. According to the Persian and Rajput accounts alike, he had letters forged that seemed to show Maldeo's chief nobles promising to betray their master. He let these letters fall into Maldeo's hands. Maldeo, always suspicious, believed them. On the night before the battle he withdrew from the field with the main part of his army.

His commanders **Jaita** and **Kumpa** refused to retreat. They swore that they would not leave the field with the stain of treachery on their names. In the early hours of **5 January 1544**, with only a few thousand men, they charged the enormous Afghan army. They fought with such ferocity that Sher Shah's line was shaken and for a time the outcome seemed in doubt. In the end the Rathores were overwhelmed, and Jaita, Kumpa and most of their men were killed. Sher Shah won, but he is said to have remarked afterwards that he had nearly lost the empire of Hindustan for a handful of millet, meaning the poor desert country of Marwar.

The **Battle of Sammel**, or Giri-Sumel, broke Maldeo's power. Sher Shah's forces occupied **Jodhpur** and Ajmer, and Maldeo retreated into the hills around Siwana. The great empire he had built in a decade fell apart in a single season. It was the darkest point of his life, and it was caused as much by his own distrust of his loyal men as by the strength of his enemy.

But Sher Shah's rule in Marwar was short. In **May 1545** the Afghan emperor was killed by an explosion during the siege of **Kalinjar**. As Afghan power weakened under his successors, Maldeo came down from the hills. He recovered Jodhpur and much of his old territory, and through the rest of the 1540s and 1550s he rebuilt his state.

He was soon at war again. In **1557**, at **Harmara**, his forces fought alongside the Afghan noble **Haji Khan** against **Rana Udai Singh** of Mewar and his allies, and the Rana was defeated. But a new and far greater power was rising in the east. Humayun had returned to Delhi in 1555, and after his death the young **Akbar** began to extend Mughal rule into Rajasthan. Mughal forces took **Ajmer** in **1557**, and in **1562** a Mughal army, aided by Biramdev's son **Jaimal Mertia**, captured **Merta**. The boy born in exile at Amarkot, whom Maldeo had once refused to shelter, now held the gateway to Marwar.

Rao Maldeo died on **7 November 1562**, at about fifty. He had chosen his younger son **Chandrasen** as heir over his elder sons, and the choice led to a long struggle within the family. Chandrasen would resist Akbar for nearly twenty years. Maldeo's elder son **Udai Singh** later made peace with the Mughals and ruled Marwar as the Mota Raja.

Maldeo was a ruler of huge ambition and great ability, a builder of forts and walls and the creator, for a few years, of the largest state Marwar had ever known. He was also suspicious, harsh with his own kin, and capable of terrible mistakes. The memory of Marwar keeps both sides: the lord who made the Rathores feared across north India, and the general who left his bravest men to die at Sammel.

## Highlights of his life

- **Khanwa (1527).** Marwar sent a contingent to Rana Sanga's army against Babur, which tradition says the young Maldeo led.
- **Great expansion (1532–1542).** He took Nagaur, Ajmer, Merta, Jalore, Siwana, Sambhar and Bikaner, making Marwar the strongest state in Rajasthan.
- **Humayun's flight (1542).** The exiled Mughal emperor came to Marwar seeking help but fled to Amarkot, where Akbar was born.
- **Battle of Sammel (1544).** Deceived by Sher Shah's forged letters, he withdrew; his commanders Jaita and Kumpa fought and died, and Marwar was occupied.
- **Recovery of Jodhpur.** After Sher Shah's death in 1545 he came down from the hills and rebuilt his kingdom.
- **Builder of defences.** He walled Jodhpur city, built the Malkot at Merta and strengthened forts across Marwar.
- **Death and succession (1562).** He died after losing Ajmer and Merta to Akbar's armies, and was succeeded by his son Chandrasen.

rao-siha.story:
## Rao Siha — the wanderer whose memorial stone began a dynasty

*Almost everything told of Rao Siha comes from the bardic khyats of Marwar, written down centuries after his death. One firm fact survives: a memorial stone at Bithu, near Pali, that records his death in 1273. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

The thirteenth century was a time of upheaval across north India. In **1192** the Chauhan king **Prithviraj III** was defeated by **Muhammad of Ghor** at the second battle of Tarain, and in **1194** the Gahadavala king **Jayachandra** of **Kannauj**, the ruler the bards call Jaichand, fell at **Chandawar**. Within a generation the Turkish rulers of the new **Delhi Sultanate** held the Ganga plain, and the old Rajput kingdoms of the north either fell, shrank, or moved into the hills and deserts of the west and south.

The Rathores of Marwar told their own origin within this story of loss. According to their khyats, Siha was a grandson of Jaichand of Kannauj, the son of a prince called **Setram** (or Seta), and he left the ruined lands of the Ganga valley with a small band of followers to seek a new home. The bards make him a fugitive prince from the greatest kingdom of the north who rode west with nothing but his sword and his name.

Historians are cautious about this. The Gahadavalas of Kannauj never used the name Rathore in their own inscriptions, and many scholars think the Rathores of Marwar descend from older **Rashtrakuta** families who were already living in Rajasthan, such as the Rashtrakutas of **Hastikundi** (Hathundi) near Pali, known from inscriptions of the tenth century, or from a Rashtrakuta line at **Badaun**. The name Rathore itself comes from Rashtrakuta. The connection with Kannauj may be a later tradition that gave a proud clan a royal ancestor. What can be said with confidence is that Siha was a Rathore chief, that his father's name was Seta, and that he lived and died in Marwar in the middle of the thirteenth century.

The country he came into was hard and divided. Marwar was a land of sand, scrub and rocky hills, cut by the seasonal **Luni** river. The Chauhans held **Nadol** and **Jalore** in the south. Other clans, Paramaras, Guhilas, Bhatis and Sankhlas, held their own pockets of land. Hill and forest peoples, the **Mers** and **Minas**, raided the plains, and from time to time Turkish armies from Delhi or from Gujarat swept through on their way to somewhere else. A man with a few hundred loyal riders could make himself a lord in such a land, if he was strong and lucky.

The bards say Siha first came into the region on a journey to the holy city of **Dwarka**, on the coast of Saurashtra. Pilgrims in those days moved in armed groups, and a band of Rajput horsemen was welcome protection on the roads. Somewhere on that road, the story continues, Siha and his men won the gratitude of local rulers by fighting off raiders, and tradition says he married a Solanki princess of Gujarat. These details cannot be checked, but the picture they give is believable: a warrior chief without a kingdom, moving through western India, offering his sword where it was needed.

The most important tradition concerns **Pali**. In the thirteenth century Pali was a rich trading town, home to a large and prosperous community of Brahmins, the **Paliwals**, who were merchants and landowners as well as priests. Their wealth made them a target. The khyats say they suffered repeated attacks from the Mers and Minas of the nearby hills and from other raiders, and that they asked Siha to protect them. He agreed, drove the raiders off, and stayed. In return the Paliwals gave him land and revenues, and Pali became the first base of the Rathores in Marwar.

It is easy to imagine how that bargain worked. A rich town needed protection. A band of warriors needed a home and an income. Siha's men patrolled the roads, guarded the caravans and rode out against raiders, and the merchants of Pali paid for security. Out of such arrangements, all over medieval India, small lordships grew. Siha's lordship was modest. He was not a king with a great fort and a court. He was the chief of a warrior clan settled around a trading town, respected by the people he defended and feared by those who raided them.

The bards also tell of great battles. One famous tale has Siha killing **Lakha Phulani**, the legendary ruler of Kutch, in single combat. But Lakha Phulani is remembered by other traditions as a figure of the tenth century, long before Siha's time, so the story cannot be true as it stands. It shows how the bards gathered heroic deeds around the founder of their line, and how carefully the khyats must be read.

Siha's life was spent in this world of local struggle. The Delhi Sultanate in his time was ruled by **Iltutmish**, then by his successors, and then by the powerful regent **Balban**. Their armies were occupied with the Mongol threat on the north-west frontier and with rebellions in the east, and they did not hold the deserts of Marwar firmly. That gave chiefs like Siha room to establish themselves. At the same time, the raids that passed through the region made life uncertain, and every chief had to be ready to fight for his land and his people.

Life for such a chief followed the rhythm of the desert. In the dry months, when the wells were low and the caravans moved, the roads had to be watched. After the monsoon, when the grass came up and the herds spread across the plains, the cattle had to be guarded against raiders from the hills. A chief like Siha lived among his kinsmen rather than above them. His followers were brothers, cousins and sworn men who shared his food and his danger, and the bond between them was the foundation of the Rajput clan system that the Rathores would carry into every state they later founded.

Siha never founded a state in the full sense. He did not build Jodhpur, which came two centuries later, and he did not rule Mandore, which the Rathores won only around the end of the fourteenth century. But he planted his clan in the soil of Marwar, among the people of Pali, and that was the beginning of everything that followed.

The firmest evidence of his life is the record of his death. At **Bithu**, a village near Pali, a memorial stone carved in **1273** records that Rao Siha, son of Seta, died there. Such stones, called *devli* or *chhatri* memorials, were raised across Rajasthan for warriors who fell and for women who became sati. Tradition says that Siha died fighting raiders in defence of the people and the cattle of the Pali region, and that his queen followed him in death. The inscription itself confirms the man, his father's name and the date. The manner of his death comes from the bards.

His sons carried the Rathore name further. His eldest son, **Asthan**, succeeded him and took **Kher**, in the Luni valley, from the Guhila chiefs who held it, giving the clan a stronger base. The khyats say that another son, **Soning**, went south to found a Rathore lordship at **Idar** in Gujarat, and that a third, **Aja**, went to Okhamandal near Dwarka, where his descendants were remembered as the Vadhel. Through Asthan's line, generation after generation, the Rathores of Kher grew stronger, until Rao Chunda took Mandore, and his grandson **Rao Jodha** founded Jodhpur in **1459**.

The rulers of Jodhpur, Bikaner, Kishangarh, Ratlam, Idar and many other Rathore states all looked back to Siha as their first ancestor in the west. He is honoured as the founder of the Marwar Rathore line, not because he built a kingdom, but because he gave his descendants a place to stand. From a pilgrim's road, a merchant town that needed a protector, and a memorial stone in a village near Pali, came one of the greatest Rajput dynasties of India.

Nothing more certain can be said about his character. The bards remember him as brave, loyal to those who trusted him and devoted to his gods. The history that can be proven is smaller: a Rathore warrior, son of Seta, who lived in the Pali region and died at Bithu in 1273. But that small record is enough to show that the story of the Marwar Rathores truly begins with him.

## Highlights of his life

- **A disputed origin.** Rathore tradition makes him a grandson of Jaichand of Kannauj; many historians link the clan instead to older Rashtrakuta families of Rajasthan.
- **Journey to the west.** The bards say he first came through Marwar on a pilgrimage towards Dwarka, fighting raiders on the road.
- **Protector of Pali.** Tradition says the Paliwal Brahmins of Pali asked him to defend their town against raiders, and gave him land in return.
- **First Rathore base in Marwar.** He settled his clan around Pali, the root from which the later Rathore states grew.
- **Death at Bithu (1273).** A memorial stone at Bithu near Pali records his death; tradition says he fell fighting raiders.
- **Father of a dynasty.** His son Asthan took Kher, and from his line came Rao Chunda of Mandore and Rao Jodha, the founder of Jodhpur.
