jaswant-singh-i.story:
## Jaswant Singh I — the poet-general caught in the war of the princes

*Maharaja Jaswant Singh's life is unusually well recorded: in the Persian chronicles of Shah Jahan's and Aurangzeb's reigns, in the Marwar khyats, in the writings of European travellers such as François Bernier, and in his own Braj poetry. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

Jaswant Singh was born on **26 December 1626** at **Burhanpur**, in the Deccan, where his father was serving the Mughal emperor. His father, **Raja Gaj Singh** of Marwar, was one of the great Rajput commanders of the empire, and Jaswant grew up in the moving world of Mughal camps, with their tents and elephants, their Persian clerks and Rajput horsemen, their endless campaigns at the edges of the empire.

By the seventeenth century the Rathores of Marwar were no longer the independent lords of the desert that Rao Jodha and Rao Maldeo had been. Since the time of **Mota Raja Udai Singh** in the 1580s, the rulers of Jodhpur had served the Mughals as high-ranking nobles, holding their homeland as a hereditary territory and commanding Mughal armies far from home. It was a relationship of service and reward, of honour and dependence, and every Rathore prince was raised to walk that line.

Gaj Singh had an elder son, **Amar Singh**, a brilliant and hot-tempered warrior. But Gaj Singh chose the younger Jaswant as his heir and sent Amar away. When Gaj Singh died in **1638**, the emperor **Shah Jahan** confirmed the eleven-year-old Jaswant as ruler of Marwar. Amar Singh received a separate fief at Nagaur, and in 1644 became famous across India when he killed the Mughal official **Salabat Khan** in open court at Agra and was himself cut down. His story became a legend in Rajasthan, and his line would later trouble Jaswant's own family.

The young Raja of Marwar grew up under the eye of the emperor. He received a high *mansab*, a rank in the Mughal hierarchy, and as he grew older he commanded troops on the empire's campaigns, including the expeditions to recover **Qandahar** from the Persians in the early 1650s. Shah Jahan favoured him, raised his rank steadily and gave him the title of **Maharaja**. By his early thirties, Jaswant was one of the most powerful Hindu nobles in the empire.

He was also a man of learning. Jaswant studied Sanskrit philosophy and the poetry of the Braj tradition, and he became a poet himself. His *Bhasha Bhushan*, a short work on the figures of speech in poetry, became one of the standard textbooks of Hindi poetics for centuries. He also wrote works on Vedanta philosophy such as the *Aparokshasiddhanta* and *Anand Vilas*. His court in Jodhpur and his camp attracted scholars and poets. His chief minister for many years was **Muhnot Nainsi**, whose great chronicle, the *Nainsi ri Khyat*, and survey of the districts of Marwar are among the most important sources for the history of Rajasthan. Jaswant later fell out with Nainsi and imprisoned him, and Nainsi took his own life in captivity in 1670, a dark episode in the reign of a learned king.

In **1657** Shah Jahan fell seriously ill, and the empire broke into civil war. His four sons, **Dara Shikoh**, **Shuja**, **Aurangzeb** and **Murad Bakhsh**, all raced for the throne. Dara, the eldest, held the capital and his father's favour. Jaswant, as a loyal noble of Shah Jahan, was sent with an imperial army into **Malwa** to stop Aurangzeb and Murad as they marched north from the Deccan and Gujarat.

On **15 April 1658**, the armies met at **Dharmat**, near Ujjain. The Rajput contingents fought with great courage. **Ratan Singh Rathore** of Ratlam and many other Rajput chiefs died on the field. But Aurangzeb's artillery was well handled, many of the Mughal nobles on Jaswant's side fought half-heartedly, and the imperial army was broken. Jaswant, wounded, left the field and rode back to Marwar.

A famous story belongs to this moment. The French traveller **François Bernier** recorded that when Jaswant reached his fort, his queen ordered the gates to be shut against him, saying that a Rajput who had lost a battle should have died rather than come home. Only after days of pleading by her mother, Bernier says, was she calmed. Whether the story happened exactly as told, it was repeated across India as a picture of the Rajput code of honour.

Aurangzeb went on to defeat Dara at **Samugarh** in June 1658, imprison his father in Agra and take the throne. Jaswant, like many nobles, had to make his peace with the new emperor, and through the mediation of **Mirza Raja Jai Singh** of Amber he was pardoned. But his loyalty remained uncertain. When Aurangzeb marched against his brother Shuja in the east, Jaswant commanded part of the army. On the night before the **Battle of Khajwa**, on **5 January 1659**, Jaswant suddenly attacked and plundered Aurangzeb's own baggage train and marched off with his Rathores towards Rajasthan. Aurangzeb kept his nerve and won the battle anyway.

Jaswant then opened contact with Dara, who was gathering a new army in Gujarat, and promised to join him at Ajmer. Dara marched north trusting that promise. But Jai Singh again persuaded Jaswant to stay out of the war and return to Aurangzeb's side, and Jaswant did not come. In **March 1659** Dara was defeated at **Deorai**, near Ajmer, and was later captured and executed. For the rest of his life, Jaswant carried the reputation of a man who had changed sides more than once in the great crisis of his age.

Yet Aurangzeb, who needed powerful Rajput commanders, forgave him again. He made Jaswant governor of **Gujarat**, and then sent him to the Deccan to serve against the rising Maratha power of **Shivaji**. In **1663**, Shivaji made his famous night raid on the Mughal commander **Shaista Khan** in Pune. Jaswant's camp was close by, and there were rumours at the time that he had not been watchful enough, or had even been in sympathy with Shivaji, though nothing was proven. His siege of the Maratha fort of **Kondhana** (later Sinhagad) failed, and he was recalled.

Later in the 1660s Jaswant returned to the Deccan with Prince **Muazzam**, and he played a part in the negotiations that brought a period of peace between the Mughals and Shivaji. He served a second term as governor of Gujarat. Through all these years he spent far more of his life in Mughal camps and provinces than in Jodhpur itself.

This was the hidden cost of Mughal service. While the Maharaja rode with imperial armies in Gujarat, the Deccan and the frontier, Marwar was governed by his ministers and his kinsmen, and the great Rathore nobles held their estates in his name. The desert state paid for his long absences, but it also gained from them: a share in the wealth of the empire, protection from its armies, and a ruler whose voice was heard at the imperial court. Jaswant himself seems to have felt the strain of living in two worlds. His philosophical writings return again and again to the idea that the world of rank and power is passing, and that the soul's true home lies beyond it.

His family life was marked by grief. His eldest son, **Prithvi Singh**, died in **1667**. A legend in Marwar says that Aurangzeb sent the young prince a poisoned robe of honour, but historians regard this as a story born of later bitterness, and the prince most likely died of illness. Other sons died young too. As Jaswant grew older, he had no surviving male heir.

In the 1670s Aurangzeb sent him to the far north-west frontier, to command at **Jamrud**, at the mouth of the **Khyber Pass**, where the Afghan tribes were in revolt. It was a hard, dangerous posting, far from Marwar. Jaswant Singh died there in **December 1678**, at the age of fifty-one.

His death opened the most dangerous crisis in the history of Marwar. With no living son at the time of his death, Aurangzeb placed the state under direct Mughal control. But two of Jaswant's queens were pregnant, and in **February 1679**, at Lahore, they gave birth to two sons. One died soon after, but the other, **Ajit Singh**, survived. The struggle of the Rathores, led by **Durgadas Rathore**, to protect that child and win back Marwar would last almost thirty years.

Jaswant Singh was not the simple hero of resistance against Aurangzeb that later tellings sometimes make him. He was a great Mughal noble, a brave but uneven general, a man who made hard and sometimes doubtful choices in a civil war, and a fine poet and philosopher. His life shows how the Rajput rulers of the seventeenth century lived between two worlds: proud of their own lineage and land, and bound at every step to the empire they served.

## Highlights of his life

- **Heir of Marwar (1638).** Chosen by his father over his elder brother Amar Singh, he became ruler of Marwar at eleven, confirmed by Shah Jahan.
- **Great noble of the empire.** He rose to high Mughal rank, served in the Qandahar campaigns and received the title of Maharaja.
- **Battle of Dharmat (1658).** Leading the imperial army against Aurangzeb and Murad, he was defeated after hard fighting by his Rajput contingents.
- **Khajwa and Deorai (1659).** He plundered Aurangzeb's baggage before Khajwa, then failed to join Dara at Ajmer, and was pardoned once more.
- **Governor and commander.** He governed Gujarat twice and served against Shivaji in the Deccan.
- **Poet and scholar.** His *Bhasha Bhushan* became a classic of Hindi poetics, and his minister Muhnot Nainsi wrote the great chronicle of Marwar.
- **Death at Jamrud (1678).** He died at the Khyber frontier; his posthumous son Ajit Singh became the centre of Marwar's long struggle with Aurangzeb.

ajit-singh.story:
## Ajit Singh — the hidden child for whom Marwar fought thirty years

*Maharaja Ajit Singh's life is told in the Persian histories of Aurangzeb's reign and its aftermath, in the Marwar khyats, in Sanskrit and Dingal court poems such as the Ajitodaya, and in the ballads of Durgadas Rathore. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

Ajit Singh was born in **February 1679** at **Lahore**, a few weeks after the death of his father. **Maharaja Jaswant Singh I** of Marwar had died in December 1678 at **Jamrud**, at the mouth of the Khyber Pass, while commanding there for the emperor **Aurangzeb**. He left no living son. Two of his queens were pregnant, and on the long road home from the frontier they gave birth at Lahore to two boys. One died within weeks. The other was named Ajit, "the unconquered".

He was born into a crisis. Aurangzeb had already placed Marwar under direct Mughal control, sending officers to occupy Jodhpur. Soon afterwards he granted the throne to **Indra Singh**, a grandson of Jaswant's elder brother Amar Singh of Nagaur, in return for a large payment. To the Rathore nobles of Marwar this was a betrayal of the dead Maharaja, who had served the empire all his life. The infant at Lahore was, in their eyes, the true heir.

The Rathore chiefs brought the baby to **Delhi** and petitioned the emperor to recognise him. Aurangzeb's answer was that the child should be raised in the imperial household, and he would decide the boy's future when he came of age. The Rathores feared the prince would be taken from them forever. In **July 1679**, when Mughal troops came to Jaswant Singh's mansion in Delhi to take the child, the Rathores fought them in the streets of the capital.

At the heart of that fight was **Durgadas Rathore**, a son of one of Jaswant Singh's ministers, a man then about forty, who would give the rest of his life to the cause of the infant prince. While his companions held back the Mughal soldiers, sacrificing themselves in the lanes around the house, a small party slipped out of Delhi with the child and rode for Marwar. Tradition says the baby was carried out disguised in a basket of sweets, and that a nurse of the household, remembered in Jodhpur as **Gora Dhay**, put her own child in the prince's place so the escape would not be noticed. These details belong to legend, but the escape itself is history.

Aurangzeb declared that the child the Rathores had taken was an impostor. He had another boy raised at court under the name **Muhammadi Raj**, presented as Jaswant Singh's son. Meanwhile the real Ajit was hidden far from any road, at **Kalindri** in the hills of **Sirohi**, in the care of **Mukunddas Khichi** and a trusted household. For years almost nobody knew where he was.

Aurangzeb's armies marched into Marwar. Jodhpur was occupied, temples were destroyed, and the land suffered greatly. The same year the emperor reimposed the *jizya*, the tax on non-Muslims, across the empire. The war that followed was not a single battle but a long, grinding struggle. The Rathores fought as guerrillas from the desert and the hills, attacking Mughal posts and supply lines, while the imperial governors held the towns.

The Rathores were not alone. **Maharana Raj Singh** of Mewar, who saw in the fate of Marwar a threat to every Rajput state, joined the struggle. In **1681** Aurangzeb's own son, **Prince Akbar**, sent to crush the Rajputs, was persuaded by them to rebel and claim the throne himself. The rebellion collapsed when Aurangzeb, by a forged letter, made the Rajputs believe that Akbar had betrayed them. When the truth was discovered, Durgadas loyally escorted the fugitive prince all the way to the Deccan, to the court of the Maratha king **Sambhaji**. It was one of the most remarkable episodes of the age: a Rajput chief protecting a rebel Mughal prince for the sake of his word.

Durgadas later returned to Marwar and resumed the war. In **1687**, when Ajit was about eight, he was revealed openly to the Rathore nobles, so that they could see the prince for whom they had been fighting. Through the 1690s the struggle went on, with periods of negotiation and of war. Durgadas had kept in his care Prince Akbar's two children, who had been left behind in Marwar, and he raised them with honour and in their own faith. When he returned them to their grandfather around **1698**, the emperor was surprised to find that the girl had even been taught the Quran. As part of the settlement that followed, Ajit received a Mughal rank and a share of Marwar's lands. But peace never lasted long, and fighting broke out again.

Ajit grew to manhood in hiding, in camps and in the hill forts of the frontier. His was not a palace childhood. He learned early to distrust, to wait and to strike when the moment came.

The moment came in **March 1707**, when Aurangzeb died in the Deccan at the age of eighty-eight. As soon as the news reached Marwar, Ajit marched on **Jodhpur**, drove out the Mughal garrison and took his father's fort of **Mehrangarh**. After twenty-eight years he sat at last on the throne of his ancestors. The khyats describe how the mosques built in the city during the occupation were pulled down and Hindu worship was restored.

The new emperor, **Bahadur Shah**, marched into Rajasthan in **1708** and occupied Jodhpur, and Ajit submitted for a time. But he and **Sawai Jai Singh II** of Amber, whose own kingdom had also been seized, left the imperial camp and made common cause with **Maharana Amar Singh II** of Mewar. Together the three Rajput rulers drove out the Mughal officers. Ajit retook Jodhpur, and Bahadur Shah, faced with a Sikh rising in the Punjab, accepted Ajit and Jai Singh in their kingdoms.

One of the saddest acts of these years was Ajit's treatment of the man who had saved him. Soon after taking power, Ajit grew suspicious of Durgadas, whose prestige among the Rathores rivalled his own, and drove him out of Marwar. The old warrior went to Mewar and later to **Ujjain**, where he died in **1718**. The ballads of Rajasthan have never forgiven the ingratitude, and they remember Durgadas, not Ajit, as the true hero of the long war.

As the Mughal empire weakened, Ajit became one of the great powers in its politics. In **1714** the Mughal general **Husain Ali Khan**, one of the two powerful **Sayyid brothers**, invaded Marwar, and as part of the peace Ajit agreed to give his daughter **Indra Kanwar** in marriage to the emperor **Farrukhsiyar**. The wedding took place in Delhi in **1715**. Ajit was appointed governor of **Gujarat** and later held **Ajmer** as well. He allied with the Sayyid brothers, and in **1719** he was in Delhi when they deposed Farrukhsiyar. Afterwards Ajit took his daughter back to Jodhpur, where she returned to the Hindu faith, an extraordinary event in the history of the imperial family.

When the Sayyids fell in **1720**, Ajit lost his strongest allies at court. He held on to Ajmer in defiance of the new emperor, **Muhammad Shah**, until a Mughal army marched against him in **1723**. He was forced to give way and to send his eldest son, **Abhay Singh**, to the imperial court.

The end came within his own family. On **23 June 1724**, Ajit Singh was killed in his sleep by his younger son **Bakht Singh**, at Jodhpur. Contemporary and later accounts say that Bakht Singh acted at the urging of his brother Abhay Singh, who wanted the throne, and some add that powerful figures at the Mughal court encouraged the plot. Several of Ajit's queens are said to have become sati on his pyre. Abhay Singh succeeded him as Maharaja.

Ajit Singh's life began with a child smuggled out of Delhi and ended with a father murdered by his son. Between those two moments lay the long war that saved Marwar's independence from Aurangzeb, the return of the Rathores to Mehrangarh, and the rise of the Rajput states as powers in their own right as the Mughal empire declined. He was a determined and able ruler, and also a suspicious and sometimes ungrateful one. But the name his mother gave him proved true: the empire that tried to take his kingdom never conquered it.

## Highlights of his life

- **Born an heir in danger (1679).** Born at Lahore after his father's death, he was claimed by Aurangzeb and saved by the Rathores in a fight through the streets of Delhi.
- **The hidden years.** Hidden at Kalindri in Sirohi, he grew up in secret while Durgadas Rathore led the war for his throne.
- **Thirty years' struggle.** The Rathores, with Mewar and at one point the rebel Prince Akbar, fought a long guerrilla war against the Mughal occupation of Marwar.
- **Recovery of Jodhpur (1707).** On Aurangzeb's death he took Mehrangarh and restored Rathore rule in Marwar.
- **Rajput alliance (1708).** With Jai Singh II of Amber and Amar Singh II of Mewar he drove out the Mughal officers and won recognition from Bahadur Shah.
- **Power in the late Mughal empire.** He governed Gujarat and Ajmer, allied with the Sayyid brothers and brought his daughter Indra Kanwar home after Farrukhsiyar's fall.
- **Death (1724).** He was murdered in his sleep by his son Bakht Singh and was succeeded by Abhay Singh.

umaid-singh.story:
## Umaid Singh — the Maharaja who built a palace in a famine

*Maharaja Umaid Singh's life is recorded in the administration reports of Jodhpur State, in the records of the British government of India, in photographs and newspapers of his time, and in the memories of the families who built his palace. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

Umaid Singh was born on **8 July 1903** in Jodhpur, the younger son of **Maharaja Sardar Singh** of Marwar. He was born into a world very different from that of his warrior ancestors. Rao Jodha had founded Jodhpur in 1459; Rao Maldeo had fought Sher Shah; Ajit Singh had won back his kingdom from Aurangzeb. But by 1903 Marwar, like all the princely states of Rajputana, was bound by treaty to the British Crown. Its rulers kept their thrones, their courts and much of their internal power, but they could no longer make war or peace on their own. The great question for a modern Maharaja was not how to defend his kingdom with the sword, but how to govern it well in a changing world.

The man who shaped young Umaid Singh most was his great-uncle, **Sir Pratap Singh**, one of the most famous Indian figures of his age. A brilliant horseman, a soldier who had served in campaigns across Asia, and a close friend of the British royal family, Pratap Singh was the guiding force behind Jodhpur's government for decades. He was also the founder of the **Jodhpur Lancers**, the state's cavalry regiment, and the man credited with making Jodhpur famous for polo and for the riding breeches that still carry the city's name.

Sardar Singh died in **1911**, when Umaid was eight. He was succeeded by Umaid's elder brother, **Sumer Singh**, who was still a boy, and Sir Pratap Singh acted as regent. When the **First World War** broke out, the young Maharaja Sumer Singh went with the Jodhpur Lancers to France, one of the youngest ruling princes to serve. In **September 1918**, in Palestine, the Jodhpur Lancers took part in the famous cavalry charge at **Haifa**, a feat still remembered in the Indian Army. Umaid Singh, then a schoolboy, had no part in the fighting, but he grew up in a household proud of that service.

Then tragedy struck. In **October 1918** Sumer Singh died suddenly, at only twenty-one. Umaid Singh, aged fifteen, became Maharaja of Marwar. Because he was a minor, Sir Pratap Singh again guided the state as regent. Umaid Singh was educated at **Mayo College** in **Ajmer**, the school founded for the sons of the Rajput princes, and he trained in administration as well as in riding, shooting and polo. In **1921** he married **Badan Kanwar**, and their eldest son, **Hanwant Singh**, was born in 1923.

Sir Pratap Singh died in 1922, and in **January 1923** Umaid Singh was given full ruling powers. He was nineteen years old, and he inherited a state with enormous problems. Marwar was one of the largest princely states of Rajputana, but much of it was desert. Rainfall was scarce and unreliable, and the people depended on wells, tanks and the monsoon. Roads were few, schools and hospitals were limited, and the state's finances were in poor condition.

The young Maharaja set out to modernise. He reorganised the administration and the finances of the state, and over the following years Jodhpur built new schools, hospitals, roads and waterworks. The **Jodhpur Railway**, owned by the state, was extended across the desert, carrying goods and passengers and linking Marwar to the ports of Sindh and to the rest of India. Electricity and modern water supply came to the capital.

Umaid Singh had a passion for flying. He learned to fly himself, and in **1931** he founded the **Jodhpur Flying Club**. Jodhpur's aerodrome became one of the most important in India, an essential stop on the international air routes between Europe and the East, where the great passenger aircraft of the age landed to refuel on their long journeys. For a desert kingdom that had once depended on camel caravans, this was a remarkable change.

Yet no railway or aerodrome could change the desert's oldest enemy. In Marwar, famine had always come with the failure of the monsoon. When the rains did not fall, the wells sank, the grass withered, cattle died in thousands and whole villages took to the roads in search of work and food. Every ruler of Marwar, from Rao Jodha onwards, had lived under that shadow, and the people measured their kings partly by what they did when the rains failed.

The project for which Umaid Singh is best remembered began in the late 1920s. Marwar suffered several years of failed rains, and the farmers and herders of the desert faced drought and famine. The story told in Jodhpur, and repeated ever since, is that the people came to the Maharaja for help, and that he decided to give them work rather than charity by building a great new palace. Whatever the exact balance of his motives, the scale of the work was immense. On **18 November 1929** the foundation stone was laid on **Chittar Hill**, overlooking the city. Thousands of workers were employed over the following years, quarrying and dressing the local sandstone, hauling it up the hill and fitting the blocks together.

The architect was the British designer **Henry Vaughan Lanchester**. He created a building that blended Indian and European ideas: a great central dome inspired by Indian temple and palace forms, wings and courts in the clean, geometric style of **Art Deco**, then fashionable across the world. The palace was built of a pale golden sandstone, fitted together with great precision. It contained hundreds of rooms, a throne room, a banquet hall, a library, a theatre and an indoor swimming pool. Work went on for well over a decade, and the **Umaid Bhawan Palace** was completed in **1943**. It became one of the largest private residences in the world.

Critics then and later have asked whether a famine-stricken state should have spent so much on a palace. Defenders have pointed out that the work fed thousands of families through hard years and left Jodhpur with one of the great buildings of twentieth-century India. Both views are part of its story.

Umaid Singh also built elsewhere. At **Sardar Samand**, beside a lake created in his father's time, he built a hunting lodge in the same modern style. He was a keen sportsman, a polo player and a shikari, as most princes of his age were. He was also a firm supporter of the British connection. When the **Second World War** began in 1939, Jodhpur placed its resources at the service of the war effort. The state forces served overseas, and the Jodhpur aerodrome became a centre for training pilots. The Maharaja was given honorary rank in the **Royal Air Force**.

But the world was changing faster than any prince could control. The Indian national movement had spread into the princely states. In Marwar, political workers led by **Jai Narayan Vyas** organised the **Marwar Lok Parishad**, demanding responsible government and civil rights. The state responded at different times with arrests and with limited reforms. Like most rulers of his generation, Umaid Singh believed in benevolent personal rule rather than democracy, and the gap between that belief and the hopes of his people grew wider with every year.

By the summer of **1947**, independence was only weeks away, and the future of the princely states hung in the balance. Umaid Singh did not live to see it. He died in **June 1947**, at the age of forty-three. His son **Hanwant Singh** succeeded him and, after some hesitation, signed Jodhpur's accession to India in August 1947. Within a few years the old state of Marwar had been merged into the new state of **Rajasthan**.

Umaid Singh's reign stands at the end of a story nearly five hundred years long, from Rao Jodha's fort on the hill of birds to a palace on Chittar Hill. He was a moderniser, an aviator, a builder and a ruler devoted to the welfare of his subjects as he understood it. The palace that bears his name still stands above Jodhpur, home to his descendants and open in part to visitors, a monument to the last great age of the Maharajas.

## Highlights of his life

- **An unexpected Maharaja (1918).** He came to the throne at fifteen after the sudden death of his elder brother, Sumer Singh, under the regency of Sir Pratap Singh.
- **Moderniser of Marwar.** After taking full powers in 1923, he reformed the state's finances and built schools, hospitals, roads, waterworks and railways.
- **Pioneer of aviation.** A pilot himself, he founded the Jodhpur Flying Club in 1931 and made Jodhpur a major stop on international air routes.
- **Umaid Bhawan Palace (1929–1943).** Begun in years of drought and famine, it gave work to thousands and became one of the largest private residences in the world.
- **Patron of a new architecture.** With the architect H. V. Lanchester he created a blend of Indian forms and Art Deco design.
- **Second World War.** Jodhpur supported the war effort, and its aerodrome became a training centre for pilots.
- **Death on the eve of independence (1947).** He died in June 1947, and his son Hanwant Singh signed Jodhpur's accession to India.

rao-satal.story:
## Rao Satal — the short reign that ended in a rescue

*Rao Satal's life comes to us mainly through the Marwar chronicles, the khyats of the Rathore court and the folk memory kept alive in the Ghudla festival. His reign was brief and poorly documented; where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

In the middle of the fifteenth century, the Rathores of Marwar were a clan that had lost almost everything and then won it back. **Rao Ranmal**, their chief, had been murdered at Chittor in 1438, and his son **Jodha** had spent years as a fugitive in the desert, gathering horsemen, losing battles and returning to fight again. By the 1450s Jodha had recovered **Mandore**, the old Rathore seat, and in **1459** he laid the foundations of a new fortress on a rocky ridge a few miles to the south. The fort was called **Mehrangarh**, and the city that grew below it took his name: **Jodhpur**.

Satal was born into this house of hard-won power as one of the many sons of Rao Jodha. The chronicles name his mother as a Hadi queen, the same queen who bore his younger brother **Suja**. The exact year of his birth is not recorded. He grew up in a court that was still half a war camp, where the talk was of raids and counter-raids, of the Sisodias of Mewar to the south, of the Bhatis of Jaisalmer to the west, and of the Muslim governors who held Ajmer and Nagaur to the east and north.

Jodha had many sons, and he used them as a frontier king uses his best horsemen. Rather than keep them all at court, he sent them out to win land of their own. **Bika** rode north into the Jangladesh country and founded the kingdom that became **Bikaner**. **Duda** and **Varsingh** went east and made **Merta** their home. Other sons were given villages and districts across Marwar, and each became the root of a branch of the Rathore clan. In this way the Rathore name spread across the desert faster than any single army could have carried it.

Satal was not the son Jodha had first marked as his heir. That place had belonged to another son, **Nimba**, who died before his father. The question of succession therefore remained open in Jodha's last years, as it so often did in Rajput houses, where a father's favour, a mother's rank and the support of the great nobles all counted. In the end it was Satal who stood next in line when the old Rao died in **1489**.

Before he came to the throne, Satal had already held lands of his own in western Marwar. Tradition credits him with founding the town and small fort of **Satalmer**, near **Pokaran**, in the sandy country that lay between Jodhpur and the lands of the Bhatis. Whether the fort was built before or after his accession is not clear, but the name has survived for more than five centuries, one of the few marks Satal left upon the map.

When Jodha died, the kingdom Satal inherited was large but loose. Marwar was not yet a centralised state. It was a web of brothers, cousins and nephews, each with his own fort, his own followers and his own pride. A new Rao had to win their respect as much as their obedience. The chronicles say little about how Satal governed in these years, and later writers have filled the gap with general praise. What can be said is that the brothers held together during his brief rule. There was no open war among Jodha's sons while Satal sat at Jodhpur, and that, in a house of so many strong-willed men, was no small thing.

To the east lay a constant danger. **Ajmer**, the ancient city of the Chauhans, was then in the hands of a Muslim governor, and its garrison raided the lands of the Rathores whenever it could. The chronicles of Marwar name the governor of Ajmer in these years as **Mallu Khan**, and they remember one raid above all others.

It came in the spring of **1492**. It was the season of the festival of **Gangaur** and the days around it, when the young women and girls of the villages went out together to worship the goddess Gauri, singing and carrying water and flowers. At **Pipar**, a town in eastern Marwar, a group of girls had gathered for the worship at a tank outside the town. Raiders from Mallu Khan's army, led by a commander whom the chronicles and the folk songs call **Ghudle Khan**, fell upon them and carried them away. The number varies in the telling; the traditional accounts speak of about a hundred and forty.

The news reached Jodhpur within hours. The bards describe the scene in the fort: a messenger falling from his horse at the gate, the weeping of the women, and the Rao rising from his seat.

"They have taken our daughters," the messenger cried, "and the road to Ajmer is open."

Satal did not wait for a council. He called for his horse and sent riders to his brother **Suja** and to his cousin **Varsingh of Merta**, whose lands lay nearest to the raiders' path. The tradition is clear on the point that mattered most: the Rao himself rode out at the head of his men.

The raiders were slowed by their captives and by their plunder. The Rathores, riding hard through the night, caught them near **Kosana**, not far from Pipar. There was no time for an ordered battle. The bards tell of horsemen charging out of the dark, of the raiders turning to fight, and of the captives running towards the Rathore lines as the fighting broke around them.

In the thick of it, the chronicles say, Ghudle Khan was struck down, his body pierced by many arrows. The raiders broke and fled towards Ajmer. The girls of Pipar were brought back, every one of them, the tradition insists, unharmed.

But the victory had a price. Rao Satal had been badly wounded in the fight. He was carried from the field, and within a short time he died of his wounds. The chronicles of Marwar record that his queens followed him in *sati* at Kosana, where a memorial to the Rao was later raised.

He had ruled for only about three years. He left no son to succeed him, and the throne passed to his brother **Suja**, who had ridden beside him on that last night.

Rao Satal's reign was short and, in most respects, quiet. His name does not appear in the great Persian histories of the age, and his building works were modest. Yet few rulers of Marwar have been remembered as warmly by ordinary people. The reason lies not in the court chronicles but in a festival.

Every year in Marwar, in the days after **Holi** and before Gangaur, girls and young women carry through the streets an earthen pot pierced with many holes, with a lamp burning inside it. The pot is called the **ghudla**. As the women walk from house to house in the evening, singing songs and collecting small gifts of oil and grain, the light shines out through the holes in a hundred small points. Folk tradition in Marwar explains the custom through the story of 1492: the pierced pot, people say, stands for the head of Ghudle Khan, shot through with Rathore arrows, and the light within it for the girls who were brought safely home.

Whether the festival began with that night, or whether an older custom of lamp-pots took on the story later, cannot now be known. Historians note that festivals of pierced lamps exist in other regions as well. But in Marwar the meaning is fixed: the ghudla belongs to Rao Satal and to the girls of Pipar, and every spring the women of the desert carry his victory through their villages.

There is something fitting in that memory. Satal did not conquer new lands like his father, or found a kingdom like his brother Bika, or build a great fort that dominates a city's skyline. He is remembered instead for answering a cry for help, for riding out himself rather than sending others, and for giving his life to bring the captured daughters of his people home. The khyats of the Rathores honour him as a dutiful son and a brave Rao. The songs of the women honour him as something closer: a protector.

After his death, Marwar continued under Rao Suja, who held the kingdom together for more than twenty years. The line of Jodhpur rulers that followed, down to the last Maharaja, who joined the Indian Union in 1947, descended not from Satal but from Suja. Satal's own line ended on the field of Kosana.

## Highlights of his life

- **Son of the founder of Jodhpur.** Born to Rao Jodha, who built Mehrangarh and founded Jodhpur in 1459, he grew up as the Rathores spread across the desert.
- **Founder of Satalmer.** Tradition credits him with the town and fort of Satalmer near Pokaran, in western Marwar.
- **Rao of Marwar (1489–1492).** He succeeded Jodha and kept the brotherhood of Rathore chiefs united during his short reign.
- **The rescue at Kosana (1492).** He pursued the raiders of Mallu Khan of Ajmer, who had carried off girls of Pipar during the Gangaur season, and won them back.
- **Death from his wounds.** He died after the fight at Kosana, leaving no son, and was succeeded by his brother Suja.
- **Remembered in the Ghudla festival.** Folk tradition in Marwar links the pierced lamp-pot carried by women each spring to his victory over Ghudle Khan.

rao-suja.story:
## Rao Suja — the brother who held the house of Jodha together

*Rao Suja's reign is known mainly from the Marwar khyats and the chronicles of Bikaner, written long after his death. They record his family, his quarrel with his brother Bika and the succession that followed him, but say little about his daily rule. Where history and tradition part ways, this story says so.*

Suja was one of the younger sons of **Rao Jodha**, the founder of **Jodhpur**. His mother, the chronicles say, was the Hadi queen **Jasmade**, a princess of the Hada Chauhans of the hill country to the south-east, and his elder full brother was **Satal**. The year of his birth is not recorded. He grew up in the decades after 1459, when the fortress of **Mehrangarh** was rising on its ridge and the city of Jodhpur was spreading below it, when the Rathores were still a clan of horsemen who had only lately become a kingdom.

His childhood was spent among brothers who were already making names for themselves. **Bika** rode north with a few hundred men and carved out a new realm in the Jangladesh country, the beginning of **Bikaner**. **Duda** and **Varsingh** settled at **Merta** in the east. Others took villages and districts across the desert. Suja stayed closer to the centre of his father's power, and the chronicles give him the name by which he is also known, **Surajmal**.

When Jodha died in **1489**, the throne passed to Satal. Suja served his brother loyally, and in the spring of **1492** he rode beside him on the most famous night of Satal's life. Raiders from **Ajmer**, sent by the governor **Mallu Khan**, had carried off the girls of **Pipar** during the season of the **Gangaur** festival. The Rathores pursued them through the night and caught them near **Kosana**. The girls were rescued and the raiders' commander, remembered in folk tradition as **Ghudle Khan**, was killed. But Satal was mortally wounded, and he died soon afterwards without a son.

So it was in grief, and almost on the battlefield, that Suja became **Rao of Marwar**.

His first great test came from within the family. Bika, the brother who had built a kingdom of his own in the north, had never forgotten that he too was a son of Jodha, and older than Suja. Tradition says that Jodha had promised Bika certain of the family's sacred heirlooms, the emblems of Rathore kingship that the clan had carried with it since its earliest days in the desert. Among them, the chronicles of Bikaner list a royal throne, a ceremonial umbrella and other objects of worship and honour. These were not mere ornaments. To hold them was to claim to be the senior line of the house of Jodha.

After Satal's death, Bika demanded them. When Suja refused, Bika marched south with his army and laid siege to Jodhpur. For a time it seemed that the sons of Jodha would destroy each other in front of the walls their father had built.

The chronicles of both houses agree on how the crisis ended. It was not a battle that settled it, but a woman. **Rani Jasmade**, the widow of Jodha and the mother of Suja, intervened. The bards imagine her standing between her son and her stepson.

"Your father built this fort for all his sons," she says in the story. "Will you pull it down to decide which of you he loved more?"

Whatever words she really used, the outcome is recorded. The heirlooms were handed to Bika, who carried them back to Bikaner, where they were kept with honour for centuries. Bika lifted the siege and went home. Suja kept Jodhpur and the lands of Marwar. Each brother came away with something. Bika had the symbols of seniority; Suja had the kingdom. It was a compromise that saved the Rathore clan from a ruinous war, and it shaped the relationship between Jodhpur and Bikaner for generations, two kingdoms of one blood, sometimes allies and sometimes rivals.

The rest of Suja's long reign is less clearly recorded. He ruled for about twenty-three years, from **1492 to 1515**, and the chronicles remember those years mainly as a time when Marwar held together. That was a real achievement. Jodha's kingdom had been made by conquest and held by brotherhood, and every brother and nephew with a fort of his own was a possible rebel. Suja's task was to keep the chiefs of the clan loyal to the throne at Jodhpur without trying to crush them, which would only have driven them into revolt. He granted lands, settled quarrels, and confirmed his kinsmen in the districts they held.

It helps to picture the land he ruled. Marwar, "the land of death" in one old explanation of its name, was a country of sand ridges, thorn scrub and scattered villages clustered around wells and tanks. Rain was uncertain, and a single failed monsoon could empty whole districts as families drove their herds towards better pasture. Its wealth lay in camels, cattle and horses, in the caravan roads that crossed the desert between Gujarat, Sindh and the north, and in the tolls that a strong ruler could collect from them. A Rao of Marwar was judged by whether those roads were safe and whether the village wells were protected from raiders. Seen in that light, a long reign without disaster was a sign of steady government, even when the chronicles have little to say about it.

At the centre of it all stood his father's fortress. Mehrangarh in Suja's day was far smaller than the vast citadel visitors see today; most of its great palaces were built by later rulers. But it was already the seat of the dynasty and the symbol of the clan's recovery, and holding it meant holding Marwar.

Around him, the political map of northern and western India was changing. In Delhi, **Sikandar Lodi** was rebuilding the strength of the Delhi Sultanate. In Gujarat, the powerful **Mahmud Begada** ruled until 1511. In Mewar to the south, **Rana Raimal** governed Chittor, and in **1508** the throne passed to his son **Rana Sanga**, who would become the greatest Rajput power of his age. Ajmer and the eastern borderlands remained contested ground between Rajput chiefs and Muslim governors. Marwar under Suja was not the strongest of these states, but it survived intact among them, and it did not lose ground.

Within the clan, the branches founded by Jodha's sons were growing into strong houses. At Merta, the line of Duda flourished, and around **1498** a daughter was born in that family who would become one of the most famous figures in Indian devotion: **Mirabai**, the granddaughter of Duda, whose songs to Krishna are still sung across India. She was born during Suja's reign, in the Rathore country of Merta, a reminder that the clan's story in these years was not only one of war.

Suja's own family was large. His sons included **Bagha**, **Biram**, **Shekha** and **Uda**, the last of whom became the founder of the **Udawat** branch of the Rathores, which held lands around Jaitaran. Bagha, the son whom many expected to be his heir, died before his father. Bagha left a young son of his own, named **Ganga**.

When Rao Suja died in **1515**, the old question of succession came back. Biram was Suja's surviving son, and by the rule of seniority he might have expected the throne. But the great nobles of Marwar, according to the chronicles, preferred Bagha's son. They placed **Ganga** on the throne at Jodhpur, and Biram had to be content with the district of **Sojat**. The decision did not end the matter. Biram and later Shekha would both resist Ganga's rule, and Marwar would see years of conflict between uncle and nephew before Ganga's position was secure.

Suja's reign is easy to overlook. He fought no great battle that history remembers by name, and he built no great monument. His brother Satal is remembered for the rescue at Kosana, his brother Bika for founding a kingdom, his great-grandson **Maldeo** for making Marwar one of the strongest powers in northern India. Suja stands between them, and his work was the kind that leaves few traces: keeping peace in a family of proud men, accepting a hard compromise rather than a ruinous war, and handing on a kingdom that was still whole after twenty-three years.

The chroniclers of Marwar, writing much later, remembered him as a just and steady ruler. They could hardly have known the details of his daily government. But they knew the outcome. When Suja came to the throne, the sons of Jodha were close to turning their swords on each other. When he died, Marwar was still one kingdom, and the line of Jodhpur, which would continue unbroken down to the twentieth century, ran through his grandson Ganga.

## Highlights of his life

- **Son of Rao Jodha.** Born to the founder of Jodhpur and the Hadi queen Jasmade, he grew up as the Rathores became a kingdom.
- **At Kosana with Satal (1492).** He rode with his brother to rescue the girls of Pipar from the raiders of Ajmer, and became Rao when Satal died of his wounds.
- **The dispute with Bika.** When Bika besieged Jodhpur to claim the family heirlooms, a settlement made through Rani Jasmade gave Bika the heirlooms and left Suja the kingdom.
- **Twenty-three years of unity (1492–1515).** He kept the many Rathore chiefs loyal to Jodhpur and handed on Marwar intact.
- **Father of new branches.** His son Uda founded the Udawat Rathores, one of the clan's important branches.
- **The succession of Ganga.** After his death in 1515, the nobles chose his grandson Ganga, son of Bagha, over his surviving son Biram.

rao-ganga.story:
## Rao Ganga — the grandson chosen by the nobles

*Rao Ganga's reign is recorded in the Marwar khyats, the chronicles of Bikaner and Merta, and in Muhnot Nainsi's seventeenth-century histories. They tell of a contested succession, a war with his own uncle and a mysterious death. Where history and tradition part ways, this story says so.*

When Ganga was born, no one expected him to rule Marwar. He was the son of **Bagha**, one of the sons of **Rao Suja**, and in the ordinary course of things the throne would have passed from Suja to one of his own sons. The exact year of Ganga's birth is not recorded. He grew up in the fortress of **Mehrangarh** at **Jodhpur**, the city his great-grandfather **Rao Jodha** had founded in 1459, in a family crowded with uncles, cousins and ambitious kinsmen.

The first turning point of his life came early and through grief. His father Bagha, whom many in Marwar had regarded as Suja's natural heir, died before his own father. Ganga was left as a young prince whose claim depended entirely on the goodwill of others.

That goodwill was tested in **1515**, when Rao Suja died. Suja's surviving son, **Biram**, expected the throne. But the great Rathore nobles of Marwar, the chiefs who held the forts and villages of the desert and whose swords made any Rao's power real, chose otherwise. According to the chronicles, they placed the young Ganga on the throne at Jodhpur. The reasons are not fully recorded. Some accounts suggest that the nobles distrusted Biram and his advisers; others that Ganga, as the son of the heir who had died, seemed the more rightful choice. Whatever their motives, the decision made Ganga the **Rao of Marwar**, and it made him a ruler with powerful rivals inside his own family.

Biram was given the district of **Sojat**, but he did not accept his loss quietly. In the early years of Ganga's reign, the chronicles describe a struggle between uncle and nephew for the lands around Sojat. With the support of the nobles who had raised him, Ganga eventually drove Biram out, and Sojat came under Jodhpur's control. It was the first sign that the young Rao, whatever the circumstances of his elevation, was prepared to fight for his throne.

In these struggles a figure appeared beside him who would shape the rest of his life and the future of Marwar: his son **Maldeo**, born in **1511**. Even as a youth, Maldeo was a fighter of extraordinary energy and ambition, and the chronicles give him a large share of the credit for the victories of his father's reign.

Beyond Marwar, the world was changing quickly. In Mewar, **Rana Sanga** had become the leading Rajput ruler of his age, defeating the Sultans of Malwa and Gujarat and the armies of Delhi. In **1526**, a new power arrived in the north: **Babur**, a prince from Central Asia, defeated **Ibrahim Lodi** at **Panipat** and took Delhi, using field guns and matchlocks on a scale never before seen in India. The next year, Rana Sanga gathered a great confederacy of Rajput rulers and Afghan allies to drive the newcomer out.

Marwar was part of that confederacy. Rao Ganga sent a contingent of Rathore horsemen to join Sanga, and the chronicles say that it was led by the young **Maldeo**. The Rathores of **Merta**, Ganga's kinsmen, came too. On **17 March 1527**, the allied army met Babur at **Khanwa**, near Fatehpur Sikri. The battle was long and bloody. Babur's guns and his disciplined flanking cavalry broke the Rajput charges, and Sanga was wounded and carried from the field. Among the many Rajput nobles killed were the Meratiya Rathore chiefs **Raimal** and **Ratan Singh**, the sons of **Duda** of Merta. Ratan Singh was the father of the poet-saint **Mirabai**. Maldeo survived and brought the remnants of the Marwar contingent home.

The defeat at Khanwa ended the hope of a single Rajput power ruling northern India, and Sanga died in 1528. For Marwar, the immediate consequences were less dramatic than for Mewar. Babur's empire was still new and did not reach into the deep desert, and Ganga's kingdom was left to face older, more familiar dangers.

The most serious of these came from within his own family again. **Shekha**, another son of Suja and Ganga's uncle, held lands around **Pipar** and had never accepted his nephew's rule. He found an ally in **Daulat Khan**, the Muslim ruler of **Nagaur**, the strong town to the north of Jodhpur that had long been held by a line of Khanzada governors. In **1529** the two of them advanced against Jodhpur.

Ganga did not face them alone. His kinsman **Rao Jaitsi of Bikaner**, the grandson of Bika, came to his aid, and Maldeo, now a seasoned commander, rode at his side. The armies met at **Sevki**, not far from Jodhpur. The bards tell of a fierce fight in the open plain and of elephants in Daulat Khan's ranks that panicked and turned back on their own men. Whatever the details, the outcome is clear. Shekha was killed on the field, Daulat Khan's army was broken, and Ganga's throne was secure. Bikaner's help at Sevki showed that the old quarrel between the houses of Bika and Suja had given way, at least for a time, to the loyalty of kinship.

With his rivals defeated, Ganga could turn to the business of ruling. His reign was not one of great conquest, but it was one of consolidation. The power of the Rao at Jodhpur over the scattered Rathore chiefs grew firmer, and the lands around Sojat and Pipar came firmly under his authority. Tradition associates Ganga with works of piety and public use in Jodhpur. The temple of **Ganga Shyamji**, dedicated to Krishna, is traditionally said to have been founded in his reign, around an image that, according to local tradition, came to Jodhpur with a queen from **Sirohi**. The tank called **Gangelav** is also linked with his name. The present temple owes much to later rebuilding, but the memory of its founder survives in its name.

Ruling Marwar in those years meant managing men more than territory. The Rao was the head of a great brotherhood rather than an absolute monarch. Each Rathore chief held his village or district as a share of the clan's land, owed service with his horsemen when the Rao called, and expected in return to be consulted, honoured and protected. A wise Rao gave rewards after a victory, settled disputes between neighbouring chiefs before they turned into blood feuds, and remembered who had stood by him in hard times. Ganga owed his throne to exactly these men, and he never forgot it. The bards picture his court at Mehrangarh as a place of long evenings, of opium shared from the palm in the old desert custom of brotherhood, of songs of Jodha's wars and of Satal's ride to Kosana. It was in this world that Maldeo learned how to command, and later how to bend the chiefs to a harder kind of rule.

The last part of Ganga's life is overshadowed by the rising power of his son. Maldeo was ambitious, impatient and immensely capable, and by the early 1530s he was the real leader of Marwar's armies. The relationship between father and son seems to have grown strained, though the chronicles do not explain why.

In **1532**, Rao Ganga died in a fall from a window of the palace in Mehrangarh. How he fell is one of the unsolved questions of Marwar's history. Some accounts say it was an accident: the Rao, they say, was sitting at the window and lost his balance, and some add that he had been drinking. Others, including later chroniclers, record the persistent rumour that Maldeo pushed his father to his death to take the throne sooner. No contemporary document settles the matter, and historians have treated the charge of patricide as unproven. What is certain is that Maldeo became Rao of Marwar in the same year, and that under him Marwar rose to the height of its power.

Ganga's reign is often seen only as a bridge between Suja and Maldeo. But it was more than a pause. He came to the throne as a young man raised up by the nobles over the head of his uncle, and he made himself a real ruler. He sent his men to stand with Rana Sanga at Khanwa, the greatest Rajput battle of the age. He defeated his uncle Shekha and the ruler of Nagaur at Sevki, and he left to his son a kingdom whose internal rivals had been subdued. When Maldeo began the great wars that would make Marwar feared across northern India, he began them from the foundation his father had laid.

## Highlights of his life

- **Chosen by the nobles (1515).** After Rao Suja's death, the Rathore chiefs raised Ganga, son of Bagha, to the throne over his uncle Biram.
- **Victory over Biram.** He brought Sojat under Jodhpur's control after a struggle with his uncle.
- **Marwar at Khanwa (1527).** His Rathore contingent, led by his son Maldeo, fought beside Rana Sanga against Babur.
- **Victory at Sevki (1529).** With his son Maldeo and Rao Jaitsi of Bikaner, he defeated his uncle Shekha and Daulat Khan of Nagaur.
- **Temples and tanks.** Tradition links the Ganga Shyamji temple and the Gangelav tank in Jodhpur with his reign.
- **A mysterious death (1532).** He died in a fall from a palace window; rumours that Maldeo was responsible were never proven.
- **Father of Rao Maldeo.** He handed on a consolidated Marwar to the son who made it one of the strongest powers in northern India.

rao-chandrasen.story:
## Rao Chandrasen — the forgotten rebel of Marwar

*Rao Chandrasen's life is known from the Marwar khyats, Muhnot Nainsi's chronicles and the Persian histories of Akbar's reign, such as the Akbarnama. Mughal writers saw him as a rebel, Marwar's bards as a hero who would not bow. Where the sources disagree, or where tradition goes beyond them, this story says so.*

Chandrasen was born in **1541**, at a time when his father's kingdom was at the height of its power and on the edge of disaster. His father was **Rao Maldeo** of Marwar, the most formidable Rajput ruler of his generation, who had extended Rathore rule over a great sweep of western India, from Nagaur and Ajmer to Jalor and the borders of Sindh. His mother, the chronicles say, was **Rani Swarupde**, a Jhala princess and Maldeo's favourite queen.

The boy's earliest years were shadowed by war. In **1544**, the Afghan emperor **Sher Shah Suri** marched against Marwar. At the battle of **Giri-Sumel**, Maldeo's great commanders **Jaita** and **Kumpa** charged the Afghan army with a few thousand men after Maldeo, deceived by forged letters into doubting their loyalty, had withdrawn. They died almost to a man. Sher Shah is said to have remarked that he had nearly lost the empire of Hindustan for a handful of millet, so poor was the desert land he had fought for. Jodhpur was occupied, and Maldeo recovered it only after Sher Shah's death in 1545. Chandrasen grew up in a kingdom that had learned both its strength and its vulnerability.

He was raised in the manner of a Rathore prince: on horseback almost as soon as he could walk, trained with lance, sword and bow, and taught the long genealogies of his clan by the bards of the court. He would have heard, again and again, the story of Jaita and Kumpa, and of how loyalty and courage had been betrayed by suspicion. The lessons of his childhood were the lessons of a frontier kingdom: that a fort could be lost and won back, that the desert itself was a refuge, and that a Rathore did not yield what his fathers had won. Those lessons would shape every choice of his life.

Maldeo had many sons, and he chose a younger son, Chandrasen, as his heir. His eldest son **Ram** had quarrelled with him and been sent away, and another son, **Udai Singh**, born in **1538** and older than Chandrasen, was passed over. It was a choice that would cost Marwar dearly. When Maldeo died in **November 1562**, Chandrasen took the throne at **Jodhpur**, and his brothers immediately turned against him.

The chronicles describe a clash with Udai Singh in the first months of the reign, in which Udai Singh was defeated. But Ram took a different and more dangerous path. He went to the court of the young emperor **Akbar**, who had come to the throne in 1556, and asked for help to claim his father's kingdom.

Akbar was glad of the opportunity. A divided Marwar was an open door into Rajasthan. A Mughal army under **Hussain Quli Khan** was sent against Jodhpur. Chandrasen held the city and its fortress for a time, but the siege dragged on and in **1565** Jodhpur fell to the Mughals. Chandrasen withdrew to **Bhadrajun**, a stronghold in the rugged country to the south. For the rest of his life, he would never again rule from his father's fort.

The loss of Jodhpur was part of a larger change sweeping across Rajasthan. Akbar was offering the Rajput rulers a new bargain: those who accepted his overlordship, sent their sons to court and served in his armies would keep their lands as hereditary fiefs, receive high ranks, and share in the wealth of a growing empire. In **1562** **Raja Bharmal** of Amber had accepted that bargain and given his daughter in marriage to the emperor. Those who refused faced the full weight of Mughal power. In **1568** Akbar took **Chittor** after a terrible siege, and in **1569** **Ranthambhore** fell. One by one, the great fortresses of Rajasthan passed under Mughal control or into Mughal alliance. Chandrasen, holding out in the rocky country of southern Marwar, watched the circle close.

In **November 1570**, Akbar came to **Nagaur** on his way to the north-west, and held court there. It was a moment of decision for the Rajput rulers of the desert. **Rao Kalyanmal of Bikaner** and his son **Rai Singh** came and submitted. So did **Rawal Har Raj of Jaisalmer**. Chandrasen's brother **Udai Singh** came too and entered Mughal service.

Chandrasen came to Nagaur as well. What happened there is told differently by different sources. The Mughal histories record his appearance at court. But Chandrasen did not stay, and he did not accept the terms that would have made him a vassal. The bards of Marwar tell the scene with relish: the proud Rao looking around a court full of Rajput princes who had already bowed, and turning his horse back towards the desert.

"I came to see the emperor," the bards make him say, "not to sell him Marwar."

Whatever his words, his choice was clear. He left Nagaur and returned to the hills. Akbar responded by placing the administration of Jodhpur in the hands of **Rai Singh of Bikaner** in **1572**, and Mughal forces began to close in on Chandrasen's remaining strongholds.

Bhadrajun was taken, and Chandrasen fell back on **Siwana**, a fort set among rocky hills in the south of Marwar, which had long served the Rathores as a last refuge. Here he made his stand. For several years, Mughal commanders and their Rajput allies besieged Siwana and raided the country around it, while Chandrasen's men struck at their supply lines and outposts. The siege was hard and long. In **1575** Siwana finally fell, and Chandrasen was driven into the hills.

The years that followed were the hardest of his life. He moved from place to place in the broken country of the **Aravallis**, through the hills of southern Marwar and along the borders of Mewar and Sirohi, sheltering with chiefs who were willing to risk Mughal anger, and sometimes finding none. His family and followers shared his wandering. The bards remember the hunger of those years, the nights in the open, and the loyalty of the small band of Rathores who refused every offer to go over to the Mughals.

He was not alone in his defiance. To the south, **Maharana Pratap** of Mewar was fighting the same struggle against the same emperor. In **1576**, the year after Siwana fell, Pratap met the Mughal army at **Haldighati**. The two rulers had much in common, and later historians have often compared them: two Rajput princes who refused the comfortable submission accepted by their neighbours and kinsmen, and chose instead a life of war in the hills. Pratap's fame came to overshadow Chandrasen's, and Marwar's rebel is sometimes called the **forgotten hero** of Rajasthan. Yet he had begun his resistance years before Pratap came to the throne.

Chandrasen never gave up hope of recovering his kingdom. Around the end of the 1570s he returned to Marwar, gathered his supporters, and attacked Mughal posts, regaining control of some districts for a time, including the country around **Sojat**. It was a brave and stubborn effort, but he could not recover Jodhpur.

He died on **11 January 1581**, at **Sachiyap**, in the hill country of the **Saran** district, not yet forty years old. His death is surrounded by uncertainty. Some accounts say that he was poisoned by a chief who had sheltered him, or by someone among his own followers. The story cannot be confirmed, but it reflects how isolated and vulnerable the last years of his life had become. A memorial was raised at the place of his death.

After his death his sons, **Ugrasen**, **Askaran** and **Rai Singh**, could not hold together what he had fought for. Jodhpur remained under direct Mughal administration until **1583**, when Akbar granted it to Chandrasen's brother **Udai Singh**, who had chosen the path of service and was given the title of **Raja**. From then on, the rulers of Marwar would be among the great Rajput commanders of the Mughal empire.

So Chandrasen's long resistance ended in apparent failure. He lost Jodhpur, then Bhadrajun, then Siwana, and died a fugitive. And yet Marwar never quite forgot him. Its bards kept his memory alive in their songs as the Rao who would not kneel, who walked out of Akbar's court at Nagaur and spent nearly twenty years in the hills rather than become another man's servant. In the twentieth century historians rediscovered him, and his name is now spoken alongside that of Pratap as one of the two great Rajput resisters of Akbar's age.

## Highlights of his life

- **Chosen heir of Rao Maldeo.** Born in 1541 to Maldeo and Rani Swarupde, he was preferred over his elder brothers Ram and Udai Singh.
- **Rao of Marwar (1562).** He took the throne at Jodhpur and faced the immediate revolt of his brothers.
- **Loss of Jodhpur (1565).** A Mughal army under Hussain Quli Khan, invited by his brother Ram, took the city after a long siege.
- **Walkout at Nagaur (1570).** He attended Akbar's court at Nagaur but refused to submit, unlike most rulers of the desert.
- **The stand at Siwana (1572–1575).** He held out in Siwana for years against Mughal forces before being driven into the hills.
- **Comrade in defiance.** His resistance began before Maharana Pratap's and ran alongside it; he is often called the forgotten hero of Rajasthan.
- **Death in the hills (1581).** He died at Sachiyap in the Saran hills, still unconquered, amid rumours that he was poisoned.

udai-singh-mota-raja.story:
## Udai Singh (Mota Raja) — the prince who won back Jodhpur through service

*The life of Udai Singh comes to us from the Marwar khyats, Muhnot Nainsi's chronicles and the Persian histories of Akbar's court. Marwar's bards have judged him harshly for choosing service over resistance; the Mughal writers praised his loyalty. Where tradition goes beyond the record, this story says so.*

Udai Singh was born on **13 January 1538**, one of the many sons of **Rao Maldeo**, the powerful ruler of Marwar. He grew up in the years of his father's greatest triumphs and worst humiliation. As a small child he lived through the invasion of **Sher Shah Suri** in 1544, the death of Maldeo's commanders **Jaita** and **Kumpa** at **Giri-Sumel**, and the Afghan occupation of Jodhpur, which ended only with Sher Shah's death in 1545. He grew to manhood in a court that had recovered its pride but not forgotten how quickly a kingdom could be lost.

He was a large, heavy man, and it was for this that he was later known across Rajasthan as **Mota Raja**, "the stout king". But in his youth his size did not prevent him from riding and fighting. The chronicles connect him with the district of **Phalodi** in the north of Marwar, where he seems to have held lands as a prince, building up a following of his own.

The great disappointment of his early life came from his father. Although Udai Singh was older than his brother **Chandrasen**, born in 1541, Maldeo chose Chandrasen as his heir. When Maldeo died in **November 1562** and Chandrasen took the throne, Udai Singh was one of the brothers who refused to accept the decision. The chronicles record a fight between the two in the first months of the new reign, in which Udai Singh was defeated. Another brother, **Ram**, went to the Mughal emperor **Akbar** for help, and in **1565** a Mughal army took Jodhpur. Chandrasen retreated into the southern hills to continue the fight.

For Udai Singh, these were uncertain years. Marwar had been broken apart, and the old kingdom of his father was now partly in Mughal hands, partly held by Chandrasen in the hills, and partly divided among chiefs who looked after themselves.

The moment of decision came in **November 1570**, when Akbar held court at **Nagaur**. The rulers of the desert came to meet the emperor. **Rao Kalyanmal of Bikaner** and his son **Rai Singh** submitted. So did **Rawal Har Raj of Jaisalmer**. Chandrasen came, but would not bow, and rode away to continue his resistance. Udai Singh came and stayed. He entered Akbar's service, accepting the emperor as his overlord.

Marwar's bards have never quite forgiven him for it. In their songs Chandrasen is the hero who would not kneel, and Udai Singh the brother who chose comfort. But the choice was not as simple as the songs make it. Akbar was offering the Rajput rulers a real bargain: those who served him kept their ancestral lands as hereditary grants, received high ranks in the imperial service, and won a share in the wealth and power of a vast empire. **Raja Bharmal** of Amber had accepted it in 1562, and his son **Bhagwant Das** and grandson **Man Singh** had already risen high. Chittor had fallen in 1568 and Ranthambhore in 1569. To many Rajput princes of the time, service under Akbar seemed the only way to keep their houses alive.

For more than a decade Udai Singh served as a Mughal officer, while his brother fought on in the hills and Jodhpur was administered by others, including for a time **Rai Singh of Bikaner**. The Persian histories record his presence on imperial campaigns, and he gained a reputation as a dependable commander. Then, on **11 January 1581**, Chandrasen died in the hills of **Saran**, and the question of Marwar's future was opened again.

Chandrasen's sons tried to hold on to their father's claim, but they lacked his strength and stubbornness. In **1583**, Akbar granted Jodhpur to Udai Singh, together with the title of **Raja**. After eighteen years of division, Marwar once again had a ruler from the house of Maldeo sitting in Mehrangarh. But it was a different kind of kingdom now. Udai Singh ruled as a Mughal mansabdar, holding Marwar as his *watan*, his hereditary homeland, under the emperor's grant. His power came not only from the swords of his clan but from the authority of Delhi and Agra.

One can imagine the day he rode up the steep road to Mehrangarh as its lord. He was forty-five, heavy in the saddle, and he had last known the fort as a young prince in his father's court. The gates through which Maldeo's armies had marched out were opened for him, and the old servants of the palace, the priests of the family shrine of **Nagnechi Mata** and the surviving nobles of Maldeo's day came out to greet him. The bards do not record what he felt. But a son who had been passed over by his father, and had watched his brother lose everything, must have known that this homecoming had been bought at a price, and that the fort was now his because an emperor had given it.

Life as a Mughal noble meant long periods away from home. A mansabdar was expected to maintain a body of horsemen in proportion to his rank, to attend the emperor at court, and to march wherever he was sent. The Rajput nobles of Akbar's empire spent years in camps and garrison towns, in the Punjab, in Gujarat or on the frontiers of the north-west, while their homelands were administered by deputies and kinsmen. Through them, too, ideas travelled in both directions. Rajput courts began to adopt the dress, ceremonial and building styles of the imperial court, while Rajput soldiers, poets and musicians became familiar figures in the Mughal capitals.

Udai Singh used that authority to rebuild. The years of war had left the countryside disordered and the Rathore chiefs divided. As Raja, he worked to bring the chiefs back under the throne at Jodhpur, rewarding those who accepted his rule and pressing those who resisted. Marwar began to be organised on new lines, with its districts administered in ways that fitted the imperial system. It was the beginning of a long period in which Marwar's rulers would be among the most important commanders in the Mughal army, and the kingdom itself would enjoy the security that imperial protection brought.

His closest bond with the imperial family came through his daughter. In **1586**, his daughter **Manmati**, known at court as **Jagat Gosain** and in popular tradition often as **Jodh Bai**, was married to Akbar's eldest son, **Prince Salim**, the future emperor **Jahangir**. On **5 January 1592**, at Lahore, she gave birth to a son, **Khurram**, who would one day rule the empire as **Shah Jahan**, the builder of the Taj Mahal. The grandson of the Mota Raja of Jodhpur thus became one of the greatest of the Mughal emperors.

Not every episode of his rule was remembered kindly. Tradition in Marwar tells of a bitter quarrel with the **Charans**, the bards and genealogists of the Rajputs, who held villages granted to them by earlier rulers. When Udai Singh is said to have taken back some of these grants, the Charans gathered in protest at **Auwa** and, according to the story, some of them took their own lives in a *dharna*, the ancient form of protest by self-sacrifice that was meant to bring guilt and misfortune upon the one who caused it. The story was told for generations as a stain on his reign. How far the details are exact cannot now be known, but the tradition shows how deeply the bards resented him, and it may explain why their songs speak of him less warmly than of Chandrasen.

In the last years of his life, Udai Singh continued to serve the emperor. He was often away from Marwar, with the imperial court or the imperial armies, and it was far from home that he died. He died at **Lahore** in **1595**, at the age of fifty-seven. He had many sons, and the throne passed to **Sur Singh**, who would rise even higher in Mughal service.

Udai Singh is not a figure of romance. He did not fight a hopeless war in the hills, and he did not die defying an emperor. His achievement was of another kind. He took a kingdom that had been broken by civil war and foreign occupation and, by accepting a powerful overlord, made it whole again. Under him and his successors, Marwar recovered its lands, its chiefs returned to their villages, and the Rathores of Jodhpur became one of the great houses of the Mughal empire. The bards preferred Chandrasen, and perhaps rightly so in the language of honour. But the kingdom that survived into the following centuries was, in large part, the kingdom that Udai Singh restored.

## Highlights of his life

- **Son of Rao Maldeo.** Born in 1538, he grew up through Sher Shah's invasion and Marwar's recovery.
- **Passed over for the throne.** His younger brother Chandrasen was made heir, and Udai Singh opposed him after Maldeo's death in 1562.
- **Submission at Nagaur (1570).** He entered Akbar's service, unlike Chandrasen, who refused.
- **Raja of Jodhpur (1583).** Akbar granted him Jodhpur and the title of Raja, ending eighteen years of division.
- **Grandfather of Shah Jahan.** His daughter Manmati, Jagat Gosain, married Prince Salim in 1586 and bore Prince Khurram in 1592.
- **The quarrel with the Charans.** Tradition remembers a protest at Auwa over the resumption of Charan grants as a stain on his reign.
- **Restorer of Marwar.** He reunited the kingdom and began the Rathores' long role in the Mughal service, dying at Lahore in 1595.
