raja-sur-singh.story:
## Raja Sur Singh — the Rathore commander of two emperors

*Raja Sur Singh's life is recorded in the Marwar khyats, Muhnot Nainsi's chronicles and the Persian histories of the reigns of Akbar and Jahangir. They tell of a ruler who spent most of his reign far from Marwar, in the service of the empire. Where tradition goes beyond the record, this story says so.*

Sur Singh was born on **24 April 1571**, the son of **Udai Singh**, the prince of Marwar later known as the **Mota Raja**. He was born into a family that had just made a fateful choice. Only a few months earlier, at Akbar's court at **Nagaur** in November 1570, his father had entered the service of the Mughal emperor, while his uncle **Chandrasen**, the Rao of Marwar, had refused to submit and ridden back to the hills to fight on.

The boy's earliest years were spent not in a palace at Jodhpur but in the shifting world of a Mughal officer's household. Jodhpur itself was in imperial hands, and Udai Singh's place depended on the emperor's favour and on his own service in the field. Sur Singh grew up hearing of two kinds of Rathore honour: the honour of his uncle, who chose the hills and hunger rather than bow, and the honour of his father, who chose service and patience in the hope of recovering what the family had lost.

His father's patience was rewarded. Chandrasen died in the hills of **Saran** in **1581**, and in **1583** Akbar granted Jodhpur to Udai Singh with the title of **Raja**. Sur Singh was twelve when his family returned to **Mehrangarh**. Three years later, in **1586**, his sister **Manmati**, known at court as **Jagat Gosain**, was married to Akbar's eldest son, **Prince Salim**. In **1592** she gave birth to **Prince Khurram**, the future emperor **Shah Jahan**. Sur Singh was thus the maternal uncle of a prince who would one day rule the empire, a bond that tied his house closely to the imperial family.

He learned the arts of war in the imperial service. Like other young Rajput princes of the age, he rode with his father's contingent, learned to command horsemen in the field, and came to know the commanders and courtiers of Akbar's empire. When Udai Singh died at **Lahore** in **1595**, Akbar confirmed Sur Singh as his successor. He was twenty-four years old.

As Raja of Marwar, Sur Singh held two roles at once. At home he was the head of the Rathores, the lord of Mehrangarh and of the chiefs of the desert. In the empire he was a **mansabdar**, an imperial officer with a rank that obliged him to maintain a body of cavalry and serve wherever the emperor sent him. For most of his reign, it was the second role that kept him away from home.

The bards imagine the moment he learned of his new rank. A young man stands in Lahore, far from the desert, still mourning his father, while the emperor's order confirming him as Raja is read out. There is no great fort around him, no gathering of Rathore chiefs, only the crowded city of the imperial court and the knowledge that his kingdom now depends on the pen of a distant court as much as on the swords of his kinsmen. Whether or not it happened in quite this way, it captures the new world in which the rulers of Marwar now lived.

While he was away, Marwar had to be governed by others. Trusted officials and kinsmen ran the districts in his name, collected the revenue and kept order among the villages, while the great Rathore chiefs held their own lands and sent their horsemen to join his contingent in the imperial armies. The system worked only if the Raja's authority was respected even in his absence, and only if the chiefs saw that service under him brought them honour and reward. Sur Singh's long years of campaigning were possible because Marwar remained quiet behind him, and that quiet was itself one of the achievements of his reign.

His first great field of service was **Gujarat**. The province had been conquered by Akbar in 1572-73, but the old ruling house kept trying to win it back. **Muzaffar Shah III**, the last Sultan of Gujarat, had led a long revolt before his death in 1593, and after him his son **Bahadur** and other followers continued to stir up trouble. Sur Singh was sent to Gujarat and campaigned against these rebels. The chronicles of Marwar remember his victories there with pride, and tradition says that Akbar, pleased with his service, honoured him with the title of **Sawai Raja**, a mark of distinction meaning "one and a quarter", a ruler worth more than one.

From Gujarat he was sent south. In the last years of the sixteenth century Akbar turned his ambitions towards the **Deccan**, the plateau kingdoms south of the Narmada. The imperial armies, under princes such as **Daniyal**, besieged **Ahmadnagar** and fought the Deccani states in a long and costly series of campaigns. Sur Singh took part in these southern wars, and the Deccan became the main theatre of his service for much of his life. The bards of Marwar tell of Rathore horsemen far from their desert, campaigning in the black-soil plains and the hill forts of the south, enduring heavy rains and fevers that were stranger to them than any enemy.

When Akbar died in **1605**, and Salim came to the throne as **Jahangir**, Sur Singh's position grew stronger still. He was the brother of the emperor's Rajput wife and the uncle of the emperor's ablest son. Jahangir continued to employ him in the Deccan and raised his rank. The Persian histories of the time record him as one of the leading Rajput nobles of the empire, a commander trusted with large forces and important posts.

The members of his family were also building new houses of their own. His brother **Kishan Singh** left Marwar and, with imperial approval, founded the state of **Kishangarh** in **1609**, a small Rathore kingdom that would later become famous for its school of painting. The Rathore name, which had once spread across the desert through the sons of Jodha, now spread again through imperial service.

Though he spent much of his life on campaign, Sur Singh did not neglect his homeland. The wealth of imperial service flowed back into Marwar. At Jodhpur, the tank and gardens of **Sursagar**, on the edge of the city, carry his name, and tradition credits him with building a palace there as well. The long years of war under his grandfather Maldeo and the divisions under Chandrasen were over, and Marwar enjoyed a period of relative peace. Villages were resettled, trade on the desert roads recovered, and the Rathore chiefs, now secure in their lands under a ruler backed by the empire, had less reason to fight one another.

Sur Singh is also remembered as a patron of poets and bards. The Charans, who had quarrelled bitterly with his father, found him more generous. The literary language of the Rajput courts, the rich and ornate Dingal of Marwar's bards, flourished in this period, and many verses were composed in praise of the rulers who rewarded their makers.

At court he was known as a man of dignity and loyalty, and his relationship with the imperial family remained close throughout his life. But it also had its strains. A Rajput noble who served far from home depended on the favour of princes who were often at odds with one another, and Sur Singh had to steer carefully through the jealousies of the imperial court. The chronicles suggest that he managed to do so without losing either the emperor's trust or his own standing among the Rajputs.

He died far from the desert, on **7 September 1619**, at **Mehkar**, in the Deccan, while still in the imperial service. He was forty-eight years old. His death in the south, on campaign, was fitting for a ruler whose life had been spent in the field. The throne of Marwar passed to his son **Gaj Singh I**, born in 1595, who would continue his father's career as one of the great Rajput commanders of the empire.

Sur Singh's reign was not one of independence or resistance, but of prosperity and security. He inherited a kingdom only recently restored to his family, and he made it rich and stable. Under him, the house of Jodhpur moved from the uncertain position of a newly reconciled vassal to the secure rank of one of the empire's leading families. The Rathore warriors who followed him fought in Gujarat and the Deccan, far from home, and the wealth and honours they won helped to sustain Marwar for generations.

## Highlights of his life

- **Son of the Mota Raja.** Born on 24 April 1571 to Udai Singh, he grew up as his family recovered Jodhpur through imperial service.
- **Uncle of Shah Jahan.** His sister Jagat Gosain was the wife of Jahangir and the mother of Prince Khurram, the future Shah Jahan.
- **Raja of Marwar (1595).** He succeeded his father at the age of twenty-four, confirmed by Akbar.
- **Campaigns in Gujarat.** He fought the rebels led by the heirs of the last Sultan of Gujarat; tradition says Akbar honoured him as Sawai Raja.
- **Commander in the Deccan.** He served for many years in the southern wars of Akbar and Jahangir and rose to high rank.
- **Builder of Sursagar.** The tank and gardens of Sursagar at Jodhpur bear his name.
- **Death on campaign (1619).** He died at Mehkar in the Deccan and was succeeded by his son Gaj Singh I.

raja-gaj-singh-i.story:
## Raja Gaj Singh I — the Rathore who held back armies

*Gaj Singh's life comes to us through the Mughal chronicles of Jahangir and Shah Jahan's reigns and through the khyats of Marwar, above all the writings of Muhnot Nainsi; where the court record and the bardic memory part ways, this story says so.*

At the very end of the sixteenth century, the Rathores of **Marwar** stood in a new kind of world. Their great-grandfather's generation had fought the Mughals; their grandfather's generation had made peace with them. **Rao Chandrasen**, the last Rathore ruler to resist Akbar to the end, had died in 1581 a hunted man in the hills. His elder brother **Udai Singh**, remembered as the *Mota Raja*, had chosen the other road. He entered Akbar's service, received Jodhpur back from the emperor, and gave his daughter **Jagat Gosain** in marriage to Prince Salim, the future Jahangir. From that marriage was born, in 1592, a prince named **Khurram**, who would one day rule India as **Shah Jahan**.

Udai Singh's son was **Raja Sur Singh**, who ruled Marwar from 1595 and spent much of his life far from the sand and stone of Jodhpur, commanding Rathore horsemen for the emperor in Gujarat and the Deccan. In **1595**, the same year his father came to the throne, a son was born to Sur Singh. The Marwar chronicles place his birth at **Lahore**, where the imperial court then lay. The boy was named **Gaj Singh**. Through his aunt Jagat Gosain he was a first cousin of Prince Khurram, a tie of blood that would shape his whole life.

Gaj Singh grew up between two worlds. In Jodhpur there was the fort of **Mehrangarh** on its red ridge, the temples, the bards reciting the deeds of Rao Jodha and Rao Maldeo, and the great Rathore nobles, each with his own fort and his own pride. In the imperial camps there were Persian manners, Mughal ranks, horses from Central Asia and the endless business of service. A Rathore prince of his generation had to learn both: how to sit a horse and swing a sword like his ancestors, and how to stand in the Mughal court, wait for the emperor's word and read the moods of powerful men. One can imagine the boy riding beside his father's tents in the Deccan, watching how Sur Singh dealt with Mughal generals, and learning that a Rajput house now survived as much by judgment as by courage.

He was given command young. While his father was away on imperial service, Gaj Singh took part in the work of holding Marwar together, and the chronicles connect him with **Jalor**, the old fortress in the south of the kingdom that the Rathores had long wanted to control. By the time he reached manhood he was a seasoned commander, known in his father's camp and known at court.

In **1619** Raja Sur Singh died in the Deccan, still in imperial service. The succession was not automatic. Under the Mughals, a Rajput ruler held his throne as an imperial grant, and it was the emperor who marked the new chief's forehead with the *tika* of succession and fixed his rank. **Jahangir** chose Gaj Singh. He confirmed him as Raja of Jodhpur, gave him a *mansab*, the rank that set the number of horsemen he must maintain, and sent him back to the war in the south.

That war was the long struggle against **Malik Ambar**, the Abyssinian minister who held the Nizam Shahi kingdom of Ahmadnagar together and fought the Mughals with the light cavalry of the Marathas. Ambar's horsemen struck at supply lines, vanished into the hills, and returned when least expected. Into this war Jahangir sent his favourite son, Prince Khurram, and with him went the Rajput contingents, among them the Rathores of Gaj Singh. For his conduct in these campaigns the emperor honoured Gaj Singh with the title **Dalthambhan**, "the one who holds back armies". It was a name a Rathore could be proud of: not a title of court favour, but of the field.

These were also years of growing danger inside the empire. As Jahangir aged and the empress **Nur Jahan** gathered power in his name, Prince Khurram, the most capable of the emperor's sons, found himself pushed aside. In **1623** he rose in rebellion. Gaj Singh faced a hard choice. Khurram was his cousin and his old commander in the Deccan. But Gaj Singh's throne was the emperor's gift, and to join the rebel prince was to risk Marwar itself. He chose loyalty to Jahangir and marched with the imperial army under Prince **Parviz** and the general **Mahabat Khan**, which hunted Khurram from Rajasthan to the Deccan and then east into Bengal and Bihar.

The bards remember one moment from that campaign with special care. In **1624**, on the banks of the **Tons** river near Allahabad, the imperial army caught up with Khurram's forces. Fighting on Khurram's side was **Raja Bhim Singh** Sisodia, a younger son of Rana Amar Singh of Mewar, the boldest of the rebel's captains. The Marwar tradition says that Gaj Singh, slighted over the place of honour in the imperial line, held his Rathores back and did not throw them into the fight, and that Bhim Singh, who had taunted him, was cut down and killed in the battle. Khurram's army broke and the prince fled. Whether Gaj Singh's restraint was wounded pride, as the bards say, or a careful refusal to destroy a cousin who might one day be emperor, nobody can now know. What is certain is that when Khurram did become emperor, he did not forget the Rathore who had not struck at him.

In **1627** Jahangir died, and in the following year Khurram was crowned at Agra as **Shah Jahan**. For Gaj Singh the change of reign brought favour. The new emperor raised his cousin step by step, until Gaj Singh held the rank of **5,000**, among the highest open to any noble of the empire. With it came lands across Marwar and beyond, and a place close to the throne.

Rank in the Mughal empire was never a rest. It was paid for in service. Soon after his accession Shah Jahan faced the revolt of **Khan Jahan Lodi**, an Afghan noble who fled to the Deccan and joined the enemies of the empire. The emperor himself went south to Burhanpur, and Gaj Singh's Rathores rode in the campaigns that hunted down the rebel and pressed on against the kingdom of Ahmadnagar. Year after year, the Raja of Marwar was in the field: in the Deccan, at the court, on the march wherever the emperor sent him. Jodhpur was governed in his absence by his ministers and nobles, and the Rathore horsemen who rode behind him brought back pay, honour and plunder that kept the kingdom prosperous.

That prosperity was the real achievement of his reign. Marwar was a dry land, its wealth in camels, cattle, salt and the trade routes that crossed it towards Gujarat. Under Gaj Singh it was spared the invasions and civil wars that had torn it apart in Chandrasen's time. The great Rathore nobles, the Champawats, Kumpawats, Udawats and others, were bound to the throne by grants of land and by the share of imperial service that their Raja could offer them. The *khyats* written in the next generation, especially those of **Muhnot Nainsi**, whose family served the Jodhpur court, preserve a picture of a well-ordered state with its parganas, villages and revenues carefully recorded. Gaj Singh was also a patron of the court culture of his time: of bards and poets in the Marwari tongue, of painters and builders, and of the temples of the kingdom. The palace complex of Mehrangarh continued to grow in the reigns of the Rathore rulers of this century, and the Jodhpur court took on the mixed Rajput and Mughal manners that would mark it for generations.

But the closing years of his life were darkened by a quarrel inside his own house. Gaj Singh's eldest son was **Amar Singh**, born in 1613, a fierce and restless young man, brave to the point of recklessness and impatient of his father's control. A younger son, **Jaswant Singh**, was born in **1626** at Burhanpur in the Deccan, to a different queen. As the years passed, the Raja came to favour the younger boy. The Marwar tradition gives a reason with a touch of romance and bitterness: it says that Gaj Singh's beloved concubine **Anara** turned his heart against Amar Singh. Whatever the truth, the father and the eldest son could not live together. Gaj Singh declared Amar Singh disinherited and sent him out of Marwar.

Amar Singh went to the imperial court, where Shah Jahan gave him a rank of his own and later the territory of **Nagaur**. He would die young, in 1644, in one of the most famous scenes of Rajput defiance at the Mughal court, after striking down the imperial paymaster Salabat Khan in the emperor's presence. But that was after his father's death. For now, Gaj Singh had chosen his heir, and he asked the emperor to accept Jaswant Singh as the next ruler of Marwar. Shah Jahan agreed.

In **May 1638**, Gaj Singh died at **Agra**, still in the service of the empire he had served all his life. He was about forty-two years old. The emperor gave the *tika* of Jodhpur to the twelve-year-old **Jaswant Singh**, who would become one of the most powerful Rajput princes of the seventeenth century, the Maharaja of Marwar who later faced the war of succession among Shah Jahan's sons. The quarrel Gaj Singh had settled by disinheriting his eldest son left its own legend in the ballads of Amar Singh Rathore, but the throne itself passed without a war.

Gaj Singh I is not remembered for a single great battle or a desperate siege, as so many Rajput heroes are. His was a different kind of life, and perhaps a harder one to tell. He ruled in the age when the Rajput houses had made their peace with the Mughal empire, and he made that peace serve Marwar. He was the emperor's cousin and his loyal general, but he was also the Raja of the Rathores, and he kept his kingdom whole, rich and quiet through nineteen years of service in distant wars. The name the emperor gave him, *Dalthambhan*, the one who holds back armies, fits him in more than one sense: in an age of rebellions and wars of succession, he kept the storm away from the gates of Jodhpur.

## Highlights of his life

- **Born into the new order (1595).** Son of Raja Sur Singh and grandson of Mota Raja Udai Singh, he was a first cousin of Prince Khurram, the future Shah Jahan, through his aunt Jagat Gosain.
- **Succession under Jahangir (1619).** On his father's death in the Deccan, Jahangir confirmed him as Raja of Jodhpur and sent him back to the southern war.
- **The title Dalthambhan.** For his service in the Deccan campaigns against Malik Ambar, he was honoured with the title meaning "the one who holds back armies".
- **Loyalty in Khurram's rebellion (1623–1625).** He stayed with Jahangir's army against his own cousin. Marwar tradition says he held his Rathores back at the battle of the Tons in 1624, where Raja Bhim Singh Sisodia was killed.
- **High rank under Shah Jahan.** He rose to the rank of 5,000 and served in the campaigns against Khan Jahan Lodi and in the Deccan.
- **A stable and prosperous Marwar.** Through long years of imperial service he kept his kingdom free of invasion and civil war, and patronised the court culture of Jodhpur.
- **Choice of heir.** He disinherited his eldest son Amar Singh and secured the succession of Jaswant Singh, who took the throne after Gaj Singh's death at Agra in May 1638.

kakil-deo-early.story:
## Kakil Deo — the king who chose the valley of Amber

*Kakil Deo's life is known only through the genealogies and chronicles of the Kachwaha house and the traditions retold by later historians; no inscription of his reign is known. This story keeps to what those traditions say and to the real history of his age, and where history and legend part ways, it says so.*

In the hill country of Dhundhar, in the first half of the twelfth century, a small Kachwaha state was taking shape. Its founder, **Dulha Rai**, had come from the old Kachwaha line of Narwar, married into a Chauhan family of the hills near Lalsot, taken **Dausa** from the Bargujar Rajputs, and won the Meena strongholds of **Manch**, which he renamed **Ramgarh**, and **Khoh**. It was a state of a few forts and a few dozen villages, held by the sword and by the loyalty of a small band of followers. Into this new and uncertain house **Kakil Deo** was born.

The chronicles name him as the son of Dulha Rai by his Chauhan wife, **Maroni**, the daughter of Ralan Singh of Moran. He was, then, a child of the alliance that had made his father's rise possible: Kachwaha by his father, Chauhan by his mother. Nothing certain is recorded of his childhood, but we can imagine it from the world around him. He would have grown up in the fortified hill towns of Khoh and Ramgarh, among warriors who had only recently won their land, listening to the stories of his father's wars and of the night at Manch when, the bards say, the goddess **Jamwai Mata** raised the wounded Kachwahas from the field. He would have learned to ride and to use the sword and the bow as every Rajput boy did, and he would have learned, too, that the hills around him still belonged in spirit to the Meenas, whose chiefs had ruled them for generations.

The traditional dates place his father's reign in the early twelfth century, and the date often given for the beginning of Kakil Deo's own rule is around **1150 CE**, though older reckonings put these events much earlier. Like all the early Kachwaha dates, it should be read as a tradition rather than a fixed fact. What the chronicles agree on is that Dulha Rai died while still in his prime, most likely from wounds received in war, and that Kakil Deo came to the gaddi of a kingdom that was young, small and still fighting for its place.

The first task of a new king in such a state was simply to survive. A founder's death was a dangerous moment. Defeated rivals might rise again, and neighbours who had respected the father might test the son. The Meena chiefs who had lost Manch and Khoh had not disappeared; they held other hills and other valleys, and the Bargujars had not forgotten Dausa. The chronicles remember Kakil Deo as a ruler who held his father's lands together through these years and then went further.

His great achievement, the one that gave his name its place in history, was the taking of **Amber**.

A few miles north of the later city of Jaipur, the hills of Dhundhar close in around a narrow valley. At its head lies a small lake, and around it the ridges rise steep and rocky, so that the valley can be entered only through a few passes. In Kakil Deo's time this valley was held by the **Susawat Meenas**, one of the most powerful Meena clans of the region, and their town in the valley was already old. Tradition has offered several explanations of its name. Some connect it with **Ambikeshwar**, a form of Shiva whose ancient shrine stands in the town; others with the goddess Amba, or with the legendary king **Ambarisha**. Whatever its origin, the name Amber would one day be known across India.

How the Kachwahas took the valley is not recorded in detail. The chronicles say simply that Kakil Deo defeated the Susawat Meenas and won Amber from them. We should imagine not a great pitched battle but a hard campaign in broken ground: Rajput horsemen working their way through the passes, Meena archers on the ridges who knew every rock and gully, the slow pressure of a determined enemy against a stronghold that had never been taken. In the end the valley fell, and Kakil Deo made a decision that would shape the next six centuries of his family's history. He did not merely hold Amber as one more fort. He made it his **capital**.

It was a wise choice. Khoh and Ramgarh were strongholds of a conquering band; Amber was a place from which a kingdom could be ruled. The ring of hills made it easy to defend, while its position gave it command of the routes across the plain to the south and to the west. Water could be stored in its lake and in tanks cut into the hills. Over the centuries his descendants would build on those ridges the great fortress-palace of **Amber Fort** and, on the hill above it, **Jaigarh**, but the first step was Kakil Deo's: he saw the valley and understood what it could become. From his time until **Sawai Jai Singh II** founded Jaipur in **1727**, Amber remained the seat of the Kachwahas, and even after that the kings of Jaipur were often called the Rajas of Amber.

Holding Amber meant ruling it. A twelfth-century Rajput state in these hills was not governed by a great bureaucracy. It was held through a web of personal loyalties: the king's kinsmen and companions, each granted villages in return for service with horse and sword; the village headmen who collected the share of the harvest; and the older inhabitants of the land, whose cooperation made every other arrangement possible. The Meenas did not vanish when they lost their towns. They remained farmers, herders and fighting men throughout Dhundhar, and in later centuries the Kachwaha rulers gave Meena clans a lasting place in the life of the state, including, by long tradition, the guarding of royal treasure. The roots of that relationship, uneasy and complicated as it was, go back to the generation of Dulha Rai and Kakil Deo.

Religion was part of the work of kingship too. The Kachwahas brought with them their devotion to Jamwai Mata, the goddess of Ramgarh, and the worship of Rama, the ancestor of their solar line. At Amber they found the old shrine of Ambikeshwar, and later tradition links its care to the early Kachwaha kings. Whether Kakil Deo himself built or restored any temple there is not certain, but he ruled in an age when every Rajput king was expected to honour the gods of his land as well as the gods of his house.

Beyond the hills, the world was changing fast. During Kakil Deo's lifetime the **Chauhans** of Shakambhari and Ajmer reached the height of their power. Around the middle of the twelfth century **Vigraharaja IV** extended Chauhan rule as far as Delhi, taking it from the Tomaras, and in **1178** the young **Prithviraj Chauhan** came to the throne of Ajmer. Dhundhar lay right in the shadow of this great power. A small kingdom like Amber survived by keeping good terms with Ajmer, and the Kachwahas were remembered as faithful followers of the Chauhans. The bards later told that Kakil Deo's descendant **Pajjun** was among the captains of Prithviraj. Kakil Deo himself did not live to see the storm that broke in **1191 and 1192**, when Muhammad of Ghor came against Prithviraj at **Tarain**, but the kingdom he had settled at Amber would have to live through what followed.

What kind of man was Kakil Deo? The chronicles do not give him speeches or a portrait. They remember him by his deeds: that he held what his father had won, took Amber from the Susawat Meenas, and made it the heart of the Kachwaha state. In the long gallery of Kachwaha kings, filled with famous names such as Raja Man Singh and Sawai Jai Singh, he is easily overlooked. But a founding needs two generations: one to win the land and one to settle it. Dulha Rai won a foothold; Kakil Deo made it a home.

His death, like his birth, is not recorded with any certainty. The traditional dates give him a reign of some three decades, ending around **1180 CE**. The Kachwaha genealogies name his son **Hanudeva** as the next ruler of Amber, and the long line of Amber's kings descended from him; the archive's own list places a ruler named **Govind Rai** after him, a name that the standard genealogies do not confirm. Whichever reckoning is followed, the kingdom passed on intact, centred on the valley he had chosen.

Today, visitors walking up to the great palace at Amber pass through the valley that the Susawat Meenas once held and Kakil Deo made into a capital. The palace they see was built centuries after him, but the choice of the place was his.

## Highlights of his life

- **Son of the founder.** Born to Dulha Rai and his Chauhan wife Maroni, he inherited a young Kachwaha state in Dhundhar and held it together after his father's death.
- **Conquest of Amber.** He won the valley of Amber from the Susawat Meenas, one of the most powerful Meena clans of the region.
- **Amber made the capital.** He moved the seat of the Kachwahas to Amber, which remained their capital until the founding of Jaipur in 1727.
- **Consolidation of the hills.** He secured the lands his father had won at Dausa, Ramgarh and Khoh, and laid the basis of Kachwaha rule over the Meena country.
- **A kingdom in the Chauhan age.** He ruled under the shadow of the Chauhans of Ajmer, whose loyal allies the Kachwahas remained.
- **Founder of a long line.** Through his son Hanudeva, according to the genealogies, descended every later king of Amber and Jaipur.

govind-rai-early.story:
## Govind Rai — a name at the dawn of Amber

*Govind Rai is known only as a name in this archive's list of early Kachwaha rulers; the standard genealogies of the house do not record him, and no inscription or chronicle tells his story. What follows is what can honestly be said.*

This archive places **Govind Rai** among the earliest Kachwaha rulers of **Dhundhar**, as the successor of **Kakil Deo** in the twelfth century. It is an uncertain place. The genealogies kept by the Kachwaha court, and followed by most historians of Jaipur, name Kakil Deo's son and successor as **Hanudeva**, followed by **Janadeva** and then **Pajjun**, the warrior the bards remember among the captains of Prithviraj Chauhan. A ruler called Govind Rai does not appear in that line, and he may be a variant name, a younger kinsman, or an error in the later lists. Nothing about his life, his deeds or his death is recorded.

What can be described is the world such a ruler would have inherited. In the second half of the twelfth century the Kachwahas were a young house. **Dulha Rai** had founded their rule in Dhundhar, winning **Dausa**, **Ramgarh** and **Khoh**, and Kakil Deo had taken the valley of **Amber** from the Susawat Meenas and made it the capital. The kingdom was small: a ring of hill forts and villages, held by kinsmen who served with horse and sword, among Meena communities who had ruled the land before them.

Beyond the hills stood the **Chauhans** of Ajmer, the great power of the region, whose king **Prithviraj III** came to the throne in **1178**. The Kachwahas lived as their loyal neighbours, and in **1191 and 1192** the wars at **Tarain** against Muhammad of Ghor shook all of northern India.

Whoever ruled Amber in those years held the valley through that storm and passed it on, and the line of Kakil Deo continued until, four centuries later, it produced **Raja Bharmal** and **Raja Man Singh**.

## Highlights of his life

- **An early Kachwaha name.** He is listed in this archive as the successor of Kakil Deo at Amber in the twelfth century.
- **An uncertain identity.** The standard Kachwaha genealogies name Hanudeva as Kakil Deo's successor and do not record a Govind Rai.
- **Ruler of a young kingdom.** Amber was then a small hill state, recently won from the Susawat Meenas.
- **The Chauhan age.** His era was dominated by the Chauhans of Ajmer and ended in the wars at Tarain.

raja-man-singh.story:
## Raja Man Singh I — the Kachwaha who carried an empire from Kabul to Bengal

*Raja Man Singh's life is unusually well recorded: in the Persian chronicles of Akbar's court, above all Abul Fazl's Akbarnama, in the memoirs of Jahangir, and in the traditions of Amber. The bards of Mewar remember him very differently from the historians of the empire; where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

When **Man Singh** was born in **December 1550**, the Kachwahas of **Amber** were a modest hill kingdom, pressed by quarrelsome kinsmen and by their powerful neighbours. His grandfather, **Raja Bharmal**, held the gaddi in the old fortified valley that **Kakil Deo** had made the Kachwaha capital four centuries earlier. His father was Bharmal's eldest son, **Bhagwant Das**. Few who saw the child then could have imagined that he would one day command armies from the Hindu Kush to the Bay of Bengal.

The turning point in the life of his family came when he was about eleven. In **1562** Bharmal, threatened by a rival claimant backed by the Mughal governor of Mewat, went to meet the young emperor **Akbar**. The meeting led to an alliance that changed the history of India. Bharmal's daughter, **Harkha Bai**, was married to Akbar at **Sambhar**, and the Kachwaha men entered imperial service. Man Singh went to the Mughal court with his father. He grew up in the camps and palaces of the empire, learning Persian manners and Mughal warfare alongside his Rajput training, while Akbar, who valued him greatly, watched him grow.

The alliance has been judged in many ways. To the bards of Mewar, who honoured those who never bowed to Delhi, it was a surrender. To the Kachwahas it was a choice that preserved their land, their religion and their honour, and raised them to a power no Rajput house had held for centuries. Man Singh lived his whole life inside that choice, and he became its greatest example.

His first great campaign came in **Gujarat**. In **1572** Akbar marched to conquer that rich province, and in the sharp fight at **Sarnal**, where the emperor himself fought with a small band, Man Singh and his father were at his side. The young Kachwaha prince proved himself a fearless soldier, and from then on he was trusted with ever greater commands.

In **1573**, on the way back from Gujarat, Akbar sent him to **Udaipur** to persuade **Maharana Pratap** of Mewar to accept Mughal overlordship. The Maharana received him with courtesy but would not submit. Later tradition in Mewar adds a famous story: that at a feast by the lake, Pratap did not sit down to eat with Man Singh, pleading illness, and that the insult was taken as a refusal to dine with a house that had given a daughter to the Mughals. The story is told in many versions and cannot be confirmed, but it shows how deep the divide between the two houses was felt to be.

Three years later the divide became war. In **1576** Akbar placed Man Singh in command of the army sent against Mewar, a choice that showed how far the emperor trusted him. On **18 June 1576**, in the narrow pass of **Haldighati** near Gogunda, the two armies met. The Mewari charge was furious, and for a time it broke the Mughal front. Pratap himself rode at Man Singh, who was mounted on an elephant; the bards tell how the Maharana's horse **Chetak** reared up against the elephant, and how Man Singh's mahout was struck down. The battle turned when the Mughal reserves came up and rumour spread that the emperor himself was arriving. Wounded, Pratap was led from the field, while the Jhala chieftain remembered as **Jhala Man** took up the royal emblems and fell in his place.

The Mughals held the field, but they did not capture Pratap, and the army, exhausted and short of supplies, did not pursue him into the hills. Akbar was displeased and for a time barred Man Singh from his presence. Haldighati has been remembered ever since as a symbol of Mewar's resistance, and Man Singh's place in it has made him, in the folk memory of Rajasthan, a figure both admired and resented.

His career did not suffer for long. In **1581** he served in Akbar's campaign against the emperor's half-brother **Mirza Hakim**, the ruler of Kabul, and after Hakim's death in **1585** the north-west was entrusted to him. He governed **Kabul** for a time and fought the Afghan tribes of the frontier passes. When an imperial force was ambushed by the Yusufzai in **1586**, a disaster in which Akbar's beloved companion **Birbal** was killed, Man Singh was among the commanders sent to restore order in the mountains. A Rajput from the hills of Dhundhar was now holding the gates of Hindustan against the tribes of the Hindu Kush.

In **1587** he was sent east as governor of **Bihar**, and there, in **1589**, news reached him that his father had died. Man Singh became **Raja of Amber**. He was nearly forty, a seasoned commander, and one of the most powerful nobles of the empire.

The east became the great stage of his life. The Afghan chiefs who had once ruled Bengal and Orissa still held much of the region. In **1590** Man Singh marched into **Orissa** against the Afghans under **Qutlu Khan Lohani**. His son **Jagat Singh** was surprised and defeated in an early clash, but Qutlu Khan died soon after, and his successors accepted Mughal overlordship. When the Afghans broke the agreement, Man Singh returned and in **1592** brought Orissa fully under imperial rule. In **1594** he was made governor of **Bengal**, and he chose a new capital at **Rajmahal** on the Ganga, which he named **Akbarnagar**. For years he fought the river chiefs of eastern Bengal, the *Bhuiyans*, above all **Isa Khan** of Bhati, a master of war on water; in one of those battles, in **1597**, another of his sons, **Durjan Singh**, was killed. In time Isa Khan made peace, and later Man Singh defeated **Kedar Rai** of Bikrampur.

From Bengal, tradition says, Man Singh brought back an image of the goddess **Shila Devi**, a form of Kali, and installed it in his palace at Amber, where she is still worshipped as a protectress of the Kachwaha house.

He was not only a soldier. As a builder he left marks across India. In **1592** he began the great palace-fortress of **Amber Fort** on the ridge above the old town, the work that later generations completed into one of the most famous palaces of Rajasthan. At **Vrindavan** he built, in **1590**, the red sandstone temple of **Govind Dev**, one of the grandest Hindu temples of the age. On the ghats of **Varanasi** he raised the palace later called **Man Mandir**. At Amber the beautiful **Jagat Shiromani** temple was built by his queen **Kanakavati** in memory of their son Jagat Singh, who died in **1599**. A devotee of Krishna, Man Singh was also a patron of poets and scholars, and later tradition counted him among the *navaratna*, the nine jewels of Akbar's court.

By **1605** he held a rank of **7,000**, higher than any noble not of the imperial family. That height brought danger. His sister **Man Bai** had been married to Akbar's son **Salim**, and her son **Khusrau** was Man Singh's nephew. As Akbar lay dying in 1605, Man Singh and the powerful noble **Mirza Aziz Koka** tried to set Khusrau on the throne in place of Salim. They failed. Salim became the emperor **Jahangir**, and although he did not punish Man Singh openly, the old trust was gone. Man Singh was sent back to Bengal for a short time and then to campaigns in the **Deccan**, far from the centre of power.

He died there, at **Ellichpur** in the Deccan, in **July 1614**, still in the field at the age of sixty-three. His son **Bhau Singh** succeeded him at Amber. He had served two emperors for more than half a century, fought in almost every corner of the empire, and raised the Kachwahas from a minor hill house to the first rank of the Mughal nobility.

How should he be remembered? In Mewar, he was long remembered as the general who led the Mughals against Pratap. In the history of the empire, he was one of its chief architects: the man who held Kabul, conquered Orissa and governed Bengal. In Amber, he is the king who built the palace on the hill and brought Shila Devi home. All three memories are true, and together they show the hard choices of a Rajput king in the age of the Mughals.

## Highlights of his life

- **Raised at Akbar's court.** Son of Bhagwant Das and grandson of Raja Bharmal, he entered imperial service as a boy after the Kachwaha-Mughal alliance of 1562.
- **Commander at Haldighati (1576).** He led the Mughal army against Maharana Pratap; the Mughals held the field, but Pratap escaped to fight on.
- **Guardian of the north-west.** He served against Mirza Hakim, governed Kabul and fought the Afghan tribes of the frontier.
- **Conqueror of Orissa and governor of Bengal.** He brought Orissa under Mughal rule by 1592, governed Bengal and founded Rajmahal as its capital.
- **Builder.** He began Amber Fort in 1592 and built the Govind Dev temple at Vrindavan and the palace on the ghats of Varanasi.
- **Highest rank in the empire.** In 1605 he held a rank of 7,000, the highest of any noble outside the imperial family.
- **Death in the Deccan.** He died at Ellichpur in 1614 and was succeeded by his son Bhau Singh.

sawai-jai-singh.story:
## Sawai Jai Singh II — the king who measured the sky and drew a city on the plain

*Sawai Jai Singh II is one of the best-documented Rajput rulers: his own letters and court papers survive in the Jaipur archives, alongside the Persian chronicles of the late Mughal court and the stone instruments he left behind. Some well-loved stories about him, such as the origin of his title, belong to tradition; where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

The boy who would become **Sawai Jai Singh II** was born at **Amber** on **3 November 1688**, in the old palace on the ridge that his ancestor **Raja Man Singh** had begun a century before. His father was **Raja Bishan Singh** of Amber, a noble in the service of the emperor **Aurangzeb**, and the Kachwaha house was still one of the great families of the Mughal empire, though its days of glory under Akbar were long past.

It was a hard time to grow up a Rajput prince. Aurangzeb's long reign had turned against the Rajput houses that had once been the empire's pillars. The emperor was absorbed in his endless wars in the **Deccan** against the Marathas, the empire was overstretched, and the trust between Delhi and the Rajput courts had worn thin. When Bishan Singh died at the end of **1699**, his son, barely eleven years old, became Raja of Amber.

The boy was soon summoned to the imperial camp in the Deccan. A famous story is told of his first meeting with the aged emperor. Aurangzeb, it is said, seized both the boy's hands and asked what he could do now that he was held fast. The young Raja answered that when a husband takes his bride's hand in marriage, he is bound to protect her all her life; now that the emperor had taken both his hands, what had he to fear? Pleased by the answer, Aurangzeb called him *Sawai*, "one and a quarter", meaning a man worth more than one ordinary man. The story is tradition, and the title may in fact have been granted for service in the Deccan, but *Sawai* became the proud title of every later ruler of Jaipur. As a young commander he served in the siege of the Maratha fort of **Khelna**, also called Vishalgad, in **1702**.

Aurangzeb died in **1707**, and the empire was plunged into a war of succession between his sons. Jai Singh made a dangerous choice. He followed **Azam Shah**, who was defeated and killed by his brother at **Jajau**, near Agra, in **June 1707**. The victor, **Bahadur Shah I**, took revenge. He declared Jai Singh's younger brother Vijay Singh the Raja, and sent an imperial officer to take over Amber itself. For the first time in centuries, the Kachwahas had lost their capital.

Jai Singh did not accept his fate. In **1708** he joined with **Ajit Singh** of Marwar, who had himself spent his youth fighting Aurangzeb to recover Jodhpur, and the two princes went to Udaipur to seek the support of **Maharana Amar Singh II** of Mewar. The three houses made a pact to stand together. As part of it, Jai Singh married a princess of Mewar, and he promised that her son, if she had one, would succeed to Amber ahead of his other sons; that promise would cause bitter trouble in the next generation. With Rajput forces behind them, the two princes drove the imperial officers out of their lands, and at **Sambhar** in **1708** the Rajputs defeated the imperial forces sent against them. Bahadur Shah, busy with other rebellions, made peace, and Jai Singh was restored to Amber.

Over the next three decades Jai Singh became one of the most important figures of a weakening empire. He was a skilled diplomat, at ease in Persian and Sanskrit, and he served a succession of emperors as governor and commander. In **1713** he was made governor of **Malwa**, where Maratha armies were beginning to push north, and he drove back a Maratha raid there in **1715**. In **1722**, as governor of **Agra**, he led a long campaign against the rising power of the **Jats** and took their stronghold of **Thun**. He was later given Malwa again, in the years when the young Peshwa **Baji Rao I** was leading Maratha armies across the Narmada.

On the Maratha question, Jai Singh's judgement changed with time. In **1734** he joined other Rajput rulers at **Hurda** in a meeting meant to unite them against the Maratha advance, but the alliance came to little. Increasingly he believed that the Marathas could not be stopped by arms alone, and he favoured negotiation with Baji Rao. His critics saw this as weakness; his admirers saw it as realism in an age when the Mughal army could no longer protect its provinces. He also involved himself in the affairs of neighbouring states, above all **Bundi**, where his interference in its succession left lasting bitterness among the Hadas.

Yet Jai Singh's fame does not rest on his wars or his diplomacy. It rests on two great works of peace.

The first was a city. Amber, squeezed into its narrow valley, had become too small for a capital that was now one of the richest states of Rajasthan, and water there was scarce. On the open plain to the south, Jai Singh decided to build a new capital. Its foundations were laid in **1727**. With the Bengali scholar-architect **Vidyadhar Bhattacharya**, he drew a city on a grid, divided into rectangular blocks crossed by broad, straight streets, following the principles of the old Indian treatises on architecture. There were planned bazaars for each trade, temples and gardens, a great palace at the centre, and strong walls with gates. The city took his name: **Jaipur**. It was among the most carefully planned cities in India of its age, and merchants, bankers and craftsmen were invited from far and wide to settle there. In the palace gardens he installed the image of **Govind Dev**, the form of Krishna that had been carried away from Vrindavan for safety in Aurangzeb's time, and Govind Dev became the guardian deity of the city.

The second work was the sky. From his youth Jai Singh had been fascinated by astronomy. He studied the Sanskrit astronomical texts and the Persian and Arabic tables used at the Mughal court, and he found that their predictions of the positions of the planets did not match what could be seen. He set out to correct them. Brass instruments, he believed, were too small and unsteady to give exact readings, so he built instruments in stone and masonry on a giant scale. His observatories, the **Jantar Mantar**, rose in **Delhi** around **1724**, then at **Jaipur**, **Ujjain**, **Varanasi** and **Mathura**. The great sundial of Jaipur, the **Samrat Yantra**, casts a shadow that moves visibly across its scale as the minutes pass. Today the Jaipur observatory is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

From years of observation, his astronomers prepared new astronomical tables, which he dedicated to the emperor **Muhammad Shah** as the *Zij-i Muhammad Shahi*. He gathered scholars of many traditions, had Euclid's geometry translated into Sanskrit, and sent a mission to Portugal that brought back European astronomical works. His learning did not reach the telescopic astronomy then changing Europe, and his great instruments were the last flowering of an older tradition rather than the beginning of a new one. But no Indian ruler of his age pursued science with such passion.

He was also a patron of the old religion. In an age when the empire had lost its power to impose its will, Jai Singh revived ancient Vedic rites, including the **ashvamedha**, the horse sacrifice of the old Indian kings, and gave generous support to Brahmins, temples and Sanskrit learning. He built at Jaipur, as at Amber, for both the gods and the state: the great **Jaivana** cannon cast at **Jaigarh** in **1720** stands beside the temples he endowed.

Sawai Jai Singh II died on **21 September 1743**, in the city he had built. His death opened the dispute his old promise to Mewar had prepared. His son **Ishwari Singh** succeeded him, but **Madho Singh**, the son of the Mewar princess, claimed the throne, and the struggle between the brothers, with Maratha armies drawn in on both sides, troubled Jaipur for years. It was a sad end for the realm of a ruler who had spent his life seeking order in the heavens and on earth.

Yet what he built lasted. The streets of Jaipur still follow his grid, its markets still bear the names of their trades, and in the courtyard of the Jantar Mantar the shadow of the great sundial still moves across the stone, exactly as he designed it to nearly three hundred years ago.

## Highlights of his life

- **Raja of Amber at eleven.** He succeeded his father Bishan Singh at the end of 1699 and served Aurangzeb in the Deccan; tradition says the emperor gave him the title Sawai.
- **Loss and recovery of Amber.** After backing Azam Shah at Jajau in 1707 he lost his capital, then won it back in 1708 in alliance with Ajit Singh of Marwar and Mewar.
- **Governor and statesman.** He governed Malwa and Agra, took the Jat stronghold of Thun in 1722, and dealt with the rising power of the Marathas.
- **Founder of Jaipur (1727).** With Vidyadhar Bhattacharya he built one of the most carefully planned cities of its age.
- **The Jantar Mantar observatories.** He built giant masonry observatories at Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Varanasi and Mathura.
- **Scholar-king.** He compiled the Zij-i Muhammad Shahi, had Euclid translated into Sanskrit, and supported scholars of many traditions.
- **Revival of Vedic rites.** He performed the ashvamedha and patronised temples and Sanskrit learning; he died in Jaipur on 21 September 1743.

dulha-rai.story:
## Dulha Rai — the bridegroom prince who carried the Kachwahas into Dhundhar

*What we know of Dulha Rai comes almost entirely from the genealogies and bardic chronicles of the Kachwaha house, written down centuries after his time, and from the retellings of colonial writers such as James Tod. The chronicles disagree on dates and on many details; where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

Long before there was a city called Jaipur, before the palace on the hill at Amber and the pink walls of the plain, the country that the Kachwahas would one day rule was called **Dhundhar**. It was a land of low, broken hills and dry valleys in eastern Rajasthan, cut by seasonal streams and dotted with tanks that filled in the rains and shrank to mud in the heat. Its villages and hill forts were held by a patchwork of powers: Meena chiefs who had ruled the hills for generations, Bargujar Rajputs at **Dausa** and other towns, and, beyond them to the west, the rising Chauhan kings of Sambhar and Ajmer.

The Kachwahas themselves came from further east. They traced their line to **Kusha**, the son of Rama, and so counted themselves among the Suryavanshi, the clans of the solar race. In the historical record, a dynasty known as the **Kachchhapaghatas** ruled around Gwalior and Narwar in the tenth and eleventh centuries, and the Kachwahas of Dhundhar have always looked back to that house as their origin. Their bards tell of a long line of kings in the fort of Gwalior, and of a time when that line lost its hold and its younger branches had to seek their fortunes elsewhere.

Dulha Rai, also remembered as **Dhola Rai**, was born into that moment of decline. The chronicles name his father as **Sodh Dev**, a Kachwaha prince of the Narwar line. The name by which the son is remembered is itself a small story. *Dulha* means "bridegroom", and the bards say it clung to him because his rise began with a marriage. The exact years of his life are uncertain. The chronicles of the Jaipur house place his arrival in Dhundhar in the first half of the twelfth century, and the date **1128 CE** is often given for the beginning of his rule; older reckonings, including Tod's, put the same events as much as a century and a half earlier. Historians treat all of these dates as traditional.

There are two very different stories of how the young Kachwaha came to Dhundhar, and both deserve to be told.

The first is the story kept by the court of Amber and Jaipur. In this telling, Sodh Dev and his son came west with a band of followers, seeking land and service. In the hills near **Lalsot** lay the small Chauhan principality of **Moran**, ruled by **Ralan Singh Chauhan**. Ralan Singh had a daughter, remembered in the chronicles as **Maroni**, and he had an enemy: the Bargujar Rajputs of Dausa, with whom his family shared or disputed that fortified town. A marriage was arranged between the Chauhan princess and the young Kachwaha, and it was more than a family alliance. It was a pact of arms.

One can imagine the wedding in the hill country: the drums and the songs of the women, the bridegroom riding to the bride's house with a sword at his side, the Chauhan elders watching to see what manner of man their daughter had married. They did not have to wait long. Soon after the marriage, Kachwahas and Chauhans marched together against the Bargujars of Dausa and drove them out. The victory gave Dulha Rai his first real seat of power. Dausa became, by the traditional account, the **first capital** of the Kachwahas in Dhundhar.

The second story is the one Tod heard and repeated, and it is darker. In this version, the young prince lost his father early and was carried west by his mother as a child, in a basket, until she came to the Meena stronghold of **Khoh**. The Meena chief, the story says, took pity on the widow, gave her shelter and treated the boy as his own. When Dhola Rai grew up, he was sent as the chief's envoy and returned with Rajput companions. On the festival day when the Meenas went down to a tank to make offerings to their ancestors, laying aside their weapons for the ritual, the Rajputs fell upon them and slaughtered them, and Khoh passed to the Kachwahas.

The two stories cannot both be wholly true, and we cannot know how much of either is. The Jaipur tradition is a court tradition and naturally tells its founder's story with honour. Tod's tale, with its betrayal at the water's edge, has the shape of a legend told in many places about the fall of the old Meena power. What both versions agree on is the larger history: that the Kachwahas came into Dhundhar as newcomers, and that their kingdom was built on the lands of the Meenas, who had held those hills before them. That memory remained alive among the Meenas for centuries, and in later times the Kachwaha rulers gave certain Meena clans a place of honour in their courts and treasuries, as if to acknowledge an old debt.

From Dausa, by the chronicles' account, Dulha Rai turned against the Meena strongholds of the hills. The first great test came at **Manch**, a fortified place among the ridges east of the later city of Jaipur. Here the story becomes a legend of faith. The bards say that the Kachwaha attack failed. The Meenas held the heights, the Rajputs were driven back, and Dulha Rai himself fell wounded on the field among his fallen men.

As he lay there, tradition says, a goddess appeared to him. She told him to rise, to fight again, and to build her a shrine on that ground when the victory was his. In the bards' telling the wounded men around him stood up as if waking from sleep, and the second attack carried the hill. Dulha Rai, true to his vow, raised a temple to the goddess, who is remembered as **Jamwai Mata**, and she became the *kuldevi*, the family goddess, of the Kachwahas. He renamed Manch in honour of his ancestor Rama, and it became **Ramgarh**; the place is still known as **Jamwa Ramgarh**, and the temple of Jamwai Mata still stands there, visited by the descendants of the house and by ordinary pilgrims alike. The miracle is legend. The shrine, and its importance to the Kachwahas, are very real.

After Manch, the chronicles say, Dulha Rai took **Khoh** from the Chanda Meenas, and Khoh became his seat. Other villages and small strongholds in the valleys around it followed. It is important to see these wars at their true scale. They were not the great battles of the later Rajput age, with tens of thousands of horsemen and war elephants. They were fights for hill forts, for wells and tanks, for the right to collect grain from a cluster of villages. A few hundred men could decide them. But in a land of small powers, each such victory changed the map, and step by step the newcomer from Narwar built something that had not existed before: a Kachwaha state in Dhundhar.

That state was born into a dangerous neighbourhood. To the west, the **Chauhans** of Shakambhari and Ajmer were the great power of the region in the twelfth century, and under kings such as **Ajayaraja** and **Arnoraja** they were extending their influence across eastern Rajasthan. Further north, the Tomaras still held Delhi, and beyond the Indus the Ghaznavid sultans remained a threat to the plains of the Punjab. A small new kingdom between these powers survived by being useful to its strong neighbours and dangerous to its weak ones. Dulha Rai's marriage into a Chauhan family, whatever its exact circumstances, gave his house a link to the most important clan of the region, and the Kachwahas would serve the Chauhans for generations.

What sort of man was Dulha Rai? The chronicles give us a warrior and a founder: bold, persistent, willing to fight again after defeat. They also give us a man of faith, whose most lasting act was the founding of a shrine. The darker tradition preserved by Tod reminds us that founders are often remembered more kindly by their own descendants than by the people they displaced. Both pictures belong to his memory.

The accounts of his death differ. Most say he died from wounds received in war, while he was still in the prime of life, and the traditional dates make his reign a short one of about two decades. He left behind him a small state, a family goddess, and a son ready to carry the work forward: **Kakil Deo**, who in the next generation would take the hill town of **Amber** from the Meenas and make it the capital of the Kachwahas for six hundred years.

From that beginning the house of Dulha Rai grew slowly through the following centuries, serving the Chauhans and later the rulers of Delhi, until in the sixteenth century **Raja Bharmal** and **Raja Man Singh** made it one of the great powers of Mughal India, and in the eighteenth **Sawai Jai Singh II** built Jaipur on the plain below the old hills. Every one of those later kings counted Dulha Rai as the founder of their line in Dhundhar, and every one of them bowed before Jamwai Mata, the goddess who, the bards say, once raised a wounded bridegroom prince from the field at Manch.

## Highlights of his life

- **A prince of the Narwar line.** Son of Sodh Dev, he came from the Kachwaha branch that looked back to the Kachchhapaghata kings of Gwalior and Narwar.
- **The marriage alliance with the Chauhans.** His marriage to the daughter of Ralan Singh Chauhan of Moran gave him allies and, according to the bards, his name of "bridegroom".
- **Capture of Dausa.** With his Chauhan allies he took Dausa from the Bargujars, and it became the first Kachwaha capital in Dhundhar.
- **Victory at Manch and the founding of Ramgarh.** After a first defeat against the Meenas he took Manch, renamed it Ramgarh, and, as tradition tells, founded the shrine of Jamwai Mata, the Kachwaha family goddess.
- **Seizure of Khoh.** He took Khoh from the Chanda Meenas and made it his seat; Tod preserves a darker legend of how it fell.
- **Founder of Kachwaha rule in Dhundhar.** Traditionally dated to the early twelfth century, his small state grew into the kingdom of Amber and later of Jaipur.

kakil-deo.story:
## Kakil Deo — the king who chose the valley of Amber

*Kakil Deo's life is known only through the genealogies and chronicles of the Kachwaha house and the traditions retold by later historians; no inscription of his reign is known. This story keeps to what those traditions say and to the real history of his age, and where history and legend part ways, it says so.*

In the hill country of Dhundhar, in the first half of the twelfth century, a small Kachwaha state was taking shape. Its founder, **Dulha Rai**, had come from the old Kachwaha line of Narwar, married into a Chauhan family of the hills near Lalsot, taken **Dausa** from the Bargujar Rajputs, and won the Meena strongholds of **Manch**, which he renamed **Ramgarh**, and **Khoh**. It was a state of a few forts and a few dozen villages, held by the sword and by the loyalty of a small band of followers. Into this new and uncertain house **Kakil Deo** was born.

The chronicles name him as the son of Dulha Rai by his Chauhan wife, **Maroni**, the daughter of Ralan Singh of Moran. He was, then, a child of the alliance that had made his father's rise possible: Kachwaha by his father, Chauhan by his mother. Nothing certain is recorded of his childhood, but we can imagine it from the world around him. He would have grown up in the fortified hill towns of Khoh and Ramgarh, among warriors who had only recently won their land, listening to the stories of his father's wars and of the night at Manch when, the bards say, the goddess **Jamwai Mata** raised the wounded Kachwahas from the field. He would have learned to ride and to use the sword and the bow as every Rajput boy did, and he would have learned, too, that the hills around him still belonged in spirit to the Meenas, whose chiefs had ruled them for generations.

The traditional dates place his father's reign in the early twelfth century, and the date often given for the beginning of Kakil Deo's own rule is around **1150 CE**, though older reckonings put these events much earlier. Like all the early Kachwaha dates, it should be read as a tradition rather than a fixed fact. What the chronicles agree on is that Dulha Rai died while still in his prime, most likely from wounds received in war, and that Kakil Deo came to the gaddi of a kingdom that was young, small and still fighting for its place.

The first task of a new king in such a state was simply to survive. A founder's death was a dangerous moment. Defeated rivals might rise again, and neighbours who had respected the father might test the son. The Meena chiefs who had lost Manch and Khoh had not disappeared; they held other hills and other valleys, and the Bargujars had not forgotten Dausa. The chronicles remember Kakil Deo as a ruler who held his father's lands together through these years and then went further.

His great achievement, the one that gave his name its place in history, was the taking of **Amber**.

A few miles north of the later city of Jaipur, the hills of Dhundhar close in around a narrow valley. At its head lies a small lake, and around it the ridges rise steep and rocky, so that the valley can be entered only through a few passes. In Kakil Deo's time this valley was held by the **Susawat Meenas**, one of the most powerful Meena clans of the region, and their town in the valley was already old. Tradition has offered several explanations of its name. Some connect it with **Ambikeshwar**, a form of Shiva whose ancient shrine stands in the town; others with the goddess Amba, or with the legendary king **Ambarisha**. Whatever its origin, the name Amber would one day be known across India.

How the Kachwahas took the valley is not recorded in detail. The chronicles say simply that Kakil Deo defeated the Susawat Meenas and won Amber from them. We should imagine not a great pitched battle but a hard campaign in broken ground: Rajput horsemen working their way through the passes, Meena archers on the ridges who knew every rock and gully, the slow pressure of a determined enemy against a stronghold that had never been taken. In the end the valley fell, and Kakil Deo made a decision that would shape the next six centuries of his family's history. He did not merely hold Amber as one more fort. He made it his **capital**.

It was a wise choice. Khoh and Ramgarh were strongholds of a conquering band; Amber was a place from which a kingdom could be ruled. The ring of hills made it easy to defend, while its position gave it command of the routes across the plain to the south and to the west. Water could be stored in its lake and in tanks cut into the hills. Over the centuries his descendants would build on those ridges the great fortress-palace of **Amber Fort** and, on the hill above it, **Jaigarh**, but the first step was Kakil Deo's: he saw the valley and understood what it could become. From his time until **Sawai Jai Singh II** founded Jaipur in **1727**, Amber remained the seat of the Kachwahas, and even after that the kings of Jaipur were often called the Rajas of Amber.

Holding Amber meant ruling it. A twelfth-century Rajput state in these hills was not governed by a great bureaucracy. It was held through a web of personal loyalties: the king's kinsmen and companions, each granted villages in return for service with horse and sword; the village headmen who collected the share of the harvest; and the older inhabitants of the land, whose cooperation made every other arrangement possible. The Meenas did not vanish when they lost their towns. They remained farmers, herders and fighting men throughout Dhundhar, and in later centuries the Kachwaha rulers gave Meena clans a lasting place in the life of the state, including, by long tradition, the guarding of royal treasure. The roots of that relationship, uneasy and complicated as it was, go back to the generation of Dulha Rai and Kakil Deo.

Religion was part of the work of kingship too. The Kachwahas brought with them their devotion to Jamwai Mata, the goddess of Ramgarh, and the worship of Rama, the ancestor of their solar line. At Amber they found the old shrine of Ambikeshwar, and later tradition links its care to the early Kachwaha kings. Whether Kakil Deo himself built or restored any temple there is not certain, but he ruled in an age when every Rajput king was expected to honour the gods of his land as well as the gods of his house.

Beyond the hills, the world was changing fast. During Kakil Deo's lifetime the **Chauhans** of Shakambhari and Ajmer reached the height of their power. Around the middle of the twelfth century **Vigraharaja IV** extended Chauhan rule as far as Delhi, taking it from the Tomaras, and in **1178** the young **Prithviraj Chauhan** came to the throne of Ajmer. Dhundhar lay right in the shadow of this great power. A small kingdom like Amber survived by keeping good terms with Ajmer, and the Kachwahas were remembered as faithful followers of the Chauhans. The bards later told that Kakil Deo's descendant **Pajjun** was among the captains of Prithviraj. Kakil Deo himself did not live to see the storm that broke in **1191 and 1192**, when Muhammad of Ghor came against Prithviraj at **Tarain**, but the kingdom he had settled at Amber would have to live through what followed.

What kind of man was Kakil Deo? The chronicles do not give him speeches or a portrait. They remember him by his deeds: that he held what his father had won, took Amber from the Susawat Meenas, and made it the heart of the Kachwaha state. In the long gallery of Kachwaha kings, filled with famous names such as Raja Man Singh and Sawai Jai Singh, he is easily overlooked. But a founding needs two generations: one to win the land and one to settle it. Dulha Rai won a foothold; Kakil Deo made it a home.

His death, like his birth, is not recorded with any certainty. The traditional dates give him a reign of some three decades, ending around **1180 CE**. The Kachwaha genealogies name his son **Hanudeva** as the next ruler of Amber, and the long line of Amber's kings descended from him; the archive's own list places a ruler named **Govind Rai** after him, a name that the standard genealogies do not confirm. Whichever reckoning is followed, the kingdom passed on intact, centred on the valley he had chosen.

Today, visitors walking up to the great palace at Amber pass through the valley that the Susawat Meenas once held and Kakil Deo made into a capital. The palace they see was built centuries after him, but the choice of the place was his.

## Highlights of his life

- **Son of the founder.** Born to Dulha Rai and his Chauhan wife Maroni, he inherited a young Kachwaha state in Dhundhar and held it together after his father's death.
- **Conquest of Amber.** He won the valley of Amber from the Susawat Meenas, one of the most powerful Meena clans of the region.
- **Amber made the capital.** He moved the seat of the Kachwahas to Amber, which remained their capital until the founding of Jaipur in 1727.
- **Consolidation of the hills.** He secured the lands his father had won at Dausa, Ramgarh and Khoh, and laid the basis of Kachwaha rule over the Meena country.
- **A kingdom in the Chauhan age.** He ruled under the shadow of the Chauhans of Ajmer, whose loyal allies the Kachwahas remained.
- **Founder of a long line.** Through his son Hanudeva, according to the genealogies, descended every later king of Amber and Jaipur.

govind-rai-amber.story:
## Govind Rai — a name from Amber's early lineage

*Govind Rai is known only from later lists of the early rulers of Amber. No inscription or chronicle of his own time names him, so this short account keeps to what can be said with confidence.*

Govind Rai is remembered as the seventh ruler of the **Kachwaha** house of **Dhundhar**, the country of hills and plains around **Amber**, in the last decades of the twelfth century. The lists place him after **Kakil Deo**, the ruler whom tradition credits with taking Amber from its **Mina** chiefs, and before **Chandrasen**. Beyond that, his life is unrecorded. The genealogies kept by the Kachwaha bards do not agree with one another for these early generations, and the best-known of them give quite different names for this period, so even his place in the line is uncertain.

What can be described is the world in which a ruler of Amber lived at this time. The Kachwahas were then a young power. Their tradition says that **Dulha Rai** came from the region of **Narwar**, where the related Kachchhapaghata line had ruled, and won land around **Dausa** and **Khoh**, and that his successors pressed on to Amber. Their small state lay in the hills between the great Chauhan kingdom of **Ajmer** and the plains towards Delhi.

That position became dangerous in the 1190s. In **1191** **Prithviraj Chauhan** defeated **Muhammad of Ghor** at the first battle of **Tarain**, and in **1192** he was defeated on the same field and killed. Ajmer passed under Ghurid control, and the old order of northern Rajasthan collapsed within a few years. Kachwaha tradition remembers a warrior of its house, **Pajjun**, as a companion of Prithviraj, but nothing links Govind Rai himself to these wars.

Whoever held Amber in these years had to survive between the falling Chauhans, the advancing Turkish garrisons and the Mina clans of the hills. That the line continued at all is the one achievement history can firmly credit to this generation.

## Highlights of his life

- **Seventh in the Amber lists.** He is placed after Kakil Deo and before Chandrasen, in the late twelfth century.
- **A name without records.** No inscription or contemporary text mentions him, and the bardic genealogies differ over this period.
- **Ruler of a young state.** The Kachwaha seat at Amber had only recently been won from the Mina chiefs, according to tradition.
- **Witness to an age of upheaval.** His time fell in the years of Tarain (1191 and 1192) and the fall of Chauhan Ajmer.

chandrasen-early.story:
## Chandrasen — Amber in the first years of the Delhi Sultanate

*Chandrasen is known only from later lists of Amber's early rulers. No inscription or chronicle of his own time records him, so this short account keeps to what can be said with confidence.*

Chandrasen appears as the eighth ruler of the **Kachwaha** line of **Dhundhar** in lists that place him in the early thirteenth century, after **Govind Rai** and before **Bishan (Vishnu) Singh**. Nothing about his birth, family, wars or death survives. The genealogies of the Kachwaha bards differ widely for these generations. He should not be confused with the far better documented **Chandrasen** of Amber who ruled at the end of the fifteenth century and was the father of Raja Prithviraj.

The years given for him, around 1200 to 1220, were the years in which a new power took shape in northern India. After the defeat of Prithviraj Chauhan at **Tarain** in **1192**, Muhammad of Ghor's general **Qutb al-Din Aibak** held Delhi and Ajmer and put down Chauhan attempts to win Ajmer back. When Muhammad died in **1206**, Aibak became the first sultan at Delhi. After Aibak's death in **1210**, **Iltutmish** took the throne and spent much of his reign bringing the Rajput states around him under his authority.

The Chauhans themselves withdrew to the fortress of **Ranthambore**, south-east of Amber, under Prithviraj's son **Govindaraja**. Dhundhar lay between Turkish Ajmer, Delhi and Chauhan Ranthambore, a hard place for a small house. The Kachwahas of Amber, still holding hill country that tradition says they had won from the **Mina** clans, could survive only by caution and by the strength of their hills.

That the lineage passed on unbroken through these years is all that history can say of Chandrasen's time. The later greatness of Amber, under rulers such as Raja Man Singh, still lay more than three centuries ahead.

## Highlights of his life

- **Eighth in the Amber lists.** He is placed after Govind Rai and before Bishan (Vishnu) Singh, in the early thirteenth century.
- **A name without records.** No inscription or contemporary text mentions him, and he is distinct from the fifteenth-century Chandrasen of Amber.
- **Ruler in the founding years of the Sultanate.** His time saw Aibak become sultan in 1206 and Iltutmish succeed in 1211.
- **Between two powers.** Amber lay between Turkish Ajmer and Delhi on one side and Chauhan Ranthambore on the other.

vishnu-singh-amber.story:
## Bishan (Vishnu) Singh — Amber in the age of Iltutmish

*Bishan (Vishnu) Singh is known only from later lists of Amber's early rulers. No inscription or chronicle of his own time records him, so this short account keeps to what can be said with confidence.*

Bishan Singh, whose name is also given in its Sanskrit form as Vishnu Singh, appears as the ninth ruler of the **Kachwaha** line of **Dhundhar**, placed around 1220 to 1240, after **Chandrasen** and before **Mal Singh**. Nothing of his personal life survives: not his birth, his marriages, his wars or the manner of his death. The genealogies of the Kachwaha bards give different names for these generations, and his position in the line cannot be confirmed. He is not to be confused with **Raja Bishan Singh** of Amber, who reigned from 1688 to 1699 and was the father of Sawai Jai Singh II.

The decades given for him were dominated by **Iltutmish**, sultan of Delhi from 1211 to 1236. Having secured his throne, Iltutmish turned on the Rajput strongholds that had recovered after the Ghurid conquest. In **1226** he took **Ranthambore** from the Chauhans, south-east of Amber, and soon afterwards he moved against **Mandore** and **Jalor** further west. The message for every chief in eastern Rajasthan was plain: the new sultanate meant to rule, not merely to raid.

After Iltutmish's death in **1236** Delhi fell into a period of disorder. His daughter **Raziya** reigned until 1240, and the nobles fought among themselves. Such years gave smaller houses on the edge of the sultanate room to breathe, and the Chauhans soon regained Ranthambore.

For the Kachwahas, still a modest power holding Amber and its hills, the safest course in this age was usually to stay out of the sultan's path. Whatever Bishan Singh did, the line passed on to his successor intact, and that continuity is what the lists remember.

## Highlights of his life

- **Ninth in the Amber lists.** He is placed after Chandrasen and before Mal Singh, around 1220 to 1240.
- **A name without records.** No inscription or contemporary text mentions him, and he is distinct from Raja Bishan Singh of Amber (1688 to 1699).
- **Ruler in the shadow of Iltutmish.** His time saw the sultan take Ranthambore in 1226 and campaign against Mandore and Jalor.
- **Continuity of the line.** The Kachwaha house at Amber came through these decades and passed to Mal Singh.
