mal-singh-amber.story:
## Mal Singh — Amber in the years of Balban's campaigns

*Mal Singh is known only from later lists of Amber's early rulers. No inscription or chronicle of his own time records him, so this short account keeps to what can be said with confidence.*

Mal Singh appears as the tenth ruler of the **Kachwaha** line of **Dhundhar**, placed around 1240 to 1260, after **Bishan (Vishnu) Singh** and before **Prithviraj Singh I**. Nothing of his birth, family, wars or death has come down to us. The bardic genealogies of the Kachwahas include a ruler named **Malesi** somewhere in these early generations, and it is tempting to see the same man behind both names, but there is no evidence to make that identification, and the lists disagree about order and dates.

The middle decades of the thirteenth century were a time of weak sultans and strong ministers at Delhi. After the fall of Raziya in 1240 the throne passed quickly from hand to hand, until **Nasir al-Din Mahmud** became sultan in **1246**. Real power lay with his deputy, **Ghiyas al-Din Balban**, who led the sultanate's armies.

Balban's campaigns came close to Dhundhar. He marched against the Chauhans of **Ranthambore**, who had recovered their fortress after Iltutmish's death, in **1248** and again in **1253**, without breaking them. Nearer still lay **Mewat**, the rough hill country north-east of Amber, whose fighters raided the roads up to Delhi itself. In **1260** Balban led a ferocious campaign there that Delhi's own chroniclers described with grim pride.

For a small house holding Amber, these were years to watch the roads and keep the hill forts strong. The Kachwahas were not yet a power that Delhi needed to reckon with, and that obscurity may itself have protected them. Mal Singh's line passed on to his successor intact.

## Highlights of his life

- **Tenth in the Amber lists.** He is placed after Bishan (Vishnu) Singh and before Prithviraj Singh I, around 1240 to 1260.
- **A name without records.** No inscription or contemporary text mentions him. A link with Malesi of the bardic lists is possible but unproven.
- **Neighbour to Balban's wars.** His time saw Delhi's attacks on Ranthambore in 1248 and 1253 and the harsh campaign in Mewat in 1260.
- **Continuity of the line.** The Kachwaha house at Amber survived these decades and passed to Prithviraj Singh I.

prithviraj-i-amber.story:
## Prithviraj Singh I — Amber under the iron rule of Balban

*Prithviraj Singh I is known only from later lists of Amber's early rulers. No inscription or chronicle of his own time records him, so this short account keeps to what can be said with confidence.*

Prithviraj Singh I appears as the eleventh ruler of the **Kachwaha** line of **Dhundhar**, placed around 1260 to 1280, after **Mal Singh** and before **Ratansingh**. Nothing of his birth, marriages, wars or death survives, and the bardic genealogies of the Kachwahas give different names for this period. The Prithviraj whom history knows well at Amber is a much later ruler, **Raja Prithviraj**, who reigned from **1503** to **1527**; this earlier namesake should not be confused with him.

The years given for him fell largely under **Ghiyas al-Din Balban**, who had commanded Delhi's armies for two decades and became sultan himself in **1266**. Balban ruled by fear. He crushed the Mewatis on the road to Delhi, cleared forests that sheltered raiders, and set up garrisoned posts across the country around the capital. His purpose was to make the sultan's authority felt in the lands nearest Delhi, and **Mewat**, on Dhundhar's north-eastern edge, felt it most harshly.

Further south, the Chauhans of **Ranthambore** held out under **Jaitrasimha**, keeping alive the last strong Chauhan kingdom in the region. A few years after the period given for Prithviraj Singh I, in the 1280s, Jaitrasimha's son **Hammir** would succeed him there and make Ranthambore famous.

For a small hill state like Amber, caught between Balban's garrisons and the Chauhan stronghold, the wisest policy was to stay quiet, keep the forts in repair and avoid giving Delhi a reason to march. Whatever the details of Prithviraj Singh I's rule, the Kachwaha line passed through these hard decades unbroken.

## Highlights of his life

- **Eleventh in the Amber lists.** He is placed after Mal Singh and before Ratansingh, around 1260 to 1280.
- **A name without records.** No inscription or contemporary text mentions him, and he is distinct from Raja Prithviraj of Amber (1503 to 1527).
- **Ruler in Balban's age.** His time saw Balban become sultan in 1266 and harshly subdue Mewat, close to Dhundhar.
- **Continuity of the line.** The Kachwaha house at Amber survived these decades and passed to Ratansingh.

ratan-singh-amber.story:
## Ratansingh — Amber on the eve of the Khalji storm

*Ratansingh is known only from later lists of Amber's early rulers. No inscription or chronicle of his own time records him, so this short account keeps to what can be said with confidence.*

Ratansingh appears as the twelfth ruler of the **Kachwaha** line of **Dhundhar**, placed around 1280 to 1300, after **Prithviraj Singh I** and before **Chandrasen II**. Nothing of his birth, family, wars or death has survived, and the bardic genealogies of the Kachwahas name different rulers for these generations. He should not be confused with the documented **Raja Ratan Singh** of Amber, son of Raja Prithviraj, who ruled in the sixteenth century.

The last two decades of the thirteenth century changed the balance of power in Rajasthan. **Balban** died in **1287**, and within three years his house was swept away. In **1290** **Jalal al-Din Khalji** seized the throne of Delhi. In **1291** he marched on **Ranthambore**, now ruled by the Chauhan **Hammir**, sacked the nearby town of **Jhain**, looked at the great fortress and turned back, judging it not worth the lives it would cost.

His nephew was less cautious. **Ala al-Din Khalji** murdered Jalal al-Din and took the throne in **1296**, and within a few years his armies would fall on the Rajput strongholds one after another: Ranthambore in **1301**, Chittor in **1303**. These blows came just after the period given for Ratansingh, in the time of his successor, but the storm was gathering throughout his last years.

Amber, lying only a short march from both Delhi's roads and Ranthambore, could not have been unaware of it. A small Kachwaha state survived by keeping its head down while far greater houses were destroyed. Whatever Ratansingh's own deeds were, the line passed on intact to Chandrasen II.

## Highlights of his life

- **Twelfth in the Amber lists.** He is placed after Prithviraj Singh I and before Chandrasen II, around 1280 to 1300.
- **A name without records.** No inscription or contemporary text mentions him, and he is distinct from the sixteenth-century Raja Ratan Singh of Amber.
- **Witness to the Khalji rise.** His time saw Jalal al-Din Khalji take Delhi in 1290 and attack Ranthambore in 1291, and Ala al-Din seize the throne in 1296.
- **Continuity of the line.** The Kachwaha house at Amber passed intact to Chandrasen II on the eve of the Khalji conquests.

chandrasen-ii.story:
## Chandrasen II — a quiet throne in the shadow of the Khalji storm

*Chandrasen II is known to this archive only as a name in a late list of Amber's rulers, placed around 1300–1315 CE; the commonly cited genealogies of the Kachwaha house do not record him, so this short account tells what is known of his house and his age rather than inventing a life.*

The Kachwahas of **Dhundhar** traced their line to the solar race of Rama and, more nearly, to the Kachchhapaghata rulers of the Gwalior and Narwar country. Tradition says that **Dulha Rai** led a branch of the clan into Dhundhar and that his son **Kakil Deo** took **Amber** from the Meenas. By 1300 the family held a small hill kingdom around Amber, Khoh and Ramgarh, still a minor power among the Rajput states. Jaipur, which the card names as capital, would not be founded until 1727; in this age the seat was Amber.

In the list followed here, Chandrasen II comes after **Ratansingh** and before **Kesar Singh**. The genealogies most historians use name different rulers for these generations, among them **Kuntal** and **Jonsi**, so his place cannot be confirmed.

What is certain is the danger of his time. **Alauddin Khalji** of Delhi was conquering the Rajput strongholds one by one: **Ranthambore**, barely a hundred miles from Amber, fell in **1301** with the death of **Hammir Dev Chauhan**; **Chittor** fell in **1303**, **Siwana** in **1308** and **Jalor** in **1311**. Small states such as Amber survived these years by caution and by not drawing the Sultan's armies upon themselves. No record tells how Amber's ruler of these years faced that storm, only that the house outlived it.

## Highlights of his life

- **Place in the line.** Listed after Ratansingh and before Kesar Singh, around 1300–1315 CE.
- **A thin record.** His name is not found in the standard Kachwaha genealogies, which give rulers such as Kuntal and Jonsi for this century.
- **Ruler of Amber, not Jaipur.** The family's seat was the hill town of Amber; Jaipur came four centuries later.
- **Survival in the Khalji age.** His house endured while Ranthambore, Chittor, Siwana and Jalor fell to Alauddin Khalji.

kesar-singh-amber.story:
## Kesar Singh — Amber in the years when Delhi changed hands

*Kesar Singh appears only in a late list of Amber's rulers, placed around 1315–1330 CE; the genealogies of the Kachwaha house that historians commonly use do not name him, so this short account describes his dynasty and his age rather than inventing a life.*

In the list followed here, Kesar Singh succeeds **Chandrasen II** and is followed by **Bhupal Singh**. He belongs to the early Kachwaha house of **Dhundhar**, which traced its descent from the solar race of Rama and, more nearly, from the Kachchhapaghata rulers of Gwalior and Narwar. Tradition says that **Dulha Rai** brought the clan into Dhundhar and that **Kakil Deo** won **Amber** from the Meenas. In the fourteenth century Amber was the family's seat; Jaipur, named on the card, was founded only in 1727. The standard genealogies give this century to rulers such as **Kuntal** and **Jonsi**, and Kesar Singh's place among them cannot be confirmed.

His period, as the list dates it, was one of upheaval in Delhi. **Alauddin Khalji** died in **1316**, and within four years his line was gone: **Mubarak Shah** was murdered in **1320**, and **Khusrau Khan** was overthrown that same year by **Ghiyasuddin Tughluq**. In **1325** Ghiyasuddin's son **Muhammad bin Tughluq** took the throne and soon ordered much of Delhi's population moved to **Daulatabad** in the Deccan.

The weakening of Delhi's hold gave Rajput houses room to recover. In Mewar, **Hammir** of the Sisodia branch won back **Chittor** from the Sultanate's nominees, around **1326** by the usual reckoning, and began Mewar's long revival. No record tells what Amber's ruler did in these years; the small hill state on the road between Ajmer and Delhi seems simply to have endured.

## Highlights of his life

- **Place in the line.** Listed after Chandrasen II and before Bhupal Singh, around 1315–1330 CE.
- **A thin record.** His name is absent from the standard Kachwaha genealogies, which name rulers such as Kuntal and Jonsi in this century.
- **Witness to Delhi's turmoil.** His years saw the end of the Khalji dynasty and the rise of the Tughluqs.
- **An age of Rajput recovery.** In his time Hammir restored Mewar's hold on Chittor, around 1326.

bhupal-singh-early.story:
## Bhupal Singh — Amber in the reign of Muhammad bin Tughluq

*Bhupal Singh is known only from a late list of Amber's rulers, which places him around 1330–1340 CE; the Kachwaha genealogies that historians commonly follow do not record him, so this short account describes his house and his age rather than inventing a life.*

In the list followed here, Bhupal Singh comes after **Kesar Singh** and before **Nar Singh**. He belongs to the early Kachwaha house of **Dhundhar**, which claimed descent from the solar race of Rama and, more nearly, from the Kachchhapaghata rulers of Gwalior and Narwar. Tradition credits **Dulha Rai** with bringing the clan into Dhundhar and **Kakil Deo** with winning **Amber** from the Meenas. In the fourteenth century the family ruled from Amber, a hill town above the plains; Jaipur, named on the card, was founded only in 1727. The standard genealogies give this century to rulers such as **Kuntal** and **Jonsi**, and Bhupal Singh's place among them cannot be confirmed.

The decade the list gives him was dominated by **Muhammad bin Tughluq**, Sultan of Delhi from **1325**. His bold and costly schemes, among them the transfer of the capital to **Daulatabad** and a token currency of copper and brass around **1330**, strained the empire, and famine and revolt followed in the 1330s. Far to the south, the kingdom of **Vijayanagara** was founded in **1336**, and the Sultan's distant provinces began to slip away.

Closer to Amber, **Mewar** was rising again under **Hammir**, who had recovered Chittor in the previous decade. For a small house such as Amber's, a distracted Delhi meant breathing space. No record tells how Amber's ruler used it, and nothing more should be claimed for him than his place in the line.

## Highlights of his life

- **Place in the line.** Listed after Kesar Singh and before Nar Singh, around 1330–1340 CE.
- **A thin record.** His name is not found in the standard Kachwaha genealogies, which name rulers such as Kuntal and Jonsi in this century.
- **Ruler of Amber.** The seat of the house was Amber; Jaipur was founded four centuries later.
- **The Tughluq decade.** His years fell in the troubled reign of Muhammad bin Tughluq, when Delhi's grip on distant lands loosened.

nar-singh-early.story:
## Nar Singh — a name that the chronicles place more than once

*Nar Singh is known to this archive from a late list of Amber's rulers, which dates him around 1340–1350 CE; the Kachwaha genealogies that historians commonly follow do know a ruler of this name, but several decades later, so this short account sets out what is known rather than inventing a life.*

In the list followed here, Nar Singh succeeds **Bhupal Singh** and is followed by **Bar Singh (Barsi)**. He belongs to the early Kachwaha house of **Dhundhar**, which traced its line to the solar race of Rama and, more nearly, to the Kachchhapaghata rulers of Gwalior and Narwar. Tradition says that **Dulha Rai** brought the clan into Dhundhar and that **Kakil Deo** took **Amber** from the Meenas. In this century the family's seat was Amber; Jaipur, named on the card, was founded only in 1727.

The standard genealogies give the middle of the fourteenth century to **Jonsi**, followed by **Udaikaran**, whose reign is usually dated from around **1366**. They do name a **Narsingh**, but as Udaikaran's son and successor, ruling from the late fourteenth century. Whether this entry is that same prince placed too early, or a different ruler altogether, the record does not allow us to say.

The decade the list gives him was the last of **Muhammad bin Tughluq**'s reign. Revolts spread through the Sultan's provinces; in **1347** the **Bahmani** sultanate broke away in the Deccan, and Muhammad himself died in **1351** in Sindh while pursuing a rebel. In Rajasthan, **Mewar** under **Hammir** and his successors was growing in strength. For the small hill state of Amber, a Delhi absorbed in its own troubles left room to survive, and nothing more certain can be said of its ruler in these years.

## Highlights of his life

- **Place in the line.** Listed after Bhupal Singh and before Bar Singh, around 1340–1350 CE.
- **A name with a puzzle.** The standard genealogies know a Narsingh, but as Udaikaran's successor in the late fourteenth century.
- **Ruler of Amber.** The family ruled from Amber; Jaipur came four centuries later.
- **The breaking of Tughluq power.** His years saw the Bahmani revolt of 1347 and the decline of Muhammad bin Tughluq's empire.

bar-singh-early.story:
## Bar Singh (Barsi) — Amber in the calmer years of Firuz Shah

*Bar Singh, also called Barsi, is known only from a late list of Amber's rulers, which places him around 1350–1360 CE; the Kachwaha genealogies that historians commonly follow do not record him, so this short account describes his house and his age rather than inventing a life.*

In the list followed here, Bar Singh succeeds **Nar Singh** and is followed by **Bhim Singh**. He belongs to the early Kachwaha house of **Dhundhar**, which claimed descent from the solar race of Rama and, more nearly, from the Kachchhapaghata rulers of Gwalior and Narwar. Tradition says that **Dulha Rai** led the clan into Dhundhar and that **Kakil Deo** won **Amber** from the Meenas. In the fourteenth century Amber was the family's seat; Jaipur, named on the card, was founded only in 1727. The standard genealogies assign these years to **Jonsi**, followed by **Udaikaran** from around **1366**, and Bar Singh's place among them cannot be confirmed.

His decade, as the list dates it, opened with a change in Delhi. **Muhammad bin Tughluq** died in Sindh in **1351**, and his cousin **Firuz Shah Tughluq** took the throne. Firuz was a builder and administrator more than a conqueror: he dug canals, founded towns such as **Hisar** and **Firozabad**, and led two expeditions against Bengal, in **1353–54** and **1359**, both of which ended without lasting conquest.

For the Rajput houses of Rajasthan, the reign of Firuz brought relatively little pressure from Delhi. States such as Mewar and Amber had room to consolidate their lands and their bonds with neighbouring clans. What Amber's ruler did with these quieter years is not recorded, and his story can honestly be no more than his place in the line and the times he lived in.

## Highlights of his life

- **Place in the line.** Listed after Nar Singh and before Bhim Singh, around 1350–1360 CE.
- **A thin record.** His name is absent from the standard Kachwaha genealogies, which give these years to Jonsi.
- **Ruler of Amber.** The seat of the house was Amber; Jaipur came four centuries later.
- **The reign of Firuz Shah.** His years fell under a Sultan who built more than he conquered, a time of lighter pressure on Rajasthan.

bhim-singh-early.story:
## Bhim Singh — a name on the eve of Udaikaran's Amber

*Bhim Singh is known to this archive only from a late list of Amber's rulers, which places him around 1360–1375 CE; the Kachwaha genealogies that historians commonly follow do not record a Bhim Singh in this century, so this short account describes his house and his age rather than inventing a life.*

In the list followed here, Bhim Singh succeeds **Bar Singh (Barsi)** and is followed by **Raja Chandrasen III**. He belongs to the early Kachwaha house of **Dhundhar**, which traced its line to the solar race of Rama and, more nearly, to the Kachchhapaghata rulers of Gwalior and Narwar. Tradition says that **Dulha Rai** brought the clan into Dhundhar and that **Kakil Deo** took **Amber** from the Meenas. Amber was the family's seat in this age; Jaipur, named on the card, was founded only in 1727.

The standard genealogies tell a different story for these years. In them **Jonsi** is followed by **Udaikaran**, whose reign is usually dated from around **1366**, squarely within the dates this list gives Bhim Singh. Udaikaran is one of the better-remembered early rulers: through his son **Balaji** descended **Rao Shekha**, founder of the **Shekhawat** branch, while another son, **Narsingh**, succeeded him at Amber. A Bhim Singh does appear in the Amber line, but in the sixteenth century. The record therefore cannot confirm this entry, and its dates conflict with the accepted chronology.

The wider age was the long reign of **Firuz Shah Tughluq** in Delhi, from **1351** to **1388**, a time of canals, new towns and relatively light pressure on the Rajput states. Mewar was strong, and the houses of Dhundhar were slowly widening their lands. Of Bhim Singh himself, nothing more can honestly be said than his place in this list and the times he is set in.

## Highlights of his life

- **Place in the line.** Listed after Bar Singh and before Chandrasen III, around 1360–1375 CE.
- **A conflicting record.** The standard genealogies give these years to Jonsi and then Udaikaran, from around 1366.
- **Ruler of Amber.** The seat of the house was Amber; Jaipur came four centuries later.
- **The age of Firuz Shah.** His years fell in a period of relatively light pressure from Delhi on Rajasthan.

chandrasen-iii.story:
## Raja Chandrasen III — a name in the long line of Amber

*Almost nothing about Raja Chandrasen III survives beyond his name and his place in the archive's list of Kachwaha rulers; this short account gives what is known of his house and his age, and says plainly where the record falls silent.*

The Kachwahas of Dhundhar traced their descent to **Kusha**, son of Rama, and their arrival in the region to **Dulha Rai** in the eleventh century. By the late fourteenth century their seat was the hill town of **Amber**, which tradition says **Kakil Dev** took from the Meenas. Jaipur, the later capital of the house, would not be founded until 1727. In the archive's list, Chandrasen III follows **Bhim Singh** and rules **c. 1375–1390 CE**, before the throne passes to **Raja Bhimdev**.

No inscription, chronicle or coin yet known names a Chandrasen ruling Amber in these years. The standard genealogies of Amber give this period to **Raja Udaykaran**, followed by Narsingh Dev, and they place the well-recorded **Raja Chandrasen** of Amber a century later, in the second half of the fifteenth century. Whatever the source of the archive's sequence, the two should not be confused, and nothing told of the later Chandrasen belongs to this one.

What can be said is how the world looked from Amber in those years. The Kachwaha state was a modest chiefdom of hill forts and farming villages, holding its lands among Meena and other cultivating communities and binding its kinsmen to the house with grants of land. To the north, the Delhi Sultanate under **Firuz Shah Tughlaq** still claimed authority over the region, and his death in **1388** opened years of quarrelling among his heirs. To the south, Mewar was growing strong again under its Sisodia ranas. For a small house like the Kachwahas, survival meant holding the hill forts, keeping the clan together, and staying clear of the anger of greater powers.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Kachwaha of Amber.** He is remembered in the archive as a ruler of the Kachwaha house, whose seat was the hill town of Amber in Dhundhar.
- **A reign of c. 1375–1390 CE.** The archive places him between Bhim Singh and Raja Bhimdev.
- **Ruler in the late Tughlaq age.** His years fell in the last decade of Firuz Shah Tughlaq's reign and the disorder that followed it.
- **Distinct from the later Chandrasen.** The well-documented Raja Chandrasen of Amber ruled in the second half of the fifteenth century and is a different man.

bhimdev-amber.story:
## Raja Bhimdev — Amber in the years of Timur

*Raja Bhimdev is known only from his name and his place in the archive's list of Kachwaha rulers; this short account sets out what is known of his house and his times, and does not invent what the record does not hold.*

The Kachwahas of Dhundhar claimed descent from **Kusha**, son of Rama, and ruled from the hill town of **Amber**, which had been their seat since the eleventh century; Jaipur was founded only in 1727. In the archive's list, Raja Bhimdev succeeds **Raja Chandrasen III** and rules **c. 1390–1405 CE**, before the throne passes to **Raja Mahipala**.

No inscription or chronicle yet known records a Bhimdev on the throne of Amber in these years. The standard genealogies of Amber assign this period to **Raja Narsingh Dev**, son of Udaykaran. The archive's sequence therefore cannot be confirmed, and nothing specific can honestly be told of Bhimdev's deeds, battles or family.

His age, however, is well known, and it was a violent one. After the death of Firuz Shah Tughlaq in 1388, the Delhi Sultanate fell into a struggle between rival claimants. In **1398** the Central Asian conqueror **Timur** crossed the Indus, defeated the Sultan's army and sacked Delhi, leaving the city ruined and the Sultanate broken. Its governors began to rule for themselves: in Malwa, **Dilawar Khan** became independent, and within a few years Gujarat had its own sultan too. Closer to Rajasthan, the Rathores under **Rao Chunda** took **Mandore** around 1395, beginning their rise in Marwar, while Mewar grew stronger under **Rana Lakha**.

For a small house such as the Kachwahas, the collapse of Delhi's power brought both danger and room to breathe. With no strong sultan to answer to, the chiefs of Dhundhar had to look to their own forts and their own kinsmen, and to the shifting powers on every side.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Kachwaha of Amber.** The archive remembers him as a ruler of the Kachwaha house of Dhundhar, seated at Amber.
- **A reign of c. 1390–1405 CE.** The archive places him between Raja Chandrasen III and Raja Mahipala.
- **Ruler in the year of Timur.** His years spanned Timur's sack of Delhi in 1398 and the breaking up of the Tughlaq Sultanate.
- **A thin record.** The standard genealogies of Amber give this period to Raja Narsingh Dev, so his own reign remains unconfirmed.

## Raja Mahipala — Amber between the sultanates

*Raja Mahipala survives only as a name and a place in the archive's list of Kachwaha rulers; this short account tells what is known of his house and his century, and marks clearly where the record ends.*

The Kachwahas of Dhundhar traced their line to **Kusha**, son of Rama, and governed from the hill town of **Amber**, their seat since the eleventh century; the city of Jaipur came only in 1727. In the archive's list, Raja Mahipala (also written Mahipal) follows **Raja Bhimdev** and rules **c. 1405–1420 CE**, before the throne passes to **Raja Prithviraj II**.

No inscription or chronicle yet known names a Mahipala as ruler of Amber in these years. The standard genealogies of Amber give the period to **Raja Narsingh Dev**, and after him, from about 1413, to **Raja Banbir**. The archive's sequence cannot therefore be confirmed, and no deeds, wars or family of Mahipala can honestly be described.

The region around him, though, is well recorded. After Timur's sack of Delhi in 1398, the old Sultanate never recovered its reach. In **1414** **Khizr Khan** took Delhi and founded the **Sayyid** dynasty, whose power barely extended beyond the country around the capital. New sultanates grew strong on Rajasthan's borders: in Gujarat, **Ahmad Shah** founded Ahmedabad in **1411**, and in Malwa **Hoshang Shah** ruled from Mandu. In Mewar, **Rana Lakha** grew rich, and tradition links the silver mines of **Zawar** to his reign.

Caught between these rising powers, the small Kachwaha state of Dhundhar had neither the wealth of Mewar nor the armies of the sultans. Its rulers in these decades kept their hold on Amber and its hill forts, and the house survived to grow great in a later age.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Kachwaha of Amber.** The archive remembers him as a ruler of the Kachwaha house, seated at Amber in Dhundhar.
- **A reign of c. 1405–1420 CE.** The archive places him between Raja Bhimdev and Raja Prithviraj II.
- **Ruler in the age of new sultanates.** His years saw the founding of the Sayyid dynasty in Delhi and the rise of Gujarat and Malwa.
- **A thin record.** The standard genealogies of Amber give this period to Raja Narsingh Dev and Raja Banbir, so his own reign remains unconfirmed.

## Raja Prithviraj II — Amber in the shadow of Mewar and Malwa

*Raja Prithviraj II is known only by his name and his place in the archive's list of Kachwaha rulers; this short account gives what is known of his house and his age, and says plainly where history is silent.*

The Kachwahas of Dhundhar traced their descent to **Kusha**, son of Rama, and ruled from the hill town of **Amber**, their seat since the eleventh century, long before Jaipur was founded in 1727. In the archive's list, Raja Prithviraj II follows **Raja Mahipala** and rules **c. 1420–1440 CE**, before the throne passes to **Raja Prithviraj III**.

No inscription or chronicle yet known records a Prithviraj ruling Amber in these years. The standard genealogies of Amber give the period to **Raja Banbir** and, from about 1424, to **Raja Udharan**. The best-known Prithviraj of Amber, **Raja Prithviraj Singh I**, ruled much later, from about 1502 to 1527, and the numbering used here does not match his. Nothing told of him should be borrowed for this reign, and no deeds, battles or family of Prithviraj II can honestly be described.

The world around Amber in these two decades is better known. Delhi's Sayyid sultans held little beyond the capital, and in **1434** Sultan **Mubarak Shah** was murdered by his own nobles. Real power in the region lay elsewhere. In Mewar, **Rana Mokal** ruled until he too was assassinated in **1433**, and his son **Rana Kumbha** began a reign that would make Mewar the leading Rajput power of the century. In Malwa, **Mahmud Khalji** seized the throne in **1436** and soon set out to fight Mewar for the mastery of the region.

For the modest Kachwaha state of Dhundhar, lying between these great rivals, the task of these years was survival: holding Amber and its hill forts, and keeping the clan and its lands together.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Kachwaha of Amber.** The archive remembers him as a ruler of the Kachwaha house, seated at Amber in Dhundhar.
- **A reign of c. 1420–1440 CE.** The archive places him between Raja Mahipala and Raja Prithviraj III.
- **Ruler in the age of Kumbha.** His years saw the murder of Rana Mokal, the rise of Rana Kumbha in Mewar and of Mahmud Khalji in Malwa.
- **Distinct from Prithviraj Singh I.** The well-documented Prithviraj of Amber ruled in the early sixteenth century.
- **A thin record.** The standard genealogies give this period to Raja Banbir and Raja Udharan, so his own reign remains unconfirmed.

## Raja Prithviraj III — Amber in the age of Kumbha and Jodha

*Raja Prithviraj III is known only by his name and his place in the archive's list of Kachwaha rulers; this short account tells what is known of his house and his age, and does not fill the silence of the record with invention.*

The Kachwahas of Dhundhar claimed descent from **Kusha**, son of Rama, and ruled from the hill town of **Amber**, their seat since the eleventh century; Jaipur would be founded only in 1727. In the archive's list, Raja Prithviraj III follows **Raja Prithviraj II** and rules **c. 1440–1460 CE**, before the throne passes to **Raja Lonkarn**, also called Lakhansi.

No inscription or chronicle yet known records a Prithviraj on the throne of Amber in these years. The standard genealogies of Amber give the period to **Raja Udharan** and, from about 1453, to **Raja Chandrasen**. The well-documented **Raja Prithviraj Singh I** of Amber ruled from about 1502 to 1527, and the numbering here does not match him. No deeds, battles or family of Prithviraj III can honestly be described.

The age itself was one of great Rajput kings. In Mewar, **Rana Kumbha** fought the sultans of Malwa and Gujarat and covered his kingdom with forts and temples. In Marwar, **Rao Jodha** recovered his father's lands and in **1459** founded the city of **Jodhpur**. In Delhi, the weak Sayyid line gave way in **1451** to **Bahlol Lodi**, an Afghan noble who began to rebuild the Sultanate's strength.

Within the Kachwaha clan itself, a new branch was rising. **Rao Shekha**, born in 1433 to a cadet line descended from Raja Udaykaran of Amber, was building his own lordship around **Amarsar** to the north. His descendants, the **Shekhawats**, would give their name to Shekhawati, and tradition remembers that Shekha would not easily accept the authority of Amber.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Kachwaha of Amber.** The archive remembers him as a ruler of the Kachwaha house, seated at Amber in Dhundhar.
- **A reign of c. 1440–1460 CE.** The archive places him between Raja Prithviraj II and Raja Lonkarn.
- **Ruler in the age of great Rajput kings.** His years saw Rana Kumbha's wars in Mewar and Rao Jodha's founding of Jodhpur in 1459.
- **The rise of the Shekhawats.** In these decades Rao Shekha, a Kachwaha kinsman, was building his own state around Amarsar.
- **A thin record.** The standard genealogies give this period to Raja Udharan and Raja Chandrasen, so his own reign remains unconfirmed.

## Raja Lonkarn — a name between Kumbha and the Lodis

*Raja Lonkarn, also called Lakhansi, is known only by his name and his place in the archive's list of Kachwaha rulers; this short account gives what is known of his house and his age, and says plainly where the record is silent.*

The Kachwahas of Dhundhar traced their line to **Kusha**, son of Rama, and ruled from the hill town of **Amber**, their seat since the eleventh century; Jaipur would not be founded until 1727. In the archive's list, Raja Lonkarn follows **Raja Prithviraj III** and rules **c. 1460–1480 CE**, before the throne passes to **Raja Pajawan**.

No inscription or chronicle yet known records a Lonkarn ruling Amber in these years. The standard genealogies of Amber give the whole period to **Raja Chandrasen**, who reigned from about 1453 to 1502. They also place a ruler named **Pajawan** (Pajjun) far earlier, around the late eleventh and twelfth centuries, so the archive's sequence here cannot be confirmed. The name Lunkaran belongs to better-known men of other times, such as **Rao Lunkaran** of Bikaner, who ruled in the early sixteenth century, and they should not be confused with him. No conquests, frontier wars or other deeds of this Lonkarn are recorded, and none are told here.

The age around Amber is well known. In Delhi, **Bahlol Lodi** was rebuilding the Sultanate's power. In Mewar, the great **Rana Kumbha** was murdered in **1468** by his own son, and years of family strife followed. In Marwar, **Rao Jodha** ruled from his new city of Jodhpur, and his son **Bika** went north into the desert to found a state of his own. Within the Kachwaha clan, **Rao Shekha** of **Amarsar** was turning his lordship into a power that tradition says challenged Amber itself.

For the rulers of Amber in these years, the danger came as much from ambitious kinsmen as from distant sultans.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Kachwaha of Amber.** The archive remembers him as a ruler of the Kachwaha house, seated at Amber in Dhundhar.
- **A reign of c. 1460–1480 CE.** The archive places him between Raja Prithviraj III and Raja Pajawan.
- **Ruler in a time of Rajput upheaval.** His years saw the murder of Rana Kumbha in 1468 and Rao Bika's departure to found a new state.
- **The Shekhawat challenge.** In these decades Rao Shekha of Amarsar was building a strong Kachwaha branch state of his own.
- **A thin record.** The standard genealogies give this whole period to Raja Chandrasen, so his own reign remains unconfirmed.

pajawan-early.story:
## Raja Pajawan — the Kachwaha who rode with Prithviraj

*Pajawan's life comes to us almost entirely through the genealogies of the Kachwaha house of Amber and through the Prithviraj Raso, a bardic epic composed and reworked long after the events it describes. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

In the twelfth century, the valley that would one day hold the palaces of Amber was a rough country of rocky ridges, thorn scrub and small walled villages. It was called **Dhundhar**, after a hill or a stream of that name, and it had no single master. Meena chiefs held many of its forts and passes. Badgujar Rajputs held others. To the north and west lay the rising power of the **Chauhans of Sakambhari and Ajmer**, the strongest Rajput house of the age.

Into this country had come a new clan. The **Kachwahas** traced their descent to **Kusha**, the son of Rama, and so to the solar race. Historians connect them with the **Kachchhapaghata** rulers who had held Gwalior and Narwar in the tenth and eleventh centuries. Family tradition says that a prince of that house, **Dulha Rai**, came west into Dhundhar, won Dausa and the valley of Ramgarh, and planted his line there. His son **Kakil Dev**, the genealogies say, took the hill of Amber from the Meenas and made it the seat of the family. After Kakil came **Hanu Dev**, and after him **Janad Dev**. Pajawan was Janad Dev's son.

The dates that the chronicles give to these men do not agree. Some later lists of Amber place Pajawan in the eleventh century; others, tying him to the Chauhan court, place him in the second half of the twelfth. Because every tradition about him links him to **Prithviraj Chauhan**, who ruled from about **1178 to 1192 CE**, most accounts set his life in those decades, and this story follows them.

Nothing is recorded of Pajawan's childhood. But it is not hard to imagine the world in which he grew. The Kachwaha house was young and its hold was thin. A boy of that family learned to ride before he could read, to judge a hillside for an ambush, and to know which village headman paid his dues and which would turn at the first sign of weakness. The bards of the clan would have sung to him of Dulha Rai and Kakil Dev, of the forts taken from the Meenas, and of the long road from Narwar. He would have learned that a small house survives either by strength or by friendship with a greater one, and usually by both.

Pajawan chose friendship with the greatest house he could reach. Tradition says that he entered the service of the Chauhan king of Ajmer, and that he married a sister of Prithviraj. The Raso and the later Kachwaha chronicles both repeat this marriage, and the colonel and antiquarian **James Tod**, writing in the nineteenth century from the bardic sources of Rajasthan, set it down as the foundation of Kachwaha fortune. Historians cannot confirm it from any inscription, and the bards are not consistent about the bride's name. But the memory itself is telling. For the Kachwahas of later centuries, the moment their house stepped onto the wider stage of Rajput history was the moment Pajawan rode into the court of Ajmer.

The Prithviraj Raso turns that court into a glittering hall of heroes. Around the young king it gathers a circle of great vassals, the *samants*, each with his own banner and his own tale. Pajawan, whom the poem calls **Pajjun** or **Pajjunrai**, is one of the brightest of them. The bards place him at the king's right hand in council, tell of his steadiness in war, and make him a leader of the Chauhan host in campaign after campaign.

It is important to understand what kind of source the Raso is. It is attributed to **Chand Bardai**, the court poet of Prithviraj, but in the form that has come down to us it was expanded over centuries. It contains dates that cannot be correct, names of people who lived at other times, and whole episodes that no historian accepts. It is a great poem and a precious record of how Rajputs remembered their past, but it is not a chronicle. Every deed that it gives Pajawan must be read in that light.

Some of the wars in which the Raso places him were real. Prithviraj's reign was full of fighting. Inscriptions found at Madanpur record that in about **1182–83 CE** he raided the lands of the **Chandela** king **Paramardi**, in Bundelkhand. The Chauhans also had a long rivalry with the **Chaulukya** kings of Gujarat, and with the Gahadavala kingdom of Kanauj. In the bardic telling, Pajawan rides in these campaigns: against Gujarat, against the Chandelas at **Mahoba**, against the enemies of Ajmer on every side. Whether the real Pajawan took part in any of them, history cannot say. The bards say he did, and his clan believed them.

One can picture the scene the bards loved: the Chauhan army drawn up in the dust of the plains, the war drums beating, elephants swaying under their howdahs, and among the banners of the great vassals the ensign of the Kachwahas, carried by a chief who had come from the hills of Dhundhar to stand beside his kinsman. "Where the king rides, the Kachwaha rides," a bard might have sung, and in later centuries Kachwaha families would quote such lines with pride.

The years of Prithviraj's reign were also the years of a new danger from the north-west. **Muhammad of Ghor**, the Ghurid ruler, had taken Ghazni and then the Punjab, and by the late 1180s his armies stood at the edge of the Chauhan lands. In **1191**, at the **first battle of Tarain**, Prithviraj defeated him and sent him back wounded across the Indus. In **1192**, at the **second battle of Tarain**, Muhammad returned with a better-prepared army and won. Prithviraj was captured and killed soon afterwards, and Ajmer passed under Ghurid control. Within a few years Delhi, too, was in the hands of Muhammad's general **Qutb al-Din Aibak**.

What happened to Pajawan in these great events is one of the places where the traditions part. The most famous version, which Tod repeats, belongs to the story of **Sanyogita**, the princess of Kanauj whom Prithviraj is said to have carried away from her own *swayamvara*. In that tale the Chauhan king rides off with the princess while his vassals fight a running battle against the pursuing army of Kanauj, falling one by one to buy him time, and Pajawan is among the heroes who die covering the retreat. The tale is one of the most beloved in Rajasthan, but historians regard the whole Sanyogita episode as legend, and there is no record that confirms it. Other Kachwaha traditions simply say that Pajawan died in the service of the Chauhans before the final disaster at Tarain. No inscription records the date, the place or the manner of his death.

What the genealogies do agree on is that Pajawan's line continued. His son **Malesi** succeeded him at Amber, and the house went on through **Bijal Dev**, **Raj Dev**, **Kilhan Dev** and their successors. The fall of the Chauhans in 1192 must have been a heavy blow. The great patron at Ajmer was gone, and the new power in the north was the Delhi Sultanate, with garrisons in Ajmer and armies moving through the region. Yet the Kachwahas did not fall with their patrons. Their small hill state was too remote and too modest to tempt a conquering army for long, and they held on in their valleys for the next three centuries, slowly enlarging their lands.

It is worth asking why a ruler about whom so little is certain became so important in Kachwaha memory. The answer lies in what Pajawan stood for. He was the first of his house whom the bards set among the heroes of all Rajasthan. Before him, the Kachwahas were a family of newcomers fighting for a foothold among the Meenas and the Badgujars. In the songs about Pajawan, they stand beside the most famous Rajput king of the age, as kinsmen by marriage and as companions in war. When the Kachwahas rose to real greatness in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, under rulers such as **Bharmal**, **Man Singh I** and later **Sawai Jai Singh II**, they looked back to Pajawan as proof that their house had always belonged among the first families of Rajputana.

The same pride shows in the way later branches of the clan remembered him. Families descended from the house of Amber would name him in their genealogies, and bards at Kachwaha courts would recite his place among the samants of Prithviraj. For a clan that had come from far away, the memory of Pajawan rooted their story in the heroic age of Rajasthan itself.

Of the man himself, only the outline remains: a young chief of a young house, who left his valley to serve a great king, who is remembered as brave and loyal, and who died, by every account, before he could see the ruin of the cause he served. His real deeds may have been smaller than the bards made them, or simply different. But the Kachwahas never forgot him, and the hills of Dhundhar still keep his name.

## Highlights of his life

- **Heir of a young house.** Son of Janad Dev, he ruled the small Kachwaha state of Amber in Dhundhar, founded only a few generations earlier by Dulha Rai and Kakil Dev.
- **Kinsman of Prithviraj Chauhan.** Tradition says he married a sister of Prithviraj, linking the Kachwahas to the greatest Rajput house of the age.
- **Hero of the Prithviraj Raso.** The epic, as Pajjun or Pajjunrai, makes him one of Prithviraj's leading vassals, though its details cannot be taken as history.
- **The Chauhan wars.** The bards place him in Prithviraj's campaigns against Gujarat and the Chandelas; the Chandela raid of about 1182–83 CE is confirmed by inscriptions, his own part is not.
- **A death in the Chauhan cause.** Traditions differ on how he died; the famous account of his fall during the flight from Kanauj belongs to the legend of Sanyogita.
- **Ancestor of later Amber.** His son Malesi succeeded him, and the house survived the fall of the Chauhans in 1192 to rise to greatness three centuries later.

## Raja Dulhan Deo — a name in the long line of Amber

*Almost nothing about a Raja Dulhan Deo ruling Amber in the early sixteenth century survives beyond his name and his place in the archive's list of Kachwaha rulers; this short account gives what is known of his house and his age, and says plainly where the record falls silent.*

The Kachwahas of **Dhundhar** traced their descent to **Kusha**, son of Rama, and their arrival in the region to **Dulha Rai**, whose name Dulhan Deo closely echoes. By the sixteenth century their seat had long been the hill town of **Amber**; Jaipur would not be founded until 1727. In the archive's list, Dulhan Deo follows **Raja Pajawan** and rules **c. 1500–1515 CE**, before the throne passes to **Raja Chandrasen IV**.

No inscription, chronicle or coin yet known names a Dulhan Deo ruling Amber in these years. The standard genealogies of Amber give this period to **Raja Prithviraj**, son of the well-recorded **Raja Chandrasen**, who came to the throne around 1503. The famous founder Dulha Rai lived some four centuries earlier, and nothing told of him belongs to this name.

What can be said is how the world looked from Amber in those years. Delhi was ruled by the Lodi sultans, **Sikandar Lodi** and then **Ibrahim Lodi**, whose power in Rajasthan was limited. To the south, Mewar was rising to its height under **Rana Sanga**, who became the leading Rajput king of the age. Within Dhundhar, the Kachwaha house was spreading into many branches, among them the Shekhawats of the north, and its rulers had to hold their kinsmen together while keeping peace with greater neighbours. The court of Amber was also turning towards the devotion of the Ramanandi teachers of **Galta**, which shaped the faith of the house for centuries.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Kachwaha of Amber.** He is remembered in the archive as a ruler of the Kachwaha house, whose seat was the hill town of Amber in Dhundhar.
- **A reign of c. 1500–1515 CE.** The archive places him between Raja Pajawan and Raja Chandrasen IV.
- **Ruler in the age of Rana Sanga.** His years fell in the late Lodi period, as Mewar rose to dominate Rajasthan.
- **Distinct from Dulha Rai.** The founder of Kachwaha rule in Dhundhar lived centuries earlier and is a different man.

## Raja Chandrasen IV — a name in the long line of Amber

*Almost nothing about a Raja Chandrasen ruling Amber in the years 1515–1530 survives beyond his name and his place in the archive's list of Kachwaha rulers; this short account gives what is known of his house and his age, and says plainly where the record falls silent.*

The Kachwahas of **Dhundhar** traced their descent to **Kusha**, son of Rama, and their arrival in the region to **Dulha Rai**. By the sixteenth century their seat had long been the hill town of **Amber**; Jaipur would not be founded until 1727. In the archive's list, Chandrasen IV follows **Raja Dulhan Deo** and rules **c. 1515–1530 CE**.

No inscription or chronicle yet known names a Chandrasen ruling Amber in these years. The well-recorded **Raja Chandrasen** of Amber ruled in the second half of the fifteenth century and died around 1502–03. The standard genealogies give the years 1515–1530 to his son **Raja Prithviraj**, who died around 1527, and then to Prithviraj's son **Puranmal**. Nothing told of the earlier Chandrasen belongs to this name.

What can be said is how the world looked from Amber in those years, which were among the most decisive in the history of northern India. In **1526**, **Babur** defeated **Ibrahim Lodi** at **Panipat** and founded Mughal rule in Delhi. In **1527**, Rana Sanga of Mewar led a great Rajput confederacy against Babur at **Khanwa** and was defeated. Tradition counts the Kachwahas of Amber among the Rajput houses that rode with Sanga. After Khanwa, Rajput power in the north was shaken, and Amber, like its neighbours, entered a troubled time of disputed successions and new overlords, the age that would end with **Bharmal**'s alliance with Akbar in 1562.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Kachwaha of Amber.** He is remembered in the archive as a ruler of the Kachwaha house, whose seat was the hill town of Amber in Dhundhar.
- **A reign of c. 1515–1530 CE.** The archive places him after Raja Dulhan Deo.
- **Ruler in the age of Panipat and Khanwa.** His years saw the fall of the Lodis and the defeat of Rana Sanga by Babur in 1527.
- **Distinct from the earlier Chandrasen.** The well-documented Raja Chandrasen of Amber died around 1502–03 and is a different man.

udaikaran-early.story:
## Raja Udaikaran — the father of many Kachwaha houses

*Udaikaran's life comes to us through the genealogies of Amber and the family chronicles of the Kachwaha branches that descend from him; no inscription of his reign is known. Where history and tradition part ways, this story says so.*

In the middle of the fourteenth century, the Kachwaha house had held the hill of **Amber** for about two hundred years. Its founders, **Dulha Rai** and **Kakil Dev**, were remembered in song, and so was **Pajawan**, the chief whom the bards set among the companions of Prithviraj Chauhan. Since the fall of the Chauhans in 1192, the family had lived in the shadow of the Delhi Sultanate, keeping to its valleys, paying what it had to, and slowly gathering villages and forts around the old seat. The line had passed from **Malesi** through **Bijal Dev**, **Raj Dev**, **Kilhan Dev** and **Kuntal Dev** to **Jansi**, and from Jansi to his son Udaikaran.

The genealogies of Amber give Udaikaran a reign of about **1366 to 1388 CE**. Like most dates for the early Kachwahas, these are traditional and cannot be checked against inscriptions, but they place him in a period whose wider history is well known, and that history explains much about the world he ruled.

Nothing is recorded of Udaikaran's birth or boyhood. He would have grown up in the old palace on the hill at Amber, in the narrow valley between the ridges, long before the great Amber Fort of later centuries was built. The town below was small: a market, temples, the houses of retainers and craftsmen, and the stepwells and tanks that held the water of the short monsoon. Beyond the ridges lay the open plains of Dhundhar, dotted with villages of Meena, Jat and Gujar cultivators, and with the small forts of Kachwaha kinsmen.

A Kachwaha prince of that age was raised for war and for rule together. He learned the bow and the lance, the management of horses, and the hunt in the scrub forests around Ramgarh, where the clan's family goddess, **Jamwai Mata**, had her shrine. He learned, too, the unwritten law of a Rajput clan state: that the raja ruled with his brothers and cousins, not over them, and that every son of the house expected a share of land. A raja's strength lay in how well he kept that brotherhood together.

The world beyond Dhundhar was changing. In Delhi, **Firuz Shah Tughlaq** had been Sultan since 1351. After the restless and ruinous schemes of his predecessor, Muhammad bin Tughlaq, Firuz ruled more gently. He built canals and towns, favoured the religious scholars, and avoided long and costly wars. Under him the Sultanate's direct grip on distant Rajputana loosened. Garrisons and governors remained in places such as Ajmer, Ranthambore and Bayana, and their armies could still punish a chief who defied them. But for the small Rajput states of the hills, these were years in which a careful ruler could quietly build.

To the south-west, the house of Mewar had already shown what such years could bring. **Hammir Singh** had recovered Chittor for the Sisodias earlier in the century, and in Udaikaran's lifetime Mewar was ruled by **Kshetra Singh** and then by **Lakha**, who made it once again the strongest Rajput kingdom of the region. To the west, the Rathores were still a rising clan; it was only around the end of the century that **Rao Chunda** would take Mandore. In this world, Amber was a modest state among many. Its rulers could not hope to challenge Delhi or Mewar, but they could make their own valleys secure.

No battle of Udaikaran's reign is recorded, and the archive's older description of him as a ruler allied with the Delhi Sultanate has no support in the sources. It is likely that, like his predecessors, he paid tribute when the Sultan's officers demanded it and avoided open conflict. It is equally likely that his reign saw the small wars that every Rajput state of the age knew: quarrels with neighbouring chiefs over villages and grazing, the punishment of a defiant headman, the defence of the valley against raiders. The chronicles do not name them, and this story will not invent them.

What the chronicles do remember about Udaikaran is his family, and through his family he became one of the most important ancestors in the whole history of the Kachwahas.

The genealogies give Udaikaran several sons. The best remembered are **Bar Singh**, **Narsingh** and **Balo**, also called **Balaji**. Each of them became the root of a distinct branch of the clan, and the way their inheritance was settled shaped the Kachwaha world for centuries.

The eldest, Bar Singh, did not succeed his father. The chronicles explain this in different ways, and none of the explanations can be confirmed. Whatever the reason, the throne of Amber passed to Narsingh, and Bar Singh received lands of his own. From Bar Singh's line, the family histories say, came **Rao Naru**, and from Naru the **Naruka** Kachwahas. Centuries later, in **1770**, a Naruka chief, **Pratap Singh**, would found the state of **Alwar**, and the rulers of Alwar always traced their descent through Bar Singh to Udaikaran.

The third son, Balo, also received an estate. His son **Mokal** held it after him, and Mokal's son was **Rao Shekha**, born in **1433**. Shekha was one of the boldest Kachwaha chiefs of the fifteenth century. He refused to remain a dependent of Amber, built up a strong domain of his own around **Amarsar**, and fought his kinsmen and his neighbours to keep it. From him came the **Shekhawat** Kachwahas, and the wide country they came to hold in the north of Rajasthan is still called **Shekhawati** after him. The Shekhawat families, the great *thikanas* of Shekhawati, and the painted towns that their merchants later built, all look back through Shekha and Balo to Udaikaran.

It is worth pausing on what this means. In Udaikaran's lifetime, his sons were simply the younger princes of a small hill state, given villages so that they would not quarrel over the throne. Yet the settlement he made, or allowed, planted three trees that would each grow tall: the main line of Amber, which would rise under Bharmal and Man Singh to stand among the first houses of the Mughal empire and later found Jaipur; the Narukas, who would rule Alwar; and the Shekhawats, who would dominate a whole region. Few rulers of so modest a state have left so large a family behind them.

Tradition also records other sons of Udaikaran whose descendants formed smaller branches of the clan, each known by the name of its founder in the Rajput manner. The details differ from chronicle to chronicle, and the archive does not attempt to list them all. What is clear is that the Kachwaha practice of naming each new branch after its founder, and of giving younger sons their own estates, made Udaikaran's reign a turning point in the shape of the clan.

How did Udaikaran keep such a family together while he lived? The chronicles do not say, but the outcome suggests a ruler who understood the brotherhood of the clan. A raja who gave his sons and cousins their share, who honoured their place at his court, and who did not try to rule them as servants could expect them to ride with him in war and to defend his valley in his name. A raja who failed to do so would see his kin go over to his enemies. Amber in Udaikaran's time did not break apart, and the branches that grew from his house remained proud of their descent from him.

Of his religious life, little is known. The Kachwahas of this age were worshippers of Vishnu and of the Goddess, and the family's devotion to Jamwai Mata and to the old temples of Amber continued under him. The great devotional movements that would later transform the court of Amber, the Ramanandi teachers of **Galta** and the worship of Krishna, belong to the following centuries. Nothing in the record links Udaikaran to any particular building or endowment, and this story does not claim any.

Udaikaran is said to have died around **1388**. By a coincidence of history, that was also the year of the death of Sultan Firuz Shah Tughlaq. The calm of Firuz's last years did not long survive him. His heirs fought one another for the throne, the Sultanate began to come apart, and ten years later, in **1398**, the armies of **Timur** would sack Delhi itself. Udaikaran did not live to see those storms. He left Amber to Narsingh at the very moment when the old order in northern India was about to break.

The older card for Udaikaran in this archive said that he prepared the Kachwahas for the Mughal age and paved the way for Bharmal. That cannot be right in any direct sense: Bharmal came to the throne in 1548, more than a century and a half after Udaikaran's death, and the Mughal empire did not yet exist. But there is a truer way to say what Udaikaran left behind. He left a house that knew how to survive in the shadow of greater powers, and a family large and strong enough to carry the Kachwaha name across half of northern Rajasthan.

## Highlights of his life

- **Raja of Amber (c. 1366–1388 CE).** Son of Jansi, he ruled the Kachwaha state of Dhundhar from the old seat at Amber, in the traditional dating of the Amber genealogies.
- **A careful ruler in the Tughlaq age.** His reign coincided with the later years of Sultan Firuz Shah Tughlaq, when a small Rajput state could build quietly; no battle of his reign is recorded.
- **Father of the Narukas.** Through his eldest son Bar Singh, he is the ancestor of the Naruka Kachwahas, whose chief Pratap Singh founded Alwar in 1770.
- **Grandfather of the Shekhawats.** Through his son Balo and grandson Mokal, he is the ancestor of Rao Shekha (born 1433) and the Shekhawat Kachwahas of Shekhawati.
- **Ancestor of the main line of Amber.** His son Narsingh succeeded him, and from Narsingh came the later rulers of Amber and Jaipur.
- **Keeper of the clan's brotherhood.** By settling his sons on their own lands, he shaped the branching structure of the Kachwaha clan for centuries.
- **Death around 1388.** He died in the same year as Firuz Shah Tughlaq, on the eve of the Sultanate's collapse and Timur's sack of Delhi.

nar-singh-ii.story:
## Raja Nar Singh II — Amber in the years of Timur

*Nar Singh's name survives in the genealogies of Amber, where he appears as Narsingh, son of Raja Udaikaran; no inscription or chronicle of his own reign is known. This story tells his life through the real history of his house and his age, and says plainly where the record falls silent.*

The archive calls him Nar Singh II, to set him apart from an earlier Nar Singh in its list. The genealogies of the Kachwaha house simply call him **Narsingh**, or **Narsingh Dev**, and they give him a clear place in the family tree: he was a son of **Raja Udaikaran**, who ruled Amber in the second half of the fourteenth century, and he succeeded his father on the throne around **1388 CE**.

He was not the eldest son. The genealogies name his elder brother as **Bar Singh**, and a younger brother as **Balo**, or Balaji. Why the throne passed to Narsingh rather than to Bar Singh, the chronicles explain in different ways, and none of their explanations can be confirmed. What they agree on is the result. Narsingh took the old seat at **Amber**, while Bar Singh and Balo received estates of their own. From Bar Singh's line would come the **Naruka** Kachwahas, who centuries later founded the state of Alwar. From Balo's line would come **Rao Shekha** and the **Shekhawats**. From Narsingh's line came the rulers of Amber and, in the end, of Jaipur.

Of Narsingh's childhood nothing is recorded, but the world of a Kachwaha prince of that time is not hard to see. Amber was then a small hill town in a narrow valley, its palace and temples on the slopes, its tanks and stepwells holding the water of the brief monsoon. The great fort that visitors see today belongs to much later centuries. Beyond the ridges lay the plains of **Dhundhar**, with villages of Meena, Jat and Gujar cultivators and the small forts of Kachwaha kinsmen. A boy of the ruling house learned to ride, to use the bow and lance, to hunt in the scrub forests, and to sit in his father's court listening to the disputes of headmen and the counsel of older kinsmen. He would have learned the songs of **Dulha Rai**, **Kakil Dev** and **Pajawan**, and the family's devotion to its goddess, **Jamwai Mata**.

Narsingh came to the throne in a year that marked the end of an era. In **1388**, the same year in which his father is said to have died, the Sultan of Delhi, **Firuz Shah Tughlaq**, also died. Firuz had ruled for thirty-seven years, and his reign had been, for the most part, a time of peace. His death opened a struggle for power among his grandsons and nobles. Sultans rose and fell in quick succession. For several years in the 1390s, two rival rulers claimed the throne at the same time, one holding Delhi and the other holding the nearby city of Firuzabad. The authority of Delhi over the provinces, already weakened, began to drain away.

For the small Rajput states of the hills, such disorder was both an opportunity and a danger. The tribute collectors and garrison commanders of the Sultanate had less power to enforce their demands. But the same weakness let ambitious neighbours rise. To the north-east of Dhundhar lay **Mewat**, whose chief **Bahadur Nahar** became a powerful figure in the quarrels around Delhi in these years. To the south-west, **Mewar** under **Rana Lakha** was growing richer and stronger. To the west, the Rathore chief **Rao Chunda** took **Mandore** in the 1390s and laid the foundations of the later kingdom of Marwar. Amber was surrounded by rising powers, and a ruler there had to watch every border.

The records do not tell us how Narsingh faced these pressures. No battle of his reign is named, no treaty, no grant. What can be said is that the house of Amber came through these years intact. It did not lose its valley to a neighbour, and the family settlement made in Udaikaran's time held. The brothers did not tear the state apart, and Narsingh's line kept the throne. In an age when many small houses disappeared, that was no small thing.

It is possible to imagine how such a ruler spent his days. In the cool season, he would ride out with his kinsmen to the villages of the plain, hearing complaints, settling quarrels over boundaries and wells, and seeing that the revenue was gathered. In the hot months, the court would retreat to the shade of the palace on the hill. When the monsoon came and the tanks filled, there would be festivals at the temples, and offerings at the shrine of Jamwai Mata. In the evenings, the bards would sing of the clan's ancestors. Such was the life of most Rajput rulers of the age, and nothing in the record suggests that Narsingh's was different. But these are pictures drawn from the age, not facts about the man.

Then, at the end of the decade, came the greatest shock that northern India had known in generations. In **1398**, the Central Asian conqueror **Timur** crossed the Indus with a great army. He moved through the Punjab, burning and killing as he went, and in December he defeated the army of Sultan **Nasir al-Din Mahmud Shah Tughlaq** outside Delhi. The city was sacked. Contemporary accounts, including Timur's own memoirs as later compiled, describe the slaughter of tens of thousands and the carrying away of craftsmen and treasure. Early in **1399**, Timur turned back towards Samarkand, leaving behind famine, disease and a ruined capital.

Timur's armies did not come to Dhundhar. Their path ran through the Punjab, Delhi and the upper Doab, far to the north-east of Amber. But the news would have reached Amber quickly, carried by traders, pilgrims and refugees, and the consequences touched every state of the region. After Timur, the Sultanate of Delhi was a shadow. Its governors in the provinces made themselves independent. In **Malwa**, **Dilawar Khan Ghuri** ruled as an independent sovereign from about 1401, and his son would take the title of Sultan. In **Gujarat**, **Zafar Khan** declared himself Sultan as **Muzaffar Shah** in 1407. In the east, the Sharqi sultans ruled at **Jaunpur**. Delhi itself would pass to **Khizr Khan** and the Sayyid dynasty in 1414.

For Amber, these changes meant that the old overlord in Delhi was no longer a real threat, but that new and ambitious sultanates now lay on the edges of Rajasthan. The fifteenth century would be a time of fierce competition between Mewar, Malwa and Gujarat, and the smaller states in between would have to choose their friends with care. Narsingh's reign stood at the beginning of that new age. The world he had been born into, with a single distant sultan in Delhi, was gone by the time he died.

The genealogies do not agree on how long Narsingh ruled. The archive gives his reign as ending around **1400**; some traditional lists of Amber run it into the second decade of the fifteenth century. Nor do the sources record his death. The standard genealogies of Amber name his successor as **Banbir**, and after Banbir come **Udharan** and then the well-documented **Raja Chandrasen**, in whose time, Shekhawat tradition says, Rao Shekha asserted his independence from Amber. The archive's list places **Khem Singh** after Narsingh; no other source known to this archive names a Khem Singh ruling Amber, and his story is told separately.

What, then, is Narsingh's place in the history of his house? He was not a builder of great forts, nor a famous warrior, nor a patron whose name is cut into stone. He was the son whom Udaikaran's settlement placed on the throne of Amber, and the man who carried the main line of the Kachwahas through the collapse of the Tughlaq Sultanate and the storm of Timur. Every later ruler of Amber and Jaipur, from **Prithviraj** and **Bharmal** to **Man Singh I** and **Sawai Jai Singh II**, traced descent through him. In a long family history, there are rulers whose task is to win glory and rulers whose task is simply to hand on what they received. Narsingh, so far as the record allows us to see, was one of the second kind, and he did that task in one of the most dangerous decades of the age.

## Highlights of his life

- **Son and heir of Udaikaran.** He succeeded his father on the throne of Amber around 1388 CE, though he was not the eldest son.
- **Brother of the founders of new branches.** His brothers Bar Singh and Balo became the ancestors of the Naruka and Shekhawat Kachwahas.
- **Ruler through the fall of the Tughlaqs.** His reign began in the year of Firuz Shah Tughlaq's death and saw the succession wars that broke the Sultanate's power.
- **Witness to Timur's invasion.** Timur's sack of Delhi in 1398 did not reach Dhundhar, but it reshaped the world around Amber.
- **Keeper of the main line.** He held Amber intact through a dangerous decade, and every later ruler of Amber and Jaipur descended from him.
- **A thin record.** No battle, building or inscription of his reign is known; his length of rule and the date of his death are uncertain.

khem-singh-amber.story:
## Raja Khem Singh — a name in the long line of Amber

*Almost nothing about Raja Khem Singh survives beyond his name and his place in the archive's list of Kachwaha rulers; this short account gives what is known of his house and his age, and says plainly where the record falls silent.*

The Kachwahas of **Dhundhar** traced their descent to **Kusha**, son of Rama, and their arrival in the region to **Dulha Rai**. By the early fifteenth century their seat had long been the hill town of **Amber**; Jaipur would not be founded until 1727. In the archive's list, Khem Singh follows **Raja Nar Singh II** and rules **c. 1400–1410 CE**, before the throne passes to **Raja Satal Deo**.

No inscription, chronicle or coin yet known names a Khem Singh ruling Amber in these years. The standard genealogies of Amber give the throne after **Narsingh**, son of Udaikaran, to **Banbir**, and after him to **Udharan** and then **Raja Chandrasen**. Whatever the source of the archive's sequence, the record is silent about this name.

What can be said is how the world looked from Amber in those years. Timur's sack of Delhi in **1398** had left the Tughlaq Sultanate a shadow. Its provinces broke away: **Dilawar Khan Ghuri** ruled Malwa independently from about 1401, and **Zafar Khan** proclaimed himself Sultan of Gujarat in 1407. Mewar was strong under **Rana Lakha**, and the Rathores had recently taken **Mandore**. For a small house like the Kachwahas, these were years in which the old overlord in Delhi could no longer enforce his demands, but in which new and ambitious neighbours were rising on every side. Survival meant holding the hill forts, keeping the branches of the clan together, and choosing friends with care.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Kachwaha of Amber.** He is remembered in the archive as a ruler of the Kachwaha house, whose seat was the hill town of Amber in Dhundhar.
- **A reign of c. 1400–1410 CE.** The archive places him between Raja Nar Singh II and Raja Satal Deo.
- **Ruler after Timur.** His years fell in the decade after Timur's sack of Delhi, as the Sultanate broke apart.
- **A silent record.** The standard genealogies of Amber do not name him; his life cannot be told beyond its setting.

## Raja Satal Deo — a name in the years after Timur

*Almost nothing about Raja Satal Deo survives beyond his name and his place in the archive's list of Kachwaha rulers; this short account gives what is known of his house and his age, and says plainly where the record falls silent.*

The Kachwahas of Dhundhar traced their descent to **Kusha**, son of Rama, and their arrival in the region to **Dulha Rai** in the eleventh century. Their seat was the hill town of **Amber**, which tradition says **Kakil Dev** took from the Meenas. Jaipur, the later capital of the house, would not be founded until 1727. In the archive's list, Satal Deo follows **Raja Khem Singh** and rules **c. 1410–1420 CE**, before the throne passes to **Raja Dhir Deo**.

No inscription, chronicle or coin yet known names a Satal Deo ruling Amber. The standard genealogies of the house give these years to **Narsingh Dev**, son of Udaikaran, and then to his son **Banbir**, whose reign they begin in about 1413. Nor should he be confused with the better-known **Rao Satal** of Marwar, who ruled Jodhpur at the end of the fifteenth century. Whatever the source of the archive's sequence, nothing more can honestly be said of the man himself.

What can be said is how the world looked from Amber in those years. In **1398** Timur had sacked Delhi, and the Sultanate that once claimed all of Rajasthan never recovered its strength. In **1414** **Khizr Khan** took Delhi and founded the Sayyid dynasty, whose armies spent much of their time collecting tribute from unwilling chiefs in the lands around the capital. To the south, Mewar under **Rana Lakha** was rich and growing; to the west, **Rao Chunda** of the Rathores held Mandore; in Gujarat, **Ahmad Shah I** founded Ahmedabad in **1411**. For a small hill state like Amber, set among these rising powers, the task of any ruler was to hold the forts, keep the kinsmen loyal and give larger neighbours no reason to march.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Kachwaha of Amber.** He is remembered in the archive as a ruler of the Kachwaha house, whose seat was the hill town of Amber in Dhundhar.
- **A reign of c. 1410–1420 CE.** The archive places him between Raja Khem Singh and Raja Dhir Deo.
- **Ruler after Timur's storm.** His years fell in the decade after the sack of Delhi, when the Sayyids rose and the Sultanate's grip on Rajasthan was weak.
- **Not in the standard genealogies.** The usual lists of Amber give these years to Narsingh Dev and Banbir, and he is distinct from Rao Satal of Marwar.

## Raja Dhir Deo — a name in the age of the Sayyids

*Almost nothing about Raja Dhir Deo survives beyond his name and his place in the archive's list of Kachwaha rulers; this short account gives what is known of his house and his age, and says plainly where the record falls silent.*

The Kachwahas of Dhundhar traced their descent to **Kusha**, son of Rama, and their arrival in the region to **Dulha Rai** in the eleventh century. Their seat was the hill town of **Amber**, guarded by the ridges of the Aravallis, which tradition says **Kakil Dev** took from the Meenas. Jaipur, the later capital of the house, would not be founded until 1727. In the archive's list, Dhir Deo follows **Raja Satal Deo** and rules **c. 1420–1430 CE**, before the throne passes to **Raja Lunkarn II**.

No inscription, chronicle or coin yet known names a Dhir Deo ruling Amber. The standard genealogies of the house give these years to **Banbir**, and after him, from about **1424**, to his son **Udharan**. Whatever the source of the archive's sequence, nothing more can honestly be said of the man himself, and no deed, building or grant can be set down in his name.

What can be said is how the world looked from Amber in those years. In Delhi, the Sayyid sultan **Mubarak Shah** (1421–1434) ruled a much-shrunken kingdom and sent his armies again and again against the chiefs of **Mewat** and the fort of **Bayana**, close to the eastern edge of Dhundhar, to force them to pay tribute. To the south, Mewar was ruled by **Rana Mokal** (1421–1433), who restored the great Shiva temple of Samiddheshwar at Chittor. To the west, the Rathore house of Mandore lost **Rao Chunda** in about **1423** and passed through troubled years. In Malwa, **Hoshang Shah** made Mandu his strong capital. For the small Kachwaha state, wedged between the Sayyid tribute-collectors and the rising Rajput kingdoms, the work of any ruler was to keep the hill forts, keep the clan united and pay or resist as the moment demanded.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Kachwaha of Amber.** He is remembered in the archive as a ruler of the Kachwaha house, whose seat was the hill town of Amber in Dhundhar.
- **A reign of c. 1420–1430 CE.** The archive places him between Raja Satal Deo and Raja Lunkarn II.
- **Ruler in the Sayyid age.** His years fell under Mubarak Shah, whose tribute-raising campaigns against Mewat and Bayana reached the borders of Dhundhar.
- **Not in the standard genealogies.** The usual lists of Amber give these years to Banbir and his son Udharan.

## Raja Lunkarn II — a name in the years of Kumbha's rise

*Almost nothing about Raja Lunkarn II survives beyond his name and his place in the archive's list of Kachwaha rulers; this short account gives what is known of his house and his age, and says plainly where the record falls silent.*

The Kachwahas of Dhundhar traced their descent to **Kusha**, son of Rama, and their arrival in the region to **Dulha Rai** in the eleventh century. Their seat was the hill town of **Amber**, which tradition says **Kakil Dev** took from the Meenas. Jaipur, the later capital of the house, would not be founded until 1727. In the archive's list, Lunkarn II follows **Raja Dhir Deo** and rules **c. 1430–1440 CE**, before the throne passes to **Raja Chandrasen V**.

No inscription, chronicle or coin yet known names a Lunkarn ruling Amber in these years. The standard genealogies of the house give the whole decade to **Raja Udharan**, who is said to have ruled from about 1424 to 1453. Whatever the source of the archive's sequence, nothing more can honestly be said of the man himself, and no deed, building or grant can be set down in his name.

What can be said is how the world looked from Amber in those years. Within the Kachwaha clan itself a new branch was taking shape: tradition places in **1433** the birth of **Rao Shekha**, a great-grandson of Raja Udaikaran through his son Balo, who would later build his own state around **Amarsar** and give his name to the **Shekhawats** and to the land of Shekhawati. Beyond the clan, the region was changing fast. In **1433** **Rana Kumbha** came to the throne of Mewar after the murder of his father Mokal, and in **1436** **Mahmud Khalji** seized the throne of Malwa; the long wars between these two would shape Rajasthan for a generation. In Delhi, the Sayyid sultans were growing weaker year by year. For the small house of Amber, the task of any ruler was to keep its hill forts, hold its kinsmen together and steer clear of the wars of greater neighbours.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Kachwaha of Amber.** He is remembered in the archive as a ruler of the Kachwaha house, whose seat was the hill town of Amber in Dhundhar.
- **A reign of c. 1430–1440 CE.** The archive places him between Raja Dhir Deo and Raja Chandrasen V.
- **Ruler as the Shekhawat branch was born.** His decade saw, by tradition, the birth of Rao Shekha, founder of the Shekhawat line of the Kachwahas.
- **Ruler in the age of Kumbha.** His years fell as Rana Kumbha rose in Mewar and Mahmud Khalji in Malwa.
- **Not in the standard genealogies.** The usual lists of Amber give these years to Raja Udharan.
