chandrasen-v.story:
## Raja Chandrasen V — a name in the shadow of the later Chandrasen

*Almost nothing about Raja Chandrasen V survives beyond his name and his place in the archive's list of Kachwaha rulers; this short account gives what is known of his house and his age, and says plainly where the record falls silent.*

The Kachwahas of Dhundhar traced their descent to **Kusha**, son of Rama, and their arrival in the region to **Dulha Rai** in the eleventh century. Their seat was the hill town of **Amber**, which tradition says **Kakil Dev** took from the Meenas. Jaipur, the later capital of the house, would not be founded until 1727. In the archive's list, Chandrasen V follows **Raja Lunkarn II** and rules **c. 1440–1450 CE**, before the throne passes to **Raja Bhupal Singh II**.

No inscription, chronicle or coin yet known names a Chandrasen ruling Amber in this decade. The standard genealogies of the house give these years to **Raja Udharan**, and they place the one well-recorded **Raja Chandrasen** of Amber just afterwards, from about **1453** to **1502**. That Chandrasen was the father of **Prithviraj**, under whom the house grew in strength. It is possible that the archive's Chandrasen V is an echo of him set a few years too early, but this cannot be shown, and nothing told of the later Chandrasen should be carried over to this entry.

What can be said is how the world looked from Amber in those years. The 1440s belonged to **Rana Kumbha** of Mewar, who fought off the repeated invasions of **Mahmud Khalji** of Malwa and raised the **Vijay Stambh** at Chittor and the great fortress of **Kumbhalgarh**. In Delhi, the last Sayyid sultans, **Muhammad Shah** and **Alam Shah**, held little beyond the capital, while the Afghan **Bahlul Lodi** gathered power in the Punjab. Within the Kachwaha clan, the young **Rao Shekha** was growing up in the Amarsar country, the future founder of the Shekhawat branch. For the small state of Amber, the task of any ruler was to keep the hill forts and the clan intact while greater powers fought around it.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Kachwaha of Amber.** He is remembered in the archive as a ruler of the Kachwaha house, whose seat was the hill town of Amber in Dhundhar.
- **A reign of c. 1440–1450 CE.** The archive places him between Raja Lunkarn II and Raja Bhupal Singh II.
- **Ruler in the age of Kumbha.** His years fell in the decade of Rana Kumbha's wars with Malwa and his great buildings at Chittor and Kumbhalgarh.
- **Distinct from the later Chandrasen.** The well-documented Raja Chandrasen of Amber ruled from about 1453 to 1502, and the usual lists give this decade to Raja Udharan.

bhupal-singh-ii.story:
## Raja Bhupal Singh II — a name in the decade of the Lodis and Jodhpur

*Almost nothing about Raja Bhupal Singh II survives beyond his name and his place in the archive's list of Kachwaha rulers; this short account gives what is known of his house and his age, and says plainly where the record falls silent.*

The Kachwahas of Dhundhar traced their descent to **Kusha**, son of Rama, and their arrival in the region to **Dulha Rai** in the eleventh century. Their seat was the hill town of **Amber**, which tradition says **Kakil Dev** took from the Meenas. Jaipur, the later capital of the house, would not be founded until 1727. In the archive's list, Bhupal Singh II follows **Raja Chandrasen V** and rules **c. 1450–1460 CE**. The next name in the list, **Raja Kank**, is dated three centuries earlier, so the list itself breaks its order at this point.

No inscription, chronicle or coin yet known names a Bhupal Singh ruling Amber. The standard genealogies of the house give these years first to **Raja Udharan** and then, from about **1453**, to his son **Raja Chandrasen**, who ruled until 1502. Whatever the source of the archive's sequence, nothing more can honestly be said of the man himself, and no deed, building or grant can be set down in his name.

What can be said is how the world looked from Amber in those years. In **1451** the Afghan **Bahlul Lodi** took the throne of Delhi and began to rebuild the Sultanate's power, which would in time press again on the lands of eastern Rajasthan. In **1459** **Rao Jodha** of the Rathores laid the foundations of **Mehrangarh** and the city of **Jodhpur**. In Mewar, **Rana Kumbha** fought on against the sultans of both Malwa and Gujarat, who in the mid-1450s joined together against him. Within the Kachwaha clan, **Rao Shekha** was making the Amarsar country his own, and Shekhawat tradition remembers his growing independence from the court at Amber. For the small state of Amber, the task of any ruler was to keep the hill forts, keep the clan from breaking apart and survive among much larger powers.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Kachwaha of Amber.** He is remembered in the archive as a ruler of the Kachwaha house, whose seat was the hill town of Amber in Dhundhar.
- **A reign of c. 1450–1460 CE.** The archive places him after Raja Chandrasen V.
- **Ruler as Delhi revived.** His years saw Bahlul Lodi take Delhi in 1451 and Rao Jodha found Jodhpur in 1459.
- **Ruler as the Shekhawats grew.** In the same decade Rao Shekha was building his own power around Amarsar.
- **Not in the standard genealogies.** The usual lists of Amber give these years to Raja Udharan and Raja Chandrasen.

kank-amber.story:
## Raja Kank — a name from Amber's early centuries

*Almost nothing about Raja Kank survives beyond his name and his place in the archive's list of Kachwaha rulers; this short account gives what is known of his house and his age, and says plainly where the record falls silent.*

The Kachwahas of Dhundhar traced their descent to **Kusha**, son of Rama, and their arrival in the region to **Dulha Rai** in the eleventh century, when, tradition says, he came west from the Gwalior and Narwar country and won lands from the Bargujars and the Meenas. His son **Kakil Dev** is remembered as the ruler who took the hill town of **Amber** from the Meenas and made it the seat of the house. Jaipur, the later capital, would not be founded until 1727. The archive places Kank at **c. 1100–1120 CE**, after **Raja Bhupal Singh II** and before **Raja Jaldeo**. Since Bhupal Singh II is dated to the fifteenth century, the list is out of order here, and Kank belongs among the early rulers of Amber.

No inscription, chronicle or coin yet known names a Kank ruling Amber, and he cannot be called a documented ruler. The standard genealogies of the house, whose early dates are themselves uncertain, give these decades to the generations that followed Kakil Dev, and some historians think even those dates are set too early. Nothing more can honestly be said of the man himself.

What can be said is how the world looked from Amber in those years. The Kachwahas claimed kinship with the **Kachchhapaghatas**, who had ruled at Gwalior and recorded their line in the great inscription of the Sas-Bahu temple in **1093**. In Dhundhar the young state was still a small chiefdom of hill forts among Meena villages. To the west, the Chahamana king **Ajayaraja** was founding the new city of **Ajmer**; to the east, the Gahadavala king **Govindachandra** ruled from Kannauj and Varanasi; and the later Ghaznavid sultans still raided out of the Punjab. For a ruler of Amber in these years, the task was to hold the new conquests, settle kinsmen on the land and keep peace with stronger neighbours.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Kachwaha of Amber.** He is remembered in the archive as a ruler of the Kachwaha house in the early centuries of its rule at Amber.
- **A reign of c. 1100–1120 CE.** The archive places him before Raja Jaldeo; his position after the fifteenth-century Bhupal Singh II is a fault in the list's order.
- **Ruler in the age of Ajmer's founding.** His years fell as the Chahamanas built Ajmer and the Gahadavalas ruled the Ganges plain.
- **Not a documented ruler.** No inscription or chronicle yet known records his name; the standard genealogies give these decades to Kakil Dev's successors.

jaldeo-amber.story:
## Raja Jaldeo — a name from the founding years in Dhundhar

*Almost nothing about Raja Jaldeo survives beyond his name and his place in the archive's list of Kachwaha rulers; this short account gives what is known of his house and his age, and says plainly where the record falls silent.*

The Kachwahas of Dhundhar traced their descent to **Kusha**, son of Rama, and looked back to the **Kachchhapaghata** kings who ruled around Gwalior and Narwar in the tenth and eleventh centuries. By the court tradition of Amber, their kingdom in eastern Rajasthan began when **Dulha Rai** came west from the Narwar line and won Dausa from the Bargujars and Khoh from the Meenas. His son **Kakil Deo** took the hill town of **Amber**, which remained the Kachwaha capital until Jaipur was founded in 1727. In the archive's list, Jaldeo follows **Raja Kank** and rules **c. 1120–1140 CE**, before the throne passes to **Raja Kshetrasimha**.

No inscription, chronicle or coin yet known names a Jaldeo ruling Amber. The standard genealogies of the house do name a **Janad Deo**, a grandson of Kakil Deo, and it is possible that "Jaldeo" is a garbled memory of that name, but this cannot be shown. There is also a deeper difficulty. The years the archive gives him are the very years in which the Jaipur tradition places Dulha Rai's arrival in Dhundhar, often dated to about 1128. The archive's sequence cannot be squared with the usual lists, and nothing more can honestly be said of Jaldeo himself.

What can be said is how the world looked from the hills of Dhundhar in those decades. To the west, the **Chauhans** of Shakambhari were the rising power: **Ajayaraja** founded **Ajmer** in the early twelfth century, and his son **Arnoraja** carried Chauhan arms further across Rajasthan. In Gujarat, **Jayasimha Siddharaja** of the Chalukyas was at the height of his power and at war with the Paramaras of Malwa. Beyond the Punjab, the Ghaznavid sultans still threatened the northern plains. For the small Rajput houses of Dhundhar, set among Meena chiefs, Bargujar towns and these great neighbours, the work of any ruler was simple to state and hard to do: hold the hill forts, guard the wells and tanks, keep the kinsmen loyal, and give stronger powers no reason to march.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Kachwaha of Dhundhar.** He is remembered in the archive as a ruler of the Kachwaha house, whose seat became the hill town of Amber.
- **A reign of c. 1120–1140 CE.** The archive places him between Raja Kank and Raja Kshetrasimha.
- **Not in the standard genealogies.** No record names a Jaldeo of Amber; the name may echo Janad Deo, grandson of Kakil Deo, but this is uncertain.
- **A ruler in the age of Ajmer's rise.** His years fell as the Chauhans founded Ajmer and became the leading power of the region.

kshetrasimha-amber.story:
## Raja Kshetrasimha — a name in the shadow of the Chauhans

*Almost nothing about Raja Kshetrasimha survives beyond his name and his place in the archive's list of Kachwaha rulers; this short account gives what is known of his house and his age, and says plainly where the record falls silent.*

The Kachwahas of Dhundhar traced their descent to **Kusha**, son of Rama, and looked back to the **Kachchhapaghata** kings of Gwalior and Narwar. By the court tradition of Amber, **Dulha Rai** founded their power in eastern Rajasthan by winning Dausa and Khoh, and his son **Kakil Deo** took the hill town of **Amber**, which remained the family's capital until Jaipur was built in 1727. In the archive's list, Kshetrasimha, also called **Shekh Singh**, follows **Raja Jaldeo** and rules **c. 1140–1160 CE**, before the throne passes to **Raja Duleh Rai**.

No inscription, chronicle or coin yet known names a Kshetrasimha or a Shekh Singh ruling Amber in the twelfth century, and the standard genealogies of the house have no ruler of either name. He should not be confused with **Rao Shekha**, the fifteenth-century Kachwaha chief from whom the Shekhawat clan and the region of Shekhawati take their name; the alias "Shekh Singh" may be an echo of that much later and much better-known figure. Nothing can honestly be said of the man himself, and the deeds and reforms once credited to him have no source.

What can be said is how the world looked from Dhundhar in those two decades. The **Chauhans** of Ajmer were the dominant power of the region. **Arnoraja** ruled from Ajmer and fought the Chalukyas of Gujarat, and around the middle of the century he was defeated by the Chalukya king **Kumarapala**. His son **Vigraharaja IV**, remembered as Visaladeva, restored Chauhan strength and took **Delhi** from the Tomaras, bringing the Chauhan frontier to the edge of the Punjab. The small Kachwaha state, by the traditions of its own bards, lived in the orbit of these Chauhan kings. For any ruler of the Dhundhar hills in such an age, the task was to hold the forts and villages already won, keep peace with the Meena and Bargujar neighbours where war could not be afforded, and stay on the right side of Ajmer.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Kachwaha of Dhundhar.** He is remembered in the archive as a ruler of the Kachwaha house of Amber.
- **A reign of c. 1140–1160 CE.** The archive places him between Raja Jaldeo and Raja Duleh Rai.
- **Not in the standard genealogies.** No record names a Kshetrasimha or Shekh Singh of Amber in this period.
- **Distinct from Rao Shekha.** He is not the fifteenth-century founder of the Shekhawats, whose name the alias recalls.
- **A ruler in the age of Vigraharaja IV.** His years fell as the Chauhans of Ajmer reached Delhi and dominated the region.

duleh-rai-revival.story:
## Raja Duleh Rai — the founder's name, carried a second time

*Almost nothing about this second Raja Duleh Rai survives beyond his name and his place in the archive's list of Kachwaha rulers; this short account gives what is known of his house and his age, and says plainly where the record falls silent.*

The name Duleh Rai belongs, above all, to the founder of the Kachwaha house in Dhundhar. **Dulha Rai**, also remembered as Dhola Rai, son of **Sodh Dev** of the Narwar line, came into eastern Rajasthan by the court tradition of Amber in the early twelfth century. He won **Dausa** from the Bargujars with the help of his Chauhan in-laws, took **Khoh** from the Meenas, and founded the shrine of **Jamwai Mata** at Ramgarh. His son **Kakil Deo** took **Amber**. In the archive's list, a second Duleh Rai, called "the Revivalist", follows **Raja Kshetrasimha** and rules **c. 1160–1180 CE**, before the throne passes to **Raja Sodo Deo**.

No inscription, chronicle or coin yet known names a second Duleh Rai ruling Amber, and the standard genealogies of the house know only the one founder of that name. Nor is any decline and revival of the Kachwaha state recorded for these years, so the title of "Revivalist" has no source. It is likely that this entry is a doubling of the founder himself, set in a different place in the list. Nothing more can honestly be said of a separate man.

What can be said is how the world looked from Dhundhar in those years. The **Chauhans** of Ajmer still dominated the region. After the death of **Vigraharaja IV** in the 1160s the Chauhan throne passed through several hands, and around **1177** the young **Prithviraj III** became king, at first under the guidance of his mother **Karpuradevi**. In the west a new danger was gathering. **Muhammad of Ghor** took **Multan** in 1175, and in **1178** his army, marching on Gujarat, was routed near Mount Abu by the forces of the Chalukya king **Mularaja II**, led in the name of the boy king by his mother **Naikidevi**. For a small hill state like the Kachwahas', the task of any ruler in these years was to hold what had been won, keep its kinsmen loyal, and keep faith with Ajmer.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Kachwaha of Dhundhar.** He is remembered in the archive as a ruler of the Kachwaha house of Amber.
- **A reign of c. 1160–1180 CE.** The archive places him between Raja Kshetrasimha and Raja Sodo Deo.
- **A doubled name.** The standard genealogies know only one Dulha Rai, the founder of the house in Dhundhar; no second ruler of the name is recorded.
- **No recorded revival.** No source tells of a decline and restoration of the Kachwaha state in these years.
- **A ruler in the years before Tarain.** His years fell as Prithviraj III came to the throne of Ajmer and Muhammad of Ghor first struck at India.

sodo-deo-amber.name: Raja Sodo Deo
sodo-deo-amber.title: Father of Dulha Rai in Kachwaha tradition
sodo-deo-amber.significance: Remembered in Kachwaha tradition as Sodh Dev, father of Dulha Rai; the archive's date and position for him cannot be reconciled with that tradition

culturalContributions: No works or grants of his are recorded

sodo-deo-amber.story:
## Raja Sodo Deo — the father remembered before the founder

*What little is said of Sodo Deo comes from the genealogies and bardic chronicles of the Kachwaha house, written down long after his time, and from James Tod's retelling of them; this short account gives what those traditions say, and says plainly where they disagree with the archive's list.*

The name Sodo Deo is best known in Kachwaha tradition as **Sodh Dev**, the father of **Dulha Rai**, the founder of the house in Dhundhar. The Kachwahas traced their line to **Kusha**, son of Rama, and to the **Kachchhapaghata** kings of Gwalior and Narwar, and Sodh Dev is remembered as a prince of the Narwar branch at a time when that line had lost its hold on its old lands. In the archive's list, however, Sodo Deo appears as the fortieth ruler, after **Raja Duleh Rai** and before **Raja Hoon Deo**, ruling **c. 1180–1200 CE**. This order cannot be right if he is the same man, since a father cannot follow his son, and the traditions place Sodh Dev a generation before Dulha Rai's arrival in Dhundhar, which the Jaipur chronicles date to about 1128 and older reckonings earlier still. No inscription, chronicle or coin yet known names any other Sodo Deo ruling Amber.

The traditions of Sodh Dev himself disagree. The court chronicles of Amber say that he came west with his son and a band of followers, and that the alliance which opened Dhundhar to them was a marriage between Dulha Rai and the daughter of **Ralan Singh Chauhan** of Moran. The darker version that Tod heard says the father died early, and that his widow carried the infant Dulha Rai to the Meena stronghold of **Khoh**. Either way, Sodh Dev never ruled Amber, which was taken only by his grandson **Kakil Deo**.

The years the archive gives him were among the most fateful in the history of northern India. In **1191** **Prithviraj III** of Ajmer defeated **Muhammad of Ghor** at **Tarain**, and in **1192** he was defeated and killed on the same field. Ajmer fell to the Ghurids, and by the end of the century their general **Qutb-ud-din Aibak** held Delhi. The later poem *Prithviraj Raso* tells of a Kachwaha chief, **Pajjun**, who served Prithviraj as a commander, but the Raso was composed long after these events and is not a reliable record.

## Highlights of his life

- **Father of the founder.** Kachwaha tradition remembers Sodh Dev as the father of Dulha Rai, founder of the house in Dhundhar.
- **A prince of the Narwar line.** He is said to have belonged to the Kachwaha branch of Narwar, descended from the Kachchhapaghatas.
- **Two traditions.** The Amber chronicles bring him west with his son; Tod's version has him die early and his widow flee to Khoh.
- **Misplaced in the archive's list.** The archive dates him c. 1180–1200 CE after Duleh Rai, but tradition places him a generation before Dulha Rai, and he never ruled Amber.

hoon-deo-amber.story:
## Raja Hoon Deo — the son of Amber's conqueror

*Almost nothing about Hoon Deo survives beyond his name and his place in the genealogies of the Kachwaha house; this short account gives what is known of his family and his age, and says plainly where the record falls silent.*

Hoon Deo is remembered in the standard genealogies of Amber as **Hanu Deo**, the son and successor of **Kakil Deo**, the Kachwaha ruler who, by tradition, took the hill town of **Amber** from the Meenas and made it the family's capital. Kakil Deo was himself the son of **Dulha Rai**, who had brought the Kachwahas into Dhundhar from the Narwar line, and the house traced its descent further back to **Kusha**, son of Rama. After Hanu Deo, the genealogies name his son **Janad Deo**, and after him **Pajjun**. Hanu Deo therefore belongs to the third generation of the Kachwaha state in Dhundhar, when Amber was still a young capital among hostile hills.

In the archive's list, however, Hoon Deo follows **Raja Sodo Deo** and rules **c. 1200–1220 CE**, before the throne passes to **Raja Manik Rai**. Neither the order nor the dates can be squared with the genealogies, which place Kakil Deo's son only a generation or two after Dulha Rai's arrival, dated by the Jaipur tradition to about 1128. No inscription, chronicle or coin of his own reign is known, and no deeds are recorded of him. Nothing more can honestly be said of the man himself.

What can be said is what his task must have been. A ruler in the generation after Amber was won had to hold it: to keep the Meena clans of the surrounding hills at peace or at bay, to guard the passes and the tanks, and to keep the loyalty of the kinsmen who had shared in the conquest. Beyond Dhundhar, the great power of the twelfth century was the Chauhan kingdom of **Ajmer**, and the Kachwahas, by their own bards' account, lived in its orbit. If the archive's later dates are followed instead, his years would fall after the defeat of **Prithviraj III** at Tarain in 1192, in the age when **Qutb-ud-din Aibak** founded the Delhi Sultanate in 1206 and **Iltutmish** began to press its claims across Rajasthan.

## Highlights of his life

- **Son of Kakil Deo.** The genealogies name him as the son and successor of the ruler who took Amber.
- **Third generation in Dhundhar.** He was a grandson of Dulha Rai, founder of the Kachwaha house in the region.
- **Father of Janad Deo.** The genealogies continue the line through his son Janad Deo and then Pajjun.
- **Misdated in the archive's list.** The archive places him c. 1200–1220 CE after Sodo Deo, an order the genealogies do not support.

manik-rai-amber.legacy: Manik Rai is not found in the standard genealogies of Amber; the name is best known from the legendary Chauhan lord of Sambhar.
manik-rai-amber.story:
## Raja Manik Rai — a name in the age of Iltutmish

*Almost nothing about Raja Manik Rai of Amber survives beyond his name and his place in the archive's list of Kachwaha rulers; this short account gives what is known of his house and his age, and says plainly where the record falls silent.*

The Kachwahas of Dhundhar traced their descent to **Kusha**, son of Rama, and looked back to the **Kachchhapaghata** kings of Gwalior and Narwar. By the court tradition of Amber, **Dulha Rai** founded their power in eastern Rajasthan in the twelfth century, and his son **Kakil Deo** took the hill town of **Amber**, which remained the family's capital until Jaipur was founded in 1727. In the archive's list, Manik Rai follows **Raja Hoon Deo** and rules **c. 1220–1240 CE**, before the throne passes to **Raja Chandrasen IX**.

No inscription, chronicle or coin yet known names a Manik Rai ruling Amber, and the standard genealogies of the house have no ruler of that name. The name is far better known from the neighbouring Chauhans: **Manik Rai** is the legendary early Chauhan lord of Sambhar to whom their bards traced much of their history. Whether the archive's entry borrows that name or preserves some other memory cannot be known. Nothing more can honestly be said of the man himself.

What can be said is how the world looked from Amber in those years, and it was a hard world for the Rajput states of eastern Rajasthan. The Chauhan kingdom of Ajmer had fallen after **Prithviraj III** was defeated at Tarain in 1192, and the **Delhi Sultanate**, founded in 1206, was now the great power of the north. Its sultan **Iltutmish**, who reigned from 1211 to 1236, set out to bring the Rajput chiefs to heel: in **1226** he took **Ranthambore**, where Prithviraj's descendants had found refuge, and in **1227** he took **Mandore** in Marwar. After his death the Sultanate passed through years of struggle, and his daughter **Raziya** ruled from 1236 until 1240. For a small hill state like Amber, set close to Delhi's armies and their routes into Rajasthan, the task of any ruler was to hold the forts, keep the kinsmen loyal, and survive in the shadow of the Sultanate without giving it cause to march.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Kachwaha of Dhundhar.** He is remembered in the archive as a ruler of the Kachwaha house of Amber.
- **A reign of c. 1220–1240 CE.** The archive places him between Raja Hoon Deo and Raja Chandrasen IX.
- **Not in the standard genealogies.** No record names a Manik Rai of Amber; the name is best known from the legendary Chauhan lord of Sambhar.
- **A ruler in the age of Iltutmish.** His years fell as the Delhi Sultanate took Ranthambore and Mandore and pressed its power across Rajasthan.

## Raja Chandrasen IX — Amber in the years of Balban's shadow

*Almost nothing about Raja Chandrasen IX survives beyond his name and his place in the archive's list of Kachwaha rulers; this short account gives what is known of his house and his age, and says plainly where the record falls silent.*

The Kachwahas of Dhundhar traced their descent to **Kusha**, son of Rama, and their arrival in the region to **Dulha Rai** in the eleventh century. Their seat was the hill town of **Amber**, which tradition says **Kakil Dev** took from the Meenas. Jaipur, the later capital of the house, would not be founded until 1727. In the archive's list, Chandrasen IX follows **Raja Manik Rai** and rules **c. 1240–1260 CE**, before the throne passes to **Raja Kakil Dev II**.

No inscription, chronicle or coin yet known names a Chandrasen ruling Amber in these decades. The standard genealogies of the house, whose names and dates themselves differ from one list to another, give the thirteenth century to rulers such as **Kilhan Dev** and **Kuntal**. The one well-recorded **Raja Chandrasen** of Amber lived two centuries later, from about **1453** to **1502**, and nothing told of him belongs to this entry.

What can be said is how the world looked from Amber in those years. After the death of **Iltutmish** in 1236, the Delhi Sultanate passed through a string of short and troubled reigns, from **Razia** to **Nasir al-Din Mahmud**, who came to the throne in **1246**. Real power in Delhi lay more and more with his minister **Ulugh Khan**, the future Sultan **Balban**. Balban led armies against the Chauhans of **Ranthambore**, south-east of Amber, and against the Mewatis on Dhundhar's north-eastern edge, whose raids reached the roads around Delhi. Mongol armies, meanwhile, pressed on the Punjab, and in **1241** they sacked Lahore. In Mewar, the Guhila ruler **Jaitrasimha** was rebuilding his kingdom after a Delhi army had laid waste to Nagda.

For a small hill state like Amber, caught between Delhi's campaigns and the Chauhan stronghold, the task of any ruler was to keep the forts in repair, keep the clan together and avoid giving a sultan's general a reason to turn aside. Whatever the details of Chandrasen IX's rule, the Kachwaha line passed through these hard decades unbroken.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Kachwaha of Amber.** He is remembered in the archive as a ruler of the Kachwaha house, whose seat was the hill town of Amber in Dhundhar.
- **A reign of c. 1240–1260 CE.** The archive places him between Raja Manik Rai and Raja Kakil Dev II.
- **Ruler in the age of Balban's rise.** His years fell in the decades when Balban, as minister of Nasir al-Din Mahmud, led Delhi's armies against Ranthambore and Mewat.
- **Distinct from the later Chandrasen.** The well-documented Raja Chandrasen of Amber ruled from about 1453 to 1502, and the standard genealogies give this period to rulers such as Kilhan Dev and Kuntal.

## Raja Kakil Dev II — a founder's name in the years of Balban

*Raja Kakil Dev II is known only by his name and his place in the archive's list of Kachwaha rulers; this short account tells what is known of his house and his age, and does not fill the silence of the record with invention.*

The Kachwahas of Dhundhar claimed descent from **Kusha**, son of Rama, and remembered **Dulha Rai** as the prince who brought their line into the region in the eleventh century. In the archive's list, Raja Kakil Dev II follows **Raja Chandrasen IX** and rules **c. 1260–1280 CE**, before the throne passes to **Raja Prithviraj Singh II**. Jaipur, the later capital of the house, would be founded only in 1727; in these centuries the family's seat was the hill town of **Amber**.

His name is an honoured one in Kachwaha memory. The first **Kakil Dev**, son of Dulha Rai, is the ruler whom the genealogies credit with taking the hill of Amber from the Meenas and making it the seat of the family, two centuries or so before the dates given here. No inscription or chronicle yet known records a second Kakil Dev on the throne of Amber in the later thirteenth century. The standard genealogies, whose names and dates vary from list to list, give these decades to rulers such as **Kilhan Dev** and **Kuntal**. No deeds, battles or family of Kakil Dev II can honestly be described.

The age itself was a hard one for the lands around Delhi. In **1260**, **Balban**, still minister to Sultan Nasir al-Din Mahmud, marched against the Mewatis, whose raids troubled the country south of the capital, and punished them with great severity. In **1266** he became sultan himself. He ruled by fear: forests that sheltered raiders were cleared, roads were guarded, and garrisoned posts were planted across the country nearest Delhi. **Mewat**, on Dhundhar's north-eastern edge, felt this most harshly. To the south-east, the Chauhans of **Ranthambore** held out under **Jaitrasimha**, and in Mewar the Guhila **Samarasimha** ruled from Chittor.

For a small hill state like Amber, wedged between Balban's garrisons and the Chauhan stronghold, the wisest course was to stay quiet, keep the forts in repair and give Delhi no reason to march. Whatever the details of these twenty years, the Kachwaha line came through them unbroken.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Kachwaha of Amber.** The archive remembers him as a ruler of the Kachwaha house, seated at Amber in Dhundhar.
- **A reign of c. 1260–1280 CE.** The archive places him between Raja Chandrasen IX and Raja Prithviraj Singh II.
- **A name from the founding of Amber.** He bears the name of Kakil Dev, son of Dulha Rai, whom tradition credits with taking Amber from the Meenas.
- **Ruler in the age of Balban.** His years fell under Balban's iron rule, which bore hard on Mewat and the country around Delhi.
- **A thin record.** The standard genealogies give this period to rulers such as Kilhan Dev and Kuntal, so his own reign remains unconfirmed.

## Raja Prithviraj Singh II — Amber in the days of Hammir and the Khaljis

*Raja Prithviraj Singh II is known only by his name and his place in the archive's list of Kachwaha rulers; this short account tells what is known of his house and his age, and does not fill the silence of the record with invention.*

The Kachwahas of Dhundhar claimed descent from **Kusha**, son of Rama, and ruled from the hill town of **Amber**, which tradition says **Kakil Dev**, son of **Dulha Rai**, had taken from the Meenas. Jaipur, the later capital of the house, would be founded only in 1727. In the archive's list, Raja Prithviraj Singh II follows **Raja Kakil Dev II** and rules **c. 1280–1300 CE**, before the throne passes to **Raja Pajawan II**.

No inscription or chronicle yet known records a Prithviraj on the throne of Amber in these years, and the claim that he expanded Amber's power has nothing to support it. The standard genealogies, whose names and dates differ between lists, give the late thirteenth century to **Kuntal**, among the more remembered of the early rulers. The Prithviraj whom history knows well at Amber is a much later ruler, **Raja Prithviraj**, who reigned from about **1503** to **1527**; this earlier namesake should not be confused with him. No deeds, battles or family of Prithviraj Singh II can honestly be described.

The age itself was a dramatic one for the country around Amber. In the early **1280s**, **Hammir Dev** came to the throne of the Chauhans at **Ranthambore**, south-east of Dhundhar, and made it the strongest Rajput fortress of the region. In Delhi, the line of Balban ended soon after his death in **1287**, and in **1290** the Khalji nobles seized the throne under **Jalal al-Din Khalji**. In **1291** Jalal al-Din marched against Ranthambore, took the nearby town of **Jhain**, and then turned back, judging the great fort not worth the lives it would cost. His nephew **Ala al-Din Khalji** murdered him and became sultan in **1296**, and Mongol armies struck at Delhi itself in **1299**. Within a year of the period given for Prithviraj Singh II, Ala al-Din would turn his armies on Ranthambore.

For a small hill state like Amber, lying between Delhi and Ranthambore, these were years for watchfulness: to keep the forts in repair, keep the clan together and stay out of the path of armies marching on the Chauhan stronghold. Whatever the details of these two decades, the Kachwaha line came through them unbroken.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Kachwaha of Amber.** The archive remembers him as a ruler of the Kachwaha house, seated at Amber in Dhundhar.
- **A reign of c. 1280–1300 CE.** The archive places him between Raja Kakil Dev II and Raja Pajawan II.
- **Neighbour of Hammir's Ranthambore.** His years saw the rise of Hammir Dev Chauhan and Jalal al-Din Khalji's failed march on Ranthambore in 1291.
- **Ruler at the dawn of the Khalji age.** Ala al-Din Khalji took the throne of Delhi in 1296, opening a time of great danger for the Rajput states.
- **Distinct from the later Prithviraj.** The well-documented Raja Prithviraj of Amber ruled from about 1503 to 1527, and the standard genealogies give this period to Kuntal.

pajawan-ii.story:
## Raja Pajawan II — Amber in the storm of Ala al-Din Khalji

*Raja Pajawan II is known only by his name and his place in the archive's list of Kachwaha rulers; this short account tells what is known of his house and his age, and does not fill the silence of the record with invention.*

The Kachwahas of Dhundhar claimed descent from **Kusha**, son of Rama, and ruled from the hill town of **Amber**, which tradition says **Kakil Dev**, son of **Dulha Rai**, had taken from the Meenas. Jaipur, the later capital of the house, would be founded only in 1727. In the archive's list, Raja Pajawan II follows **Raja Prithviraj Singh II** and rules **c. 1300–1320 CE**, before the throne passes to **Raja Udaikaran II**.

His name recalls one of the most celebrated of the early Kachwahas. The first **Pajawan**, son of **Janad Dev**, is remembered in the genealogies and in the bardic epic *Prithviraj Raso* as a companion of **Prithviraj Chauhan** in the late twelfth century. No inscription or chronicle yet known records a second Pajawan on the throne of Amber more than a century later, and the claims that he strengthened the frontier or expanded the state have nothing to support them. The standard genealogies, whose names and dates differ between lists, give these years to rulers such as **Kuntal** and **Jonsi**. No deeds, battles or family of Pajawan II can honestly be described.

The age itself was among the most violent the Rajput states had known. **Ala al-Din Khalji**, sultan of Delhi since 1296, besieged **Ranthambore** and took it in **1301**; **Hammir Dev Chauhan** died defending it. In **1303** the sultan captured **Chittor**, the great fortress of Mewar. **Siwana** fell in **1308**, and **Jalore**, where **Kanhadadeva Chauhan** fell, in about **1311**. Old ruling houses across Rajasthan were broken or driven into the hills. After Ala al-Din's death in **1316** his empire fell into confusion under his son **Mubarak Shah**, and in **1320** **Ghiyas al-Din Tughlaq** seized the throne and founded a new dynasty.

For a small hill state like Amber, which lay within easy reach of the roads from Delhi to Ranthambore and Chittor, survival in these decades meant keeping out of the sultan's path and giving his generals no cause to turn aside. Whatever the details of these twenty years, the Kachwaha line, unlike many greater houses, came through them unbroken.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Kachwaha of Amber.** The archive remembers him as a ruler of the Kachwaha house, seated at Amber in Dhundhar.
- **A reign of c. 1300–1320 CE.** The archive places him between Raja Prithviraj Singh II and Raja Udaikaran II.
- **A name from the Prithviraj era.** He bears the name of Pajawan, son of Janad Dev, remembered as a companion of Prithviraj Chauhan.
- **Ruler in the Khalji storm.** His years saw the fall of Ranthambore in 1301, Chittor in 1303 and Jalore around 1311.
- **A thin record.** The standard genealogies give this period to rulers such as Kuntal and Jonsi, so his own reign remains unconfirmed.

udaikaran-ii.story:
## Raja Udaikaran II — Amber in the reign of Muhammad bin Tughlaq

*Almost nothing about Raja Udaikaran II survives beyond his name and his place in the archive's list of Kachwaha rulers; this short account gives what is known of his house and his age, and says plainly where the record falls silent.*

The Kachwahas of Dhundhar traced their descent to **Kusha**, son of Rama, and their arrival in the region to **Dulha Rai** in the eleventh century. Their seat was the hill town of **Amber**, which tradition says **Kakil Dev** took from the Meenas. Jaipur, the later capital of the house, would not be founded until 1727. In the archive's list, Udaikaran II follows **Raja Pajawan II** and rules **c. 1320–1340 CE**, before the throne passes to **Raja Kumbhakarna**.

No inscription or chronicle yet known records an Udaikaran ruling Amber in these decades. The standard genealogies, whose names and dates differ between lists, give the first half of the fourteenth century to **Jonsi**. They do know a **Raja Udaikaran**, but as Jonsi's successor, whose reign is usually dated from around **1366**. That Udaikaran is one of the better-remembered early rulers: through his son **Balo** descended **Rao Shekha**, founder of the **Shekhawat** branch, while another son, **Narsingh**, succeeded him at Amber. It is possible that the archive's Udaikaran II is an echo of him set a generation too early, but this cannot be shown. The old claim that Udaikaran II "paved the way for Bharmal" is also mistaken: **Raja Bharmal** came to the throne of Amber only in **1548**, more than two centuries later.

What can be said is how the world looked from Amber in those years. In **1320** **Ghiyas al-Din Tughlaq** took the throne of Delhi, and in **1325** his son **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** succeeded him. Muhammad was learned and restless, and his bold schemes shook the whole Sultanate: in **1327** he moved much of Delhi's population to **Daulatabad** in the Deccan, and soon afterwards he issued a token coinage of brass and copper that had to be withdrawn. Famine struck the country around Delhi in the 1330s, and revolts broke out across the empire. In Mewar, meanwhile, **Hammir** of the Sisodia branch recovered **Chittor** from the sultan's governors, around the 1320s or 1330s, and began the revival of the Rajput power that the Khalji conquests had broken.

For a small hill state like Amber, the weakening grip of Delhi brought both danger and room to breathe. The task of any ruler was to keep the forts in repair, hold the clan together and stay clear of the sultan's armies as they marched to put down one rising after another.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Kachwaha of Amber.** He is remembered in the archive as a ruler of the Kachwaha house, whose seat was the hill town of Amber in Dhundhar.
- **A reign of c. 1320–1340 CE.** The archive places him between Raja Pajawan II and Raja Kumbhakarna.
- **Ruler in the age of Muhammad bin Tughlaq.** His years saw the move to Daulatabad, the token coinage and the famines and revolts that weakened Delhi.
- **Witness to Mewar's revival.** In these decades Hammir of the Sisodias won back Chittor.
- **Distinct from the later Udaikaran.** The standard genealogies give this period to Jonsi and place the known Raja Udaikaran, ancestor of the Shekhawats, from around 1366.

kumbhakarna-amber.story:
## Raja Kumbhakarna of Amber — a quiet name as Delhi's empire cracked

*Raja Kumbhakarna of Amber is known only by his name and his place in the archive's list of Kachwaha rulers; this short account tells what is known of his house and his age, and does not fill the silence of the record with invention.*

The Kachwahas of Dhundhar claimed descent from **Kusha**, son of Rama, and ruled from the hill town of **Amber**, which tradition says **Kakil Dev**, son of **Dulha Rai**, had taken from the Meenas. Jaipur, the later capital of the house, would be founded only in 1727. In the archive's list, Raja Kumbhakarna, also called Kumbha, follows **Raja Udaikaran II** and rules **c. 1340–1360 CE**, before the throne passes to **Raja Prithviraj IV**.

No inscription or chronicle yet known records a Kumbhakarna on the throne of Amber in these years, and the claim that he consolidated Amber's rule has nothing to support it. The standard genealogies, whose names and dates differ between lists, give the middle of the fourteenth century to **Jonsi**, followed by **Udaikaran**, whose reign is usually dated from around **1366**. This Kumbhakarna must also be kept apart from the far more famous **Rana Kumbha** of Mewar, whose full name was also Kumbhakarna and who ruled from **1433** to **1468**, building **Kumbhalgarh** and the **Vijay Stambh** at Chittor. Nothing told of the Rana belongs to this entry. No deeds, battles or family of Kumbhakarna of Amber can honestly be described.

The age itself saw the great empire of Delhi begin to crack. **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** spent his last years marching from one rebellion to the next. The Deccan broke away: the **Vijayanagara** kingdom had been founded in the south in **1336**, and the **Bahmani** sultanate rose in **1347**. Muhammad died in Sindh in **1351**, still on campaign, and his cousin **Firuz Shah Tughlaq** took the throne. Firuz gave up distant conquests, built canals, towns and hunting lodges, and ruled a smaller but calmer realm. In Mewar, **Hammir** of the Sisodias, master of Chittor once more, was rebuilding the strength of his house.

For a small hill state like Amber, the slackening of Delhi's grip meant fewer punishing expeditions and more room to manage its own lands. The task of any ruler was still the same: to keep the hill forts in repair, bind kinsmen to the house with grants of land, and keep the line alive. Whatever the details of these two decades, the Kachwaha line came through them unbroken.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Kachwaha of Amber.** The archive remembers him as a ruler of the Kachwaha house, seated at Amber in Dhundhar.
- **A reign of c. 1340–1360 CE.** The archive places him between Raja Udaikaran II and Raja Prithviraj IV.
- **Ruler as Delhi's empire cracked.** His years saw the revolts of Muhammad bin Tughlaq's last decade and the calmer rule of Firuz Shah Tughlaq from 1351.
- **Distinct from Rana Kumbha.** The famous Kumbhakarna, Rana Kumbha of Mewar, ruled from 1433 to 1468 and is a different man.
- **A thin record.** The standard genealogies give this period to Jonsi, so his own reign remains unconfirmed.

prithviraj-iv-amber.story:
## Raja Prithviraj IV — Amber in the age of Firuz Shah

*Raja Prithviraj IV is known only by his name and his place in the archive's list of Kachwaha rulers; this short account tells what is known of his house and his age, and does not fill the silence of the record with invention.*

The Kachwahas of Dhundhar claimed descent from **Kusha**, son of Rama, and had ruled from the hill town of **Amber** since the eleventh century; the city of Jaipur would be founded only in 1727. In the archive's list, Raja Prithviraj IV follows **Raja Kumbhakarna (Kumbha)** and rules **c. 1360–1380 CE**, before the throne passes to **Raja Chandrasen VI**.

No inscription, chronicle or coin yet known names a Prithviraj on the throne of Amber in these decades. The standard genealogies of the house give this period to **Raja Junsi** and then to his son **Raja Udaikaran**, who came to the throne in the later 1360s. The well-documented **Raja Prithviraj Singh I** of Amber ruled much later, from about 1502 to 1527, and the numbering here does not match him. No deeds, battles or family of Prithviraj IV can honestly be described.

The age itself is better known. In Delhi, **Sultan Firuz Shah Tughlaq** ruled from 1351 to 1388, a time of canals, gardens and comparative calm in the north, though the Sultanate's hold on Rajasthan was loose. In Mewar, the house of **Rana Hammir** had recovered Chittor, and his son **Rana Kshetra Singh** carried its power forward from 1364. The Hadas were establishing themselves at **Bundi**. For a small state like Amber, set among these neighbours, the work of any ruler was to keep the hill forts, the clan and its lands intact.

Within the Kachwaha house, the reign of Udaikaran in these years is remembered as a time of branching. Tradition says that his son **Balaji** received **Amarsar** to the north, and from Balaji's line would come **Rao Shekha**, founder of the **Shekhawat** branch, in the following century.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Kachwaha of Amber.** The archive remembers him as a ruler of the Kachwaha house, seated at Amber in Dhundhar.
- **A reign of c. 1360–1380 CE.** The archive places him between Raja Kumbhakarna and Raja Chandrasen VI.
- **Ruler in the age of Firuz Shah.** His years fell under the long reign of Firuz Shah Tughlaq in Delhi and the revival of Mewar under Hammir's line.
- **A thin record.** The standard genealogies give this period to Raja Junsi and Raja Udaikaran, so his own reign remains unconfirmed.

chandrasen-vi.story:
## Raja Chandrasen VI — Amber as the Tughlaq order crumbled

*Raja Chandrasen VI is known only by his name and his place in the archive's list of Kachwaha rulers; this short account tells what is known of his house and his age, and says plainly where the record falls silent.*

The Kachwahas of Dhundhar traced their line to **Kusha**, son of Rama, and their seat was the hill town of **Amber**, which tradition says **Kakil Dev** took from the Meenas in the eleventh century. Jaipur, the later capital of the house, would not be founded until 1727. In the archive's list, Chandrasen VI follows **Raja Prithviraj IV** and rules **c. 1380–1395 CE**, before the throne passes to **Raja Prithviraj V**.

No inscription, chronicle or coin yet known names a Chandrasen ruling Amber in these years. The standard genealogies of the house give the period to **Raja Udaikaran** and, from about the end of the 1380s, to his son **Raja Narsingh**. The one well-recorded **Raja Chandrasen** of Amber ruled much later, from about 1453 to 1502, and nothing told of him should be carried over to this entry.

The world around Amber was changing fast in these years. In Delhi, **Firuz Shah Tughlaq** died in **1388**, and his heirs fought one another for the throne. Within a few years, several sultans rose and fell, and the governors of the provinces began to act as kings. Close to Dhundhar, the Khanzada chiefs of **Mewat**, led by **Bahadur Nahar**, raided towards Delhi itself. In Mewar, **Rana Lakha** came to the throne in **1382**, and in Marwar the Rathore **Rao Chunda** won **Mandore** in about **1395**, laying the foundation of the Rathore state.

For a small hill kingdom like Amber, the weakening of Delhi meant both danger and opportunity. There was less tribute to pay and less fear of imperial armies, but also more raiders, more ambitious neighbours and no higher power to keep the peace. Any ruler of Amber in these years had to defend his own forts and keep the many branches of the Kachwaha clan loyal to the seat at Amber.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Kachwaha of Amber.** The archive remembers him as a ruler of the Kachwaha house, seated at Amber in Dhundhar.
- **A reign of c. 1380–1395 CE.** The archive places him between Raja Prithviraj IV and Raja Prithviraj V.
- **Ruler as Delhi weakened.** His years saw the death of Firuz Shah Tughlaq in 1388 and the breakdown of Tughlaq authority.
- **Distinct from the later Chandrasen.** The usual lists give this period to Raja Udaikaran and Raja Narsingh, and the well-documented Raja Chandrasen ruled from about 1453 to 1502.

## Raja Prithviraj V — Amber in the shadow of Timur

*Raja Prithviraj V is known only by his name and his place in the archive's list of Kachwaha rulers; this short account tells what is known of his house and his age, and does not fill the silence of the record with invention.*

The Kachwahas of Dhundhar claimed descent from **Kusha**, son of Rama, and ruled from the hill town of **Amber**, their seat since the eleventh century; Jaipur would be founded only in 1727. In the archive's list, Raja Prithviraj V follows **Raja Chandrasen VI** and rules **c. 1395–1410 CE**, before the throne passes to **Raja Chandrasen VII**.

No inscription, chronicle or coin yet known records a Prithviraj on the throne of Amber in these years. The standard genealogies of the house give this period to **Raja Narsingh**, son of Raja Udaikaran. The well-documented **Raja Prithviraj Singh I** of Amber ruled from about 1502 to 1527, and the numbering here does not match him. No deeds, battles or family of Prithviraj V can honestly be described.

The years themselves were among the most violent of the age. In late **1398**, the Central Asian conqueror **Timur** crossed into India. He stormed the fort of **Bhatner** on the northern edge of the Thar desert and in December sacked **Delhi**, leaving the Tughlaq capital ruined and its people slaughtered or carried away. Timur did not march into Dhundhar, but the blow broke what remained of Delhi's power. In the years that followed, the governors of the provinces became independent kings: **Zafar Khan** took the title of **Sultan Muzaffar Shah** in **Gujarat** in about **1407**, and **Dilawar Khan Ghuri** made **Malwa** a separate sultanate.

Nearer home, **Rana Lakha** ruled Mewar, where the silver and lead mines of **Zawar** brought new wealth, and **Rao Chunda** was building up the Rathore state from **Mandore**. Amber stood between these rising powers and the shattered capital in the north. For any ruler of the Kachwahas in these years, survival meant guarding the hill forts, keeping the clan's branches loyal, and watching the new sultanates take shape around Rajasthan.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Kachwaha of Amber.** The archive remembers him as a ruler of the Kachwaha house, seated at Amber in Dhundhar.
- **A reign of c. 1395–1410 CE.** The archive places him between Raja Chandrasen VI and Raja Chandrasen VII.
- **Ruler in the years of Timur.** His years saw Timur's sack of Bhatner and Delhi in 1398 and the rise of the Gujarat and Malwa sultanates.
- **A thin record.** The standard genealogies give this period to Raja Narsingh, so his own reign remains unconfirmed.

## Raja Chandrasen VII — Amber in the age of the new sultanates

*Raja Chandrasen VII is known only by his name and his place in the archive's list of Kachwaha rulers; this short account tells what is known of his house and his age, and says plainly where the record falls silent.*

The Kachwahas of Dhundhar traced their line to **Kusha**, son of Rama, and ruled from the hill town of **Amber**, their seat since the eleventh century; Jaipur would be founded only in 1727. In the archive's list, Chandrasen VII follows **Raja Prithviraj V** and rules **c. 1410–1425 CE**, before the throne passes to **Raja Chandrasen VIII**.

No inscription, chronicle or coin yet known names a Chandrasen ruling Amber in these years. The standard genealogies of the house give the period to **Raja Narsingh** and his successor **Raja Banbir**, with **Raja Udharan** coming to the throne in the 1420s; the exact years differ from one list to another. The one well-recorded **Raja Chandrasen** of Amber ruled from about 1453 to 1502, and nothing told of him belongs to this entry.

The age around Amber is well known. In Delhi, the Tughlaq line ended, and in **1414** **Khizr Khan** founded the rule of the **Sayyids**, whose power reached little beyond the country around the capital. In Gujarat, **Sultan Ahmad Shah I** founded the city of **Ahmedabad** in **1411**, and his armies pressed on the Rajput lands of the west. In Malwa, **Hoshang Shah** ruled from **Mandu**. In Mewar, **Rana Lakha** died in about **1421** and was followed by his young son **Rana Mokal**, while the Rathore **Rao Chunda** of Mandore was killed in battle near Nagaur in the early 1420s.

Amber in these years was still a modest state, ringed by sultanates on one side and the greater Rajput houses of Mewar and Marwar on the other. Its rulers kept their hill forts, their clan and their temples, and waited for a stronger age. That age would come, but more than a century later.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Kachwaha of Amber.** The archive remembers him as a ruler of the Kachwaha house, seated at Amber in Dhundhar.
- **A reign of c. 1410–1425 CE.** The archive places him between Raja Prithviraj V and Raja Chandrasen VIII.
- **Ruler in the age of the new sultanates.** His years saw the rise of the Sayyids in Delhi in 1414 and the founding of Ahmedabad in 1411.
- **Distinct from the later Chandrasen.** The usual lists give this period to Raja Narsingh and Raja Banbir, and the well-documented Raja Chandrasen ruled from about 1453 to 1502.

chandrasen-viii.story:
## Raja Chandrasen VIII — Amber in the years of Mokal and Kumbha

*Raja Chandrasen VIII is known only by his name and his place in the archive's list of Kachwaha rulers; this short account tells what is known of his house and his age, and says plainly where the record falls silent.*

The Kachwahas of Dhundhar traced their line to **Kusha**, son of Rama, and ruled from the hill town of **Amber**, their seat since the eleventh century; Jaipur would be founded only in 1727. In the archive's list, Chandrasen VIII follows **Raja Chandrasen VII** and rules **c. 1425–1440 CE**. In this sequence the next name is **Raja Bharmal**, who came to the throne in **1548**; the standard genealogies place several rulers between them, among them Udharan, Chandrasen, Prithviraj Singh I, Puranmal, Bhim Singh and Ratan Singh.

No inscription, chronicle or coin yet known names a Chandrasen ruling Amber in these years. The standard genealogies give the whole period to **Raja Udharan**, who ruled until about **1453**. Udharan was followed by the one well-recorded **Raja Chandrasen** of Amber, who ruled from about 1453 to 1502. It is possible that this entry is an echo of him placed too early, but this cannot be shown, and nothing told of him should be carried over here.

The years themselves were full of drama in Rajasthan. In **1433**, **Rana Mokal** of Mewar was murdered by his own kinsmen, and his son **Rana Kumbha** came to the throne, beginning one of the greatest reigns in Rajput history. In **1438**, the Rathore **Rao Ranmal**, long the power behind the throne at Chittor, was killed there, and his son **Rao Jodha** fled to begin the long struggle to recover Marwar. In Malwa, **Mahmud Khalji** seized the throne in **1436** and soon began his wars against Mewar. In Delhi, the Sayyid sultan **Mubarak Shah** was murdered in **1434**, and the dynasty grew weaker still.

Within the Kachwaha clan itself, **Rao Shekha** was born in **1433** in the Amarsar line descended from Raja Udaikaran. His descendants, the **Shekhawats**, would one day rule a large part of northern Rajasthan. Amber itself remained a modest state, guarding its hills and waiting for its rise.

## Highlights of his life

- **A Kachwaha of Amber.** The archive remembers him as a ruler of the Kachwaha house, seated at Amber in Dhundhar.
- **A reign of c. 1425–1440 CE.** The archive places him after Raja Chandrasen VII; the next name in this sequence, Raja Bharmal, ruled from 1548.
- **Ruler in the age of Kumbha.** His years saw the murder of Rana Mokal in 1433, the accession of Rana Kumbha, and the death of Rao Ranmal at Chittor in 1438.
- **The birth of Rao Shekha.** In 1433 the founder of the Shekhawat branch of the Kachwahas was born.
- **Distinct from the later Chandrasen.** The usual lists give this period to Raja Udharan, and the well-documented Raja Chandrasen ruled from about 1453 to 1502.

raja-bharmal-amber.story:
## Raja Bharmal — the king who chose the alliance

*Raja Bharmal's life comes to us through the Mughal chronicles, above all Abul Fazl's Akbarnama, and through the genealogies and chronicles of the Kachwaha house; where these sources disagree or fall silent, this story says so.*

At the end of the fifteenth century, Amber was a small hill kingdom in the dry, rocky country of **Dhundhar**. Its rulers, the **Kachwahas**, claimed descent from **Kusha**, son of Rama, and had held the old fort above the Maota lake for nearly four hundred years. They were respected, but they were not great. To the south, Mewar under the Sisodias towered over Rajasthan; to the west, the Rathores of Marwar were rising; and to the north, in Delhi and Agra, Afghan and then Mughal sultans fought for the empire of Hindustan.

Bharmal was born around **1498**, a son of **Raja Prithviraj Singh I** of Amber. His mother, the chronicles say, was a princess of the Rathore house of **Bikaner**, a daughter of Rao Lunkaran. Prithviraj was a warrior and a devout man. He fought beside **Rana Sanga** of Mewar against Babur at **Khanwa in 1527**, the battle that opened the way for Mughal rule in India. He was also a disciple of the Vaishnava saint **Krishnadas Payahari** of **Galta**, the holy valley in the hills near Amber, and his court was filled with the sound of devotion to Rama and Krishna.

Bharmal grew up among many brothers. Prithviraj, tradition says, divided the lands and honours of the clan among his sons and their lines in the arrangement later remembered as the **Baran Kotri**, the twelve chambers of the Kachwaha house. It was a way of giving every branch a share in the state. It was also a recipe for quarrels, and the young Bharmal saw them begin as soon as his father died in 1527.

The throne went first to his brother **Puranmal**, and after Puranmal's death in 1534 to another brother, **Bhim Singh**, rather than to Puranmal's young son **Sujamal**. Bhim Singh was followed by his son **Ratan Singh**. These were unsettled years. The Mughal Babur died in 1530, his son Humayun lost Hindustan to the Afghan **Sher Shah Suri** in 1540, and Sher Shah's armies marched across Rajasthan. A small hill state like Amber could only watch the great powers and try not to be crushed between them.

Bharmal did not come to the throne as a young man. He was about fifty when his chance came, in **1548**. According to the Kachwaha chronicles, Ratan Singh was poisoned by his own brother **Askaran**, who seized the throne. The nobles of Amber would not accept a ruler who had come to power through the murder of his brother. They set Askaran aside and raised the older, steadier uncle, Bharmal, to the gaddi of Amber. Askaran was not killed. Years later he would receive the lordship of Narwar.

The kingdom Bharmal took over was weak and divided. Inside the clan, Sujamal, the son of Puranmal, still believed the throne was rightfully his, and he found friends wherever Bharmal had enemies. Outside, the Afghan Sur empire of **Islam Shah**, Sher Shah's son, was breaking apart, and after Islam Shah's death in 1553 northern India fell into confusion. In 1555 Humayun returned to Delhi. A year later he was dead, and his thirteen-year-old son **Akbar**, guided by **Bairam Khan**, defeated the general **Hemu** at the **Second Battle of Panipat** in November 1556.

Bharmal's first contact with the Mughals came in these months. An Afghan commander, **Haji Khan**, a former officer of Sher Shah, besieged the Mughal officer **Majnun Khan Qaqshal** in the town of **Narnaul**, north of Amber. The Akbarnama records that Bharmal stepped in. He arranged for Majnun Khan and his people to leave the town in safety, and his men escorted them. It was a small act, but a wise one. Majnun Khan did not forget it, and he spoke of the Kachwaha raja at the new emperor's court.

Soon afterwards Bharmal went to Delhi and was presented to the young Akbar. Abul Fazl tells a story of that visit. Akbar, who loved to ride fierce elephants, was mounted on a wild, maddened animal that suddenly turned and charged the crowd. Everyone scattered, except the Rajputs of Bharmal's party, who stood still and did not run. The boy emperor noticed. Bharmal left Delhi with honours, and with the memory of a teenage ruler who admired courage more than anything else.

For a few years, nothing more came of it. Then the trouble at home grew worse. Around **1561**, the Mughal governor of the region around Ajmer and Mewat, **Mirza Sharafuddin Husain**, took up the cause of Sujamal. With Mughal troops at his back, he pressed Amber hard. He demanded tribute, and Bharmal was forced to hand over his son **Jagannath** and other young kinsmen as hostages. Imagine the old raja's position: almost sixty-five, with his own heir held in a Mughal camp and his nephew waiting to take his throne. He could fight the Mughals, as the Rajputs of Chittor and Merta would soon choose to do, and almost certainly lose everything. Or he could go over the governor's head, straight to the emperor.

In **January 1562**, Akbar set out from Agra on his pilgrimage to the shrine of **Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti** at Ajmer. His road passed close to Amber. Through the officer **Chaghatai Khan**, Bharmal asked for an audience, and on the road to Ajmer he came before the emperor. He spoke of the harassment of Sharafuddin and of his loyalty, and he offered Akbar the hand of his eldest daughter. The bards of later centuries would tell this moment in many ways, some proud and some bitter. What the Mughal record shows is a careful old ruler, making the hardest decision of his life for the survival of his house.

Akbar accepted. On his way back from Ajmer, early in 1562, the marriage took place at **Sambhar**, the great salt lake on the edge of Kachwaha country. The princess was **Harkha Bai**, known to later history by the title **Mariam-uz-Zamani**. The name "Jodha Bai", by which she is often called today, is a much later label and is not found in the sources of her own time. Sharafuddin was ordered to release the hostages, and Bharmal's son came home.

Bharmal accompanied the emperor's camp, and with him came his son **Bhagwant Das** and his young grandson **Man Singh**, then about twelve years old. They were taken into Akbar's service. This was something new. Rajput chiefs had served sultans before, but the Kachwahas were not treated as defeated vassals. They became members of the imperial family and officers of the empire, keeping their own lands, their own religion and their own customs. Within a few months, Sharafuddin himself rebelled against Akbar and fled. The man who had tried to destroy Bharmal was gone, and Bharmal was the emperor's kinsman.

The alliance changed the fate of Amber. Bharmal was given a high rank in the imperial service; Abul Fazl lists him among the commanders of five thousand. Akbar trusted him with responsibility at the heart of the empire. When the emperor marched against **Gujarat in 1572**, the Akbarnama records that Bharmal was left in charge of **Agra**, the capital. Very few nobles of the empire, and no other Rajput of that time, received such a trust.

It was not a peaceful time for his family. The empire of Akbar was built through war, and the Kachwahas fought in its front ranks. Bhagwant Das and Man Singh rode with the imperial armies. In **December 1572**, in the fierce fight at **Sarnal** in Gujarat, Bharmal's son **Bhupat** was killed fighting at Akbar's side. Bharmal was by then an old man, and the alliance he had chosen had cost him a son.

Meanwhile, in the palace at Sikri, his daughter waited for a child. Akbar had longed for an heir, and he had gone on foot to pray at the hermitage of the Sufi **Shaikh Salim Chishti**. On **30 August 1569**, Harkha Bai gave birth to a son in Sikri. He was named **Salim** after the saint. He would rule the empire as **Jahangir**. The grandson of the Kachwaha raja of Amber was heir to the throne of Hindustan.

Many in Rajasthan did not forgive the choice. Mewar under **Rana Udai Singh** and later **Maharana Pratap** refused any such bond, and the bards of Mewar spoke of Amber with scorn. It is a debate that has never really ended. But Bharmal had not made his decision in a time of strength. He had made it as the ruler of a small, divided state, with a rival claimant backed by Mughal arms and his son in a hostage camp. His choice saved his throne, ended the claims of Sujamal, and gave his house a place in the empire that no Kachwaha before him could have imagined.

In religion and custom, Bharmal remained what he had always been. The Kachwahas kept their gods, their Vaishnava devotion inherited from Prithviraj's time, and their family goddess. Akbar's court, with its growing openness to many faiths, gave room to Rajput customs, and Harkha Bai kept her own worship inside the imperial palace. The bond between Amber and the Mughals was not a conversion. It was an alliance of houses.

Bharmal died in **1574**, in his mid-seventies. He had ruled Amber for twenty-six years. He was succeeded by his son **Raja Bhagwant Das**, who continued the alliance, and whose own daughter **Man Bai** would marry Prince Salim in 1585. After Bhagwant Das came **Raja Man Singh**, the greatest general of Akbar's empire, governor of Kabul, Bihar and Bengal, and the builder of the palaces that still crown the hill at Amber.

None of that splendour existed when Bharmal took the throne. Amber's later palaces, the wealth of the Kachwaha nobles, and in time the city of Jaipur, all grew from the choice he made on the road to Ajmer in 1562. He was not the most glorious king of his line. But he may have been the one who changed its history most.

## Highlights of his life

- **Late accession (1548).** After Ratan Singh's death and Askaran's brief seizure of power, the nobles of Amber raised Bharmal, then about fifty, to the throne.
- **The Narnaul rescue (c. 1556–57).** He secured the safe withdrawal of the Mughal officer Majnun Khan Qaqshal from Narnaul, which first brought him to Akbar's notice.
- **The meeting with Akbar (January 1562).** Pressed by Mirza Sharafuddin Husain and his nephew Sujamal, he went directly to the emperor on the road to Ajmer.
- **The marriage at Sambhar (1562).** His daughter Harkha Bai, later Mariam-uz-Zamani, married Akbar and became the mother of Jahangir.
- **A Rajput at the heart of the empire.** He held a rank of five thousand and was left in charge of Agra during the Gujarat campaign of 1572.
- **Founder of Kachwaha greatness.** His alliance raised Bhagwant Das and Man Singh to the highest offices of the Mughal empire and secured Amber's future.

bhagwant-das-amber.story:
## Raja Bhagwant Das — the Kachwaha who rode beside Akbar

*Bhagwant Das's life comes to us mainly through the Persian chronicles of Akbar's reign, above all the Akbarnama of Abul Fazl and the history of Badauni, and through the family traditions of Amber. Where the record is uncertain, this story says so.*

In the first half of the sixteenth century, the Kachwaha Rajputs held the hill country of **Dhundhar**, around their fortress-capital of **Amber**, a few miles north of where Jaipur stands today. They traced their line to Kush, son of Rama, and had ruled this rocky land of ridges and lakes for centuries. But in those years Amber was a minor power. It was squeezed between stronger neighbours, troubled by quarrels inside its own ruling house, and watched hungrily by the governors of the Afghan Sur kings and then of the Mughals in Ajmer and Mewat.

**Bhagwant Das** was born into this uneasy house, the son of **Raja Bharmal**, also called Bihari Mal. His birth is usually placed around **1527**, though no contemporary record fixes the year. He grew up in a family where the throne was never safe. Bharmal had come to power through a bitter struggle with his own kinsmen, and rivals within the clan sought help from outside to unseat him. A young prince of Amber learned early that survival depended on choosing friends wisely.

The great turning point of his family's history came in **1562**. The young emperor **Akbar**, travelling to the shrine of Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti at Ajmer, passed through the country near Amber. Bharmal, pressed by the Mughal governor of the region and by his own rivals, chose to seek the emperor's protection rather than his anger. He offered an alliance sealed by marriage. His daughter was married to Akbar at **Sambhar** early that year. In later times she would be honoured as **Mariam-uz-Zamani**, the mother of the future emperor Jahangir.

With that marriage, Bhagwant Das and his young son **Man Singh** entered the imperial service. For a Rajput house this was a new kind of world. The Mughal court was a place of Persian etiquette, ranks and salaries, intrigue and opportunity. The chroniclers tell that soon after, when a maddened elephant charged through a crowd at the camp, the Kachwaha party alone stood their ground while others ran, and the emperor noticed them. Whether or not every detail of that story is true, Akbar came to trust the men of Amber as he trusted few others.

Bhagwant Das proved his worth in war. In **1572** Akbar marched into **Gujarat**, a rich province torn between rival nobles and rebellious Mirza princes of the Timurid house. In December of that year, near the town of **Sarnal**, the emperor learned that a Mirza army was close by. Impatient, he crossed the river with only a small band of companions, far fewer than the enemy. Bhagwant Das was beside him.

The fight at Sarnal was fought in narrow lanes and broken ground, among thorn hedges where horsemen could barely turn. At one moment the emperor himself was hard pressed, with enemies closing in. Bhagwant Das and his men fought around him and drove the attackers back. The cost to the Kachwahas was heavy: his brother **Bhupat** fell in that fight. When the battle was won, Akbar honoured Bhagwant Das with a **banner and kettledrums**, marks of high rank in the Mughal army that were rarely given, and that set him among the foremost nobles of the empire.

The next year brought a different kind of duty. In **1573** Akbar sent a series of envoys to **Maharana Pratap** of Mewar, hoping to bring the proudest of the Rajput houses into his alliance without war. Man Singh went first, and then Bhagwant Das himself travelled into the hills of Mewar. The Persian histories say he was received with courtesy, and they claim that Pratap sent his son Amar Singh back with him to the court. Mewar's own tradition remembers these embassies very differently, as attempts that Pratap politely turned away. What is certain is that no submission followed, and three years later Man Singh would lead the imperial army against Pratap at Haldighati.

Around **1574**, Raja Bharmal died, and Bhagwant Das became the ruler of Amber. He was already a senior general, and his life as a king was lived as much in the camps of the empire as in his own palace. His home country was governed by trusted officers and kinsmen while he served far away. Yet the bond with the emperor brought Amber something it had never had before: security. No rival claimant could hope to unseat a Kachwaha ruler who stood so close to Akbar, and the small hill kingdom began to grow in wealth and standing.

His most important work in these years lay in the **Punjab** and on the north-western frontier. Akbar's half-brother **Mirza Muhammad Hakim** ruled Kabul and more than once looked eastward towards the rich plains of Lahore. In **1581**, when Hakim marched into the Punjab, Bhagwant Das and Man Singh were among the commanders who held the province until the emperor arrived with his main army and drove the Mirza back to Kabul. After Hakim's death in **1585**, Man Singh was sent to govern Kabul, and Bhagwant Das was made governor of the Punjab, with his seat at **Lahore**. He held a rank of **5,000** in the Mughal system, one of the highest ranks then given.

The year 1585 also brought a marriage that bound Amber even more closely to the throne. Bhagwant Das's daughter, **Man Bai**, was married to **Prince Salim**, the heir to the empire. The wedding was celebrated with great splendour, and Akbar himself took part in the ceremonies. In 1587 she bore a son, **Khusrau**. For a time it seemed that a grandson of the house of Amber might one day sit on the Mughal throne.

The same years brought the episode that, more than any other, reveals the kind of man Bhagwant Das was. In **1585–86** Akbar sent an army to bring **Kashmir** under his rule, and Bhagwant Das was one of its leading commanders. The army struggled through the snows and narrow passes of the Pir Panjal, short of food and battered by the winter. In the end the Kashmiri ruler, **Yusuf Shah Chak**, came to Bhagwant Das's camp and agreed to submit, on the promise that he would be treated with honour.

Bhagwant Das gave his word. But when Yusuf Shah was brought before the emperor, Akbar did not accept the terms his general had made. The Kashmiri king was kept under guard and never allowed to return to his country. For a Rajput, a broken promise given in his name was a deep wound. The chroniclers record that Bhagwant Das, feeling his honour stained, fell into a kind of madness and stabbed himself. He survived the wound and in time recovered, but the story was remembered at court for years. Badauni, who was often critical of Akbar's policies, told it as proof that even the emperor's closest Rajput allies had their own code that no favour could buy.

Bhagwant Das was a devout Hindu all his life, and the Mughal alliance did not change that. He remained a worshipper of Krishna, and his name is linked with the holy land of **Braj**, around Mathura and Vrindavan, which in his time was being revived by the followers of Chaitanya and Vallabha. The **Harideva temple at Govardhan**, one of the important early temples of that revival, is credited to him. His son Man Singh would carry this patronage further, building the great temple of Govind Dev at Vrindavan in 1590.

Historians have long debated one question about his family. Most sources call Man Singh his son, and that is how the Kachwaha house itself has always remembered him. A few later writers claimed that Man Singh was in fact a nephew whom Bhagwant Das adopted. The question has never been settled, and it changes little: in every account, Man Singh grew up in his household and was his heir.

Bhagwant Das's last years were spent in Lahore, where the court itself stayed for much of the late 1580s while Akbar watched the north-west. In **1589** the empire lost two of its great servants within a few days. Raja **Todar Mal**, the finance minister, died at Lahore, and Bhagwant Das, who attended his funeral rites, fell ill soon after. He died at Lahore in late **1589**, and Man Singh succeeded him as ruler of Amber.

He did not live to see the sorrow that came to his daughter. Years later, as Prince Salim quarrelled with his own son Khusrau, Man Bai, caught between husband and son, took her own life with opium in **1605**. Khusrau's rebellion against his father would end in blindness and, eventually, death. The hope that a grandson of Amber might rule the empire died with them.

Bhagwant Das's choices are still argued over. Some see in his life the surrender of Rajput independence. Others see a ruler who found a way to protect a small and threatened state, and who turned it into one of the strongest houses in northern India. What is not in doubt is that he served with courage, as Sarnal showed, and with a sense of honour that did not disappear when he entered the emperor's service, as Kashmir showed. The Amber of Man Singh and of the Jai Singhs, with its great palaces and its place at the centre of Mughal India, was built on the foundation that he and his father had laid.

## Highlights of his life

- **The Mughal alliance.** After his father's agreement with Akbar in 1562, he entered imperial service and became one of the emperor's most trusted Rajput nobles.
- **Courage at Sarnal (1572).** He fought beside Akbar in the Gujarat campaign, protecting the emperor in a dangerous fight in which his brother Bhupat was killed, and was honoured with a banner and kettledrums.
- **Envoy to Mewar (1573).** He travelled as Akbar's envoy to Maharana Pratap in one of the embassies that sought peace with Mewar.
- **Ruler of Amber (c. 1574–1589).** He brought the small Kachwaha kingdom security and new standing through its bond with the empire.
- **Governor of the Punjab.** He helped hold the Punjab against Mirza Muhammad Hakim and later governed the province from Lahore, with a rank of 5,000.
- **A promise in Kashmir.** When Akbar refused the terms he had given Yusuf Shah Chak, he felt his honour wounded so deeply that he stabbed himself, an episode remembered by the chroniclers.
- **Patron of Braj.** The Harideva temple at Govardhan is credited to him, part of the revival of Krishna worship in Braj.
