## Raja Bhau Singh — the son who stood in a giant's shadow

*Bhau Singh's reign was short, and most of what we know about him comes from the memoirs of the emperor Jahangir and from the family records of Amber. Much of his inner life is lost, and this story does not pretend otherwise; where it describes his world, it describes what is known of that world.*

To be born a son of **Raja Man Singh** was to be born in the shadow of one of the most famous men in India. In the last decades of the sixteenth century, Man Singh of Amber was Akbar's greatest Rajput general. He had governed Kabul, fought at Haldighati, conquered Odisha, and ruled Bihar and Bengal for the empire. His rank stood above almost every other noble of the court. His palace was rising on the ridge at **Amber**, and his name was known from the Khyber to the Bay of Bengal.

**Bhau Singh** was one of his sons. The year of his birth is not recorded with certainty, but he grew up in the 1580s and 1590s, in the years of his father's greatest power. Like other boys of the Kachwaha house, he would have been trained in riding, the sword and the lance, in the management of men and horses, and in the courtly Persian that every noble needed in the emperor's service. He would also have been raised in the faith of his family, which worshipped Krishna and honoured the goddess. It was Man Singh who brought the image of **Shila Devi** from Bengal and installed her at Amber, where she became the guardian goddess of the Kachwahas.

He was not his father's chosen heir. That place belonged to his elder brother, **Jagat Singh**, a brave commander who served with Man Singh in the eastern provinces. But Jagat Singh died young, in **1599**, and his death left a question that would shape the rest of Bhau Singh's life. By Rajput custom, the right of the eldest line passed to Jagat Singh's son, **Maha Singh**. Yet Maha Singh was a youth, and Bhau Singh was a grown son of the reigning raja.

The early years of the seventeenth century were difficult for the house of Amber. When Akbar lay dying in **1605**, Man Singh supported the claim of his own nephew, **Prince Khusrau**, the son of his sister Man Bai, against Khusrau's father, Prince Salim. The plan failed. Salim became the emperor **Jahangir**, and although he did not punish Man Singh openly, he never fully trusted him again. Man Singh was sent away from the centre of power, first to Bengal and later to the Deccan. Khusrau's own rebellion in 1606 ended in his capture and blinding. For the Kachwahas, favour at court, once almost unlimited, now had to be earned again.

Bhau Singh grew to manhood in this cooler climate. As a son of Man Singh he held his own rank in the imperial service and served with the armies of the empire. In these years the Mughal court had two great unfinished wars. One was with **Mewar**, where Maharana Amar Singh I still refused to submit, until the long campaigns ended in the treaty of **1615**. The other was in the **Deccan**, where the able Abyssinian minister **Malik Ambar** of Ahmadnagar was fighting the Mughal armies to a standstill with swift raids and guerrilla warfare. Rajput contingents were sent to both fronts, and the house of Amber had its part in each.

In **1614**, Man Singh died while on campaign in the Deccan, at **Ellichpur**, after a life of nearly fifty years in the emperor's service. Tradition says that many of his queens and women followed him into the fire. His death brought the old question of succession into the open. Should the throne of Amber go to Maha Singh, grandson through the eldest line, as Rajput custom would suggest? Or to Bhau Singh, the surviving son?

The choice did not belong to the Kachwahas alone. In the Mughal system, the emperor confirmed every succession to a great Rajput house by granting the *tika*, the mark of investiture, and the rank that went with it. Jahangir recorded the decision in his own memoirs. He knew, he wrote, that by the custom of the Hindus the succession should go to the grandson, but he did not approve of it, and he gave the honour to Bhau Singh. Bhau Singh received the title of **Mirza Raja**, a high mark of favour that would later be famous in the name of his successor, and a rank among the senior nobles of the empire. Maha Singh was compensated with an increase in his own rank.

Why Jahangir chose as he did, we can only guess. Perhaps he preferred an experienced man to a youth. Perhaps he wished to show that the succession of the great Rajput houses depended on the emperor's will, and not on custom alone. Perhaps he simply trusted Bhau Singh more than the grandson of the man who had once stood against him. Whatever the reason, in **1614** Bhau Singh became the ruler of Amber.

He inherited a state very different from the hill kingdom his great-grandfather had known. Amber was now rich and secure. Its rulers held large estates in other parts of the empire, its revenues had grown, and its capital boasted the new palace on the ridge, the temple of Shila Devi and the strong walls that guarded the valley. The rough, uncertain years of Bharmal's time were gone. The task of the new raja was to keep this inheritance safe, and to hold the family's place at a court where its old influence had faded.

Bhau Singh's reign was spent largely in that service. The records of the period place him among the nobles employed in the imperial armies, and the Deccan, where his father had died, remained the great field of Mughal effort. Between **1616** and **1621**, Prince **Khurram**, the future Shah Jahan, led two major campaigns there against Malik Ambar and his allies, forcing them to give up territory and pay large sums. The Rajput chiefs who served in those armies spent years far from home, in camps where the rains, disease and long marches killed as many men as the enemy did.

At home, the government of Amber was carried on by the raja's officers and kinsmen, as it had been in his father's time. The records preserve little of his own work in Dhundhar: no great building, no major endowment, no famous judgement is firmly linked to his name. This silence is not unusual. In the age of the Mughal alliance, many Rajput rulers spent the greater part of their reigns away from their capitals, and their personal mark on their own lands was often slight. What the family remembered of Bhau Singh was that he kept the throne secure and the house's bond with the empire unbroken through a delicate time.

His reign also saw a turning point in the history of the Rajput states. In **1615**, Maharana **Amar Singh I** of Mewar, worn down by years of war, accepted peace with the empire on honourable terms. He was not required to attend court in person, and his son Karan Singh went in his place. The last of the great Rajput houses to resist had now come to terms. From this time onward, the leading Rajput rulers, Kachwaha, Rathore, Hada and Sisodia alike, were all part of the Mughal system, and the competition between them for rank and favour at court would decide much of their history in the century to come.

The darker side of court life touched Bhau Singh's family closely. Jahangir, who himself struggled with wine and opium for much of his life, noted with disapproval the heavy drinking of several men of Man Singh's line. Maha Singh, the passed-over grandson, died in the Deccan in **1617**, while still young, and Jahangir blamed drink for his death.

Bhau Singh did not long outlive him. He died in **1621**, after a reign of about seven years. Jahangir's memoirs, as they are usually read, say that he too died from excessive drinking. Whatever the exact cause, his death once more left Amber with a question of succession, and once more the emperor answered it.

Bhau Singh left no son who succeeded him. Jahangir turned back to the eldest line, the line he had passed over seven years earlier. The new ruler of Amber was **Jai Singh**, the young son of Maha Singh and great-grandson of Man Singh, a boy of about ten. That boy would grow into **Mirza Raja Jai Singh I**, one of the greatest Rajput generals of the Mughal age, the commander who would one day bring Shivaji to terms at Purandar.

In this way, Bhau Singh's short reign stands as a bridge between two famous men. On one side stands Man Singh, his father, the conqueror of the east. On the other stands Jai Singh I, the great-nephew who succeeded him. Between them, for seven uncertain years, Bhau Singh held the house of Amber steady while its old favour faded and before its new glory began.

He is not remembered for great battles or great buildings. He is remembered, if at all, as a ruler of transition: a son who inherited a giant's throne, kept it in a difficult time, and handed it on unbroken to the line from which Amber's next great age would come.

## Highlights of his life

- **Son of Man Singh.** He was born to Raja Man Singh, Akbar's greatest Rajput general, and grew up during his father's years of power.
- **Chosen by the emperor (1614).** After Man Singh's death in the Deccan, Jahangir chose him over his nephew Maha Singh, setting aside the custom that favoured the eldest line.
- **Mirza Raja.** He received the title of Mirza Raja and a senior rank among the nobles of the empire.
- **Service in the imperial armies.** His reign fell in the years of the long Mughal wars in the Deccan against Malik Ambar, where the Rajput contingents served for years.
- **A reign of continuity.** He kept the throne of Amber secure and the house's bond with the empire unbroken while its old influence at court had faded.
- **Death and succession (1621).** He died after about seven years on the throne, and was succeeded by Jai Singh I, great-grandson of Man Singh, who became the most famous Kachwaha of his age.

## Raja Ram Singh I — the guardian of Shivaji and the general of Assam

*Ram Singh's life comes to us through the Persian histories of Aurangzeb's reign, the letters of the Kachwaha court, Maratha chronicles, and the Ahom chronicles of Assam, the buranjis, which tell of his long war on the Brahmaputra. Where these sources disagree, or where tradition adds to them, this story says so.*

**Ram Singh** was born into the house of Amber as the eldest son of **Mirza Raja Jai Singh I**, at a time when his father was rising to become one of the greatest generals of the Mughal empire. The year of his birth is not firmly recorded. He grew up in the world of the imperial court: among Persian scribes, Rajput horsemen, poets and soldiers, in the great camps that moved with the emperor and in the mansions of the nobles at Agra and Delhi.

As the heir of a great noble, he had a special duty. While his father was away on campaign, in the Deccan, on the north-western frontier, or chasing princes across India in the war of succession, Ram Singh was often at court as the Kachwaha representative. He held his own rank, attended the emperor, and watched over his family's interests. It was a school in politics as much as war. He learned how to read the moods of a court, how to make friends among the nobles, and how quickly favour could change.

That lesson came home to him in **1666**, in the most famous episode of his life. The year before, Jai Singh had brought the Maratha king **Shivaji** to terms at **Purandar**, and had then persuaded him to travel north to meet the emperor **Aurangzeb** at Agra. Jai Singh gave his word that Shivaji would be safe. Since he himself had to stay in the Deccan, he made his son responsible. Ram Singh was to receive Shivaji, look after him at Agra, and stand guarantee for him.

Shivaji arrived near Agra in **May 1666**, with his young son **Sambhaji**. On the day of his audience the emperor was celebrating his birthday, and the hall was full of the great nobles of the empire. Ram Singh brought Shivaji forward. But the Maratha king was given a place among nobles of the rank of 5,000, behind men he regarded as his inferiors, and he received none of the honour he had been led to expect. Angry and humiliated, he turned away and protested aloud, in front of the whole court.

It was a moment of great danger, and Ram Singh stood in the middle of it. Men at court urged the emperor to punish Shivaji severely. Ram Singh, bound by his father's promise, tried to calm the situation and to protect his guest. Shivaji was placed under guard in Agra, and for weeks his fate hung in the balance. Ram Singh, as the Maratha chronicles and the Kachwaha letters both show, gave a written guarantee for him and kept his own men around his lodging. Jai Singh wrote from the Deccan again and again, urging that the promise be honoured.

Then, in **August 1666**, Shivaji vanished. The famous story says that he had begun sending out great baskets of sweets as gifts to holy men and nobles, and that one day he and Sambhaji were carried out hidden in them, while a companion lay in his bed to deceive the guards. However it was done, he escaped from Agra and made his way back to the Deccan.

Aurangzeb was furious, and he suspected that the Kachwahas had helped. Ram Singh was forbidden to come to court and his rank was reduced. Whether he had quietly helped Shivaji or simply failed to stop him, no one has ever proved. But the stain of the escape stayed with him. In the next year his father, recalled in disgrace from the Deccan, died at **Burhanpur** on **28 August 1667**, and Ram Singh became ruler of Amber with the emperor's trust badly shaken.

Aurangzeb soon found him a task. In **1667** the **Ahom** kingdom of Assam, in the valley of the Brahmaputra, had struck back against the Mughals. Under their great general **Lachit Borphukan**, the Ahoms recaptured **Guwahati**, which the Mughals had taken a few years earlier. The emperor ordered Ram Singh to lead an army to Assam and win it back. Many at the time, and many historians since, have seen this as a punishment: a distant, dangerous posting, in a land of rivers, forests and heavy rains, far from Amber and far from court.

Sikh tradition remembers that **Guru Tegh Bahadur**, the ninth Sikh Guru, travelled with Ram Singh on this journey to the east, and that a memorial at **Dhubri** on the Brahmaputra marks a place where he stayed. The Guru is said to have been a friend of the Kachwaha house.

Ram Singh reached the borders of Assam in **1669** with a large army of Rajputs and Mughal troops, and a fleet of boats to carry them on the river. He found himself facing a kind of war that Rajput training had not prepared him for. The Ahoms had built strong earthen ramparts along both banks of the Brahmaputra, closing the approaches to Guwahati, and they fought from these defences and by night attacks, using the forests, hills and the river itself as weapons. Lachit Borphukan avoided pitched battles where the Mughal cavalry would have the advantage.

For two years the campaign dragged on. There were negotiations, broken off and begun again. There were battles, and Ram Singh won some of them. At **Alaboi**, in 1669, the Mughals defeated a large Ahom force and killed many thousands of their men. But victory on land could not break the defences of Guwahati, and the Mughal army was slowly wasting away from disease and the monsoon. The Ahom chronicles record that Ram Singh came to respect the discipline and organisation of his enemy, and that he praised their skill.

The decisive battle came in **March 1671**, at **Saraighat**, on the Brahmaputra near Guwahati, where the river narrows between the hills. Ram Singh sent his fleet to break through. The Ahom boats, lighter and quicker, met them on the water. Lachit Borphukan, gravely ill, had himself carried onto a boat to lead his men, and the Assamese tradition tells how his presence turned a wavering defence into an attack. The Mughal fleet was broken and driven back with heavy losses. Saraighat became one of the most celebrated victories in the history of Assam.

Ram Singh withdrew down the river. He held on for several more years at the edge of Assam, but the campaign was lost. In **1676** he was finally recalled. He had spent nearly a decade in the east, and had come home without the victory the emperor wanted, but with an army that had fought hard in a war few generals of the age could have won.

The years that followed were hard for all the Rajput houses. Aurangzeb's policies grew harsher toward his Hindu subjects. Orders went out against temples, and in Braj, the holy land of Krishna, the great shrines built by the Kachwahas were threatened. The image of **Govind Dev**, worshipped in the temple that Man Singh had built at Vrindavan, was carried away by its priests and eventually found shelter in Kachwaha lands, where the rulers of Amber would later give it a new home. In **1679** the emperor reimposed the **jizya** tax on non-Muslims, and in the same year he began a long war with **Marwar** after the death of Jaswant Singh. Through all of this, Ram Singh kept Amber loyal to the empire. It was a hard choice, but it kept his own lands safe while the Rathores and Sisodias fought.

At home, Ram Singh was a patron of letters. The poet **Kulpati Mishra**, a writer on the art of poetry in Hindi, is remembered as one of the scholars of his court. In this the house of Amber continued the tradition of his father, the patron of Bihari.

His last years brought personal grief. His son **Kishan Singh**, the heir to Amber, died before him, and the succession passed to Kishan Singh's young son, **Bishan Singh**. Ram Singh himself was sent once more to a distant frontier, this time to the north-west, among the Afghan tribes beyond the Indus. He died there, at **Kohat**, in **1688**, still in the service of the empire that had never quite forgiven him.

Ram Singh I has often been overshadowed by his father and by his famous great-grandson, Sawai Jai Singh II. Yet his life touched some of the great moments of seventeenth-century India. He was the guardian of Shivaji at Agra in the year that changed the Maratha story, and the commander who faced Lachit Borphukan at Saraighat. In both, he stood on the losing side of history's memory. But he carried his duty through two of the hardest assignments of the age, and he kept his house intact through the dark years of Aurangzeb's reign.

## Highlights of his life

- **Heir of Mirza Raja Jai Singh I.** He grew up at the imperial court and represented the Kachwaha house there while his father was on campaign.
- **Guardian of Shivaji at Agra (1666).** Bound by his father's promise, he was responsible for the Maratha king's safety; after Shivaji's escape he was disgraced and his rank reduced.
- **Ruler of Amber (1667).** He succeeded after his father's death at Burhanpur in 1667.
- **The Assam campaign (1669–1676).** Sent against the Ahom kingdom, he won at Alaboi but could not break the defences of Guwahati.
- **Saraighat (1671).** His fleet was defeated on the Brahmaputra by Lachit Borphukan, one of the most celebrated victories in Assam's history.
- **Companion of Guru Tegh Bahadur.** Sikh tradition remembers that the ninth Guru travelled with him to the east.
- **Death on the frontier (1688).** He died at Kohat on the north-western frontier and was succeeded by his grandson Bishan Singh.

## Raja Bishan Singh — the young raja between two great names

*Bishan Singh ruled for only about eleven years, and he left a light footprint in the records. What we know comes mostly from the Persian histories of Aurangzeb's reign and from the papers of the Kachwaha court. This story keeps to what those sources say, and describes the world he lived in where his own life is silent.*

**Bishan Singh** was born into the house of Amber in the later years of the seventeenth century, the son of **Kunwar Kishan Singh** and grandson of **Raja Ram Singh I**. The exact year of his birth is not certain, but he was still a young man when he came to the throne. His family carried both great fame and a long shadow. His great-grandfather, **Mirza Raja Jai Singh I**, had been one of the greatest generals of the Mughal empire. His grandfather, Ram Singh, had been the guardian from whom Shivaji escaped at Agra in 1666, and had spent nearly a decade fighting a losing war against the Ahoms in Assam.

His path to the throne was shaped by loss. His father, the heir to Amber, died before Ram Singh. When the old raja himself died on the north-western frontier in **1688**, the throne passed directly to his grandson. The emperor **Aurangzeb** confirmed the succession, and Bishan Singh became the ruler of Amber. In that same year, on **3 November 1688**, his first son was born. The child was named Jai Singh, and he would become **Sawai Jai Singh II**, the astronomer-king who founded Jaipur.

Bishan Singh came to power at a difficult time. Aurangzeb was spending the rest of his life in the **Deccan**, fighting the Marathas. Bijapur had fallen in 1686 and Golconda in 1687, and in **1689** the Maratha king **Sambhaji** was captured and executed. But the Marathas fought on, and the emperor's armies were tied down in the south. Northern India, left without its emperor, was growing restless.

Nowhere was this more true than around **Agra and Mathura**, close to the borders of Amber. Here the **Jat** peasants and chiefs had risen against Mughal authority. Under **Rajaram** they raided Mughal roads and towns, and in **1688** they attacked and plundered the tomb of **Akbar** at **Sikandra**. Later writers said they even burned the emperor's bones; that is uncertain, but the attack was a heavy blow to Mughal prestige. Rajaram was killed the same year, but the Jats fought on from **Sinsini** and other fortified villages in the ravines of the Braj country.

Aurangzeb turned to the young ruler of Amber. Bishan Singh was appointed to lead the campaign against the Jats and keep order in the Mathura region, and he was promised that the lands he subdued would go to his house. It was a test. The Kachwahas had lost favour since the Agra affair, and this was a chance to win it back.

The campaign was hard. The Jat villages were defended by mud walls, ditches and thorn, and their defenders fought stubbornly. Bishan Singh served alongside Aurangzeb's grandson **Prince Bidar Bakht**, who held the overall command. Together they besieged **Sinsini**, and after a long siege the stronghold fell in early **1690**. The campaign brought Bishan Singh rank, favour and new rights for Amber in the country towards Agra. But it did not end the Jat struggle. Within a few years **Churaman** gathered the Jats again, and in the next century his successors would found the kingdom of **Bharatpur**.

Of Bishan Singh's life at Amber we know little. Like his ancestors, he spent much of his time in the emperor's service, and his state was run by ministers and kinsmen. The worship of Shila Devi, the guardian goddess of the house, continued as it had since Man Singh's day. In these years, when Aurangzeb's orders reached the temples of Braj, the image of **Govind Dev** had found shelter in Kachwaha territory, cared for by its priests.

He was also a father. His sons **Jai Singh** and **Vijay Singh** were brought up at Amber and at court. The elder boy was quick, curious and well educated, and he would later show a deep love of mathematics and astronomy.

Bishan Singh died in **1699**, still a young man, after a reign of about eleven years. The records say little about his last years or the manner of his death. His son Jai Singh, then about eleven, was confirmed by Aurangzeb as ruler of Amber, and before long the emperor gave him the title **Sawai**, "one and a quarter", which stayed with the rulers of Jaipur ever after.

Bishan Singh's reign has always lived in the shadow of the men around him. Yet it was not an empty pause. He came to the throne young, in a house that had lost the emperor's trust, and won back favour through a hard campaign in a time of unrest. He left his son a secure throne, new lands, and a place at court from which the boy could rise.

## Highlights of his life

- **Grandson of Ram Singh I.** He succeeded his grandfather in 1688, because his father Kishan Singh had died before him.
- **Father of Sawai Jai Singh II.** His eldest son, born in 1688, became the astronomer-king who founded Jaipur.
- **Campaign against the Jats.** With Prince Bidar Bakht he took part in the siege and capture of the Jat stronghold of Sinsini in 1690.
- **Restoring the family's standing.** His service won back imperial favour lost after Shivaji's escape from Agra.
- **New lands for Amber.** The Jat campaign brought his house new rights in the country towards Agra.
- **Early death (1699).** He died young after about eleven years on the throne, leaving Amber to his son.

## Mirza Raja Jai Singh I — the general of three emperors

*Jai Singh I is one of the best-documented Rajputs of the Mughal age. His life comes to us through the Persian histories of Shah Jahan's and Aurangzeb's reigns, through his own letters, through Maratha chronicles, and through the poetry written at his court. Where tradition adds to the record, this story says so.*

On **15 July 1611**, a son was born in the palace at **Amber** to **Maha Singh**, the grandson of the great Raja Man Singh. The boy was named **Jai Singh**. His birth did not seem to promise a throne. His father's line, the eldest line of the house, had been passed over: when Man Singh died in 1614, the emperor Jahangir gave Amber to Man Singh's son **Bhau Singh** instead of to Maha Singh. Maha Singh died in the Deccan in 1617, and the boy grew up as the son of a disappointed prince.

Then fortune turned. In **1621** Bhau Singh died without an heir to follow him, and Jahangir, choosing again, gave the throne to the eldest line after all. Jai Singh, a child of about ten, became the ruler of Amber. For several years the state was managed, according to family tradition, by his mother and by the officers of the house, while the young raja was trained for the life that awaited every Kachwaha ruler: service in the imperial armies.

He began that service early. While still in his teens he was riding with the Mughal forces, and when **Shah Jahan** came to the throne in **1628**, Jai Singh's career began to rise quickly. He fought in the Deccan against rebels and against the Deccan sultanates, and he showed the qualities that would mark his whole life: courage in battle, patience in a long campaign, and an unusual skill in persuading enemies to become allies. Shah Jahan rewarded him with higher and higher ranks, and with the title of **Mirza Raja**, by which he is remembered. The title, which joined a Persian honour to a Hindu one, suited a man who lived comfortably in both worlds. Tradition says he spoke several languages, and his letters show a mind at ease in Persian statecraft.

Through the 1630s, 1640s and 1650s he served wherever the empire sent him. He took part in the hard campaigns in the far north-west, where the Mughals struggled with the Safavid shahs of Persia over the fortress of **Kandahar**. In 1649, 1652 and 1653 imperial armies besieged Kandahar, and each time they failed, defeated by strong walls, distance and the cold. Jai Singh was among the commanders who knew these bitter marches. They taught him that war was won as much by supplies, roads and diplomacy as by courage.

In **1657** Shah Jahan fell seriously ill, and his four sons, **Dara Shikoh**, **Shah Shuja**, **Aurangzeb** and **Murad Bakhsh**, began a war for the throne. Jai Singh was sent with Dara's son **Sulaiman Shikoh** to stop Shah Shuja, who was marching from Bengal. In **February 1658**, at **Bahadurpur** near Benares, Jai Singh and Sulaiman Shikoh surprised Shuja's camp at dawn and routed his army. It was the first great victory of the war.

But elsewhere, everything was changing. In May 1658 Aurangzeb and Murad defeated Dara at **Samugarh**, near Agra. Dara fled, Shah Jahan was confined in the fort of Agra, and Aurangzeb took power. Jai Singh, far away with Sulaiman's army, had to decide where his future lay. He chose Aurangzeb. He left the young prince and went over to the new ruler, bringing much of the army with him. It was a hard and calculated decision, and it has been judged harshly by some. But Jai Singh had served the empire for thirty years, and he served it now under the man who held it.

He proved valuable at once. When **Jaswant Singh of Marwar**, who had changed sides during the war, was ready to join Dara again, Jai Singh wrote to him and persuaded him to stay away. Without Jaswant's Rathores, Dara faced Aurangzeb almost alone, and in **March 1659** he was defeated at **Deorai**, near Ajmer. Jai Singh was sent in pursuit as Dara fled west. Dara was finally betrayed by an Afghan chief and handed over, and Aurangzeb had him executed in 1659. In the new reign, Jai Singh stood among the first nobles of the empire.

His greatest task came a few years later. In the Deccan, a new power had risen: the Maratha leader **Shivaji**. He had defeated the Bijapur general Afzal Khan in 1659, surprised and wounded the Mughal governor **Shaista Khan** in his own quarters at Pune in 1663, and sacked the rich port of **Surat** in 1664. Aurangzeb needed a commander who could deal with him. He chose Jai Singh.

Jai Singh arrived in the Deccan in **1665** with a large army and with the Afghan general **Diler Khan**. He did not waste time chasing Shivaji's swift horsemen through the hills. Instead he struck at the heart of Maratha power: its forts. He laid siege to **Purandar**, one of the strongest, and at the same time sent forces to burn and lay waste the surrounding country so that the Marathas could not support their garrisons. The defenders fought bravely. The Maratha commander **Murarbaji Deshpande** was killed in a desperate sally, and the fort was close to falling.

Shivaji understood that he could not hold out. He came in person to Jai Singh's camp to negotiate. The meeting of the two men, the old Rajput general and the young Maratha king, has been told many times. Jai Singh received him with courtesy and firmness. In **June 1665** they agreed the **Treaty of Purandar**. Shivaji gave up twenty-three of his forts, with the lands around them, and kept twelve. His young son **Sambhaji** received a Mughal rank of 5,000, and Shivaji agreed to help the Mughals against Bijapur.

It was the greatest diplomatic success of Jai Singh's life. But it was followed by two disappointments. The first was the campaign against **Bijapur** in 1665–66. Jai Singh's army marched almost to the walls of the city, but Bijapur's forces burned the countryside, poisoned the wells and harried the Mughal columns, and Jai Singh, short of supplies and money, had to retreat.

The second was far worse. Jai Singh had persuaded Shivaji to go north to meet the emperor at **Agra**, giving his word that he would be safe. His son **Ram Singh** was to look after the Maratha king at court. In **May 1666** Shivaji came before Aurangzeb, but he was given a place among nobles of lower rank, and he protested angrily before the whole court. He was placed under guard. Jai Singh wrote from the Deccan, urging that his promise be honoured. In August 1666 Shivaji escaped from Agra, according to the famous story hidden in great baskets of sweets, and made his way back to the Deccan.

Aurangzeb suspected that the Kachwahas had helped. Ram Singh was disgraced, and Jai Singh, his campaign against Bijapur a failure, was recalled from the Deccan. Worn out, the old general set out for the north. He never reached it. On **28 August 1667** he died at **Burhanpur**. Rumours spread that he had been poisoned, and some later writers accused the emperor or men around him. Nothing has ever been proven. What is certain is that he died in the service he had given his whole life to, at the age of fifty-six.

For all his years in camps, Jai Singh did not forget Amber. Tradition credits him with some of the finest parts of the **Amber palace**, among them the halls of the inner palace with their mirror-work and carved marble, which made Amber one of the most beautiful palaces in India. He was also a patron of poets. The great Hindi poet **Bihari** lived at his court, and his *Satsai*, a collection of some seven hundred couplets, is one of the treasures of Hindi literature. Tradition tells that when the raja, newly married to a young queen, neglected the business of the state, Bihari sent him a couplet about a bee so lost in an unopened bud that it forgot everything else, and that Jai Singh, understanding, returned to his duties and rewarded the poet.

His title and his fame passed to his son Ram Singh, who succeeded him. In later centuries the name **Mirza Raja** became almost his own, and historians of the Mughal age place him among the ablest generals and diplomats the empire ever had. He served Jahangir, Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb, held the highest rank open to a noble, and through all of it remained a Rajput ruler devoted to his own house and faith. His life shows both the greatness and the cost of the Mughal alliance: a Kachwaha who could bring Shivaji to terms, but who could not make an emperor keep his word.

## Highlights of his life

- **Child ruler (1621).** Born in 1611, he became ruler of Amber at about ten, when Jahangir returned the throne to the eldest line of Man Singh's house.
- **Mirza Raja.** Shah Jahan gave him the title by which he is remembered, and he rose to the highest rank of the Mughal nobility.
- **Victory at Bahadurpur (1658).** With Sulaiman Shikoh he defeated Shah Shuja near Benares in the war of succession, before joining Aurangzeb.
- **Keeping Jaswant Singh away from Dara.** His persuasion helped leave Dara without Rathore support before his defeat at Deorai in 1659.
- **Treaty of Purandar (1665).** After besieging Purandar he brought Shivaji to terms, gaining twenty-three Maratha forts for the empire.
- **The Agra affair (1666).** He gave his word for Shivaji's safety; Shivaji's detention and escape ended his last campaign in disappointment.
- **Patron of Bihari.** The poet Bihari wrote his *Satsai* at his court, and tradition credits him with some of the finest halls of the Amber palace.

## Maharaja Ishwari Singh — the king of the tower and the poison cup

*Ishwari Singh's short and tragic reign is known from Persian and Marathi records of the time, from the papers of the Jaipur court, and from the memory of the city itself, where his victory tower still stands. Where tradition adds to the record, this story says so.*

**Ishwari Singh** was born around **1721**, the eldest son of **Sawai Jai Singh II**, the astronomer-king who had built the new city of **Jaipur** and its great observatory. He grew up in the most splendid court in Rajasthan, among scholars, architects and poets, in a city whose broad, straight streets were still being laid out.

But a promise made before his birth would poison his whole life. In **1708**, when Jai Singh II was seeking allies against the emperor Bahadur Shah, he married **Chandra Kunwari**, a princess of **Mewar**. As the price of that alliance, Mewar demanded that her son, whatever his birth order, should inherit Jaipur. In **1728** she bore a son, **Madho Singh**. Jai Singh II did not keep the promise. He raised Ishwari Singh as his heir, and Madho Singh was given the estate of Rampura by his mother's family in Mewar.

When Jai Singh II died in **September 1743**, Ishwari Singh became Maharaja. At once Madho Singh, backed by his uncle **Maharana Jagat Singh II** of Mewar, claimed the throne. The old order that had protected Rajasthan was gone. The Mughal emperors were now weak, and the **Marathas** were sweeping north, selling their swords to whichever side paid more. Every Rajput quarrel became a door through which they could enter.

The war of succession was fought for seven years. Ishwari Singh's first great test came in **March 1747** at **Rajmahal**, on the banks of the Banas. There he faced a coalition gathered for Madho Singh, including the forces of Mewar and of the Hada chiefs of Kota and Bundi. Ishwari Singh won a clear victory. To celebrate it he raised a tall tower near the Tripolia gate of Jaipur, the **Isarlat**, also called the **Swargasuli**, "the spire that pierces heaven". Completed around **1749**, it still looks down over the city's bazaars.

The next year brought a different enemy. In early **1748** the Afghan king **Ahmad Shah Abdali** invaded the Punjab, and the Mughal emperor called on his nobles to meet him. Ishwari Singh marched with the imperial army. At **Manupur**, near Sirhind, in March 1748, the Mughals won, but the old wazir Qamar-ud-din Khan was killed, and contemporary accounts say that Ishwari Singh left the field during the fighting. It was a stain on his name that his enemies did not forget.

In **August 1748** the war at home turned against him. Madho Singh returned, this time with the Maratha general **Malhar Rao Holkar** and his allies. The armies met near **Bagru**, west of Jaipur. For days the fighting went on through the rains, and Ishwari Singh's forces were worn down. At last he was forced to agree to terms. Madho Singh was to receive several districts of the Jaipur state, and the Marathas were promised large sums of money. In the same year, Holkar helped **Umed Singh** recover the throne of Bundi, which Jaipur had long controlled.

The peace of Bagru solved nothing. The treasury Jai Singh II had left was empty, and the Marathas pressed for payment. Inside the court, rivalries grew bitter. Ishwari Singh's minister **Keshavdas** was accused of treachery by his rival **Hargovind Natani**, and the Maharaja allowed him to be put to death, by poison according to most accounts. Later he came to believe that Keshavdas had been innocent and that he had been deceived. Hargovind, now in control of the army, did little to raise the forces the kingdom needed.

In **December 1750**, Malhar Rao Holkar marched on Jaipur once more, demanding what had been promised. Ishwari Singh found that he had neither money nor an army ready to fight. His commander had failed him, his allies were gone, and his enemies were at the gates. He was still a young man, not yet thirty.

He chose not to be taken. According to the accounts of the time, the Maharaja took poison in his palace. Tradition adds that he also had a cobra brought to bite him, so that there could be no mistake. He died in mid-**December 1750**. Several of his queens and women followed him into the funeral fire.

Madho Singh entered Jaipur and took the throne as **Sawai Madho Singh I**. The Marathas who came with him soon wore out their welcome. In January 1751 the people of Jaipur rose against the Maratha soldiers in the city and killed a large number of them, a sign of how bitter the years of war and demands had become.

Ishwari Singh is often remembered as a weak ruler, a man who fled at Manupur and gave up at Bagru. But his story is also a tragedy. He inherited a broken promise, a divided family and a rich kingdom in an age when the empire that had protected it was falling apart. He won his greatest battle at Rajmahal, and he lost to forces far larger than any one Rajput state. The tower he raised, the Isarlat, still rises over Jaipur, a monument to the one victory of a king whose reign ended in a poison cup.

## Highlights of his life

- **Heir of Sawai Jai Singh II.** The eldest son of Jaipur's founder, he became Maharaja in 1743.
- **War with Madho Singh.** He fought his half-brother, whose claim rested on a promise made to Mewar in 1708.
- **Victory at Rajmahal (1747).** He defeated a coalition gathered for Madho Singh on the banks of the Banas.
- **The Isarlat.** He raised the Isarlat, or Swargasuli, the victory tower of Jaipur, completed around 1749.
- **Bagru (1748).** Facing Madho Singh and Malhar Rao Holkar, he was forced to give up districts and promise large payments.
- **Tragic end (1750).** As Holkar marched on Jaipur, he took his own life by poison, and Madho Singh I succeeded him.

## Maharaja Sawai Madho Singh I — the prince of a broken promise who won the throne of Jaipur

*Madho Singh's life is recorded in the Persian and Rajasthani chronicles of the eighteenth century, in Maratha correspondence and in the archives of the Jaipur court; the poets of his age added their own colour, and where they go beyond the record, this story says so.*

In the spring of **1708**, long before Madho Singh was born, a marriage was arranged that would shape his whole life. **Sawai Jai Singh II** of Amber, then a young ruler struggling to recover his own throne from the Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah, sought the help of **Maharana Amar Singh II** of Mewar. The price of that help was a bride and a promise. Jai Singh married the Maharana's daughter, **Chandra Kunwar**, and agreed that any son she bore would succeed to the throne of Amber ahead of his sons by other wives. It was an old Mewar demand, the pride of the Sisodias asserted over a house that had long served the Mughals, and Jai Singh accepted it because he needed Mewar's swords.

For twenty years the promise slept. Jai Singh recovered Amber, rose to be one of the greatest nobles of the empire, governed Malwa and Agra for the emperors, built observatories at Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Mathura and Varanasi, and in **1727** laid out the new city of **Jaipur** on the plain below the old hill capital. He had other sons, and the eldest surviving, **Ishwari Singh**, was raised as the heir. Then, around **1728**, the Sisodia queen at last bore a son. He was named **Madho Singh**, and from the day of his birth he was a living question mark over the succession of the most splendid state in Rajputana.

Jai Singh did not openly break with his eldest son. Instead he made provision for the younger. With Mewar's agreement, the boy received the district of **Rampura**, on the borders of Mewar and Malwa, as his own estate. Madho Singh grew up partly at his mother's side in the new palaces of Jaipur and partly in the orbit of his maternal kin at Udaipur, where the Maharanas never forgot that their daughter's son had been promised a throne. He learned to ride and to shoot, to read Persian and Sanskrit, and to watch the faces of men at court. Those who knew him later spoke of a sharp mind, a long memory and a patience that could wait years for its moment.

His moment seemed to come in **1743**, when Sawai Jai Singh II died. Ishwari Singh was proclaimed Maharaja in Jaipur. Madho Singh, then about fifteen, was at Udaipur, and his uncle, **Maharana Jagat Singh II**, took up his cause. What followed was seven years of family war, fought with Rajput armies and, increasingly, with the hired strength of the Marathas, who were now the great military power of central India.

In the first round, Ishwari Singh had the better of it. In **1747**, at **Rajmahal** on the Banas, he defeated a coalition that had gathered in Madho Singh's name, including forces of Mewar, Kota and Bundi. To celebrate the victory he raised a tall tower in Jaipur, the **Isarlat**, which still stands above the bazaars. But Madho Singh did not give up. He turned to **Malhar Rao Holkar**, the Maratha chief who would bargain with anyone who could pay. In **1748**, at **Bagru**, a few miles from Jaipur, an army of Holkar's horsemen and Madho Singh's Rajput allies forced Ishwari Singh to terms. The elder brother agreed to hand over several districts to the younger, and to pay the Marathas for their trouble.

The settlement did not hold, because the money could not be paid. Jaipur's treasury, emptied by war and by Jai Singh's great building projects, could not meet Maratha demands. In **December 1750**, Holkar's army approached Jaipur once more. Ishwari Singh, exhausted, abandoned by many of his nobles and unwilling to face humiliation, took his own life. The chroniclers say he died by poison, and that some of his queens chose to die with him.

So it was that, in the last days of 1750, Madho Singh entered Jaipur not as a conqueror but as the heir of a tragedy. He was crowned as **Sawai Madho Singh**, and he inherited, along with the throne, the Maratha armies camped at the city's gates and the debts that had destroyed his brother.

The first weeks of his reign were among the most violent in Jaipur's history. Maratha soldiers had entered the city in large numbers, and in **January 1751** the townspeople, provoked by their behaviour and encouraged, many believed, by the court itself, rose against them. Many Maratha soldiers were killed in the streets before order was restored. Whether Madho Singh planned the rising or merely allowed it, it sent a message: the new Maharaja had used the Marathas to gain power, but he did not intend to be their client. The relationship between Jaipur and the Maratha chiefs, especially the Holkars and the Scindias, would remain tense and expensive for the rest of the century.

Madho Singh's reign of eighteen years was a long struggle to hold together what his father had built. Jaipur was rich in trade and craft, but it was surrounded by ambitious neighbours. To the east, the **Jats of Bharatpur** under **Suraj Mal** had grown from rebels into a real power, holding forts and lands that had once looked to Jaipur. To the south, the Marathas demanded tribute. In Delhi, the Mughal throne had become weak and divided, its emperors raised and removed by their own ministers.

Madho Singh used the weakness of Delhi to his advantage. One of his greatest gains was the old fortress of **Ranthambhore**, which had been held by Mughal garrisons for nearly two centuries. In the 1750s, the emperor's grant gave the fort to Jaipur, and after a long contest with Maratha claims Madho Singh secured it. Near its foot, in **1763**, he founded a new town and named it after himself: **Sawai Madhopur**. It remains one of the major towns of eastern Rajasthan, and the gateway to the forests around the old fort.

In **1761**, when the Maratha armies and the Afghan king **Ahmad Shah Abdali** met at **Panipat** in one of the bloodiest battles of the century, Madho Singh did not send his army to the field. Like most Rajput rulers, he had no love for the Maratha demands that had bled his state, and he kept his distance from both sides. The crushing Maratha defeat at Panipat gave Rajputana a breathing space of some years, and Jaipur used it to recover.

But the Jats pressed harder. After Suraj Mal's death in **1763**, his son **Jawahar Singh** sought to prove himself. In **1767** he marched his army through Jaipur territory to bathe at the sacred lake of **Pushkar**, without asking leave, a deliberate insult to the Kachwaha house. On his return, in **December 1767**, the Jaipur army met him at **Maonda**, near the hills of Shekhawati. The battle was fierce. The Jats were driven from the field and Jawahar Singh's power never recovered from the blow, but the victory cost Jaipur dearly: many of its leading nobles fell that day, and the chroniclers remembered Maonda as a victory paid for with the flower of the Kachwaha clans.

Madho Singh himself was by now unwell. He had spent his life in conflict, first with his brother, then with the Marathas and the Jats, and his health was failing. Yet he did not neglect the city his father had founded. Jaipur under Madho Singh continued to grow as a centre of trade, banking and craft. The court workshops of painters, jewellers and textile makers flourished, and the Maharaja patronised poets and musicians, maintained the temples of the city, and kept up the festivals, the processions of **Teej** and **Gangaur**, that gave Jaipur its public life. He extended and adorned the palace and buildings of the city, and the grand style of Jaipur's architecture, with its painted walls and broad bazaars, was carried forward in his time.

He was also a careful manager of his nobles. The Kachwaha state was a federation of powerful clans, the **Rajawats**, **Nathawats**, **Shekhawats** and others, each with its own forts and followers. A Maharaja who could not hold their loyalty could not hold Jaipur. Madho Singh, who had once been an outsider supported by foreign arms, worked to bind them to the throne through honours, land grants and marriage alliances.

His character divided those who wrote about him. To his supporters he was the rightful heir by his father's sworn word, a prince who waited, endured defeat and finally prevailed. To others he was the man who had brought the Marathas into Rajputana's family quarrels, a door that could not afterwards be closed. Both views hold some truth. The Maratha intervention that he invited became a burden on Jaipur, and on all of Rajputana, for the next seventy years. Yet he also ended the civil war, saved the state from partition, added Ranthambhore to its lands, and fought off the Jat challenge.

Madho Singh died on **5 March 1768**, still in middle age. He left two young sons, **Prithvi Singh**, a boy of about six, and the even younger **Pratap Singh**. Both would rule Jaipur in turn. The kingdom he left them was intact and still wealthy, but it was ringed by enemies and governed, for many years to come, by regents and ministers rather than by a grown king. The prince of the broken promise had fought his whole life to win the throne and keep it, and in the end he had done both.

## Highlights of his life

- **Son of the Mewar promise.** Born around 1728 to Sawai Jai Singh II and the Sisodia princess Chandra Kunwar, under a 1708 agreement that her son would succeed in Amber.
- **War of succession.** He contested the throne with his elder brother Ishwari Singh, lost at Rajmahal (1747), and with Maratha help forced a settlement at Bagru (1748).
- **Accession in 1750.** He became Maharaja after Ishwari Singh's suicide in December 1750, and soon showed that he would not be a Maratha client.
- **Ranthambhore and Sawai Madhopur.** He secured the old fortress of Ranthambhore for Jaipur and founded the town of Sawai Madhopur in 1763.
- **Victory at Maonda (1767).** His army defeated Jawahar Singh of Bharatpur, ending the Jat challenge to Jaipur at heavy cost to the Kachwaha nobility.
- **Patron of Jaipur.** He kept the new city growing as a centre of trade and craft, and supported its painters, poets, temples and festivals.
- **Death in 1768.** He died on 5 March 1768, leaving the throne to his young sons Prithvi Singh and Pratap Singh.

## Maharaja Sawai Prithvi Singh — the boy king of a besieged inheritance

*Prithvi Singh ruled as a child, and his reign is known mostly through the chronicles of the Jaipur court and the records of the powers that pressed upon it; little of his own voice survives, and where the accounts are uncertain, this story says so.*

When **Sawai Madho Singh I** died in **March 1768**, the palace of Jaipur filled with the sound of mourning and, behind it, the quieter sound of men calculating. The Maharaja had fought for eighteen years to win and hold his throne. Now he left it to a boy. His elder son, **Prithvi Singh**, born around **1762**, was about six years old. His younger son, **Pratap Singh**, was younger still. Neither could lead an army, sit in judgement or face the envoys of the Marathas. Yet one of them had to be Maharaja, and so, in the spring of 1768, the child Prithvi Singh was carried to the throne of the Kachwahas and proclaimed **Sawai Prithvi Singh**.

We can imagine the scene as the court poets would have described it: the small boy in heavy brocade, the turban jewel almost too large for his head, the nobles of the great clans filing past to offer their swords hilt first in token of loyalty, the priests chanting, the drums of the city sounding from the gateways of the palace. But the boy on the throne did not rule. Power lay with those who stood around him.

The government of Jaipur passed into the hands of a regency. The queen mother, the widows of Madho Singh, the chief ministers and the great nobles all claimed a share. The chroniclers of Jaipur describe a court divided into factions, each trying to control the young Maharaja and the treasury that went with him. Some accounts speak of the rise of palace favourites, men of humble origin who won the trust of the women of the zenana and used it to gain wealth and influence, to the fury of the old Rajput nobility. The details are coloured by the hostility of those who wrote them, but the picture is clear enough: for ten years, Jaipur was governed by a regency that was neither united nor strong.

This was a dangerous weakness, because the world around Jaipur was changing fast. Madho Singh's last great battle, at **Maonda** in **December 1767**, had broken the momentum of the **Jats of Bharatpur**. Their ruler **Jawahar Singh** was murdered in **1768**, the same year Prithvi Singh came to the throne, and the Jat state fell into its own quarrels. For a short time Jaipur's eastern border was quieter. But other forces were gathering.

The Marathas, crushed at **Panipat** in **1761**, had recovered. By **1770** their armies were again marching north of the Chambal, and in **1772** they escorted the Mughal emperor **Shah Alam II** back into Delhi, making him for a time their protégé. For Jaipur this meant the return of the old demands: tribute, arrears and the threat of the horsemen who came to collect them. A child king and a quarrelling court were in no position to refuse.

At the same time a new figure rose in the imperial service: **Mirza Najaf Khan**, a gifted Persian general who rebuilt the emperor's army in the 1770s. Najaf Khan drove the Jats from **Agra** and then from their great fortress of **Deeg**, and he looked to the Rajput states, Jaipur above all, as a source of the tribute the empire needed to survive. Envoys rode between Delhi and Jaipur, demanding payments the regency could not easily make. Every year of Prithvi Singh's reign brought another messenger with another claim.

The most lasting loss of these years came not from outside but from within the Kachwaha family itself. In the north-east of the state lay the lands of the **Narukas**, a Kachwaha branch descended from the same house as the Maharajas of Jaipur. Their chief, **Pratap Singh Naruka** of **Macheri**, was ambitious and capable. He had served Jaipur in war, including, it is said, at Maonda, and he had been rewarded. But he quarrelled with the court, and in the confusion of the regency he began to act as an independent ruler. He gathered lands, built up his own army, and in **1775** took the fort of **Alwar**. From that moment Alwar was a separate state, and the Naruka chiefs who ruled it would never again bow to Jaipur as their master. A boy king could not stop a seasoned soldier from carving a kingdom out of his inheritance, and the regency was too divided to try.

Inside Jaipur, life went on. The city that **Sawai Jai Singh II** had founded in 1727 was by now a busy centre of trade and craft. Its bankers lent money across northern India. Its jewellers cut stones for princes, its dyers and printers made the textiles that were sold in markets far away, and its painters worked in the palace workshops. The festivals continued: the procession of **Gangaur** in spring, when the goddess was carried through the streets, and the swings and songs of **Teej** in the rains. Whatever the troubles of the court, the city kept its rhythm. The young Maharaja would have watched these processions from the palace windows, learning the rituals that a Kachwaha king was expected to perform.

His education followed the pattern of a Rajput prince. He learned to ride and to use the sword and the bow, to read and write, and to perform the daily worship of the family deities. Tutors taught him the history of his house: of **Raja Man Singh**, the great general of Akbar; of **Mirza Raja Jai Singh**, who had served Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb; and of his own grandfather Sawai Jai Singh II, astronomer and city-builder. These were large shadows for a boy to grow up beneath.

We know little of Prithvi Singh's own character. The sources treat him mostly as a name at the centre of other men's struggles. Some later accounts describe him as gentle and devout. Others note only that he was too young to rule, and that the real decisions were made by others. Whether he would have grown into a strong king, able to master his nobles and face the Marathas, no one can say, because he was never given the time.

In **April 1778**, when he was about sixteen, Prithvi Singh died. The accounts differ on how. The most common tradition says that he was injured in a fall from his horse and did not recover. Others, in the atmosphere of suspicion that surrounded the court, whispered of poison, though there is no proof of this. What is certain is that the young Maharaja died before he had ever truly ruled, and that the throne passed to his younger brother, **Pratap Singh**, then a boy of about thirteen.

The reign of Prithvi Singh is often passed over in the histories of Jaipur, because so little happened that he himself decided. Yet the years from 1768 to 1778 mattered. They were the years when the Marathas returned to the north, when the Mughal emperor became a pawn of his generals, and when Jaipur lost the lands that became the state of Alwar. They showed how much the Kachwaha state depended on the strength of its ruler, and how quickly ambitious nobles and foreign armies moved in when that strength was missing.

When Pratap Singh came to the throne, he inherited the same problems: the Maratha demands, the claims of Delhi, a court of quarrelling factions, and a treasury that was never full enough. He would face them with more energy, fighting the Scindias on the battlefield and filling Jaipur with poetry and buildings, including the **Hawa Mahal**. But the story of his brother is a reminder that kingship in eighteenth-century Rajputana was not only a matter of crowns and ceremony. It was a fragile thing, held together by the ruler's own person. For ten years, Jaipur's king was a child, and Jaipur paid the price.

## Highlights of his life

- **Child king.** Born around 1762, he succeeded his father Sawai Madho Singh I in 1768 at about six years old.
- **A divided regency.** His reign was governed by the queen mother, ministers and nobles, whose quarrels weakened the state.
- **Return of the Marathas.** After 1770 the Marathas came back to the north and renewed their demands for tribute from Jaipur.
- **Pressure from Delhi.** The imperial general Mirza Najaf Khan, who drove the Jats from Agra and Deeg, pressed Jaipur for tribute.
- **Loss of Alwar.** The Naruka chief Pratap Singh of Macheri broke away and took Alwar in 1775, founding a separate state.
- **Early death.** He died in April 1778 at about sixteen, most accounts say after a fall from his horse, and was succeeded by his younger brother Pratap Singh.

pratap-singh-amber.story:
## Maharaja Sawai Pratap Singh — the poet king of the Palace of Winds

*Pratap Singh's reign is recorded in the Jaipur court archives, in Maratha and British records, and in his own verses written under the name Brajnidhi; the legends of the court add colour, and where they go beyond the record, this story says so.*

In **April 1778**, the throne of Jaipur passed for the second time in ten years to a boy. **Sawai Prithvi Singh**, who had ruled in name since the age of six, was dead at sixteen. His younger brother, **Pratap Singh**, born on **2 December 1764** to **Sawai Madho Singh I**, was now about thirteen. He was led into the hall of audience, seated on the cushion of the Kachwaha kings and proclaimed **Sawai Pratap Singh**. Around him stood the same divided court that had ruled in his brother's name: ministers, queens, favourites and nobles, each with an eye on the treasury.

The boy who sat there would surprise them. Pratap Singh grew into one of the most remarkable men ever to rule Jaipur, not because he won great wars, for he did not, but because in an age of constant danger he made his court one of the brightest centres of poetry, music and painting in northern India, and left the city a building that has become its symbol.

His first years were spent learning to survive. The factions that had ruled for Prithvi Singh fought on, and the young Maharaja learned to watch, to listen and to wait. Outside the palace, the great question of the age was who would control the remains of the Mughal empire. The imperial general **Mirza Najaf Khan** died in **1782**, and after a period of confusion his place was taken by the most powerful Maratha chief of the north, **Mahadji Scindia**. By **1784** Mahadji was master of Delhi in the emperor's name, and he turned to the Rajput states to pay for his armies. Jaipur, the richest of them, was asked first and asked most.

Pratap Singh, now a young man, refused to be bled without a fight. He found an ally in **Maharaja Vijay Singh** of **Jodhpur**, whose Rathore cavalry was famous across India. In **1787**, the armies of Jaipur and Jodhpur gathered against Mahadji. They met near **Tunga**, south-east of Jaipur, in the heat of **July 1787**. The Rathore horsemen charged with their old ferocity, and the fighting was hard. In the middle of the campaign, Mughal troops in Mahadji's service went over to the Rajput side, and one of his commanders, **Muhammad Beg Hamadani**, was killed. Mahadji was forced to withdraw. For a few years it seemed that the Rajput states had thrown off the Maratha yoke.

The relief did not last. Mahadji rebuilt his power with a new kind of army: infantry brigades trained in the European manner by the French soldier **Benoît de Boigne**, with disciplined musketeers and well-served artillery. In **1790** these brigades won a crushing victory at **Patan**, in the Shekhawati country of Jaipur's north, over Mahadji's enemy **Ismail Beg** and his Rajput allies, and soon after broke the Rathores at **Merta**. The old Rajput way of war, the great charge of mailed horsemen, could not stand against massed musketry and cannon. Jaipur had to agree to pay tribute again.

For the rest of his life Pratap Singh lived under this pressure. Maratha armies came to collect money, and when it was not paid they occupied districts, besieged forts and plundered villages. Adventurers of every kind rode through Rajputana: the Irish soldier **George Thomas**, who carved out a small state of his own at Hansi, raided Jaipur's northern lands around **1799**. In **1800** Jaipur's army fought the forces of **Daulat Rao Scindia**, Mahadji's successor, at **Malpura**, and was defeated. The Kachwaha nobles fought bravely, but bravery was no longer enough.

It is a strange thing that a ruler so often defeated in war should be remembered with such affection. The reason lies in the other half of his life. Pratap Singh was a devoted follower of **Krishna**, and in particular of **Govind Devji**, the image of Krishna brought from Vrindavan and installed in the palace gardens of Jaipur by his great-grandfather **Sawai Jai Singh II**. To Pratap Singh, the true king of Jaipur was Govind Devji, and he himself was the god's servant.

Out of this devotion came poetry. Under the pen name **Brajnidhi**, "the treasure of Braj", Pratap Singh wrote a large body of verse in **Braj Bhasha**, the language of Krishna's homeland. His poems sing of the love of Radha and Krishna, of the seasons in Vrindavan, of longing and devotion. They were collected in many works, later gathered as the *Brajnidhi Granthavali*. They are not the verses of a king playing at poetry; they are the work of a real poet, and they are still read today.

He gathered around him a court of artists. His **Gunijan Khana**, the department of musicians and scholars, was one of the largest in India. Under his patronage the great treatise on music, the *Radha Govind Sangeet Sar*, was compiled by court scholars, bringing together the theory and practice of Indian music of the age. Painters in the palace workshops produced portraits, scenes of court life and illustrations of the Krishna legend in a refined Jaipur style, among them the painter **Sahibram**, whose large portraits of the Maharaja survive. The **Suratkhana**, the painting studio, was busy in his reign as never before.

And he built. In **1799** he raised the building that has become the face of Jaipur: the **Hawa Mahal**, the Palace of Winds. Designed by the architect **Lal Chand Ustad**, it rises five storeys high on the edge of the palace, its pink sandstone front pierced by hundreds of small windows and screens. Behind those screens, the women of the palace could watch the processions and the life of the bazaar below without being seen, and the breeze passing through the windows kept the rooms cool in the summer heat. Tradition says the shape of the façade recalls the crown of Krishna, a fitting tribute from a devotee king. Whether or not that was the intention, the building is a perfect image of Pratap Singh's world: delicate, devotional, and turned towards the life of the city.

The Maharaja also added to the palace complex and its temples, and the city's crafts flourished under his rule. Jaipur's jewellers, enamellers, block-printers and stone-carvers kept their trade alive through all the years of war, and the royal workshops set the fashion for the whole region.

His character, as it comes down to us, was gentle, devout and artistic, but not weak. He fought when he could, and he kept his state intact through a quarter-century in which other Rajput houses were humbled. His enemies called him extravagant, and the cost of his court added to the debts of a treasury already drained by Maratha demands. Yet he understood that a kingdom is not only its army. In a time when Jaipur could not win its wars, he made it a city that people would remember for its beauty.

His son, **Jagat Singh**, was born in **1786**, and was raised in this world of poets and painters. In the last years of his father's life, events far away were changing everything. The British East India Company was moving towards war with the Maratha chiefs, and the old order that had pressed on Jaipur for half a century was about to be overturned.

Pratap Singh did not live to see it. He died on **1 August 1803**, at the age of thirty-eight. Within weeks, British armies under **General Lake** were fighting the Scindias in the north, and before the year was out, his son had signed Jaipur's first treaty with the Company. The poet king had lived his whole life under the shadow of Maratha power; it ended almost exactly as he did. He left behind a body of poetry, a great collection of paintings, a famous treatise on music and a palace of windows, and these, more than any battle, are his memorial.

## Highlights of his life

- **Accession as a boy.** Born on 2 December 1764, he succeeded his brother Prithvi Singh in 1778 at about thirteen.
- **Battle of Tunga (1787).** Allied with Vijay Singh of Jodhpur, he forced Mahadji Scindia to withdraw, briefly freeing Jaipur from Maratha demands.
- **Defeats at Patan and Malpura.** Against the European-trained brigades of the Scindias, Jaipur and its allies were defeated at Patan (1790) and Malpura (1800).
- **The poet Brajnidhi.** Under this pen name he wrote a large body of devotional poetry in Braj Bhasha to Krishna.
- **Patron of music and painting.** His court produced the *Radha Govind Sangeet Sar* and a flourishing school of Jaipur painting.
- **Builder of the Hawa Mahal (1799).** He raised the five-storey Palace of Winds, designed by Lal Chand Ustad, now the symbol of Jaipur.
- **Death in 1803.** He died on 1 August 1803, just before the British wars that ended Maratha dominance, and was succeeded by his son Jagat Singh.

jagat-singh-ii-jaipur.story:
## Maharaja Sawai Jagat Singh — the rival suitor and the end of an age

*Jagat Singh's reign is described in the Jaipur archives, in British records and in the pages of James Tod, who knew Rajputana in these very years and judged him harshly; the stories of his court are partly legend, and where they go beyond the record, this story says so.*

When **Sawai Pratap Singh** died on **1 August 1803**, he left to his son a city full of poetry and a treasury full of debts. **Jagat Singh**, born in **1786**, was seventeen years old when he took the throne of Jaipur as **Sawai Jagat Singh**. He had grown up among his father's musicians and painters, in palaces where the verses of Brajnidhi were sung in the evenings and the walls were covered with scenes of Krishna's love. He was handsome, proud and fond of pleasure, and he came to power at the exact moment when the world his father had known was breaking apart.

In the very months of his accession, the **British East India Company** went to war with the Maratha chiefs. Within weeks, **General Gerard Lake** had defeated the armies of **Daulat Rao Scindia** at **Delhi** and **Laswari**, and the Maratha power that had pressed on Jaipur for half a century was broken in the north. The young Maharaja saw his chance. In **December 1803** Jaipur signed a treaty of alliance with the Company, the first in its history. For the first time in decades, it seemed that someone stronger than the Marathas might protect the Kachwaha state.

The hope was short-lived. In **1804** the Company went to war with **Yashwant Rao Holkar**, and a British force under **Colonel Monson** was driven back in a disastrous retreat through the lands south of Jaipur. The British accused Jaipur of failing to help as the treaty required. Then, in **1805**, a new government in Calcutta under **Sir George Barlow** decided to withdraw from the affairs of Rajputana altogether, and the alliance with Jaipur was abandoned. The Rajput states were left to face the Marathas, the Pathan adventurers and the Pindari raiders alone. Tod would later call it a betrayal; for Jaipur, it opened twelve of the worst years in its history.

Into this dangerous world Jagat Singh brought a quarrel of his own making. In Udaipur lived **Krishna Kumari**, the young daughter of **Maharana Bhim Singh** of Mewar, famed across Rajputana for her beauty. She had been betrothed to **Maharaja Bhim Singh** of **Jodhpur**, but he had died in **1803** before the marriage. Her hand was then offered to Jagat Singh of Jaipur. But the new ruler of Jodhpur, **Maharaja Man Singh**, claimed that the betrothal had been made to the throne of Jodhpur, not to one man, and that the princess was rightfully his. Neither king would give way. What began as a question of honour became a war that drew in half of Rajputana.

Jagat Singh found allies among Man Singh's enemies. A powerful Rathore noble, **Sawai Singh of Pokaran**, supported a rival claimant to the Jodhpur throne, **Dhonkal Singh**, and brought many Jodhpur nobles over to the Jaipur side. Jagat Singh also hired the Pathan commander **Amir Khan**, whose army of mercenaries was one of the strongest forces in Rajputana. Early in **1807** a great army marched west from Jaipur. Near **Gingoli**, on the borders of Marwar, Man Singh's forces broke up as his nobles deserted him, and the Jodhpur king fled to the shelter of his great fortress of **Mehrangarh**.

For a few months Jagat Singh seemed to stand at the height of his fortune. His army besieged Jodhpur and plundered the city below the fort. But the siege of Mehrangarh, perched on its rock, was a long and costly business, and the alliances that had brought him there were fragile. Man Singh, from inside the fort, opened talks with Amir Khan. The Pathan changed sides, as he often did, and turned his army on Jaipur's own territory, plundering its towns and threatening the capital. Jagat Singh was forced to raise the siege in the autumn of **1807** and hurry home. He had spent enormous sums and gained nothing. The treasury, already empty, was now deep in debt.

The quarrel ended in tragedy, though not on a battlefield. With Mewar exhausted, Jodhpur and Jaipur still claiming the princess and Amir Khan's army camped near Udaipur, the Maharana was told that only the death of his daughter could end the danger to his state. In **July 1810**, **Krishna Kumari**, a girl of about sixteen, was given poison and died. Her death shocked Rajputana. Tod, who wrote of it with deep feeling, saw it as the symbol of a whole order in decay. Jagat Singh had not ordered it, but his rivalry was one of the causes, and the story of the princess has been joined to his name ever since.

The years that followed were years of plunder. The armies of Amir Khan and the Maratha chiefs, together with bands of **Pindaris**, crossed and recrossed Jaipur's lands, collecting tribute at the point of the sword. Villages were burned, trade was disrupted, and the great nobles of the state, each holding his own fort, made their own bargains with the raiders. The authority of the Maharaja weakened year by year.

At court, Jagat Singh's personal life became a scandal. Tradition tells of his passion for **Ras Kapur**, a dancing girl of great beauty and wit. The stories say that he raised her to a position no courtesan had ever held, seating her beside him in public and, it is said, granting her a share of the kingdom itself. The nobles were outraged. In the end, the tale goes, Ras Kapur was accused of plotting against the state and was confined in the fort of **Nahargarh** on the ridge above Jaipur. How much of this is history and how much is the gossip of an angry court is hard to say, but the legend of Ras Kapur has been told in Jaipur for two centuries.

Not everything in his reign was decay. The craftsmen of Jaipur kept working, the painters of the palace continued to produce portraits and scenes of court life, and the temple of **Govind Devji** remained the centre of the city's devotion. Jagat Singh had inherited his father's love of music and festivals, and the processions of Gangaur and Teej still filled the streets. But the money to support them came harder every year.

By **1817** the Company had changed its mind once more. Under **Lord Hastings**, the British decided to destroy the Pindaris and to bring the Rajput states under their protection. Treaties were offered to each in turn. Jagat Singh was reluctant, unwilling to give up the independence that his house had held, at least in name, for centuries. But the alternative was to be left once more to the raiders. On **2 April 1818**, Jaipur signed a treaty of "perpetual friendship, alliance and unity of interests" with the Company. Jaipur would pay an annual tribute and accept British protection; in return, the British would guard the state from outside attack. **Amir Khan** was settled as ruler of **Tonk**, and the Pindari bands were broken. The age of plunder was over, but so was the age of independence.

Jagat Singh did not live long under the new order. He died on **21 December 1818**, aged about thirty-two. He left no living son. The nobles of Jaipur, in their haste, placed a distant kinsman on the throne, but within months one of the late Maharaja's queens, a Bhati princess, was found to be expecting a child. In **April 1819** she gave birth to a son, who was proclaimed Maharaja as **Sawai Jai Singh III**. The kingdom that Jagat Singh left him was poorer and weaker than at any time in the century, but it was at peace, and under the shadow of a new power.

History has not been kind to Jagat Singh. Tod called him the most dissolute prince of his race, and the stories of Krishna Kumari and Ras Kapur have shaped his memory. Yet he ruled in an impossible time, between the collapse of Maratha power and the arrival of British supremacy, when no Rajput king could have held his state together without loss. His reign marks the end of the old Rajputana, of wars between proud houses over honour and brides, and the beginning of the age of treaties.

## Highlights of his life

- **Accession in 1803.** Born in 1786, he succeeded his father Pratap Singh in August 1803, at the start of the Anglo-Maratha War.
- **First treaty with the British (1803).** Jaipur's first alliance with the East India Company, abandoned by the Company in 1805.
- **War over Krishna Kumari (1807).** As a rival suitor to Man Singh of Jodhpur, he invaded Marwar, won at Gingoli and besieged Jodhpur, but had to withdraw when Amir Khan changed sides.
- **Years of plunder.** Jaipur suffered heavily from the armies of Amir Khan, the Marathas and the Pindaris between 1805 and 1817.
- **The legend of Ras Kapur.** Tradition remembers his passion for the dancing girl Ras Kapur, later confined in Nahargarh.
- **Treaty of 1818.** On 2 April 1818 he placed Jaipur under British protection, ending the age of plunder.
- **Death and succession.** He died on 21 December 1818; his posthumous son Jai Singh III was born in April 1819.
