jai-singh-iii-amber.story:
## Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh III — the child born to a vacant throne

*Jai Singh III ruled only as a child, and his story is told mostly in the records of the British agents who watched over Jaipur and in the memory of the city that mourned him; much about his death remains uncertain, and this story says so.*

On **21 December 1818**, **Sawai Jagat Singh** died in his palace at Jaipur, and the throne of the Kachwahas stood empty. The Maharaja was barely thirty-two. He had no living son, and the treaty he had signed with the **East India Company** only eight months earlier was still new. Across the great courtyards of the palace, the nobles gathered in anxious groups. A throne without a king was an invitation to every ambitious kinsman and every faction at court.

The nobles acted quickly. Within days they chose a distant kinsman, **Mohan Singh** of the Kachwaha branch of **Narwar**, and placed him on the throne. But the choice was rushed and disputed, and many of the great clans resented it. Then news spread through the zenana that changed everything. One of Jagat Singh's widows, a princess of the **Bhati** house of Jaisalmer, was expecting a child.

For months, Jaipur waited. If the child was a daughter, Mohan Singh's claim might stand. If it was a son, he would be the rightful heir of Jagat Singh. Rumour filled the bazaars. Some whispered that the pregnancy was a trick of the queen and her supporters, and that a child would be smuggled into the palace if none was born. The British, now the protecting power, watched closely. **Sir David Ochterlony**, the veteran general who represented the Company in Rajputana, took a keen interest in the outcome.

In **April 1819** the queen gave birth to a son. After enquiries, the British and the majority of the nobles accepted him as the true son of the late Maharaja, and Mohan Singh was set aside. The infant was proclaimed **Sawai Jai Singh III**, taking the name of his great ancestor, the founder of Jaipur. He was a king before he could open his eyes.

A baby cannot rule, and so Jaipur entered another long regency, the third in fifty years. Power passed to the queen mother, the **Bhatiyani Rani**, who governed in her son's name from behind the screens of the zenana. She was strong-willed and determined to keep power in her own hands. To do so she relied on people whom the old nobility regarded as upstarts. The most important was **Jhutha Ram**, a man of the merchant class who rose to become the chief minister. The British records also speak of the great influence of women of the queen's household.

The nobles of Jaipur, proud heads of the Rajawat, Nathawat, Shekhawat and other clans, bitterly resented being governed by a minister of humble birth. The court split into factions. Some supported the queen mother and Jhutha Ram; others opposed them and appealed to the British to intervene. The British, for their part, were torn. Their treaty promised not to interfere in Jaipur's internal affairs, but they wanted the annual tribute to be paid, and they did not want disorder in a state they had sworn to protect. A British officer was stationed at Jaipur to watch over affairs, and the Agents in Rajputana sent long reports to Calcutta describing the quarrels of the court.

The tribute itself was a constant burden. The 1818 treaty had fixed an annual payment to the Company, rising over the years. But Jaipur's revenues had been ruined by twenty years of plunder, and much of the land was held by nobles who paid little to the state. Arrears built up. Every year the British pressed for payment, and every year the regency struggled to find it. Meanwhile, without the Maratha and Pindari raids, the countryside began, slowly, to recover. Villages that had been abandoned were resettled, and the trade of Jaipur's bankers and craftsmen revived under the new peace.

The young Maharaja grew up in the middle of these conflicts. He was raised in the zenana under his mother's close care, and taught the arts expected of a Rajput prince: riding, the use of arms, reading, the worship of the family gods and the great festivals of the city. He would have taken part in the processions of **Gangaur** and **Teej**, carried in state through the streets so that his people could see their king. He was married young, as Rajput princes were, and in **September 1833**, when he was only fourteen, a son was born to him: **Ram Singh**.

In **1832** the Governor-General, **Lord William Bentinck**, came to **Ajmer** and held court for the Rajput princes. The nobles of Jaipur brought their complaints against the queen mother's government, and the British began to take a more active part in Jaipur affairs. When the queen mother died, Jhutha Ram's position became weaker, and the young Maharaja, now approaching manhood, might soon have begun to rule for himself.

He never did. On **6 February 1835**, Sawai Jai Singh III died suddenly, at the age of only fifteen. His death came without warning, and almost at once the city was filled with rumours of poison. Suspicion fell on **Jhutha Ram**, who had most to lose if the young king took power into his own hands. Whether the boy was murdered or died of some sudden illness has never been proved, and historians still debate it. But the people of Jaipur were convinced that a crime had been committed.

Their anger burst out a few months later. In **June 1835**, as the British Agent for Rajputana, **Major Alves**, came to Jaipur to settle the affairs of the state, he was attacked in the streets by an armed crowd and wounded. His assistant, **Mr. Blake**, was killed. The attack shocked the British and the court alike. In the enquiry that followed, Jhutha Ram and several of his associates were found responsible for the conspiracy behind the attack, and were sent away as prisoners. Whatever the truth about the boy king's death, the reign of the favourites ended with it.

The throne passed to Jai Singh's infant son, **Ram Singh II**, who was not yet two years old. This time the British did not leave Jaipur to the factions of the court. They set up a **Council of Regency** made up of leading nobles, under the supervision of a British political agent, to govern the state until the new Maharaja came of age. It was a new kind of government, and it marked a change in the relationship between Jaipur and the British: from distant protection to close supervision.

It is hard to speak of the achievements of a king who died at fifteen, having never truly ruled. Jai Singh III built no great palaces and fought no battles. His reign was the reign of his mother and her ministers, and of the British agents who watched them. Yet his life marks an important turning point in Jaipur's history. He was the first Maharaja to reign entirely under British paramountcy. The disorder of his regency and the violence that followed his death persuaded the British to take a direct hand in governing the state, and that direct hand would, under his son, help to make Jaipur one of the most modern states in Rajputana.

The people of Jaipur remembered him with sorrow, as a boy who had come into the world to save the throne of his father and left it before he could take it up. His short life began with a vacant throne and ended with another, and between the two lay the quiet years in which Jaipur slowly recovered from the age of plunder.

## Highlights of his life

- **Posthumous birth.** Born in April 1819, four months after the death of his father Jagat Singh, he displaced the hastily chosen Mohan Singh of Narwar.
- **A long regency.** His mother, the Bhatiyani Rani, governed in his name with the minister Jhutha Ram, against the opposition of many nobles.
- **First reign under British paramountcy.** His whole reign followed the treaty of 1818, under the burden of tribute and the watch of British agents.
- **Recovery after the age of plunder.** With the end of the Maratha and Pindari raids, Jaipur's villages and trade slowly revived.
- **Father of Ram Singh II.** His son Ram Singh, born in September 1833, became one of Jaipur's greatest rulers.
- **Sudden death in 1835.** He died on 6 February 1835 at fifteen, amid suspicions of poison that were never proved; the unrest that followed led to direct British supervision of Jaipur.

## Maharaja Sawai Ram Singh II — the king who brought the modern age to the Pink City

*Ram Singh II's reign is richly documented in the Jaipur state archives, in British records and in the buildings and institutions he left behind, and even in the photographs he took himself; where popular stories go beyond the record, this story says so.*

On **6 February 1835**, the boy king **Sawai Jai Singh III** died suddenly in Jaipur, at only fifteen. He left behind a son who was not yet two years old. **Ram Singh**, born on **28 September 1833**, was carried to the throne of the Kachwahas in the arms of his attendants and proclaimed **Sawai Ram Singh II**. Few in that grieving, suspicious city could have imagined that this infant would reign for forty-five years and transform Jaipur more than any ruler since its founder.

His first years were shadowed by violence. The city believed his father had been poisoned, and suspicion fell on the minister **Jhutha Ram**. In **June 1835**, an armed crowd attacked the British Agent for Rajputana, **Major Alves**, in the streets of Jaipur; his assistant, **Mr. Blake**, was killed. After an enquiry, Jhutha Ram and his associates were removed and imprisoned. The British, who had watched three regencies in Jaipur descend into faction, decided that this time they would not stand aside. A **Council of Regency** of leading nobles was set up to govern the state, under the supervision of a British political agent.

The most important of these agents was **Major John Ludlow**, who took charge in the 1840s. Ludlow was a reformer, and under his guidance the regency council did things that no Jaipur government had done before. In the **1840s**, Jaipur prohibited **sati**, the burning of widows on their husbands' funeral pyres, and acted against **female infanticide** and the trade in slaves. These were deeply rooted customs, and the reforms met resistance, but they were carried through, and Jaipur became one of the first Rajput states to adopt them. The finances of the state were put in order, the arrears of tribute were reduced, and roads and public works were begun.

The young Maharaja grew up in the middle of these changes. He was given an education unlike that of any of his ancestors. Alongside the traditional training of a Rajput prince, in riding, arms, Sanskrit and the rituals of kingship, he learned English and studied subjects that were new to the courts of Rajputana: geography, science and the history of other nations. He was curious about everything: machines, chemistry, painting, music and, above all, the new art of **photography**. He grew into a man who could converse with British officials in their own language, yet remained deeply rooted in the traditions of his house.

In **1851**, at the age of eighteen, Ram Singh took the full powers of government into his own hands. He kept many of the reforms of the regency and pushed them further. He believed that a ruler's duty was not only to defend his state but to improve the lives of its people, and that Jaipur, which had been founded by a scholar king as a planned city, should once more lead the way.

His first great test came in **1857**. When the sepoys of the Bengal Army rose against the East India Company and the revolt spread across northern India, the Rajput princes had to choose a side. Ram Singh chose to support the British. He sent troops to help keep order, protected Europeans who sought refuge in his territory, and kept Jaipur quiet while the great rising raged around it. His decision has been judged in different ways since. To the British he was a loyal ally, and after the revolt they rewarded him with the district of **Kot Kasim** and high honours. To later nationalists it was a choice for the foreign power against those who had risen against it. Ram Singh himself seems to have seen it as the protection of his state and his people from war, the duty of a ruler bound by treaty.

With peace restored, he threw himself into building a new Jaipur. The list of what he founded is long. A school he had supported from **1844** grew into the **Maharaja's College**, one of the earliest modern colleges in Rajputana. In **1857** he founded a **School of Arts**, later famous as the Maharaja's School of Arts and Crafts, to train the craftsmen of Jaipur in drawing, design, metalwork and other arts, keeping the city's old crafts alive while teaching new ones. In **1867** a school for girls was opened, the **Maharani's Girls' School**, at a time when the education of girls was rare in all of India. A Sanskrit college was supported, and schools were opened in the towns of the state.

He built for the health of his people as well. Dispensaries were opened in the districts, and in Jaipur the **Mayo Hospital** was built in the 1870s. He brought piped water and **gas lighting** to the streets of the city, and Jaipur became one of the first cities in India to have its streets lit by gas. Roads were laid, linking Jaipur to Agra and the other cities of the region. To carry out these works he created a Public Works Department and employed the engineer **Samuel Swinton Jacob**, whose designs would shape Jaipur's architecture for decades.

When famine struck Rajputana in **1868**, Ram Singh used the relief works to give work and wages to the hungry. Among those works was the great public garden of **Ram Niwas Bagh**, laid out just outside the walls of the city. In **February 1876** the **Prince of Wales**, later King Edward VII, visited Jaipur, and laid the foundation stone of a museum building in the garden, the **Albert Hall**, which was completed in the reign of Ram Singh's successor. It is commonly said that for this visit the city's buildings were washed in the warm pink colour that gave Jaipur its name, the **Pink City**; whether or not the colour began then, it was in his reign that Jaipur became famous by that name.

Ram Singh loved the theatre and built the **Ram Prakash Theatre** in the city. He was a skilled photographer, setting up his own studio and darkroom in the palace and taking hundreds of photographs of his courtiers, his nobles, the women of his household and the life of Jaipur. Many of his glass plates survive in the palace collections today, a remarkable record of a royal court seen through the eyes of its own king.

His religious life was more complicated. Raised in the Vaishnava devotion to Krishna that had long been central to the Jaipur court, he turned in middle age towards the worship of **Shiva**, and for a time his government put pressure on some of the Vaishnava sects of the city. This caused deep resentment among his subjects and his nobles, and it is remembered as one of the more troubled episodes of his reign.

The British valued his counsel, and he was appointed to the **Viceroy's Legislative Council**, one of the first Indian princes to sit on it. He was honoured with British titles and a salute of guns. Yet he never ceased to be a Rajput king, and the ceremonies of the Kachwaha court, the processions of Gangaur and Teej and the worship of the family gods, went on through all the changes of his reign.

Ram Singh had no son. As his health failed in **1880**, he adopted as his heir **Kayam Singh**, a younger son of the Kachwaha **Thakur of Isarda**, who would reign as **Sawai Madho Singh II**. Ram Singh died on **17 September 1880**, just short of his forty-seventh birthday. He had found Jaipur a city still recovering from an age of plunder, governed by quarrelling factions. He left it with schools and colleges, a hospital, lit streets, piped water, a great public garden and a reputation across India as the most progressive of the Rajput states. Of all the Maharajas who followed Sawai Jai Singh II, none did more to make Jaipur the city it is today.

## Highlights of his life

- **Infant king.** Born on 28 September 1833, he succeeded his father Jai Singh III in 1835, and was raised under a Council of Regency.
- **Social reform.** Under the regency and in his own reign, Jaipur prohibited sati and acted against female infanticide and slavery.
- **Full powers in 1851.** He took charge of the state at eighteen and governed for nearly three decades as a reforming ruler.
- **The revolt of 1857.** He supported the British during the revolt, and was rewarded with the district of Kot Kasim.
- **Education.** He built up the Maharaja's College, founded the School of Arts (1857) and opened a girls' school (1867).
- **A modern city.** He brought gas lighting, piped water, the Mayo Hospital, roads and the Ram Niwas Bagh to Jaipur; the Albert Hall's foundation stone was laid in his reign in 1876.
- **Photographer king.** His own photographs of the Jaipur court survive as a unique record of his age.
- **Death in 1880.** He died on 17 September 1880, having adopted Madho Singh II as his heir.

## Madho Singh II — the thakur's son who carried the Ganga to London

*Madho Singh II's reign is well recorded in the archives of Jaipur State, in British administrative reports and in the buildings he left behind; the stories told about his piety and his habits come partly from court memory and family tradition, and where they do, this story says so.*

In the summer of **1880**, the old Maharaja of Jaipur, **Sawai Ram Singh II**, lay dying in his palace in the pink city. He had ruled for forty-five years. He had brought gas lamps, a school of art, a college, hospitals and wide paved roads to Jaipur, and he had kept his state loyal to the British through the storm of 1857. But he had no son. In the Kachwaha house, as in every Rajput house, a ruler without an heir left behind a question that could tear a state apart.

The answer Ram Singh chose surprised many at the court. On his deathbed he named as his adopted son a young man named **Kayam Singh**, the younger son of **Thakur Raghunath Singh of Isarda**, a modest estate in the east of the state. The Isarda thakurs were Rajawat Kachwahas, a branch of the ruling line itself, so the blood of the founders of Amber ran in the boy's veins. But Isarda was far from the splendour of the City Palace, and Kayam Singh, born in **1861**, had grown up as the son of a minor noble, not as a prince expecting a throne.

Ram Singh died in **September 1880**. The British government, whose approval was needed for every adoption in a princely state, accepted his choice, and the young man from Isarda was enthroned in Jaipur under a new name: **Sawai Madho Singh II**. He was about nineteen years old. The name itself was a statement. The first Madho Singh had ruled Jaipur in the eighteenth century, and by taking his name the new Maharaja placed himself firmly in the line of Sawai Jai Singh's successors.

The first years were not easy. A young ruler raised outside the palace had to win over ministers who had served his predecessor, nobles who had their own candidates, and British political agents who watched every princely court closely. Madho Singh was given a council to help him govern, and for a time the able ministers of Ram Singh's day continued to run much of the administration. The new Maharaja learned slowly and carefully. He was not a reformer by temperament, as his predecessor had been. He was a cautious, deeply religious man, and he would remain one all his life.

Yet he did not undo what Ram Singh had begun. The most visible example stands in the Ram Niwas Garden outside the walled city. In **1876**, during the visit of the Prince of Wales, the foundation stone of a great hall had been laid in his honour. The building, designed by the engineer **Samuel Swinton Jacob** in a blend of Indian and Islamic forms, rose slowly through the early years of Madho Singh's reign. In **1887** it was opened as the **Albert Hall Museum**, the first public museum of Rajasthan, filled with carpets, metalwork, pottery, arms and paintings. Ram Singh had dreamed it; Madho Singh completed it and gave it to the public.

Jacob became one of the most important figures of the reign. As head of the state's public works, he and his department built roads, dams, irrigation works and public buildings across the territory. Within the City Palace, Madho Singh commissioned the **Mubarak Mahal**, a reception hall finished around **1900**, whose carved white and cream stone combined Rajput, Mughal and European ideas. Today it houses the palace's collection of royal textiles. On the ridge above the city, at the old fort of **Nahargarh**, he built the **Madhavendra Bhawan**, a set of nine matching suites for his queens, linked by corridors to a central apartment for the king himself.

The railway, too, came closer during these years. Lines built in agreement with the British linked Jaipur to the rest of India, and the state later built its own railway lines through its territory. Grain, cloth, marble, gems and pilgrims moved more freely than ever before, and Jaipur's markets, already famous for jewellery and textiles, grew richer.

The greatest test of the reign came at the very end of the nineteenth century. In **1899 and 1900**, the monsoon failed across Rajasthan. The famine of those years, remembered in Rajasthani as the *Chhappaniya Akal* after the Vikram year 1956 in which it began, was one of the worst in the region's history. Wells ran dry, cattle died in the fields, and families walked hundreds of miles in search of food and work. Princely states and British districts alike struggled to cope.

Madho Singh opened relief works and grain distribution in his own state, but his most remembered act reached beyond Jaipur. He gave a very large sum of money to found the **Indian People's Famine Trust**, a permanent fund meant to help the victims of future famines anywhere in India. It was one of the largest charitable gifts made by an Indian ruler in that age, and the British government honoured him for it. For the rest of his life, Madho Singh was known as a generous giver, especially to causes connected with relief, religion and education.

It was his religion that shaped the most famous episode of his life. In **1902**, King **Edward VII** was to be crowned in London, and the princes of India were invited. For an orthodox Hindu of Madho Singh's kind, the journey was a serious matter. Many in that time believed that crossing the "black water" of the ocean would cost a high-caste Hindu his purity. Madho Singh resolved to go, but on his own terms.

He chartered a ship, the **SS Olympia**, for himself and his large retinue, and had it cleansed and purified before boarding. A shrine was set up on board for the worship of the household deity. Above all, he would not drink the water of a foreign land. For the journey, the silversmiths of Jaipur made two enormous silver urns, the **Gangajalis**, each about five feet tall and holding several thousand litres, beaten from thousands of melted silver coins. They were filled with water from the Ganga, and that sacred water served the Maharaja for drinking and ritual throughout his stay in England. The two urns survive today in the **Diwan-i-Khas** of the City Palace, and they are counted among the largest silver objects in the world.

Court tradition adds many details to the voyage: that a storm in the Arabian Sea was calmed after a silver vessel was offered to the waves, and that the Maharaja's household carried their own cooks, priests and supplies so that nothing foreign touched his food. Some of these stories may be embroidered, but the basic facts are well recorded. The English press was fascinated by the visiting prince, and Madho Singh attended the coronation, honoured by the King, without breaking a single rule of his faith.

He was loyal to the British Crown throughout his reign, and he was rewarded with the highest honours of the Raj. He attended the great **Delhi Durbars of 1903 and 1911**, and when the First World War broke out in 1914, Jaipur, like other princely states, contributed men, money and supplies to the British war effort. His imperial service troops served the Empire, and the British in turn treated him as one of the senior princes of Rajputana.

But Madho Singh was not merely a loyal prince. He gave generously to Indian causes as well. Tradition and the records of the time remember his gifts to **Madan Mohan Malaviya's** project of a Hindu university at Banaras, founded in 1916, and his support for Sanskrit learning, temples and pilgrim places. Within Jaipur he maintained the Maharaja's College, the School of Art and the hospitals that Ram Singh had founded, and he added to them. He was conservative in social matters, and he did not lead campaigns against old customs as some reforming princes did, but under him the institutions of a modern city continued to grow.

In private, Madho Singh was a man of strong habits. He was known for his love of ceremony, his strict routine of worship, and his faith in astrologers and auspicious hours. Like many princes of his age he kept a large household, with several queens and many women of the zenana, and he had a number of children by women who were not his formally married queens. None of his children, however, was born of a marriage that allowed him to succeed under Rajput custom. As the years passed, the old question that had brought Madho Singh himself to the throne returned to haunt the house.

He answered it in the same way Ram Singh had done, and from the same place. In **1921**, Madho Singh adopted a boy from his own family's estate of Isarda: **Mor Mukut Singh**, the second son of **Thakur Sawai Singh of Isarda**, born in 1912. The boy, renamed **Man Singh**, was brought to Jaipur and kept under close protection. Court memory says that the old Maharaja, fearful of intrigue in the zenana, ordered that the child's food be prepared and tested with great care.

Madho Singh did not live long after the adoption. He died on **7 September 1922**, aged about sixty-one, after a reign of forty-two years. His adopted son was only ten years old, and a council of regency governed the state until the boy came of age.

Madho Singh II is remembered today in two quite different ways. To some he was a conservative ruler who resisted change, more concerned with ritual purity than with reform. To others he was the steady hand that carried Jaipur from the age of Ram Singh into the twentieth century, completing great buildings, giving generously in times of famine, and keeping the dignity of an ancient house intact at the height of the British Raj. Both images are true in part. What is beyond doubt is that when a visitor today walks past the Albert Hall, enters the Mubarak Mahal, climbs to the Madhavendra Bhawan at Nahargarh, or stands before the two great silver urns in the Diwan-i-Khas, they are standing among the works of the thakur's son from Isarda who became the Maharaja of Jaipur.

## Highlights of his life

- **From Isarda to the throne (1880).** Born Kayam Singh in 1861, the son of the Thakur of Isarda, he was adopted by the dying Ram Singh II and became Maharaja of Jaipur at about nineteen.
- **Completion of the Albert Hall Museum (1887).** He completed and opened the museum whose foundation had been laid in 1876, the first public museum in Rajasthan.
- **Builder of palaces.** He commissioned the Mubarak Mahal in the City Palace and the Madhavendra Bhawan with its nine queens' suites at Nahargarh.
- **Famine relief (1899–1900).** During the great famine he funded relief in Jaipur and gave a large endowment to found the Indian People's Famine Trust.
- **The Ganga in London (1902).** He travelled to the coronation of Edward VII with two giant silver Gangajalis of Ganga water, now kept in the City Palace.
- **Patron of learning and faith.** He supported temples, Sanskrit learning and the Hindu university at Banaras, and maintained Jaipur's colleges, school of art and hospitals.
- **Securing the succession.** In 1921 he adopted Mor Mukut Singh of Isarda, who succeeded him in 1922 as Man Singh II.

## Man Singh II — the polo-playing Maharaja who saw the princely age end

*Man Singh II lived in an age of newspapers, photographs and government records, so his life is well documented; the memoirs of his wife Gayatri Devi add a personal view, and where a detail rests on family memory alone, this story says so.*

On **21 August 1912**, a second son was born to **Thakur Sawai Singh of Isarda**, a nobleman of the Rajawat branch of the Kachwahas who held a modest estate in the east of Jaipur State. The boy was named **Mor Mukut Singh**. Nobody at his birth imagined that he would one day sit on the throne of Jaipur. He was a younger son of a minor house, and his future seemed to lie in the quiet life of the countryside.

But Isarda had given Jaipur a ruler once before. The reigning Maharaja, **Sawai Madho Singh II**, had himself been born in Isarda and adopted by his predecessor. Now old, and without a son born of a marriage that could inherit, he looked once more to the family he had come from. In **March 1921**, the eight-year-old Mor Mukut Singh was formally adopted as the Maharaja's heir and given a new name: **Man Singh**, the name of the great Kachwaha general of Akbar's age.

The boy's life changed overnight. He was brought into the City Palace, surrounded by guards and servants, and kept apart from the intrigues of the zenana. Family memory recalls that the old Maharaja was so anxious for his heir's safety that the child's food was watched with great care. The adoption had come just in time. On **7 September 1922**, Madho Singh II died, and the ten-year-old boy became **Maharaja Sawai Man Singh II** of Jaipur. A council of regency, working under the eye of the British, governed the state until he came of age.

He was sent for his education to **Mayo College** at Ajmer, the school founded for the sons of Rajputana's princes, and he also received military training, including a period at the **Royal Military Academy, Woolwich**, in England. He grew into a tall, athletic, charming young man who loved horses above all things. He was married young, in the custom of the time, to **Marudhar Kanwar**, a princess of the Rathore house of **Jodhpur**, in 1924. From this marriage was born, in **1931**, his eldest son **Bhawani Singh**, the first male heir born directly to a ruling Maharaja of Jaipur in generations. In 1932 he married a second Jodhpur princess, **Kishore Kanwar**, niece of his first wife.

On **14 March 1931**, Man Singh received full ruling powers. The young Maharaja took charge of a large state of more than two million people, with a modern capital, an old feudal nobility and a growing educated middle class. He also brought Jaipur a new kind of fame. In the early 1930s he formed a polo team that became one of the best in the world. In **1933**, the Jaipur team toured England and won the major open tournaments of that season, an achievement that made the Maharaja's name known far beyond India. Man Singh himself was one of the finest polo players of his generation, reaching the highest handicaps in the game.

In **1940** he married for the third time. His bride was **Gayatri Devi**, a princess of **Cooch Behar**, whom he had first met when she was a girl and he was a visiting polo player. She was educated, independent and spirited, and she became one of the most famous Indian women of the century. In 1949 she gave birth to a son, **Jagat Singh**. Gayatri Devi founded a girls' school in Jaipur in **1943**, now the Maharani Gayatri Devi Girls' School, and later entered politics herself.

When the Second World War began in 1939, Jaipur, like the other princely states, placed its forces at the service of the British Crown. The state's troops served overseas, and Man Singh himself went on active service with them for a period, in keeping with the tradition of the Rajput ruler as a soldier. He was honoured by the British with military rank and titles.

At home, the years around the war brought important changes to the city. In **1942** Man Singh appointed **Sir Mirza Ismail**, a celebrated administrator who had earlier served Mysore, as his prime minister. Under Mirza Ismail, Jaipur was given new roads, gardens and civic works; the city's main road outside the walls still carries his name. Man Singh founded and supported new institutions of learning and health. The **Sawai Man Singh Medical College** and the **Sawai Man Singh Hospital** bear his name, and the **University of Rajputana**, later the University of Rajasthan, was founded at Jaipur in **1947**.

But the world around the princes was changing faster than any palace could control. India's freedom movement had grown into a mass struggle. In Jaipur, as in other states, the **Praja Mandal** demanded responsible government and an end to autocratic rule. Man Singh was a ruler of the old order, but he was also a realist. In the 1940s steps were taken towards constitutional government in Jaipur, with ministers drawn partly from the people's representatives.

In **August 1947**, as British rule ended, Man Singh signed the **Instrument of Accession**, joining Jaipur to the new Dominion of India. It was the first step. Over the next two years, the government of India, led in this work by **Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel** and **V. P. Menon**, persuaded the princes of Rajputana to merge their states into larger unions. On **30 March 1949**, Jaipur, together with Jodhpur, Jaisalmer and Bikaner, joined the union that formed **Greater Rajasthan**, with Jaipur as its capital. That date is celebrated today as Rajasthan Day.

Man Singh was appointed **Rajpramukh** of the new state, its constitutional head, a post similar to that of a governor. He held it from 1949 until **1956**, when the reorganisation of states abolished the office. The ruler whose ancestors had governed Dhundhar for centuries now presided, as a constitutional figure, over the democratic state that had replaced their kingdoms. He accepted the change with dignity, and the peaceful integration of Jaipur became one of the quiet successes of the founding of the Indian republic.

The princes kept their titles and received an annual allowance from the government, called the **privy purse**, in return for surrendering their states. But the cost of keeping up great palaces was heavy. Man Singh found an answer that many others would later copy. In **1957**, he turned the **Rambagh Palace**, his own residence since the 1920s, into a luxury hotel, one of the first palace hotels in India. The family moved to a smaller residence, and the palace began a new life welcoming guests from all over the world. Part of the City Palace was opened as a museum, now the **Maharaja Sawai Man Singh II Museum**.

Politics, however, did not leave the family alone. In **1962**, Gayatri Devi stood for parliament from Jaipur as a candidate of the **Swatantra Party**, which opposed the ruling Congress, and won by one of the largest margins ever recorded. Relations between the former ruling family and the Congress government in Delhi became tense. Man Singh himself remained in public service, and in **1965** he was appointed **India's Ambassador to Spain**, serving in Madrid for several years.

He never gave up polo. Even in his late fifties he continued to play. In **June 1970**, while playing a match at **Cirencester** in England, he fell from his horse and died on **24 June 1970**, at the age of fifty-seven. He had died, many said, as he would have wished, on a polo field. His body was brought back to Jaipur, and he was cremated with full honours at the royal cremation ground of **Gaitore**, where the Kachwaha rulers have been laid to rest since the founding of the city.

His eldest son, **Bhawani Singh**, succeeded him as head of the family. But within a year, the government of India ended the privy purses and the recognition of princely titles through the 26th Amendment to the Constitution in 1971. Man Singh II was therefore the last Maharaja of Jaipur to rule a state, and the last to be recognised as a ruler by the government of India before his death.

His legacy is all around Jaipur. The stadium, the hospital and the medical college that bear his name; the university founded in his time; the palace hotel that set a pattern for heritage tourism across Rajasthan; and above all the memory of the peaceful passage of an ancient kingdom into the Indian republic. He was born the younger son of a country thakur, and he lived to see the end of the world of kings. That he accepted that ending with grace is perhaps the most important thing he did.

## Highlights of his life

- **From Isarda to the throne.** Born Mor Mukut Singh in 1912, he was adopted by Madho Singh II in 1921 and became Maharaja in 1922 at the age of ten.
- **World-famous polo player.** His Jaipur team swept the major English tournaments of 1933, and he was one of the leading players of his generation.
- **Service in the Second World War.** He placed Jaipur's forces at the service of the war effort and served on active duty himself.
- **Builder of institutions.** The Sawai Man Singh Hospital and Medical College bear his name, and the University of Rajputana was founded at Jaipur in 1947.
- **Accession and merger.** He acceded to India in 1947 and merged Jaipur into Greater Rajasthan on 30 March 1949.
- **Rajpramukh of Rajasthan (1949–1956).** He served as the constitutional head of the new state.
- **Pioneer of heritage tourism.** In 1957 he turned Rambagh Palace into one of India's first palace hotels.
- **Ambassador and sportsman to the end.** He served as India's ambassador to Spain from 1965 and died after a polo fall in England in 1970.

## Bhawani Singh — the soldier-Maharaja of the desert raid

*Bhawani Singh's life belongs to modern history and is recorded in army citations, newspapers and public records; some colourful details, such as the story of his nickname, come from family memory, and where they do, this story says so.*

On **22 October 1931**, the cannons of Jaipur fired a royal salute, and the old city erupted in celebration. A son had been born to **Maharaja Sawai Man Singh II** and his first queen, **Marudhar Kanwar** of Jodhpur. For generations, the rulers of Jaipur had come to the throne by adoption: Ram Singh II had adopted Madho Singh II, and Madho Singh II had adopted Man Singh II. This child was the first male heir born directly to a ruling Maharaja of Jaipur for a very long time.

Family memory tells that the celebrations in the palace were so lavish, and the champagne flowed so freely, that the baby was nicknamed **"Bubbles"** by an English nanny. The name stayed with him all his life. Friends, fellow officers and even newspapers used it long after he had become a decorated soldier and the head of one of India's oldest royal houses. His formal name was **Bhawani Singh**, after the goddess Bhavani, the fierce form of the Mother whom the Rajputs have worshipped as a giver of victory.

He grew up in a world that was about to disappear. His father was a ruling prince, a world-famous polo player and a favourite of British society, and Jaipur was one of the great states of Rajputana. But by the time Bhawani Singh was a teenager, India had become independent, Jaipur had acceded to the new nation, and in **1949** the state was merged into Rajasthan. The boy who had been born to inherit a throne would instead inherit a title, a family, a set of palaces and a great deal of history.

He was educated at the **Doon School** in Dehradun and in England, and from his youth he chose the profession that the Rajputs had always regarded as their own: soldiering. In **1951** he was commissioned as an officer in the Indian Army, in the cavalry. He later served with the **President's Bodyguard**, the oldest regiment of the Indian Army, the mounted unit that escorts the President of India on ceremonial occasions. It was a natural home for a young man who had grown up in the stables of the Jaipur polo team.

But Bhawani Singh wanted more than ceremony. He moved to the **Parachute Regiment**, and in time he rose to command its **10th Battalion**, which had been converted into a commando unit trained for operations deep behind enemy lines in the desert. Its men were trained to move at night across sand and scrub, to strike suddenly and to vanish again. For a Rajput officer whose ancestors had fought across the Thar for centuries, the desert was not a strange land.

In **1966** he married **Padmini Devi**, a princess of the royal house of **Sirmur** in the hills of Himachal. Their only child, a daughter named **Diya Kumari**, was born in **1971**. By then the family's world had changed again. In **June 1970**, his father Man Singh II died after a fall during a polo match in England, and Bhawani Singh became the head of the Kachwaha house, the titular **Maharaja Sawai Bhawani Singh** of Jaipur. In 1971, the twenty-sixth amendment to the Constitution ended the privy purses and the official recognition of princely titles. From then on, his title was a matter of family and public affection, not law.

That same year brought the moment for which he is best remembered. In **December 1971**, war broke out between India and Pakistan over the crisis in East Pakistan, which would soon become Bangladesh. While the main campaign was fought in the east, the Indian Army also opened operations on the western front. Lieutenant Colonel Bhawani Singh led his commandos of **10 Para** into the desert of the **Tharparkar** district of **Sindh**, in Pakistan.

The raids that followed became famous in the history of the Indian Army's special forces. Moving by night in jeeps and on foot across the sands, his men struck at Pakistani positions far inside enemy territory, around **Chachro** and the surrounding areas. The aim was to unsettle the enemy, seize ground and throw his defences into confusion. The commandos covered great distances, attacked outposts and captured territory, and the speed and daring of the operation caught the defenders off guard. Bhawani Singh led from the front, travelling with his men and directing the attacks himself.

For his leadership in these operations, he was awarded the **Maha Vir Chakra**, India's second-highest award for gallantry in war. It was a rare honour for any officer, and rarer still for a man who could have lived a life of comfort in the palaces of Jaipur. The people of Rajasthan saw in it a link between the old and the new: the descendant of the Kachwaha generals had once more ridden into battle, this time in the uniform of the Indian Republic. He later retired from active service, and was afterwards given the honorary rank of **Brigadier**.

Civilian life was not always kind to the family. During the **Emergency** of **1975**, when civil liberties were suspended across India, Bhawani Singh and his stepmother **Gayatri Devi**, who had become a strong opposition politician, were arrested on charges relating to tax and foreign exchange laws. Both spent months in **Tihar Jail** in Delhi. Many saw the arrests as political, aimed at a family that had openly opposed the ruling party. When the Emergency ended in 1977, they returned to public life.

Bhawani Singh made his own attempt at politics. In **1989** he contested the Lok Sabha seat of Jaipur as a candidate of the **Congress** party, but he was defeated by the BJP candidate. He did not stand again. His service to the nation continued in another form: from **1994 to 1997** he served as **India's High Commissioner to Brunei**, following his father, who had been ambassador to Spain.

Most of his later life was devoted to the care of the family's heritage. The **City Palace** of Jaipur, part of which remained the family's home, was managed through a trust, and its museum, named after his father, drew visitors from across the world. Bhawani Singh supported the conservation of the palace, its collections of textiles, arms, manuscripts and paintings, and the family's charitable trusts. He took part in the festivals of the city, appearing in the old ceremonies of **Dussehra**, **Gangaur** and **Teej**, which kept alive the link between the house of Jaipur and its people. For many in Jaipur, his presence at these occasions was a reassurance that something of the old city remained.

He was known as a warm, approachable man, fond of good company and of the army, and proud of his regiment all his life. His regiment, in turn, remembered him as one of its heroes. Visitors to the palace often noted that among the portraits of armoured kings and jewelled princes, the Maharaja himself was most at ease talking about the desert war.

One question troubled his later years: the succession. He and Padmini Devi had no son. Their daughter Diya Kumari married **Narendra Singh**, and in **1998** she gave birth to a son, **Padmanabh**. In **November 2002**, following a custom that the Jaipur house had used many times, Bhawani Singh formally adopted his grandson as his son and heir. The old Rajput practice of adoption, which had brought Madho Singh II and Man Singh II to the throne, now secured the line once again.

His last years were also marked by long legal disputes within the extended family over the division of the family's properties, disputes that continued after his death. Through them he remained a public figure in Jaipur, respected as a soldier and as the head of the house.

Bhawani Singh died on **16 April 2011**, aged seventy-nine, in a hospital in **Gurgaon** near Delhi, after an illness. His body was brought back to Jaipur, where thousands of people lined the streets for the funeral procession. He was cremated with military honours at **Gaitore**, the royal cremation ground below Nahargarh, beside the memorials of his ancestors. His grandson and adopted son **Padmanabh Singh**, then twelve years old, succeeded him as the titular head of the house.

Bhawani Singh's life spans the passage from princely India to the modern republic. He was born to a reigning king amid cannon salutes and champagne, but he earned his most lasting honour as an ordinary soldier of the Indian Army, leading men by night across the sands of Sindh. In that sense he was perhaps the most fitting heir of the Kachwahas: a ruler without a kingdom, who still served his country with a sword.

## Highlights of his life

- **The long-awaited heir (1931).** Born on 22 October 1931 to Man Singh II and Marudhar Kanwar, he was the first son born to a ruling Maharaja of Jaipur in generations, and was nicknamed "Bubbles".
- **Army officer.** Commissioned in 1951, he served with the cavalry and the President's Bodyguard before joining the Parachute Regiment.
- **The desert raid (1971).** As commanding officer of 10 Para, he led commando raids deep into Sindh around Chachro in the 1971 India–Pakistan war.
- **Maha Vir Chakra.** He received India's second-highest wartime gallantry award for his leadership in those operations.
- **Head of the house (1970).** He became the titular Maharaja of Jaipur on his father's death in 1970, shortly before princely titles were abolished in 1971.
- **Public service.** He contested the Jaipur Lok Sabha seat in 1989 and served as India's High Commissioner to Brunei from 1994 to 1997.
- **Securing the succession.** In 2002 he adopted his grandson Padmanabh Singh, who succeeded him on his death on 16 April 2011.

## Padmanabh Singh — the boy who inherited three centuries of a city

*Padmanabh Singh is a living person, and his story is still being written; what follows rests on public records and reporting, and it does not guess at what is private or still to come.*

In the spring of **2011**, the old courtyards of the **City Palace** of Jaipur filled once more with the sound of conch shells, drums and priests chanting in Sanskrit. Nobles in bright *safas* stood in rows. At the centre of it all sat a boy of twelve, a little uncertain under the weight of the ceremony, while the elders of the Kachwaha house performed the rites that marked him as the new head of their family. His name was **Padmanabh Singh**, and he had just inherited a title that his ancestors had carried since before the city of Jaipur itself was built.

To understand how a twelve-year-old came to that seat, one has to go back a generation. His grandfather, **Maharaja Sawai Bhawani Singh**, had been the head of the house since 1970. Bhawani Singh was a decorated soldier, the commander of a famous commando raid in the desert war of 1971, and a beloved figure in Jaipur. But he and his wife, **Padmini Devi** of the royal house of Sirmur, had only one child, a daughter, **Diya Kumari**.

Diya Kumari married **Narendra Singh**, and their first son was born on **12 July 1998**. The boy was named Padmanabh, a name of Vishnu, "the one from whose navel the lotus springs". Two more children followed, a younger brother, **Lakshyaraj**, and a sister, **Gauravi**. Within the family, the eldest boy was given a pet name that would follow him into adulthood: **"Pacho"**.

The question of succession in the Jaipur house had often been answered by adoption. Ram Singh II had adopted Madho Singh II in 1880; Madho Singh II had adopted Man Singh II in 1921. Bhawani Singh now followed the same path. In **November 2002**, when Padmanabh was four years old, his grandfather formally adopted him as his son and heir. From that day the small boy was, in the eyes of the family and its traditions, the future head of the Kachwahas of Jaipur.

His childhood was divided between two worlds. On one side were the courtyards of the City Palace, the festivals in which the family still took part, and the stories of ancestors whose portraits lined the walls: **Sawai Jai Singh II**, who founded the city in 1727 and built its observatories; **Ram Singh II**, who lit its streets with gas; **Man Singh II**, the polo-playing Maharaja who saw the age of princes end. On the other side was the ordinary life of a boy in modern India, with school, friends and sport.

He was sent to **Mayo College** at Ajmer, the school that had been founded in the nineteenth century for the sons of the princes of Rajputana, and where his great-grandfather Man Singh II had also studied. Later he continued his education abroad. Like many of his family before him, he was drawn early to horses, and above all to **polo**, the game that had once made the Jaipur name famous across the world.

His grandfather's health declined in his last years, and on **16 April 2011** Bhawani Singh died in a hospital near Delhi. Thousands lined the streets of Jaipur for his funeral procession to the royal cremation ground at **Gaitore**. Days later, in the ceremony in the City Palace, the twelve-year-old Padmanabh was installed as the titular **Maharaja Sawai Padmanabh Singh**, the head of the house.

It is important to understand what that title means today. Since **1971**, when the twenty-sixth amendment to the Constitution of India ended the privy purses and the official recognition of princely rulers, the title of Maharaja has had no legal force. Padmanabh Singh rules no territory and holds no government office by birth. What he inherited was something different: the leadership of a family, the care of great historic buildings and collections, a place in the ceremonies of the city, and a deep bond of affection with many of the people of Jaipur who still see the house as part of the city's identity.

In practice, much of that inheritance is held in trusts. The City Palace, part of which remains the family's residence, includes the **Maharaja Sawai Man Singh II Museum**, with its textiles, arms, manuscripts, paintings, carriages and the two great silver urns of Madho Singh II. The family also has links with other historic properties, such as the fort of **Jaigarh** above Amber, which belongs to the family's trust. As he grew older, Padmanabh Singh took on a growing public role in these institutions, together with his mother.

His mother, meanwhile, entered public life in her own right. Diya Kumari was elected to the Rajasthan Legislative Assembly from **Sawai Madhopur** in **2013**, to the Lok Sabha from **Rajsamand** in **2019**, and in **December 2023** became a **Deputy Chief Minister of Rajasthan**. Her younger son, Lakshyaraj, was chosen by the house of his grandmother's family to be the titular head of **Sirmur**, so that the two brothers now carry the names of two different royal houses.

Padmanabh Singh's own path has not been politics but heritage, culture and sport. In polo he has followed his great-grandfather into the saddle, playing in India and abroad and representing the colours of Jaipur and India in international matches. The game is a living link with the past: the Jaipur team of the 1930s, led by Man Singh II, was one of the greatest in the world, and the Rambagh polo ground still hosts matches in the winter season.

He has also tried to bring the old palace into the modern world in new ways. In **2021**, a suite within the City Palace was opened to paying guests through an international online booking service, allowing travellers to stay inside a working royal palace. Through such efforts, and through his presence in fashion, travel and the media, he has become one of the best-known faces of Rajasthan's royal heritage among young people, both in India and abroad. Some see this as a clever way of keeping old buildings alive in an age when they must pay for their own upkeep. Others see in it a new chapter in a story that began when Man Singh II turned Rambagh Palace into a hotel in 1957.

Through all of this, the old ceremonies continue. On **Dussehra**, the family performs the worship of weapons that the Rajputs have kept for centuries. At **Gangaur**, the image of the goddess Gauri is carried in procession out of the palace into the streets of the walled city, watched by crowds of women in bright clothing who pray for good husbands and long marriages. At **Teej**, the coming of the monsoon is welcomed with another procession. At these moments, the head of the house still appears before the people of Jaipur, not as a ruler but as the keeper of a tradition.

The city he represents has itself been recognised by the world. In **2019**, the walled city of Jaipur, laid out by Sawai Jai Singh II almost three centuries earlier, was inscribed as a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**, joining the **Jantar Mantar** observatory and the **Amber** fort, already honoured among the world's heritage. The history that the Kachwaha house carries is now part of the inheritance of all humanity.

Padmanabh Singh is still a young man, and the most important parts of his life may lie ahead of him. He stands at the end of a long line: seventy names in the list of this dynasty, from the founders who came to Dhundhar a thousand years ago, through the kings of Amber who served and fought beside the Mughal emperors, to the builders of the pink city and the princes of the British age. He is the first in that line to have grown up entirely as a citizen of the Republic of India. What he makes of that inheritance, in a democracy that has no place for kings but still loves its history, is the part of the story that remains to be told.

## Highlights of his life

- **Born into the house of Jaipur (1998).** He was born on 12 July 1998 to Diya Kumari and Narendra Singh, grandson of Maharaja Sawai Bhawani Singh.
- **Adopted as heir (2002).** At the age of four he was formally adopted by his grandfather, continuing the Jaipur tradition of succession by adoption.
- **Head of the house at twelve (2011).** After Bhawani Singh's death on 16 April 2011, he was installed as the titular Maharaja of Jaipur in the City Palace.
- **Keeper of heritage.** With his family he plays a leading role in the trusts that care for the City Palace, its museum and other historic properties.
- **Polo player.** He has carried on the Jaipur polo tradition of Man Singh II, playing in India and abroad.
- **Opening the palace to the world.** In 2021 a suite in the City Palace was opened to paying guests, part of an effort to sustain the palace and share its heritage.
- **Face of living tradition.** He takes part in Jaipur's festivals of Dussehra, Gangaur and Teej, linking the city's past with its present.

rao-bika.story:
## Rao Bika — the prince who answered a taunt with a kingdom

*Rao Bika's life comes to us through the Rathore chronicles of Bikaner and Marwar, the khyats of the bards and the traditions kept at the shrine of Karni Mata in Deshnoke. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

In the middle of the fifteenth century the Rathores of Marwar were a rising house. **Rao Jodha**, after years of exile and war, had won back his father's lands, and in **1459** he founded a new capital on a rocky ridge, the city that still bears his name, **Jodhpur**. Around his court gathered a crowd of sons, brothers and kinsmen, each of them a Rajput with a sword, a horse and an ambition. A kingdom can only be divided so many times, and every son of Jodha knew that only one of them would sit on his father's throne.

Bika was one of these sons. The Bikaner chronicles place his birth in **1438**, and name his mother as Rani **Naurangde** of the Sankhla Parmars. He grew up in the hard school of his father's wars, riding with his uncles and cousins, learning how to hold a desert well, how to read a horizon for dust and how to judge a man by the way he kept his word. He was not the heir, and he knew it.

The story of how Bika left Jodhpur is the most famous in Bikaner's memory. Tradition says that one day in **1465**, as Rao Jodha sat in court, he noticed his son Bika whispering with his uncle **Kandhal**, Jodha's own brother. Half in jest, the old Rao asked what the two of them were plotting so earnestly. Were they, he said, planning to conquer some new kingdom for themselves? The court laughed. Kandhal did not. He rose and said that by the grace of his elder brother, that was exactly what they would do. Whether the words were spoken quite like that, the bards cannot say. But the taunt became a vow, and the vow became Bikaner.

The chronicles say Bika set out with Kandhal, a few kinsmen and a small band of horsemen and foot soldiers, numbered in the hundreds rather than the thousands. They rode north-west into the country called **Jangaldesh**, the "land of scrub", the dry tract between Marwar, the Bhati lands of Jaisalmer and the plains of the Punjab. It was not empty. Bhati Rajputs held the forts of the west. Johiya and other clans held the north. And across much of the land lay the cantons of the **Jat** clans, the Godaras, Sarans, Beniwals, Punias and others, each under its own headman, farming where the rain allowed and grazing herds across the sand.

On the way, tradition says, Bika went to **Deshnoke** to seek the blessing of **Karni Mata**, the Charan holy woman revered across the desert as a living goddess. She is said to have foretold that his power would surpass his father's. From that day the Rathores of Bikaner took Karni Mata as the protecting goddess of their house, and her temple at Deshnoke, famous today for the rats that are believed to be her devotees, remained bound to the dynasty ever after.

Bika's first base was at **Kodamdesar**, where he raised a small fort. The early years were a struggle for survival. The Bhatis of **Pugal** and Jaisalmer saw the newcomers as intruders and raided them. Bika answered with arms and with marriage. The chronicles say he married the daughter of **Rao Shekha**, the Bhati chief of Pugal, and the alliance eased the pressure from the west, though quarrels with the Bhatis never quite ended.

The heart of the matter, however, was the Jat country. The Jat cantons were not united. The Godaras and the Sarans in particular were bitter rivals, and the bards tell a story of how that rivalry began over a woman, Malki, the wife of the Saran chief **Pula**, who left him for the Godara chief **Pandu**. Whatever the truth of the tale, the quarrel gave Bika his opening. The Godaras chose to accept him as their overlord, seeking his protection against their enemies. In return, tradition says, the Godara headmen were given the honour of marking the forehead of each new ruler of Bikaner with the *tilak* at his coronation, an honour remembered in the state for centuries.

With the Godaras beside him, Bika turned on those who resisted. The Sarans and other cantons were brought under his rule through years of hard campaigning. These were not great set-piece battles but a slow war of raids, sieges of village strongholds and negotiated surrenders. Bika's skill lay as much in diplomacy as in fighting: he left local headmen in place where they submitted, took revenue rather than land, and offered protection in return for loyalty. Step by step, the scattered Jat country became a Rathore state.

A state needed a capital. Around **1485** Bika began building a fort on a rise of ground called **Rati Ghati**, and in **1488**, on the traditional date of the second day of the bright half of Vaishakh, the city of **Bikaner** was founded around it. Local tradition says the land belonged to a Jat named **Nera**, who agreed to give it only if his name was joined to the new town. So the city became *Bika-Ner*. Historians treat the story with caution, since other explanations of the name exist, but it shows how deeply the founding of the state was tied, in local memory, to agreement with the Jat people of the land.

Bika's small stone fort was modest. The great fort of Bikaner that stands today, Junagarh, was built a century later by his descendant Raja Rai Singh. But the walled town around Bika's fort grew quickly. It stood on routes that carried caravans between the Punjab, Sindh and Gujarat, and merchants were glad of a ruler strong enough to keep the roads safe.

Not every year brought success. Bika's uncle **Kandhal**, the man who had answered Jodha's taunt, continued to carve out lands of his own towards the north-east, on the edge of the territory ruled from **Hisar**. There, around **1490**, he was killed in a clash with **Sarang Khan**, the governor of Hisar. Kandhal's death was a heavy blow to Bika. The chronicles say that Rao Jodha himself joined his son to avenge his brother, and that the Rathores defeated Sarang Khan's forces. The descendants of Kandhal, the **Kandhalots**, remained among the leading nobles of Bikaner.

Jodha died in **1489**, and Bika faced a new kind of struggle, this time with his own family. Tradition says that Jodha had promised Bika certain sacred heirlooms of the Rathore house, among them a royal throne, an umbrella of state, a sword and the family's household deity, in return for Bika's renouncing any claim to the throne of Jodhpur. After Jodha's death, his successor **Rao Suja** would not give them up. Bika marched on Jodhpur to claim what he believed was his. The bards say that bloodshed between brothers was avoided through the mediation of the dowager queen, **Jasmade**, and that the heirlooms were handed over. They were kept at Bikaner ever afterwards as the most precious possessions of the dynasty, and the rulers of Bikaner were proud that the ancestral regalia of the Rathores lay with them.

By the end of his life Bika had built something no one in Jodhpur had expected when he rode out in 1465. His rule stretched across a wide stretch of the northern Thar, from the Bhati frontier towards the edges of the Punjab plains. His kinsmen had also founded their own holdings nearby: his brother **Bida** had established the Bidawat Rathores in the lands of the Mohil Chauhans around Chhapar and Dronpur, a branch that would later be drawn closely into Bikaner's orbit.

Bika was a devout man in the manner of his age. Beyond his devotion to Karni Mata, he is credited with beginning the **Lakshminath temple** in Bikaner, dedicated to Vishnu and Lakshmi, which became the principal temple of the city and was completed by his son Lunkaran. He honoured the Charans and bards who would, in turn, keep his story alive for five centuries.

He is remembered as a ruler of plain habits and great stubbornness, a man who had been given no kingdom and so made one. The chronicles describe him dividing his life between the saddle and the council, settling disputes between clans, receiving merchants, inspecting wells and walls. In a country where water decided everything, the digging and protection of wells and tanks was as important as any war.

Rao Bika died in **1504** at Bikaner. He was succeeded by his eldest son, **Rao Naro**, whose reign would last only a few months, and then by his younger son **Rao Lunkaran**, who would expand what his father had begun. The state Bika founded outlasted the Delhi Sultanate, the Mughal Empire and the British Raj, and remained a princely state until it joined independent India in 1949. Every one of its rulers looked back to the day when a son of Jodha, stung by a joke in his father's court, rode out into the sand to find a kingdom of his own.

## Highlights of his life

- **Departure from Jodhpur (1465).** Tradition says a jest by his father, Rao Jodha, about "conquering a new kingdom" set him and his uncle Kandhal on the road to Jangaldesh.
- **Blessing of Karni Mata.** He sought the blessing of the Charan holy woman at Deshnoke, and she became the protecting goddess of the Bikaner Rathores.
- **Union with the Jat cantons.** Through alliance with the Godaras and campaigns against those who resisted, he brought the scattered Jat country under one rule.
- **Founding of Bikaner (1488).** He built a fort at Rati Ghati and founded the city of Bikaner, which became the capital of a state lasting more than four and a half centuries.
- **Avenging Kandhal.** After his uncle Kandhal was killed by Sarang Khan of Hisar, he and Rao Jodha defeated the governor's forces.
- **Winning the Rathore regalia.** After Jodha's death he secured the sacred heirlooms of the Rathore house from Rao Suja, and they were kept at Bikaner ever after.
- **Founder of a dynasty.** He died in 1504, leaving a state that remained a princely kingdom until 1949.

rao-naroji-bikaner.story:
## Rao Naroji — the founder's heir and his brief reign

*Rao Naro, or Naroji, appears in the Bikaner chronicles only briefly, as the eldest son of Rao Bika and his first successor; little more about him has come down to us.*

When **Rao Bika** died in **1504**, the young Rathore state of Bikaner was less than forty years old. Bika had ridden out of Jodhpur in 1465 with a small band of followers, won over or subdued the Jat cantons of Jangaldesh, held off the Bhatis of Pugal and Jaisalmer, and founded the city of **Bikaner** in 1488. What he left behind was still a frontier state, held together by the loyalty of kinsmen and clan headmen as much as by any settled government.

By custom, the throne passed to Bika's eldest son, **Naro**. The chronicles record his accession at Bikaner in 1504 and little else. His reign lasted only a few months. He died in **1505**, and since he left no son to succeed him, the throne passed to his younger brother, **Lunkaran**.

The chronicles record no wars, buildings or reforms from these months, and it would be wrong to invent them. What can be said is that the succession passed without civil war at a fragile moment. Bikaner's neighbours, the Bhatis to the west, the Rathores of Jodhpur to the south and the governors of the Delhi Sultanate to the north-east, were all watching. A disputed throne could have undone Bika's work. Instead the Rathore nobles accepted Naro and then, after his death, Lunkaran, and the state passed intact to the ruler who would greatly enlarge it.

## Highlights of his life

- **Eldest son of the founder.** He was the eldest son of Rao Bika, the founder of Bikaner.
- **Second ruler of Bikaner (1504).** He succeeded his father as the second Rao of the young state.
- **A reign of months.** He died in 1505, a few months after taking the throne.
- **An unbroken succession.** With no son of his own, the throne passed peacefully to his brother Rao Lunkaran.

## Rao Lunkaran — the generous king who widened the desert kingdom

*Rao Lunkaran's reign is known through the Bikaner khyats, the songs of the Charan bards who praised his gifts and the later histories built on them. Where history and tradition part ways, this story says so.*

Lunkaran was born around **1470**, a son of **Rao Bika**, in the years when his father was still fighting to turn a band of horsemen into a kingdom. He grew up in a household that lived in the saddle. Bika had left Jodhpur in 1465 with his uncle Kandhal and a few hundred men, and by the time Lunkaran was a boy, the Rathores were winning over the Jat cantons of Jangaldesh one by one, quarrelling with the Bhatis of Pugal and Jaisalmer, and laying out the lines of a fort on the rise called Rati Ghati.

He would have been about eighteen when the city of **Bikaner** was founded in **1488**. He saw the walls go up, the merchants arrive, the wells dug and guarded. He saw his father ride to Jodhpur after Rao Jodha's death to claim the ancestral regalia of the Rathore house, and return with them. These were the lessons of his youth: that a kingdom in the desert was held together by water, by trade, by the loyalty of kinsmen and by the willingness to fight.

Lunkaran was not the eldest son. When Bika died in **1504**, the throne passed to his elder brother, **Rao Naro**. But Naro died only a few months later, in **1505**, without a son, and Lunkaran became the third ruler of Bikaner. He was about thirty-five, a grown man with long experience of his father's campaigns, and he took over a state that was still young, still surrounded by rivals and still unsure of its borders.

The world beyond the sand was changing too. In Delhi, **Sikandar Lodi** ruled the Sultanate, and after him, from 1517, his son **Ibrahim Lodi**. Their power reached into the plains of Haryana and the edges of the desert through governors and local chiefs. In Mewar, **Rana Sanga** was building the strongest Rajput power of the age. In Marwar, Bikaner's kinsmen ruled from Jodhpur. Between these great neighbours lay a patchwork of smaller lordships: the Chauhans of the north-east, the **Kayamkhani** Muslim chiefs of Fatehpur and Jhunjhunu, the Bhatis of the west, and the governors of the towns of the Delhi plains. Lunkaran's reign would be spent pushing Bikaner's borders out into this patchwork.

The chronicles tell of a campaign against the Chauhans of **Dadrewa**, in the country to the east, which Lunkaran brought under his control. They tell of war with the Kayamkhanis of **Fatehpur**, from whom he is said to have taken a large number of villages. These were hard-won gains. The Kayamkhanis were a proud and warlike house, descended from a Chauhan ancestor who had converted to Islam, and they fought for every well and every hamlet. Lunkaran's men rode out in the cold months, when the desert could be crossed, struck at forts and villages, and either took them or forced their chiefs to pay tribute.

The most remembered of his campaigns, though, was against **Jaisalmer**. The Bhatis had been Bikaner's rivals since the days of Bika, and the frontier between them was a constant source of raids. The chronicles say that Lunkaran marched into Bhati territory and captured **Rawal Jait Singh** of Jaisalmer. A lesser ruler might have held him for ransom or killed him. Lunkaran, the bards say, released him after the Rawal agreed to terms, and the two houses settled their quarrel for a time. The story was told in Bikaner as proof of both his strength and his restraint. Imagine the scene as the bards might have: the defeated Rawal brought before the Rao, expecting humiliation, and instead hearing that he was free to return to his golden fort, provided the raids on Bikaner's villages stopped.

What the bards loved most about Lunkaran, however, was not his wars but his generosity. They called him the **Karna of the Kali Age**, after the hero of the Mahabharata who could never refuse a gift. The Charans and Bhats who came to his court went away with horses, camels, gold and grants of land, and in return they filled their songs with his name. Historians read such praise with caution, since bards praised their patrons for a living. But the consistency of the tradition suggests that Lunkaran's open-handedness was real, and that it was part of how he ruled. In a land where a ruler's reputation travelled faster than his armies, generosity was also a kind of power.

He was a builder as well. He completed the **Lakshminath temple** in Bikaner, begun by his father, which became the principal temple of the city and the place where the rulers of Bikaner would worship for generations. He is remembered as the founder of **Lunkaransar**, a town to the north-east of Bikaner that still bears his name, with its salt lake beside it. Every new settlement in the desert needed water and protection, and each one that took root extended the reach of the state.

Inside his kingdom, Lunkaran had to manage a nobility made up largely of his own kinsmen. The Kandhalots, descendants of his great-uncle Kandhal, the Bidawats of his uncle Bida's line and the families of his own brothers all held lands and expected a voice in the state. The Jat headmen who had accepted Bika's rule still mattered. Lunkaran kept this balance through a long reign of twenty-one years, and the state he handed on was larger and more secure than the one he had received.

Ruling Bikaner meant understanding the desert itself. Rain came in a few weeks of the monsoon, and in many years it hardly came at all. The wealth of the state lay in its herds of camels, cattle, sheep and goats, in the thin crops of millet and pulses that the sandy fields could bear, and in the caravans that crossed its tracks carrying salt, wool, horses and cloth between Sindh, the Punjab, Gujarat and the Delhi plains. A Rao's revenue came from a share of the harvest, from dues on herds and from tolls on the caravans. Each of these depended on peace on the roads and on the wells. Much of Lunkaran's ruling life was spent on things the bards rarely sang about: settling quarrels over wells and grazing, appointing and watching the men who collected the dues, and making sure the traders who brought money into Bikaner felt safe enough to come back.

His relations with **Jodhpur** were those of proud kinsmen. The rulers of Marwar, first **Rao Suja** and then, from 1515, **Rao Ganga**, were his cousins, descended like him from Rao Jodha. The memory of Bika's march to claim the Rathore regalia had not been forgotten in either court, and each house watched the other's growth with a careful eye. But during Lunkaran's reign the two Rathore states were not at open war. Their great quarrel would come a generation later, under his son, when the ambitions of a new ruler of Jodhpur would threaten Bikaner's very existence.

The end came in **1526**, the same year that **Babur** defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat and the Delhi Sultanate collapsed. That collapse did not happen in a single day. In the months around it, the towns and districts of the Delhi plains were held by governors and local chiefs, each trying to keep or expand their power. Lunkaran turned east towards **Narnaul**, held by a chief whom the chronicles call **Shaikh Abhimira**. Near **Dhosi**, close to Narnaul, the armies met. The chronicles say the fight went badly for Bikaner, and that some of those who should have stood with the Rao did not. Lunkaran was killed in the battle, and several of his sons died beside him.

It was a hard death for a man who had spent his life widening his kingdom, and a sharp reminder of how fragile the desert states remained. The bards made the most of it, as they always did, describing a ruler who would not turn his horse from the field. What is certain is that Bikaner lost its ruler and several of its princes on a single day, and that the throne passed to his son **Rao Jait Singh**, who would soon face a far greater threat from the new rulers of Delhi and Lahore.

Lunkaran's reign has none of the drama of Bika's founding or the fame of the Mughal-era rulers who came after him. But in many ways it was the reign that made Bikaner last. He took a state that was still a frontier camp and gave it borders, towns, temples and a reputation. He showed that the house of Bika could expand without breaking apart, and that a Rao of Bikaner could deal with the Bhatis, the Kayamkhanis and the chiefs of the Delhi plains on equal terms.

## Highlights of his life

- **Third ruler of Bikaner (1505).** He took the throne after the short reign of his brother Naro, who died without a son.
- **Eastern expansion.** The chronicles credit him with bringing Dadrewa under Bikaner and winning many villages from the Kayamkhanis of Fatehpur.
- **Capture and release of the Rawal of Jaisalmer.** Tradition says he captured Rawal Jait Singh and freed him on terms, ending the Bhati raids for a time.
- **The "Karna of the Kali Age".** The bards remembered him for his lavish gifts to poets, Charans and the needy.
- **Builder of Bikaner.** He completed the Lakshminath temple and founded the town of Lunkaransar.
- **Death at Dhosi (1526).** He fell near Narnaul fighting Shaikh Abhimira, with several of his sons, in the year the Delhi Sultanate fell.
