## Rao Jait Singh — the Rao who drove a Mughal prince from Bikaner

*Rao Jait Singh, often called Jaitsi, is known to us through the Bikaner khyats, the Persian histories of the early Mughals and, above all, a Rajasthani heroic poem written in his honour by the Charan poet Bithu Suja. Where history and the poets part ways, this story says so.*

Jait Singh came to the throne of Bikaner in **1526** in the worst of circumstances. His father, **Rao Lunkaran**, had just been killed in battle at **Dhosi**, near Narnaul, fighting the chief whom the chronicles call Shaikh Abhimira, and several of Jait Singh's brothers had died with him. The young state founded by his grandfather **Rao Bika** less than sixty years earlier had lost its ruler and a group of its princes in a single day. The nobles looked to Jait Singh, as the eldest surviving son, to hold it together.

He was a grown man by then, raised in the saddle like his father and grandfather, and he knew the state he inherited. Its heart was the walled city of **Bikaner** with its small fort on Rati Ghati, its temples of Lakshminath and its devotion to **Karni Mata** of Deshnoke. Around it lay the Jat cantons that had accepted Bika's rule, the lands of Rathore kinsmen such as the Kandhalots and Bidawats, and the frontier towns that Lunkaran had won from the Chauhans and Kayamkhanis. To the north-east, on the route to the Punjab, stood the old fort of **Bhatner**, where Hanumangarh is today, a key to the desert roads.

The world around Bikaner was turning upside down. In the same year that Lunkaran died, **Babur** defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat and founded Mughal rule in Delhi. In **1527**, Babur defeated **Rana Sanga** of Mewar and his Rajput allies at **Khanwa**. Some Bikaner traditions say that a contingent from Bikaner rode with Sanga that day, but the details are uncertain. What is certain is that the old balance of power in northern India had been broken, and that the new rulers from Kabul were looking for land and revenue in every direction.

After Babur's death in 1530, his son **Humayun** became emperor, and Humayun's brother **Kamran Mirza** took control of Kabul and the Punjab, ruling from **Lahore**. Kamran was ambitious, restless and eager for conquests of his own. The desert lands to the south of the Punjab, with their forts and caravan routes, lay within his reach.

In **1534**, Kamran's army struck. It first fell on **Bhatner**. The fort was held for Bikaner by a Kandhalot noble, **Khetsi**, who refused to surrender. The defenders fought until the fort fell, and Khetsi died in its defence. With Bhatner taken, the road to Bikaner lay open. Kamran's forces marched across the sand and occupied the city and its fort.

It was a moment that could have ended the house of Bika. A Mughal prince, a brother of the emperor, held the Rathore capital. Jait Singh had withdrawn rather than be trapped in the fort, and now he had to decide what to do. The chronicles say that he gathered his nobles, his kinsmen and the fighting men of the Jat cantons, and that he chose not to wait for the Mughals to come out and hunt him down, but to strike first.

The poets tell the rest of the story in fire and thunder. Imagine the night as they describe it: the Mughal camp around the captured fort, the tents and horses and guards half-asleep after their easy victory, and out of the darkness of the dunes the Rathore horsemen coming down at a gallop. The attack fell on Kamran's camp near **Ratighati**, close to the fort itself. Surprised and thrown into confusion, the Mughal forces broke. Kamran fled back towards Lahore, leaving behind his baggage and, the bards claim, his royal umbrella.

The victory at Ratighati in **1534** was the greatest achievement of Jait Singh's life. The Rathores of Bikaner had defeated a prince of the new imperial house and taken back their capital within a single campaign. The Charan poet **Bithu Suja** celebrated it in *Rao Jaitsi ro Chhand*, one of the finest works of early Rajasthani heroic poetry. The poem is a work of praise, not a dispatch from the battlefield, and its numbers and speeches belong to poetry. But it preserves the memory of a real event, and it shows how deeply the victory moved the people of the desert. Jait Singh's reward to the poet was itself remembered as a sign of his generosity, in the tradition of his father.

Jait Singh's reign was not only war. He continued the work of his father and grandfather in the city of Bikaner, kept up the worship at the Lakshminath temple and the shrine of Karni Mata, and held together the balance between his Rathore nobles and the Jat headmen. He honoured the Charans and bards, who in return made his name immortal. In the years after Ratighati, Bikaner stood stronger and prouder than ever.

But a much more dangerous enemy was rising, and he was a kinsman. In **1532**, **Rao Maldev** had become ruler of **Jodhpur**. He was one of the most able and ambitious rulers Marwar ever had. Through the 1530s he built a large army and swept across western Rajasthan, taking **Nagaur**, **Merta**, **Ajmer**, **Jalore**, **Siwana** and many other towns and forts. The Rathores of Merta were driven out. The rulers of smaller states either submitted or fell. Maldev's aim was clear: to make Marwar the master of the whole region.

Bikaner, an independent Rathore state founded by a younger son of Jodha, stood in his way. The old rivalry between the two houses, going back to Bika's march on Jodhpur for the ancestral regalia, now turned into open war. Jait Singh understood the danger. The chronicles say he sent his trusted minister, **Nagraj**, to seek help from **Sher Shah Suri**, the Afghan ruler who had driven Humayun out of India in 1540 and was now the master of Delhi.

Jait Singh could have chosen another road. Many chiefs of the region had bowed to Maldev, sent tribute and kept their lands as his vassals. Imagine the council in the hall of the small fort at Bikaner: the older nobles counting the strength of Jodhpur's army, someone suggesting that a gift and a promise of loyalty might buy peace, and the Rao answering that the house of Bika had not crossed the desert to become the servant of Jodhpur. Whatever words were truly spoken, his choice is clear from what followed. He would not submit. He strengthened his forts, called up his kinsmen and the Jat levies, and prepared to fight for the independence that his grandfather had won and his father had widened.

Help did not come in time. Early in **1542**, Maldev's army marched on Bikaner, commanded by his great generals, among whom the chronicles name **Kumpa** and **Jaita**. Jait Singh gathered his forces and went out to meet them. The armies met near **Pahoba**, also called Sohwa, in Bikaner territory. The battle was fierce, and the Bikaner forces were outnumbered. Jait Singh was killed on the field, fighting at the head of his men.

Bikaner fell to Maldev. The Rathores of Jodhpur occupied the capital that Jait Singh had once won back from a Mughal prince. Jait Singh's son, **Kalyan Mal**, took refuge with his family at **Sirsa**, on the edge of the Punjab plains. For a moment it seemed that the house of Bika had been swallowed by the house of Jodhpur.

But Jait Singh's last act of statecraft, the mission of Nagraj to Sher Shah, bore fruit after his death. In **1544**, Sher Shah marched against Maldev, and at the hard-fought battle of **Giri-Sumel** the Marwar army was broken. Kalyan Mal, who had joined Sher Shah's camp, was restored to Bikaner. The kingdom survived, though its ruler had not.

Jait Singh's life is often overshadowed by those of his famous descendants, the rulers of the Mughal age. But he stood at a turning point. Between 1526 and 1542 the Lodis fell, the Mughals came, Rana Sanga was defeated, Humayun was driven out, Sher Shah rose and Maldev built his empire in Marwar. Through all of this, Jait Singh held Bikaner together, won back its capital from Kamran and died defending it from Maldev. His people remembered him as the Rao who would not let his grandfather's city stay in foreign hands.

## Highlights of his life

- **Accession in crisis (1526).** He took the throne after his father Rao Lunkaran and several of his brothers were killed at Dhosi.
- **Loss of Bhatner (1534).** Kamran Mirza's army took Bhatner, where the Kandhalot noble Khetsi died defending the fort, and then occupied Bikaner.
- **Victory at Ratighati (1534).** In a sudden attack he defeated Kamran Mirza, the brother of Humayun, and drove him from Bikaner.
- **Immortalised in poetry.** The Charan poet Bithu Suja celebrated his victory in *Rao Jaitsi ro Chhand*, a landmark of Rajasthani heroic verse.
- **Mission to Sher Shah.** Facing Rao Maldev of Jodhpur, he sent his minister Nagraj to seek help from Sher Shah Suri.
- **Death at Pahoba (1542).** He fell fighting the army of Maldev, and Bikaner was occupied until Sher Shah's victory at Giri-Sumel in 1544 restored his son Kalyan Mal.

## Rao Kalyan Mal — the exile who won back his father's kingdom

*Rao Kalyan Mal's life is known through the Bikaner khyats and the Persian histories of Sher Shah's and Akbar's reigns. Where history and tradition part ways, this story says so.*

Kalyan Mal was born around **1519**, the son of **Rao Jait Singh** of Bikaner. He grew up in a state that was both proud and threatened. When he was a boy of about fifteen, in **1534**, the Mughal prince **Kamran Mirza** seized Bhatner and then Bikaner itself, and his father won the city back in a sudden attack at **Ratighati**. The young prince learned early that a desert kingdom could be lost in a season and recovered in a night.

The greater danger came from his own kin. **Rao Maldev** of Jodhpur, who took the throne of Marwar in 1532, was building an empire across western Rajasthan. Early in **1542** his army invaded Bikaner, and Jait Singh was killed fighting it near **Pahoba**. Bikaner fell to Maldev. Kalyan Mal, now Rao of Bikaner in name only, took refuge with his family at **Sirsa**, on the edge of the Punjab plains.

These were the hardest years of his life. He was a king without a capital, depending on the loyalty of kinsmen who had escaped with him and on the hope of outside help. That hope rested on a mission his father had begun: the minister **Nagraj** had gone to **Sher Shah Suri**, the Afghan ruler of Delhi, to ask for aid against Maldev. Sher Shah had reasons of his own to fear the master of Marwar, whose army was among the strongest in northern India.

In **1544**, Sher Shah marched into Rajasthan. Kalyan Mal joined his camp, as did **Biram Dev** of Merta, another Rathore driven from his lands by Maldev. Imagine the young Rao in the great Afghan encampment, a desert prince among Pathan nobles, waiting for the day that would decide whether he ever saw Bikaner again. At **Giri-Sumel**, Maldev's commanders **Jaita** and **Kumpa** led a fierce attack that nearly broke Sher Shah's army before they were overwhelmed and killed. Sher Shah is said to have remarked that he had almost lost the empire of Hindustan for a handful of millet, a saying the histories attach to the battle. Maldev withdrew, and Kalyan Mal was restored to **Bikaner**.

He returned to a damaged kingdom. Two years of occupation had loosened the loyalty of some nobles and villages, and the borders had to be secured again. Kalyan Mal spent the following years rebuilding: winning back his kinsmen, restoring the shrines, and reasserting his authority over the Jat headmen and the frontier towns. Sher Shah died in 1545, and the Sur empire soon fell into civil war, but Bikaner did not slip back under Jodhpur. Maldev, though weakened, remained a rival until his death in **1562**, and the bitterness between the two Rathore houses lasted for a generation.

In **1556**, **Akbar** came to the throne of a restored Mughal empire. Kalyan Mal watched carefully as the young emperor's power spread into Rajasthan. The chronicles record that in **1560**, when Akbar's former guardian **Bairam Khan** fell from power and left the court, he passed through Bikaner and was received by Kalyan Mal on his way west. The Rao was learning to deal with the great men of the imperial world.

The decisive step came in **November 1570**, when Akbar held court at **Nagaur**. Many Rajput chiefs came there to meet him. Kalyan Mal came with his son **Rai Singh** and accepted Mughal overlordship. A marriage sealed the alliance: a daughter of Kalyan Mal's brother **Kanha** was married to Akbar. Rai Singh entered Mughal service and soon rose high in it.

It is easy to judge such choices from a distance. Kalyan Mal had seen his father die fighting Jodhpur, his own capital occupied, and his kingdom saved only by the help of a Delhi ruler. For him, an alliance with the strongest power in India meant that Bikaner would never again be at the mercy of Marwar. The bards who praised the defiance of Mewar also kept Kalyan Mal's memory with respect, as the ruler who brought Bikaner safely through its most dangerous years.

At home, he kept up the worship of **Karni Mata** and the temples his grandfather and great-grandfather had founded. His court remained a home for Charan poets. His younger son **Prithviraj Rathore** would become one of the great poets of the age, author of the devotional work *Veli Krisan Rukmani ri*, and a celebrated figure at Akbar's court.

By the early 1570s, Rai Singh was leading Bikaner's armies in Mughal campaigns and directing much of its affairs, and the dynasty's lists count him as ruler from **1571**. Some chronicles place Kalyan Mal's death a few years later, around **1574**. Either way, he left behind a state that had survived occupation and exile and had found a secure place in the new order of Mughal India.

## Highlights of his life

- **Exile at Sirsa (1542).** After his father fell fighting Rao Maldev, he took refuge outside his occupied kingdom.
- **Ally of Sher Shah (1544).** He joined Sher Shah Suri's campaign against Maldev, which ended at Giri-Sumel.
- **Restored to Bikaner (1544).** After Maldev's defeat, he regained his capital and rebuilt his kingdom.
- **Holding off Jodhpur.** He kept Bikaner independent of Marwar until Maldev's death in 1562.
- **Nagaur durbar (1570).** He met Akbar at Nagaur with his son Rai Singh and joined the Mughal alliance.
- **Father of poets and generals.** His sons included Raja Rai Singh, the builder of Junagarh, and the poet Prithviraj Rathore.

## Raja Rai Singh — the general of Akbar who built Junagarh

*Raja Rai Singh's life is known through the Bikaner khyats, the Persian histories of Akbar's and Jahangir's reigns, and the inscription on the gate of the fort he built. Where history and tradition part ways, this story says so.*

Rai Singh was born on **20 July 1541**, the son of **Rao Kalyan Mal** of Bikaner. Within a year of his birth his grandfather, **Rao Jait Singh**, was killed fighting the army of **Rao Maldev** of Jodhpur, and Bikaner was occupied. The infant prince spent his first years in exile with his family at **Sirsa**. He was three when **Sher Shah Suri** defeated Maldev at **Giri-Sumel** in 1544 and Kalyan Mal returned to Bikaner. He grew up hearing that his house had nearly been destroyed by its own kinsmen, and that it had been saved by an alliance with the ruler of Delhi.

That lesson shaped his life. In **November 1570**, when **Akbar** held court at **Nagaur**, Rai Singh came with his father and Bikaner joined the Mughal alliance. He entered imperial service, and from then on he spent most of his life on campaign far from the desert. The dynasty's lists count him as ruler of Bikaner from **1571**, though his father may have lived a few years longer.

Akbar trusted him quickly. In **1572** he was given charge of **Jodhpur**, the capital of the house that had once conquered Bikaner, at a time when Akbar was pressing Maldev's son **Chandrasen**, who refused to submit. Rai Singh campaigned against Chandrasen in the hills of Marwar for several years. In the same period he served in Akbar's conquest of **Gujarat** in 1572–73 and fought against the rebellious **Mirzas**, princes of the Timurid house who had risen against the emperor. Later he campaigned against **Rao Surtan** of **Sirohi**, another Rajput ruler who resisted Mughal authority.

These were wars that set Rajput against Rajput, and the bards who sang of resistance remembered them with mixed feelings. Rai Singh's own younger brother, the poet **Prithviraj Rathore**, served at Akbar's court too, yet tradition credits him with verses honouring **Maharana Pratap** of Mewar. The story of Prithviraj's letter to Pratap is legend rather than record, but it shows how the age was remembered: as a time when loyalty to the emperor and pride in Rajput independence lived side by side, even within one family.

Rai Singh's service took him to the far ends of the empire. In **1581** he marched with Akbar's army to **Kabul** against the emperor's half-brother **Mirza Muhammad Hakim**. He served on the north-western frontier and in other campaigns, and his rank in the imperial hierarchy rose steadily. He became the first ruler of Bikaner to bear the title **Raja**. The bond with the imperial family deepened when, in **1586**, a daughter of Rai Singh was married to Akbar's son **Prince Salim**, the future Jahangir.

His wealth and rank allowed him to do what none of his ancestors could. Bika's old fort on Rati Ghati was small and exposed. In **1589**, Rai Singh began a new fortress on the plain nearby, under the supervision of his minister **Karam Chand**. It was completed in **1594**, with a moat, massive walls and palaces within. Today it is called **Junagarh**, the "old fort", though it was then the new one. Unlike most great Rajput forts it does not stand on a hill, yet in its long history it was never taken by storm. An inscription on its gate records its building and Rai Singh's deeds.

His life at home was not free of danger. Karam Chand, the minister who had built the fort, was later accused of plotting to replace Rai Singh with his son **Dalpat Singh**. When the plot came to light, the minister fled to Akbar's court and found protection there. The affair left a lasting bitterness in Bikaner, and years later Karam Chand's family would pay for it under Rai Singh's successors.

Rai Singh was a man of culture as well as war. Tradition credits him with works on Sanskrit learning, including a treatise on medicine, and his court welcomed scholars and poets. He honoured **Karni Mata** and the temples of his ancestors, and the palaces of Junagarh show the meeting of Rajput and Mughal styles that marked his age.

After Akbar's death in **1605**, Rai Singh served **Jahangir**, his son-in-law. His relationship with the new emperor was not always smooth; during Prince Khusrau's rebellion in 1606 he is recorded as leaving his post without leave, and was later pardoned. In his last years he was posted to the **Deccan**, where the Mughals were fighting the sultanates of the south. He died at **Burhanpur** in **1612**, far from the desert he had made great.

He had wished his younger son **Sur Singh** to succeed him, but Jahangir recognised **Dalpat Singh**, the elder, as Raja. Dalpat's reign would be short and troubled. Rai Singh's achievement, however, endured. He took a desert state that had nearly been swallowed by Jodhpur and made it an honoured partner of the Mughal empire, and he gave Bikaner the fortress that still stands at its heart.

## Highlights of his life

- **Childhood in exile.** Born in 1541, he spent his first years at Sirsa while Bikaner was held by Rao Maldev.
- **Nagaur durbar (1570).** With his father Kalyan Mal, he joined the Mughal alliance and entered Akbar's service.
- **Imperial general.** He served in Akbar's Gujarat campaign, against the Mirzas, Chandrasen of Marwar and Rao Surtan of Sirohi, and in the Kabul campaign of 1581.
- **First Raja of Bikaner.** He rose high in the Mughal hierarchy, and his daughter married Prince Salim in 1586.
- **Builder of Junagarh (1589–1594).** He built the great fortress of Bikaner, which was never taken by storm.
- **Death in the Deccan (1612).** He died at Burhanpur in Jahangir's service and was succeeded by Dalpat Singh.

## Raja Dalpat Singh — the elder son who lost the desert throne

*Dalpat Singh's short and troubled reign is known to us from the Bikaner chronicles and from the memoirs of the emperor Jahangir, which see the same events from opposite sides. Where the two disagree, or where the bards add what the records do not say, this story says so.*

In the second half of the sixteenth century, the Rathore kingdom of Bikaner stood at the edge of the Thar desert, a land of sand ridges, thorn scrub and scattered wells. It had been carved out a century earlier by **Rao Bika**, a son of Rao Jodha of Marwar, and it had survived because its rulers knew how to fight, how to bargain and when to bend. Under **Rao Kalyan Mal** the house had come to terms with the Mughal emperor **Akbar**, and under Kalyan Mal's son **Rai Singh** it rose higher than ever before.

Dalpat Singh was born into this rising house in the middle of the 1560s, the eldest son of Rai Singh. His childhood was spent in a court that was changing fast. His father was becoming one of Akbar's most trusted generals, a commander who fought in Gujarat, on the north-western frontier and in the Deccan, and who brought home both wealth and honour. Between **1589 and 1594**, Rai Singh and his capable minister **Karam Chand Bachhawat** built a new fortress at Bikaner, the great stronghold later called **Junagarh**, whose red sandstone walls still stand at the heart of the city. Dalpat grew up with the sound of masons and the coming and going of imperial messengers.

A Rajput prince of that age was trained to ride before he could read well, to handle the sword, the lance and the bow, and to know the genealogy of his clan by heart. He was also expected to learn the ways of the imperial camp, where Rajput chiefs, Persian nobles and Mughal princes served side by side under one master. Dalpat learned the first lessons well. The second, it seems, never came easily to him.

As a young man he was sent to serve with the imperial armies. He saw campaigns in the far west of the empire, towards **Sindh**, in the years when Akbar's forces were bringing the lower Indus under their control. The sources that survive do not paint a gentle picture of him. The Mughal accounts remember a proud and quarrelsome young man who resented orders, who did not hide his displeasure, and who was accused more than once of leaving imperial service without permission. Around the turn of the century he fell out of favour, and his father had to answer for him at court. Whatever the details of these quarrels, the reputation stayed with him, and it would matter later.

There was another shadow over Dalpat's future, and it came from inside his own family. Rai Singh had several queens and several sons. Late in his life, a younger son, **Sur Singh** (later remembered as Surat Singh), was born to a queen whom Rai Singh greatly favoured. As the old king aged, he came to prefer this younger boy, nearly thirty years Dalpat's junior, as his heir. In a Rajput state the eldest son normally inherited the *gaddi*, but the wishes of the dying ruler, the support of the nobles and, by now, the decision of the emperor all weighed heavily. Bikaner's court divided quietly into those who looked to the elder son and those who looked to the younger.

Rai Singh died in **January 1612** at **Burhanpur**, far away in the Deccan, where he was serving the new emperor, **Jahangir**. The news travelled north across hundreds of miles of road to the desert capital. Tradition says that on his deathbed the old king named Sur Singh as his successor. But the throne of Bikaner was no longer decided in Bikaner alone. Jahangir, according to his own memoirs, chose to recognise the elder son. Dalpat received the imperial *tika*, the mark of investiture, and was confirmed as Raja of Bikaner.

So Dalpat Singh came to the throne at last, a man in his forties who had waited a long time and who knew that many in his own court had hoped for someone else. One can imagine the scene in the halls of Junagarh: the conch shells, the saffron, the nobles coming forward one by one to present their swords hilt-first, and behind the ceremony a hundred private calculations. The brothers of the old queen, the ministers, the chiefs of the outlying *thikanas*, all were watching to see what kind of ruler the new Raja would be.

He did not have long to show them. The details of the next months are uncertain, and the Bikaner chronicles and the Mughal record tell them differently. What is clear is that Dalpat soon lost the emperor's confidence. The imperial accounts speak of disobedience and of failure to perform the service expected of a Rajput vassal. Bikaner's own tradition speaks of the intrigues of the younger prince's party, who never accepted the elder son and who worked to turn the emperor against him. Both may be true. A ruler with a difficult past and a divided court made an easy target, and a ruler who did not travel to court and stand before the emperor in person was always at a disadvantage against rivals who did.

In **1613** Jahangir reversed his decision. He recognised Sur Singh as Raja of Bikaner and gave him imperial support to take possession of his inheritance. Mughal troops from the neighbouring imperial districts moved with the young prince towards the desert. Dalpat gathered those who were still loyal to him and prepared to fight.

The chronicles describe the struggle that followed as short and bitter. The sand country was hard to campaign in, and every well and village mattered. Dalpat's strength depended on the loyalty of his nobles, and that loyalty was thin. When the forces met, many of the chiefs who had sworn to him failed him, some going over to his brother, others simply withdrawing to their own estates. Dalpat was defeated and taken prisoner. The bards later told the moment with bitterness: the eldest son of Rai Singh, betrayed by men of his own clan, led away by the soldiers of a foreign court.

He was taken to **Ajmer**, where Jahangir held court in these years, close to the shrine of Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti. There, in **1614**, Dalpat Singh was put to death on the emperor's order. Bikaner's tradition adds a tragic detail that the imperial record does not dwell on: that a band of his loyal Rajputs tried to free him from his captivity, and that in the fighting that followed the captive Raja himself was killed, together with those who had come to rescue him. Whichever account is closer to the truth, his life ended in the prison of the power his father had served so loyally.

The tradition of Bikaner also remembers the women of his household. When word of his death reached the desert, it is said that several of his queens chose to become *sati*, as was still the custom among Rajput royal families of that age. Memorial stones and cenotaphs at the royal cremation ground of Bikaner preserve the memory of such deaths across the generations, a grim reminder of what the politics of men cost the women of their families.

It is easy to remember Dalpat Singh only as a failure, a man who held the throne for a single year and lost it. But his story says a great deal about the world in which the Rajput states now lived. In the days of Rao Bika, a desert chief who held his forts and his wells could defy any rival. By the time of Rai Singh's death, Bikaner was part of a vast imperial order. Its rulers commanded thousands of horsemen in the emperor's wars and received honours and lands in return, but the emperor also decided who would sit on their throne. Dalpat inherited a kingdom whose fate was settled as much in the imperial camp as in Junagarh, and he never learned to play that game as well as his rivals did.

His story is also a story of a family divided. The rivalry between the elder and younger sons of Rai Singh was not unusual: many Rajput houses of the Mughal age were torn by such disputes, and the emperors often used them to keep their vassals dependent. In Bikaner the dispute was settled quickly and harshly, and the younger son, Sur Singh, went on to rule for nearly two decades. The house of Bika survived, and the kingdom remained in Rathore hands. Yet the bards did not forget the elder brother who lost everything in a single year, and his name was kept in the genealogies of the dynasty as the seventh ruler of Bikaner.

In the long gallery of the rulers of Bikaner, Dalpat Singh stands between two strong figures: his father Rai Singh, the builder of Junagarh and the general of Akbar, and his brother Sur Singh, who would consolidate the kingdom after him. His reign was brief, and it was not peaceful. It was a hinge in the history of the desert kingdom, the moment when it became clear that no Rajput throne, however old its lineage, could be held without the favour of the emperor in Agra.

## Highlights of his life

- **Eldest son of Rai Singh.** Born in the mid-1560s, he grew up while his father rose to be one of Akbar's leading generals and built the fortress of Junagarh.
- **Service in the imperial armies.** As a young prince he served on Mughal campaigns in the west, but earned a reputation for pride and disobedience.
- **Recognised by Jahangir (1612).** After Rai Singh's death at Burhanpur, Jahangir gave the elder son the *tika*, even though tradition says Rai Singh had wanted Sur Singh to succeed.
- **Overthrown in 1613.** Having lost the emperor's favour, he was opposed by his brother Sur Singh with Mughal support, abandoned by many of his nobles, and captured.
- **Death at Ajmer (1614).** He was put to death at the imperial court at Ajmer; Bikaner's tradition says his loyal Rajputs died trying to rescue him.
- **A turning point for Bikaner.** His fall showed how far the succession of the Rajput states now depended on the will of the Mughal emperor.

## Raja Surat Singh — the favoured son who settled his father's scores

*The life of Sur Singh, often called Surat Singh, comes to us through the Bikaner chronicles, through Jain accounts of the Bachhawat ministers, and through scattered references in the Mughal record. The chronicles of the court and the memory of its victims do not always agree; where they part ways, this story says so.*

When **Sur Singh** was born in **1594**, his father **Rai Singh** was at the height of his power. The Raja of Bikaner was one of the great generals of the emperor **Akbar**, a commander of thousands who had fought in Gujarat, on the north-western frontier and in the Deccan, and who had just completed the great fortress of **Junagarh** at the heart of his desert capital. Sur Singh was the son of a queen whom Rai Singh loved deeply, and from the first he was the darling of his ageing father.

He was not, however, the heir. His half-brother **Dalpat Singh** was nearly thirty years older, a grown man with a career of his own in the imperial armies. In a Rajput house the eldest son normally took the throne, but Dalpat was proud and difficult, and he had quarrelled more than once with the Mughal authorities. As the years passed, Rai Singh turned more and more towards his youngest son, and the court of Bikaner began to divide into two camps.

There was another wound in the house of Bika that would shape Sur Singh's life. Rai Singh's long-serving minister, **Karam Chand Bachhawat**, a Jain of the Oswal community, had been the builder of Junagarh beside his master and one of the most capable administrators in Rajasthan. Yet at some point in the 1590s, Bikaner's chronicles say, Karam Chand was suspected of plotting against Rai Singh. He fled the desert and took refuge at the imperial court, where Akbar received him with favour. For Rai Singh this was a betrayal he never forgave. The bards say that the old king carried the grievance to his deathbed and passed it to his favourite son as a debt of honour.

Rai Singh died at **Burhanpur** in the Deccan in **January 1612**, while serving the new emperor **Jahangir**. Tradition says he named Sur Singh as his heir, but Jahangir recognised the elder son, and Dalpat Singh became Raja. Sur Singh, still a young man of about eighteen, had to watch his brother take the throne he believed was his.

He did not wait long. Dalpat soon fell out of favour with the emperor, and in **1613** Jahangir reversed his decision and recognised Sur Singh as the rightful Raja of Bikaner. With Mughal troops at his side, the young prince marched into the desert. Many of Dalpat's nobles deserted him, and the elder brother was defeated and captured. He was taken to **Ajmer**, where Jahangir was holding court, and there, in **1614**, he was put to death. Sur Singh had won his throne, but he had won it with the help of the imperial power and at the cost of his brother's life. It was a hard beginning, and the chronicles do not hide it.

As Raja, Sur Singh set about making his position secure. He rewarded the nobles who had supported him and dealt firmly with those who had stood with Dalpat. In a land of scattered villages and powerful clan chiefs, the authority of the ruler depended on his ability to command loyalty from the *thakurs* of the outlying estates, and the young Raja worked to rebuild the order that his father had left and that the succession struggle had shaken.

He also served the emperor, as every Rajput ruler of his rank was now expected to do. Bikaner's contingents of desert horsemen were a valued part of the imperial armies, and Sur Singh held a *mansab*, an imperial rank, that obliged him to provide troops and to serve wherever he was sent. He spent long periods away from Bikaner, attending the court and taking part in imperial campaigns, especially in the Deccan, where the Mughals were fighting the sultanates of Ahmadnagar and Bijapur and their great general **Malik Ambar**. The details of his individual service are thinly recorded, but it was this service that kept Bikaner in the emperor's favour.

The most famous and most terrible episode of his reign was the settling of his father's score with the house of Karam Chand. Karam Chand himself had died at the imperial court. But his sons, **Bhag Chand** and **Lakshmi Chand**, were living in the north as men of standing. The story is told both in Bikaner's chronicles and in Jain accounts of the Bachhawat family, and it is told with very different feeling. According to these traditions, Sur Singh met the brothers, treated them with honour, and invited them to return to Bikaner and serve the state as their ancestors had done. They accepted, and came home to the desert with their families.

Some time later, around **1620** by the usual reckoning, the Raja's soldiers surrounded the Bachhawat mansion in Bikaner. The brothers and their followers, knowing what this meant, armed themselves and fought. The Jain tradition remembers that they defended their home to the last and died with their swords in their hands, and that the women of the household chose death rather than capture. Very few of the family survived. One can imagine the narrow lanes of the old city filled with smoke and the clash of arms, and the silence afterwards. In the eyes of the court chronicles, Sur Singh had fulfilled his father's last wish and punished a treachery. In the memory of the Jain community, it was a cruel betrayal of a family that had served Bikaner with great distinction. Both memories have survived, side by side, for four hundred years.

Yet Sur Singh was not only a man of vengeance. Like his father, he understood that a ruler of the desert must care for water. Bikaner's tradition credits him with the tank of **Sursagar**, near the walls of Junagarh, which bears his name. In a city where every drop of rain had to be caught and kept, a great tank was not a luxury but a gift of life, and the people of Bikaner remembered the rulers who gave them one. He also continued to strengthen and adorn the fortress his father had built, as each generation of the house of Bika would do after him.

His court followed the pattern that his father had set. Rajasthani bards and *charans* recited the deeds of the Rathores and composed verses in praise of their patron. Brahmin scholars and Jain monks lived side by side in the city, and the Jain communities, despite the fate of the Bachhawats, continued to play an important part in the trade and administration of the state. The ties with the imperial court also brought new fashions in dress, painting and architecture to the desert, and the styles of Bikaner began slowly to blend Rajput and Mughal tastes.

In **1627** Jahangir died, and after a brief struggle his son **Shah Jahan** took the throne. Sur Singh remained in imperial service under the new emperor. Shah Jahan's early years were spent in fighting in the Deccan, where the rebellious noble **Khan Jahan Lodi** and the Deccan sultanates challenged Mughal power, and the Rajput contingents were once again called south.

Sur Singh died in **1631**, while on imperial service in the Deccan, still a man in his late thirties. He had ruled for about eighteen years. His son **Karan Singh** succeeded him and would rule Bikaner for nearly four decades, through the age of Shah Jahan and into the troubled first years of **Aurangzeb**.

The memory of Sur Singh is mixed, as the memory of strong men often is. He was the favoured son who took the throne from his elder brother with Mughal help. He was the son who carried out his father's vengeance on the family of a minister who had once been the greatest servant of the state. He was also the ruler who held Bikaner together after a dangerous succession crisis, kept it in the favour of two emperors, and gave its people water. In the long line of the rulers of Bikaner, his reign marks the moment when the kingdom settled firmly into the role it would play for the next century: a loyal and valued Rajput ally of the Mughal empire, proud of its desert independence, but bound to the imperial throne.

## Highlights of his life

- **Favoured son of Rai Singh.** Born in 1594 to a beloved queen, he was preferred by his father as heir over his much older half-brother Dalpat Singh.
- **Won the throne in 1613.** After Jahangir withdrew his support from Dalpat Singh, Sur Singh took Bikaner with Mughal help; Dalpat was captured and put to death at Ajmer in 1614.
- **Restored order in the kingdom.** He rewarded his supporters and rebuilt the authority of the throne after the succession struggle.
- **The fall of the Bachhawats (c. 1620).** He destroyed the family of his father's former minister Karam Chand, an episode remembered by the court as justice and by the Jain community as betrayal.
- **Builder of Sursagar.** Tradition credits him with the tank of Sursagar near Junagarh, a vital source of water for the desert city.
- **Servant of two emperors.** He served Jahangir and Shah Jahan, and died in 1631 while on imperial service in the Deccan.

## Raja Karan Singh — the desert king between Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb

*Karan Singh's long reign is known from the Bikaner chronicles, from the Persian histories of the Mughal court, and from a rich body of Rajasthani tradition. Some of the most famous stories about him, such as the title "Jangaldhar Badshah", belong to tradition rather than recorded history; where they do, this story says so.*

**Karan Singh** was born in **1616**, in the reign of the emperor **Jahangir**, as the son of **Sur Singh**, the Raja of Bikaner. His father had come to the throne only three years earlier, after a bitter struggle with his elder half-brother Dalpat Singh, and the court in which the boy grew up was still settling after that storm. Bikaner was by now firmly part of the Mughal order. Its rulers held high imperial ranks, led their desert horsemen in the emperor's wars, and spent years at a time far from home.

The prince was raised in the great fortress of **Junagarh**, built by his grandfather Rai Singh, and he learned the arts expected of a Rathore heir: riding the tough horses and camels of the desert, handling sword and lance, hunting in the scrub around the city, and listening to the bards recite the deeds of **Rao Bika** and his successors. He also learned that the fortunes of his house were made as much at the imperial court as on the battlefield.

Sur Singh died in **1631** while serving in the Deccan, and Karan Singh, then about fifteen, became Raja of Bikaner. The new emperor, **Shah Jahan**, confirmed him in his inheritance and his rank. For the next quarter of a century Karan Singh served the Mughal throne as his father and grandfather had done. The empire's chief military business in those years lay in the Deccan, where Shah Jahan was bringing the last of the Ahmadnagar sultanate under his control and pressing on Bijapur and Golconda. Bikaner's contingents served in these southern wars, and Karan Singh spent long periods away from his desert home in the camps and forts of the Deccan plateau.

Back in Rajasthan, the old rivalries between neighbouring Rajput houses did not disappear simply because all of them now served the same emperor. The most famous quarrel of Karan Singh's reign was with **Rao Amar Singh Rathore** of **Nagaur**, a proud and fiery prince of the Jodhpur house who held Nagaur as an imperial grant. The lands of Bikaner and Nagaur touched each other in the open sandy country, and the villages along that border were often at odds.

In **1644**, tradition says, a dispute broke out over a watermelon vine that had grown from the fields of one village into the fields of the other. Whose was the fruit? The villagers quarrelled, the local chiefs took sides, and the quarrel became a fight between the forces of the two states. Rajasthan remembers it as **Matire ri Rad**, "the war of the watermelon". The details of the fighting are known mainly from tradition, but the story agrees that the men of Bikaner had the better of it. Neither ruler, it seems, was present in person: both were away in imperial service. The affair is remembered partly because of what happened next. In the same year, at the imperial court in Agra, Amar Singh Rathore killed the Mughal paymaster **Salabat Khan** in open court, and was himself killed soon after. Some traditions link the insult that provoked him to the quarrel with Bikaner. Whatever the truth, the episode shows how small border quarrels in the desert could reach all the way to the emperor's hall.

Karan Singh's own relationship with the Mughal court changed sharply at the end of the 1650s. In **1657** Shah Jahan fell ill, and his four sons began a war for the throne. The Rajput rulers were drawn in on every side. Many Rajputs fought for the eldest prince, **Dara Shikoh**, and for the imperial army sent against **Aurangzeb**, and many of them died at the battles of **Dharmat** and **Samugarh** in 1658. Karan Singh was then serving in the Deccan, where Aurangzeb had been governor. The sources suggest that he did not commit himself wholeheartedly to Aurangzeb's cause, and kept his distance while the struggle was decided. Aurangzeb won, crowned himself emperor, and did not forget who had stood beside him and who had not.

It is from these years that one of the best-loved Bikaner legends comes. The bards tell that Aurangzeb, marching with a host of Rajput chiefs, planned to take them across the Indus at **Attock** and there force them to give up their faith. Karan Singh, the story goes, learned of the plan, warned the other chiefs, and had the boats destroyed so that no one could be carried across. The grateful Rajput rulers then hailed him as **"Jangaldhar Badshah"**, the emperor of the jungle-land, as the desert country of Bikaner was called. There is no evidence for this plot in the historical record, and historians treat the tale as legend. But the title stuck, and the rulers of Bikaner proudly used it for generations. The legend tells us how Bikaner wished to remember Karan Singh: as a Rajput who would bend to the emperor in service but never in faith.

The real history of his later years was quieter but sadder. Relations with Aurangzeb remained cold. Karan Singh continued in imperial service in the Deccan, but he was no longer trusted, and his position at home weakened. Imperial pressure fell on him through rivals and claimants within his own family, and for long periods he lived far from Bikaner. Tradition says that he settled near **Aurangabad**, the great Mughal city of the Deccan, where a settlement called **Karanpura** is said to take its name from him.

His sons became famous warriors in the Deccan wars. **Padam Singh** and **Kesari Singh** in particular were celebrated in Rajasthani verse for their courage in the battles of Aurangzeb's armies. Tradition tells of another son, **Mohan Singh**, who was killed in a quarrel in the imperial camp, and of Padam Singh avenging him on the spot with his own sword, an act that won him the admiration of the bards and the anger of the court. These stories reflect the world of Karan Singh's family: proud Rajput princes living far from home, serving an emperor they did not fully trust, and quick to defend their honour with steel.

Karan Singh was not only a soldier. Like several rulers of his line, he valued learning. Brahmin scholars at his court composed Sanskrit works in his name, on subjects such as ritual, law and poetics, and the collection of manuscripts that would later grow into the famous library of Bikaner owed a debt to his patronage. The Rajasthani bards, too, found in him a generous patron. At Junagarh, the fortress continued to grow under each new ruler, and Karan Singh added to its palaces. Above all he kept the old ways of the desert court: the worship of **Karni Mata**, the patron goddess of the Rathores of Bikaner, whose shrine at Deshnoke stood a few miles from the capital; the rituals of kingship; and the bond between the Raja and the clan chiefs who held the sandy *thikanas* around him.

He died in **1669**, in the Deccan near Aurangabad, after a reign of nearly four decades. His son **Anup Singh**, who had already won Aurangzeb's favour by his service, succeeded him and would go on to become one of the most celebrated rulers in Bikaner's history, a soldier and a patron of learning whose library still bears his name.

Karan Singh's reign was not one of great conquests or sweeping reforms, and the sources do not credit him with remaking the army or the administration of his state. What they do show is a ruler who lived through one of the great turning points of Mughal history. He served Shah Jahan faithfully for a quarter of a century, kept his distance in the war of succession, and paid for it with the cold suspicion of Aurangzeb. His reign shows how a Rajput state of the desert survived in the shadow of the empire: by service and by caution, by the courage of its princes, and by the stories it told itself about its own pride.

## Highlights of his life

- **Raja at fifteen (1631).** Born in 1616, he succeeded his father Sur Singh and was confirmed by Shah Jahan.
- **Service in the Deccan.** He spent much of his reign leading Bikaner's contingents in Shah Jahan's wars in the south.
- **Matire ri Rad (1644).** A border quarrel with Rao Amar Singh Rathore of Nagaur, remembered in tradition as the "war of the watermelon", ended in Bikaner's favour.
- **The war of succession (1657–58).** Serving in the Deccan, he did not commit himself fully to Aurangzeb, and lost the new emperor's trust.
- **"Jangaldhar Badshah".** Legend says he saved the Rajput chiefs from forced conversion at Attock and was given this title; the story is tradition, not recorded history.
- **Patron of learning.** Sanskrit works were composed at his court, and his patronage helped lay the foundation of Bikaner's great manuscript collection.
- **Death in the Deccan (1669).** He died near Aurangabad and was succeeded by his son Anup Singh.

## Maharaja Anup Singh — the soldier who carried the Deccan's books home

*Anup Singh's life is known from the Bikaner chronicles, from the Persian histories of Aurangzeb's reign, and above all from the great library and collections that bear his name. Where tradition adds to the record, this story says so.*

**Anup Singh** was born in **1638**, in the reign of **Shah Jahan**, as a son of **Raja Karan Singh** of Bikaner. His father spent much of his life in the Deccan in imperial service, and the young prince grew up between the desert fortress of **Junagarh** and the camps of the Mughal army in the south. He learned the sword and the saddle like every Rathore prince, but from early on he also showed a love of books, music and learned conversation that would set him apart from almost every ruler of his age.

His father lost the trust of the emperor **Aurangzeb** after the war of succession of 1657–58, but Anup Singh won it. He served with distinction in the Deccan, and when Karan Singh died near **Aurangabad** in **1669**, Aurangzeb recognised Anup Singh as Raja of Bikaner. His brothers **Padam Singh** and **Kesari Singh**, famous in Rajasthani verse for their courage, fought beside him in the imperial wars.

Most of Anup Singh's reign was spent far from the desert. Aurangzeb was determined to conquer the Deccan, and from **1681** he moved there himself with his court and armies, never to return north. The Rajput contingents were essential to these long wars against the sultanates of **Bijapur** and **Golconda** and against the rising power of the **Marathas**. Anup Singh served in many of these campaigns. He took part in the operations that ended with the fall of Golconda in **1687**, and in recognition of his service Aurangzeb gave him the title of **Maharaja**. He was the first ruler of Bikaner to bear it.

The emperor also trusted him with important posts. Anup Singh served as governor at **Aurangabad**, the chief Mughal city of the Deccan, and later as commander of **Adoni**, a strong fortress in the south that had belonged to Bijapur and passed into Mughal hands after 1686. For years he held these southern posts amid constant Maratha raids, in country very different from the dunes of his home.

It was in the Deccan that he did the work for which he is chiefly remembered. The wars of conquest brought ruin to old cities and courts, and with them to libraries, temples and the households of scholars. Anup Singh, tradition says, could not bear to see learning destroyed. Wherever his duties took him, he sought out Sanskrit manuscripts, buying them, rescuing them from ruined collections and sending them north on long caravans to Bikaner. Thousands of works on philosophy, ritual, law, astronomy, medicine, poetry and music reached the desert in this way. He gathered sacred metal images too, which tradition says he saved from destruction in the south; many were kept at Junagarh, where they are still shown today.

These manuscripts became the heart of the **Anup Sanskrit Library** at Bikaner, one of the finest collections of Sanskrit manuscripts in India. Scholars still travel to consult rare texts that survive there and almost nowhere else. The library is Anup Singh's true monument.

He was a patron of living scholars as well as of old books. His court drew learned men from many parts of India. Among them was the musicologist **Bhavabhatta**, who composed for him several treatises on music, such as the *Anupa Sangita Ratnakara*, the *Anupa Sangita Vilasa* and the *Anupankusha*. Works on law, ritual and medicine were written in his name, and some are attributed to the Maharaja himself. In a time when war filled most of his days, he made his camp a place of learning.

At home, Bikaner was governed in his absence by ministers and loyal nobles, and the desert state remained largely at peace. The great fortress continued to grow, and Anup Singh added to its palaces. The worship of **Karni Mata**, the patron goddess of Bikaner's Rathores, remained at the centre of the court's religious life, and Anup Singh was remembered by the people as a just and pious ruler.

His long years in the south took their toll. Anup Singh died at **Adoni** in **1698**, still on imperial service, at about sixty. His young son **Sarup Singh**, still a child, succeeded him, and Bikaner entered a difficult time. But the caravans of books had already reached home. A soldier who spent his life in Aurangzeb's wars left behind not a list of conquests but a library, and through it he preserved a part of India's learning that the age of war might otherwise have destroyed.

## Highlights of his life

- **A prince of learning.** Born in 1638, the son of Raja Karan Singh, he combined the training of a Rathore warrior with a deep love of books and music.
- **Raja in 1669.** He succeeded his father with the favour of Aurangzeb, which his own service in the Deccan had earned.
- **Service in the Deccan wars.** He fought in Aurangzeb's campaigns against Bijapur, Golconda and the Marathas.
- **First Maharaja of Bikaner.** Aurangzeb gave him the title of Maharaja after the fall of Golconda in 1687.
- **Governor in the south.** He held Aurangabad and later the fortress of Adoni for the emperor.
- **Founder of the Anup Sanskrit Library.** He collected thousands of manuscripts in the Deccan and sent them to Bikaner, where they remain a priceless collection.
- **Patron of music and scholarship.** Bhavabhatta and other scholars wrote major works for him on music, law and ritual.
- **Death at Adoni (1698).** He died on imperial service and was succeeded by his son Sarup Singh.

## Maharaja Sarup Singh — the boy king who died far from the desert

*Sarup Singh's short life is known only in outline, from the Bikaner chronicles and the history of Aurangzeb's Deccan wars. Where the details rest on tradition, this story says so.*

**Sarup Singh** was born in the late 1680s, the eldest son of **Maharaja Anup Singh** of Bikaner. His father was then one of the most respected Rajput servants of the emperor **Aurangzeb**, a soldier who had fought at the fall of **Golconda** in 1687, the first ruler of Bikaner to bear the title of Maharaja, and a patron of learning who was sending caravans of Sanskrit manuscripts home from the Deccan to the desert. The boy grew up in a family whose head was almost always far away, holding the fortress of **Adoni** and other posts in the south for the emperor.

At home, in the great fortress of **Junagarh**, the young prince was raised in the women's quarters among his mother, the other queens and his younger brother **Sujan Singh**. Tutors taught him letters and the genealogy of the Rathores; the household guards taught him to ride and to hold a sword. The bards recited the deeds of **Rao Bika**, of **Rai Singh**, the builder of Junagarh, and of his grandfather **Karan Singh**. Around him, ministers and nobles ran the state in his father's name, sending men and money south to the endless war.

That war shaped everything. Since **1681** Aurangzeb had been in the Deccan, determined to destroy the Deccan sultanates and then the **Marathas**. Bijapur and Golconda had fallen, but the Maratha struggle went on year after year, and the Mughal armies were worn down by sieges, raids and disease. For a Rajput state, imperial service meant prestige and lands, but also sons and fathers who spent their lives in distant camps and often died there.

In **1698** Anup Singh died at Adoni. Sarup Singh, still a child of about nine or ten, became Maharaja of Bikaner. A boy could not lead armies or attend the imperial court in person, so real power passed to his mother, acting as regent, and to the ministers and senior nobles of the state. Such regencies were always dangerous times. The *thakurs* of the outlying estates, the rival branches of the royal family and the imperial officials all watched for weakness.

The danger came from the south. Anup Singh had held important grants in the Deccan, above all around Adoni, in return for his service. With the old Maharaja dead and his heir a child unable to serve, these holdings were at risk. Bikaner's chronicles say that the imperial authorities took them back. For the court at Bikaner this was a serious blow, both to its income and to its honour.

Tradition says that the queen mother resolved that her son should go south to win back what his father had held. Some accounts give the decision to the boy himself, eager to prove himself worthy of his father. Whatever the truth, the young Maharaja set out for the Deccan with an escort of Rathore horsemen, crossing hundreds of miles from the dunes of Bikaner to the dry plateau of the south. For a boy of eleven or twelve it was a long and hard road, through country full of armies and marked by famine and epidemic.

He never returned. In **1700**, while in the Deccan, Sarup Singh fell ill with **smallpox**, one of the great killers of that age, which spared neither princes nor peasants. He died far from home, still a boy, after a reign of about two years. His followers carried the news back to Bikaner, where the court went into mourning for a ruler who had never had the chance to rule.

Sarup Singh's younger brother, **Sujan Singh**, himself only about ten, succeeded him. The regency and the dependence on ministers and nobles continued, and Bikaner entered the new century in a weaker position than it had held under Anup Singh. Within a few years Aurangzeb himself would die in the Deccan, in 1707, and the long decline of Mughal power would begin, bringing new dangers and new freedoms to the Rajput states.

The record of Sarup Singh's reign is thin, and it would be wrong to credit him with deeds or reforms. To call his rule peaceful says little: it was a reign without real power, held in the name of a child while others governed. Yet his story is worth telling. It shows the cost of the Deccan wars for the Rajput houses that served in them: a father who died on duty at Adoni, and a son who followed him south and died there too. In the long line of the rulers of Bikaner, Sarup Singh is the boy king who stands between the great scholar-soldier Anup Singh and the long reign of his brother Sujan Singh, a short life spent in the shadow of an empire's last great war.

## Highlights of his life

- **Son of Anup Singh.** Born in the late 1680s, he was the eldest son of Bikaner's first Maharaja, the soldier and patron of learning.
- **Maharaja as a child (1698).** He succeeded his father at about nine or ten, with his mother and the ministers governing in his name.
- **Loss of the Deccan holdings.** After his father's death, Bikaner's lands in the south around Adoni were taken back by the imperial authorities.
- **Journey to the Deccan.** Tradition says he went south to win back his father's holdings.
- **Death from smallpox (1700).** He died in the Deccan after a reign of about two years and was succeeded by his brother Sujan Singh.

## Maharaja Sujan Singh — the desert king in the twilight of the Mughals

*Sujan Singh's long reign is recorded mainly in the Bikaner chronicles, which tell us much about the troubles of his time but little about the man himself. Where the details are uncertain, this story says so.*

**Sujan Singh** was born around **1690**, a younger son of **Maharaja Anup Singh** of Bikaner, the soldier and scholar who served the emperor **Aurangzeb** in the Deccan and sent home the manuscripts that became the **Anup Sanskrit Library**. Like his elder brother **Sarup Singh**, he grew up in the fortress of **Junagarh** while his father was far away in the south. He was still a small child when his father died at **Adoni** in **1698**, and Sarup Singh, himself only a boy, became Maharaja.

Two years later, in **1700**, Sarup Singh died of smallpox in the Deccan. Sujan Singh, now about ten years old, became Maharaja of Bikaner. For several years the state was governed in his name by the queen mother, the ministers and the senior nobles. It was a fragile beginning. The kingdom had lost its southern holdings, its ruler was a child, and the chiefs of the outlying *thikanas* grew used to acting on their own.

As he grew older, Sujan Singh took up the duty expected of every Rajput ruler of his rank: service in the imperial armies. Aurangzeb was still fighting his long war against the **Marathas**, and Bikaner's horsemen were called south. The young Maharaja spent years in the Deccan, as his father and grandfather had done. Bikaner's chronicles remember these years as hard ones, far from home, in a war that brought little reward.

Everything changed when Aurangzeb died in the Deccan in **1707**. The great empire he had ruled for nearly half a century began to come apart. His sons fought for the throne, and over the following decades emperor followed emperor in quick succession while powerful nobles made and unmade rulers at Delhi. The Mughal grip on Rajasthan loosened. The Rajput rulers were drawn less and less to the imperial court and turned their attention back to their own lands and their own rivalries.

For Bikaner this brought both freedom and danger. The greatest danger came from its old neighbour and kinsman, **Marwar**. The Rathores of Jodhpur, led by **Maharaja Ajit Singh**, had fought a long war against Aurangzeb and recovered their capital after his death. Under Ajit Singh and then his son **Abhay Singh**, Marwar became one of the strongest states in Rajasthan, and its rulers looked on Bikaner, founded by a younger son of their own house, with ambition. Bikaner's chronicles speak of armed clashes with Jodhpur in Sujan Singh's reign and of Marwar forces threatening his territory. The details vary from one account to another, but the pressure was real, and it would grow worse under his successors.

Inside the kingdom, the problem was the power of the nobles. During the long years when Bikaner's rulers had served far away, the *thakurs* of the great estates had grown strong. Many held their lands almost as independent lords, collecting their own revenues and keeping their own armed retainers. Some quarrelled with each other; some defied the Maharaja's officers. Sujan Singh's task was to hold this world together: to keep the nobles loyal without driving them into rebellion, to defend the borders with an army made up largely of their men, and to collect enough revenue from a poor desert land to keep the state going. The chronicles show a ruler who managed this balance rather than one who overcame it. He did not crush the nobles, but he kept Bikaner intact.

The desert itself was always a challenge. Rain was uncertain, famine came often, and the wealth of the land depended on wells, tanks and the trade caravans that crossed between Sindh, Punjab and Gujarat. A ruler who kept the roads safe and the wells in repair served his people as much as one who won battles. The court at Junagarh continued its traditions: the worship of **Karni Mata**, the patron goddess of Bikaner's Rathores at nearby Deshnoke; the patronage of bards and *charans* who sang the deeds of the dynasty; and the care of the great library his father had built.

Sujan Singh ruled for thirty-five years, a long reign for an age of such uncertainty. He died in **1735** and was succeeded by his son **Zorawar Singh**. Only four years later, in 1739, the Persian ruler **Nadir Shah** would sack Delhi, showing the whole of India how weak the Mughal empire had become, and a new age of Maratha expansion and Rajput wars would begin.

Sujan Singh is not remembered for great victories or monuments. His reign was a long holding operation: a child king who grew into a cautious ruler, guiding a small desert state through the collapse of the empire it had served for a century. In the history of Bikaner he stands at the hinge between two worlds. Before him, the rulers of Bikaner were imperial generals. After him, they would be rulers of a kingdom left largely to defend itself, against Marwar, against the Marathas and against its own nobles.

## Highlights of his life

- **Son of Anup Singh.** Born around 1690, he grew up at Junagarh while his father served Aurangzeb in the Deccan.
- **Maharaja as a child (1700).** He succeeded his brother Sarup Singh, who died of smallpox in the Deccan.
- **Service in the Deccan.** As a young ruler he served in Aurangzeb's long war against the Marathas.
- **Through the Mughal decline.** After Aurangzeb's death in 1707, he guided Bikaner as imperial power collapsed.
- **Pressure from Marwar.** He faced the ambitions of Jodhpur under Ajit Singh and Abhay Singh.
- **Holding the nobles together.** He kept the powerful *thakurs* of Bikaner loyal through a difficult age.
- **A long reign.** He ruled for thirty-five years and died in 1735, succeeded by his son Zorawar Singh.

## Maharaja Zorawar Singh — the desert king who held his walls in a breaking age

*Maharaja Zorawar Singh's reign comes to us through the chronicles of Bikaner and Marwar and the records of the Jaipur court, which tell us more about the wars around him than about the man himself. Where the record is thin, this story says so.*

When Zorawar Singh was born, early in the eighteenth century, the kingdom of Bikaner was already more than two hundred years old. It had been founded in **1488** by **Rao Bika**, a son of Rao Jodha of Marwar, who had ridden north into the dry country of Jangaldesh with a few hundred companions and carved a state out of sand, scrub and the scattered villages of the Jats. Bika's descendants had made that state into something real. **Raja Rai Singh**, the great general of Akbar, had raised the fortress of **Junagarh** in the 1590s, and its red sandstone walls now stood at the centre of a walled city that traded in wool, camels, grain and salt along the desert routes.

Zorawar Singh was the son of **Maharaja Sujan Singh**, who had ruled Bikaner since 1700. The boy grew up inside Junagarh, among its courtyards and painted halls, in a court that still looked to Delhi for honours and rank. The Rathores of Bikaner had served the Mughal emperors for generations. They had fought in the Deccan, in the Punjab and on the northwestern frontier, and their princes had learned the manners and the Persian of the imperial camp as well as the songs of their own bards.

But the world in which Zorawar grew up was very different from the one his ancestors had known. After the death of Aurangzeb in 1707, the Mughal empire began to come apart. Emperors rose and fell within months. Great nobles carved out provinces of their own. In the south, the **Marathas** grew stronger every year, and from the 1720s their armies were crossing into Malwa and pressing on the edges of Rajputana. The old certainty that service to Delhi meant safety at home was gone.

Closer to home, the danger came from Bikaner's own kinsmen. The Rathores of **Jodhpur** were the senior branch of the house of Jodha, and they had never quite accepted Bikaner as an equal. Under **Maharaja Abhay Singh** of Jodhpur and his ambitious brother **Bakht Singh**, who held Nagaur on Bikaner's southern border, Marwar pressed hard on its northern neighbour. In the last years of Sujan Singh's reign, Bikaner had already felt that pressure on its frontier. A prince growing up in Junagarh in those years learned early that the greatest threat to his house might come from those who shared its blood.

Sujan Singh died in **1735**, and Zorawar Singh succeeded him. We know little of his first years on the throne. The chronicles say nothing of great building works or famous feasts. What they show instead is a ruler occupied with keeping his kingdom whole: managing the powerful **thakurs** who held their estates from the crown, keeping the frontier villages loyal, and watching the road from Nagaur.

It was a hard country to rule. Bikaner had no rivers. Its fields depended on the few weeks of the monsoon, and when the rains failed, as they often did, whole villages packed their goods onto camels and moved away in search of water. The wealth of the state lay in its herds and in the caravans that passed through it, and both could be scattered in a single season of drought or war. A Maharaja of Bikaner had to be part soldier, part landlord and part peacemaker among his own nobles, many of whom were descended from the sons and brothers of earlier kings and considered themselves almost his equals.

The great test of Zorawar Singh's reign came at the end of the 1730s. Abhay Singh of Jodhpur, encouraged by his brother Bakht Singh, resolved to bring Bikaner to heel. A Marwar army marched north into the desert and laid siege to Bikaner itself, around **1739–40**.

We can imagine the scene from what we know of such sieges. The gates of the city were closed. The villagers from the surrounding country crowded inside the walls with their animals. From the ramparts of Junagarh the defenders could see the smoke of the enemy's camps and the dust of their foragers riding out to strip the countryside. In the desert, a siege was a contest of water and grain as much as of swords. The besiegers had to feed their horses in a land that barely fed its own people. The besieged had to make their wells and stores last longer than the patience of the enemy.

Zorawar Singh knew that he could not break the siege with the strength of Bikaner alone. Instead he turned to diplomacy, and he chose his ally well. He sent to **Sawai Jai Singh II** of Jaipur, the most powerful and most respected Rajput prince of the age, the builder of a new capital and of the great observatories, and a man who had long played the part of senior statesman among the Rajput courts.

"Tell the Sawai Raja," we may imagine Zorawar saying to his envoy, "that if Bikaner falls today, every small state in Rajputana will know that the strong may swallow the weak at will. Tell him that we ask not for charity but for the order he himself has always defended."

Jai Singh had his own reasons to check the growing power of Jodhpur, and he answered. Instead of marching to Bikaner, he struck at the heart of Marwar. A Jaipur army advanced towards Jodhpur itself. Faced with a threat to his own capital, Abhay Singh had no choice but to recall his forces and come to terms. The siege of Bikaner was lifted, and Jodhpur was forced to make peace with Jai Singh in **1740**.

The quarrel did not end there. Bakht Singh, proud and furious at the humiliation, refused to accept it. In **1741** he led a fierce attack on Jai Singh's army at **Gangwana**. The battle that followed became famous in Rajput memory for the reckless courage of Bakht Singh's charge, which threw the Jaipur army into confusion even though Bakht Singh himself was forced to leave the field. For Bikaner, though, the result that mattered had already been won. The kingdom had survived, and it had survived not by a hopeless sortie but by the skill of its ruler in bringing a greater power into the balance.

This was the pattern of Zorawar Singh's whole reign. Bikaner was not strong enough to dominate its neighbours, and it was too poor to buy their friendship. What it could do was use the rivalries between the great states to protect itself. Zorawar Singh appears in the chronicles as a ruler who understood this, and who acted on it with patience and timing.

The world beyond Rajputana was meanwhile growing darker. In **1739**, the Persian conqueror **Nadir Shah** invaded India, defeated the Mughal army at Karnal and sacked Delhi. The massacre and plunder of the imperial capital showed every Indian court how hollow Mughal power had become. In the years that followed, the Maratha armies pressed further into Rajputana, demanding tribute and taking sides in every succession quarrel. Jai Singh himself died in **1743**, and with him went one of the few voices that could still hold the Rajput princes together.

For Bikaner, distance was a kind of protection. The desert that made the kingdom poor also made it hard to reach. The Maratha cavalry, which lived off the land, found little to live off in Jangaldesh. While Jaipur, Jodhpur, Kota and Udaipur were drawn deeper into the wars of the age, Bikaner under Zorawar Singh stayed largely at the edge of the storm. That was not an accident of geography alone. It was also the result of a ruler who chose his quarrels carefully.

Inside his kingdom, Zorawar Singh maintained the order his father had left. The court of Bikaner in these years kept up its old patronage of scholars, physicians and poets, and the great library of Junagarh, gathered by earlier rulers such as **Anup Singh**, remained one of the treasures of Rajputana. Later Bikaner tradition remembers Zorawar Singh as a cultivated man with an interest in learning, and some works are attributed to his court, though how much of this was his own work is not certain. What is clear is that in an age when many states were losing their libraries and temples to war, Bikaner kept its own.

He was also a Rathore prince of his time in his faith. The rulers of Bikaner were devoted to the goddess **Karni Mata**, whose shrine at Deshnoke, south of the city, had blessed the founding of the kingdom in the days of Rao Bika. Every ruler of the house, Zorawar Singh among them, honoured her as the protector of the dynasty, and the people of the desert believed that the walls of Bikaner stood under her care.

Zorawar Singh's reign was short. He died in **1746**, after about eleven years on the throne, and he left no son to succeed him. In a Rajput state, a death without an heir was one of the most dangerous moments possible. Brothers, cousins and nobles could all press their claims, and every neighbour with an army could find a reason to interfere.

The choice fell on **Gaj Singh**, a young prince of the royal house descended from Maharaja Anup Singh, and so a close kinsman of Zorawar Singh. His accession did not go entirely unchallenged, and Bikaner's chronicles record rival claims within the family in the years that followed. But the kingdom held together. Gaj Singh would rule for more than forty years, and he would inherit a state that had come through the most dangerous decade of the century with its walls, its lands and its independence intact.

That was Zorawar Singh's legacy. He was not remembered for conquests or for great monuments. He was remembered for something harder to see: for holding a small and poor desert kingdom together in an age when larger and richer states were breaking apart, and for knowing when to stand on his walls and when to send a letter.

## Highlights of his life

- **Son of Sujan Singh.** He succeeded his father, Maharaja Sujan Singh, on the throne of Bikaner in 1735.
- **Survived the siege of Bikaner.** Around 1739–40 a Jodhpur army under Abhay Singh besieged his capital, and the city held.
- **Alliance with Sawai Jai Singh II.** He brought the Jaipur ruler into the conflict, and Jai Singh's march on Marwar forced Jodhpur to lift the siege and make peace in 1740.
- **Steered clear of the great wars.** Through the years of Nadir Shah's invasion and the Maratha advance, he kept Bikaner largely outside the wars that were consuming Rajputana.
- **Kept the court and its learning.** Bikaner tradition remembers him as a patron of scholars and physicians in an age when much of the region's learning was being lost.
- **A peaceful succession.** He died without a son in 1746, and the throne passed to his kinsman Gaj Singh with the kingdom intact.
