## Maharaja Gaj Singh — forty years on the throne of the desert

*Maharaja Gaj Singh's long reign is recorded in the chronicles of Bikaner and its neighbours, which preserve the main lines of his wars and alliances but few personal details. Where history gives way to tradition, this story says so.*

Gaj Singh was not born to be king. He came into the world around **1723** as the son of **Anand Singh**, a younger son of **Maharaja Anup Singh**, the scholar-king who had filled the library of Junagarh with manuscripts gathered from across India. Through his father, the boy belonged to the royal house of Bikaner, the Rathore line founded by **Rao Bika** in 1488. But the throne belonged to another branch of the family. His uncle **Sujan Singh** ruled Bikaner when Gaj Singh was a child, and after him came Sujan Singh's son **Zorawar Singh**. A cousin of the reigning king could expect an estate, a place at court and a share in the kingdom's wars, but not the crown.

He grew up in the world of the desert nobility. Boys of his rank learned to ride both horses and camels, to hunt blackbuck and wild boar across the dunes, to use the sword and the matchlock, and to read the chronicles and the poetry in which the deeds of their ancestors were preserved. Above all they learned the delicate art of living among proud kinsmen, in a state where every noble family was descended from some earlier prince and every quarrel over land or honour could turn into a feud.

The Bikaner of his youth was a frightened place. Under Zorawar Singh, around 1739–40, a Jodhpur army besieged the capital, and the city was saved only when **Sawai Jai Singh II** of Jaipur marched on Marwar and forced the besiegers to withdraw. In the same years, the Persian conqueror **Nadir Shah** sacked Delhi, and the Maratha armies were spreading across Malwa and into Rajputana. A young man of the royal house watching these events would have learned that Bikaner's survival depended on vigilance, on its desert, and on choosing allies with care.

In **1746**, Zorawar Singh died without a son. The nobles of Bikaner, gathered in the hall of Junagarh, had to choose a successor from among the kinsmen of the dead king. Their choice fell on Gaj Singh, then a young man in his early twenties. Bikaner tradition tells that his accession did not go unchallenged, and that a rival within the family looked to Jodhpur for support. But Gaj Singh had the backing of the leading nobles, and he held the throne.

The early years of his reign were dominated by the troubles of Marwar. In **1749** Maharaja **Abhay Singh** of Jodhpur died, and his son **Ram Singh** succeeded him. Ram Singh was young, rash and quarrelsome, and he soon fell out with his uncle **Bakht Singh** of Nagaur, the same warrior prince who had once pressed so hard on Bikaner. Bakht Singh claimed the throne of Jodhpur for himself, and Marwar was plunged into civil war.

Gaj Singh saw his chance. For decades, Jodhpur had treated Bikaner as a junior branch to be bullied. Now, by joining one side of Marwar's quarrel, Bikaner could help shape its outcome. Gaj Singh threw his support behind Bakht Singh, and Bikaner forces joined the campaign that drove Ram Singh from his capital. In **1751** Bakht Singh took Jodhpur and became its Maharaja.

His triumph was short. Bakht Singh died in **1752**, and the war passed to his son **Bijay Singh**. The exiled Ram Singh called in the Marathas, and in **1754** a Maratha army under **Jayappa Scindia** entered Marwar. The war that followed was long and bitter. Jayappa was assassinated in his camp at Nagaur in **1755**, and the Marathas took heavy revenge on Marwar. Bikaner, which had backed Bakht Singh's line, could not stay entirely clear of these quarrels, but its distance and its poverty kept it from bearing the worst of the Maratha storm.

These were the years in which Gaj Singh learned the lesson that his predecessor had learned before him. A small desert state could not afford to tie itself permanently to any one side. It had to watch, wait, and lean towards whichever power would keep its neighbours in check. It was a policy of balance rather than heroics, but in the second half of the eighteenth century it was the only policy that kept a state like Bikaner alive.

Gaj Singh's other wars were fought on his own frontiers. To the north and northwest of Bikaner lay a wild border country where the desert faded into the plains of the Punjab and the valley of the Indus. There the **Bhatti** chiefs held the old fortress of **Bhatner**, and from the 1740s the new **Daudpotra** rulers of **Bahawalpur** were building a state of their own across the desert to the west. Raids for cattle and camels were constant, and every village well and grazing ground could become a cause of war. Gaj Singh spent much of his reign defending these frontiers, sending his nobles against raiders and building up the strength of the border forts. The chronicles of Bikaner record clashes with the Bhattis and with Bahawalpur, though they often leave the details vague, and the frontier was still unsettled when he died.

Within his kingdom, Gaj Singh was forced to deal with the same problem that had troubled every ruler of Bikaner: his own nobles. The great **thakurs** of the state, lords of estates like Bidasar, Mahajan and Bhukarka, held their lands in return for military service, and they guarded their privileges jealously. When the king was strong, they served him. When he was weak, they defied him. Over his long reign, Gaj Singh managed this balance with patience, sometimes rewarding loyalty, sometimes confiscating the lands of rebels, but never entirely solving the problem. It would trouble his successors for another hundred years.

The wider world kept changing around him. In **1761**, at the **Third Battle of Panipat**, the Afghan ruler **Ahmad Shah Abdali** crushed the Maratha army in one of the bloodiest battles of the century. For a time, the Maratha pressure on Rajputana eased, before returning under new leaders such as **Mahadji Scindia**. The Mughal emperor in Delhi was now emperor in name only, but his court could still grant titles and honours, and the rulers of Bikaner continued to value them. Bikaner tradition holds that Gaj Singh received high titles of honour from the imperial court, and the long, grand titles of later Bikaner rulers owe something to his reign.

Gaj Singh was also a builder, though on a modest scale suited to a desert state. He added to the palaces of **Junagarh**, and the name of **Gajner**, the lake and hunting retreat to the west of Bikaner where the rulers of the state would later build a famous palace, is traditionally linked with his. In the dry country, a lake where the rains could be gathered and wild game drawn to the water was a gift as valuable as any monument. In the court, poets and bards wrote in praise of him, and the painters of Bikaner, whose fine and delicate style had grown out of a meeting of Mughal and Rajput traditions, continued to work under his patronage.

Like the rulers before him, Gaj Singh was a devotee of **Karni Mata**, the goddess of Deshnoke whom the house of Bika regarded as its protector. He honoured the temples of the kingdom and the shrines of the desert saints. In the folk memory of Bikaner he appears as a ruler of the old style: a hunter, a patron and a father of a large family, surrounded by sons and grandsons who would later fight each other for his throne.

That large family was the great weakness of his last years. As Gaj Singh grew old, his sons began to look to the succession. The eldest, **Raj Singh**, quarrelled bitterly with his father, and for a time he lived in disgrace away from the court. Another son, **Surat Singh**, was ambitious and capable, and he watched the struggle closely. The nobles took sides. The old Maharaja, after four decades on the throne, found that the hardest enemy to manage was the quarrel inside his own palace.

Gaj Singh died in **1787**, after a reign of about forty-one years, one of the longest in the history of Bikaner. Raj Singh succeeded him, but ruled only a matter of weeks before he too died, and Bikaner's chronicles have long suspected poison. His infant son was placed on the throne with Surat Singh as regent, and within months Surat Singh had made himself Maharaja. The kingdom that Gaj Singh had held together through so many storms passed into a dark and violent chapter.

Yet the forty years of his reign mattered. Gaj Singh came to the throne when Bikaner had only just survived a siege, when the Mughal empire was collapsing and the Marathas were sweeping across Rajputana. When he died, Bikaner was still independent, still whole, and still ruled by the house of Bika. In an age that destroyed so many Indian states, that was no small achievement.

## Highlights of his life

- **An unexpected king.** A grandson of Maharaja Anup Singh, he was chosen by the nobles to succeed his kinsman Zorawar Singh in 1746.
- **Intervention in Marwar.** He backed Bakht Singh against Ram Singh in the Jodhpur civil war, helping Bakht Singh take Jodhpur in 1751.
- **Survival in the Maratha age.** Through the Maratha wars of the 1750s and after Panipat in 1761, he kept Bikaner largely outside the storms that overwhelmed its neighbours.
- **Defender of the frontiers.** He spent much of his reign holding the northern and western borders against the Bhattis and the rising state of Bahawalpur.
- **Gajner.** Tradition links his name with Gajner, the lake and hunting retreat west of Bikaner.
- **A forty-one-year reign.** He ruled from 1746 to 1787, one of the longest reigns in Bikaner's history.

## Maharaja Surat Singh — the iron hand that carried Bikaner into a new century

*Maharaja Surat Singh's reign is known from the chronicles of Bikaner, the records of its neighbours and the early reports of the British, many of which are hostile to him. Where the record is a matter of suspicion rather than proof, this story says so.*

Surat Singh was one of the many sons of **Maharaja Gaj Singh**, who ruled Bikaner for forty-one years, from 1746 to 1787. He grew up in the palace of **Junagarh**, in a crowded royal household where brothers and half-brothers competed for their father's favour and the loyalty of the nobles. He was not the eldest. That place belonged to **Raj Singh**, the heir. But from early in life Surat Singh showed the qualities that would define him: energy, cunning, ambition, and an unwillingness to accept second place.

The Bikaner of his youth was a state held together by careful balance. His father had kept the kingdom independent through the Marwar civil wars and the Maratha invasions of the eighteenth century, but he had never fully tamed the great **thakurs**, the nobles who held their estates in return for military service and who often behaved as rulers in their own right. In the last years of Gaj Singh's reign, the old king quarrelled bitterly with his eldest son, and the court split into factions. Surat Singh watched, and waited.

When Gaj Singh died in **1787**, Raj Singh came to the throne. Within a few weeks he was dead. The chronicles of Bikaner, and the British officers who later collected its history, believed that he had been poisoned, and many pointed to Surat Singh. Raj Singh's infant son, **Pratap Singh**, was proclaimed Maharaja, and Surat Singh became his regent. Before long the child too was dead, and Surat Singh took the throne in his own name. The tradition that he had the boy killed was widely repeated in later accounts. It cannot be proved, but it shadowed his name for the rest of his life.

A king who comes to power in this way begins his reign with enemies. Many nobles refused to accept him. Some of his own brothers turned against him. The first years of Surat Singh's rule were a long war against rebellion inside his own kingdom. He moved against the defiant thakurs one by one, besieging their fortified villages, seizing their estates and forcing them to submit. He was harsh, and he was remembered as harsh. But he was also effective. By the end of the century, the authority of the crown in Bikaner was stronger than it had been for decades.

The world outside was in turmoil. The Mughal empire had become a shadow, and the Maratha chiefs, especially **Mahadji Scindia** and later **Daulat Rao Scindia**, dominated much of northern India. Adventurers of every kind raised armies and carved out territories for themselves. One of them, the Irish soldier of fortune **George Thomas**, built a short-lived principality around **Hansi** in Haryana, on Bikaner's northeastern border, and around **1799** his troops raided into the lands of Bikaner. The desert kingdom had to pay to see them go. It was a sign of how far the old order had fallen: a foreign mercenary could now demand tribute from the house of Bika.

Surat Singh responded by strengthening his frontier. To the north of his capital he built a new fortress in the open desert, and around it grew a town that still carries his name: **Suratgarh**. Built of brick in the years around the turn of the nineteenth century, it guarded the routes along the dry bed of the old **Ghaggar** river, where travellers and armies moved between the Punjab and the desert.

His greatest military success came a few years later. Further up the same river stood **Bhatner**, one of the oldest forts in northern India, a great brick stronghold that had stood on the road between Central Asia and the Ganges plain for centuries. Timur had stormed it in 1398. For much of the eighteenth century it had been held by the **Bhatti** chiefs, who used it as a base for raids into Bikaner territory. In **1805**, after a siege of several months, Surat Singh's forces took Bhatner from its Bhatti chief, **Zabita Khan**.

The fort fell on a Tuesday, the day sacred to **Hanuman**, and Surat Singh renamed it **Hanumangarh**, the fort of Hanuman. He built a temple to the god within its walls. The name has stuck for more than two hundred years. For the house of Bika, it was the fulfilment of a long ambition: the northern gateway of the desert was finally theirs.

Surat Singh's successes did not make him safe. In **1807**, Rajputana was torn apart by a war between **Jaipur** and **Jodhpur**, sparked by the rival suits of their rulers for the hand of **Krishna Kumari**, the daughter of the Maharana of Udaipur. The war was really about power, and every state chose a side. Surat Singh joined the coalition led by **Maharaja Jagat Singh** of Jaipur against **Maharaja Man Singh** of Jodhpur, and supported a rival claimant to the Jodhpur throne. At first the coalition swept all before it, and Man Singh was besieged in his own fort. But the alliance broke apart, and Man Singh survived.

He did not forget his enemies. In the following year, a Jodhpur army marched into Bikaner territory and pressed Surat Singh hard. He was forced to make peace and pay an indemnity. The tragic end of the Krishna Kumari affair in **1810**, when the young princess was given poison to end the war that had grown around her, became one of the saddest stories of Rajput history. For Bikaner, the lesson was plainer. In the age of mercenary armies and broken alliances, a small state that joined the wars of its neighbours risked being destroyed by them.

Those years were the worst in the history of Rajputana. Bands of **Pindaris** and the forces of freebooting commanders such as **Amir Khan** moved across the region, plundering villages and extracting money from rulers who could no longer defend their own lands. Inside Bikaner, the thakurs rose again, encouraged by the chaos. Surat Singh's harsh taxes, needed to pay for his wars and his soldiers, made him more enemies. By the 1810s, Bikaner was exhausted.

The answer, when it came, came from outside. In **1817**, the **British East India Company** launched a great campaign to destroy the Pindaris and break the power of the Maratha chiefs. As part of this campaign, the British offered the Rajput states treaties of protection. In return for accepting British supremacy and giving up the right to make war or alliances on their own, the states would be protected against outside attack.

For Surat Singh, the offer was a lifeline. On **9 March 1818**, Bikaner signed its treaty with the Company. The kingdom accepted British protection and gave up its independent foreign policy, and the British promised to defend it. Almost immediately the treaty proved its worth for Surat Singh personally. When his nobles rose against him again, British troops were sent to help him restore order, and the rebellious thakurs were forced to submit.

It was a turning point in the history of Bikaner. For more than three centuries the state had defended itself with its own swords, its desert and its skill in diplomacy. From 1818 it lived under the shelter of a foreign power. Some would see that as a loss of independence. Others would see it as the only way to save the kingdom from the anarchy that had nearly destroyed it. Surat Singh, who had spent his life fighting for power, chose to secure it on the terms the age allowed.

He spent his last years in a kingdom that was, for the first time in decades, at peace. His forts at Suratgarh and Hanumangarh guarded the north. His nobles, however resentful, had been forced to obey. Like the rulers before him, he honoured **Karni Mata** of Deshnoke as the protector of his house, and the temple he founded at Hanumangarh still recalls the Tuesday on which the old fort fell.

Surat Singh died in **1828**, after a reign of about forty-one years, the same length as his father's. He was succeeded by his son **Ratan Singh**. He left behind a complicated memory. To his enemies and to many later historians, he was a usurper whose path to the throne passed through the deaths of his brother and his infant nephew. To others, he was the ruler who crushed the rebellious nobles, won Bhatner, founded Suratgarh, and carried Bikaner through the worst years of Rajputana's history into a new and more peaceful age. Both memories are true, and neither can be understood without the other.

## Highlights of his life

- **Seized the throne (1787).** After the sudden deaths of his brother Raj Singh and his infant nephew Pratap Singh, he became Maharaja, though later accounts accused him of causing those deaths.
- **Crushed the rebel nobles.** He spent years subduing the thakurs who rejected his rule, strengthening the authority of the crown.
- **Founded Suratgarh.** He built a fortress on the northern frontier around which grew the town that bears his name.
- **Captured Bhatner (1805).** He took the ancient fort from the Bhatti chief Zabita Khan and renamed it Hanumangarh.
- **The war of 1807–08.** He joined Jaipur's coalition against Man Singh of Jodhpur and was forced to make peace when Jodhpur struck back.
- **Treaty with the British (9 March 1818).** He placed Bikaner under the protection of the East India Company, ending decades of anarchy.

## Maharaja Ratan Singh — the king who made his nobles swear at Gaya

*Maharaja Ratan Singh's reign is known from the chronicles of Bikaner and the reports of British political officers in Rajputana. Where the details rest on tradition rather than record, this story says so.*

Ratan Singh was the son of **Maharaja Surat Singh**, the hard and ambitious ruler who had seized the throne of Bikaner in 1787, crushed its rebellious nobles, captured **Bhatner** and renamed it **Hanumangarh**, and in **1818** placed the kingdom under the protection of the **British East India Company**. Ratan Singh grew up in the palace of **Junagarh** during the most violent years of his father's reign, when Pindari bands and mercenary armies roamed Rajputana and the thakurs of Bikaner rose again and again against the crown. He was a young man when the treaty of 1818 brought that age to an end.

When Surat Singh died in **1828**, Ratan Singh inherited a kingdom that was quieter than it had been for generations, but not at rest. The nobles still resented the crown's demands. The frontiers with the neighbouring desert states were still disputed. And above the throne now stood a new power: the British, represented by political agents whose advice could not easily be ignored.

The first test came almost at once. Bikaner and **Jaisalmer** had long quarrelled over grazing grounds and border villages in the empty country between them. In **1829** the quarrel turned to open fighting, and the forces of the two states clashed near the frontier. The fighting did not go well for Bikaner. Under the old order, such a quarrel might have grown into years of raids and reprisals. Now the British stepped in. They forbade further fighting, and the dispute was settled by arbitration, with the **Maharana of Udaipur** acting as arbiter. It was a sign of how much had changed. A Rajput king could no longer settle his quarrels with the sword alone.

Ratan Singh accepted the new order and tried to make the best of it. He kept up good relations with the British, and when they went to war beyond the frontier, Bikaner helped. During the **First Anglo-Afghan War** (1839–42), and again during the wars against the **Sikhs** in the 1840s, Bikaner supplied camels for the British armies. In the desert, the camel was wealth and strength, and Bikaner's camel herds were famous. The British valued the help, and Ratan Singh's standing with them rose.

The deed for which Ratan Singh is best remembered, however, was not a war but a vow. Across much of Rajputana, among the proud Rajput clans, the killing of infant daughters was a terrible and long-standing practice. Families feared the ruinous cost of a daughter's wedding and the dishonour of marrying her below their rank, and many baby girls did not survive their first days. British officials had begun to press the princes to stop it, but the practice was deeply rooted, and few rulers dared to confront their nobles over it.

In **1836**, Ratan Singh made a great pilgrimage to **Gaya**, the holy city on the Phalgu river where Hindus offer rites for the souls of their ancestors. He travelled with a large retinue of his nobles. There, tradition and the British reports agree, at one of the holiest places of his faith, he made his thakurs swear that they would no longer kill their infant daughters.

We may imagine the scene: the river, the crowded ghats, the smoke of the funeral offerings, the priests chanting the names of the dead. And among them the Maharaja of Bikaner, turning to the proud men of his court. "We have come here for our fathers," he might have said. "Let us not return home with the blood of our daughters on our hands." An oath sworn at Gaya, before the ancestors, carried a weight that no order from the palace could match. How far it was kept in every village is impossible to know, but it was among the earliest public commitments of its kind by a Rajput ruler.

At home, Ratan Singh was a builder and a man of faith. In **Bikaner** city he built the **Ratan Bihari** temple, dedicated to Krishna, in the 1840s. Its white marble and red sandstone still stand near the old city, a quiet memorial to a ruler who preferred devotion to display. Like all rulers of his house, he honoured **Karni Mata** of Deshnoke as the protector of the dynasty. The court painters and poets of Bikaner continued their work under his patronage, and the old library of Junagarh was preserved.

His relations with his nobles were never easy. The thakurs had been forced to submit by his father, with British help, but they had not forgotten their grievances. Ratan Singh tried to rule with a lighter hand than Surat Singh, but the tension between the crown's need for revenue and the nobles' sense of their ancient rights remained. It would be inherited, unresolved, by his son.

Ratan Singh died in **1851**, after a reign of about twenty-three years. He was succeeded by his son **Sardar Singh**. His reign had none of the drama of his father's. There were no usurpations, no great sieges, no famous conquests. But it was the reign in which Bikaner learned to live under the new order of British supremacy, in which a desert king used his authority to challenge one of the cruellest customs of his society, and in which the kingdom enjoyed a peace it had not known for a hundred years.

## Highlights of his life

- **Son of Surat Singh.** He succeeded his father in 1828, inheriting a kingdom newly at peace under the treaty of 1818.
- **The Jaisalmer dispute (1829).** A border war with Jaisalmer was halted by the British and settled by arbitration, with the Maharana of Udaipur as arbiter.
- **The vow at Gaya (1836).** On pilgrimage to Gaya, he made his nobles swear to give up the killing of infant daughters.
- **Ally of the British.** Bikaner supplied camels for the British in the First Anglo-Afghan War and the Sikh wars.
- **Ratan Bihari temple.** He built the Krishna temple of Ratan Bihari in Bikaner in the 1840s.
- **A peaceful reign.** He ruled until his death in 1851 and was succeeded by his son Sardar Singh.

## Maharaja Sardar Singh — the desert king who rode out in 1857

*Maharaja Sardar Singh's reign is known from the chronicles of Bikaner and the records of the British government in India, which naturally dwell on his part in the events of 1857. Where the details are uncertain, this story says so.*

Sardar Singh was born in **1818**, the year in which his grandfather, **Maharaja Surat Singh**, placed Bikaner under the protection of the **British East India Company**. He was the son of **Maharaja Ratan Singh**, and he grew up in the palace of **Junagarh** in the first generation of Bikaner princes who had never known the wars and anarchy of the old Rajputana. He knew instead the new order: British political agents, treaties, and a peace that rested on a foreign power.

He would have seen his father's reign at close quarters: the border war with **Jaisalmer** in 1829, ended by British intervention, the camels sent to the British armies in Afghanistan and the Punjab, and the famous pilgrimage to **Gaya** in 1836, where Ratan Singh made his nobles swear to give up the killing of infant daughters. The lessons of those years shaped him. A ruler of Bikaner now had to deal with the British as well as with his own thakurs, and his standing with the one could decide his strength against the other.

Ratan Singh died in **1851**, and Sardar Singh, then in his early thirties, came to the throne. He inherited a kingdom at peace, but with old problems. The crown needed money, and the nobles resisted every new demand. The countryside was poor, and drought was never far away.

Six years later, northern India was shaken by the great uprising of **1857**. In May, sepoys of the Bengal Army rose at **Meerut** and marched on **Delhi**, where they proclaimed the old Mughal emperor, **Bahadur Shah Zafar**, as their leader. Within weeks, the revolt had spread across much of the north. In **Hisar** and the surrounding districts of what is now Haryana, on Bikaner's eastern border, British authority collapsed, and British officers and their families fled for their lives.

Every Indian prince had to choose. Some stood aside to see which way the storm would turn. Some were swept along with it. Sardar Singh chose the British, and he chose decisively. He gave shelter to British fugitives who reached his territory, and he did something almost no other Rajput ruler did: he led his own troops in person beyond the borders of his state, into the disturbed districts around Hisar, to help restore British control.

We can imagine the column leaving Bikaner in the summer heat: camel riders and horsemen, the Maharaja at their head, moving east across the sand towards the plains. To his nobles, it may have seemed strange to ride out for a foreign power. To Sardar Singh, it was a calculation as old as his dynasty. Bikaner had survived for centuries by choosing the side that would win, and in 1857 he judged that the British would prevail.

He was right. By 1858 the uprising had been crushed, the East India Company abolished, and India placed under the direct rule of the British Crown. The new government did not forget its friends. In recognition of his services, Sardar Singh was granted the **Tibi** pargana, a tract of villages on Bikaner's border taken from the Hisar district, along with other honours. The coins of Bikaner from these years came to bear the name of **Queen Victoria**, a small sign of the new age.

At home, Sardar Singh continued his father's efforts against cruel customs. Under British encouragement, orders were issued in Bikaner against **sati**, the burning of widows, against female infanticide, and against the living burial of ascetics. Such orders could not change society overnight, but they set the law of the state against practices that had long been tolerated.

His relations with his nobles were less successful. To meet the needs of his treasury, Sardar Singh tried to raise the dues that the thakurs paid to the crown. The nobles resisted bitterly, and some appealed to the British political agent. In the 1860s the dispute grew serious, and the British stepped in to mediate between the Maharaja and his nobles. It was a pattern that would continue under his successor: the crown and the nobles locked in a struggle over money and rights, with the British as the referee.

Like all rulers of his line, he honoured **Karni Mata** of Deshnoke as the protector of the dynasty, and he maintained the temples, the palaces and the library of Junagarh. But he did not live to see his kingdom's problems resolved. Sardar Singh died in **1872**, after a reign of about twenty-one years, and he left no son.

A succession without an heir had once been a moment of great danger for Bikaner. Now it was managed within the new order. The senior widow of Sardar Singh and the nobles chose a young kinsman, **Dungar Singh**, a descendant of Maharaja Gaj Singh, and the British government approved the choice. The throne passed peacefully, and Dungar Singh would begin the work of building a modern state in the desert.

## Highlights of his life

- **Born into the new order (1818).** Son of Maharaja Ratan Singh, he was born in the year Bikaner signed its treaty with the British.
- **Accession (1851).** He succeeded his father and ruled for about twenty-one years.
- **Led his troops in 1857.** He sheltered British fugitives and personally led Bikaner's forces into the Hisar region to support the British during the uprising.
- **The Tibi grant.** The British rewarded him with the Tibi pargana from the Hisar district.
- **Against cruel customs.** Orders against sati, female infanticide and the living burial of ascetics were issued in Bikaner during his reign.
- **A peaceful succession.** He died without a son in 1872, and the throne passed to his kinsman Dungar Singh.

dungar-singh-bikaner.story:
## Maharaja Dungar Singh — the young king who opened the doors of Junagarh to a new age

*Maharaja Dungar Singh's reign is recorded in the chronicles of Bikaner and in the reports of British officials in Rajputana. Where later memory has added to the record, this story says so.*

Dungar Singh was born in **1854**, the son of **Lal Singh**, a nobleman of the royal house of Bikaner descended from **Maharaja Gaj Singh**, who had ruled the kingdom in the eighteenth century. Like Gaj Singh before him, the boy was not born in the direct line of succession. The throne belonged to **Maharaja Sardar Singh**, the ruler who had led his troops in person to help the British in 1857. Dungar Singh grew up as a young kinsman of the king, in the world of the desert nobility, learning to ride and hunt and to take his place at court.

His life changed in **1872**. Sardar Singh died without a son, and the question of the succession arose. The senior widow of the dead king and the nobles of Bikaner chose Dungar Singh, then about eighteen years old, and the British government approved the choice. The young man who had expected to live as a nobleman found himself seated on the throne of Rao Bika, in the great fortress of **Junagarh**.

He inherited a difficult kingdom. Bikaner was vast, dry and poor. Its revenue was small, its administration old-fashioned, and its powerful **thakurs** were still locked in the quarrel that had troubled Sardar Singh's reign: the crown wanted more revenue, and the nobles refused to pay more than their ancient dues. Above them all stood the British political agent, whose advice carried the weight of the Raj.

Dungar Singh was young, but he was determined to rule. He set out to reform the government of his state, bringing it closer to the model of British India. During his reign Bikaner began to acquire the institutions of a modern state: regular courts of justice, a police force, a jail, a hospital and schools. These were modest beginnings in a desert kingdom with few roads and fewer trained officials, but they marked a real change from the old government of household officers and noble privilege.

He did not find it easy. His efforts to strengthen the crown's finances revived the old struggle with the thakurs. In **1883** the discontent broke into open revolt, as several nobles defied the Maharaja's authority. The revolt was put down with British support, and in its aftermath the British took a closer hand in the administration of Bikaner. For a proud young ruler, it was a bitter experience. But it also broke the power of the nobles to defy the crown by force, and the reforms continued.

Bikaner was now firmly part of the British imperial system. When the British fought the **Second Anglo-Afghan War** (1878–80), Bikaner, like its rulers before, sent camels to support their armies. Under an agreement with the British government, the state also gave up the manufacture of salt in return for compensation, part of the British effort to control the salt trade across India. In these years the long isolation of the desert kingdom was beginning to end.

Dungar Singh was also a builder. He added new apartments to **Junagarh**, decorated in the rich style of the late nineteenth century, where traditional Rajput painting and gilding met imported glass, clocks and European furniture. Bikaner tradition remembers him as one of the first rulers in Rajputana to bring electric light into his palace, though the details of that story have grown with the telling. What is certain is that he was curious about the new technology of the age and eager to bring it to his capital.

He was a man of faith in the tradition of his house, devoted to **Karni Mata** of Deshnoke, the protector of the Bikaner dynasty, and he supported the temples of his kingdom. At the same time, he looked outward. Education mattered to him, and the schools of his reign were the seed of a system his successor would greatly expand.

But Dungar Singh's reign was short. He fell ill, and in **1887** he died, at only about thirty-three years of age, after fifteen years on the throne. He had no son. Before his death, he chose his younger brother, **Ganga Singh**, a boy of only seven, as his heir, and the British government confirmed the choice.

It was perhaps the most important decision of his life. Ganga Singh would rule Bikaner for fifty-six years, until 1943. He would bring the railway and the **Gang Canal** to the desert, build the **Lalgarh Palace**, named after his and Dungar Singh's father, serve in two world wars and sign the Treaty of Versailles. In **1928** he founded a college in Bikaner and named it **Dungar College** in honour of the brother who had made him king.

Dungar Singh's reign is often overshadowed by the brilliant career of his successor. Yet it was in his fifteen years that the work of modernising Bikaner began: the courts, the police, the hospital, the schools and the new ideas that would transform the desert kingdom in the century that followed.

## Highlights of his life

- **Chosen as king (1872).** A descendant of Gaj Singh, he was chosen by the widow of Sardar Singh and the nobles, with British approval, at about eighteen.
- **Administrative reform.** He began building a modern government in Bikaner, with courts, police, a jail, a hospital and schools.
- **The nobles' revolt (1883).** He faced a rebellion of the thakurs, which was put down with British support.
- **Builder of Junagarh.** He added new apartments to the fort, and tradition credits him with bringing electric light to the palace.
- **Chose Ganga Singh as heir.** Before his death in 1887, he chose his younger brother Ganga Singh, who became Bikaner's greatest modern ruler.
- **Dungar College.** The college in Bikaner was founded by Ganga Singh in 1928 and named in his memory.

ganga-singh-bikaner.story:
## Ganga Singh — the desert king who brought the river home

*Maharaja Ganga Singh's life is unusually well documented, in the records of his own state, the papers of the British Empire and the memories of those who knew him. This story follows that record, and adds only the colour of scene and feeling.*

In the late nineteenth century, the kingdom of **Bikaner** lay across one of the harshest stretches of the Thar Desert. It had been founded in 1488 by **Rao Bika**, a son of Rao Jodha of Marwar, and for four hundred years its Rathore rulers had governed a land of shifting dunes, scattered villages and deep wells, where a failed monsoon could empty whole districts. The fort of **Junagarh**, built by Raja Rai Singh in the late sixteenth century, showed that men could hold this country, but not that they could tame it.

It was here, on **13 October 1880**, that a boy named **Ganga Singh** was born. He was a younger son of **Maharaj Lal Singh**, a nobleman of the ruling house, and he was not expected to rule. The throne belonged to his elder brother, **Maharaja Dungar Singh**, who had become king in 1872. But Dungar Singh had no son of his own, and when he died in **August 1887**, the choice of the family and the approval of the British government fell upon the young brother. Ganga Singh was not yet seven years old when he became Maharaja of Bikaner.

A child cannot rule, and so for the next eleven years Bikaner was governed by a regency council working under the eye of the British Political Agent. The court decided that he should be educated as a modern prince. In 1889 he was sent to **Mayo College** at Ajmer, the school created for the sons of the Rajput princes. Later his studies continued at home under private tutors, among them the Englishman **Brian Egerton** and the scholar **Pandit Ram Chandra Dube**, who taught him the languages and traditions of his own land.

A Rathore king was still expected to be a soldier, and in 1898 the young Maharaja went through a year of military training with the **Deoli Regiment**. In **December 1898**, at the age of eighteen, he was invested with full ruling powers. He came into his kingdom at the worst possible moment.

The monsoon of 1899 failed across western India. In the Hindu calendar the year was Samvat 1956, and in Rajasthan the famine that followed is still remembered as the **Chhappania Akal**, the famine of fifty-six. Wells ran dry, cattle died in their thousands, and families fled the desert. In Bikaner the young Maharaja did not stay behind the walls of Junagarh. He organised relief works, opened grain stores, and is remembered for riding out personally to inspect the camps and the roads being built by the starving so that they could earn their bread. For his work in the famine he was awarded the **Kaisar-i-Hind** medal. But the lesson he took from those months was deeper than any honour. Ganga Singh became convinced that Bikaner would never be safe as long as its life depended on the rain. The desert needed a river.

That conviction would take him almost thirty years to realise. In the meantime, he set about making his state and himself known in the wider world. Bikaner had already raised a famous camel corps, the **Ganga Risala**, as part of the Imperial Service Troops that princely states maintained for the defence of the Empire. In **1900** the Maharaja went with his camel corps to **China**, where Western powers and their allies were fighting the Boxer uprising. The young king served there in person, and he returned with a reputation as a prince who would share the hardships of his own soldiers. A few years later the camel corps also served in **Somaliland**, in the campaigns of the Horn of Africa.

At home, he married into other Rajput houses and raised a family. His heir, **Sadul Singh**, was born in 1902. Another son, **Bijey Singh**, died young, and the father's grief later took the form of a hospital in his name, the **Prince Bijey Singh Memorial Hospital** in Bikaner. Ganga Singh was a demanding master who read files late into the night and wanted to know the details of every department.

Those departments were multiplying. In the first decades of the twentieth century Bikaner was transformed from a feudal desert kingdom into something close to a modern administration. A **Chief Court** was set up in 1910, and later a **High Court**. A **Representative Assembly** was created in 1913, one of the earliest such bodies in any princely state, though its powers remained limited and the final word always belonged to the Maharaja. Municipal committees, a police force on modern lines, schools for boys and later for girls, and hospitals followed. The railway, which had first come to Bikaner in his brother's time, was extended across the state, and in 1924 the **Bikaner State Railway** was separated from the joint line it had shared with Jodhpur. Electricity, telegraphs and paved roads reached the capital. In 1912 a college was founded at Bikaner and named after his brother, **Dungar College**.

He built too. Outside the old walled city he raised the **Lalgarh Palace**, named after his father, Lal Singh. It was designed by the British architect **Sir Samuel Swinton Jacob** and built over many years of the early twentieth century in the deep red sandstone of the region, with carved stone screens, wide courtyards and long verandas, a blend of Rajput tradition and European comfort. At **Gajner**, by a lake outside the city, he improved the old hunting lodge into a palace where viceroys and princes came for the famous winter shoots of sandgrouse. In the world of the Raj a ruler's guests were his allies, and he used every season at Gajner to build friendships.

Then the world went to war. When the **First World War** began in 1914, Ganga Singh immediately offered his troops and his own service. The Ganga Risala was sent to **Egypt**, where it helped defend the **Suez Canal** against the Ottoman attacks of 1915. The Maharaja himself served with the Indian forces in **France** and in Egypt, and was honoured for it. Bikaner, a small and poor state, gave men, money and animals far beyond its size.

His reward was a place at the table of the Empire. In **1917** he was chosen as one of India's representatives at the **Imperial War Conference** in London, and he sat in the **Imperial War Cabinet**, the only Indian prince to do so. When the war ended, he went to the peace conference at Paris, and in **1919** he signed the **Treaty of Versailles** on behalf of India, alongside the Secretary of State Edwin Montagu and Lord Sinha.

Back in India he became the leading voice of the princes. When the **Chamber of Princes** was created in 1921, he was elected its first **Chancellor**, and he held that office for five years. In 1930 he led the Indian delegation to the **League of Nations** at Geneva, and in 1930 and 1931 he took part in the **Round Table Conferences** in London, where the future constitution of India was debated. At first he spoke in favour of an all-India federation that would bring the princely states and British India together. Later, as the princes quarrelled and feared for their powers, the plan stalled and the federation was never established.

Through all these years, the river remained his greatest ambition. The nearest great water lay far to the north, in the **Sutlej**, which flowed through the Punjab. To bring it to Bikaner meant dealing with the British government of the Punjab, with the state of Bahawalpur, and with engineers who doubted that a canal through such sandy soil could ever hold water. Ganga Singh argued, negotiated and paid. In 1920 an agreement was finally reached under the **Sutlej Valley Project**, and work began on a canal from the headworks at **Ferozepur**. To prevent the precious water from soaking away into the sand, a long stretch of it was lined, a remarkable engineering effort for its time.

On **26 October 1927**, the Viceroy **Lord Irwin** formally opened the **Gang Canal**. People in the north of Bikaner who had never seen running water in their lives came to the banks to watch it arrive. Local memory tells of old men who wept to see it. Around the canal, new villages were planned and settlers were invited to farm the land. A new town was laid out and named after the king: **Sri Ganganagar**. Within a generation, the dry plains of the north became fields of wheat, cotton and gram. The canal did not turn the whole desert green, and much of Bikaner remained as dry as before, but it changed the life of a whole region and became the model for the later and far larger Indira Gandhi Canal.

His long reign had a harder side as well. Ganga Singh believed in progress from above, given by a wise ruler, not demanded by his subjects. When the movement for responsible government began to stir in the princely states, he met it with firmness. In 1932 his government passed a **Public Safety Act**, and a group of political workers was tried in what became known as the **Bikaner Conspiracy Case**. Nationalist critics called him an autocrat in modern clothes. He reformed the state, but he did not share its power.

In **1937** Bikaner celebrated his **Golden Jubilee**, fifty years on the throne. A museum was founded in his honour. By then he held a long list of British honours and the honorary rank of **general**, and he was perhaps the best known of all the Indian princes abroad.

When the **Second World War** came in 1939, he was nearly sixty, but he again placed his forces at the service of the Allies, and the Bikaner state troops served overseas. Old as he was, he travelled to visit soldiers in the Middle East. The years of strain told on his health. On **2 February 1943** Maharaja Ganga Singh died in **Bombay**, at the age of sixty-two, after a reign of fifty-six years, one of the longest in the history of Rajputana.

He was succeeded by his son, **Maharaja Sadul Singh**, who would sign Bikaner's accession to the new Dominion of India in 1947 and see it merge into the state of Rajasthan. Ganga Singh did not live to see the end of the princely order that he had served and defended. But his statue stands in Bikaner, the city of Sri Ganganagar carries his name, and every season when the water flows through the old Gang Canal, the desert remembers the king who refused to accept that it must always be dry.

## Highlights of his life

- **A boy king.** Born in 1880, he succeeded his elder brother Dungar Singh in 1887 at the age of six, and received full powers in December 1898.
- **The great famine.** He led relief work during the Chhappania Akal of 1899–1900 and was awarded the Kaisar-i-Hind medal.
- **Soldier of the Empire.** He served in China in 1900 and in the First World War, while the Ganga Risala defended the Suez Canal in 1915.
- **Signatory at Versailles.** He sat in the Imperial War Cabinet in 1917 and signed the Treaty of Versailles for India in 1919.
- **Voice of the princes.** He was the first Chancellor of the Chamber of Princes (1921–1926) and attended the Round Table Conferences.
- **The Gang Canal.** Opened in 1927, it brought Sutlej water to northern Bikaner and gave birth to the town of Sri Ganganagar.
- **A modern state.** Courts, an assembly, railways, schools, hospitals and the Lalgarh Palace marked his reign, though he kept power firmly in his own hands.

jaisal-singh.story:
## Rawal Jaisal — the exile who raised a golden fort on the hill of three peaks

*Much of Rawal Jaisal's life comes to us through the Bhati chronicles of Jaisalmer, the songs of the bards and the account James Tod compiled from them in the nineteenth century. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

Long before there was a golden city in the Thar, the Bhati Rajputs were already a people of the desert. They traced their descent from the Yadavas, the lunar race of Lord Krishna, and through a chieftain named **Bhati** from whom their clan took its name. Pushed out of the lands near the Indus over generations of war, they had moved south and east into the sand country, building one stronghold after another: **Tanot**, then **Derawar**, and finally **Lodurva**, a walled town on the edge of a dry riverbed, set among the caravan tracks that crossed the desert between Sindh, Gujarat and the plains of the north.

By the early twelfth century Lodurva was the seat of the Bhati rawals. The chronicles name its ruler in this period as **Rawal Dusaj**, and give him several sons. Among them were **Jaisal** and **Vijayraj**, who is remembered by the nickname *Lanjha*. Tradition says that Jaisal was the elder, and that he had every reason to expect the turban of Lodurva. But kingship among the desert clans was not always settled by birth order alone. The father's favour, the backing of the nobles and the alliances made by marriage all counted, and when Dusaj died it was Vijayraj, not Jaisal, who took his seat.

The bards remember Vijayraj Lanjha's reign with pride. He is said to have married a princess of the Solanki house of **Anhilwara Patan**, the great kingdom of Gujarat, and from that court the Bhatis are said to have received a title they would carry for centuries: *Uttar Bhad Kiwad*, "the bolt on the northern door". The Bhatis, in other words, were to be the barrier that stood between the rich lands of Gujarat and the invaders who came down from the north-west. It was a proud name, and a dangerous one, for those who hold a door must also bear the blows that fall on it.

For Jaisal, these were years in the shadow of another man's throne. He had his own followers, his own horses and his own pride, but no kingdom. When Vijayraj died and his son **Bhojdev** succeeded him, the young ruler was Jaisal's nephew, a man much younger than himself. The chronicles say that relations between uncle and nephew were bitter from the start. Bhojdev feared his uncle's ambition; Jaisal resented a crown that he believed had been his by right. In the end Jaisal left Lodurva, or was driven out of it.

What followed is the darkest part of his story, and the part where the chronicles are least certain. Tradition says that Jaisal, determined to win back what he had lost, went in search of an ally strong enough to break Lodurva's walls, and that he found one in a sultan from beyond the Indus. Tod, following the bards, names this ally as the ruler of Ghor. Here history must speak plainly: the famous **Muhammad of Ghor** did not begin his campaigns into India until the 1170s, nearly twenty years after the date the chronicles give for the founding of Jaisalmer. Either the ally was some other lord of the north-west, perhaps a governor of the Ghaznavid lands in Sindh or the Punjab, or the bards drew the most famous name of the age into a story where it does not belong. What the tradition agrees on is the result. Lodurva was attacked and sacked, Bhojdev was killed fighting in its defence, and Jaisal became master of a ruined capital.

It was not the victory he had dreamed of. The town had been plundered, its walls were broken, and it lay on open ground that any army could reach. The very alliance that had brought him to power had shown how easily Lodurva could be taken. A Bhati ruler who wished to hold the northern door could not sit behind walls like these. Jaisal began to look for a new seat, a place that the desert itself would help to defend.

He found it about fifteen kilometres to the south-east, at a long ridge of yellow sandstone that rose some eighty metres above the plain. The local people called it **Trikuta**, the hill of three peaks. Seen from the dunes, it was a natural fortress: steep on every side, wide enough on top to hold a town, and visible for miles in every direction, so that no enemy could approach unseen.

The bards say that the hill was not empty when Jaisal first climbed it. On its summit lived a hermit named **Eesul** (or Isal), who had made his home beside a small spring. When the hermit learned who the visitor was, the story goes, he told Jaisal of a prophecy older than any Bhati chronicle. Long ago, he said, **Lord Krishna** had come to this very hill with the hero **Arjuna**, and had foretold that in a distant age a prince of his own Yadava blood would build a kingdom here. Some versions add that Krishna struck the rock to bring out the spring, and that the old well on the hill, still called **Jaisal Kuan**, is that same water. It is a legend, and it is told as one. But it gave the new city a sacred beginning, and it bound the Bhatis, the children of the Yadavas, to the land in the most powerful way their age knew: through the word of a god.

The chronicles give the year of foundation as **1156 CE**. Jaisal laid out a fort along the crest of the hill, and the town that grew within and beneath it took his name: **Jaisalmer**, the hill-fort of Jaisal. The stone was quarried from the ridge itself, a yellow sandstone that turns the colour of honey in the late afternoon light, and so the fort and the city around it came to be called *Sonar Qila*, the golden fort, and the golden city.

Building a capital in the Thar was not a matter of walls alone. Water was life, and the fort needed wells and tanks that could last through a siege. People had to be persuaded to come: the families of the Bhati warriors, the Brahmins who served the clan's temples, and above all the merchants. Jaisalmer stood astride the caravan routes that linked Sindh and the lands beyond it with Gujarat and the Ganges plain. Camels carried salt, cloth, dried fruit, spices, opium and horses along these routes, and every caravan that passed beneath the golden hill brought tolls and trade. Much of the city's later wealth, and its famous havelis and temples, would come from these merchants. The foundations of that prosperity were laid when Jaisal chose a hill that commanded the roads.

The old capital was not entirely abandoned. Lodurva lived on as a sacred place, and its Jain temple, dedicated to Parshvanath, was later rebuilt and is still visited by pilgrims today. But from Jaisal's time the heart of the Bhati state moved to the golden hill, and it would stay there for nearly eight hundred years, until the princely state of Jaisalmer joined the Indian Union in 1949.

Of Jaisal's character we know mainly what the bards chose to remember, and they remembered a man of hard decisions. He was a warrior who had spent most of his life waiting, and who, when his moment came, took it at a terrible price. The chronicles do not hide the fact that he won his throne with the help of a foreign ally and over the body of his own nephew. In the code of the bards, that was a stain. Yet they also credit him with the act that made the Bhatis great: the choice to leave a broken town and build on the hill that would protect his people for centuries.

His reign on Trikuta was short. The chronicles give him only about a dozen years in the new capital, years spent raising walls, digging wells and drawing settlers to a place that had been empty rock. The fort he built was much smaller than the one visitors see today. Its great ring of bastions, ninety-nine in number, was added over the following centuries by his successors, who strengthened it again and again as new enemies came to test the northern door.

Rawal Jaisal died in **1168 CE**, according to the traditional chronology. He was succeeded by his son, **Rawal Shalivahan II**. The dynasty he set on the hill would face terrible trials there. Twice, at the end of the thirteenth century and again in the fourteenth, the chronicles say, the defenders of Jaisalmer chose *saka*, the last charge of the men and the *jauhar* of the women, rather than surrender. But each time the Bhatis returned to the golden fort, and their rawals, later the maharawals, ruled from it without a break in the line of descent until the end of princely India.

Today Jaisalmer is one of the few living forts in the world, where families still make their homes inside walls that were begun in the twelfth century. At the foot of the hill, the city's people still tell the story of the hermit, the prophecy and the spring. They tell it as their grandparents told it, as a legend. But the golden fort itself is no legend. It stands where a disinherited prince, having lost one home and won another at great cost, chose to build.

## Highlights of his life

- **A prince denied his throne.** Tradition says that Jaisal, a son of Rawal Dusaj of Lodurva, was passed over in favour of his brother Vijayraj Lanjha.
- **Struggle with his nephew.** He fought his nephew Rawal Bhojdev for Lodurva with the help of an ally from the north-west; the chronicles say Bhojdev was killed and Lodurva sacked. The chronicles name the sultan of Ghor as the ally, but the dates do not fit.
- **Founder of Jaisalmer (1156 CE).** He abandoned the exposed town of Lodurva and built a new fort on the three-peaked hill of Trikuta, which took his name.
- **The legend of the prophecy.** The bards tell that the hermit Eesul showed him Krishna's prophecy that a Yadava prince would rule from the hill, a story linked to the well called Jaisal Kuan.
- **Master of the caravan roads.** His new capital commanded the desert trade routes between Sindh, Gujarat and northern India, the source of the city's later wealth.
- **A lasting dynasty.** He died in 1168 CE and was succeeded by his son Shalivahan II; his line ruled from the golden fort until 1949.

## Maharaja Sadul Singh — the last ruling Maharaja of Bikaner, who led his state into India

*Sadul Singh's life is well recorded: in the papers of the Bikaner state, the records of the Indian princely states, the proceedings of the Constituent Assembly and the biographies written after his death. This story follows that record.*

The Rathore kingdom of **Bikaner** was born in the desert in the late fifteenth century, when **Rao Bika**, a son of Rao Jodha of Marwar, rode north into the sand country of Jangladesh and founded a city that bore his name in **1488**. For more than four centuries his descendants held that dry land of dunes, wells and camel tracks. By the time **Sadul Singh** was born, the kingdom was ruled by one of the most remarkable princes of his age, his father **Maharaja Ganga Singh**.

Sadul Singh was born on **7 September 1902** in the old fort of **Junagarh** at Bikaner. His mother was Maharani Vallabh Kunwar, a princess of the Sisodia house of Pratapgarh. He was the eldest surviving son: an elder brother, Ram Singh, had died at birth. The boy grew up in a court that was changing fast. Ganga Singh, who had come to the throne as a child in 1887, was turning his desert state into a modern one, with railways, schools, hospitals, a reformed administration and, above all, a dream of bringing water to Bikaner's parched fields. He was also a soldier and statesman whose reputation reached far beyond India.

The young prince, known as the **Maharaj Kumar**, was raised to follow in those footsteps. He was educated at **Mayo College** in Ajmer, the school founded for the sons of the Rajput princes, and he was taken early into the wider world his father moved in. In 1911, when he was only nine, he attended the coronation of King George V in London, and later that year he served as a page of honour to the King-Emperor at the great **Delhi Durbar**. In **1919**, still a teenager, he was in Paris when the Peace Conference met after the First World War, where his father was one of the representatives of India. In **1924** he attended the meeting of the League of Nations at Geneva.

At home, his father gave him real responsibility. From **1920 to 1925** the young Maharaj Kumar served as **Chief Minister** of Bikaner and president of the state council, learning the business of government at the side of a ruler who demanded much of those around him. In 1921 and 1922 he served as an honorary aide to the Prince of Wales during the royal tour of India. In April **1922** he married **Sudarshan Kumari**, a princess of the Baghel house of **Rewa** in central India. Their first child, a daughter named **Sushila Kumari**, was born in 1923. A son, **Karni Singh**, followed in April 1924, and a second son, **Amar Singh**, in December 1925.

The years that followed were the years of Ganga Singh's greatest achievement. In **1927** the **Gang Canal** opened, carrying the waters of the Sutlej from the headworks at Ferozepur in the Punjab into the north of Bikaner, and turning a stretch of desert into farmland around a new town, Sri Ganganagar. Sadul Singh grew up watching his father fight for that canal and then build a new province around it. It would shape his own concerns in the years ahead, for the life of northern Bikaner now depended on water that flowed from outside the state.

In all, Sadul Singh spent about thirty years in his father's service before he became ruler himself. It was a long apprenticeship, and the family suffered losses along the way: his younger brother Bijey Singh died at the age of thirty-one. On **2 February 1943** Maharaja Ganga Singh died, and Sadul Singh succeeded him. He took his seat on the throne in the **Karan Mahal** of Junagarh on 13 February 1943, at the age of forty.

He became ruler in the middle of the Second World War. Bikaner's state forces, including its famous camel corps, the **Ganga Risala**, and the **Sadul Light Infantry**, served with the Allied armies, and the new Maharaja himself went to the front. In 1943 he served in the Middle East and Persia, and in 1944 in Burma. He was made an honorary major-general in 1945 and an honorary lieutenant-general in 1946. At home he founded new orders of honour for the state: the **Vikram Badge**, later the Order of the Vikram Star, in 1944, and later the Order of the Sadul Star.

But the great test of his reign was not the war. It was what came after it. By 1946 it was clear that British rule in India was ending, and the more than five hundred princely states faced a question their ancestors had never faced: what would become of them when the paramount power withdrew? Some princes hoped to stand apart, as independent states or in a separate union of their own. The **Chamber of Princes**, under its chancellor, the Nawab of Bhopal, urged the rulers to keep their distance from the **Constituent Assembly** that was drafting India's new constitution.

Sadul Singh took a different path. Guided by his own judgement and advised by his dewan, the scholar and diplomat **K. M. Panikkar**, he decided that Bikaner's future lay with India. In **April 1947**, when most princes were still holding back, Bikaner was among the very first states to send representatives to take their seats in the Constituent Assembly, breaking ranks with the princes who wished to stay out. It was a public and deliberate choice, and it encouraged other rulers to follow.

Partition brought the danger close to home. The new border between India and Pakistan would run along Bikaner's western edge, and the headworks of the Gang Canal stood at **Ferozepur**, in the Punjab that was about to be divided. Accounts of the time say that Sadul Singh pressed hard for the canal's source to remain in India, since the fields of northern Bikaner could not live without it. When the boundary award was announced, Ferozepur remained on the Indian side. Exactly how much the Maharaja's appeals counted in that decision is still debated by historians, but his concern for the canal was real and well known.

On **7 August 1947**, a week before independence, Sadul Singh signed the **Instrument of Accession** to the Dominion of India, among the first princes to do so. Bikaner joined India on matters of defence, foreign affairs and communications, and soon found itself a border state of the new nation. In the months that followed, refugees crossed the frontier in both directions, and the state had to keep order across a long desert border in a time of terrible violence in the Punjab.

Accession was only the first step. Under **Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel** and **V. P. Menon**, the government of India began to merge the princely states into larger units. In Rajputana this happened in stages, as one group of states after another joined together. On **30 March 1949**, Sadul Singh signed away his ruling powers and merged Bikaner, along with Jaipur, Jodhpur and Jaisalmer, into the **United State of Greater Rajasthan**, which later became the state of Rajasthan. The kingdom that Rao Bika had founded in 1488 ceased to exist as a separate state after four hundred and sixty-one years.

He was not bitter about it. The biographers who wrote about him later called him a co-architect of India's unity, and that is how he wished to be remembered. He kept the title of Maharaja and remained head of the house of Bikaner, but the government of the land passed to the people's representatives. It was the outcome he had chosen two years earlier, when he walked into the Constituent Assembly while others stood outside.

He did not live long to see the new India. Sadul Singh died in **London** on **25 September 1950**, only forty-eight years old. His body was brought home, and his elder son, **Karni Singh**, succeeded him as Maharaja of Bikaner. His daughter Sushila Kumari had married **Bhagwat Singh**, who would become Maharana of Mewar, binding the Rathores of Bikaner to the Sisodias of Udaipur.

His reign as a ruling prince lasted only six years, from 1943 to 1949, and his father's long shadow has often hidden it. But those six years were among the most important in the long history of Bikaner. The prince who had sat at the Paris Peace Conference as a boy spent his own reign deciding that the age of kingdoms was over, and that his people would be safer and stronger inside a free India than outside it.

## Highlights of his life

- **Heir to a moderniser.** Born at Junagarh on 7 September 1902, the son of Maharaja Ganga Singh, he was educated at Mayo College and raised for public life.
- **Early on the world stage.** As a young man he attended King George V's coronation in 1911, the Paris Peace Conference in 1919 and the League of Nations in 1924.
- **Chief Minister of Bikaner (1920–1925).** He learned government at his father's side in thirty years of service before succeeding him on 2 February 1943.
- **Service in the Second World War.** As ruler he served with the Allied forces in the Middle East and Persia in 1943 and in Burma in 1944.
- **A pioneer in the Constituent Assembly.** In April 1947 Bikaner was among the first princely states to take its seats in the Assembly, breaking with the princes who stayed away.
- **Accession to India.** He signed the Instrument of Accession on 7 August 1947, among the first rulers to do so.
- **Merger into Rajasthan.** On 30 March 1949 he merged Bikaner into the United State of Greater Rajasthan. He died in London on 25 September 1950 and was succeeded by his son Karni Singh.

karni-singh-bikaner.story:
## Maharaja Karni Singh — the prince who found new battlefields in Parliament and on the shooting range

*Karni Singh's life is recorded in the proceedings of the Lok Sabha, the results of the Olympic Games and world championships, his own books and the records of the house of Bikaner. This story follows that record.*

**Karni Singh** was born on **21 April 1924** at the Lallgarh Palace in **Bikaner**, the elder son of the Maharaj Kumar **Sadul Singh** and his wife **Sudarshan Kumari**, a princess of Rewa. His grandfather, **Maharaja Ganga Singh**, was still on the throne, one of the best-known princes in India. The child was named after **Karni Mata**, the warrior goddess revered by the Rathores of Bikaner, whose blessing, tradition says, guided the founding of their kingdom.

He grew up in a world of palaces and camel corps, but he was given a modern education. After his first schooling in Bikaner he studied at **St Stephen's College** in Delhi and at **St Xavier's College** in Bombay, graduating with honours in history and politics. During the Second World War he saw active service in the Middle East with his grandfather. In February **1944** he married **Sushila Kumari**, a daughter of Maharawal Lakshman Singh of **Dungarpur**. They had a son, **Narendra Singh**, born in 1946, and two daughters, **Rajyashree Kumari** and **Madhulika Kumari**.

The India he came of age in was changing faster than any prince could have imagined. In 1947 his father, now Maharaja Sadul Singh, took Bikaner into India, and in March 1949 he merged the state into the new union of Rajasthan. When Sadul Singh died in London on **25 September 1950**, Karni Singh succeeded him as Maharaja at the age of twenty-six. He was installed in the Karan Mahal of Junagarh fort that October, but he inherited a title and a family heritage, not a kingdom. The government of Bikaner now belonged to the voters.

Karni Singh chose to go to the voters himself. In the first general election of free India, in **1952**, he stood for the **Bikaner** seat in the **Lok Sabha** as an independent candidate, and won. He held the seat for twenty-five years, through five elections, until **1977**. He never joined a party, and he served on the consultative committees of several ministries. For the people of Bikaner he was something new, a maharaja who asked for their votes instead of commanding their loyalty.

Alongside politics he followed a scholar's path. He returned to study the history of his own house, and in **1964** **Bombay University** awarded him a doctorate for a thesis on the relations of the Bikaner rulers with the central powers of India, from the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals to the British. It was later published as *The Relations of the House of Bikaner with the Central Powers, 1465–1949*. From then on he was known as **Dr Karni Singh**.

Yet it was in sport that he became famous across the country. The Rathore princes had always been hunters and marksmen, and Karni Singh turned that old skill into a modern sport: clay pigeon shooting, in the trap and skeet events. He won the national championship **seventeen** times. He represented India at five **Olympic Games**: Rome in **1960**, Tokyo in **1964**, where he captained the team, Mexico City in **1968**, Munich in **1972** and Moscow in **1980**. He was the first Indian to compete at five Olympics. His best finish was eighth place, in Rome.

His greatest international result came at the **World Shooting Championships** in **Cairo** in **1962**, where he tied for first place in trap and took the **silver medal** after the shoot-off, while captaining the Indian team. He won gold at the Asian Shooting Championships in Seoul in 1971 and silver at the **Asian Games** in Tehran in 1974. In **1961** he received the **Arjuna Award**, the first shooter ever to be given that national honour. He wrote about his sporting life in a memoir, *From Rome to Moscow*.

The love of the sport ran through his family: his daughter **Rajyashree Kumari** also became a champion shooter and an Arjuna Award winner.

The hardest blow to the old order came in his political years. In **1971** Parliament passed the **26th Amendment** to the Constitution, which ended the recognition of the former rulers and abolished the **privy purses** that had been promised to them at the time of merger. Karni Singh was among the princes who opposed the change, arguing that the promises made in 1949 should be kept. The amendment passed all the same, and from the end of 1971 he was Maharaja only by the custom of his family and the affection of his people, not in the law of India. He remained in Parliament until 1977, still the member for Bikaner.

In his later years he gave his time to his family trusts, to the palaces and collections of Bikaner, and to the sport he loved. When India prepared to host the **1982 Asian Games** in Delhi, the new shooting range built near Tughlaqabad was named the **Dr Karni Singh Shooting Range**, a rare honour for a living sportsman. It was later rebuilt for the 2010 Commonwealth Games and remains India's leading shooting venue.

Karni Singh died at Bikaner House in **New Delhi** on **4 September 1988**, at the age of sixty-four. His son **Narendra Singh** succeeded him as head of the house of Bikaner. He had been born a prince of a kingdom, and he died a citizen of a republic who had found new ways to serve: in Parliament, in scholarship, and on the shooting range.

## Highlights of his life

- **A prince of the last generation.** Born at Bikaner on 21 April 1924, he succeeded his father Sadul Singh as Maharaja on 25 September 1950.
- **Member of Parliament for 25 years.** He won the Bikaner Lok Sabha seat as an independent in 1952 and held it until 1977.
- **Historian of his house.** He earned a doctorate from Bombay University in 1964 for a study of Bikaner's relations with the central powers of India.
- **Five-time Olympian.** He competed in trap shooting at the Olympics from 1960 to 1980, the first Indian to appear at five Games.
- **World silver medallist.** He took silver at the 1962 World Shooting Championships in Cairo and was the first shooter to receive the Arjuna Award, in 1961.
- **A lasting legacy in sport.** The Dr Karni Singh Shooting Range in Delhi bears his name. He died in New Delhi on 4 September 1988.
