narendra-singh-bikaner.story:
## Maharaja Narendra Singh — keeper of an old house in a new republic

*Narendra Singh lived most of his life outside the public eye, and his story comes to us mainly through the genealogical records of the house of Bikaner and the history of his family. This story keeps to what that record shows.*

**Narendra Singh** was born on **13 January 1946** at Karni Niwas, a wing of the **Lallgarh Palace** in **Bikaner**. He was the only son of **Karni Singh**, then the Maharaj Kumar, and his wife **Sushila Kumari** of Dungarpur. His great-grandfather, **Maharaja Ganga Singh**, had died three years earlier, and his grandfather, **Maharaja Sadul Singh**, was now on the throne of a princely state that had been ruled by the Rathores since Rao Bika founded it in 1488.

The boy was born at the very end of that long story. When he was eighteen months old, his grandfather signed Bikaner's accession to the Dominion of India. When he was three, in March 1949, the state was merged into Rajasthan, and its ruler ceased to govern. In September 1950, when Narendra was four, his grandfather died in London, and his father became Maharaja. So Narendra Singh grew up as the heir to a famous title, but in a democratic India where that title no longer carried power.

His childhood was shaped by his father's busy public life. Karni Singh was elected to the Lok Sabha for Bikaner in 1952 and became one of India's best-known sportsmen, competing in trap shooting at five Olympic Games. Narendra's two younger sisters, **Rajyashree Kumari** and **Madhulika Kumari**, were born in the 1950s, and Rajyashree would follow their father to fame as a champion shooter. Narendra was educated at **Mayo College** in Ajmer, the school where generations of Rajput princes had studied, and then at **Shri Ram College** in Delhi.

On **27 April 1971** he married **Padma Kumari**, a daughter of Raja Lakshman Singh of **Chamba**, the old hill kingdom in the Himalayas. Later that same year Parliament passed the **26th Amendment** to the Constitution, which withdrew the official recognition of the former rulers and abolished their privy purses. His father opposed the change in Parliament, but it passed. From then on, the title Narendra Singh would one day inherit was a matter of family tradition and local respect, not of law.

Narendra and Padma Kumari had three daughters. The eldest, **Daksha Kumari**, was born in New Delhi in 1972. She was severely disabled, and the family cared for her throughout her life; she died in June 2000. The second daughter, **Siddhi Kumari**, was born in 1973, and the youngest, **Mahima Kumari**, in 1975.

On **4 September 1988** Karni Singh died in New Delhi, and Narendra Singh succeeded him as head of the house of Bikaner. On 29 September 1988 he took his seat on the *gadi* in the **Karan Mahal** of **Junagarh** fort, in the same hall where his father and grandfather had been installed. The ceremony no longer made him a ruler. But it kept alive a link between the people of Bikaner and a family that had stood at the centre of their history for five centuries.

The role he inherited was a quiet one. The great buildings of the dynasty still stood: the fort of Junagarh, begun by Raja Rai Singh in the late sixteenth century and filled with painted halls, armour and the treasures of generations; and the red sandstone Lallgarh Palace, built by Ganga Singh, part of which had become a hotel. Family trusts looked after the fort's museum and other heritage of the house. At festivals and at the temple of **Karni Mata** at Deshnoke, the people of Bikaner still looked to the family of their old rulers. Narendra Singh's place in this was that of a custodian, the living link in a line that went back to Rao Bika.

Unlike his father, he did not seek a career in national politics or sport, and the public record of his fifteen years as head of the house is slight. Those years held personal sorrow as well as duty: the death of his eldest daughter in 2000 was a heavy blow.

Narendra Singh died at the **Apollo Hospital** in Delhi on **24 October 2003**, at the age of fifty-seven. He was brought home to Bikaner and cremated at **Devi Kund Sagar**, the royal cremation ground east of the city, where the cenotaphs of the Bikaner rulers stand among the dunes. He left no son and had adopted no heir. His widow and his mother chose not to exercise the right of adoption, and by the custom of the family the headship of the house passed to his cousin, **Ravi Raj Singh**, a grandson of Karni Singh's younger brother, Amar Singh.

His family's public life continued through his daughter. **Siddhi Kumari** entered politics and was elected to the Rajasthan Legislative Assembly from **Bikaner East** in 2008, carrying the name of her grandfather, the five-time member of Parliament, into a new generation.

Narendra Singh's life was not one of battles or great reforms. He was born into the last months of a kingdom and lived the whole of his adult life as a private citizen of the republic that replaced it. Yet in the long line of Bikaner's rulers his place matters. He was the bridge between the generation that had governed and the generations that would only remember, the head of an old house who kept its ceremonies and its memory alive through the years when India decided what its princes would become.

## Highlights of his life

- **Born at the end of an era.** Born at Lallgarh Palace on 13 January 1946, he was a child when Bikaner joined India and merged into Rajasthan.
- **Heir to a famous father.** The only son of Karni Singh, MP and Olympic shooter, he was educated at Mayo College and Shri Ram College, Delhi.
- **Marriage into the house of Chamba.** In April 1971 he married Padma Kumari of Chamba, months before the privy purses were abolished.
- **Head of the house of Bikaner (1988–2003).** He succeeded his father on 4 September 1988 and was installed in the Karan Mahal of Junagarh.
- **Custodian of the family's heritage.** As head of the house he kept the dynasty's ceremonies and memory alive at Junagarh, Lallgarh and Deshnoke.
- **Death and succession.** He died in Delhi on 24 October 2003 and was cremated at Devi Kund Sagar. With no son, the headship passed to his cousin Ravi Raj Singh.

deoraj-bhati.story:
## Rawal Deoraj — the survivor who gave the Bhatis their title and their first great capital

*Deoraj lived long before the Bhatis kept written records, and his story comes to us through the chronicles and bardic songs of Jaisalmer, much of it gathered by James Tod in the nineteenth century. Almost all of it is tradition; this story says so where it matters.*

In the ninth century, long before the golden fort of Jaisalmer was built, the Bhati Rajputs were a clan fighting for room in the western desert. They claimed descent from the Yadavas, the race of Lord Krishna, and they had been pushed out of the lands near the Indus into the sand country of the Thar. There they competed with other warrior clans for the same wells, pastures and caravan tracks. The Bhati stronghold of this age was **Tanot**, founded, the chronicles say, by **Rawal Tanu**. Tanu's son and successor was **Vijayrai**, and Vijayrai's son was **Deoraj**.

The first great story the bards tell of Deoraj is one of betrayal. Tradition says the young prince was betrothed to the daughter of a neighbouring chief, and rode with a large party of Bhati kinsmen to the bride's home for the wedding. There, in the middle of the celebrations, the hosts and their allies, whom the chronicles name as the Varahas, turned on their guests. The wedding became a massacre. Most of the Bhati party was killed, and Deoraj escaped only with the help of a few loyal men.

The bards tell what followed with great tenderness. The fugitive prince, they say, found shelter in the house of a Brahmin. When his pursuers came looking for him, the Brahmin hid him in plain sight, presenting him as his own son. To prove it, the Brahmin sat down and ate from the same dish as the young man, something no Brahmin of that age would do with a stranger of another caste. The pursuers were convinced and rode away, and the Bhatis never forgot the debt.

Tradition adds that the enemies of the Bhatis then attacked Tanot itself, and that Vijayrai was killed. Deoraj was left a young man without a home, a father or most of his clan. What he still had was his name, a few followers, and the support of his mother's family, which the chronicles describe as being of Panwar descent.

The next story is told as a legend of blessing. While wandering in the desert, the bards say, Deoraj met a wandering **jogi**, an ascetic of the Nath tradition, and served him faithfully. In return the holy man gave him his blessing, and with it a title: **Rawal**. From that day, the chronicles say, the Bhati rulers were called Rawals, and later Maharawals. Some versions add that the jogi gave Deoraj a magic gift that turned base metal to gold, which paid for his forts. That part is pure legend. The title itself is real, and it is one of the clearest marks the Bhatis carried from this age.

Deoraj's first new stronghold was **Derawar**, also remembered as Deogarh, the fort of Deo. The bards tell a famous story about how he won the land for it. He asked a local chief, they say, for only as much ground as could be covered by the hide of a bull. Deoraj then cut the hide into thin strips, laid them end to end, and enclosed enough land for a fortress. The same trick is told of founders in many lands and should be read as a folk tale, not a record. But Derawar itself was real: its fort, rebuilt many times, still stands in the Cholistan desert, now in Pakistan. Tod's reading of the chronicles places its founding in **853 CE**, though other reckonings differ.

From Derawar, Deoraj looked east to a richer prize. **Lodurva**, on the edge of a dry river course north-west of where Jaisalmer now stands, belonged to the **Lodra Rajputs**. The chronicles tell that Deoraj won Lodurva partly through a marriage alliance with the Lodra ruling house and partly by force, and that once inside he made it his own. However it happened, Lodurva became the seat of the Bhati Rawals, and it remained their capital for nearly three hundred years.

As ruler of Lodurva and Derawar, Deoraj held a harsh land. Water had to be guarded, rival clans defeated or bound by marriage, and the caravans between Sindh, Gujarat and the north protected and taxed. To the west, Sindh had been under Arab rule since 712, and the frontier between the Muslim governors of Sindh and Multan and the Rajput clans of the desert was never fully quiet. The Bhatis learned in these years the role they would later claim with pride: to be the guardians of the desert's northern and western edge.

Of the end of Deoraj's life, the chronicles say little that can be trusted, and traditions differ on how he died. They name his son, **Mund**, as his successor at Lodurva. The line continued through many generations of Rawals at Lodurva until, in the twelfth century, **Rawal Jaisal** moved the capital to the hill of Trikuta and founded Jaisalmer in 1156.

Deoraj's dates and deeds cannot be checked against inscriptions, and much of his story is told the way all founding stories are told, with escapes, blessings and clever tricks. But the bards remember him for real things: the survival of the Bhati house after near destruction, the title of Rawal that its rulers carried for a thousand years, the fort of Derawar, and the capture of Lodurva, which gave the Bhatis their first great capital in the Thar.

## Highlights of his life

- **Survivor of a massacre.** Tradition says he escaped when the Bhati wedding party was slaughtered by rival clans, and that his father Vijayrai was killed when Tanot was attacked.
- **Saved by a Brahmin.** The bards tell that a Brahmin hid him by eating from the same dish and claiming him as his son.
- **The title of Rawal.** The chronicles say a Nath jogi gave him the title of Rawal, which the Bhati rulers carried for centuries afterwards.
- **Founder of Derawar.** He built the fort of Derawar (Deogarh), which Tod's reading of the chronicles dates to 853 CE.
- **Conqueror of Lodurva.** He took Lodurva from the Lodra Rajputs; it remained the Bhati capital until Jaisal founded Jaisalmer in 1156.
- **Ancestor of the Jaisalmer line.** Succeeded, the chronicles say, by his son Mund, he stands at the head of the line of Lodurva Rawals.

rawal-lakhman-bhati.story:
## Rawal Lakhman — A Name in the Bhati Genealogies

*Rawal Lakhman of the pre-Jaisalmer era is known only from the genealogies preserved by Bhati bards, the seventeenth-century Khyat of Muhnot Nainsi, later court histories of Jaisalmer and James Tod's Annals; no inscription or contemporary chronicle records his deeds, and even his place in the line differs between lists.*

The story of **Rawal Lakhman** is less the story of a single man than of a lineage remembering itself. In the account that the Bhati court passed down, he belongs to the long age before **1156**, when the clan had not yet raised its famous fort on the Trikuta hill at **Jaisalmer** and its power was centred instead on **Lodurva**, an older town about fifteen kilometres to the north-west. His biography quickly reaches the edge of the evidence; what can be done honestly is to place the name within the world that produced it.

### The Bhatis and their remembered origins

The **Bhatis** claim descent from the Yadavas, the lunar lineage of **Krishna**, and their bards traced the line through a series of migrations from the north-west — through Ghazni and the Punjab, as tradition has it — into the Thar. The eponymous ancestor, **Bhati**, gave the clan its name. Historians treat the earliest links of this chain as legend shaped by the needs of later courts, which wished to connect a desert kingdom with the epic heroes of the Mahabharata. But from about the eighth and ninth centuries the outline becomes firmer. A series of strongholds is associated with the clan: **Tanot**, still known for its temple to the clan goddess **Tanot Mata**; **Derawar**, now in Pakistan's Cholistan desert; and Lodurva, taken, the bards say, from a Rajput clan called the Lodra (sometimes linked with the Paramaras).

The figure usually credited with making the Bhatis a regional power is **Rawal Devaraja (Deoraj)**, who, according to tradition, took the title *Rawal* and fixed the capital at Lodurva. His successors held the town through the eleventh and early twelfth centuries, and the dynasty's chronicle lists several rulers in this period — names such as Mund, Bachhraj, Dusaj and Vijayaraja Lanjha appear in most versions. Lists of this kind were recited at coronations and weddings by the clan's genealogists, and they were copied, corrected and sometimes reorganised over centuries. The name Lakhman (a vernacular form of Lakshmana) appears in some of these lineage records for the Lodurva generations, but historians cannot fix his reign, his relationship to the better-known rulers, or anything he did. It should also be noted that modern king-lists place two later rulers of similar name at Jaisalmer itself — **Lakhan Sen** in the 1270s and **Lachman (Lakshman) Singh** in the early fifteenth century — and later compilations occasionally blur men who shared a name.

### Lodurva and the desert economy

Whatever the exact dates, a ruler of Lodurva in this period governed a particular kind of state. The Thar could not support large armies or dense agriculture; power rested on control of wells, grazing grounds and, above all, the **caravan routes** that linked Sindh and Multan with Gujarat and the Gangetic plain. Camels carried cloth, salt, dried fruit, opium, horses and spices along tracks that depended on known waterholes. A Bhati rawal earned revenue by protecting — and taxing — this traffic, and by drawing tribute from the herding and farming settlements around him. His following consisted of kinsmen who held their own villages; the ruler was in many ways a first among equals in a clan brotherhood.

Lodurva was also a religious centre. Its **Jain temple** dedicated to **Parshvanatha** is the best-known surviving monument of the site, although the present building is largely a seventeenth-century reconstruction on an older foundation. The presence of Jain merchant communities, who financed trade and later built the great temples inside the Jaisalmer fort, shows how closely the Bhati state was tied to commerce from an early date.
### A frontier under pressure

The Lodurva centuries were not peaceful. From the eleventh century onward the north-western frontier of India felt the impact of the **Ghaznavid** raids, and the Bhatis also competed with neighbouring powers — the Paramaras, Chauhans and others — as well as with Baloch and Sindhi groups to the west. Bardic tradition remembers repeated raids, but no specific campaign can be assigned to Rawal Lakhman.

That vulnerability shaped the decision for which this whole era is remembered. Tradition holds that **Rawal Jaisal**, a member of the ruling family who disputed the succession at Lodurva, abandoned the old town and in **1156** founded a new fortress on the **Trikuta hill**, a ridge of yellow sandstone that offered height, defensible walls and a view across the desert. The city that grew below it took his name. Lodurva declined thereafter, though it was never wholly deserted. The rulers before Jaisal, Lakhman among them, thus became in Bhati memory the ancestors of the "old capital" — the generations whose holdings made the move possible.

### How such rulers were remembered

Rajput genealogies were written to confirm the legitimacy of the ruling line and the land rights of collateral branches, not to answer modern historians' questions. When nineteenth-century writers such as **James Tod** and the compilers of the **Tawarikh-i-Jaisalmer** turned these recitations into narrative history, they inherited both their value and their gaps. Older drafts of Lakhman's story described a detailed education, military reforms and regiments with artillery; none of this has any source, and guns reached the Thar centuries later.

### Death and succession

Neither the manner of Lakhman's death nor the exact name of his successor can be stated with confidence, because the versions of the genealogy disagree. What is certain is the direction of the dynasty: within a few generations of the rulers remembered at Lodurva, the Bhatis had moved their seat to Jaisalmer, where the line continued without permanent break until the integration of the princely state into India in 1949.

### Key points
- **Lodurva era.** He is placed among the Bhati rulers of Lodurva before Jaisal founded Jaisalmer in 1156.
- **Thin evidence.** His name survives only in genealogies and later court histories; no inscription or contemporary record describes his reign.
- **Name confusion.** Later Jaisalmer rulers named Lakhan Sen (1270s) and Lachman Singh (fifteenth century) may be blurred with him in some lists.
- **Desert state.** Bhati power rested on caravan routes, wells and kin-based chiefs rather than large armies.
- **Legacy.** His importance lies in the continuity of the lineage that later built the Jaisalmer fort.

## Rawal Vijayraj — the door-bar of the north

*Rawal Vijayraj's life comes to us almost entirely through the chronicles and bardic genealogies of Jaisalmer, written down long after his time; where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

Some fifteen kilometres north-west of the golden fort of Jaisalmer, the ruins of **Lodurva** lie along the dry bed of the **Kak**, a stream that runs only when the rains are kind. Today a rebuilt Jain temple and a scatter of old stones are most of what remains. In the early twelfth century, before Jaisalmer existed, Lodurva was the capital of the **Bhati** Rajputs, a walled town of merchants, temples and wells on the caravan routes of the Thar. It was here that Rawal Vijayraj ruled.

The Jaisalmer genealogies know two rulers of this name, and it is worth keeping them apart. The earlier, **Vijay Rai**, remembered as *Chudala*, was the father of **Deoraj** and ruled from Tanot in the ninth century. The later, the subject of this story, is remembered by the nickname **Lanjha**, and he ruled at Lodurva in the generations just before the founding of Jaisalmer. The lists of rulers around him are not always consistent; in the main chronicles he is the son of **Rawal Dusaj**, and the line that leads up to him runs from Deoraj through **Mund** and **Bachhu**.

The house into which he was born had a long memory. The Bhatis traced their descent from **Yadu**, and through him claimed kinship with **Krishna** himself. Their bards told how the Yadavas, scattered after the fall of Dwarka, wandered north and west, held lands in the Punjab, lost them, and came down at last into the desert. It was **Deoraj**, the chronicles say, who took the title of **Rawal** from a Nath yogi who blessed him, and who won Lodurva from an older Rajput clan that held it. By the time Vijayraj was born, Lodurva had been the seat of his family for several generations.

Nothing is recorded of the year of his birth or the name of his mother. We can only picture the world of his boyhood. Lodurva woke before dawn to the creak of the wells and the groaning of camels being loaded. Merchants from Sindh and Gujarat bargained in the bazaar, and Jain monks walked barefoot between the temples their patrons had built. A Bhati boy of the ruling house learned to ride a horse and a camel before he could read, to find water by the colour of the sand and the flight of birds, and to listen to the *charans* and bards who sang the deeds of his ancestors at night beside the fire.

He also learned that the desert was never empty. Herding clans moved across it with their flocks, and other Rajput houses held the lands to the east and south. A ruler of Lodurva lived by the caravans, and the caravans lived by safety. Whoever could keep the roads open, the wells guarded and the raiders away would be rich. Whoever could not would soon be ruling nothing but sand.

When **Rawal Dusaj** died, the seat of Lodurva passed to Vijayraj. The chronicles make **Jaisal**, the future founder of Jaisalmer, a son of Dusaj and so a brother of Vijayraj, and they agree that it was Vijayraj who took the throne. Why Jaisal was passed over, if he was, the bards explain in different ways. What is clear is that the question did not die with their father, and that it would return to trouble the house a generation later.

The world beyond the dunes was changing fast in these years. More than eighty years had passed since the death of **Mahmud of Ghazni** in 1030, but the Ghaznavid sultans still held **Lahore** and the Punjab, and raids from the north-west remained a constant fear for the kingdoms of the plains. In Sindh, to the west, the **Sumra** dynasty had taken power. To the east, the **Chauhans** were rising: **Ajayaraja** founded **Ajmer** early in the twelfth century, and his son **Arnoraja** fought off a Turkish force near that city. To the south, in Gujarat, the Chalukya (Solanki) king **Siddharaja Jayasimha**, who reigned from the 1090s until 1143, was the greatest power in western India, the conqueror of Malwa and the patron of poets and scholars at **Anahilavada Patan**.

It was towards Gujarat that Vijayraj turned for the alliance that made his name. The chronicles of Jaisalmer tell that he married a Solanki princess, and most of them name her father as Siddharaja himself. The marriage cannot be confirmed from Gujarat's own records, but the tradition is old and firmly held, and it fits the politics of the time: the rulers of Patan had every reason to want a strong friend on the desert road from the north.

The bards set the most famous scene of his life at that wedding. The celebrations at Patan, they say, went on for days. When the time came to send the bride away, the queen of the Solanki house, following the custom of the bride's family, marked the forehead of her son-in-law and spoke to him. Tradition remembers her charge in a few words that the Bhatis have repeated ever since: he was to be the **Uttar Bhad Kivad**, the door-bar of the north.

We may imagine the moment. "The Turks come from the north," she might have said, "and between them and us there is only sand and the Bhatis. Be the bar across that door, my son, and let nothing pass." And we may imagine the young Rawal, the red mark still wet on his forehead, answering that as long as a Bhati stood in the desert, the door would hold.

Whatever words were truly spoken, the title stayed. For centuries afterwards the rulers of Jaisalmer were praised in verse as *Uttar Bhad Kivad Bhati*, the Bhatis who were the barrier of the north. It described a real place in the map of India. The Thar and its western fringe lay between the Turkish powers of the Punjab and Sindh on one side and the kingdoms of Rajasthan and Gujarat on the other, and the Bhati country sat across the routes that joined them.

Living up to that title was hard work and little glory. The chronicles do not preserve the names of particular battles in Vijayraj's reign, and it would be false to invent them. But the shape of the work is clear enough from the conditions of the age. A desert ruler's war was a war of movement: riders sent out at night to answer a raid on a caravan, watchmen on the high dunes, wells defended or denied, and the long pursuit of raiders who knew the land as well as his own men did. It was a war in which a cut well could do more harm than a lost skirmish, and in which the loyalty of the herding clans mattered as much as the strength of a wall.

At home, his wealth depended on trade. Lodurva stood where caravans from Sindh and Multan met the roads running south to Gujarat and east into Marwar. Salt, wool, horses, cloth, spices and indigo moved through its gates, and the duties paid on them kept the Rawal's riders in the saddle. The merchants who made this possible were often **Jains**, and Lodurva was an important centre of their faith. Its temple of **Parshvanath** was one of the great shrines of the desert. The present building is a seventeenth-century reconstruction, but the tradition of worship on the site goes back to these older days, and the rulers of Lodurva are remembered as its protectors.

The Bhatis themselves worshipped the mother goddess of the desert in her many forms, together with Krishna, the divine ancestor their bards never let them forget. Like most Rajput rulers of the time, Vijayraj seems to have honoured every faith that kept his kingdom peaceful and prosperous: the Jain merchants, the Brahmin priests, the Nath yogis whom his ancestor Deoraj had revered, and the bards who would one day turn his life into song.

The Solanki queen bore him a son, **Bhojdeo**. A son of a Patan princess was a prince with powerful friends, and the chronicles make him Vijayraj's heir. For a ruler whose own succession had once left a brother waiting in the shadows, this was a source of both pride and danger. Jaisal was still alive, still ambitious, and still certain, if the bards are to be believed, that Lodurva should have been his.

Of Vijayraj's last years and death we know almost nothing. The chronicles do not say how he died or exactly when, only that he was followed on the throne at Lodurva by Bhojdeo. Within a short time the quarrel he had held off broke open. According to the Jaisalmer tradition, Jaisal sought help from a Turkish power in the north, and in the fighting that followed Bhojdeo was killed. The chroniclers name the Ghori sultan as Jaisal's ally, though the dates of the story do not fit together neatly, and historians treat this part of it with caution.

Jaisal, now master of the Bhatis but wary of an old town in open country, looked for a stronger seat. He found it on the **Trikuta** hill, a ridge of yellow sandstone a few kilometres away, and there, by the traditional date of **1156 CE**, he began the fort of **Jaisalmer**. Lodurva declined. Its people moved to the new city, its walls crumbled, and in time it became the quiet ruin it is today, remembered in folk song as the home of the beautiful **Moomal** of the old desert romance.

Vijayraj Lanjha, then, stands at a hinge in the history of his people. He was the last great ruler of the Lodurva age, a king whose name is tied less to a conquest or a monument than to a promise. When later rulers of Jaisalmer held their fort against sultans and armies, and when bards sang of them as the door-bar of the north, they were repeating the words first spoken, tradition says, to a young Rawal at a wedding in Patan.

## Highlights of his life

- **Ruler of Lodurva.** He ruled the Bhati capital of Lodurva on the caravan routes of the Thar in the generations before Jaisalmer was founded.
- **Son of Rawal Dusaj.** In the main Jaisalmer genealogies he is the son of Dusaj and a brother of Jaisal, distinct from the earlier Vijay Rai Chudala, father of Deoraj.
- **Marriage alliance with the Solankis.** Tradition says he married a princess of the Chalukya (Solanki) house of Patan, most often named as a daughter of Siddharaja Jayasimha.
- **"Uttar Bhad Kivad".** At that wedding, the bards say, he was charged to be the door-bar of the north, a title the Bhatis of Jaisalmer carried with pride for centuries.
- **Guardian of the trade roads.** His power rested on keeping the caravan routes between Sindh, Gujarat and Marwar open and safe.
- **Protector of Lodurva's faiths.** The rulers of his age are remembered as patrons of Lodurva's Jain temple of Parshvanath as well as the Bhatis' own gods.
- **Father of Bhojdeo.** His son by the Solanki queen succeeded him, and the conflict that followed led to the founding of Jaisalmer in 1156.

## Rawal Durga Das — a name from the desert years before Jaisalmer

*Rawal Durga Das is known only as a name in later lists of the early Bhati rulers; this short account gives what can honestly be said about his place and time.*

Rawal Durga Das belongs to the long, dimly lit age of the **Bhati** Rajputs before **Rawal Jaisal** founded **Jaisalmer** in **1156 CE**. In this archive's list he follows **Rawal Vijayraj** and comes before **Rawal Bhati**, the ancestor from whom the clan takes its name. That order cannot be right as a line of succession, since the eponymous ancestor must stand near the beginning of the clan's story, and it shows how confused the lists of these early rulers have become.

No ruler named Durga Das appears in the main genealogies of Jaisalmer that have come down to us. Those chronicles trace the Bhatis from the eponym through **Mangal Rao**, **Majam Rao**, **Kehar** and **Tanu**, to **Vijay Rai Chudala** and **Deoraj**, and then through the rulers of **Lodurva** down to Jaisal. Durga Das may be a local or branch chief remembered in one tradition, a different form of another ruler's name, or an error in compilation. Nothing reliable is known of his birth, his deeds or his death, and it would be wrong to invent them.

What can be said is what his world was like. The Bhatis of these centuries moved their seats again and again: from the Punjab plains to **Kehror**, then to **Tanot**, then to **Derawar** and finally to **Lodurva**. They lived by herding, by the caravan trade between Sindh, Multan, Gujarat and Marwar, and by their swords, often in conflict with neighbouring clans and with the Turkish powers that held Sindh and the Punjab. Any chief of the Bhati house in this period would have spent his life guarding wells, roads and herds in the Thar.

## Highlights of his life

- **An early Bhati name.** He is listed among the Bhati rulers before the founding of Jaisalmer in 1156.
- **Not in the main chronicles.** His name does not appear in the standard Jaisalmer genealogies, and nothing certain is known of his reign.
- **A ruler of the desert age.** His time was the age when the Bhatis moved between Kehror, Tanot, Derawar and Lodurva.
- **Part of a confused list.** His position before the clan's eponym shows that the early lists need careful use.

## Rawal Bhati — the warrior who gave a clan its name

*Everything we know of Bhati comes from the genealogies of the Jaisalmer bards, set down many centuries after him; this story follows their tradition and says plainly where history cannot follow.*

Every Rajput clan carries the name of someone. The Rathores, the Chauhans and the Sisodias all look back to a founder or a place, and the **Bhatis** of Jaisalmer look back to a warrior called **Bhati**, sometimes written **Bhatti**. From him, the bards say, came the name that his descendants carried from the plains of the Punjab into the heart of the Thar, and which still belongs to Rajput families in Rajasthan and to Bhatti families across the Punjab today.

He did not carry the title Rawal in his lifetime. In the Jaisalmer tradition that title came much later, when **Deoraj** received it from a Nath yogi in the ninth century. The bards remembered Bhati simply as a king and a conqueror, and the honour of "Rawal" was given to him only by the descendants who looked back on him.

The story of Bhati begins, in the bards' telling, long before his birth. The Bhatis claimed descent from **Yadu**, and so from the same Yadava line as **Krishna**. When Dwarka was swallowed by the sea and the Yadavas destroyed one another, tradition says, some of the survivors wandered north-west beyond the Indus. One of their kings, **Gaj**, is said to have founded a city called **Gajni**, which the bards identify with Ghazni in Afghanistan, and to have died defending it. His son **Salivahan** came east into the Punjab and founded a new capital, and Punjabi folklore makes the hero **Raja Rasalu**, of Sialkot, one of Salivahan's sons. Salivahan's heir, in the Jaisalmer lists, was **Baland**, and Bhati was the son of Baland.

None of this can be checked against coins or inscriptions. It is the memory of a people, shaped over centuries, and it mixes real places with heroic invention. What it tells us clearly is how the Bhatis saw themselves: as Yadavas of the Punjab, a royal house that had once ruled great cities in the north-west and had been pushed, step by step, towards the desert.

Of Bhati's childhood the bards say nothing that can be trusted, and we can only imagine it: a prince of a frontier kingdom, raised among horses and riders on the wide plains between the rivers, hearing from his elders how the family's lost cities lay to the west, in the hands of others. A boy brought up on such stories would grow up knowing that a throne was something to be won and kept by force.

As a king, Bhati is remembered above all as a conqueror. James Tod, who collected the Jaisalmer traditions in the early nineteenth century, recorded that Bhati was a famous warrior who subdued many neighbouring princes, and that his fame was so great that his descendants took his name in place of the older name of Yadu. This is the heart of his legend. A clan does not lightly rename itself, and the fact that the Bhatis chose to be called after him rather than after an older and holier ancestor shows how strongly his memory was held.

When he lived is uncertain. The chronicles do not agree, and some place him many centuries earlier than is likely. A clue may lie in the **Bhatika era**, a calendar used in later inscriptions of the Jaisalmer region that began in about **623–624 CE**. Some historians have linked its starting point to an important moment in the history of the Bhati house, perhaps to Bhati himself, but this is only an argument, not a proven fact. The safest statement is that he belongs to the early centuries of the clan, long before the move into the Thar.

The world of the Punjab in the seventh century was unsettled. The great empire of **Harsha** in the Ganga plain broke up after his death in 647. The north-west was a frontier of small kingdoms, and after the Arab conquest of **Sindh** in 712 and the fall of **Multan**, the lands west of the Sutlej came under new pressure. Whatever the true dates of Bhati's reign, it was in this changing frontier that his family fought for its place.

The bards say little about Bhati's religion beyond the faith of the Yadavas in Krishna and the worship of the mother goddess that the clan carried with it. Nor do they record how he died. They tell only that he was followed by his son **Mangal Rao**, and that in Mangal Rao's time the family lost its seat in the north and fled south and east, across the rivers, to the edge of the great desert. There, under **Majam Rao**, **Kehar** and **Tanu**, the Bhatis built new strongholds at **Kehror** and **Tanot**, and began the long journey that ended with Deoraj at Derawar and Lodurva and, at last, with **Jaisal** and the golden fort of **Jaisalmer** in **1156**.

The places that remember the name are scattered across that journey. **Bhatner**, the old fort at Hanumangarh, is traditionally linked to the Bhatis, and the name of **Bhatinda** has long been connected with them by tradition as well. Across the Punjab, Hindu, Sikh and Muslim families named Bhatti still trace themselves to the same ancestor. Few men of whom so little is certainly known have left their name on so many people.

In the end, Bhati is less a figure of history than a figure of identity. The bards placed him at the turning point of their story, the moment when the scattered Yadavas of the north became a clan with a name of its own. Every Bhati ruler who later held Lodurva or Jaisalmer, and every bard who sang the praises of the "door-bar of the north", was in a sense repeating his name.

## Highlights of his life

- **Ancestor of the clan.** By tradition, the Bhati (Bhatti) Rajputs take their name from him.
- **Yadava descent.** The bards make him a son of Baland and a descendant of Yadu, in the same line as Krishna.
- **Remembered as a conqueror.** Tradition says he subdued many neighbouring princes, and his fame led his descendants to adopt his name.
- **Uncertain date.** His period is unknown; some link the Bhatika era of about 623–624 CE to his house, but this is not proven.
- **Father of Mangal Rao.** In his son's time, tradition says, the Bhatis lost their northern seat and moved towards the desert.
- **A name across many peoples.** Rajput Bhatis in Rajasthan and Bhatti families across the Punjab still claim him as their ancestor.

rawal-kehar-bhati.story:
## Rawal Kehar — the builder of Kehror on the edge of the desert

*Rawal Kehar is known to us only through the genealogies of the Jaisalmer bards and the traditions James Tod gathered from them; where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

When the bards of Jaisalmer told the long story of their masters, there was a moment they always lingered on: the time when the **Bhatis**, driven from their old lands in the Punjab, stopped running and began to build. The man they placed at that moment was **Kehar**, and the stronghold they gave him was **Kehror**, on the plains near the old course of the Sutlej and Beas, at the very edge of the great sand country.

He did not bear the title Rawal in his own day. In the Jaisalmer tradition, that honour came to the family later, when his descendant **Deoraj** received it from a Nath yogi. To his own people Kehar was a *rao*, a chief, the head of a proud but much-reduced Yadava house.

The family into which he was born had fallen far. The bards traced it back to **Yadu** and to **Krishna**, and to kings who had ruled cities in the north-west and the Punjab. They remembered **Bhati**, the conqueror whose name the clan had taken, and his son **Mangal Rao**, in whose time, tradition says, the family lost its seat in the north and fled south across the rivers. Mangal Rao's son, **Majam Rao**, kept the remnant of the clan together, and Kehar was Majam Rao's son.

Nothing is recorded of Kehar's birth or mother, but the world of his childhood is not hard to imagine. He grew up among exiles, in a clan that remembered palaces and now lived in camps and small forts, moving with its herds of cattle and camels between the river lands and the dunes. The elders told the young prince of what had been lost, and the boy learned early that a family with no walls of its own lived at the mercy of its neighbours.

The tradition places him in roughly the eighth century, and the times were hard on the frontier. In **712 CE** the Arab general **Muhammad bin Qasim** conquered **Sindh**, and soon afterwards **Multan** fell to the Arabs as well. For the next centuries Multan, not far from the lands where Kehar would build, was ruled by Arab governors and then by Arab emirs. To the north lay rival Rajput and Jat clans, and across the whole region raiding was a way of life. A small clan in such a place had to be strong or it would be swallowed.

Kehar's answer, the bards say, was to build. He raised the fort and town of **Kehror**, which carried his name. The site is traditionally identified with **Kahror Pakka** in the present-day Lodhran district of Pakistan's Punjab, close to the edge of the Cholistan desert. Historians cannot date the founding precisely, and the link between the town and Kehar rests on tradition, but it fits the pattern of the Bhati story: a clan moving step by step from the river plains towards the desert, and building a new stronghold at each stage.

We can picture the building of such a place: mud-brick walls rising on a low mound above the floodplain, a gate facing the caravan road, wells sunk deep, and storehouses for grain against the years of drought. Around it the herders brought in their animals at night, and traders from Multan and the river towns found a market where a Bhati chief took his duty and promised them safety.

War was never far away. The bards remember the Bhatis of these centuries fighting neighbouring clans, among them the **Varahas** (Barahas), whose feud with the Bhati house runs through the early chronicles and would later cost Kehar's grandson his life. The chronicles do not preserve the names of particular battles for Kehar himself, and it would be wrong to invent them. But the work of his life is clear from the conditions of the land: defending herds and wells, punishing raids, and holding his new fort against those who wanted the trade it controlled.

Kehar also had to keep his own people together. A clan that had lost its kingdom could easily break up into rival branches, each following its own chief. Kehar, the bards say, held the Bhatis as one house, and the fact that the line continues in an unbroken chain from him through his son to the later rulers of Jaisalmer suggests that he succeeded.

His religion was the faith of his ancestors: devotion to Krishna, the divine head of the Yadava line, and worship of the mother goddess of the desert, whose shrines his descendants would build at Tanot and elsewhere. The bards, who were also the keepers of the family's honour, were part of every Rajput court, and it was through them that Kehar's name survived when everything he built had crumbled.

The chronicles record his heir as **Tanu**, also called **Tanno**, who led the Bhatis further into the desert and founded **Tanot**, a fort and shrine that still stands today. Under Tanu's son **Vijay Rai Chudala** and grandson **Deoraj**, the clan moved on to **Derawar** and **Lodurva**, and in **1156 CE** **Jaisal** founded **Jaisalmer**. Each of those steps grew from the first one, the decision to stop and build at Kehror. How and when Kehar died the bards do not say.

Kehror itself had a long history after him. It appears in later centuries as a town of the Multan region, and the name survives in Kahror Pakka today. For the Bhatis of Jaisalmer, the fort on the river plain became a distant memory, but the bards kept Kehar's name in their recitations as the chief who turned a fleeing clan into a settled house once again.

## Highlights of his life

- **Son of Majam Rao.** In the Jaisalmer genealogies he follows Majam Rao, grandson of Mangal Rao and great-grandson of Bhati.
- **Founder of Kehror.** Tradition credits him with the fort and town of Kehror, identified with Kahror Pakka in Pakistan's Punjab.
- **A turning point for the clan.** He is remembered as the chief under whom the exiled Bhatis began to build strongholds again.
- **Ruler in a hard age.** His era, by tradition the eighth century, followed the Arab conquest of Sindh and Multan.
- **Keeper of the Bhati house.** He held the clan together and passed it on unbroken to his son.
- **Father of Tanu.** His son founded Tanot and led the Bhatis deeper into the Thar.

rawal-tansukh-bhati.story:
## Rawal Tansukh — the founder of Tanot in the deep desert

*The ruler named here as Tansukh is known only through the genealogies of the Jaisalmer bards, where he appears as Tanu or Tanno; where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

Far out in the Thar, about a hundred and twenty kilometres north-west of Jaisalmer and close to the border with Pakistan, a white temple stands among the dunes. Soldiers of India's Border Security Force keep it, pilgrims travel for hours across the sand to reach it, and the goddess worshipped there is called **Tanot Mata**. The village and the shrine take their name from a Bhati chief whom the bards remember as their founder.

In the Jaisalmer genealogies, the ruler who comes after **Kehar** and before **Vijay Rai Chudala** is called **Tanu**, or **Tanno**. The name Tansukh used in this archive's list appears to be another form of the same name, and this story follows what the chronicles say of Tanu. He did not carry the title Rawal in his lifetime; in the Jaisalmer tradition that title came to the family two generations later with his grandson **Deoraj**.

Tanu was the son of Kehar, the chief who, tradition says, had built the fort of **Kehror** on the plains at the desert's edge, after the **Bhatis** lost their old lands in the Punjab. The family claimed descent from **Yadu** and from **Krishna**, and remembered kings who had ruled cities in the north-west. By Tanu's time those cities were only stories, and the Bhatis were a clan of the borderlands, living by herding, by the caravan trade and by the sword.

Nothing is recorded of Tanu's birth or his mother. We can imagine a boy raised at Kehror among horses, camels and cattle, listening at night to the bards who sang of Dwarka and of Bhati, the warrior who gave the clan its name. He would have learned to ride and fight before he learned anything else, and he would have learned that in the borderlands a chief's first duty was to keep his people alive.

The times demanded it. After the Arab conquest of **Sindh** in 712 and of **Multan** soon afterwards, the lands around the lower Indus and its rivers were ruled by Arab governors and later by Arab emirs at Multan. Rival Rajput clans held the country around the Bhatis, and the bards remember a long and bitter feud with the **Varahas** (Barahas). For a small clan, the open plain near the rivers was dangerous ground.

Tanu's answer, the bards say, was to go deeper into the desert, where few enemies would follow. There, in the sea of dunes, he founded **Tanot**, a fort and settlement that took his name. The tradition places its founding in the eighth century; the exact date given in the chronicles cannot be confirmed, and should be taken as tradition rather than record.

It was a hard place to build. There were no rivers and few wells, the summer heat was savage, and the winds shifted the dunes from season to season. But a fort in such a place had one great advantage: an enemy who came to besiege it had to carry his water with him. For a clan that had been driven from one home after another, the desert itself could be a wall.

Tanu also made Tanot a holy place. The Bhatis worshipped the mother goddess of the desert, and the shrine at Tanot became the seat of the goddess whom the people still call Tanot Mata. Local belief connects her with **Hinglaj Mata**, the goddess of the great shrine in Baluchistan, and with **Avad Mata**, whom the Charan communities of the desert revere. Tradition gives Tanu the honour of first raising her temple. The building that stands today is much later, but the worship on the site is remembered as going back to him.

The goddess of Tanot has a modern story too. During the India–Pakistan war of **1965**, the area around the temple was shelled, and it is widely believed that many shells that fell near the shrine failed to explode. Some of them are displayed at the temple today. This is a matter of faith rather than of history, but it has made Tanot Mata one of the best-known shrines of the Indian frontier, and the temple has been kept by the Border Security Force ever since.

Of Tanu's wars and achievements beyond the founding of Tanot, the chronicles say little, and it would be wrong to invent battles or treaties for him. What is clear is that under him the Bhatis became a clan of the deep Thar. The caravans that crossed the desert between Sindh, Multan and the lands to the east needed water, guides and protection, and a chief at Tanot could offer all three, for a price.

The bards do not record how or when he died. His son, **Vijay Rai Chudala**, followed him at Tanot, and in Vijay Rai's time, tradition says, the feud with the Varahas came to a terrible end when the Varahas fell upon the Bhatis and killed him. His son **Deoraj** escaped, founded **Derawar** in the desert of Cholistan, took the title of Rawal and won **Lodurva**. From Lodurva, centuries later, **Jaisal** moved to the hill of Trikuta and founded **Jaisalmer** in **1156 CE**.

Of all the early Bhati chiefs, Tanu has left the most living memory. The fort of Kehror is a distant name, and Derawar stands in another country, but every day pilgrims and soldiers bow before the goddess at Tanot, in the desert village that still carries his name.

## Highlights of his life

- **Tanu of the chronicles.** The ruler listed here as Tansukh appears in the Jaisalmer genealogies as Tanu or Tanno, son of Kehar.
- **Founder of Tanot.** Tradition credits him with founding the fort and village of Tanot deep in the Thar, in about the eighth century.
- **The temple of Tanot Mata.** He is remembered as the first builder of the shrine of the goddess, still one of the best-known temples of the desert frontier.
- **Into the deep desert.** Under him the Bhatis moved from the river plains into the dunes, using the desert itself as a defence.
- **Father of Vijay Rai Chudala.** His son ruled after him at Tanot, and his grandson Deoraj founded Derawar and won Lodurva.
- **A living memory.** The shrine at Tanot, kept today by the Border Security Force, has made his name the best remembered of the early Bhati chiefs.

rawal-jand-bhati.story:
## Rawal Jand — a Bhati name from the age of Tanot

*Rawal Jand is known only as a name in later lists of the early Bhati rulers; this short account gives what can honestly be said about his place and time.*

Rawal Jand belongs to the early history of the **Bhati** Rajputs, long before **Rawal Jaisal** founded **Jaisalmer** in **1156 CE**. In this archive's list he follows **Rawal Tansukh**, the ruler the chronicles call **Tanu**, founder of **Tanot**, and comes before **Rawal Manikrai**.

No ruler named Jand appears in the main genealogies of Jaisalmer that have come down to us. In those chronicles Tanu is followed by his son **Vijay Rai Chudala**, and Vijay Rai by **Deoraj**, who founded **Derawar**, took the title of Rawal from a Nath yogi and won **Lodurva**. Jand may be a chief of a branch line, another form of a known ruler's name, or an error in the compilation of the list. Nothing reliable is known of his birth, his deeds or his death, and it would be wrong to invent them. The title Rawal, too, belongs to the family only from Deoraj's time onward.

What can be described is the world he would have lived in. In the eighth and ninth centuries the Bhatis held Tanot and the surrounding dunes of the Thar. Their neighbours to the west and north were the Arab emirs of **Multan** and the rulers of **Sindh**, and closer to home they carried on a long feud with the **Varahas**, which, tradition says, cost Vijay Rai Chudala his life. A Bhati chief of this age lived by herding, by guarding the wells and caravan routes across the desert, and by keeping the trust of the herding and Charan communities who shared the land with his clan. Any Bhati chief of these years would have spent his life in that work.

## Highlights of his life

- **An early Bhati name.** He is listed among the Bhati rulers of the Tanot age, before Jaisalmer was founded in 1156.
- **Not in the main chronicles.** His name does not appear in the standard Jaisalmer genealogies, and nothing certain is known of his reign.
- **A ruler of the desert frontier.** His time was the age when the Bhatis held Tanot amid pressures from Multan, Sindh and rival clans.
- **Before the title of Rawal.** By tradition the Bhatis took the title Rawal only with Deoraj, so the title here is a later honour.

rawal-manikrai-bhati.story:
## Rawal Manikrai — a name in the long Bhati line

*Rawal Manikrai is known only from the genealogical lists of the Bhati house. No inscription or contemporary chronicle describes his reign, so this short account keeps to what can honestly be said.*

The Bhatis are one of the oldest clans of the Thar. They claim descent from the lunar race through the Yadavas of Krishna, and their bards trace a long migration from the north-west, through the Punjab and the country beyond the Indus, into the desert that would one day be called Jaisalmer. Before **Rawal Jaisal** raised his fort on the Trikuta hill in **1156 CE**, the Bhati rulers held a chain of desert strongholds, among them **Tanot**, **Derawar** and above all **Lodurva**, the old capital in the dunes north-west of the later city.

In the archive's list, **Rawal Manikrai** stands thirteenth in the line, after **Rawal Jand** and before **Rawal Hinglaj**, in the centuries before 1156. His name does not appear in the better-known versions of the Bhati genealogy, such as the one James Tod drew from the Jaisalmer chronicles, and the order and names of the early Rawals differ from one bardic list to another. Nothing reliable survives about his birth, his wars, his marriages or his death.

What can be said is what his age demanded of any Bhati chief. The desert rulers of this period lived by holding wells, grazing grounds and the caravan tracks that ran between Sindh, Multan and Gujarat. They fought neighbouring clans for water and pasture, and from the eighth century onwards they lived on the edge of the lands ruled from Sindh and Multan. Whoever Manikrai was, he would have spent his reign keeping his people and their herds alive in that hard country, and passing the line on to the next Rawal.

## Highlights of his life

- **A ruler of the early Bhati line.** He is listed thirteenth among the Rawals, in the period before the founding of Jaisalmer in 1156.
- **Between Jand and Hinglaj.** The archive's list names Rawal Jand as his predecessor and Rawal Hinglaj as his successor.
- **A thin record.** His name is absent from the best-known Bhati genealogies, and no details of his reign survive.
- **Ruler of the desert frontier.** Like every early Bhati chief, he governed a land of wells, herds and caravan routes on the edge of Sindh.

rawal-hinglaj-bhati.story:
## Rawal Hinglaj — a ruler named for the goddess of the west

*Rawal Hinglaj survives only as a name in the lists of the early Bhati Rawals. No inscription or contemporary account describes him, so this short account keeps to what can honestly be said.*

In the archive's list of the Bhati rulers, **Rawal Hinglaj** stands fourteenth, after **Rawal Manikrai** and before **Rawal Bachhraj**, in the centuries before **Rawal Jaisal** founded Jaisalmer in **1156 CE**. His name is not found in the best-known versions of the Bhati genealogy, and the early part of that genealogy differs from one bardic list to another. Nothing reliable is known of his birth, his reign, his wars or his death.

His name is itself the most telling thing about him. **Hinglaj** is the name of the goddess whose cave shrine lies in the Hingol valley of Las Bela, in present-day Balochistan, one of the most revered places of pilgrimage for the peoples of Sindh, Kutch and western Rajasthan. Pilgrims walked for weeks across desert and coast to reach it. In the traditions of the Charans, the bards and genealogists so closely bound to the Rajput houses of the Thar, the goddess **Awad** or **Swangiya**, the protective mother of the Bhatis, is honoured as a form of Hinglaj. A ruler bearing this name reflects that world of faith, in which the desert clans looked west towards the great goddess beyond the Indus.

The card once credited him with spreading the worship of Hinglaj Mata. No source supports this, and it should be read as a guess drawn from his name. What can be said is that he ruled in the age when the Bhatis held desert strongholds such as **Tanot**, **Derawar** and **Lodurva**, living by wells, herds and the caravan routes between Sindh, Multan and Gujarat, and that he handed the line on to the next Rawal.

## Highlights of his life

- **A ruler of the early Bhati line.** He is listed fourteenth among the Rawals, before the founding of Jaisalmer in 1156.
- **Between Manikrai and Bachhraj.** The archive's list names Rawal Manikrai as his predecessor and Rawal Bachhraj as his successor.
- **A name of the goddess.** He bore the name of Hinglaj, the great goddess of the shrine in Las Bela, revered across Sindh and western Rajasthan.
- **A thin record.** No details of his reign survive, and claims about his religious works rest on his name alone.

rawal-bachhraj-bhati.story:
## Rawal Bachhraj — a link in the Lodurva years

*Rawal Bachhraj is known only from the Bhati genealogies kept by the bards of Jaisalmer. No inscription or contemporary account describes his reign, so this short account keeps to what can honestly be said.*

The Jaisalmer chronicles, as James Tod later set them down, name a ruler called **Bachhu Raj** (Bachhraj or Vachharaj) among the Rawals who ruled from **Lodurva** in the generations after **Rawal Deoraj**. In that version he is the son of **Rawal Mundh** and the father of **Rawal Dusaj**, whose line led through **Vijayrao Lanjha** and **Bhojdev** to **Rawal Jaisal**, the founder of Jaisalmer in **1156 CE**. This would place him roughly in the late tenth or eleventh century, though the chronicles' dates for this period are uncertain. The archive's own list places him fifteenth, after **Rawal Hinglaj**, and the early genealogies differ in their names and order, so the two placements cannot easily be reconciled.

Nothing reliable survives about his birth, his wars, his marriages or his death. The card once credited him with diplomacy and trade relations; no source describes these, and they should be read as a guess.

What can be said is the world he ruled. Lodurva, the Bhati capital of this age, stood on the trade route across the Thar, and its Jain merchants are remembered for the temple of **Parshvanatha**, whose rebuilt shrine still stands among the dunes. To the west lay Sindh and Multan, ruled by Muslim dynasties since the eighth century; in the early eleventh century **Mahmud of Ghazni** passed through this region on his raids, including the march to Somnath in 1025–26. To the east and south stood the Paramaras, the Chalukyas of Gujarat and the rising Chauhans. A Bhati Rawal of these years had to hold his wells and caravan tracks among all of them.

## Highlights of his life

- **A ruler of the Lodurva age.** The Jaisalmer chronicles name a Bachhu Raj among the Rawals who ruled from Lodurva.
- **Son of Mundh, father of Dusaj.** In Tod's version of the genealogy he links Rawal Mundh to Rawal Dusaj, ancestor of Rawal Jaisal.
- **A disputed place in the line.** The archive's list sets him after Rawal Hinglaj, while the chronicles give a different order.
- **A thin record.** No details of his reign survive beyond his name and place in the genealogy.

rawal-ratan-sen-bhati.story:
## Rawal Ratan Sen — a name on the eve of Jaisalmer

*Rawal Ratan Sen appears in the archive's list of Bhati rulers, but no inscription or chronicle describes a ruler of this name at this point in the line. This short account keeps to what can honestly be said and corrects what cannot.*

In the archive's list, **Rawal Ratan Sen** stands sixteenth among the Bhati Rawals, after **Rawal Bachhraj** and before **Rawal Salbahan**, and is placed in the twelfth century. His card once described him as the builder of **Lodurva** and the founder of the first Bhati capital. That cannot be right. Lodurva was an older town, held by the **Lodra** Rajputs before the Bhatis, and the Jaisalmer chronicles say it was taken from them by **Rawal Deoraj**, generations before the twelfth century. Before Lodurva the Bhatis had already held **Tanot** and **Derawar**. Lodurva remained their seat until **Rawal Jaisal** moved the capital to his new fort on the Trikuta hill in **1156 CE**.

The chronicles also make **Salbahan** the son and direct successor of Jaisal, which leaves no clear place for a Ratan Sen between Bachhraj and Salbahan. The name may be a confusion with a later and far better remembered ruler: **Rawal Ratan Singh** (Ratansi), who, the bards of Jaisalmer say, shared the defence of the fort with his brother **Rawal Mularaj** during the long siege by the armies of **Alauddin Khalji** around 1299, ending in the first *saka* of Jaisalmer.

Nothing reliable can therefore be said about the birth, deeds or death of a twelfth-century Ratan Sen. What can be said is that the Bhati line in these decades stood at a turning point: the old capital of Lodurva, troubled by family strife and exposed on the desert plain, was about to give way to the golden fort that would carry the dynasty's name for the next eight centuries.

## Highlights of his life

- **A name in the archive's list.** He is listed sixteenth among the Bhati Rawals, between Rawal Bachhraj and Rawal Salbahan.
- **Not the builder of Lodurva.** Lodurva was an older town taken by Rawal Deoraj, and Tanot and Derawar were earlier Bhati seats.
- **A doubtful placement.** The chronicles make Salbahan the son and successor of Rawal Jaisal, leaving no clear room for a Ratan Sen here.
- **A possible confusion.** The name may echo Rawal Ratan Singh, remembered in tradition from the Khalji siege of Jaisalmer around 1299.

rawal-salbahan.title: Ruler of Jaisalmer
rawal-salbahan.significance: Son and successor of Rawal Jaisal, the founder of Jaisalmer
rawal-salbahan.legacy: Held the new fort of Jaisalmer through its first decades; remembered for losing his throne to his son Bijal and dying on the frontier.
rawal-salbahan.story:
## Rawal Salbahan — the heir of the golden fort

*Rawal Salbahan's life comes to us almost entirely through the chronicles of the Jaisalmer bards, as James Tod and later writers set them down; no inscription of his reign is known. Where the chronicles tell a story that cannot be checked, this account says so.*

When **Salbahan** was born, sometime in the first half of the twelfth century, the Bhati Rajputs still ruled from **Lodurva**, the old town among the dunes of the western Thar. It was a place of wells and gardens, of caravans resting on their way between Sindh and Gujarat, and of Jain merchants whose temple to **Parshvanatha** stood near the palace. It was also a place of quarrels. The Bhati house was large, its princes many, and the throne of Lodurva had more claimants than it could hold.

Salbahan's father was **Jaisal**, a son of **Rawal Dusaj**. The chronicles say that Dusaj's throne went first to Jaisal's elder half-brother, **Vijayrao Lanjha**, and then to Vijayrao's son, **Bhojdev**. Jaisal, the uncle, did not accept being passed over. The bards tell that he sought outside help against his nephew, that an army came against Lodurva, that Bhojdev died in its defence, and that the old capital was plundered. The chronicles name the ally as a Muslim ruler of the west, but their names and dates for this episode do not fit well with what is known from other sources, and historians treat the details with caution. What is not in doubt is the result: Jaisal became Rawal, and he decided that Lodurva, open on every side, could no longer be the seat of his house.

So the boy Salbahan grew up in the years when his father was building a new home for the dynasty. About ten miles to the south-east of Lodurva rose a long, flat-topped ridge of yellow sandstone called **Trikuta**, the three-peaked hill. Tradition says that a hermit named **Eesul** lived there, and that he told Jaisal of an old prophecy: a descendant of the Yadavas would one day build a fortress on that hill. In **1156 CE**, by the date the dynasty has always kept, Jaisal began the walls of **Jaisalmer**.

For a young prince this must have been a remarkable thing to watch. Quarrymen cut blocks from the ridge itself, so that the fort grew out of the hill in the same golden stone. The first ring of walls climbed the slope, and inside them rose the first houses of the nobles, the first wells cut into the rock, and the first shrines. Merchants who had lived at Lodurva began to move to the new town below the fort, bringing their trade and their temples with them. Over the centuries Jaisalmer would grow into one of the great caravan cities of the Thar, but in Salbahan's youth it was raw and new, a camp of masons and soldiers on a bare hill.

Jaisal had at least two sons, **Kailan** (Kelan) and Salbahan. Kailan was the elder, yet the chronicles agree that it was Salbahan whom Jaisal chose as his heir. They give different explanations for this, and none of them can be confirmed. Whatever the reason, the choice planted a seed of rivalry that would shape the rest of Salbahan's life, because Kailan did not leave the story. He lived on, with his own followers, as a reminder that the eldest son had been set aside.

Jaisal died, according to the traditional reckoning, around **1168 CE**, and Salbahan became Rawal of the new fort. He inherited a young state on a dangerous frontier. To the west and north-west, the lands of Sindh and Multan were changing hands. In **1175** the Ghurid ruler **Muhammad of Ghor** took Multan, and soon afterwards Uch, the great river towns whose markets the desert caravans had always served. Three years later, in **1178**, he led an army through the desert towards Gujarat, aiming at the rich Chalukya capital of Anahilapataka. The Chalukya forces met and defeated him near Mount Abu, at **Kasahrada**, and the Ghurid army retreated across the sands with heavy losses.

No record says whether that army passed through Bhati country or what Salbahan did while it marched. But the campaign shows the world he lived in. The Thar was not an empty barrier. It was a road, used by traders in peace and by armies in war, and the small states that held its wells had to watch the horizon constantly. In the years that followed, the Ghurids turned their strength against the Chauhans of Ajmer and Delhi. In **1191** **Prithviraj Chauhan** defeated Muhammad of Ghor at the first battle of **Tarain**; in **1192** he was defeated and killed on the same field. Within a few years Ghurid generals held Delhi and Ajmer, and in **1197** **Qutb-ud-din Aibak** sacked Anahilapataka itself. The great Rajput kingdoms around the Bhatis were being broken one after another.

Through all of this, Jaisalmer survived. The reason lay partly in its poverty and its remoteness. A ruler who wished to take it had to cross long stretches of waterless sand, then climb to walls built on solid rock, and the reward at the end was a small desert kingdom rather than the treasures of Gujarat or the Ganga plain. The Bhati Rawals understood this. Their strength was not great armies but knowledge of the land: where the wells were, which tracks could carry horses in summer, and which neighbouring clans could be trusted.

Salbahan's own reign is told by the bards mainly through one great misfortune. The chronicles say that he led an expedition away from Jaisalmer, to fight against rivals of the Bhatis beyond his borders, and that he was away a long time. While he was gone, his son **Bijal** (Baijal) seized power in the fort. The bards describe the young man as proud and impatient, encouraged by companions who told him that his father's absence was his opportunity. When Salbahan returned, the gates of Jaisalmer, the fort his own father had built for him, were shut against him.

It is not hard to imagine the scene the bards set before their listeners: the old Rawal and his tired riders below the yellow walls, the watchmen on the ramparts who had once saluted him now looking down in silence, and messengers going up and down the slope while father and son refused to yield. The chronicles say that Salbahan did not try to storm the fort. Perhaps he would not shed the blood of his own clan at the gate of his father's city; perhaps he simply did not have the strength. Instead he withdrew to a holding on the frontier.

There, tradition says, he spent his last years guarding the western marches of the Bhati land against the **Baloch**, the tribes who pressed in from the direction of Sindh and the Indus, raiding herds and wells. And there, according to the chronicles, he died fighting them, a Rawal without a throne who still kept the frontier for the kingdom that had turned him away. The exact date of his death is not known; the traditional reckoning closes his reign around **1200 CE**.

The bards do not leave Bijal unpunished. They say that his usurpation brought him no peace, and that after a short and troubled rule he was rebuked by his **dhai**, the foster-mother who had nursed him, for his treatment of his father. Stung by her words and by his own shame, the story goes, he took his own life. The tale is told as a lesson as much as a history, and it cannot be checked, but its meaning was clear to every listener: a son who betrays his father has destroyed his own right to rule.

With Bijal gone, the nobles of Jaisalmer turned to the one man whose claim no one could deny. **Kailan**, the elder son of Jaisal, who had been passed over a generation earlier, was at last raised to the throne. In this way the old injustice was undone, and the line of the Jaisalmer Rawals continued through him.

What did Salbahan leave behind? Not great monuments, for none can be firmly linked to his name, and not great victories that the wider history of India records. His legacy is quieter but real. He held the new fort through its first difficult decades, while the great kingdoms around the Thar were falling to the Ghurid armies. Under him Jaisalmer passed from being Jaisal's bold experiment to being the settled capital of the Bhati house, the seat it would remain for nearly eight hundred years, until the state joined independent India in 1949.

And in the bardic memory he stands as a figure of tragedy and loyalty: the favoured son who received a crown, lost it to his own child, and died defending the frontier of a kingdom that no longer called him king.

## Highlights of his life

- **Son of the founder.** He was a son of Rawal Jaisal, who founded Jaisalmer in 1156, and was chosen as heir over his elder brother Kailan.
- **Rawal of the new fort (c. 1168).** He succeeded his father and ruled Jaisalmer in its first decades as the Bhati capital.
- **A frontier in turmoil.** His reign saw the Ghurid conquest of Multan (1175), the failed Ghurid march on Gujarat (1178), the battles of Tarain (1191–92) and the sack of Anahilapataka (1197).
- **Betrayed by his son.** The chronicles say his son Bijal seized the fort while he was away on campaign and shut the gates against him.
- **Death on the frontier.** Tradition says he withdrew to the western marches and died fighting Baloch raiders, around 1200 by the traditional reckoning.
- **The throne returns to the elder line.** After Bijal's death, his elder brother Kailan became Rawal and carried the dynasty forward.

## Rawal Kelan — the elder son who waited for his crown

*Rawal Kelan's life comes to us through the chronicles of the Jaisalmer bards, as James Tod and later writers set them down; no inscription of his reign is known. Where the chronicles tell what cannot be checked, this account says so.*

**Kelan** (Kailan) was the elder son of **Rawal Jaisal**, the Bhati chief who in **1156 CE** began the yellow sandstone fort of **Jaisalmer** on the Trikuta hill. He grew up in two worlds: the old capital of **Lodurva** among the dunes, where his family had ruled for generations and quarrelled bitterly over the throne, and the raw new fort rising on its ridge, where masons, soldiers and merchants were building a city from nothing.

By the custom of most Rajput houses the throne should one day have been his. It was not. The chronicles agree that Jaisal chose his younger son, **Salbahan**, as heir, though they explain the choice in different ways, and none of the explanations can be confirmed. When Jaisal died, around **1168** by the traditional reckoning, Salbahan became Rawal, and Kelan, the eldest son of the founder, was left to live as a noble under his brother's rule.

For a proud young prince this was a hard fate, and the bards remember that it was not forgotten. Yet Kelan did not, so far as the chronicles tell, rise against his brother. He waited, and the years passed. Around the Thar the great powers of northern India were being overturned. Muhammad of Ghor took Multan in 1175, was defeated in Gujarat in 1178, and in **1192** destroyed **Prithviraj Chauhan** at the second battle of **Tarain**. Delhi and Ajmer fell to the Ghurids. The small desert kingdom of the Bhatis watched these storms from behind its sands.

Then the crisis came from within. The chronicles say that while Salbahan was away on campaign, his son **Bijal** seized Jaisalmer and shut the gates against his own father. Salbahan withdrew to the western frontier and died there fighting **Baloch** raiders. Bijal's rule was short. The bards tell that his foster-mother rebuked him for betraying his father, and that in shame he took his own life.

The nobles of Jaisalmer now needed a ruler whose right no one could question, and there was only one: the founder's eldest son. Around **1200 CE**, by the traditional reckoning, Kelan was at last raised to the throne he had been denied a generation earlier. The bards tell it as a righting of an old wrong. It is easy to picture the scene they imply: a man no longer young climbing to the palace of his father's fort, the same gates that had been shut on his brother now thrown open for him.

The kingdom he took over was small, poor in water and surrounded by danger. In **1206** the Ghurid conquests in India became the **Delhi Sultanate**, and from **1211** it was ruled by **Iltutmish**. To the west, Multan and Uch were held by **Nasir-ud-din Qabacha**, a rival of Delhi. In **1221** the struggle reached the Indus itself: **Jalal-ud-din Mangburni**, the Khwarazmian prince fleeing from Genghis Khan, crossed the river and for some years raided through Sindh, and Mongol forces followed him to the borderlands. In **1228** Iltutmish took Uch, and Qabacha drowned in the Indus. Iltutmish also campaigned in Rajasthan, against Ranthambhor, Mandore and Jalor.

No record says that any of these armies attacked Jaisalmer in Kelan's time, and it would be wrong to invent such a war. But every one of these events shaped his reign. Each upheaval in Sindh and Multan sent refugees, raiders and broken bands across the desert, and the trade on which the Bhatis lived depended on caravans passing safely between the Indus towns and Gujarat. Kelan's task was the one his card rightly names: to hold the frontier and keep the routes open. The chronicles remember the Bhatis of this age fighting the Baloch along their western edge, the same enemy that had killed Salbahan.

A desert Rawal did this not with great armies but with the loyalty of his kinsmen. The Bhati clan had many branches, each holding wells and villages under the Rawal, and each expected respect and a share of the land in return for service. Kelan, who had lived for decades as a noble among nobles, understood these men well. His long years outside the palace may have made him a better judge of the clan than a prince raised only for the throne.

Within the fort, Jaisalmer continued to grow. Merchants settled beneath its walls, and the town became a halt for caravans carrying goods between Sindh, Multan and Gujarat. No building can be firmly credited to Kelan, but the fort his father founded passed through his reign intact and stronger, while greater kingdoms around it fell.

Kelan ruled, by the traditional dates, until about **1235**. The chronicles give no clear account of his death, and nothing should be invented for it. He was followed by **Rawal Chachak Dev**, under whom the Bhatis would continue to fight on their western and southern frontiers. The line of the Jaisalmer Rawals, which almost broke in the strife of Salbahan's last years, ran on through Kelan for more than seven centuries.

His story is a quiet one, without a famous battle or a great monument. But the bards valued it for its meaning: the son who was passed over, who did not take by force what he believed was his, and who in the end received his father's throne from the hands of his clan.

## Highlights of his life

- **Eldest son of the founder.** He was the elder son of Rawal Jaisal, who founded Jaisalmer in 1156.
- **Passed over for the throne.** His younger brother Salbahan was chosen as heir and became Rawal around 1168.
- **Raised to the throne (c. 1200).** After Bijal's usurpation and death, the nobles made Kelan Rawal, restoring the elder line.
- **A frontier in turmoil.** His reign saw the founding of the Delhi Sultanate, the Khwarazmian and Mongol upheavals in Sindh (1221 onwards) and Iltutmish's capture of Uch (1228).
- **Keeper of the desert routes.** He held the Bhati frontier against the Baloch and kept the caravan trade alive.
- **Continuity of the line.** He ruled until about 1235 and was followed by Rawal Chachak Dev.
