## Rawal Chachak Dev — the desert king who chose his own heir

*Almost everything we know of Rawal Chachak Dev comes from the Bhati chronicles of Jaisalmer, preserved by the court bards and retold by James Tod in the nineteenth century. No inscription of his reign has been found; where the chronicle may be shaping the past, this story says so.*

When Chachak Dev was born, Jaisalmer was still a young city. According to the chronicle, his grandfather **Rawal Jaisal** had founded the fort on the golden ridge of Trikuta in **1156**, moving the Bhati capital away from exposed Lodurva. The Bhatis were Yaduvanshi Rajputs, who traced their line to Krishna. Their kingdom was a land of sand, scrub and scattered wells, where wealth was counted in cattle and camels, and in the caravans that crossed the Thar between Sindh, Multan and Gujarat.

Chachak was the eldest of the six sons of **Rawal Kelan**. His father's path to the throne had been strange. Though he was Jaisal's elder son, he was sent away in his youth, and Kelan was recalled to rule only at the age of fifty, after his younger brother Salivahan was killed fighting Baloch raiders and Salivahan's son Bijal took his own life in a fit of shame. Chachak therefore grew up in a court that knew how quickly fortune could turn in the desert. He would have learned to ride and hunt in the dunes around the fort, to read the wind and the stars, and to understand the old feuds of the Thar, as every Bhati prince did.

When Kelan died, Chachak Dev became Rawal. Tod's chronicle places his accession in **1219**; other reckonings, including the one this archive follows, place it somewhat later. The dates of this age in the Bhati records are not exact, and it is wiser to say simply that he ruled in the first half of the thirteenth century, the decades when the Delhi Sultanate of **Iltutmish** was taking shape far to the east.

The new king's first wars were with his neighbours of the desert. The chronicle says he fell upon the **Chana Rajputs**, a clan now long vanished, and drove them from their lands; they fled to take shelter with the Johiyas further north. It claims thousands slain and fourteen thousand cows taken. The numbers are the bards' numbers, but the picture is true to the Thar. In a land where grazing and water were life, wars were fought for pasture, and cattle were the prize.

Next he turned south-west, against the **Sodhas of Umarkot**, a Parmara clan whose fortress stood on the edge of Sindh. The chronicle tells that he caught their chief, **Rana Armsi**, by surprise. The Sodha gathered his horsemen, but was beaten and forced to shelter behind the walls of Umarkot. Peace was bought in the way desert peace was often bought: the Rana offered his daughter to the Bhati king in marriage. The bond between Jaisalmer and Umarkot, made and broken many times, would run through the history of both houses for centuries.

The chronicle also places in his reign the first trouble with the **Rathors**, a clan newly arrived in the land of Kher, near the Luni river. With Sodha help, it says, Chachak marched against them, and the Rathor chiefs turned his anger aside by giving him a daughter in marriage. Tod himself noticed that the Rathor names in this passage belong to a somewhat later time, and the episode may have been moved backwards by the bards. But it records something real: the thirteenth century was when the Rathors began to make the western desert their home, and the Bhatis would deal with them, in war and in marriage, for the rest of their history.

We should imagine Chachak Dev's kingdom as it really worked. The Rawal held the fort and its town, and his kinsmen held villages and wells across the desert, each with its own little band of riders. Power rested on loyalty, on marriage, and on the respect a king could win by leading his men in person. His younger brothers founded branches of the family; the chronicle says the descendants of two of them became the **Jaser** and **Sihana** Bhatis. Such branches were the strength of a Rajput state, and later, as Jaisalmer would learn, sometimes its danger.

The chronicle says Chachak Dev ruled for thirty-two years. His later life was shadowed by private grief. He had only one son, **Tej Rao**, and Tej Rao died of smallpox at about forty-two, before his father. The old king was left with two grandsons, **Jaitsi** the elder and **Karan** the younger.

Here the chronicle tells its most human story about him. Chachak loved the younger boy most. As he lay dying, he called his chiefs to his bedside and begged them, as his last wish, to make Karan his successor rather than Jaitsi. We can imagine the scene in the dim chamber of the fort, the old man's voice weak, the chiefs uneasy, for the custom of the eldest was strong. Yet they gave their word, and when Chachak Dev died, **Karan** was placed on the throne.

The choice had long consequences. Jaitsi, passed over, left Jaisalmer and took service with the Muslim rulers of Gujarat. Many years later, after Karan's son **Lachhman Dev** (Lakhansen of the chronicles) and grandson Punpal had both failed as kings, the nobles would send for the exiled Jaitsi and make him Rawal at last. It was in his reign that Jaisalmer faced the great siege that ended in its first saka.

Chachak Dev himself left no great monument that can be named with certainty. His legacy was the kingdom he held together: a young desert state that had beaten back its rivals, bound its neighbours by marriage, and survived its second and third generations, the years in which many new kingdoms fell apart.

## Highlights of his life

- **Son of Rawal Kelan.** The eldest of six sons, he inherited a young kingdom only a few decades after the founding of Jaisalmer.
- **War against the Chanas.** The chronicle says he drove the Chana Rajputs from their lands and took their herds.
- **Victory over the Sodhas.** He defeated Rana Armsi of Umarkot, who made peace by giving him his daughter in marriage.
- **First dealings with the Rathors.** The chronicle places in his reign a campaign against the newly arrived Rathors, ended by a marriage alliance.
- **A long reign.** Tradition gives him thirty-two years on the throne, in the first half of the thirteenth century.
- **A disputed succession.** After his only son died of smallpox, he asked his chiefs to crown his younger grandson Karan instead of the elder Jaitsi, a choice that shaped the next generations of Jaisalmer.

## Rawal Lachhman Dev — the strange king of the jackals' quilts

*Rawal Lachhman Dev appears in the Bhati chronicles of Jaisalmer as Lakhansen, and his story comes to us through the court bards as retold by James Tod. The chronicle remembers him unkindly; where its tales read like satire or legend, this story says so.*

Lachhman Dev was born into the house of Jaisalmer in the middle of the thirteenth century, when the fort on the golden ridge of Trikuta was barely a hundred years old. His father was **Rawal Karan**, and his great-grandfather was **Rawal Chachak Dev**, the desert king who on his deathbed had asked his chiefs to crown his younger grandson Karan in place of the elder, **Jaitsi**. That choice hung over Lachhman Dev's whole life. His father's throne had been given by the wish of a dying man, and the passed-over Jaitsi was still alive, living in exile in Gujarat.

Karan's reign, as the chronicle remembers it, was a vigorous one. Its most famous episode tells of a Baraha Rajput landholder whose daughter was carried off by **Muzaffar Khan**, a commander then holding Nagaur, and of Karan riding out to avenge the wrong. Lachhman Dev grew up in a court that told such stories with pride. He would have learned what every Bhati prince learned: horsemanship, the sword and the lance, the reading of desert omens, and the long memory of feuds and marriages that bound the clans of the Thar.

After a long reign, Karan died, and Lachhman Dev became Rawal. The Bhati chronicle, as Tod gives it, dates his accession to **1271** and allows him only four years on the throne; the reckoning used in this archive gives him a longer reign. The exact dates cannot be settled, but the chronicle is clear about one thing. It considered him unfit to rule.

The bards tell the story by which he is remembered. On cold winter nights the jackals howled in the scrub around the fort. The king asked why they cried so, and his courtiers, perhaps teasing him, told him the animals were cold. Lachhman Dev was moved to pity. He ordered that quilted coats be made for the jackals. Yet the howling went on night after night. His servants assured him that his orders had been obeyed and the coats delivered. Puzzled, the king commanded that houses be built for the animals in the royal hunting preserve. Tod, writing more than five centuries later, was told that some of those shelters still stood.

The story is told as a joke against a simple-minded king, and that is how the chronicle meant it. But a modern reader may notice something else in it: a ruler moved by the suffering of creatures in a hard land, however strangely he acted on that feeling. Legends of this kind often grow up around rulers whom their nobles have decided to remove, and we cannot know how much of it is true.

The chronicle says that the real power in his court lay with his queen, a **Sodha** princess from Umarkot. The Sodhas and the Bhatis had been bound by marriage since the days of Chachak Dev. The chronicle also makes Lachhman Dev a contemporary of **Kanhad Dev Songara**, the famous ruler of Jalore, and tells that the queen's skill in reading omens once saved Kanhad Dev's life. It gives no details, and the tale cannot be checked, but it shows the queen as a woman of knowledge and influence, respected beyond her own court.

Her influence led to the darkest episode of the reign. The queen invited her brothers from Umarkot to Jaisalmer. The chronicle says that the king, in a fit of madness, had them put to death and their bodies thrown over the walls. It is a terrible charge, and we have only the bards' word for it. But it would explain much: the killing of a queen's kinsmen was a deadly insult to an allied house, and it would have made the Rawal's position among his own nobles impossible.

In a Rajput state the Rawal was first among his kinsmen, not their absolute master, and when the clan lost faith in him, his reign could end without a battle. That is what happened. The chronicle says Lachhman Dev "was allowed to rule four years", and was then replaced by his son **Punpal**. How he spent the rest of his life, and when and how he died, it does not tell. He simply passes out of the story.

His son fared no better. Punpal, the chronicle says, had so violent a temper that within about a year the nobles deposed him too, giving him a residence in a remote corner of the state. Then they did what Chachak Dev's dying wish had prevented a generation before. They sent to Gujarat for the exiled **Jaitsi**, the elder grandson, and placed him on the throne. The line of Lachhman Dev lost Jaisalmer for good.

Yet his line did not vanish. Punpal's grandson, **Rao Raningdeo**, according to the chronicle, took **Marot** from the Johiyas and **Pugal** from a robber clan, and made Pugal the seat of his family. The Bhatis of Pugal became one of the important branches of the clan in the northern desert, and later rulers of that line would play their own part in the history of the Thar, including in the founding of Bikaner two centuries later.

Lachhman Dev's reign was short and unhappy, and the chronicle remembers him with mockery. But his story is a useful window into how a desert kingdom worked. A Rawal ruled only as long as his clan accepted him. Marriages with neighbouring houses were the pillars of peace, and breaking them was dangerous. And the bards, who kept the memory of every king, could turn a ruler's life into a lesson or a joke for centuries to come.

## Highlights of his life

- **Son of Rawal Karan.** He came to the throne through the line chosen by his great-grandfather Chachak Dev over the elder grandson Jaitsi.
- **The jackals' quilts.** The bards remember him for ordering quilted coats, and then shelters, for the howling jackals of the royal preserve.
- **A Sodha queen.** His queen from Umarkot was, the chronicle says, the real power at court, and was remembered for her skill with omens.
- **A broken alliance.** The chronicle accuses him of killing his queen's brothers, an act that destroyed his standing.
- **Deposed by his nobles.** He was replaced by his son Punpal, whose own fall brought the exiled Jaitsi to the throne.
- **Ancestor of the Pugal Bhatis.** Through his grandson's son Raningdeo, his line founded the Bhati house of Pugal.

## Rawal Jaitsi — the exile who came home to face the Sultan

*Rawal Jaitsi's life comes to us through the Bhati chronicles of Jaisalmer, kept by the court bards and retold by James Tod. The Persian histories of Delhi say little about Jaisalmer in these years, so the great siege of his reign is known mainly from Rajput tradition; where that tradition exaggerates or cannot be checked, this story says so.*

Jaitsi was born to be king, and then was told he would not be. He was the elder son of **Tej Rao**, the only son of **Rawal Chachak Dev**. When Tej Rao died of smallpox, the old Rawal was left with two grandsons, and he loved the younger, **Karan**, more. On his deathbed, the chronicle says, Chachak Dev begged his chiefs to crown Karan instead of Jaitsi, and they agreed.

Jaitsi left Jaisalmer. The chronicle says he went to Gujarat and took service there with Muslim lords. In those decades Gujarat itself was still ruled by the Vaghela kings, so we cannot be sure whom he served, but the picture is clear enough: a prince without a throne, earning his bread with his sword in a foreign court.

The years of exile were long. Karan reigned for decades, but his son **Lachhman Dev** and grandson **Punpal** were each deposed by the nobles. With no fit king left in that line, the Bhati chiefs remembered the elder grandson in Gujarat. Messengers rode south, and Jaitsi came home.

The chronicle gives his accession as **1276**; the reckoning used in this archive places it a little later. He came back a seasoned man, with two grown sons, **Mulraj** and **Ratan Singh** (Ratansi), and a grown grandson, **Deoraj**, son of Mulraj, whose own son **Hamir** would become a famous warrior. Deoraj married a princess of the **Songara** house of Jalore, binding Jaisalmer to one of the strongest Rajput states of the west.

The chronicle shows Jaitsi as a generous host: when **Rana Rupsi**, the Parihar ruler of **Mandor**, was driven from his land by an invading army, he fled with his twelve daughters to Jaisalmer, and Jaitsi gave him the village of Baru as a home.

The storm that would define his reign was gathering in the east. In **1296**, **Alauddin Khalji** seized the throne of Delhi and set out to break the Rajput fortresses one by one. The chronicle says the trouble began with the reckless courage of Jaitsi's own sons. A great convoy carrying the tribute of Thatta and Multan to Delhi, said to be fifteen hundred horses and fifteen hundred mules loaded with treasure, was passing along the rivers of the Punjab. The Bhati princes disguised their men as grain merchants, camped beside the convoy, rose upon its guards at night and carried the treasure back to Jaisalmer.

The Sultan, say the bards, swore revenge. When word came that the royal army was camped by the **Anasagar** lake at Ajmer, Jaitsi prepared for the greatest test a desert fort could face.

Jaitsi filled the fort's granaries. He had great round stones piled along the ramparts, ready to be hurled down on attackers. He sent the old, the sick and the young girls of his family deep into the desert. The land around Jaisalmer for many miles was laid waste, the wells and villages abandoned, so that the enemy would find nothing to eat or drink. Jaitsi himself, with his sons and some five thousand warriors, stayed inside the fort. Deoraj and Hamir led a force in the open desert, to strike at the enemy's supply lines.

The army that came was huge, its soldiers in steel armour, and in the bards' words they "rolled on like the clouds in Bhadon". The chronicle says every one of the fort's fifty-six bastions was manned, and the first assaults were thrown back with heavy losses. The Bhati force outside cut off the convoys coming from Mandor, while the garrison was fed from the desert lands of Khadal, Barmer and Dhat. The siege settled into a long, grinding blockade.

The chronicle claims it lasted eight years. That is surely the bards' exaggeration, and historians do not know its true length. But it was long enough for strange friendships to grow. The bards tell that Jaitsi's son Ratan Singh met daily with a commander of the besieging army, **Mahbub Khan**, under a khejri tree between the lines. The two men played chess together and spoke as friends, and then went back to fight each other with full courage.

Jaitsi did not live to see the end. Somewhere in the long years of the siege the old king died, and since there was no way out through the enemy lines, his body was burned within the walls of the fort he had come home to defend. The chronicle says he had ruled eighteen years.

His son **Mulraj** was crowned inside the besieged fort. Soon afterwards supplies ran out. Mulraj and Ratan Singh chose the path of honour: the women performed **jauhar**, and the men opened the gates and rode out to die. This was the **first saka of Jaisalmer**. The chronicle dates it to 1295, which does not fit Alauddin's reign, and historians usually place it some years later. Ratan Singh, before the last battle, sent his two young sons, Gharsi and Kanhar, to his friend Mahbub Khan, who kept his word and raised them in safety. The Delhi army held the fort for a time, then dismantled its defences and left it empty.

Jaitsi's life began with a throne taken from him and ended in a fort surrounded by enemies, yet he is remembered with honour. The exiled prince came home when his clan needed him, restored order, prepared his people for the storm, and held the walls until his last breath. The defence he planned became one of the great stories of Rajput courage, told in Jaisalmer to this day.

## Highlights of his life

- **The passed-over heir.** Though the elder grandson of Chachak Dev, he was set aside in favour of his brother Karan and went into exile in Gujarat.
- **Recalled by the nobles.** After two of Karan's line were deposed, the Bhati chiefs brought him home and made him Rawal.
- **Host to the Parihar of Mandor.** He gave shelter to Rana Rupsi when he was driven from his kingdom.
- **The great raid.** His sons seized a tribute convoy bound for Delhi, bringing on the wrath of Alauddin Khalji.
- **Defender of Jaisalmer.** He prepared the fort and the desert for a long siege, keeping a field army outside the walls to harass the besiegers.
- **Death in the siege.** He died during the blockade and was cremated inside the fort; soon after, his sons fell in Jaisalmer's first saka.

rawal-duda-i.title: Ruler of Jaisalmer
rawal-duda-i.story:
## Rawal Duda — The Second Saka of Jaisalmer

*Rawal Duda's story comes from Bhati bardic tradition, Muhnot Nainsi's seventeenth-century Khyat, James Tod's Annals of Jaisalmer and later court histories; Persian chronicles of the Delhi Sultanate do not describe his siege, and his dates — including the 1294–1313 range given here — are uncertain and disputed.*

**Rawal Duda** belongs to the most turbulent chapter in the history of **Jaisalmer**: the decades around **1300**, when the armies of the Delhi Sultanate pressed into Rajasthan and fort after fort — Ranthambhore, Chittor, Siwana, Jalore — fell after long sieges. In Bhati memory Jaisalmer endured two great disasters in this period, each remembered as a **saka**, the last stand in which the garrison rode out to die while the women of the fort chose **jauhar**. The first is associated with Rawal Mulraj and his brother Ratan Singh. The second is associated with Duda.

### A fort left empty

According to the Jaisalmer tradition, after the first siege the fortress on the **Trikuta hill** lay ruined and largely deserted. Imperial forces did not hold such a remote desert stronghold for long, and the surviving Bhati chiefs had scattered to their villages. Duda, a member of a collateral branch of the Bhati ruling family, is said to have gathered followers and reoccupied the fort, restoring Bhati rule over the town and its trade routes. His elevation therefore came not through an ordinary succession from father to son but through a seizure of an abandoned seat — a reminder that Rajput kingship in this period often depended on the ability to hold ground as much as on genealogy.

The bards remember Duda's companion **Tilaksi** (Tilak Singh), a famous raider whose exploits fill the ballads. The pair are portrayed as leading attacks on the herds and caravans of their neighbours, including the Rathores who were beginning to settle in western Marwar, and even on the property of the Sultanate. Tod repeats a story that Tilaksi carried off horses or cattle belonging to the imperial establishment, provoking retaliation. Such raiding was part of the desert economy and of Bhati honour culture, but it brought the anger of a much stronger power down on Jaisalmer.

### The second siege

The tradition holds that an army from Delhi besieged Jaisalmer and that, when supplies ran out, the women of the fort performed jauhar and Duda, Tilaksi and the remaining warriors went out to fight to the death. This was the **second saka** of Jaisalmer.

Here historians must be cautious. Tod and some later writers attribute this siege to the reign of **Firuz Shah Tughlaq**, who ruled from 1351 to 1388; others place it in the last years of **Alauddin Khalji** (died 1316) or of his successors. Modern king-lists, which sometimes give his name as **Durjan Sal**, place his reign around 1295–1306, immediately after Mulraj; the 1294–1313 range used here belongs to the same Khalji-era framework, and neither fits the Firuz Shah version at all. No Persian source currently known gives a detailed account of a Jaisalmer siege matching the bardic one, so the event rests on Rajput memory alone. That does not mean it did not happen — sieges of distant forts were often left out of court histories — but the sequence and dates cannot be fixed with confidence. What the tradition consistently preserves is that Jaisalmer suffered two sakas within a relatively short span and that Duda died in the second.

The memory of jauhar should be understood historically. It was a response by besieged Rajput households to the near-certainty of captivity and enslavement after a fort's fall, practised at several Rajasthani forts in this era. Later literature turned it into a symbol of honour; modern readers can recognise both the courage and the immense human cost it represented.

### Reign and government

Of Duda's administration almost nothing is recorded. His power was that of a desert chief holding a fortified capital, taxing the camel caravans that crossed between **Sindh**, **Multan**, **Gujarat** and the plains, and relying on kinsmen who held villages across the region. Diplomacy with neighbours, which some modern summaries credit to him, is not documented in detail; it is more accurate to say that the Bhatis of this age balanced between hostility and accommodation with the Rathores, the Sodhas of Umarkot, Baloch groups to the west and the Sultanate's governors in Sindh and Multan. Any building he undertook at the fort would have been reconstruction after the damage of the first siege, but none can be attributed to him with certainty.

### Aftermath and succession

After the second saka the fort is again said to have stood empty for a time. The Bhati line was restored by **Rawal Gharsi**, a kinsman who, according to tradition, obtained recognition from Delhi — a sign of the more pragmatic relationship with the Sultanate that followed. Gharsi is remembered as the builder of the great reservoir **Gharsisar (Gadisar)**, which supplied the town with water for centuries. From Gharsi's time the dynasty settled into a more continuous line, and the sakas became part of Jaisalmer's identity: later poets, temple inscriptions and the city's own pride all looked back to the two sieges as proof of Bhati steadfastness.

Duda's own legacy is therefore that of a restorer and a defender rather than a builder. He reoccupied a fort others had abandoned and held it until it fell. The old draft of his story spoke of frontier diplomacy and tribal balance; those phrases capture something real about the Bhati position in the desert, but the specific achievements credited to Duda in such summaries have no documentary basis.

### Key points
- **Restorer.** Tradition says Duda reoccupied Jaisalmer after the first saka left the fort deserted.
- **Tilaksi.** His companion Tilaksi is remembered in ballads as a bold raider whose actions provoked Delhi.
- **Second saka.** Duda died in the second great siege of Jaisalmer, when the women performed jauhar and the men fought to the end.
- **Uncertain date.** Sources disagree whether the attackers were Khalji or Tughlaq forces; the dates cannot be fixed.
- **Succession.** Rawal Gharsi later restored the dynasty and built the Gharsisar lake.

## Rawal Devidas — A Desert Kingdom in a Century of New Neighbours

*Rawal Devidas is known from the Jaisalmer genealogies, Muhnot Nainsi's Khyat, James Tod's Annals and later court histories; few details of his reign are recorded, and his dates are uncertain — standard modern king-lists place him c. 1457–1497, not in the 1313–1325 range sometimes attached to his name.*

**Rawal Devidas** is one of the rulers of **Jaisalmer** whose name is securely fixed in the Bhati line but whose deeds are only faintly visible. A first problem is chronology. Some summaries place him in the early fourteenth century, between the sieges of the Khalji era and the restoration of the dynasty. The fuller king-lists used by most modern historians, however, set the sequence of that period as Mulraj, Duda (Durjan Sal), Gharsi and Kehar, and they place a Rawal Devidas much later — in the second half of the fifteenth century, after **Chachak Dev II** and before **Jait Singh II**. This account follows that later placement, while noting that the dynastic record is not uniform.

### Accession and the Bhati state

Devidas came to the throne of a kingdom that had recovered from the catastrophes of the early fourteenth century. Under **Rawal Gharsi** and his successors the fort on the **Trikuta hill** had been reoccupied and strengthened, and the **Gharsisar** reservoir had given the growing town a reliable water supply. The fifteenth-century rawals ruled a state whose wealth came above all from the **caravan trade**: Jaisalmer sat on routes between **Sindh** and **Multan** to the west and **Gujarat**, Marwar and the Gangetic plain to the east, and the duties on camel trains carrying textiles, salt, spices, opium, dried fruit and horses sustained the court.

Power within the kingdom was shared with the Bhati nobility. Kinsmen descended from earlier rulers held villages and estates across the desert, owed military service and expected to be consulted. A rawal's success depended on keeping these lineages loyal, and many of the political crises recorded in the chronicles are quarrels within the clan rather than wars with outsiders.

### A changing map

The defining development of Devidas's lifetime happened just beyond his borders. In **1459** **Rao Jodha** founded the city and fort of **Jodhpur**, giving the **Rathores** a permanent capital in Marwar. Jodha's sons spread Rathore power further: **Rao Bika** carved out a new state in the dry country to the north and in **1488** founded **Bikaner**. Much of that land had earlier been dominated by Bhati branches, notably those around **Pugal**, and the expansion of the Rathores pressed directly against Bhati interests. Tradition records both conflict and marriage alliances between the two clans in this period — Bika's ties with the Bhatis of Pugal are the best-known example — but no specific campaign can be confidently assigned to Devidas himself.

To the west, the Sultanate of Delhi had lost its grip on Sindh and Multan, where local dynasties such as the **Sammas** of Thatta and the **Langahs** of Multan now ruled. Baloch groups were also moving into the lands between the Indus and the Thar. For Jaisalmer this meant a frontier of many smaller powers rather than a single imperial threat — less dangerous than the age of the great sieges, but requiring constant vigilance over wells, grazing and caravan routes.

### Culture and the Jain temples

The fifteenth century was the great age of temple building inside the Jaisalmer fort. Wealthy **Jain** merchant families, who financed and managed much of the desert trade, built a cluster of shrines in yellow sandstone that remains one of the finest groups of Jain architecture in western India. The **Chintamani Parshvanatha** temple was completed in the early fifteenth century, and several others followed through the century and into the next. In the same period the scholar-monk **Jinabhadra Suri** gathered the collection of manuscripts that became the celebrated **Jain library (gyan bhandar)** of Jaisalmer, preserving palm-leaf and paper texts that are still studied today.

These were not royal foundations in the strict sense; they were the work of merchant patrons and monastic orders. But they flourished under the protection and with the permission of the Bhati rawals, whose rule made the fort a safe place for such investment. A ruler like Devidas presided over this partnership between a Rajput warrior aristocracy and a Jain commercial elite — a partnership that gave Jaisalmer much of its character. Specific inscriptions naming the reigning rawal survive in some temples, but the dating of particular shrines to Devidas's reign should be checked against the epigraphic studies rather than assumed.

### Fortification

Older drafts describe Devidas as a great fortifier of Jaisalmer. The fort was indeed strengthened in successive phases between the twelfth and eighteenth centuries, with additional bastions and walls added by many rulers. No specific work, however, is documented as his. It is safer to say that, like every rawal, he maintained a fortress that had been the dynasty's refuge since the time of Jaisal.

### Death and succession

Devidas was succeeded by **Rawal Jait Singh II**, under whom Jaisalmer entered the sixteenth century. The next generations would see the Bhatis drawn into the wider politics of the **Mughal** age, culminating in the accommodation reached by **Rawal Harraj** with Akbar. In that longer story Devidas represents the quieter decades: a reign of maintenance, of uneasy coexistence with the rising Rathore states, and of growing prosperity in the fort's temples and bazaars.

### Key points
- **Dating.** Standard king-lists place Rawal Devidas c. 1457–1497, between Chachak Dev II and Jait Singh II; earlier dates in some summaries do not fit the dynastic sequence.
- **Rathore expansion.** His lifetime saw the founding of Jodhpur (1459) and Bikaner (1488), which reshaped the Bhatis' eastern and northern frontiers.
- **Trade state.** Jaisalmer's wealth rested on caravan duties along the routes between Sindh and Gujarat.
- **Jain culture.** The fifteenth century saw major Jain temples and the famous manuscript library flourish in the fort under Bhati protection.
- **Thin record.** No specific battle or building can be securely credited to Devidas personally.

rawal-kanhad-dev.significance: Military preparedness and protection of trade
rawal-kanhad-dev.story:
Early life and the depth of lineage
Rawal Kanhad Dev was born in the heart of the Thar, with endless dunes and caravan tracks, a landscape where the memory of the Jaisalmer (Bhati) was kept alive not by stone inscriptions alone, but by bards who walked from village to village, by mothers who sang lullabies of old battles, and by clan-councils held under the ancient banyan. 1325-1340 CE was an age when every fort had its own ghost, every pass its own tradition, and every shrine its own protective vow. The clan deity, Sri Tanot Mata, the desert guardian of the Bhatis, was worshipped with a lamp that never went out; caravans stopped before entering the hills; and sentinels watched every waterhole through the night. It was in such a world that Rawal Kanhad Dev grew up, sitting at the knee of Ruler Bhati Rajputs Ancestor and learning the first, cruel truth of Rajput kingship: that the throne is not comfort, but a vow.
Their education was deliberately rounded. The four martial sciences - bow, horse, sword, and mace - were taught before the letters of the alphabet. Then came the shastras, but never only from books. Economics was taught from the account-books of a merchant caravan. Statecraft was taught from a rebel chieftain's forgiven letter. Justice was taught from the actual hearing of a widow's land dispute in the village chaupal. Music and painting were not ornaments; they were meant to train eye and ear, so that a king could read the lie in a courtier's salute and the truth in the murmur of a crowd.
From the queen-mother, Rawal Kanhad Dev received an even more difficult lesson: a king's courage is not proven on the battlefield alone. It is proven when he listens silently to a complaint he does not want to hear, when he feeds the hungry before his own table, when he keeps his word to a weaker ally even if every minister advises him otherwise. These quiet disciplines were rehearsed long before the coronation, and they gave Rawal Kanhad Dev a steadiness of temper that would later be noted by every chronicler of Jaisalmer (Bhati).

Ascension and the trials of succession
When the reign of Ruler Bhati Rajputs Ancestor closed, Rawal Kanhad Dev was invested with the five symbols of the Jaisalmer (Bhati) at Jaisalmer: the clan-tilak, the talismanic armour, the ancestral sword, the signet ring, and the turban of honour. The ceremonies were magnificent, but no sooner had the last hymn ended than the new ruler was tested. A group of feudatories - calculating on the sovereign's youth - withheld tribute. Others launched cattle-raids along the border. Still others opened secret correspondence with a neighbouring kingdom, hoping to carve out independent shares.
Rawal Kanhad Dev refused a hasty punitive war. Instead, a threefold policy was announced. Every rebel chief - without exception - received a personal letter, written in ink but sealed with the same signet that would later seal the punishment: it reaffirmed their ancient rights, welcomed them to the council, and invited them to the capital. Those who accepted were received with the same dignity they had known under Ruler Bhati Rajputs Ancestor. Those who persisted in open rebellion were dealt with by a carefully chosen commander, with strict orders that the fields of ordinary cultivators should not be trampled and no market-town be looted. The families of the leading chiefs were also invited to send their sons to be trained in the royal court, as pages, cavalry officers, and scholars.
Within a single year the troubles collapsed. The border was sealed, the tribute-chests were full again, and even the most sceptical old chieftain admitted that Rawal Kanhad Dev had the two rarest qualities in a king: patience without softness, and resolution without cruelty. From this episode a new convention grew up within the Jaisalmer (Bhati): no loyal family would ever be displaced merely because the crown had changed hands.

Military campaigns, strategy, and the mark of valour
Under Rawal Kanhad Dev the Jaisalmer (Bhati) army was reshaped into a far more cohesive instrument of war. The old feudal contingents were supplemented by standing regiments organised by arm: heavy infantry, bowmen, cavalry squadrons, elephant corps, batteries of light guns, companies of skirmishers, siege-engineering teams, and a dedicated espionage wing. Each of these was placed under a professional commandant reporting directly to Rawal Kanhad Dev, so that in a crisis blame could not travel down and credit could not travel up.
Campaigns such as “border-security expeditions”, “suppression of local uprisings” illustrate the methodical nature of that military mind. Before every major operation, reconnaissance parties travelled far ahead - disguised as mendicants, as grain-merchants, as cattle-drovers - counting the enemy's tents, inspecting the wells, watching the routes by which fodder and water reached their camps, and even counting the daily movements of their cavalry patrols. Only after that data had been compared with the reports of the astrologer, the priest performing the campaign-havan, the chief engineer, the field-hospital surgeon, and the paymaster would Rawal Kanhad Dev unfurl the royal standard.
Victory was never treated as a licence. Enemy kings who surrendered were guaranteed their lives, their families' safety, and often a place in the council of the victor. Wounded soldiers of the winning side received lifelong stipends; the families of the dead received rent-free lands and annual gifts. Even the war-horses and elephants were pensioned off in royal elephant-stables and stud-farms. The result was an army that fought for more than loot: it fought for the very name of Rawal Kanhad Dev.

Forts, roads, water, and the labour of building for posterity
The reign of Rawal Kanhad Dev was a long festival of building. “repair of the old capital fort”, “border outposts and village ponds” are the obvious and still-standing witnesses, but behind them lay an entire system. Every fort, large or small, was planned as a self-contained town: quarters for the royal family, barracks for the garrison, a shrine for Sri Tanot Mata, the desert guardian of the Bhatis, houses for brahmin householders, huge granaries, dispensaries of herbal medicine, feeding-halls for the poor, and wells deep enough to withstand a siege of many years.
The road network was equally transformed. Between the principal towns, milestones, arched rest-houses, masonry step-wells, and roadside groves of shade-giving trees were set up at fixed intervals. Passes on the old caravan routes received small fortified outposts, so that merchants could move silver and spices without extra private guards. Market-places were laid out with proper lanes for separate trades, with overseers to keep weights and measures honest, grain-storehouses safe from damp, and the lanes free from encroachments.
Water management, however, was the most intimate form of building. In dry belts, johads, earthen dams, covered kunds, and lined tanks were constructed one after another. Canals drawn from the rivers began to reach villages that had always depended on the monsoon alone. Most importantly, traditional water-rights were written down for each village, witnessed by the chaupal, and registered by the royal clerk. So when drought came, the last peasant and the first thakur drew water by the same measure.

Administration, revenue, and the fundamentals of justice
Under Rawal Kanhad Dev the Jaisalmer (Bhati) state was split into six clear departments: military, religious endowments, revenue and treasury, commerce and caravan tolls, land settlement, and water-forest stewardship. Each was placed under a senior minister whose registers were balanced every six months by Rawal Kanhad Dev personally, not by clerks alone. Beyond these, provincial governors for distant tracts were appointed for fixed terms, and required to submit written returns every lunar month.
The fiscal policy was deliberately mild. Taxes on agriculture were kept low; tolls on the long-distance routes were standardised so that a merchant could predict his costs from the first milestone; and hereditary classes engaged in public service - brahmins engaged in teaching and sacrifice, village teachers, cow-sanctuaries, hospitals, and pilgrim-hostels - were kept free of any impost. Embezzlement, however, was not. A corrupt officer was not merely transferred; the whole district was audited, the sums recovered, and the offender brought to the same open court that heard the poorest cultivator.
The jewel of the reign, however, was the visible even-handedness of justice. The proudest thakur and the most ragged cowherd stood before the same bench and under the same written rules. A public audience was held every single day, without exception, where every subject - irrespective of rank, wealth, or recommendation - could walk in and place a petition into the hands of Rawal Kanhad Dev. Hundreds of cases were settled by the ruler in person, with the full papers spread open on the carpet before them. It was this visible, daily, approachable justice that gave the Jaisalmer (Bhati) regime a moral weight no mere army could ever buy.

Dharma, the arts, and the patronage of letters
Rawal Kanhad Dev was a devout ruler, yet never a sectarian one. Works such as “sustained worship of the clan deity”, “honours for local poets and musicians” made that policy visible across the entire kingdom. Temples, mosques, dargahs, and gurdwaras were all repaired; the ministers of every faith received allowances; cow-sanctuaries and hospitals for sick animals were maintained from the treasury; and dispensaries of Unani and Ayurvedic medicines were staffed by salaried physicians.
In the realm of art and craftsmanship, Rawal Kanhad Dev summoned masters of every school under royal protection. Architecture in stone, fresco-painting on plaster, stone-sculpture, perforated jalis, silver filigree, wood-carving, embroidery of cloth, beaten copper and brass, manuscript illumination, the forging of arms, and the exact science of fort-building - all were given workshops within the palace precincts, where apprentices learned the trade from masters in the old guru-shishya style.
Poets, bards, musicians, instrumentalists, and reciters of oral epic were given permanent stipends, seats of honour at festivals, and freedom to criticise the court as sharply as they pleased. As a result, folk literature flourished. Village-songs, bardic lays, khyals, nautch parties, and folk-plays picked up the memory of Rawal Kanhad Dev and carried it from the capital to the most remote hamlet. It was a cultural policy too often forgotten: true glory is not built from palaces alone, but from the voices of the people themselves.

Feudal loyalties, neighbouring states, and the diplomacy of moderation
Under Rawal Kanhad Dev, the compact between the Jaisalmer (Bhati) throne and its feudatories was rewritten on the clearest possible terms. Each chief's ancient dignity, his land-rights, the honours due to his family at court, and the protection of his clan during minority successions - all were confirmed in a formal patent sealed by the crown. The leading chiefs were also given seats on the permanent war-council and the revenue council, so that policy was never made behind their backs.
Marriage alliances were also used with great care. Younger members of the royal family were linked by marriage to other ruling houses, not as a bribe, but as a public guarantee that quarrels of the past would not be revived. Friendly kingdoms were kept completely autonomous; defeated kingdoms were often given back their old ruling families, only under a treaty of friendship. No ancient line was displaced merely for the crime of having lost a battle.
These exact principles were also taught, with endless patience, to Next Ruler. For Rawal Kanhad Dev often said that a sword's edge fades in a single campaign, but a treaty well kept, kept by both sides for a whole lifetime, can outlast a hundred victories. It was this doctrine - not force alone - that extended the shadow of the Jaisalmer (Bhati) far beyond its formal borders.

Character, daily discipline, and the living fountain of ideals
The day of Rawal Kanhad Dev was as regular as a temple bell. Awakening in the stillness before dawn, Rawal Kanhad Dev bathed, said the morning prayers, and visited the shrine of Sri Tanot Mata, the desert guardian of the Bhatis with a simple offering. Then came a ride and weapons-drill, followed by a tour of the city - often in disguise, sometimes accompanied by one old bodyguard and no other retinue. In that disguise Rawal Kanhad Dev visited the grain markets, tasted the water at the public wells, sat in village schools, and listened to the women drawing water at the step-well. Nothing gave a truer picture of the kingdom.
The midday court was long, and grew longer when there were many petitions. Rawal Kanhad Dev never hurried a hearing. The youngest chowkidar's complaint outranked the longest minister's speech; a forged document was detected as often by the tone of the petitioner's voice as by the royal clerk's seals. One story has it that a small cultivator once came before the throne with a petition against a great chief, claiming his land had been seized. The chief produced sealed papers; Rawal Kanhad Dev studied them, sent a confidential commission to measure the actual fields, and then - in full court, before all the crown officers - restored the land to the cultivator and imposed a heavy fine on the chief. It became a byword: 'The court of Rawal Kanhad Dev is the only pilgrim centre where a poor man can hope to arrive first.'
In the evenings Rawal Kanhad Dev withdrew to the private library: Puranas, old chronicles, the aphorisms of Chanakya, grammar, poetics. Sometimes poets recited new compositions; sometimes instrumentalists played into the small hours. Popular traditions such as “that they were humble, just, and truly brave” still remember Rawal Kanhad Dev not as a triumphant warrior-king, but as a ruler who was gentle with the weak, immovable with the dishonest, and always, always, within reach of his people.

rawal-bhim-dev.name: Rawal Bhim Dev
rawal-bhim-dev.title: Ruler of Jaisalmer
rawal-bhim-dev.significance: Maintained the stability of the state
rawal-bhim-dev.story:
## Rawal Bhim Dev — a name in the years after the sakas

*Rawal Bhim Dev appears in the archive's list of Bhati rulers, but the chronicles of Jaisalmer name no ruler called Bhim at this point in the line. This short account keeps to what can honestly be said.*

In the archive's list, **Rawal Bhim Dev** stands twenty-fifth among the Bhati Rawals, after **Rawal Kanhad Dev** and before **Rawal Lunakaran**, and is given the years **1340–1360 CE**. Nothing is recorded of his birth, his deeds or his death, and the name does not appear among the rulers of these decades in the Bhati genealogies.

The best-known Rawal of Jaisalmer called Bhim lived more than two centuries later. **Rawal Bhim** ruled from around **1577** to the early **1600s**, in the age of **Akbar** and **Jahangir**, when Jaisalmer had become an ally of the Mughal empire. The name in this list may be an echo of him, placed in the wrong century.

The middle decades of the fourteenth century were, in truth, a time of ruin and recovery for the Bhatis. The golden fort had suffered its first *saka* around **1299**, against the armies of **Alauddin Khalji**, and a second under **Rawal Duda** in a later war with the sultans of Delhi. The chronicles say that the kingdom was restored by **Rawal Gharsi**, who returned to Jaisalmer, rebuilt it and began the great tank of **Gadisar** below the fort, and that he was followed by **Rawal Kehar II**. These are the rulers the chronicles place in the years the archive gives to Bhim Dev.

The card's description of "stability and discipline" cannot be tested against any record. What can be said is that these were years in which the Bhatis slowly returned to their fort, and the caravan trade that would make Jaisalmer rich began to flow again.

## Highlights of his life

- **A name in the archive's list.** He is listed twenty-fifth among the Bhati Rawals, between Rawal Kanhad Dev and Rawal Lunakaran.
- **Not found in the chronicles.** The Bhati genealogies name no Rawal Bhim in the mid-fourteenth century.
- **A possible confusion.** The well-known Rawal Bhim of Jaisalmer ruled from about 1577, in the Mughal age.
- **The real rulers of the period.** The chronicles credit Rawal Gharsi with restoring Jaisalmer after the sakas, followed by Rawal Kehar II.

rawal-lunakaran.title: Ruler of Jaisalmer
rawal-lunakaran.significance: Defended Jaisalmer in the age of Humayun and Maldeo; fell in the 'half saka'
rawal-lunakaran.legacy: Died defending the golden fort against a treacherous attack, completing Jaisalmer's 'two and a half sakas'.
rawal-lunakaran.story:
## Rawal Lunakaran — the lord of the golden fort and the half saka

*Rawal Lunakaran's life comes to us through the Bhati chronicles of Jaisalmer, the Marwar khyats, the memoirs of the Mughal court and the account James Tod compiled from the bards. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

The archive once placed Rawal Lunakaran in the fourteenth century. The chronicles of Jaisalmer place him two hundred years later. He ruled the golden fort in the first half of the **sixteenth century**, from around **1530** until his death around **1550**, in the age when Babur's sons and the Afghans of Sher Shah fought for Delhi and the Rathores of Marwar were growing into the strongest power in the desert.

He was a son of **Rawal Jaitsi**, known as Jait Singh, and he grew up in a fort that remembered humiliation. The chronicles of Bikaner say that **Rao Lunkaran** of Bikaner, a namesake of our Rawal, marched into Bhati country and captured Jaitsi, releasing him only on terms. The young prince inherited the lesson of that day: Jaisalmer sat between hungry neighbours, the Rathores to the north-east and east, the Baloch and the lords of Sindh to the west, and it survived only by the strength of its walls and the cleverness of its rulers.

From the ramparts of **Sonar Qila**, the fort of yellow stone on the Trikuta hill, the boy could watch the caravans wind in from the dunes, carrying cloth, salt, dried fruit and horses between Sindh, Gujarat and the north. Every caravan paid its toll at the foot of the hill, and the merchants, many of them Jains, built temples within the walls that still stand. A Rawal of Jaisalmer had to be a warrior, but he also had to keep the roads open.

Lunakaran came to the throne around 1530, after his father's death. The bards remember him as proud, watchful and quick to suspect. His greatest neighbour was **Rao Maldeo** of Marwar, who became ruler of Jodhpur in **1532** and spent the next decades swallowing the lands around him. Lunakaran met him with a marriage. His daughter **Umade** was given to Maldeo, and the wedding became one of the most famous stories in Rajasthan.

The bards tell that on the wedding night a misunderstanding over a maidservant so wounded the Bhati princess that she refused ever to live with Maldeo as his wife. She is remembered as the **Ruthi Rani**, the queen who stayed offended. One version of the tale adds a darker thread: that Lunakaran had planned to have Maldeo killed at the wedding, and that his own queen, fearing for her daughter, warned the bridegroom. These are ballads rather than records, but they show how the two houses saw each other: kinsmen by marriage, and rivals still.

Then the wider world came to the edge of the desert. **Humayun**, defeated by **Sher Shah Suri** in **1540** and driven out of Hindustan, wandered for months in Sindh and then turned to Marwar, hoping for help from Maldeo. Help did not come, and in **1542** the fugitive emperor fled back across the Thar towards **Amarkot**, where his son **Akbar** would be born that October. The Mughal memoirists remember that march as a torment of thirst, and record that the Rawal of Jaisalmer's men barred the way and fought the exhausted travellers in Bhati country. To Lunakaran, Humayun was not yet the father of an empire; he was one more armed band crossing his land without leave.

The real danger, when it came, came from a friend. Tradition names him **Amir Ali**, an Afghan chief who had been given shelter by the Rawal. The bards tell that Amir Ali asked that the women of his household might visit the queens inside the fort, a courtesy no host could easily refuse. Covered palanquins were carried up the hill and through the gates, one after another. Inside them, the story goes, were not women but armed soldiers.

The palanquins opened inside the walls, and fighting broke out in the lanes of the fort. Lunakaran understood at once that there was no time. A *jauhar*, in which the women gave themselves to the fire, needed hours to prepare. The enemy was already within the gates. The chronicles say that the Rawal and his kinsmen did what they believed honour left them: with their own swords they took the lives of the women of the palace so that none would fall into the attackers' hands, and then they went out to fight until they fell.

Lunakaran died in that fight, around **1550**. But the fort was not lost. Bhati warriors from outside, the chronicles say, came up in time to retake the gates, and Amir Ali was killed. Because the men made their last stand but the women did not die by jauhar, Jaisalmer counts this as only half a *saka*. With the two earlier sakas, under **Rawal Mularaj** and **Rawal Ratan Singh** against **Alauddin Khalji** and later under **Rawal Duda**, it gives the golden fort its famous tally of **two and a half sakas**. Historians accept a treacherous attack on the fort and the Rawal's death defending it; the palanquins and the hour of the sword are told differently by different chroniclers.

He was succeeded by his son, **Rawal Maldev**. A generation later, under **Rawal Harraj**, Jaisalmer made its peace with Akbar, the son of the emperor whose fleeing camp Lunakaran's men had fought. The old world of desert rivalries was giving way to the Mughal age, and Lunakaran was one of the last Rawals who knew only the old one. His fort still stands above the town, and in its lanes people still speak of the night of the palanquins.

## Highlights of his life

- **Ruler of Jaisalmer (c. 1530–1550).** Son of Rawal Jaitsi, he ruled the golden fort in the first half of the sixteenth century, not the fourteenth.
- **Marriage alliance with Marwar.** He gave his daughter Umade to Rao Maldeo of Jodhpur; she is remembered in song as the Ruthi Rani.
- **Opposition to Humayun.** Mughal memoirs record that his men fought the fleeing emperor's party in the desert in 1542.
- **The half saka (c. 1550).** Tradition says the Afghan Amir Ali entered the fort with soldiers hidden in palanquins; Lunakaran fell defending it.
- **The fort held.** Bhati reinforcements retook the gates, completing Jaisalmer's famous tally of two and a half sakas.
- **Succession.** He was followed by his son, Rawal Maldev.

rawal-duda-ii.title: Ruler of Jaisalmer

## Rawal Duda II — a name across the age of the temples

*Rawal Duda II appears in the archive's list of Bhati rulers, but the chronicles of Jaisalmer know only one Rawal Duda, and he lived and died earlier. This short account keeps to what can honestly be said.*

In the archive's list, **Rawal Duda II** stands twenty-seventh among the Bhati Rawals, after **Rawal Lunakaran** and before **Rawal Jaisal II**, with a reign of fifty-five years, **1381–1436 CE**. No inscription or chronicle describes a second Duda, and nothing is recorded of such a ruler's birth, deeds or death.

The Duda whom Jaisalmer remembers is the hero of its second *saka*. The bards tell that **Rawal Duda** and his brother **Tilaksi** defied the sultans of Delhi in the fourteenth century, and that when the fort was besieged, Duda led the last charge while the women died in *jauhar*. His story belongs to the archive's earlier entry for Rawal Duda, not to the years given here.

The chronicles fill these decades with other names. **Rawal Kehar II** ruled until around **1397**, in the years of recovery after the sakas. He was followed by his son **Rawal Lakshman**, and then by **Rawal Bersi** (Vairisi), whose reigns carried Jaisalmer into the middle of the fifteenth century. These were years of peace and growing wealth. The caravan trade between Sindh, Gujarat and the north revived, and in the early fifteenth century the Jain merchants of the city began to raise the great carved **Jain temples** inside the fort, the first of them dedicated to **Parshvanath**. They remain among the finest monuments of Rajasthan.

The card's claim of a long reign that "strengthened administration and defences" cannot be tested against any record. What can be said is that the half-century it covers was one of the most fruitful in the golden fort's history, when Jaisalmer turned from war to building.

## Highlights of his life

- **A name in the archive's list.** He is listed twenty-seventh among the Bhati Rawals, between Rawal Lunakaran and Rawal Jaisal II.
- **No second Duda in the chronicles.** The only Rawal Duda the chronicles know is the hero of the second saka, in an earlier age.
- **The real rulers of the period.** The chronicles place Rawal Kehar II, Rawal Lakshman and Rawal Bersi in these decades.
- **An age of temples.** In the early fifteenth century the great Jain temples of Jaisalmer fort began to rise.

## Rawal Jaisal II — a founder's name in the fifteenth century

*Rawal Jaisal II appears in the archive's list of Bhati rulers, but the chronicles of Jaisalmer name no second Jaisal among the Rawals. This short account keeps to what can honestly be said.*

In the archive's list, **Rawal Jaisal II** stands twenty-eighth among the Bhati Rawals, after **Rawal Duda II** and before **Rawal Kehar II**, with the years **1436–1463 CE**. No inscription or chronicle describes a ruler of this name, and nothing is recorded of his birth, deeds or death.

The only Jaisal the Bhatis remember is the founder of their city. **Rawal Jaisal** left the old capital of **Lodurva** and raised a new fort on the Trikuta hill in **1156 CE**, and the city that grew beneath it still carries his name. A second Jaisal three centuries later may be a confusion with him, or a name that entered the list by mistake.

The chronicles give these decades to other rulers. **Rawal Bersi** (Vairisi) ruled until around the middle of the fifteenth century, and was followed by **Rawal Chachig Dev** and then by **Rawal Devidas**, who came to the throne around the late 1450s. In their time the Jain temples of the fort continued to rise, paid for by merchants grown rich on the caravan trade between Sindh, Gujarat and the north.

The neighbourhood was changing too. To the east, the Rathores were becoming a great power: **Rao Jodha** founded **Jodhpur** in **1459**, and within a few years his son **Bika** would ride north-west into the scrub country beyond the Bhati frontier to found a kingdom of his own. The Bhatis of Jaisalmer and of **Pugal** would spend the next generations contending with these new neighbours.

The card's description of "cultural patronage and frontier security" cannot be attached to any ruler named Jaisal in these years. What can be said is that the period was one of temple-building at home and of rising Rathore power beyond the borders.

## Highlights of his life

- **A name in the archive's list.** He is listed twenty-eighth among the Bhati Rawals, between Rawal Duda II and Rawal Kehar II.
- **No second Jaisal in the chronicles.** The only Rawal Jaisal is the founder of Jaisalmer in 1156 CE.
- **The real rulers of the period.** The chronicles place Rawal Bersi, Rawal Chachig Dev and Rawal Devidas in these decades.
- **A changing frontier.** Rao Jodha founded Jodhpur in 1459, and the rise of the Rathores reshaped the Bhatis' eastern borders.

rawal-kehar-ii.story:
## Rawal Kehar II — the Rawal of the long recovery

*Rawal Kehar II is known chiefly from the Bhati genealogies and chronicles of Jaisalmer, which James Tod later set down. No inscription tells his story in detail, so this account keeps close to what the chronicles say and to the real history of his age, and says so where the record is thin.*

The archive once placed Rawal Kehar II in the late fifteenth century. The chronicles of Jaisalmer place him a hundred years earlier, in the second half of the **fourteenth century**, roughly from the **1360s** to the **1390s**. His reign belongs to the years when the golden fort was slowly coming back to life after the darkest chapter in its history.

To understand Kehar, one must begin with the ruins he inherited. Twice within living memory, the bards say, Jaisalmer had chosen death over surrender. Around **1299**, after a long siege by the armies of **Alauddin Khalji**, **Rawal Mularaj** and **Rawal Ratan Singh** had led the first *saka*, and the women of the fort had died in *jauhar*. Some decades later, under **Rawal Duda**, the same fate fell on the fort a second time, in a war with the sultans of Delhi. For a time, the chronicles suggest, the fort stood half empty, its Bhati lords scattered among the villages and sand-hills of the Thar.

The man who brought them back was **Rawal Gharsi**. The bards say he won the favour of the court of Delhi, returned to Jaisalmer and set about rebuilding it. His most lasting work was water. Below the fort he began the great tank that still bears his name, **Gadisar**, the lake of Gharsi, which for centuries held the rain that kept the city alive. But tradition says Gharsi was killed by rivals among his own kinsmen, and the throne passed out of his direct line.

Here Kehar enters the story. The chronicles make him a prince of a collateral branch of the Bhati house, raised to the throne after Gharsi's death. Tradition gives an important part in this to Gharsi's widow, the queen remembered as **Rani Vimla**, who is said to have completed her husband's tank and supported Kehar's succession. The details vary from one telling to another, and the exact year is uncertain, but it was in this way, the bards say, that the line of Jaisalmer was carried forward.

The young Rawal came to power in a changing world. In Delhi, **Firoz Shah Tughlaq** ruled a sultanate that was large but no longer hungry for distant conquest. Firoz was a builder of canals and mosques rather than a besieger of desert forts, and in his long reign the pressure that had twice destroyed Jaisalmer eased. When he died in **1388**, the sultanate fell into civil war between his grandsons, and the hold of Delhi over Rajasthan loosened further. For the desert kingdoms, these were years in which a careful ruler could rebuild.

That, as far as the record shows, is what Kehar did. The chronicles do not credit him with famous battles or great conquests. They remember him instead as a ruler under whom Jaisalmer recovered its people and its strength. Imagine the fort in those years: Bhati families returning to houses that had stood empty, masons repairing walls scarred by siege, priests relighting lamps in the temples, and below the hill the waters of Gadisar spreading after the rains. The caravans between Sindh, Gujarat and the north came back too, paying toll at the gates. Trade, more than war, would make the city rich again.

Kehar's most enduring legacy lay in his sons. The chronicles give him many, and their descendants spread the Bhati name across the desert. One of them, **Kelan**, rode out to the north-east and won lands of his own. His line became the Kelan Bhatis, and they established themselves at **Pugal** and the country around it. A few generations later the Bhati chief of Pugal, **Rao Shekha**, would give his daughter in marriage to **Rao Bika**, the founder of Bikaner, and his house would play a part in the making of that new Rathore state. From a single Rawal's family, the Bhati clans thus spread across the borderlands of the Thar.

The end of the fourteenth century brought a storm that showed how fragile the desert world still was. In **1398**, the Central Asian conqueror **Timur** crossed into India. On his way to Delhi he stormed **Bhatner**, the fort on the old north-western road, held by a Bhati chief, and massacred many of its people. Jaisalmer itself lay far to the south-west, outside Timur's path, and the golden fort was spared. But the news of Bhatner, coming at the end of Kehar's reign or just after it, would have reminded every Bhati lord that the peace of the recovery years could vanish in a single season.

Kehar died in the closing years of the fourteenth century; the chronicles' date is commonly given as around **1397**. He was succeeded by his son, **Rawal Lakshman**. In the reign of Lakshman and the rulers after him, the merchants of Jaisalmer began building the great **Jain temples** inside the fort, whose carved stone still draws visitors today. Those temples were the fruit of the long peace and the revived trade that Kehar's reign had helped to restore.

He is not one of the heroes of the Jaisalmer ballads. But a kingdom that had twice been destroyed needed a ruler who could let it heal, and the chronicles remember Kehar as that ruler.

## Highlights of his life

- **Ruler of Jaisalmer in the late fourteenth century.** The chronicles place his reign roughly from the 1360s to around 1397, not in the fifteenth century.
- **Successor of Rawal Gharsi.** Tradition says he came from a collateral branch and was raised to the throne after Gharsi's death, with the support of Gharsi's widow.
- **Years of recovery.** His reign fell in the quieter decades after the two sakas, when the fort was repopulated and trade revived.
- **Father of the Kelan Bhatis.** His son Kelan founded the line that established itself at Pugal on the north-eastern frontier.
- **A spared fort.** Timur's invasion of 1398 sacked the Bhati fort of Bhatner but did not reach Jaisalmer.
- **Succession.** He was followed by his son, Rawal Lakshman, in whose time the great Jain temples of the fort began to rise.

## Rawal Devidas II — a name on the eve of the Mughal age

*Rawal Devidas II appears in the archive's list of Bhati rulers, but the chronicles of Jaisalmer know only one Rawal Devidas, and the years given here belong largely to his son. This short account keeps to what can honestly be said.*

In the archive's list, **Rawal Devidas II** stands thirtieth among the Bhati Rawals, after **Rawal Kehar II** and before **Rawal Harraj**, with the years **1492–1530 CE**. No inscription or chronicle describes a second Devidas, and nothing is recorded of such a ruler's birth, deeds or death.

The chronicles do remember a **Rawal Devidas**, who came to the throne around the late **1450s** and ruled until the 1490s. His reign, as far as it is known, belongs to the end of the period the archive gives here, not to its whole span. He was followed by his son **Rawal Jaitsi**, known as Jait Singh, and it is Jaitsi whom the chronicles place on the throne in most of the years from the 1490s to around **1530**.

Those were hard years on the eastern frontier. The new Rathore kingdom of **Bikaner**, founded by **Rao Bika** in **1488**, pressed against the Bhati lands, and the Bikaner chronicles say that **Rao Lunkaran** of Bikaner marched into Bhati country and captured Rawal Jaitsi, releasing him only on terms. Inside the fort, meanwhile, the merchants of Jaisalmer continued to build and endow the Jain temples that had been rising for nearly a century, for the caravan roads between Sindh, Gujarat and the north still brought wealth to the golden city.

When Jaitsi died, around 1530, he was followed by his son **Rawal Lunakaran**, who would fall defending the fort in the "half saka" around 1550. The card's description of "stabilisation of power" cannot be tested against any record of a Devidas II. What can be said is that these were the last decades before the Mughal empire reached the desert.

## Highlights of his life

- **A name in the archive's list.** He is listed thirtieth among the Bhati Rawals, between Rawal Kehar II and Rawal Harraj.
- **Only one Devidas in the chronicles.** The chronicles' Rawal Devidas ruled from around the late 1450s into the 1490s.
- **The real ruler of these years.** Most of the period belongs to Rawal Jaitsi, whom the Bikaner chronicles say Rao Lunkaran captured and released on terms.
- **Succession.** Jaitsi was followed around 1530 by his son Rawal Lunakaran.

rawal-harraj.title: Ruler of Jaisalmer
rawal-harraj.significance: Accepted Akbar's overlordship at Nagaur in 1570, keeping Jaisalmer under Bhati rule
rawal-harraj.legacy: Secured his dynasty through the Mughal alliance and patronised the poet Kushallabh, author of Dhola Maru ri Chaupai.
rawal-harraj.story:
## Rawal Harraj — the desert king who made terms with Akbar

*Rawal Harraj's life comes to us through the chronicles of Jaisalmer, the Mughal histories of Akbar's reign and the colophons of the poets he patronised. His birth date and much of his private life are not recorded; where tradition fills the gaps, this story says so.*

Far to the west of Rajasthan, where the sand rolls on towards Sindh, the golden fort of **Jaisalmer** rises from the Trikuta hill. It had been founded by **Rawal Jaisal** in 1156, and for four centuries it had been the seat of the **Bhati** Rajputs, who traced their line to the Yadavas and to Krishna himself. Their kingdom was poor in rain and rich in distance. Caravans of camels crossed it on their way between Sindh, Multan, Gujarat and the plains of the north, and the merchants of the city, many of them Jains, grew wealthy on that trade.

Harraj was born into this house in the first half of the sixteenth century, a son of **Rawal Maldev**. The year of his birth is not recorded. He grew up inside the honey-coloured walls of the fort, among bastions, temples and narrow lanes, and he grew up in a time of hard memories. The chronicles of Jaisalmer tell that in the reign of his grandfather, **Rawal Lunkaran**, an Afghan chief who had been given shelter by the Bhatis tried to seize the fort by treachery. Lunkaran died fighting, and tradition says there was no time for the women to perform jauhar, so they died at the hands of their own men. The bards remember it as the **"half saka"** of Jaisalmer. For a boy of the royal house, it was a lesson that a desert fort could be lost not only to great armies but to a single act of trust misplaced.

The family had ties across Rajasthan. Harraj's aunt, **Umade**, a daughter of Lunkaran, had been married to **Rao Maldev** of Marwar, the most powerful Rathor ruler of his age. Their marriage became famous for its quarrel: tradition says that Umade, offended on her wedding night, refused ever to live with her husband, and she is remembered in Rajasthan as the **Ruthi Rani**, the queen who sulked. Behind the story lay a harder truth. Marwar's ruler was pressing on every neighbour, and the Bhatis had to watch their eastern frontier with care.

The wider world was changing too. In **1541**, before Harraj came to the throne, the fugitive Mughal emperor **Humayun**, driven out of Hindustan by Sher Shah Sur, had crossed the deserts of western Rajasthan on his way to Sindh, harassed and turned away by the chiefs whose land he crossed. Few in the fort could have guessed that his son would one day decide the fate of every Rajput house.

Harraj became Rawal of Jaisalmer in **1561**, after the death of his father. Akbar had taken power in his own right only the year before, and over the following decade the young emperor turned his attention to Rajasthan. Amber made an alliance with him in 1562. Merta fell. In 1568 Chittor was stormed after a long siege, and in 1569 Ranthambore surrendered. Every Rajput ruler now had to decide whether to resist the Mughals in the open, as Mewar chose to do, or to make terms that would keep his house on its throne.

The decision came in **1570**, when Akbar held court at **Nagaur**, on the edge of the desert. There **Rao Kalyan Mal** of Bikaner and his son **Rai Singh** came to submit, and Rawal Harraj of Jaisalmer also accepted the emperor's overlordship. As a mark of the alliance, a daughter of Harraj was married to Akbar. The Mughal histories record that **Raja Bhagwant Das** of Amber was sent to escort the bride from Jaisalmer.

One can imagine the debate in the fort before that choice was made: old nobles remembering the half saka and the long Bhati tradition of standing alone, younger men pointing out that no fort in the desert could hold out against an empire that had just taken Chittor. Whatever was said, Harraj chose survival. The result was that Jaisalmer kept its own rulers, its own law and its own customs, while its frontier was now backed by the power of the empire rather than exposed to it. The cost was the independence that the Bhatis had known for four hundred years.

Harraj was not only a ruler of treaties. His reign is remembered in the history of Rajasthani literature. The Jain poet **Kushallabh**, who lived at Jaisalmer, composed his celebrated version of the love story of **Dhola and Maru**, *Dhola Maru ri Chaupai*, around 1561, and his own verses say that he wrote it at the wish of Harraj. The same poet is credited with *Pingal Shiromani*, a work on prosody associated with the Rawal's court. Through such patronage, the songs of the desert, of Dhola riding through the night to find Maru, were set down in a form that has lasted to this day.

In the city below the fort, the Jain merchant families went on building and endowing their temples and libraries, and the caravan trade that fed the kingdom continued. The Mughal peace, uneasy as it was, made the roads safer for the camel trains, and Jaisalmer's markets drew goods from Sindh, Gujarat and beyond. Harraj's rule seems to have been steady rather than dramatic, and the chronicles do not record great wars fought by him after the settlement with Akbar.

Rawal Harraj died in **1577**. He was succeeded by his son **Rawal Bhim**, who rose high in Mughal service and whose daughter would later marry Prince Salim, the future emperor Jahangir. The bond that Harraj had made at Nagaur thus passed to the next generation, and for more than a century afterwards the Bhatis of Jaisalmer held their desert kingdom as allies of the Mughal throne.

## Highlights of his life

- **Heir of a wounded house.** Grew up in the shadow of the "half saka" of his grandfather Rawal Lunkaran, when the fort was nearly lost to treachery.
- **Accession in 1561.** Succeeded his father Rawal Maldev at a time when Akbar was beginning his campaigns in Rajasthan.
- **The Nagaur settlement of 1570.** Accepted Akbar's overlordship and gave a daughter in marriage to the emperor, securing his dynasty's rule over Jaisalmer.
- **Patron of literature.** The Jain poet Kushallabh wrote *Dhola Maru ri Chaupai* at his wish, preserving one of Rajasthan's best-loved love stories.
- **Keeper of the caravan kingdom.** His reign kept Jaisalmer's trade and temples flourishing under the new Mughal order.
- **Succession.** He died in 1577 and was followed by his son Rawal Bhim.
