rawal-manohardas.title: Ruler of Jaisalmer
rawal-manohardas.significance: Ruled Jaisalmer as a Mughal ally through the reign of Shah Jahan
rawal-manohardas.legacy: Kept the desert kingdom steady; his death without a son led to Sabal Singh's Mughal-backed accession.
rawal-manohardas.story:
## Rawal Manohardas — the last of Kalyandas's line on the golden throne

*Rawal Manohardas is a quiet name in the chronicles of Jaisalmer. The genealogies of the Bhatis and the wider history of Shah Jahan's empire give us the frame of his reign, but few deeds of his own are recorded; this story keeps to that frame and does not invent what the sources do not say.*

In the early seventeenth century the fort of **Jaisalmer** stood as it had stood since **Rawal Jaisal** founded it in 1156: a crown of yellow sandstone on the Trikuta hill, looking out over an ocean of dunes. The **Bhati** Rajputs who ruled there traced their descent from the Yadavas and from Krishna, and they had held this harsh land through siege, famine and the long wars of the desert. By the time Manohardas was born, however, their world had changed. Since **1570**, when **Rawal Harraj** accepted Akbar's overlordship at Nagaur, the rulers of Jaisalmer had been allies of the Mughal empire, holding their kingdom under its protection.

Manohardas was the son of **Rawal Kalyandas**. His birth year is not recorded, but he grew up in a family whose path to power had been shaped directly by the Mughal court. His uncle, **Rawal Bhim**, had served the empire with distinction, and Bhim's daughter had been married to Prince Salim, who became the emperor **Jahangir**. When Bhim died and his infant son did not survive, it was Jahangir who summoned Kalyandas and gave him the title of Rawal. The boy Manohardas therefore learned early that the throne of Jaisalmer rested on two foundations: the loyalty of the Bhati nobles at home, and the favour of the emperor far away in Agra or Lahore.

The fort in which he grew up was a city in itself. Its palaces looked down on the temples of the Jain merchant families, whose carved stone shrines and libraries of palm-leaf manuscripts were already centuries old. Below the walls, the bazaars handled goods that came by camel from Sindh, Multan and Gujarat: cloth, salt, dried fruit, indigo and horses. The Rawal's revenue came less from the thin harvests of the desert than from these caravans, and every ruler of Jaisalmer had to keep the roads open and the raiders in check.

Manohardas succeeded his father around **1627**. Within a year the Mughal throne also changed hands, when **Shah Jahan** became emperor in 1628. For the next two decades Manohardas ruled as one of the many Rajput princes bound to the court of the builder of the Taj Mahal. That meant sending contingents of Bhati horsemen when the emperor called, paying respect at court, and keeping his own kingdom quiet. The records do not tell us which campaigns his men joined, but Shah Jahan's reign was full of them, from the Deccan in the south to Balkh and Kandahar in the north-west, and the Rajput states supplied many of the soldiers who fought them.

At home, the pressures were older than the Mughals. Jaisalmer's neighbours, the Rathor kingdoms of **Bikaner** and **Marwar**, had long disputed the border lands and the towns between them. Pokaran and the villages around it had changed hands more than once in earlier generations, and the Bhatis guarded their claims jealously. In the west lay the open country towards Sindh, where pastoral clans moved with their herds and raids could come without warning. A Rawal of Jaisalmer had to keep his frontier chiefs loyal, his wells guarded and his forts manned.

We do not know the details of how Manohardas met these tasks. The chronicles name no great war of his, no famous siege and no new treaty. This silence is itself a kind of history. It suggests that his reign, coming in the long noon of Mughal power, was a time when the desert kingdom kept its place without great upheaval. The camel trains continued, the merchants of the city prospered, and the walls of the fort, repaired and maintained as every generation had to maintain them, still stood unbroken.

One can imagine the life of the court in those years: the Rawal holding darbar in the palace of the fort, receiving the reports of his frontier chiefs, hearing petitions from merchants and herders, and listening in the evenings to the bards who sang of the old Bhati heroes. The desert taught patience. A ruler who could not command rain had to command loyalty instead, and the chronicles' silence about rebellion in his time suggests that he did.

The great weakness of his reign lay in his own family. Manohardas had no son to succeed him. In a Rajput state, a failure of the direct line was a dangerous moment, because every branch of the royal clan might press its own candidate, and an emperor might decide the matter in his own interest.

Rawal Manohardas died around **1650**, leaving no direct heir. The nobles of Jaisalmer placed **Ramchandra**, a kinsman, on the throne, but his rule was brief. **Sabal Singh**, a Bhati of another branch of the royal house who had served in the Mughal armies, won the support of Shah Jahan and took the throne for himself. With Manohardas, the line of Kalyandas came to an end, and the succession of Jaisalmer passed once again through the hands of the Mughal emperor.

## Highlights of his life

- **Son of Rawal Kalyandas.** He belonged to the branch of the Bhati house raised to power by Jahangir after the death of Rawal Bhim.
- **Accession around 1627.** He came to the throne on the eve of Shah Jahan's accession and ruled through most of that emperor's reign.
- **Ally of the Mughal court.** Like his predecessors since 1570, he held Jaisalmer as a Mughal ally, and Bhati contingents served the empire.
- **Keeper of the desert frontier.** His reign is not remembered for wars, and Jaisalmer's caravan trade and Jain merchant community continued to flourish.
- **A failed succession.** He died around 1650 without a son, opening a struggle that ended with Sabal Singh taking the throne with Mughal support.

rawal-kalyan-das.title: Ruler of Jaisalmer
rawal-kalyan-das.significance: Raised to the throne by Jahangir after the death of his brother Rawal Bhim
rawal-kalyan-das.legacy: Held Jaisalmer in peace as a Mughal ally and passed the throne to his son Manohardas.
rawal-kalyan-das.story:
## Rawal Kalyan Das — the brother called to the throne by an emperor

*Rawal Kalyan Das appears in the chronicles of Jaisalmer and, briefly, in the memoirs of the emperor Jahangir, who tells how he came to the throne. The rest of his life must be read through the history of his family and his age; where the record is silent, this story says so.*

The Bhati Rajputs of **Jaisalmer** were among the oldest ruling houses of Rajasthan. Their fort, raised by **Rawal Jaisal** in 1156 on the Trikuta hill, glowed gold above the Thar desert, and their bards traced the clan back through the Yadavas to Krishna. For centuries the Bhatis had lived by the sword and by the caravan trade, guarding the routes that carried goods between Sindh, Multan, Gujarat and the north.

Kalyan Das was born in the sixteenth century, a son of **Rawal Harraj**, the ruler who in **1570** had accepted Akbar's overlordship at Nagaur and given a daughter in marriage to the emperor. The year of Kalyan's birth is not recorded. He grew up as a younger son in the palace of the fort, in a kingdom that had just made the great decision of its century: to survive as an ally of the Mughals rather than to fight them in the open, as Mewar did.

When Harraj died in **1577**, the throne went to Kalyan's elder brother, **Rawal Bhim**. For a younger son, the path was the usual one for Rajput princes of the age: service, loyalty to the head of the house, and patience. Bhim proved a strong and respected ruler. He served the Mughal empire with distinction, and his standing at court was high. His daughter was married to Prince **Salim**, Akbar's heir, who gave her the title **Malika-i-Jahan**, "queen of the world". The bond between Jaisalmer and the Mughal house was now a family bond in two generations.

For more than thirty years Kalyan Das lived in his brother's shadow. We do not know what offices he held or what campaigns he joined, but Bhati princes of the time commonly led their clan's contingents or held lands and forts on behalf of the ruler. The deserts around Jaisalmer demanded constant watchfulness. To the east, the Rathor kingdoms of **Marwar** and **Bikaner** disputed border towns and grazing lands. To the west, the open country towards Sindh brought raids from pastoral clans. A prince of the house learned to ride through the dunes at night, to read the wells and the stars, and to hold a frontier with a handful of horsemen.

Then, around **1613**, Rawal Bhim died. He left a son who was only an infant, and the child did not live long. Jaisalmer was suddenly without a clear heir, and in such moments a Rajput state could easily fall into faction and civil war.

The decision was taken not in the fort but at the Mughal court. **Jahangir**, now emperor, wrote of the matter in his memoirs. He remembered Bhim as a man of rank and standing, recalled that as a prince he had married Bhim's daughter, and recorded that he sent for Kalyan of Jaisalmer, Bhim's brother, and gave him the title of **Rawal**. With that imperial recognition, Kalyan Das became ruler of Jaisalmer.

It is easy to picture the scene: the desert prince, no longer young, travelling to the imperial camp, bowing before the emperor who was also his niece's husband, and receiving the robe of honour and the mark of kingship. For Jaisalmer, it showed how much had changed since the days of Rawal Jaisal. The throne still belonged to the Bhatis, and the nobles still had to accept their ruler, but the emperor's word now carried decisive weight.

As ruler, Kalyan Das governed a kingdom that was at peace with its overlord and prosperous in its trade. The Jain merchants of the city continued to build and endow their temples and libraries, and the caravans continued to cross the desert under the protection of the Mughal order. Later summaries credit him with attention to administration and the economy, but the chronicles preserve no specific reforms in his name, and this story does not invent them. What can be said is that his reign was not remembered as a time of disaster: no siege of the fort, no saka and no lost war is recorded under him.

The duties of a Mughal ally continued. Bhati horsemen were expected to serve when the emperor called, and Jahangir's reign saw campaigns in the Deccan, in Mewar until the peace of 1615, and on the north-western frontier. At home, the Rawal had to keep his frontier chiefs loyal and the border with the Rathors quiet, and to manage the scarce water and thin harvests of a land where a single failed monsoon could mean famine.

Kalyan Das ruled for roughly fourteen years. He died around **1627**, at almost the same time as Jahangir himself, and was succeeded by his son **Manohardas**. The branch of the Bhati house that an emperor had raised to the throne would hold it for one more generation, until Manohardas died without a son around 1650.

## Highlights of his life

- **Son of Rawal Harraj.** He was born into the Bhati house that had made its alliance with Akbar at Nagaur in 1570.
- **Brother of Rawal Bhim.** He spent decades as a younger prince during the strong reign of his brother, whose daughter married Jahangir.
- **Raised to the throne by Jahangir.** After Bhim's death around 1613 and the death of Bhim's infant son, Jahangir summoned Kalyan and gave him the title of Rawal, as the emperor records in his memoirs.
- **A peaceful reign.** No siege or major war is recorded in his time, and Jaisalmer's trade and Jain community continued to prosper.
- **Succession.** He died around 1627 and was succeeded by his son Rawal Manohardas.

rawal-bairisal-i.name: Rawal Bairisal
rawal-bairisal-i.title: Ruler of Jaisalmer
rawal-bairisal-i.significance: Ruled Jaisalmer when the Jain temple of Sambhavnath and the Jinabhadra Suri library were founded in the fort
rawal-bairisal-i.legacy: His reign belongs to the fifteenth-century revival of Jaisalmer as a city of temples, trade and learning.
rawal-bairisal-i.story:
## Rawal Bairisal — a desert king in the age of temple-builders

*Rawal Bairisal, called Vairisimha in Sanskrit inscriptions, is known to us mainly from the Bhati genealogies and from the Jain temple inscriptions of Jaisalmer fort, which name the Rawal in whose reign they were raised. Some later lists misplace a Rawal Bairisal in the Mughal age, but the ruler of this name belongs to the fifteenth century. Few personal details survive, and this story does not invent them.*

In the fifteenth century the fort of **Jaisalmer** was already nearly three hundred years old. **Rawal Jaisal** had founded it in 1156 on the Trikuta hill, and its walls of yellow sandstone had since seen siege and sack. The bards of the **Bhati** Rajputs told of the terrible sakas of earlier generations, when the men of the fort had ridden out to die and the women had chosen the fire of jauhar rather than captivity. By the time Bairisal was born, those days were memories, and Jaisalmer had been rebuilt and repeopled. The Bhatis, who traced their descent from the Yadavas and from Krishna, ruled once more from the golden rock.

Bairisal was born into the royal house in the late fourteenth or early fifteenth century. The exact year, the name of his mother and the details of his childhood are not recorded. He grew up in a kingdom whose wealth came less from its sparse fields than from its position. Caravans of camels crossed the Thar between Sindh and Multan in the west and Gujarat, Malwa and the Ganga plains in the east, and Jaisalmer sat across their path. The merchants who handled this trade, many of them Jains of the Oswal community, had settled inside the fort and in the town below, and their prosperity was the kingdom's prosperity.

The world beyond the dunes had become more open and more dangerous at once. The Delhi Sultanate had been shattered by the invasion of **Timur** in 1398, and in its place new regional powers had risen. The Sultans of **Gujarat** and **Malwa** were building strong kingdoms to the south and south-east. In Mewar, **Rana Kumbha** came to the throne in 1433 and began the great forts and temples for which he is remembered. Closer to Jaisalmer, the **Rathors** of Marwar were growing in strength under Rao Ranmal and his son Rao Jodha, and to the west the rulers of Sindh and Multan watched the desert routes. A Bhati ruler had to defend his frontier against all of them while keeping the caravan roads safe.

Bairisal succeeded **Rawal Lakshman**, in whose reign the first of Jaisalmer's great Jain temples, dedicated to **Parshvanath**, had been consecrated in the fort. The traditional lists place Bairisal's own reign in the 1430s and 1440s. He came to power, therefore, at the same time as Rana Kumbha in Mewar, and his reign belonged to that same age of building.

The clearest mark of his rule is in stone. During his reign the Jain community of Jaisalmer raised the temple of **Sambhavnath** inside the fort, and its inscriptions name the Rawal in whose kingdom it was built. Beneath this temple was placed the great library of manuscripts gathered by the Jain teacher **Jinabhadra Suri**, which became one of the most precious collections of palm-leaf and paper manuscripts in India. Texts in Sanskrit, Prakrit and Apabhramsha, on religion, grammar, poetry and science, were copied and kept there, some of them older than the fort itself. The desert's dry air and the care of generations of monks preserved them.

That such work could happen tells us something about the ruler. A temple of this kind took years to build and required the security of the town, the goodwill of the court and the confidence of the merchants who paid for it. The Rawals of Jaisalmer were Hindus and worshipped the gods of their own tradition, but they allowed and protected the faith of the Jains who lived under them. In the shared space of the fort, the Rawal's palace, the shrines of his household gods and the carved Jain temples stood within a few hundred paces of one another.

We can imagine the court of those years: the Rawal sitting in darbar among his Bhati nobles, receiving news of the caravans, of the rains or their failure, of raiders seen near the wells to the west; Jain merchants coming to seek permission for a new shrine; bards reciting the deeds of Jaisal and the heroes of the old sakas. The chronicles, however, record no named battles of Bairisal and no famous campaigns. Whatever wars he fought on his frontiers have not come down to us in detail, and it would be false to invent them.

What the record does show is continuity. Under Lakshman and Bairisal, and the rulers who followed them, Jaisalmer recovered from the disasters of the fourteenth century and became the city of carved stone that travellers still admire. The temples built in the fort in the fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, one after another, form one of the finest groups of Jain architecture in western India, and Bairisal's reign stands near the beginning of that great age.

Rawal Bairisal died around the middle of the fifteenth century, and the traditional lists name **Rawal Chachig Dev** as his successor. The kingdom he left was still small, poor in rain and surrounded by stronger neighbours, but it was secure, its trade was flowing, and its fort held treasures of learning that would outlast every army that crossed the desert.

## Highlights of his life

- **Ruler in the fifteenth century.** He reigned over Jaisalmer in the second quarter of the fifteenth century, after Rawal Lakshman, in the age of Rana Kumbha and the rising Rathors.
- **The Sambhavnath temple.** The Jain temple of Sambhavnath in Jaisalmer fort was built during his reign, and its inscriptions name him.
- **Protector of the Jinabhadra Suri library.** The great manuscript library of Jaisalmer was established beneath that temple in his time, preserving texts of immense value.
- **Keeper of the caravan kingdom.** He held the desert routes between Sindh, Multan and Gujarat in an age of new regional powers.
- **Part of Jaisalmer's revival.** His reign belongs to the period in which Jaisalmer recovered from earlier sakas and grew into a city of carved stone.
- **Succession.** He was followed, according to the traditional lists, by Rawal Chachig Dev.

rawal-amar-singh.name: Rawal Amar Singh
rawal-amar-singh.title: Ruler of Jaisalmer
rawal-amar-singh.story:
Early life and the depth of lineage
Rawal Amar Singh was born in the heart of the Thar, with endless dunes and caravan tracks, a landscape where the memory of the Jaisalmer (Bhati) was kept alive not by stone inscriptions alone, but by bards who walked from village to village, by mothers who sang lullabies of old battles, and by clan-councils held under the ancient banyan. 1619-1648 CE was an age when every fort had its own ghost, every pass its own tradition, and every shrine its own protective vow. The clan deity, Sri Tanot Mata, the desert guardian of the Bhatis, was worshipped with a lamp that never went out; caravans stopped before entering the hills; and sentinels watched every waterhole through the night. It was in such a world that Rawal Amar Singh grew up, sitting at the knee of Ruler Bhati Rajputs Ancestor and learning the first, cruel truth of Rajput kingship: that the throne is not comfort, but a vow.
Their education was deliberately rounded. The four martial sciences - bow, horse, sword, and mace - were taught before the letters of the alphabet. Then came the shastras, but never only from books. Economics was taught from the account-books of a merchant caravan. Statecraft was taught from a rebel chieftain's forgiven letter. Justice was taught from the actual hearing of a widow's land dispute in the village chaupal. Music and painting were not ornaments; they were meant to train eye and ear, so that a king could read the lie in a courtier's salute and the truth in the murmur of a crowd.
From the queen-mother, Rawal Amar Singh received an even more difficult lesson: a king's courage is not proven on the battlefield alone. It is proven when he listens silently to a complaint he does not want to hear, when he feeds the hungry before his own table, when he keeps his word to a weaker ally even if every minister advises him otherwise. These quiet disciplines were rehearsed long before the coronation, and they gave Rawal Amar Singh a steadiness of temper that would later be noted by every chronicler of Jaisalmer (Bhati).

Ascension and the trials of succession
When the reign of Ruler Bhati Rajputs Ancestor closed, Rawal Amar Singh was invested with the five symbols of the Jaisalmer (Bhati) at Jaisalmer: the clan-tilak, the talismanic armour, the ancestral sword, the signet ring, and the turban of honour. The ceremonies were magnificent, but no sooner had the last hymn ended than the new ruler was tested. A group of feudatories - calculating on the sovereign's youth - withheld tribute. Others launched cattle-raids along the border. Still others opened secret correspondence with a neighbouring kingdom, hoping to carve out independent shares.
Rawal Amar Singh refused a hasty punitive war. Instead, a threefold policy was announced. Every rebel chief - without exception - received a personal letter, written in ink but sealed with the same signet that would later seal the punishment: it reaffirmed their ancient rights, welcomed them to the council, and invited them to the capital. Those who accepted were received with the same dignity they had known under Ruler Bhati Rajputs Ancestor. Those who persisted in open rebellion were dealt with by a carefully chosen commander, with strict orders that the fields of ordinary cultivators should not be trampled and no market-town be looted. The families of the leading chiefs were also invited to send their sons to be trained in the royal court, as pages, cavalry officers, and scholars.
Within a single year the troubles collapsed. The border was sealed, the tribute-chests were full again, and even the most sceptical old chieftain admitted that Rawal Amar Singh had the two rarest qualities in a king: patience without softness, and resolution without cruelty. From this episode a new convention grew up within the Jaisalmer (Bhati): no loyal family would ever be displaced merely because the crown had changed hands.

Military campaigns, strategy, and the mark of valour
Under Rawal Amar Singh the Jaisalmer (Bhati) army was reshaped into a far more cohesive instrument of war. The old feudal contingents were supplemented by standing regiments organised by arm: heavy infantry, bowmen, cavalry squadrons, elephant corps, batteries of light guns, companies of skirmishers, siege-engineering teams, and a dedicated espionage wing. Each of these was placed under a professional commandant reporting directly to Rawal Amar Singh, so that in a crisis blame could not travel down and credit could not travel up.
Campaigns such as “border-security expeditions”, “suppression of local uprisings” illustrate the methodical nature of that military mind. Before every major operation, reconnaissance parties travelled far ahead - disguised as mendicants, as grain-merchants, as cattle-drovers - counting the enemy's tents, inspecting the wells, watching the routes by which fodder and water reached their camps, and even counting the daily movements of their cavalry patrols. Only after that data had been compared with the reports of the astrologer, the priest performing the campaign-havan, the chief engineer, the field-hospital surgeon, and the paymaster would Rawal Amar Singh unfurl the royal standard.
Victory was never treated as a licence. Enemy kings who surrendered were guaranteed their lives, their families' safety, and often a place in the council of the victor. Wounded soldiers of the winning side received lifelong stipends; the families of the dead received rent-free lands and annual gifts. Even the war-horses and elephants were pensioned off in royal elephant-stables and stud-farms. The result was an army that fought for more than loot: it fought for the very name of Rawal Amar Singh.

Forts, roads, water, and the labour of building for posterity
The reign of Rawal Amar Singh was a long festival of building. “repair of the old capital fort”, “border outposts and village ponds” are the obvious and still-standing witnesses, but behind them lay an entire system. Every fort, large or small, was planned as a self-contained town: quarters for the royal family, barracks for the garrison, a shrine for Sri Tanot Mata, the desert guardian of the Bhatis, houses for brahmin householders, huge granaries, dispensaries of herbal medicine, feeding-halls for the poor, and wells deep enough to withstand a siege of many years.
The road network was equally transformed. Between the principal towns, milestones, arched rest-houses, masonry step-wells, and roadside groves of shade-giving trees were set up at fixed intervals. Passes on the old caravan routes received small fortified outposts, so that merchants could move silver and spices without extra private guards. Market-places were laid out with proper lanes for separate trades, with overseers to keep weights and measures honest, grain-storehouses safe from damp, and the lanes free from encroachments.
Water management, however, was the most intimate form of building. In dry belts, johads, earthen dams, covered kunds, and lined tanks were constructed one after another. Canals drawn from the rivers began to reach villages that had always depended on the monsoon alone. Most importantly, traditional water-rights were written down for each village, witnessed by the chaupal, and registered by the royal clerk. So when drought came, the last peasant and the first thakur drew water by the same measure.

Administration, revenue, and the fundamentals of justice
Under Rawal Amar Singh the Jaisalmer (Bhati) state was split into six clear departments: military, religious endowments, revenue and treasury, commerce and caravan tolls, land settlement, and water-forest stewardship. Each was placed under a senior minister whose registers were balanced every six months by Rawal Amar Singh personally, not by clerks alone. Beyond these, provincial governors for distant tracts were appointed for fixed terms, and required to submit written returns every lunar month.
The fiscal policy was deliberately mild. Taxes on agriculture were kept low; tolls on the long-distance routes were standardised so that a merchant could predict his costs from the first milestone; and hereditary classes engaged in public service - brahmins engaged in teaching and sacrifice, village teachers, cow-sanctuaries, hospitals, and pilgrim-hostels - were kept free of any impost. Embezzlement, however, was not. A corrupt officer was not merely transferred; the whole district was audited, the sums recovered, and the offender brought to the same open court that heard the poorest cultivator.
The jewel of the reign, however, was the visible even-handedness of justice. The proudest thakur and the most ragged cowherd stood before the same bench and under the same written rules. A public audience was held every single day, without exception, where every subject - irrespective of rank, wealth, or recommendation - could walk in and place a petition into the hands of Rawal Amar Singh. Hundreds of cases were settled by the ruler in person, with the full papers spread open on the carpet before them. It was this visible, daily, approachable justice that gave the Jaisalmer (Bhati) regime a moral weight no mere army could ever buy.

Dharma, the arts, and the patronage of letters
Rawal Amar Singh was a devout ruler, yet never a sectarian one. Works such as “sustained worship of the clan deity”, “honours for local poets and musicians” made that policy visible across the entire kingdom. Temples, mosques, dargahs, and gurdwaras were all repaired; the ministers of every faith received allowances; cow-sanctuaries and hospitals for sick animals were maintained from the treasury; and dispensaries of Unani and Ayurvedic medicines were staffed by salaried physicians.
In the realm of art and craftsmanship, Rawal Amar Singh summoned masters of every school under royal protection. Architecture in stone, fresco-painting on plaster, stone-sculpture, perforated jalis, silver filigree, wood-carving, embroidery of cloth, beaten copper and brass, manuscript illumination, the forging of arms, and the exact science of fort-building - all were given workshops within the palace precincts, where apprentices learned the trade from masters in the old guru-shishya style.
Poets, bards, musicians, instrumentalists, and reciters of oral epic were given permanent stipends, seats of honour at festivals, and freedom to criticise the court as sharply as they pleased. As a result, folk literature flourished. Village-songs, bardic lays, khyals, nautch parties, and folk-plays picked up the memory of Rawal Amar Singh and carried it from the capital to the most remote hamlet. It was a cultural policy too often forgotten: true glory is not built from palaces alone, but from the voices of the people themselves.

Feudal loyalties, neighbouring states, and the diplomacy of moderation
Under Rawal Amar Singh, the compact between the Jaisalmer (Bhati) throne and its feudatories was rewritten on the clearest possible terms. Each chief's ancient dignity, his land-rights, the honours due to his family at court, and the protection of his clan during minority successions - all were confirmed in a formal patent sealed by the crown. The leading chiefs were also given seats on the permanent war-council and the revenue council, so that policy was never made behind their backs.
Marriage alliances were also used with great care. Younger members of the royal family were linked by marriage to other ruling houses, not as a bribe, but as a public guarantee that quarrels of the past would not be revived. Friendly kingdoms were kept completely autonomous; defeated kingdoms were often given back their old ruling families, only under a treaty of friendship. No ancient line was displaced merely for the crime of having lost a battle.
These exact principles were also taught, with endless patience, to Next Ruler. For Rawal Amar Singh often said that a sword's edge fades in a single campaign, but a treaty well kept, kept by both sides for a whole lifetime, can outlast a hundred victories. It was this doctrine - not force alone - that extended the shadow of the Jaisalmer (Bhati) far beyond its formal borders.

Character, daily discipline, and the living fountain of ideals
The day of Rawal Amar Singh was as regular as a temple bell. Awakening in the stillness before dawn, Rawal Amar Singh bathed, said the morning prayers, and visited the shrine of Sri Tanot Mata, the desert guardian of the Bhatis with a simple offering. Then came a ride and weapons-drill, followed by a tour of the city - often in disguise, sometimes accompanied by one old bodyguard and no other retinue. In that disguise Rawal Amar Singh visited the grain markets, tasted the water at the public wells, sat in village schools, and listened to the women drawing water at the step-well. Nothing gave a truer picture of the kingdom.
The midday court was long, and grew longer when there were many petitions. Rawal Amar Singh never hurried a hearing. The youngest chowkidar's complaint outranked the longest minister's speech; a forged document was detected as often by the tone of the petitioner's voice as by the royal clerk's seals. One story has it that a small cultivator once came before the throne with a petition against a great chief, claiming his land had been seized. The chief produced sealed papers; Rawal Amar Singh studied them, sent a confidential commission to measure the actual fields, and then - in full court, before all the crown officers - restored the land to the cultivator and imposed a heavy fine on the chief. It became a byword: 'The court of Rawal Amar Singh is the only pilgrim centre where a poor man can hope to arrive first.'
In the evenings Rawal Amar Singh withdrew to the private library: Puranas, old chronicles, the aphorisms of Chanakya, grammar, poetics. Sometimes poets recited new compositions; sometimes instrumentalists played into the small hours. Popular traditions such as “that they were humble, just, and truly brave” still remember Rawal Amar Singh not as a triumphant warrior-king, but as a ruler who was gentle with the weak, immovable with the dishonest, and always, always, within reach of his people.

One story has it that a small cultivator once came before the throne with a petition against a great chief, claiming his land had been seized. The chief produced sealed papers; Rawal Mulraj I studied them, sent a confidential commission to measure the actual fields, and then - in full court, before all the crown officers - restored the land to the cultivator and imposed a heavy fine on the chief. It became a byword: 'The court of Rawal Mulraj I is the only pilgrim centre where a poor man can hope to arrive first.'
In the evenings Rawal Mulraj I withdrew to the private library: Puranas, old chronicles, the aphorisms of Chanakya, grammar, poetics. Sometimes poets recited new compositions; sometimes instrumentalists played into the small hours. Popular traditions such as “that they were humble, just, and truly brave” still remember Rawal Mulraj I not as a triumphant warrior-king, but as a ruler who was gentle with the weak, immovable with the dishonest, and always, always, within reach of his people.

rawal-akhai-singh.name: Rawal Akhai Singh
rawal-akhai-singh.title: Ruler of Jaisalmer
rawal-akhai-singh.story:
Early life and the depth of lineage
Rawal Akhai Singh was born in the heart of the Thar, with endless dunes and caravan tracks, a landscape where the memory of the Jaisalmer (Bhati) was kept alive not by stone inscriptions alone, but by bards who walked from village to village, by mothers who sang lullabies of old battles, and by clan-councils held under the ancient banyan. 1743-1762 CE was an age when every fort had its own ghost, every pass its own tradition, and every shrine its own protective vow. The clan deity, Sri Tanot Mata, the desert guardian of the Bhatis, was worshipped with a lamp that never went out; caravans stopped before entering the hills; and sentinels watched every waterhole through the night. It was in such a world that Rawal Akhai Singh grew up, sitting at the knee of Ruler Bhati Rajputs Ancestor and learning the first, cruel truth of Rajput kingship: that the throne is not comfort, but a vow.
Their education was deliberately rounded. The four martial sciences - bow, horse, sword, and mace - were taught before the letters of the alphabet. Then came the shastras, but never only from books. Economics was taught from the account-books of a merchant caravan. Statecraft was taught from a rebel chieftain's forgiven letter. Justice was taught from the actual hearing of a widow's land dispute in the village chaupal. Music and painting were not ornaments; they were meant to train eye and ear, so that a king could read the lie in a courtier's salute and the truth in the murmur of a crowd.
From the queen-mother, Rawal Akhai Singh received an even more difficult lesson: a king's courage is not proven on the battlefield alone. It is proven when he listens silently to a complaint he does not want to hear, when he feeds the hungry before his own table, when he keeps his word to a weaker ally even if every minister advises him otherwise. These quiet disciplines were rehearsed long before the coronation, and they gave Rawal Akhai Singh a steadiness of temper that would later be noted by every chronicler of Jaisalmer (Bhati).

Ascension and the trials of succession
When the reign of Ruler Bhati Rajputs Ancestor closed, Rawal Akhai Singh was invested with the five symbols of the Jaisalmer (Bhati) at Jaisalmer: the clan-tilak, the talismanic armour, the ancestral sword, the signet ring, and the turban of honour. The ceremonies were magnificent, but no sooner had the last hymn ended than the new ruler was tested. A group of feudatories - calculating on the sovereign's youth - withheld tribute. Others launched cattle-raids along the border. Still others opened secret correspondence with a neighbouring kingdom, hoping to carve out independent shares.
Rawal Akhai Singh refused a hasty punitive war. Instead, a threefold policy was announced. Every rebel chief - without exception - received a personal letter, written in ink but sealed with the same signet that would later seal the punishment: it reaffirmed their ancient rights, welcomed them to the council, and invited them to the capital. Those who accepted were received with the same dignity they had known under Ruler Bhati Rajputs Ancestor. Those who persisted in open rebellion were dealt with by a carefully chosen commander, with strict orders that the fields of ordinary cultivators should not be trampled and no market-town be looted. The families of the leading chiefs were also invited to send their sons to be trained in the royal court, as pages, cavalry officers, and scholars.
Within a single year the troubles collapsed. The border was sealed, the tribute-chests were full again, and even the most sceptical old chieftain admitted that Rawal Akhai Singh had the two rarest qualities in a king: patience without softness, and resolution without cruelty. From this episode a new convention grew up within the Jaisalmer (Bhati): no loyal family would ever be displaced merely because the crown had changed hands.

Military campaigns, strategy, and the mark of valour
Under Rawal Akhai Singh the Jaisalmer (Bhati) army was reshaped into a far more cohesive instrument of war. The old feudal contingents were supplemented by standing regiments organised by arm: heavy infantry, bowmen, cavalry squadrons, elephant corps, batteries of light guns, companies of skirmishers, siege-engineering teams, and a dedicated espionage wing. Each of these was placed under a professional commandant reporting directly to Rawal Akhai Singh, so that in a crisis blame could not travel down and credit could not travel up.
Campaigns such as “border-security expeditions”, “suppression of local uprisings” illustrate the methodical nature of that military mind. Before every major operation, reconnaissance parties travelled far ahead - disguised as mendicants, as grain-merchants, as cattle-drovers - counting the enemy's tents, inspecting the wells, watching the routes by which fodder and water reached their camps, and even counting the daily movements of their cavalry patrols. Only after that data had been compared with the reports of the astrologer, the priest performing the campaign-havan, the chief engineer, the field-hospital surgeon, and the paymaster would Rawal Akhai Singh unfurl the royal standard.
Victory was never treated as a licence. Enemy kings who surrendered were guaranteed their lives, their families' safety, and often a place in the council of the victor. Wounded soldiers of the winning side received lifelong stipends; the families of the dead received rent-free lands and annual gifts. Even the war-horses and elephants were pensioned off in royal elephant-stables and stud-farms. The result was an army that fought for more than loot: it fought for the very name of Rawal Akhai Singh.

Forts, roads, water, and the labour of building for posterity
The reign of Rawal Akhai Singh was a long festival of building. “repair of the old capital fort”, “border outposts and village ponds” are the obvious and still-standing witnesses, but behind them lay an entire system. Every fort, large or small, was planned as a self-contained town: quarters for the royal family, barracks for the garrison, a shrine for Sri Tanot Mata, the desert guardian of the Bhatis, houses for brahmin householders, huge granaries, dispensaries of herbal medicine, feeding-halls for the poor, and wells deep enough to withstand a siege of many years.
The road network was equally transformed. Between the principal towns, milestones, arched rest-houses, masonry step-wells, and roadside groves of shade-giving trees were set up at fixed intervals. Passes on the old caravan routes received small fortified outposts, so that merchants could move silver and spices without extra private guards. Market-places were laid out with proper lanes for separate trades, with overseers to keep weights and measures honest, grain-storehouses safe from damp, and the lanes free from encroachments.
Water management, however, was the most intimate form of building. In dry belts, johads, earthen dams, covered kunds, and lined tanks were constructed one after another. Canals drawn from the rivers began to reach villages that had always depended on the monsoon alone. Most importantly, traditional water-rights were written down for each village, witnessed by the chaupal, and registered by the royal clerk. So when drought came, the last peasant and the first thakur drew water by the same measure.

Administration, revenue, and the fundamentals of justice
Under Rawal Akhai Singh the Jaisalmer (Bhati) state was split into six clear departments: military, religious endowments, revenue and treasury, commerce and caravan tolls, land settlement, and water-forest stewardship. Each was placed under a senior minister whose registers were balanced every six months by Rawal Akhai Singh personally, not by clerks alone. Beyond these, provincial governors for distant tracts were appointed for fixed terms, and required to submit written returns every lunar month.
The fiscal policy was deliberately mild. Taxes on agriculture were kept low; tolls on the long-distance routes were standardised so that a merchant could predict his costs from the first milestone; and hereditary classes engaged in public service - brahmins engaged in teaching and sacrifice, village teachers, cow-sanctuaries, hospitals, and pilgrim-hostels - were kept free of any impost. Embezzlement, however, was not. A corrupt officer was not merely transferred; the whole district was audited, the sums recovered, and the offender brought to the same open court that heard the poorest cultivator.
The jewel of the reign, however, was the visible even-handedness of justice. The proudest thakur and the most ragged cowherd stood before the same bench and under the same written rules. A public audience was held every single day, without exception, where every subject - irrespective of rank, wealth, or recommendation - could walk in and place a petition into the hands of Rawal Akhai Singh. Hundreds of cases were settled by the ruler in person, with the full papers spread open on the carpet before them. It was this visible, daily, approachable justice that gave the Jaisalmer (Bhati) regime a moral weight no mere army could ever buy.

Dharma, the arts, and the patronage of letters
Rawal Akhai Singh was a devout ruler, yet never a sectarian one. Works such as “sustained worship of the clan deity”, “honours for local poets and musicians” made that policy visible across the entire kingdom. Temples, mosques, dargahs, and gurdwaras were all repaired; the ministers of every faith received allowances; cow-sanctuaries and hospitals for sick animals were maintained from the treasury; and dispensaries of Unani and Ayurvedic medicines were staffed by salaried physicians.
In the realm of art and craftsmanship, Rawal Akhai Singh summoned masters of every school under royal protection. Architecture in stone, fresco-painting on plaster, stone-sculpture, perforated jalis, silver filigree, wood-carving, embroidery of cloth, beaten copper and brass, manuscript illumination, the forging of arms, and the exact science of fort-building - all were given workshops within the palace precincts, where apprentices learned the trade from masters in the old guru-shishya style.
Poets, bards, musicians, instrumentalists, and reciters of oral epic were given permanent stipends, seats of honour at festivals, and freedom to criticise the court as sharply as they pleased. As a result, folk literature flourished. Village-songs, bardic lays, khyals, nautch parties, and folk-plays picked up the memory of Rawal Akhai Singh and carried it from the capital to the most remote hamlet. It was a cultural policy too often forgotten: true glory is not built from palaces alone, but from the voices of the people themselves.

Feudal loyalties, neighbouring states, and the diplomacy of moderation
Under Rawal Akhai Singh, the compact between the Jaisalmer (Bhati) throne and its feudatories was rewritten on the clearest possible terms. Each chief's ancient dignity, his land-rights, the honours due to his family at court, and the protection of his clan during minority successions - all were confirmed in a formal patent sealed by the crown. The leading chiefs were also given seats on the permanent war-council and the revenue council, so that policy was never made behind their backs.
Marriage alliances were also used with great care. Younger members of the royal family were linked by marriage to other ruling houses, not as a bribe, but as a public guarantee that quarrels of the past would not be revived. Friendly kingdoms were kept completely autonomous; defeated kingdoms were often given back their old ruling families, only under a treaty of friendship. No ancient line was displaced merely for the crime of having lost a battle.
These exact principles were also taught, with endless patience, to Next Ruler. For Rawal Akhai Singh often said that a sword's edge fades in a single campaign, but a treaty well kept, kept by both sides for a whole lifetime, can outlast a hundred victories. It was this doctrine - not force alone - that extended the shadow of the Jaisalmer (Bhati) far beyond its formal borders.

Character, daily discipline, and the living fountain of ideals
The day of Rawal Akhai Singh was as regular as a temple bell. Awakening in the stillness before dawn, Rawal Akhai Singh bathed, said the morning prayers, and visited the shrine of Sri Tanot Mata, the desert guardian of the Bhatis with a simple offering. Then came a ride and weapons-drill, followed by a tour of the city - often in disguise, sometimes accompanied by one old bodyguard and no other retinue. In that disguise Rawal Akhai Singh visited the grain markets, tasted the water at the public wells, sat in village schools, and listened to the women drawing water at the step-well. Nothing gave a truer picture of the kingdom.
The midday court was long, and grew longer when there were many petitions. Rawal Akhai Singh never hurried a hearing. The youngest chowkidar's complaint outranked the longest minister's speech; a forged document was detected as often by the tone of the petitioner's voice as by the royal clerk's seals. One story has it that a small cultivator once came before the throne with a petition against a great chief, claiming his land had been seized. The chief produced sealed papers; Rawal Akhai Singh studied them, sent a confidential commission to measure the actual fields, and then - in full court, before all the crown officers - restored the land to the cultivator and imposed a heavy fine on the chief. It became a byword: 'The court of Rawal Akhai Singh is the only pilgrim centre where a poor man can hope to arrive first.'
In the evenings Rawal Akhai Singh withdrew to the private library: Puranas, old chronicles, the aphorisms of Chanakya, grammar, poetics. Sometimes poets recited new compositions; sometimes instrumentalists played into the small hours. Popular traditions such as “that they were humble, just, and truly brave” still remember Rawal Akhai Singh not as a triumphant warrior-king, but as a ruler who was gentle with the weak, immovable with the dishonest, and always, always, within reach of his people.

rawal-mulraj-ii-1762.story:
## Rawal Mulraj II — A Long Reign Between Palace Feuds and the Company's Treaty

*Mulraj II's reign is reasonably well documented: the Bhati chronicles of Jaisalmer, James Tod's "Annals of Jaisalmer" (1829–32), and the British treaty of 1818 give its outline, though Tod relied heavily on court informants and many personal details survive only in khyat and bardic tradition.*

### The desert kingdom in 1762

When **Mulraj II** succeeded his father **Rawal Akhai Singh** at **Jaisalmer** in **1762**, the Bhati kingdom was large on the map and poor in reality. It stretched across the sand seas of the western **Thar**, its wealth resting on the caravan trade that crossed between Sindh, Multan, Gujarat and the Gangetic plain, and on the bankers and merchants who lived in the walled town below the golden fort. Rainfall was scanty, the population thin, and the treasury dependent on transit duties.

The wider political world was also in upheaval. The Mughal empire, to which Jaisalmer had long paid formal allegiance, had dissolved into rival successor powers. Marathas raided and levied tribute across Rajputana, while to the west and north-west the **Daudputra** rulers of **Bahawalpur** and the Talpur Mirs of **Sindh** pressed on Bhati frontier districts. Neighbouring **Bikaner** and **Jodhpur** were rivals for the same scattered villages and wells. Jaisalmer's remoteness spared it the worst of the Maratha storms, but it could do little to stop the steady nibbling away of its outer territories during the eighteenth century.

### Ministers and a rebellious heir

The decisive feature of Mulraj's long reign was the power of his ministers. The office of **diwan** was held by **Swarup Singh**, a Mehta of the Jain mercantile community, who controlled revenue and administration. His influence alienated many of the Bhati nobles, and the heir-apparent, **Rai Singh**, became the focus of their resentment.

According to Tod and the local chronicles, Rai Singh killed Swarup Singh in open court, in his father's presence. In the turmoil that followed, a faction of nobles confined Mulraj and set up Rai Singh in charge of the state. This interlude lasted only a few months. A loyal party of chiefs, among them **Zorawar Singh**, restored the old ruler, and Rai Singh was driven into exile. He later died in confinement, and his sons were also imprisoned; the chronicles blame their deaths on the vengeance of the new minister. The exact years of these episodes are given differently in different works, and historians treat the details with caution.

That new minister was **Salim Singh**, son of the murdered Swarup Singh. Raised to the diwanship while still young, he became the most powerful man in Jaisalmer for more than three decades. Tod, who corresponded with him, portrayed him as clever, grasping and ruthless, an image that has stuck. Salim Singh broke the power of many nobles, confiscated estates and laid heavy demands on merchants and cultivators. Local tradition links his exactions to the flight of the **Paliwal Brahmins**, the prosperous farming community whose deserted villages such as **Kuldhara** still stand near Jaisalmer. The story is widely told, but the precise causes of the Paliwal departure are debated and documentary evidence is thin.

Mulraj himself, by most accounts, ruled more than he governed. He was an elderly and devout king through much of this period, and the real direction of affairs lay with Salim Singh.

### The treaty of 1818

The great turning point of the reign came at its end. After the defeat of the Marathas and the Pindaris in 1817–18, the **East India Company** under the Governor-General **Lord Hastings** offered treaties of "subordinate alliance" to the Rajput states. Jaisalmer signed on **12 December 1818**, one of the last major Rajput courts to do so.

The treaty was short. The Company guaranteed the principality to Mulraj and his posterity and promised protection against serious invasion, while the Maharawal agreed to act in subordinate cooperation with the British government and to accept its arbitration in disputes with other states. For a weak desert kingdom repeatedly pressed by stronger neighbours, the guarantee of its existence was valuable; for the Company, it closed a remote but strategic gap on the road to Sindh.

The treaty did not end internal tensions. Salim Singh remained in office and continued to dominate the court. But it fixed Jaisalmer's place in the new order of Rajputana, where it would remain for the next 130 years.

### Building and culture

Jaisalmer's built heritage owes much to the decades around Mulraj's reign, though often through his ministers and merchants rather than the ruler himself. The most famous monument of the age is **Salim Singh ki Haveli**, the minister's mansion in the lower town, with its upper storeys swelling outwards over the lane in carved yellow sandstone. Merchant families of the town, enriched by trade and banking, began to build the elaborate havelis for which Jaisalmer is now celebrated; the best known, the **Patwon ki Haveli** group, was raised in the early nineteenth century.

Within the fort, the Jain temples continued to be maintained by the merchant community, and the royal palace complex was added to over successive reigns. Court culture remained rooted in the Bhati bardic tradition, which recorded genealogies and the deeds of the clan, and in the worship of the clan's protective goddesses, especially **Swangiya** or Awad Mata, whose shrines, such as the one at **Tanot**, dot the Bhati country.

### Death and succession

Mulraj II died in **1820** after a reign of nearly sixty years, one of the longest in Jaisalmer's history. Because his son Rai Singh had predeceased him, the throne passed to his grandson **Gaj Singh**, a son of Rai Singh. The new ruler was young, and Salim Singh's grip on the state continued into the early 1820s.

Mulraj's reign is remembered less for battles than for survival: Jaisalmer lost outlying lands and suffered court violence, yet emerged with its dynasty intact and guaranteed by treaty.

### Key points
- **Accession.** Mulraj II succeeded Rawal Akhai Singh in 1762 and ruled until 1820.
- **Court crisis.** His heir Rai Singh killed the diwan Swarup Singh and briefly displaced his father before loyal nobles restored Mulraj.
- **Salim Singh.** The diwan's son dominated the state for decades; tradition links his oppression to the Paliwal exodus.
- **Treaty of 1818.** On 12 December 1818 Jaisalmer entered subordinate alliance with the East India Company, which guaranteed the state.
- **Legacy.** Salim Singh ki Haveli and the first great merchant havelis date from this era; the throne passed to Mulraj's grandson Gaj Singh.

rawal-gaj-singh.story:
## Rawal Gaj Singh — Jaisalmer's First Years Under the British Umbrella

*The outline of Gaj Singh's reign comes from the Jaisalmer chronicles, James Tod's "Annals of Jaisalmer", and later British gazetteers and treaty collections; these give the main political events, but intimate details of the ruler's character and court life survive mostly in tradition and are less certain.*

### A grandson on the throne

**Gaj Singh** came to the throne of **Jaisalmer** in **1820** on the death of his grandfather, **Maharawal Mulraj II**, who had reigned for almost sixty years. His father, the heir **Rai Singh**, had died long before in confinement after a violent quarrel at court, and, according to the chronicles, some of Gaj Singh's brothers had not survived the faction struggles of the previous reign. He thus inherited a throne stained by family tragedy, and a state still in the hands of the formidable diwan **Salim Singh Mehta**.

The rulers of Jaisalmer used the title Rawal, and increasingly the grander **Maharawal**; Gaj Singh appears with both in the records.

### The end of Salim Singh

For the first years of the reign Salim Singh remained the effective master of the kingdom. He controlled revenues, appointments and the fort, and many of the Bhati nobility had been impoverished or driven into exile by his policies. The British, who had signed the treaty of 1818 with Mulraj, were aware of his reputation but at first preferred stability to intervention.

Salim Singh died in **1824**. Accounts of his end vary: tradition says he was wounded in an attack by a Rajput aggrieved by his rule, and some versions add that he was finally poisoned within his own household. Whatever the truth, his death removed the dominant figure of Jaisalmer politics for a generation and allowed Gaj Singh to assume real authority. Later ministers were never again permitted to accumulate quite the same power, though the office of diwan remained in the hands of trusted administrative families.

### Living within the new order

Gaj Singh's reign was the first full reign of a Jaisalmer ruler under British paramountcy, and much of its significance lies in how the state adjusted to that position. From **1832** the Company appointed an **Agent to the Governor-General for Rajputana**, based at Ajmer, through whom relations with the Rajput states were increasingly channelled. Disputes that would once have been settled by raids or war now went to British arbitration.

The clearest example was the quarrel with **Bikaner**. Cattle-raiding and disputed villages along the long desert border produced an armed clash around **1829**. Rather than allow a wider war, the British referred the dispute to arbitration, with the **Maharana of Udaipur** acting as umpire, and compensation was settled through that process. For Jaisalmer, a militarily weaker state, this machinery was protection as much as constraint.

The new order also opened opportunities. When the British assembled the **Army of the Indus** for the **First Anglo-Afghan War** in 1838–39, routes through and near the western Thar and Sindh mattered, and Jaisalmer assisted with supplies and transport animals, especially camels. After the British conquest of **Sindh** in **1843**, Jaisalmer was rewarded in **1844** with the restoration of several frontier tracts and forts, including **Shahgarh**, **Ghotaru** and **Garsia**, which had been lost to the Sindhi rulers in earlier decades. This was a modest gain in territory, but it reversed a long pattern of loss along the western frontier.

### Administration and the desert economy

The phrase "administrative adaptation" fits the reign better than "modernisation". Jaisalmer remained a feudal state in which the Maharawal, the Bhati nobles holding jagirs, and the merchant and banking families of the capital shared power according to custom. What changed was the context: the external threat that had justified harsh revenue demands receded, and the court had to keep the British agent satisfied that the state was orderly.

The economy still depended on the caravan trade. Merchants of Jaisalmer ran banking houses with branches far beyond the desert, and the transit duties collected on goods moving between Sindh, Multan and the Indian interior sustained the treasury. Over the following decades, the shift of trade towards sea routes and later the railways would erode this base, but in Gaj Singh's time the town's merchant families were still prosperous enough to keep building. The great **Patwon ki Haveli** complex, begun in the early nineteenth century, continued to rise in the lower town during these years.

### Court and culture

Little is recorded of Gaj Singh's personal tastes beyond the conventional praise of the chronicles. The court continued its patronage of bards, genealogists and temple worship, both of the Bhati clan goddesses and of the Jain shrines in the fort maintained by the merchant community. Like other Rajput courts of the period, Jaisalmer maintained painters and craftsmen, and the yellow sandstone carving tradition of the town remained vigorous. Claims that specific palaces or tanks were founded by Gaj Singh appear in popular literature but are not always well supported, and should be treated with care.

### Death and succession

Gaj Singh died in **1846** without a surviving son. Following Rajput custom, an heir was adopted from the nearest collateral line: his nephew **Ranjit Singh** was placed on the throne. The adoption was recognised by the British, who by then were in a position to approve or question successions in the states.

Gaj Singh's reign is best understood as a transition. He began it as a young ruler in the shadow of a powerful minister and ended it as a recognised member of the system of British-protected princely states, with his frontiers somewhat restored and his kingdom at peace. The cost was the loss of the old freedom of action; the gain was a security Jaisalmer had rarely known.

### Key points
- **Accession.** Gaj Singh succeeded his grandfather Mulraj II in 1820, inheriting a court dominated by the diwan Salim Singh.
- **End of an era.** Salim Singh's death in 1824 freed the ruler from ministerial domination.
- **Arbitration.** A border clash with Bikaner around 1829 was settled through British-sponsored arbitration by the Maharana of Udaipur.
- **Frontier gains.** Help during the First Anglo-Afghan War was followed in 1844 by the restoration of Shahgarh, Ghotaru and Garsia.
- **Succession.** He died in 1846 without a son; his nephew Ranjit Singh was adopted as heir.

rawal-ranjit-singh.name: Rawal Ranjit Singh
rawal-ranjit-singh.title: Ruler of Jaisalmer
rawal-ranjit-singh.story:
## Rawal Ranjit Singh — A Quiet Reign Through the Storm of 1857

*Ranjit Singh's reign is thinly documented. The main sources are the Jaisalmer genealogies and khyats, British administrative reports, and later gazetteers such as those of the Rajputana Agency; they record his adoption, the state's conduct in 1857 and his death, but say little about his personality, so this account relies on the wider context of the period.*

### Adoption and accession

When **Maharawal Gaj Singh** of **Jaisalmer** died in **1846** without a surviving son, the Bhati nobles and the royal household turned to a collateral branch of the ruling family. **Ranjit Singh**, a nephew of the late ruler, was adopted and placed on the throne. Adoption was an ordinary and honoured practice in Rajput dynasties, but by the 1840s it also required the consent of the British, who as the paramount power had a strong interest in orderly successions in the states bound to them by treaty.

The circumstances of his accession explain much of the reign. Ranjit Singh came to power by family arrangement rather than direct descent, and he ruled a small, poor desert principality whose foreign relations were managed through British political officers. His room for independent action was limited, and the record suggests that he used what he had cautiously.

### The state he inherited

Jaisalmer in 1846 was still recovering from the troubled era of the diwan **Salim Singh**, whose death in 1824 had ended decades of ministerial domination. Gaj Singh had used the British connection to recover some frontier territory, notably the tracts of **Shahgarh**, **Ghotaru** and **Garsia** restored after the British conquest of **Sindh**. The western frontier was therefore now bordered by British Sindh, and the old threat of raids from the Sindhi Mirs had disappeared.

The economy remained what it had been for centuries: thin agriculture and pastoralism in the desert villages, and in the capital a merchant and banking community whose fortunes depended on caravan routes between Sindh, Multan, Gujarat and the interior. Transit duties were a key source of revenue. Over Ranjit Singh's reign the slow decline of these overland routes, as trade was increasingly drawn to the ports and to British-controlled markets, began to make itself felt, although its full impact would come later with the railways.

### Administration and diplomacy

The common description of the reign as one of "administrative reform and diplomacy" should be read modestly. There is no evidence of sweeping reforms on the model later attempted in larger states such as Jaipur or Bikaner. What can be said is that Ranjit Singh's government maintained order, kept the nobles in balance and preserved good relations with the British authorities and with neighbouring **Jodhpur** and **Bikaner**, with whom Jaisalmer had long had frontier disputes. Day-to-day administration continued to rest with ministers drawn from experienced administrative families, while the Bhati jagirdars managed their estates under customary obligations to the throne.

In this period British officers also began to compile more systematic information on the states, including revenue, population and boundaries. Jaisalmer's sparse resources and vast area were noted in these reports, which form much of what we know about the state's condition in the mid-nineteenth century.

### The year 1857

The great political test of the reign came in **1857**, when the uprising against Company rule spread across northern India. In Rajputana, mutinies broke out among troops at **Nasirabad** and **Neemuch**, and the Erinpura force rose; in Marwar the Thakur of **Auwa** became a centre of resistance. Many Rajput princes, however, kept their states aloof from the revolt, and several actively supported the British.

Jaisalmer, remote from the main centres of the rising, remained quiet. Ranjit Singh's court did not join the revolt and is recorded as loyal to the British. Its isolation, the absence of a sepoy garrison and the experience of the previous decades all contributed to this choice. In the settlement that followed, the British Crown took over the government of India from the East India Company in **1858**, and Queen Victoria's proclamation promised to respect the rights and dignities of the princes.

One concrete outcome reached Jaisalmer in **1862**, when the Viceroy **Lord Canning** issued **sanads of adoption** to loyal Hindu princes, guaranteeing that their adopted heirs would be recognised if natural heirs failed. For a dynasty in which Ranjit Singh himself had come to the throne by adoption, this guarantee was especially meaningful: it removed the fear, born of Lord Dalhousie's "doctrine of lapse", that a state without a natural heir could be annexed.

### Court and culture

Little specific is known about Ranjit Singh's patronage. The court maintained the customary ceremonies of the Bhati house, the worship of the clan goddesses and the employment of bards and genealogists. The Jain community continued to maintain the temples within the fort, and merchant families continued work on havelis in the lower town. Whether any particular building should be credited to Ranjit Singh is uncertain, and popular claims to that effect are best treated as unverified.

### Death and succession

Ranjit Singh died in **1864** without a son. He was succeeded by his younger brother, **Bairi Sal**, whose long reign carried Jaisalmer through the famines and changes of the later nineteenth century. Ranjit Singh's eighteen years on the throne thus passed without dramatic events, which for a small desert state in an age of upheaval was itself an achievement of sorts: Jaisalmer emerged from 1857 with its dynasty secure, its adoption rights guaranteed and its relations with its neighbours stable.

### Key points
- **Adoption.** Ranjit Singh, a nephew of Gaj Singh, was adopted and became ruler of Jaisalmer in 1846.
- **Thin record.** Surviving sources give the main events of the reign but little about the ruler himself.
- **1857.** Jaisalmer remained quiet and loyal to the British during the uprising.
- **Sanad of adoption.** In 1862 Lord Canning's adoption sanads secured the dynasty's right to adopt heirs.
- **Succession.** He died in 1864 and was succeeded by his younger brother Bairi Sal.
